But you MUST understand imagePullSecrets for private registries: kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=... --docker-username=... --docker-password=... and reference it in your Pod spec with imagePullSecrets: [name: regcred]. For easypj/jobpost local practice, use kind load docker-image easypj/api:v1.0 --name kind-cka-lab to load images directly without a registry.

1.2 Choose & Use the Right Workload ResourceQ13-Q20

🟢 Novice | LF Subtopic: Choose and use the right workload resource (Deployment, DaemonSet, CronJob, etc.).

Design 🟢 Q13 of 200
You need to choose the right Kubernetes workload resource for each tier of the easypj/jobpost application. Which workload resource should you use for each scenario?
A) Use Deployment for everything — PostgreSQL, Redis, Django API, and the web frontend. Deployment is the universal workload resource that works for every type of application
B) Use Deployment for stateless tiers (Django API, web frontend) because they need horizontal scaling and rolling updates; StatefulSet for stateful tiers (PostgreSQL) because it needs stable network identity and persistent storage; DaemonSet for node-level agents (logging, monitoring); Job for one-time tasks (DB migrations); CronJob for scheduled tasks (nightly backups)
C) Use Pod directly for all tiers — Pods are the simplest resource and provide everything you need for production workloads
D) Use ReplicaSet for all tiers because it's the most basic controller that ensures a specified number of pods are always running, and you don't need the extra features of Deployment or StatefulSet
✅ Correct Answer: B

Kubernetes provides different workload resources for different use cases. There is no "one size fits all." Choosing the right resource is a core CKAD skill. Each resource builds on the one below it: Pod → ReplicaSet → Deployment; Pod → StatefulSet; Pod → DaemonSet; Pod → Job → CronJob.

📝 Workload Resource Decision Matrix — Which One When?
Kubernetes Workload Resources — Complete Decision Matrix
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  RESOURCE       BEST FOR                  KEY FEATURES        easypj USE   │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Pod            One-off debugging,        Smallest unit,      Rarely used  │
  │                 quick tests               1+ containers       directly in  │
  │                 (NOT for production!)     sharing network     production   │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Deployment     Stateless web apps,       Rolling updates,    ✅ easypj-web │
  │  (→ReplicaSet   APIs, microservices       rollbacks, scale,   ✅ easypj-api │
  │   →Pod)                                   self-healing        ✅ easypj-redis (cache)│
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  StatefulSet    Databases, message        Stable pod names    ✅ easypj-db │
  │                 queues, any app needing   (postgres-0, -1,    (PostgreSQL) │
  │                 stable identity +         -2), ordered deploy,             │
  │                 persistent storage        persistent PVCs                  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  DaemonSet      Log collectors,           One pod per node,   ✅ Fluentd   │
  │                 monitoring agents,        runs on every node  ✅ Prometheus │
  │                 CSI drivers, CNI plugins  (or selected nodes)   node-exporter│
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Job            Database migrations,      Runs to completion, ✅ DB migrate│
  │                 data processing,          retry on failure,   ✅ Data import│
  │                 one-time tasks            parallelism support              │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  CronJob        Scheduled recurring       Cron syntax,        ✅ Nightly   │
  │                 tasks: nightly backups,   concurrencyPolicy,  DB backup   │
  │                 report generation,        history limits      ✅ Daily     │
  │                 cache warming                                  cache warm │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  DECISION FLOWCHART:
  ┌─ Is it stateful (needs stable identity + persistent storage)?
  │  YES → StatefulSet
  │  NO  ↓
  ├─ Does it need to run on every node?
  │  YES → DaemonSet
  │  NO  ↓
  ├─ Does it run once and stop?
  │  YES → Is it scheduled? YES → CronJob, NO → Job
  │  NO  ↓
  └─ → Deployment (default choice for stateless apps)

CKAD exam tip: The exam will ask you to create specific workload resources. Memorize the imperative commands: kubectl create deploy for Deployments, kubectl create job for Jobs, kubectl create cronjob for CronJobs. StatefulSets and DaemonSets must be created from YAML (no imperative command). For easypj/jobpost: the Django API and web tiers are Deployments, PostgreSQL is a StatefulSet, and database backups are CronJobs.

Design 🟢 Q14 of 200
When should you use a multi-container Pod instead of deploying containers in separate Pods?
A) Always use multi-container Pods — they're more efficient because containers share CPU and memory, reducing total resource usage
B) Never use multi-container Pods — each container should always run in its own Pod to follow the microservices principle of complete isolation
C) Use multi-container Pods when containers share a tight coupling — they need to communicate via localhost, share the same lifecycle (start/stop together), share volumes directly, or one container acts as a helper (sidecar/init container) for the main container. Otherwise, deploy in separate Pods for independent scaling and fault isolation
D) Multi-container Pods are only used for legacy applications that cannot be containerized individually — modern cloud-native apps should always use single-container Pods
✅ Correct Answer: C

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. All containers in a Pod share: (1) the same network namespace (same IP, same localhost, same ports), (2) the same IPC namespace (can use shared memory), and (3) can share Volumes mounted in the Pod spec. Containers in the same Pod are always co-located on the same node and share the same lifecycle — when the Pod is scheduled, all containers start; when it terminates, all stop. The key question: do these containers need to be scaled together, or independently?

📝 Single-Container vs Multi-Container — Decision Guide
When to Use Multi-Container Pods
  ✅ USE MULTI-CONTAINER POD WHEN:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SIDECAR: Helper enhances the main app                          │
  │  Example: Nginx sidecar serving static files for Django         │
  │  → Pod: [Django :8000] + [Nginx :80] sharing /static volume     │
  │  → They scale together: 3 Django replicas = 3 Nginx sidecars   │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  INIT CONTAINER: Setup before main app starts                   │
  │  Example: Run DB migration before Django starts                 │
  │  → Pod: [init: migrate] then [Django]                           │
  │  → Init containers run to COMPLETION before app containers      │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  ADAPTER: Transform output from main container                  │
  │  Example: Convert Django text logs to JSON for Elasticsearch    │
  │  → Pod: [Django] + [Fluentd adapter] sharing /var/log volume    │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  AMBASSADOR: Proxy external connections                         │
  │  Example: Redis proxy for connection pooling                    │
  │  → Pod: [Django] connects to localhost:6379 → [Redis proxy] → Redis│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ❌ USE SEPARATE PODS WHEN:
  • You need to scale independently (web scales to 10, cache to 3)
  • Different update cycles (API updates weekly, DB rarely)
  • Fault isolation (DB crash shouldn't kill the web server)
  • Different resource profiles (CPU-heavy vs memory-heavy)
  • Different nodes (DB needs SSD, web runs anywhere)

CKAD exam tip: The exam explicitly tests multi-container Pod design patterns. You will be asked to add an init container or sidecar to an existing Pod spec. Remember: all containers in a Pod share localhost — if your sidecar needs to reach the main app, use http://localhost:<port>, not a Service DNS name. For easypj/jobpost, the classic example is Django + Nginx sidecar sharing an emptyDir volume for static files.

Design 🟢 Q15 of 200
What is the Pod lifecycle in Kubernetes, and what are the possible Pod phases?
A) Pod phases: Pending (scheduling/waiting for resources, pulling images) → Running (at least one container running) → Succeeded (all containers terminated successfully, restartPolicy=Never) OR Failed (all containers terminated, at least one with non-zero exit) — plus Unknown if the node cannot communicate with the API server
B) Pod phases: Created → Starting → Healthy → Stopping → Deleted. If a container crashes, the Pod enters "Crashed" phase until manually recovered
C) Pod phases: Init → Running → Restarting → Terminated. Pods cycle through these phases repeatedly during their lifetime
D) Pod phases are not relevant to CKAD — Kubernetes manages pods automatically and developers don't need to know about lifecycle states
✅ Correct Answer: A

A Pod's status.phase is a high-level summary of where the Pod is in its lifecycle. There are exactly 5 phases: Pending, Running, Succeeded, Failed, and Unknown. It's important to understand that phase ≠ container state — a Pod can be "Running" even if one container is restarting (as long as at least one container is running). Use kubectl describe pod to see detailed container states (Waiting, Running, Terminated) alongside the pod phase.

📝 Pod Lifecycle — Complete State Machine
Pod Lifecycle Phases & Container States
  ═══════════════════════ POD LIFECYCLE STATE MACHINE ═══════════════════════

       kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
                │
                ▼
    ┌──────────────────────┐
    │      PENDING          │  ← Pod accepted by API server but not yet running
    │  • Scheduling         │     • Scheduler finding a node
    │  • Image pulling      │     • Container images being downloaded
    │  • Volume provisioning│     • PVC binding, volume attachment
    └──────────┬───────────┘
               │ (all containers created & at least one started)
               ▼
    ┌──────────────────────┐
    │      RUNNING          │  ← Pod bound to a node, at least 1 container running
    │  • Containers running │     • Can have containers starting/restarting
    │  • Probes active      │     • Liveness & readiness probes checking health
    └──────┬───────┬───────┘
           │       │
    (containers exit 0)    (containers exit non-zero)
    with restartPolicy:    with restartPolicy:
    Never/OnFailure        Never
           │       │
           ▼       ▼
    ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
    │ SUCCEEDED│  │  FAILED   │  ← Terminal states (Pod not restarted)
    │ (Job     │  │ (Job/     │     • Pod stays on node until deleted
    │  complete)│  │  Pod fail)│     • Container logs still accessible
    └──────────┘  └──────────┘

    ┌──────────┐
    │ UNKNOWN   │  ← Node cannot communicate with API server
    │ (rare)    │     • Network partition, kubelet down
    └──────────┘

  ═══════════════ CONTAINER STATES (inside a Running Pod) ═══════════════
  Waiting    → Container not yet running (pulling image, waiting for init)
  Running    → Container executing without issues
  Terminated → Container finished (success or failure); shows exit code

CKAD exam tip: When debugging, don't just look at kubectl get pod (shows phase only). Use kubectl describe pod to see the full detail: each container's State, Reason, Exit Code, and the Events log at the bottom — this is where you'll find why a container is CrashLoopBackOff or ImagePullBackOff. For easypj/jobpost, if Django shows "Running" but returns 503, check the readiness probe and container state, not just the Pod phase.

Design 🟢 Q16 of 200
What are the four required top-level fields in every Kubernetes YAML manifest, and what does each represent?
A) name, namespace, image, and ports — these are the minimum fields needed to run any container in Kubernetes
B) pod, service, deployment, and configmap — these are the four core resource types that every Kubernetes application uses
C) spec, status, labels, and annotations — Kubernetes automatically generates these for every object
D) apiVersion (which API group and version to use), kind (what type of resource — Pod, Deployment, Service), metadata (name, namespace, labels, annotations), and spec (the desired state — what you want Kubernetes to create). The status field is populated by Kubernetes to reflect the actual state
✅ Correct Answer: D

Every Kubernetes object you create has the same structure: apiVersion, kind, metadata, and spec are written by you (the desired state). After creation, Kubernetes adds a status field that reflects the current actual state. Understanding this structure is essential because every single CKAD task involves writing or editing YAML.

📝 Kubernetes YAML — Anatomy of Every Resource
Every Kubernetes Object — The 4 Required Fields (+1 Auto-Generated)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  apiVersion: apps/v1          ← WHICH API? apps/v1, v1, batch/v1    │
  │                                 Use "kubectl api-resources" to find  │
  │                                 the correct apiVersion for any kind  │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kind: Deployment             ← WHAT TYPE? Pod, Service, ConfigMap, │
  │                                 Deployment, Job, Ingress, etc.       │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  metadata:                    ← WHO/WHERE? Identity & organization  │
  │    name: easypj-web           ← Unique name within the namespace    │
  │    namespace: easypj          ← Which namespace (default if omitted)│
  │    labels:                    ← Key-value for selection/grouping    │
  │      app: easypj                                                   │
  │      tier: frontend                                                │
  │    annotations:               ← Non-identifying metadata (optional) │
  │      git-commit: a3f2b9c                                          │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  spec:                        ← WHAT SHOULD BE? Desired state you   │
  │    replicas: 3                ← define. Structure DEPENDS on kind.  │
  │    selector:                  ← Use "kubectl explain deploy.spec"   │
  │      matchLabels:             ← to see what fields are available.   │
  │        app: easypj                                                  │
  │    template:                                                        │
  │      metadata:                                                      │
  │        labels:                                                      │
  │          app: easypj                                                │
  │      spec:                    ← Pod spec (containers, volumes, etc.)│
  │        containers:                                                  │
  │        - name: django                                               │
  │          image: easypj/api:v2.1                                     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  status:                      ← WHAT IS NOW? CURRENT actual state   │
  │    availableReplicas: 3       ← Populated BY Kubernetes (read-only) │
  │    conditions:                ← Never write status — K8s manages it │
  │    - type: Available                                               │
  │      status: "True"                                                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: You'll write YAML constantly. The fastest way to get correct YAML: kubectl create deploy myapp --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml. This generates a valid manifest with all 4 required fields filled in. Then edit only what you need. Never type YAML from scratch on the exam — always use --dry-run=client -o yaml or copy from kubernetes.io/docs. For easypj/jobpost, generate the Deployment YAML imperatively, then add your ConfigMap refs, probes, and resource limits.

Design 🟡 Q17 of 200
What is a DaemonSet and when should you use it in your Kubernetes cluster?
A) A DaemonSet is a Kubernetes resource that runs a specified number of identical pods scattered randomly across the cluster, useful for distributing load evenly
B) A DaemonSet ensures that a copy of a specific Pod runs on ALL (or a subset of) nodes in the cluster. It's used for cluster-level services like log collectors (Fluentd), monitoring agents (Prometheus node-exporter), CSI storage drivers, and CNI network plugins — anything that needs one instance per node
C) A DaemonSet is a background process that runs inside the Kubernetes control plane and manages automatic pod restarts when nodes fail
D) A DaemonSet is identical to a Deployment but with a fixed replica count equal to the number of nodes — there's no practical difference between them
✅ Correct Answer: B

A DaemonSet guarantees that one Pod runs on every node (or on specific nodes matching a nodeSelector). When a new node joins the cluster, the DaemonSet controller automatically creates a Pod on it. When a node is removed, the Pod is garbage collected. This is fundamentally different from a Deployment — Deployments care about total replica count; DaemonSets care about per-node coverage. If you have 10 nodes, a DaemonSet runs 10 Pods (one per node). A Deployment with 10 replicas might run any number on any node.

📝 DaemonSet Use Cases — Real-World Examples
DaemonSet — One Pod Per Node
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  3-NODE CLUSTER WITH DAEMONSET (example: Fluentd log collector)      │
  │                                                                     │
  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐              │
  │  │   NODE-1      │  │   NODE-2      │  │   NODE-3      │              │
  │  │               │  │               │  │               │              │
  │  │ ┌───────────┐ │  │ ┌───────────┐ │  │ ┌───────────┐ │              │
  │  │ │ fluentd    │ │  │ │ fluentd    │ │  │ │ fluentd    │ │              │
  │  │ │ (DaemonSet)│ │  │ │ (DaemonSet)│ │  │ │ (DaemonSet)│ │              │
  │  │ │ reads:     │ │  │ │ reads:     │ │  │ │ reads:     │ │              │
  │  │ │ /var/log/  │ │  │ │ /var/log/  │ │  │ │ /var/log/  │ │              │
  │  │ │ containers │ │  │ │ containers │ │  │ │ containers │ │              │
  │  │ └───────────┘ │  │ └───────────┘ │  │ └───────────┘ │              │
  │  │               │  │               │  │               │              │
  │  │ ┌───────────┐ │  │ ┌───────────┐ │  │               │              │
  │  │ │ easypj-web │ │  │ │ easypj-api │ │  │               │              │
  │  │ │ (Deploy)   │ │  │ │ (Deploy)   │ │  │               │              │
  │  │ └───────────┘ │  │ └───────────┘ │  │               │              │
  │  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  COMMON DAEMONSET USE CASES:
  📋 Log Collection    → Fluentd / Fluent Bit (reads /var/log/containers)
  📊 Monitoring        → Prometheus node-exporter, Datadog agent
  🔒 Security          → Falco (runtime security), OPA/Gatekeeper agent
  💾 Storage           → CSI drivers (EBS, EFS, NFS node plugins)
  🌐 Networking        → CNI plugins (Calico, Cilium, Weave), kube-proxy
  🔧 Node Maintenance  → Node problem detector, node cleanup jobs

CKAD exam tip: DaemonSets cannot be created imperatively — you must write YAML. Use kubectl create deploy ... --dry-run=client -o yaml, then change kind: Deployment to kind: DaemonSet, remove replicas and strategy (DaemonSets use updateStrategy instead), and the selector must match a label on the template. For easypj/jobpost, you'd use a Fluentd DaemonSet to collect all application logs from every node.

Design 🟡 Q18 of 200
What makes a StatefulSet different from a Deployment, and why is it essential for database workloads like easypj's PostgreSQL?
A) StatefulSet is just a Deployment with a different name — there is no functional difference, and you can use them interchangeably
B) StatefulSet is a Deployment that automatically creates PersistentVolumes without needing a StorageClass or PVC
C) StatefulSet provides three guarantees that Deployments do not: (1) Stable, unique network identifiers — pods are named {name}-0, {name}-1, {name}-2 and keep these names even if rescheduled, (2) Stable, persistent storage — each pod gets its own PVC that survives pod deletion and rescheduling, and (3) Ordered, graceful deployment and scaling — pods are created/deleted in order (0→1→2, 2→1→0). These are critical for databases, which require stable identity for replication and dedicated storage per instance
D) StatefulSet is a special resource that runs pods only on master/control-plane nodes for cluster administration tasks
✅ Correct Answer: C

A StatefulSet is designed for applications that need sticky identity and stable storage. Unlike a Deployment where pods are interchangeable (web-7d8f9-xk2m, web-7d8f9-j3lp...), StatefulSet pods have predictable, stable names: postgres-0, postgres-1, postgres-2. Even if postgres-1 crashes and is recreated on a different node, it keeps the name "postgres-1" and its own PVC. These guarantees are essential for clustered databases (PostgreSQL with replication, MongoDB, Cassandra, Kafka) where each instance has a unique role and dedicated storage.

📝 StatefulSet — Stable Identity & Storage
StatefulSet vs Deployment — Side-by-Side Comparison
  ═══════════════ DEPLOYMENT (Stateless) ═══════════════
  Service: easypj-api  →  DNS resolves to Service IP (load-balanced)
  
  Pod names (random suffixes, interchangeable):
  easypj-api-7d8f9-xk2m   ← Pod dies → replaced by:
  easypj-api-7d8f9-j3lp   ← NEW random name, same PVC? ❌ New empty PVC!
  easypj-api-7d8f9-mq7r
  
  Storage: All pods share the same PVC template
  (OR worse, no storage at all — each restart = fresh start)

  ═══════════════ STATEFULSET (Stateful) ═══════════════
  Headless Service: easypj-db (clusterIP: None)
  → DNS resolves to individual pod IPs:
    postgres-0.easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local
    postgres-1.easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local
    postgres-2.easypj-db.easypj.svc.cluster.local
  
  Pod names (predictable, ordinal, stable):
  ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
  │ postgres-0   │    │ postgres-1   │    │ postgres-2   │
  │ (Primary)    │    │ (Replica)    │    │ (Replica)    │
  │ PVC: pvc-0   │    │ PVC: pvc-1   │    │ PVC: pvc-2   │
  │ 20 Gi data   │    │ 20 Gi data   │    │ 20 Gi data   │
  └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘
  
  CRITICAL: Even if postgres-1 moves to a different node,
  it STAYS "postgres-1" with ITS OWN pvc-1.
  Scaling: 0→1→2 (ordered creation); 2→1→0 (ordered deletion)

  volumeClaimTemplates in StatefulSet spec:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  volumeClaimTemplates:                              │
  │  - metadata:                                        │
  │      name: data                                     │
  │    spec:                                            │
  │      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]                 │
  │      storageClassName: fast-ssd                     │
  │      resources:                                     │
  │        requests:                                    │
  │          storage: 20Gi                              │
  │  → Each pod automatically gets: data-postgres-0,    │
  │    data-postgres-1, data-postgres-2                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: StatefulSets require a headless Service (clusterIP: None) for stable network identity. This Service doesn't load-balance — it creates DNS A records for each pod. Also, StatefulSet PVCs are NOT automatically deleted when you delete the StatefulSet (to prevent accidental data loss). You must manually clean up PVCs. For easypj/jobpost, PostgreSQL MUST be a StatefulSet — never use a Deployment for databases.

Design 🟢 Q19 of 200
What is a Kubernetes Job, and how do you configure it to run a database migration with retries on failure?
A) A Job creates one or more Pods and ensures a specified number of them successfully terminate. It's for finite tasks (migrations, data processing, batch jobs). Configure retries with backoffLimit (default 6) and parallelism/completions for multi-pod workloads. When the Job completes, the Pods stop but remain for log inspection
B) A Job is the same as a Deployment but with restartPolicy: Never — it runs continuously and restarts on failure just like a web server
C) A Job is a one-shot Pod that runs exactly once and deletes itself immediately after completion, leaving no trace for debugging
D) A Job is a Kubernetes controller that automatically retries any Pod failure indefinitely until manual intervention stops it
✅ Correct Answer: A

A Job is designed for finite, run-to-completion tasks. Unlike a Deployment (which keeps pods running forever), a Job's purpose is to run until a specified number of completions is reached, then stop. The Job controller tracks successful and failed pods, retries on failure (up to backoffLimit), and allows you to run work in parallel. Pods from completed Jobs are NOT deleted by default — this allows you to inspect logs with kubectl logs job/myjob after completion.

📝 Job Patterns — Three Ways to Use Jobs
Kubernetes Jobs — Complete Reference
  ═══════════════ PATTERN 1: SINGLE COMPLETION JOB (migration) ═══════════════
  apiVersion: batch/v1
  kind: Job
  metadata:
    name: easypj-db-migrate
  spec:
    backoffLimit: 3        ← Retry 3 times on failure (default: 6)
    template:
      spec:
        restartPolicy: Never  ← Don't restart container, create new Pod instead
        containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: easypj/api:v2.1
          command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate"]

  Result: 1 Pod runs → if fails, retries up to 3 times → if succeeds, COMPLETE
          Pod stays for log inspection. Job shows: COMPLETIONS: 1/1

  ═══════════════ PATTERN 2: PARALLEL WORK QUEUE ═══════════════
  apiVersion: batch/v1
  kind: Job
  metadata:
    name: easypj-data-import
  spec:
    completions: 100        ← 100 items must be processed
    parallelism: 10         ← 10 Pods run simultaneously
    template:
      spec:
        restartPolicy: OnFailure
        containers:
        - name: worker
          image: easypj/worker:v1
          command: ["python", "process_chunk.py"]

  Result: 10 Pods run at once → each processes one item → when 100 total
          completions reached, Job finishes. Great for batch data processing.

  ═══════════════ PATTERN 3: CRONJOB (see Q20) ═══════════════

  KEY JOB PARAMETERS:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  backoffLimit: 3       Max retries before marking Job Failed│
  │  completions: 5        How many successful pods needed      │
  │  parallelism: 2        How many pods run at once            │
  │  activeDeadlineSeconds: 300  Kill all pods after 5 min      │
  │  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 60   Auto-delete after 60 seconds  │
  │  restartPolicy: Never  Create new pod on failure (default)   │
  │                 OnFailure  Restart SAME container on failure │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: Jobs are created imperatively: kubectl create job myjob --image=busybox -- /bin/sh -c "echo hello". Use --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate the YAML. For easypj/jobpost, run Django migrations as a Job BEFORE rolling out a new Deployment: kubectl create job migrate --image=easypj/api:v2.1 -- python manage.py migrate. Check completion with kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/migrate.

Design 🟡 Q20 of 200
What is a CronJob, and how would you configure a nightly PostgreSQL backup for easypj/jobpost using cron syntax?
A) A CronJob is a Kubernetes resource that runs continuously like a Deployment but only processes data at specific times of day using an internal scheduler
B) A CronJob is a Linux cron daemon running inside the container — you configure it by editing /etc/crontab inside the container image
C) A CronJob is a special type of Service that schedules network requests to pods at specified intervals using HTTP calls
D) A CronJob creates Jobs on a repeating schedule defined by cron syntax (5 fields: minute hour day month weekday). It's perfect for recurring tasks like backups, report generation, and cache warming. Key settings include concurrencyPolicy (Allow/Forbid/Replace), startingDeadlineSeconds, and history limits for keeping completed/failed Jobs
✅ Correct Answer: D

A CronJob is a Job scheduler — it creates Jobs on a time-based schedule using standard Unix cron syntax. Think of it as: "every day at 2 AM, create a Job that runs pg_dump to back up the database." The CronJob controller watches the clock and creates a new Job object each time the schedule triggers.

📝 CronJob — Complete Reference with Cron Syntax
CronJob — Schedule Syntax & Configuration
  ═══════════════ CRON SYNTAX (5 fields) ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  *    *    *    *    *                                           │
  │  │    │    │    │    │                                           │
  │  │    │    │    │    └─── Day of Week   (0=Sun, 1=Mon, ..., 6=Sat)│
  │  │    │    │    └──────── Month          (1=Jan, ..., 12=Dec)     │
  │  │    │    └───────────── Day of Month   (1-31)                   │
  │  │    └────────────────── Hour           (0-23)                   │
  │  └─────────────────────── Minute         (0-59)                   │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  COMMON SCHEDULES:                                               │
  │  "0 2 * * *"      Every day at 2:00 AM                          │
  │  "*/5 * * * *"    Every 5 minutes                               │
  │  "0 0 1 * *"      First day of every month at midnight          │
  │  "0 9-17 * * 1-5" Every hour 9AM-5PM, Monday-Friday              │
  │  "0 0 * * 0"      Every Sunday at midnight                      │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ⚠️  All times are in UTC (the control plane's timezone)         │
  │     There is NO timezone field in CronJob — plan accordingly    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ easypj/jobpost NIGHTLY BACKUP CRONJOB ═══════════════
  apiVersion: batch/v1
  kind: CronJob
  metadata:
    name: easypj-db-backup
    namespace: easypj
  spec:
    schedule: "0 2 * * *"           ← 2:00 AM UTC every day
    concurrencyPolicy: Forbid        ← Skip if previous backup still running
    startingDeadlineSeconds: 300     ← Deadline to start (5 min tolerance)
    successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 7    ← Keep last 7 successful backups
    failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3        ← Keep last 3 failed attempts
    jobTemplate:
      spec:
        backoffLimit: 2
        template:
          spec:
            restartPolicy: Never
            containers:
            - name: backup
              image: postgres:15-alpine
              env:
              - name: PGPASSWORD
                valueFrom:
                  secretKeyRef:
                    name: easypj-db-credentials
                    key: password
              command:
              - /bin/sh
              - -c
              - |
                DATE=$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)
                pg_dump -h easypj-db -U postgres easypj > /backup/easypj-${DATE}.sql
                echo "Backup complete: easypj-${DATE}.sql"
            volumes:
            - name: backup-volume
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: easypj-backup-pvc

  KEY CronJob PARAMETERS:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  schedule                   Cron expression (5 fields)          │
  │  concurrencyPolicy: Allow   Allow overlapping Jobs (default)    │
  │                    Forbid   Skip run if previous still running  │
  │                    Replace  Kill previous, start new            │
  │  startingDeadlineSeconds    Max delay to start (missed if late) │
  │  successfulJobsHistoryLimit How many completed Jobs to keep     │
  │  failedJobsHistoryLimit     How many failed Jobs to keep        │
  │  suspend: true/false        Pause/resume the CronJob            │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: CronJobs are created imperatively: kubectl create cronjob mybackup --image=busybox --schedule="*/5 * * * *" -- /bin/sh -c "date". To manually trigger a CronJob (for testing): kubectl create job --from=cronjob/easypj-db-backup manual-backup. For easypj/jobpost, you'd have CronJobs for: nightly database backups, daily report generation, weekly cache warming, and monthly data archival.

1.3 Multi-Container Pod Design PatternsQ21-Q28

🟡 Intermediate → 🔴 Advanced | LF Subtopic: Understand multi-container Pod design patterns (sidecar, init, ambassador, adapter).

Design 🟡 Q21 of 200
What is the Sidecar pattern in Kubernetes, and how does it enhance the easypj/jobpost web frontend?
A) The Sidecar pattern means running a separate Deployment that communicates with the main application over the network, providing loosely coupled services like caching or logging
B) The Sidecar pattern places a helper container inside the SAME Pod as the main application container. They share the same network namespace (localhost), same volumes, and same lifecycle. A classic example: an Nginx sidecar in the same Pod as Django, serving static files from a shared emptyDir volume — both containers scale together, start together, and stop together
C) The Sidecar pattern is a Kubernetes DaemonSet that runs one helper pod per node, providing node-level services to all application pods on that node
D) The Sidecar pattern is when you run an identical copy of your main container for high availability, placed "side-by-side" on the same node for redundancy
✅ Correct Answer: B

The Sidecar pattern is the most common multi-container Pod pattern. The "sidecar" is a helper container that extends or enhances the main application without modifying it. Both containers share: (1) the same Pod IP and localhost — the sidecar can reach the main app at http://localhost:<port>, (2) the same Volumes — they can read/write shared files, and (3) the same lifecycle — when the Pod is scheduled, both start; when it terminates, both stop. Since they scale together, 3 Django replicas = 3 Nginx sidecars.

📝 Sidecar Pattern — easypj-web with Nginx for Static Files
Sidecar Pattern — Django + Nginx Sharing emptyDir Volume
  ═══════════════ easypj-web POD (Sidecar Pattern) ═══════════════
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  POD: easypj-web-7d8f9-xk2m                                 │
  │  Pod IP: 10.244.1.5                                         │
  │                                                             │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  MAIN CONTAINER      │  │  SIDECAR CONTAINER           │  │
  │  │  django              │  │  nginx                       │  │
  │  │  image: easypj/web   │  │  image: nginx:alpine         │  │
  │  │  port: 8000          │  │  port: 80                    │  │
  │  │                      │  │                              │  │
  │  │  • Runs Gunicorn     │  │  • Serves static files      │  │
  │  │  • Handles requests  │  │  • Proxies /api to Django   │  │
  │  │  • Writes static     │  │  • Reads static files from   │  │
  │  │    files to /static  │  │    SHARED /static volume    │  │
  │  └────────┬────────────┘  └────────────┬────────────────┘  │
  │           │                             │                   │
  │           │    ┌─────────────────┐      │                   │
  │           └───→│  emptyDir       │←─────┘                   │
  │                │  /static        │  SHARED VOLUME            │
  │                │  (in-memory)     │                          │
  │                └─────────────────┘                          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WHY SIDECAR (not separate Pod)?
  ✅ localhost communication (Nginx proxies to http://localhost:8000)
  ✅ Shared filesystem (no network file copy needed for static files)
  ✅ Same lifecycle (scale together, deploy together)
  ✅ Atomic unit (Pod succeeds or fails as a whole)

  COMMON SIDECAR USE CASES:
  📁 Static file serving (Nginx + Django/Node.js)
  📋 Log forwarding (Fluentd/Fluent Bit sidecar reading app logs)
  🔄 Config reloading (sidecar watches ConfigMap, signals app to reload)
  🔒 TLS termination (Envoy/Nginx sidecar handling HTTPS for the main app)
  📊 Metrics scraping (Prometheus sidecar scraping app metrics endpoint)

CKAD exam tip: The exam may ask you to add a sidecar to an existing Pod. Remember: (1) add the container to spec.containers[], (2) if they share files, add an emptyDir volume and mount it in both containers, (3) communication is on localhost since they share the network namespace. For easypj/jobpost, the Nginx sidecar serves static files at lightning speed while Django focuses on dynamic requests.

Design 🔴 Q22 of 200
What is the Ambassador pattern, and how would you use it to provide a Redis connection proxy for easypj/jobpost?
A) The Ambassador pattern deploys a separate Kubernetes Service that acts as a load balancer between your application and external services, routing traffic based on HTTP headers
B) The Ambassador pattern is when you run an ambassador container on the control plane node that manages all external API connections for the entire cluster
C) The Ambassador pattern uses a proxy container inside the SAME Pod that abstracts and manages connections to external services. Your main app connects to the ambassador on localhost, and the ambassador handles connection pooling, retries, encryption, and service discovery to the actual backend. Example: a Redis proxy (like Twemproxy/envoy) as an ambassador — Django connects to localhost:6379 and the ambassador forwards to the real Redis cluster
D) The Ambassador pattern means deploying an API gateway (like Kong or Ambassador Edge Stack) as a separate Deployment to handle all incoming traffic to the cluster
✅ Correct Answer: C

The Ambassador pattern is a specialized sidecar that proxies connections to external services. Your application doesn't need to know the real backend address, authentication credentials, or connection pooling logic — it just connects to localhost:<port> and the ambassador handles everything else. This is especially powerful for: (1) simplifying application code (no Redis cluster awareness in Django), (2) adding resilience (retries, circuit breaking, connection pooling), and (3) enabling zero-downtime backend migrations (switch the ambassador config without touching app code).

📝 Ambassador Pattern — Redis Proxy for easypj/jobpost
Ambassador Pattern — Django → localhost:6379 → Redis Proxy → Redis Cluster
  ═══════════════ easypj-api POD (Ambassador Pattern) ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  POD: easypj-api-7d8f9-j3lp                                      │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  MAIN CONTAINER       │  │  AMBASSADOR CONTAINER           │   │
  │  │  django               │  │  redis-proxy (Twemproxy/envoy)  │   │
  │  │                       │  │                                 │   │
  │  │  App connects to:     │  │  Listens on: localhost:6379     │   │
  │  │  REDIS_URL=           │  │  Forwards to REAL Redis:        │   │
  │  │  redis://localhost:6379│  │  redis-0.easypj.svc:6379       │   │
  │  │                       │  │  redis-1.easypj.svc:6379       │   │
  │  │  Django code:         │  │  redis-2.easypj.svc:6379       │   │
  │  │  import redis         │  │                                 │   │
  │  │  r = redis.Redis(     │  │  Features:                     │   │
  │  │    host='localhost',  │  │  • Connection pooling           │   │
  │  │    port=6379)          │  │  • Automatic failover           │   │
  │  │                       │  │  • Retry logic                  │   │
  │  │  ← Simple! No cluster │  │  • Read/write splitting         │   │
  │  │     awareness needed  │  │  • TLS encryption to backend    │   │
  │  └──────────────────────┘  └────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    │ localhost:6379 (inside Pod)
                    ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  EXTERNAL REDIS CLUSTER (or StatefulSet)                          │
  │  redis-0.easypj.svc.cluster.local:6379                           │
  │  redis-1.easypj.svc.cluster.local:6379                           │
  │  redis-2.easypj.svc.cluster.local:6379                           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  AMBASSADOR vs SIDECAR:
  ┌────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
  │  SIDECAR   │ Enhances main app     │ Nginx serving static files  │
  │  AMBASSADOR│ Proxies external comm │ Redis/Database proxy        │
  │  ADAPTER   │ Transforms output     │ Log format converter        │
  └────────────┴──────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: The Ambassador pattern is less common on the exam than sidecar/init containers, but understand the distinction: Ambassador = proxies external connections OUT, Sidecar = enhances the main app. For easypj/jobpost, an ambassador simplifies Django's Redis connection to a single localhost:6379 while the ambassador handles the complexity of connecting to a Redis cluster or AWS ElastiCache behind the scenes.

Design 🔴 Q23 of 200
What is the Adapter pattern, and how would you use it to standardize application logs for a centralized logging system?
A) The Adapter pattern places a container in the same Pod that transforms, normalizes, or adapts the output of the main container — such as converting plain-text Django logs into structured JSON format for Elasticsearch, or translating metrics from one format to another — without modifying the main application code
B) The Adapter pattern is a Kubernetes controller that automatically adjusts Pod resource limits based on actual usage, "adapting" the configuration to the workload
C) The Adapter pattern is when you use a load balancer to adapt incoming traffic from different protocols (HTTP, gRPC, WebSocket) into a single unified format for your backend
D) The Adapter pattern means replacing the main container's entrypoint with a wrapper script that adapts environment variables before starting the actual application
✅ Correct Answer: A

The Adapter pattern is about transforming output — taking something the main container produces in one format and converting it to a standardized format that external systems expect. The key insight: you don't modify the application code (it keeps logging in its native format), and the adapter handles the conversion. This is essential for teams running heterogeneous applications (Python/Django, Node.js, Go) that all need to send logs to the same Elasticsearch cluster in a consistent JSON format.

📝 Adapter Pattern — Standardizing Logs for easypj/jobpost
Adapter Pattern — Django Text Logs → JSON for Elasticsearch
