2.1 Deployments & Rolling UpdatesQ41-Q50

🟢 Novice → 🟡 Intermediate | LF Subtopic: Understand Deployments and how to perform rolling updates.

Deploy 🟢 Q41 of 200
How does the Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod hierarchy work, and why does Kubernetes use this layered approach?
A) Deployment, ReplicaSet, and Pod are three independent controllers that compete to manage the same containers — whichever responds fastest wins
B) Deployment creates Pods directly, and ReplicaSets are only used for StatefulSets — there is no layering between them
C) Each layer adds functionality: Pod is the smallest unit (containers), ReplicaSet ensures a specified number of identical Pods are always running (self-healing), and Deployment adds rolling updates, rollbacks, pause/resume, and version history on top of ReplicaSets. When you create a Deployment, it creates a ReplicaSet, which creates Pods. Each layer owns the layer below it
D) Pod → ReplicaSet → Deployment is the correct hierarchy — Pods create ReplicaSets, and ReplicaSets create Deployments
✅ Correct Answer: C

Kubernetes uses a layered controller pattern: each layer builds on the one below it, adding new capabilities. A Pod is just containers. A ReplicaSet adds "keep N copies running" (self-healing: if a Pod dies, create a new one). A Deployment adds "update those copies in a controlled way" (rolling updates, rollbacks, version history). When you kubectl create deploy, Kubernetes creates a Deployment → which creates a ReplicaSet → which creates Pods. The Deployment OWNS the ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet OWNS the Pods.

📝 Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod — Layered Ownership
Deployment Hierarchy — Each Layer Adds Features
  ═══════════════ THE LAYERED CONTROLLER MODEL ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DEPLOYMENT: easypj-api                                          │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  FEATURES ADDED AT THIS LAYER:                             │  │
  │  │  • Rolling updates (maxSurge, maxUnavailable)              │  │
  │  │  • Rollback (kubectl rollout undo)                         │  │
  │  │  • Pause / Resume rollout                                  │  │
  │  │  • Revision history (revisionHistoryLimit)                 │  │
  │  │  • Strategy: Recreate or RollingUpdate                     │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                         │ OWNS                                    │
  │                         ▼                                         │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  REPLICASET: easypj-api-7d8f9c4b6                          │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
  │  │  │  FEATURES ADDED AT THIS LAYER:                       │  │  │
  │  │  │  • Maintain N replicas (self-healing)                │  │  │
  │  │  │  • Pod selector (matchLabels)                        │  │  │
  │  │  │  • If Pod dies → create replacement Pod              │  │  │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
  │  │                         │ OWNS                              │  │
  │  │                         ▼                                   │  │
  │  │  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ │  │
  │  │  │ POD: -xk2m       │ │ POD: -j3lp      │ │ POD: -mq7r    │ │  │
  │  │  │ ┌─────────────┐ │ │ ┌─────────────┐ │ │ ┌───────────┐ │ │  │
  │  │  │ │ django      │ │ │ │ django      │ │ │ │ django    │ │ │  │
  │  │  │ │ (container) │ │ │ │ (container) │ │ │ │ (container)│ │ │  │
  │  │  │ └─────────────┘ │ │ └─────────────┘ │ │ └───────────┘ │ │  │
  │  │  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └───────────────┘ │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WHY THE LAYERING?
  • Separation of concerns — each controller does one thing well
  • During rolling update: old RS scales down, new RS scales up
  • Rollback: Deployment switches back to the old RS (pods already there!)
  • Version tracking: each RS represents one version

CKAD exam tip: When you do kubectl get all, you'll see Deployment, ReplicaSet, and Pods for each app. The ReplicaSet name includes a hash: easypj-api-7d8f9c4b6. This hash changes when the Pod template changes, creating a new RS. The old RS stays (scaled to 0) for rollback purposes. For easypj/jobpost, every tier (web, api, redis) uses this Deployment→RS→Pod hierarchy.

Deploy 🟢 Q42 of 200
What is the fastest way to create a properly-structured Deployment for easypj/jobpost on the CKAD exam?
A) Write the complete Deployment YAML from scratch — this is the most reliable method and the only one accepted on the CKAD exam
B) Use imperative command with dry-run to generate the YAML: kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj/web:v2 --replicas=3 --port=8000 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml — then edit the generated YAML to add probes, env vars, volumes, and other configuration. This is the FASTEST and most ACCURATE method because Kubernetes writes the YAML for you with correct structure and defaults
C) Copy a Deployment YAML from the Kubernetes documentation and manually replace all values — this is the recommended CKAD workflow
D) Use the Kubernetes dashboard web UI to create the Deployment visually, then download the YAML — this is the supported CKAD exam workflow
✅ Correct Answer: B

The imperative + dry-run pattern is your #1 speed hack on the CKAD exam. It generates valid YAML with correct structure, apiVersion, selectors, and labels in 2 seconds instead of 2 minutes of typing. You then edit only the fields you need (probes, resources, env vars). This approach eliminates YAML syntax errors, selector mismatches, and missing required fields — the most common exam mistakes.

Generate → Edit → Apply — The CKAD Workflow

Deploy 🟢 Q43 of 200
What is a ReplicaSet, and how does it provide self-healing for your application?
A) A ReplicaSet is a controller that ensures a specified number of identical Pods are running at all times. It continuously monitors Pods and if a Pod dies (node failure, eviction, deletion), it immediately creates a replacement Pod to maintain the desired count. ReplicaSets use label selectors to identify which Pods belong to them — they can even "adopt" existing orphaned Pods that match their selector
B) A ReplicaSet is a Kubernetes scheduler that decides which node each Pod should run on, ensuring Pods are evenly distributed across the cluster
C) A ReplicaSet is a monitoring tool that sends alerts when Pods fail — it does not create or manage Pods directly
D) A ReplicaSet is an older, deprecated Kubernetes resource — Deployments now handle replication directly without ReplicaSets
✅ Correct Answer: A

A ReplicaSet is the workhorse of Kubernetes reliability. Its job is simple: "I must have exactly N Pods matching my selector at all times." If there are too few (Pod crashed), it creates more. If there are too many (someone manually created extra Pods), it deletes the excess. This reconciliation loop runs continuously — the ReplicaSet controller compares desired state (spec.replicas) with actual state (count of matching Pods) and takes action to close the gap. This is why Kubernetes is "self-healing" — no human needs to restart a crashed Pod.

📝 ReplicaSet — The Self-Healing Engine
ReplicaSet Reconciliation Loop — Desired vs Actual
  ═══════════════ REPLICASET RECONCILIATION LOOP ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReplicaSet: easypj-api-7d8f9c4b6                                │
  │  spec.replicas: 3    ← DESIRED STATE                             │
  │                                                                  │
  │  CONTINUOUS LOOP (runs forever):                                 │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  1. Count Pods matching selector {app: easypj-api}         │  │
  │  │  2. Compare with spec.replicas (3)                         │  │
  │  │  3. IF count < 3 → create Pod(s)                           │  │
  │  │  4. IF count > 3 → delete Pod(s)                           │  │
  │  │  5. IF count == 3 → do nothing                             │  │
  │  │  6. Wait, then go to step 1                                │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ SELF-HEALING SCENARIOS ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SCENARIO 1: NODE FAILURE                                       │
  │  Node-2 crashes (hardware failure)                               │
  │  → Pod easypj-api-j3lp (on Node-2) becomes Unknown               │
  │  → ReplicaSet: "I have 2 running, I need 3! Creating new Pod..." │
  │  → New Pod created on healthy Node-1 or Node-3                   │
  │  → Back to 3 running Pods ✓                                     │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  SCENARIO 2: ACCIDENTAL DELETION                                 │
  │  Someone runs: kubectl delete pod easypj-api-xk2m                │
  │  → Pod deleted immediately                                       │
  │  → ReplicaSet: "I have 2 Pods, I need 3! Creating new Pod..."    │
  │  → New Pod created within seconds                                │
  │  → Back to 3 Pods ✓                                             │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  SCENARIO 3: MANUAL SCALE UP                                     │
  │  kubectl scale rs easypj-api-7d8f9c4b6 --replicas=5              │
  │  → ReplicaSet: "I have 3, I need 5! Creating 2 more Pods..."     │
  │  → But Deployment sees this and says: "Wait, I said 3 replicas!" │
  │  → Deployment scales ReplicaSet BACK to 3                        │
  │  💡 Lesson: Always scale the DEPLOYMENT, not the ReplicaSet!     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: You rarely interact with ReplicaSets directly — Deployments manage them for you. But understanding ReplicaSets is essential for debugging: if pods keep being created/deleted, check if the ReplicaSet spec.replicas is correct. For easypj/jobpost, the ReplicaSet ensures that even if a node crashes, your Django API pods are automatically recreated on healthy nodes.

Deploy 🟢 Q44 of 200
What is the difference between the Recreate and RollingUpdate deployment strategies?
A) There is no difference — both strategies work exactly the same way and the names are interchangeable
B) Recreate updates pods one-at-a-time for zero downtime, while RollingUpdate deletes all pods at once for maximum speed
C) RollingUpdate is only available on cloud providers (AWS, GCP, Azure), while Recreate works on all Kubernetes clusters including local ones
D) Recreate: ALL old Pods are deleted FIRST, then ALL new Pods are created. There is DOWNTIME between deletion and creation. RollingUpdate: Pods are replaced gradually — a few new Pods are created, then a few old Pods are deleted, in batches. There is ZERO downtime if configured correctly. Recreate is simpler but causes outages; RollingUpdate is the default and recommended for production
✅ Correct Answer: D

Deployment strategies control HOW pods are replaced during an update. Recreate is the nuclear option: kill everything, then start fresh. There WILL be downtime. RollingUpdate is the surgical approach: replace pods one batch at a time, ensuring service continuity. RollingUpdate is the default because it provides zero-downtime deployments — your users never experience an outage.

📝 Recreate vs RollingUpdate — Visual Comparison
Deployment Strategies — Recreate vs RollingUpdate
  ═══════════════ STRATEGY 1: RECREATE (downtime!) ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TIME ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────►    │
  │                                                                  │
  │  BEFORE:    [v1] [v1] [v1]   ← 3 Pods running                    │
  │                                                                  │
  │  STEP 1:    [  ] [  ] [  ]   ← ALL 3 Pods DELETED                │
  │             ⚠️  DOWNTIME — Service has NO endpoints!             │
  │                                                                  │
  │  STEP 2:    [v2] [v2] [v2]   ← 3 new Pods CREATED                │
  │             ✓ Service back online                                 │
  │                                                                  │
  │  DOWNTIME DURATION: Pod startup time (seconds to minutes)        │
  │  BEST FOR: Database schema changes, breaking migrations,         │
  │            when old and new versions CANNOT run simultaneously   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ STRATEGY 2: ROLLING UPDATE (zero downtime!) ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TIME ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────►    │
  │                                                                  │
  │  BEFORE:    [v1] [v1] [v1]   ← 3 Pods running (all v1)          │
  │                                                                  │
  │  STEP 1:    [v1] [v1] [v2]   ← 1 new v2 Pod CREATED              │
  │                                 1 old v1 Pod DELETED              │
  │             ✓ Service has 2 v1 + 1 v2 = 3 total Pods running     │
  │                                                                  │
  │  STEP 2:    [v1] [v2] [v2]   ← 1 new v2 Pod CREATED              │
  │                                 1 old v1 Pod DELETED              │
  │             ✓ Service has 1 v1 + 2 v2 = 3 total Pods running     │
  │                                                                  │
  │  STEP 3:    [v2] [v2] [v2]   ← 1 new v2 Pod CREATED              │
  │                                 1 old v1 Pod DELETED              │
  │             ✓ All 3 Pods now v2 — NO DOWNTIME!                   │
  │                                                                  │
  │  maxSurge: 1        ← Up to 1 EXTRA Pod beyond desired count     │
  │  maxUnavailable: 0  ← NO Pods below desired count during update  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ WHEN TO USE EACH ═══════════════
  ┌────────────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │  RECREATE       │  ROLLINGUPDATE       │  (DEFAULT!)              │
  ├────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  Breaking changes│  Compatible changes  │                          │
  │  DB schema v1→v2 │  API v1→v1.1         │                          │
  │  Can't coexist   │  Can coexist         │                          │
  │  Downtime OK     │  ZERO downtime needed│                          │
  └────────────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: RollingUpdate is the default — you don't need to specify it. Only set strategy: Recreate when old and new pods absolutely cannot run simultaneously. For easypj/jobpost: use RollingUpdate for the web and API tiers (stateless), and Recreate for the database tier when schema changes are breaking (rare, since PostgreSQL migrations are usually backward-compatible).

Deploy 🟡 Q45 of 200
How do maxSurge and maxUnavailable control a RollingUpdate, and what values ensure zero downtime?
A) maxSurge controls maximum CPU usage during updates, and maxUnavailable controls maximum memory usage — they have nothing to do with pod counts
B) maxSurge (default 25%) limits how many EXTRA Pods can be created ABOVE the desired count during the update. maxUnavailable (default 25%) limits how many Pods can be UNAVAILABLE BELOW the desired count. For ZERO downtime: set maxUnavailable=0 (never drop below desired count) and maxSurge=1 (allow one extra Pod). During a 3-replica update, Kubernetes creates 1 new Pod, waits for it to be Ready, then deletes 1 old Pod — repeating until all are updated
C) maxSurge must always equal maxUnavailable — Kubernetes rejects any Deployment where these values differ
D) maxSurge=100% and maxUnavailable=100% is the recommended setting for all production deployments because it provides the fastest possible rollout
✅ Correct Answer: B

maxSurge and maxUnavailable are the two knobs that control RollingUpdate behavior. They can be absolute numbers (like 1) or percentages (like 25%). The formula for how many pods exist during update: desired ± maxSurge (above) and desired − maxUnavailable (below). For zero-downtime, you need to ensure at least 1 Pod is always available to serve traffic.

📝 maxSurge & maxUnavailable — Visual Examples
RollingUpdate Parameters — maxSurge & maxUnavailable
  ═══════════════ CONFIGURATIONS COMPARED ═══════════════
  replicas: 3

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CONFIG A: maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0  (ZERO DOWNTIME!)    │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │  Step 0: [v1] [v1] [v1]          (3 pods)                   │
  │  Step 1: [v1] [v1] [v1] [v2]     (4 pods! surge +1)         │
  │          wait for v2 Ready → [v1] [v1] [v2]  (delete 1 v1)  │
  │  Step 2: [v1] [v1] [v2] [v2]     (4 pods)                   │
  │          wait → [v1] [v2] [v2]   (delete 1 v1)              │
  │  Step 3: [v1] [v2] [v2] [v2]     (4 pods)                   │
  │          wait → [v2] [v2] [v2]   (delete last v1)            │
  │  ✓ Never went below 3 pods — ZERO DOWNTIME                   │
  │  ✓ Max pod count during update: 4 (3 desired + 1 maxSurge)  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  CONFIG B: maxSurge=25%, maxUnavailable=25%  (DEFAULT)       │
  │  25% of 3 = 0.75 → rounds UP to 1                           │
  │  Same behavior as Config A (for 3 replicas)                  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  CONFIG C: maxSurge=0, maxUnavailable=1                      │
  │  Step 0: [v1] [v1] [v1]          (3 pods)                   │
  │  Step 1: [v1] [v1]                (2 pods! -1 unavailable)   │
  │          wait for v2 Ready → [v1] [v1] [v2]                 │
  │  ✓ Uses fewer resources during update                        │
  │  ⚠️  Temporary reduced capacity (2 pods serving instead of 3)│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ RECOMMENDED VALUES ═══════════════
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  USE CASE                  maxSurge  maxUnavailable  BEHAVIOR   │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Zero-downtime production   1         0              100% uptime│
  │  Fast rollout, limited nodes 25%      25%            Balanced   │
  │  Resource-constrained       0         1               Save CPU/RAM│
  │  Maximum speed              50%       0               Fastest   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠️  CANNOT be zero simultaneously: maxSurge=0 AND maxUnavailable=0
      would make it impossible to replace any pods!

CKAD exam tip: For easypj/jobpost production: set maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 for zero-downtime API updates. The default (25%/25%) is usually fine for 3+ replicas but can cause brief reduced capacity with fewer replicas. The CKAD exam may ask you to configure specific values in a Deployment YAML.

Deploy 🟡 Q46 of 200
What are the kubectl rollout subcommands, and how do you monitor a rolling update?
A) kubectl rollout status (watch progress in real-time), kubectl rollout history (view revision list with change-cause), kubectl rollout undo (rollback to previous revision), kubectl rollout pause (temporarily stop the rollout mid-update), kubectl rollout resume (continue a paused rollout). Use kubectl rollout status deploy/name --watch to monitor the update until it completes or fails
B) kubectl rollout has only one subcommand: kubectl rollout restart — it restarts all pods immediately with no progress tracking or rollback capability
C) kubectl rollout commands work only on StatefulSets and DaemonSets — they cannot be used with Deployments
D) kubectl rollout is an alias for kubectl apply — there is no separate rollout functionality in Kubernetes
✅ Correct Answer: A

kubectl rollout is your mission control center for Deployment updates. It provides 5 subcommands that cover the entire update lifecycle: monitor progress, check history, undo mistakes, pause problematic rollouts, and resume after investigation. These are essential CKAD tools — you'll use them on nearly every Deployment-related exam task.

📝 kubectl rollout — Complete Reference
kubectl rollout Subcommands — The Complete Toolkit

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  COMMAND                          WHAT IT DOES                    │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl rollout status           Shows real-time rollout        │
  │    deploy/easypj-api              progress. Exits 0 on success,  │
  │                                   non-zero on failure/stuck.     │
  │                                   Use --watch for live updates.  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl rollout history          Lists all revisions with       │
  │    deploy/easypj-api              CHANGE-CAUSE (if annotation    │
  │                                   kubernetes.io/change-cause     │
  │                                   was set). Shows revision #.    │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl rollout undo             Rolls back to PREVIOUS         │
  │    deploy/easypj-api              revision. Use --to-revision=N  │
  │                                   for specific version.          │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl rollout pause            Pauses a mid-progress rollout. │
  │    deploy/easypj-api              Existing pods stay as-is.      │
  │                                   New changes are queued.        │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl rollout resume           Continues a paused rollout.    │
  │    deploy/easypj-api              Processes queued changes.      │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl rollout restart          Restarts all Pods (rolling      │

     → Waiting for rollout to finish: 2 of 3 updated...
     → deployment "easypj-api" successfully rolled out ✓

  3. (If something goes wrong)
     kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-api
     → REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
     → 1        Initial deployment
     → 2        Updated to v2.1

     kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api --to-revision=1
     → Rolled back to revision 1 ✓

CKAD exam tip: kubectl rollout restart is your go-to when you update a ConfigMap or Secret and need pods to pick up the changes (since pods don't auto-restart on ConfigMap changes). For easypj/jobpost, after updating the Django settings ConfigMap: kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api — this triggers a clean rolling restart with zero downtime.

Deploy 🟡 Q47 of 200
How does kubectl rollout undo work, and what happens to the ReplicaSets during a rollback?
A) Rollout undo deletes the current Deployment and creates a brand new one from scratch — all ReplicaSets and Pods are recreated
B) Rollout undo only changes the Deployment's image tag back to the previous version — it does not touch ReplicaSets or Pods
C) Rollout undo reverts the Deployment to a previous revision by scaling UP the old ReplicaSet (from the target revision) and scaling DOWN the current ReplicaSet. This is FAST because the old Pods often still exist (just scaled to 0) — Kubernetes doesn't need to pull images or create Pods from scratch. The old ReplicaSet becomes the active one, and the current one is scaled to 0 (preserved for future rollbacks)
D) Rollout undo is a manual process — you must kubectl delete the current Deployment, then kubectl apply the old YAML file from your Git history
✅ Correct Answer: C

Rollback is incredibly fast because the old ReplicaSet and its Pods still exist — they were just scaled to 0 during the previous update. When you kubectl rollout undo, the Deployment controller simply scales the old ReplicaSet back up and scales the current one down. No image pulling, no Pod creation — just changing the replica count on existing ReplicaSets. This is why revisionHistoryLimit matters: it controls how many old ReplicaSets are kept. Default is 10 — you can rollback up to 10 revisions back.

📝 Rollout Undo — How Rollback Works
kubectl rollout undo — Instant Rollback via ReplicaSet Switching
  ═══════════════ ROLLBACK MECHANISM ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  BEFORE ROLLBACK:                                                │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  DEPLOYMENT: easypj-api (current revision: 3)              │  │
  │  │                                                            │  │
  │  │  ReplicaSet v1 (rev 1):  SCALED TO 0 ← Old pods preserved! │  │
  │  │  ReplicaSet v2 (rev 2):  SCALED TO 0 ← Old pods preserved! │  │
  │  │  ReplicaSet v3 (rev 3):  3 PODS RUNNING ← Current active   │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                           │
                           │  kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api
                           │  (or: --to-revision=1)
                           ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  AFTER ROLLBACK (to revision 1):                                 │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  DEPLOYMENT: easypj-api (current revision: 4 = rev 1 data) │  │
  │  │                                                            │  │
  │  │  ReplicaSet v1 (rev 1):  3 PODS RUNNING ← NOW ACTIVE!      │  │
  │  │  ReplicaSet v2 (rev 2):  SCALED TO 0                      │  │
  │  │  ReplicaSet v3 (rev 3):  SCALED TO 0 ← Just rolled back   │  │
  │  │  ReplicaSet v4 (rev 4):  SCALED TO 0 ← New record of undo │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ KEY COMMANDS ═══════════════
  # View revision history
  kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-api
  → REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
  → 1         Initial deploy (v1.0)
  → 2         Updated image to v2.0
  → 3         Updated image to v2.1 (BROKEN!)

  # Rollback to previous revision
  kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api

  # Rollback to SPECIFIC revision
  kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api --to-revision=1

  ⚠️  ROLLBACK IS FAST (seconds, not minutes!)
      Because old pods often still exist and just need scaling up.

CKAD exam tip: Set the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation to make kubectl rollout history useful: kubectl annotate deploy/easypj-api kubernetes.io/change-cause="Updated to v2.1". Without this, history shows <none> for each revision. For easypj/jobpost, always annotate your deployments so you can quickly identify which revision is which during an incident.

Deploy 🟡 Q48 of 200
What is revisionHistoryLimit and what happens if you set it too low?
A) revisionHistoryLimit controls how many Pods can be updated simultaneously during a rolling update — setting it too low makes rollouts slower
B) revisionHistoryLimit is the maximum number of times you can rollback — once exceeded, the Deployment becomes permanently locked at the current version
C) revisionHistoryLimit controls how many seconds Kubernetes waits before forcing a rollback after detecting a failed Deployment
D) revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) controls how many old ReplicaSets are kept. Each old ReplicaSet represents one revision. If set too low (e.g., 2), older ReplicaSets are DELETED — you cannot kubectl rollout undo to revisions beyond the limit. Set it higher (e.g., 20) for better audit trail and rollback flexibility. Setting it to 0 prevents rollbacks entirely
✅ Correct Answer: D

revisionHistoryLimit is your rollback safety net. Each time you update a Deployment, a new ReplicaSet is created and the old one is preserved (scaled to 0). This limit controls how many old ReplicaSets to keep. The default (10) means you can rollback up to 10 revisions back. There's a tradeoff: more history = better audit trail + deeper rollback, but more etcd storage. Setting it to 0 means NO rollback capability at all.

📝 revisionHistoryLimit — Tradeoffs
revisionHistoryLimit — How Many Revisions to Keep
  ═══════════════ revisionHistoryLimit VALUES ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  VALUE    BEHAVIOR                                               │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  10       DEFAULT. Keeps last 10 ReplicaSets. Good for most apps.│
  │           Oldest RS (#11) is automatically deleted.              │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  0        ❌ NO old ReplicaSets kept.                             │
  │           ❌ kubectl rollout undo WILL NOT WORK.                  │
  │           ❌ kubectl rollout history shows nothing.               │
  │           ✓ Saves etcd storage (minimal benefit).                │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  20       ✅ Keeps 20 revisions. More rollback flexibility.       │
  │           ✅ Better audit trail (what changed and when).          │
  │           ⚠️  More ReplicaSet objects in etcd.                   │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  100      ✅ Maximum audit trail.                                 │
  │           ⚠️  Significant etcd storage if you deploy often.       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ VISUAL: WHAT GETS DELETED ═══════════════
  revisionHistoryLimit: 3

  Revisions:  [RS-v1] [RS-v2] [RS-v3] [RS-v4] [RS-v5]
                                    ↑ kept   ↑ kept   ↑ kept
               DELETED ❌   DELETED ❌

  Only revisions 3, 4, 5 are available for rollback.
  Revisions 1 and 2 are GONE FOREVER.

  ═══════════════ easypj/jobpost RECOMMENDATION ═══════════════
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: easypj-api
  spec:
    revisionHistoryLimit: 20    ← Keep 20 revisions
    # Why 20? We deploy 2-3 times per day. 20 revisions = ~1 week
    # of rollback capability. Enough for any incident investigation.

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam may ask you to configure or explain revisionHistoryLimit. Remember: it's a Deployment spec field, not an annotation. Set it to at least 5 for exam scenarios. For easypj/jobpost production: 20 is a good balance between rollback safety and etcd storage.

Deploy 🟡 Q49 of 200
How does a Blue/Green deployment work, and how does it achieve instant rollback?
A) Blue/Green deployment means running half your pods in one availability zone (blue) and half in another (green) for geographic redundancy
B) Blue/Green deployment uses TWO complete environments: BLUE (current live version serving all traffic) and GREEN (new version, fully deployed but receiving NO traffic). After testing Green thoroughly, you switch the Service selector from Blue to Green — instantly moving 100% of traffic to the new version. Rollback is just as fast: switch the Service selector back to Blue. No pod restarts, no image pulling — just a selector change
C) Blue/Green is another name for RollingUpdate — there is no difference between the two strategies
D) Blue/Green deployment requires a cloud load balancer — it cannot be implemented on local clusters like kubeadm or kind
✅ Correct Answer: B

Blue/Green is the simplest zero-downtime strategy. You deploy the new version (Green) alongside the current version (Blue) — two full stacks. Green is fully tested while Blue handles all traffic. When ready, you change the Service selector from version: blue to version: green — instant switch! Rollback is just as fast: change the selector back. This is simpler than canary and provides instant rollback, but costs twice the resources during the deployment window.

📝 Blue/Green Deployment — Instant Switch
Blue/Green Deployment — Service Selector Switch
  ═══════════════ PHASE 1: BLUE SERVES ALL TRAFFIC ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Service: easypj-api                                             │
  │  selector:                                                       │
  │    app: easypj-api                                               │
  │    version: blue          ← Points to BLUE deployment            │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────┐              │
  │  │  BLUE (v2.0)         │    │  GREEN (v2.1)       │              │
  │  │  replicas: 3         │    │  replicas: 3         │              │
  │  │  🟦🟦🟦 SERVING       │    │  🟩🟩🟩 IDLE           │              │
  │  │  ← ALL traffic       │    │  ← NO traffic       │              │
  │  └─────────────────────┘    └─────────────────────┘              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ PHASE 2: SWITCH TO GREEN ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  kubectl patch svc easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}'│
  │                                                                  │
  │  Service: easypj-api                                             │
  │  selector:                                                       │
  │    app: easypj-api                                               │
  │    version: green         ← NOW points to GREEN!                 │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────┐              │
  │  │  BLUE (v2.0)         │    │  GREEN (v2.1)       │              │
  │  │  replicas: 3         │    │  replicas: 3         │              │
  │  │  🟦🟦🟦 IDLE          │    │  🟩🟩🟩 SERVING      │              │
  │  │  ← NO traffic        │    │  ← ALL traffic      │              │
  │  └─────────────────────┘    └─────────────────────┘              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ ROLLBACK: SWITCH BACK TO BLUE ═══════════════
  kubectl patch svc easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"blue"}}}'
  → Instant! Blue pods still running, just idle. No restart needed.
  → Rollback time: <1 second (just a selector change!)

  ═══════════════ PROS & CONS ═══════════════
  ✅ Instant switch (no pod restarts, no image pulling)
  ✅ Instant rollback (just switch selector back)
  ✅ Green fully tested before traffic hits it
  ❌ Double resources during deployment window
  ❌ Database migrations must be backward-compatible
     (Blue AND Green connect to the SAME database!)

CKAD exam tip: Blue/Green is not a built-in Kubernetes strategy — you implement it manually using two Deployments and a shared Service (or two Services and a traffic router). The CKAD exam may ask you to set this up. Key: use different label values (version: blue vs version: green) and switch the Service selector. For easypj/jobpost, use Blue/Green for database migration safety — test Green against a database snapshot before switching.

Deploy 🟡 Q50 of 200
How does a Canary deployment differ from Blue/Green, and how do you implement it?
A) Canary deployment gradually shifts a SMALL percentage of traffic to the new version (e.g., 10% to v2, 90% stays on v1) while monitoring error rates. If the canary performs well, increase the percentage; if it fails, rollback instantly. Unlike Blue/Green (all-or-nothing), Canary is progressive and reduces blast radius. Implementation: deploy a small number of new-version pods alongside old-version pods, both matching the Service selector, so traffic is split proportionally
B) Canary deployment requires a special Kubernetes plugin called "CanaryController" that must be installed separately — it's not possible with standard Kubernetes resources
C) Canary is the same as Blue/Green — both deploy two full stacks and switch all traffic at once
D) Canary deployment randomly deletes pods to "test" if the cluster can self-heal, like a canary in a coal mine testing for toxic gas
✅ Correct Answer: A

Canary deployment is the cautious cousin of Blue/Green. Instead of switching all traffic at once, you send a small percentage to the new version and watch for problems. The name comes from "canary in a coal mine" — if the canary dies (errors spike), you know the new version is bad and you roll back before it affects everyone. This is the safest production deployment strategy.

📝 Canary Deployment — Gradual Traffic Shift
Canary Deployment — Progressive Traffic Shifting
  ═══════════════ PHASE 1: 10% CANARY ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Service: easypj-api (selector: app=easypj-api)                  │
  │                                                                  │
  │  STABLE (v2.0):  9 pods    ← 90% of traffic (~9/10 requests)    │
  │  CANARY (v2.1):  1 pod     ← 10% of traffic (~1/10 requests)    │
  │                                                                  │
  │  🟦🟦🟦🟦🟦🟦🟦🟦🟦  +  🟩                                     │
  │  9x v2.0 stable        1x v2.1 canary                            │
  │                                                                  │
  │  MONITOR for 10 minutes:                                         │
  │  • Error rate:  v2.0: 0.1%  |  v2.1: 0.1%  ✅ OK               │
  │  • Latency:     v2.0: 45ms  |  v2.1: 48ms  ✅ OK               │
  │  • Memory:      v2.0: 200MB |  v2.1: 210MB ✅ OK               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ PHASE 2: 50% CANARY ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Scale canary to 5, scale stable to 5                            │
  │  🟦🟦🟦🟦🟦 + 🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩                                         │
  │  Monitor for 10 more minutes... still good ✅                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ PHASE 3: 100% PROMOTED ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Scale canary to 10, scale stable to 0                           │
  │  🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩🟩 (10x v2.1)                               │
  │  v2.1 is now the new stable!                                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ ROLLBACK (if needed) ═══════════════
  If canary shows errors at 10%:
  → kubectl scale deploy easypj-api-canary --replicas=0
  → Only 10% of users affected. Rollback in seconds.

  ═══════════════ CANARY vs BLUE/GREEN ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────┬─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
  │  BLUE/GREEN  │  100% instant switch │  Double resources, risky  │
  │  CANARY      │  Gradual % shift     │  Safest, slower rollout   │
  └──────────────┴─────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: The simplest canary on CKAD: create two Deployments (stable and canary) with different replica counts but the SAME labels matching the Service selector. Traffic splits proportionally: 9 stable pods + 1 canary pod = 90/10 split. For easypj/jobpost, use canary for risky changes — start with 1 canary pod, monitor for 10 minutes, then gradually increase.

2.2 Deployment Operations & DebuggingQ51-Q58

🟢→🟡 | Supporting topic: kubectl scale, set image, edit, patch, apply vs create, diff, deployment conditions.

Deploy 🟢 Q51 of 200
How do you manually scale a Deployment using kubectl?
A) You must edit the Deployment YAML file and run kubectl apply — there is no imperative scale command
B) kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api --replicas=5 — this immediately changes the desired replica count and the Deployment controller creates/terminates Pods to match. Use --replicas=0 to scale down completely (stop all pods without deleting the Deployment). Always scale the DEPLOYMENT, not the underlying ReplicaSet
C) kubectl resize deploy/easypj-api --count=5 — scale is not the correct kubectl verb
D) kubectl update replicas deploy/easypj-api 5 — the replicas field cannot be changed imperatively
✅ Correct Answer: B

kubectl scale is the imperative way to change replica counts. It works on Deployments, ReplicaSets, StatefulSets, and replication controllers. The change is immediate and the controller begins creating/terminating pods right away. An important gotcha: if an HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) also manages this Deployment, the HPA will fight your manual scaling and revert to its calculated target.

📝 kubectl scale — Quick Reference
kubectl scale — Change Replica Counts Instantly
  ═══════════════ COMMON SCALE COMMANDS ═══════════════
  # Scale UP
  kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api --replicas=5
  → Deployment controller creates 2 new Pods (was 3 → now 5)

  # Scale DOWN
  kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api --replicas=1
  → Deployment controller terminates 2 Pods (was 3 → now 1)

  # Scale to ZERO (stop without deleting)
  kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api --replicas=0
  → All Pods terminated. Deployment still exists — scale back up anytime.

  # Scale multiple Deployments at once
  kubectl scale deploy/easypj-web deploy/easypj-api --replicas=5

  ═══════════════ SCALE vs HPA CONFLICT ═══════════════
  ⚠️  If HPA manages this Deployment:
      1. You: kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api --replicas=10
      2. HPA (after 15s): "CPU is low, I want 3 replicas"
      3. HPA: kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api --replicas=3
      4. Your manual 10 is OVERWRITTEN by HPA!
      → Solution: kubectl delete hpa easypj-api (remove HPA first)

CKAD exam tip: Always scale the Deployment, NOT the ReplicaSet. If you scale the ReplicaSet directly, the Deployment controller will revert it to the Deployment's desired replica count. For easypj/jobpost, use kubectl scale for manual scaling during traffic spikes and for scaling down to 0 during maintenance windows.

Deploy 🟢 Q52 of 200
How do you update a container image in a running Deployment without editing the YAML file?
A) kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api django=easypj/api:v2.1 — this updates the container image and triggers a rolling update. For multi-container Pods, specify the container name: kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web django=easypj/web:v3 nginx=nginx:1.25. Use --record (deprecated) or annotation to track the change
B) You cannot update a container image imperatively — you must delete and recreate the entire Deployment with the new image
C) kubectl update-image deploy/easypj-api easypj/api:v2.1 — set image is not the correct kubectl verb
D) kubectl replace container deploy/easypj-api --image=easypj/api:v2.1
✅ Correct Answer: A

kubectl set image is the fastest way to update a container image and trigger a rolling update — no YAML editing needed. The format is RESOURCE/NAME CONTAINER_NAME=IMAGE:TAG. For multi-container Pods, you MUST specify which container to update; otherwise kubectl will error. After the command, the Deployment begins a rolling update immediately.

📝 kubectl set image + kubectl set resources
kubectl set — Update Deployments Imperatively
  ═══════════════ SET IMAGE ═══════════════
  # Single container Deployment
  kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api django=easypj/api:v2.1

  # Multi-container Deployment (MUST specify container name)
  kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web \
    django=easypj/web:v3 \
    nginx=nginx:1.25-alpine

  # All containers in a Deployment
  kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api *=easypj/api:v2.1

  ═══════════════ SET RESOURCES ═══════════════
  # Set resource requests/limits imperatively
  kubectl set resources deploy/easypj-api \
    --requests=cpu=200m,memory=256Mi \
    --limits=cpu=500m,memory=512Mi

  # For a specific container
  kubectl set resources deploy/easypj-web \
    -c django \
    --requests=cpu=500m,memory=512Mi

  ═══════════════ SET ENV ═══════════════
  # Set environment variables
  kubectl set env deploy/easypj-api DEBUG=false LOG_LEVEL=info

  ═══════════════ SET SERVICEACCOUNT ═══════════════
  kubectl set serviceaccount deploy/easypj-api easypj-api-sa

  ⚠️  kubectl set triggers a ROLLING UPDATE immediately!
      The Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet with the changes.

CKAD exam tip: kubectl set commands are CKAD essentials. They're fast, imperative, and trigger rolling updates. Use kubectl set image for quick image updates during the exam. For easypj/jobpost: update the API image with kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api django=easypj/api:v2.1 and monitor with kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api.

Deploy 🟡 Q53 of 200
What happens when you run kubectl edit deploy/easypj-api, and what should you be careful about?
A) kubectl edit opens a read-only view of the Deployment — you cannot actually modify anything, it's just for inspection
B) kubectl edit saves changes to a local file only — you must run kubectl apply separately to push changes to the cluster
C) kubectl edit opens the LIVE resource YAML in your default editor (vim/nano). When you save and exit, changes are APPLIED IMMEDIATELY to the cluster. A rolling update is triggered if the Pod template changed. ⚠️ DANGER: you're editing the LIVE object which includes status, resourceVersion, and many read-only fields — only modify fields under spec:
D) kubectl edit is deprecated and no longer works in Kubernetes 1.25+ — you must use kubectl patch or kubectl apply instead
✅ Correct Answer: C

kubectl edit is the "quick fix" tool — it opens the live resource in your editor and applies changes on save. It's convenient but dangerous because the live object contains many auto-generated fields (status, resourceVersion, uid, managedFields) that you should NEVER modify. Always scroll down past those fields and only edit spec: and metadata.labels/annotations. Tip: use KUBE_EDITOR="nano" if you prefer a different editor on the exam.

📝 kubectl edit — Lifecycle & Dangers
What Happens When You kubectl edit
  ═══════════════ KUBECTL EDIT FLOW ═══════════════
  kubectl edit deploy/easypj-api
        │
        ▼
  kubectl GETs the live object from API server
        │
        ▼
  Opens in $EDITOR (vim/nano) — shows FULL YAML:
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  apiVersion: apps/v1                       │
  │  kind: Deployment                          │
  │  metadata:                                 │
  │    name: easypj-api                        │
  │    uid: a1b2c3d4...     ◄── DO NOT TOUCH  │
  │    resourceVersion: "12345"  ◄── NO TOUCH  │
  │    managedFields: [...]   ◄── HANDS OFF    │
  │  spec:                                     │
  │    replicas: 3          ◄──✅ SAFE TO EDIT │
  │    template:                               │
  │      spec:                                 │
  │        containers:                         │
  │        - image: easypj/api:v1  ◄──✅ EDIT │
  │  status: {...}           ◄── DO NOT TOUCH  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
  YOU edit spec fields → Save → Exit (:wq)
        │
        ▼
  kubectl sends PATCH to API server
        │
        ▼
  API server applies changes → triggers Rolling Update!
        │
        ▼
  Status: deployment "easypj-api" edited ✓

  ══════════ EDIT vs PATCH vs APPLY ══════════
  ┌────────┬──────────────────┬────────────────────────────┐
  │  edit   │ Opens editor     │ ⚡ Quick fix, human-driven │
  │         │ on LIVE object   │ ⚠️  Easy to break things   │
  ├────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
  │  patch  │ CLI, scriptable   │ Precision, CI/CD friendly │
  │         │ Single field      │ Cannot see full context    │
  ├────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
  │  apply  │ From YAML file    │ GitOps, reproducible       │
  │         │ Declarative state │ Must maintain full YAML    │
  └────────┴──────────────────┴────────────────────────────┘

  ⚠️  DANGER ZONE: If you accidentally delete or modify
      resourceVersion, uid, or status fields, your edit
      will FAIL or cause unexpected behavior.

CKAD exam tip: Use kubectl edit for quick field changes during the exam (it's faster than writing YAML). But if the task asks for a "declarative approach," use kubectl apply instead. Set export KUBE_EDITOR=nano at exam start if you're not comfortable with vim.

Deploy 🟡 Q54 of 200
What is kubectl patch, and how does it differ from kubectl edit and kubectl apply?
A) kubectl patch makes targeted, programmatic changes to specific fields without opening an editor or needing the full YAML. Three patch types: strategic merge (default, K8s-specific), JSON merge (RFC 7386), and JSON patch (RFC 6902). Best for scripts, CI/CD, and precise single-field changes like: kubectl patch deploy/easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"replicas":5}}'
B) kubectl patch is the same as kubectl edit — both open an editor for manual changes
C) kubectl patch can only modify labels and annotations — it cannot change spec fields like replicas or image
D) kubectl patch requires a full YAML manifest file just like kubectl apply — there's no way to make targeted changes
✅ Correct Answer: A

kubectl patch is the scalpel of Kubernetes operations — precise, scriptable, and fast. It updates only the fields you specify without touching anything else. The default strategic merge patch intelligently merges lists (like containers) by name. JSON patch (RFC 6902) uses operations like add, remove, replace, copy, move for surgical changes.

📝 kubectl patch — Three Patch Types
kubectl patch — Examples
  ══════════ STRATEGIC MERGE (default) ══════════
  kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"replicas":5}}'
  → Changes only replicas. Merges intelligently.

  kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"django","image":"easypj/api:v2.1"}]}}}}'
  → Updates only the django container image. Other containers untouched.

  ══════════ JSON PATCH (RFC 6902) ══════════
  kubectl patch deploy easypj-api --type json -p '[
    {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/replicas","value":5},
    {"op":"add","path":"/metadata/labels/version","value":"v2"}
  ]'

  ══════════ PATCH vs EDIT vs APPLY ══════════
  ┌──────────┬────────────────────┬────────────────────────┐
  │  patch    │ Targeted field     │ CI/CD, scripts, one-liner│
  │  edit     │ Manual (editor)    │ Quick human changes      │
  │  apply    │ Full YAML manifest │ GitOps, declarative state│
  └──────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘
Deploy 🟡 Q55 of 200
When should you use kubectl apply vs kubectl create vs kubectl replace?
A) All three commands are identical — you can use any of them interchangeably with the same result
B) kubectl apply is deprecated — you should always use kubectl create for new resources and kubectl replace for existing ones
C) kubectl create works only on Pods, kubectl apply works only on Deployments, and kubectl replace works only on Services
D) kubectl create — creates a NEW resource (fails if it already exists). kubectl replace — replaces EXISTING resource (fails if it doesn't exist). kubectl apply — DECLARATIVE: creates if it doesn't exist, updates if it does (maintains last-applied-configuration annotation). apply is the standard GitOps/declarative approach; create and replace are imperative and less commonly used
✅ Correct Answer: D

kubectl apply is the declarative standard. It manages resources by tracking the last-applied-configuration annotation, which allows it to compute a 3-way merge (original, live, desired) and remove fields you deleted from your YAML. This is essential for GitOps workflows. kubectl create and kubectl replace are imperative and don't track changes over time.

📝 create vs replace vs apply — Decision Guide
kubectl create vs replace vs apply
  ═══════════ QUICK REFERENCE ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  COMMAND       BEHAVIOR                    USE CASE              │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl       Creates NEW resource.       Imperative quick      │
  │  create        Errors if already exists.   create. Good for      │
  │                                            testing/debugging.    │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl       Replaces EXISTING resource. Rarely used. Requires │
  │  replace       Errors if not found.        full YAML.            │
  │               Deletes & recreates.                               │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl       Creates if new, UPDATES     DECLARATIVE standard. │
  │  apply         if exists. Tracks changes   GitOps. CI/CD.        │
  │               via annotation. Merges       Production.           │
  │               smartly (3-way diff).                              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ CKAD EXAM RECOMMENDATION ═══════════
  • Use kubectl create --dry-run=client -o yaml to GENERATE YAML
  • Use kubectl apply -f to DEPLOY/UPDATE from YAML files
  • Avoid kubectl replace (rarely needed on CKAD)
Deploy 🟡 Q56 of 200
What is the difference between imperative and declarative Kubernetes management?
A) There is no difference — imperative and declarative are two names for the same approach
B) Imperative: "kubectl run nginx --image=nginx" — tell Kubernetes exactly WHAT to do, step by step (YOU define the operations). Declarative: "kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml" — tell Kubernetes WHAT you want (desired state), and Kubernetes figures out HOW to achieve it. Imperative is faster for one-off tasks; declarative is better for reproducibility, GitOps, and production
C) Imperative is the only way to manage Kubernetes — declarative was deprecated in v1.20
D) Declarative requires a PhD in computer science — imperative is the simple approach for beginners
✅ Correct Answer: B

Imperative = "Do this, then this, then this." You control the steps. Declarative = "Here's what I want — make it so." Kubernetes handles the how. On the CKAD exam, use both: imperative for speed (generating YAML, quick tests), declarative for final answers (apply YAML files). The exam tests your ability to use the right approach for each task.

📝 Imperative vs Declarative — CKAD Strategy
When to Use Each Approach on CKAD
  ═══════════ IMPERATIVE (fast, one-off) ═══════════
  kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- sh
  kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > f.yaml
  kubectl scale deploy/api --replicas=5
  kubectl set image deploy/api django=api:v2

  ═══════════ DECLARATIVE (reproducible, GitOps) ═══════════
  kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
  kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml
  kubectl apply -k ./overlays/prod/    (Kustomize)

  ═══════════ CKAD STRATEGY ═══════════
  1. Generate YAML imperatively:  kubectl create ... --dry-run -o yaml
  2. Edit the YAML (add probes, env vars, resources)
  3. Apply declaratively:          kubectl apply -f file.yaml
  4. Verify:                        kubectl get/describe/logs

  💡 "Generate imperatively, apply declaratively"
Deploy 🟡 Q57 of 200
How do you preview what changes kubectl apply will make before actually applying them?
A) Use kubectl preview -f deploy.yaml — this shows a visual diff of changes before applying
B) You cannot preview changes — kubectl apply always applies immediately with no preview capability
C) Use kubectl diff -f deploy.yaml — this compares the proposed YAML against the live object on the server and shows exactly what lines will be added (+), removed (-), or changed. It's like "git diff" for Kubernetes. Also: kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f deploy.yaml validates the YAML against the API server without applying
D) Use kubectl apply --preview -f deploy.yaml — this applies changes in preview mode where they are only visible for 30 seconds
✅ Correct Answer: C

kubectl diff is your safety check before applying changes. It shows exactly what will change in the cluster — added lines, removed lines, modified fields. On the CKAD exam, use this to verify your YAML edits are correct before potentially breaking a running application.

📝 kubectl diff — Preview Before Apply
kubectl diff — See Changes Before Applying
  ═══════════════ WORKFLOW ═══════════════
  1. Edit deploy.yaml (increase replicas from 3 to 5)
  2. kubectl diff -f deploy.yaml
     → -  replicas: 3
     → +  replicas: 5
  3. Review: "Yes, that's what I intended"
  4. kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml

  ═══════════════ COMMAND COMPARISON ═══════════════
  ┌────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  COMMAND                │ WHAT IT DOES                     │
  ├────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl diff -f f.yaml │ Show DIFF vs live object (no     │
  │                         │ change applied)                  │
  ├────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl apply          │ Validate YAML schema against     │
  │  --dry-run=server       │ API server (no change applied)   │
  ├────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl apply          │ Validate YAML locally (no API    │
  │  --dry-run=client       │ server contact)                  │
  ├────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubectl apply -f f.yaml│ APPLY changes to cluster         │
  └────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ CKAD SAFETY WORKFLOW ═══════════
  kubectl diff -f deploy.yaml       ← Check what WILL change
  kubectl apply --dry-run=server    ← Validate YAML
  kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml      ← Apply for real
  kubectl rollout status deploy/name ← Monitor progress
Deploy 🟡 Q58 of 200
What are Deployment conditions and how do you check if a rollout is stuck?
A) Deployment conditions include: Available (minimum replicas available), Progressing (rollout is making progress), and ReplicaFailure (a ReplicaSet has failed to create pods). Check with kubectl describe deploy or kubectl rollout status. If Progressing=False with reason "ProgressDeadlineExceeded", the rollout is STUCK — Kubernetes has given up trying to deploy
B) Deployment conditions are only visible in the Kubernetes dashboard web UI — kubectl cannot display them
C) Deployment conditions are set by the developer using kubectl annotate — they are not automatic
D) There are only two conditions: Healthy and Unhealthy — these are binary states with no additional information
✅ Correct Answer: A

Deployment conditions are Kubernetes' way of telling you "here's what's happening with your rollout." The Progressing condition is the most important — when it's False, your rollout is stuck. Common reasons: insufficient resources (cluster can't schedule the new pods), ImagePullBackOff (can't pull the new image), or probe failures (new pods fail health checks). The progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600s = 10 min) determines how long Kubernetes waits before declaring the rollout stuck.

📝 Deployment Conditions — Diagnosing Rollout Issues
Deployment Conditions — Check with kubectl describe
  ═══════════════ READING DEPLOYMENT CONDITIONS ═══════════════
  kubectl describe deploy easypj-api

  Conditions:
    Type           Status  Reason
    ────           ──────  ──────
    Available      True    MinimumReplicasAvailable  ← 3/3 pods ready ✅
    Progressing    False   ProgressDeadlineExceeded  ← ROLLOUT STUCK! ❌
    ReplicaFailure False   (not present = no failure)

  ═══════════════ CONDITION MEANINGS ═══════════════
  ┌─────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CONDITION       │ MEANING                                  │
  ├─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Available       │ Minimum required replicas are running    │
  │  Progressing     │ Rollout is making forward progress       │
  │  ReplicaFailure  │ A ReplicaSet failed to create pods       │
  └─────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ WHEN PROGRESSING=FALSE ═══════════
  1. kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-api → Any pods stuck?
  2. kubectl describe pod <stuck-pod> → Events tell why
  3. Common reasons: ImagePullBackOff, Insufficient CPU,
     CrashLoopBackOff, Failed probes
  4. Fix root cause → rollout resumes automatically

CKAD exam tip: If kubectl rollout status hangs, the rollout is stuck. Ctrl+C and check kubectl describe deploy for conditions, then kubectl get pods for the actual pod status. For easypj/jobpost, the most common stuck rollout cause is an invalid image tag.

2.3 Namespaces & Resource ManagementQ59-Q64

🟢→🟡 | Supporting topic: namespaces, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, cross-namespace communication.

Deploy 🟢 Q59 of 200
What are Kubernetes Namespaces and how should easypj/jobpost use them?
A) Namespaces are Kubernetes clusters within clusters — each namespace runs its own API server, scheduler, and controller manager
B) Namespaces are virtual clusters within a physical cluster — they isolate resources (Pods, Services, Deployments) by name and provide scope for RBAC, ResourceQuotas, and NetworkPolicies. For easypj/jobpost: use easypj-dev (development), easypj-staging (testing), easypj-prod (production) namespaces. Resources in different namespaces can communicate via DNS (svc.ns.svc.cluster.local)
C) Namespaces are only used for organizing kubectl output — they have no impact on resource isolation or security
D) Namespaces are automatically created per user — every developer gets their own namespace with full admin access
✅ Correct Answer: B

Namespaces partition cluster resources between multiple users, teams, or environments. Key facts: (1) Resource names must be unique WITHIN a namespace but can repeat ACROSS namespaces, (2) Not all resources are namespaced — Nodes, PVs, StorageClasses are cluster-scoped, (3) Default namespaces: default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease. Use kubectl create ns easypj-dev and kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-dev to set default namespace.

📝 Namespaces — Logical Cluster Partitioning
Namespaces in the easypj/jobpost Cluster
  ═══════════════ CLUSTER-WIDE (NOT namespaced) ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Nodes · PersistentVolumes · StorageClasses              │
  │  ClusterRoles · ClusterRoleBindings · Namespaces         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ NAMESPACED RESOURCES ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ┌─ easypj-dev ──────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  Pods: web-dev, api-dev, db-dev                    │   │
  │  │  Services: web-svc, api-svc                        │   │
  │  │  Deployments, ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs...         │   │
  │  │  ResourceQuota: 2 CPU / 4Gi / 10 pods              │   │
  │  │  RBAC: dev-team (read-write)                       │   │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │  ┌─ easypj-staging ──────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  Pods: web-stg, api-stg, db-stg                    │   │
  │  │  (Same names OK — different namespace!)             │   │
  │  │  ResourceQuota: 4 CPU / 8Gi / 20 pods              │   │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │  ┌─ easypj-prod ─────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  Pods: web-prod, api-prod, db-prod                 │   │
  │  │  ResourceQuota: 20 CPU / 40Gi / 50 pods            │   │
  │  │  NetworkPolicy: strict ingress rules               │   │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ══════════ DEFAULT SYSTEM NAMESPACES ══════════
  ┌─────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  kube-system     │ Control plane & system pods      │
  │  kube-public     │ Publicly readable (cluster info) │
  │  kube-node-lease │ Node heartbeat leases (1.13+)    │
  │  default         │ Fallback namespace (AVOID it)    │
  └─────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: Always create a dedicated namespace for each exam task unless told otherwise. Check kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true vs --namespaced=false to see which resources are namespace-scoped.

Deploy 🟢 Q60 of 200
How do you set a default namespace to avoid typing -n on every kubectl command?
A) kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj — this permanently sets the default namespace for the current context. All subsequent kubectl commands will use this namespace unless you explicitly override with -n. Verify with kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace
B) export NAMESPACE=easypj — kubectl reads this environment variable as the default namespace
C) You cannot set a default namespace — you must always specify -n on every command
D) kubectl namespace set easypj — this sets the namespace globally for all users on the cluster
✅ Correct Answer: A

Setting the default namespace saves keystrokes and prevents mistakes. On the CKAD exam, always set your namespace at the start of each task. The command modifies your kubeconfig file. To switch back: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=default.

📝 Namespace Context Switching — CKAD Must-Know
Managing kubectl Context & Namespace
  ═══════════════ SET DEFAULT NAMESPACE ═══════════════
  # Set current context to easypj-dev
  kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj-dev

  # Verify (look for "namespace:" in output)
  kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace
  → namespace: easypj-dev  ✓

  # Now ALL commands default to easypj-dev:
  kubectl get pods
  → Lists pods in easypj-dev (no -n needed!)

  ═══════════ OVERRIDE PER COMMAND ═══════════
  kubectl get pods -n easypj-prod
  → Overrides default just for this one command

  ═══════════ LIST RESOURCES IN ALL NAMESPACES ═══════════
  kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
  kubectl get pods -A    (short form)

  ═══════════════ CKAD WORKFLOW ═══════════════
  # Task 1: "Create resources in namespace 'ckad-task1'"
  kubectl create ns ckad-task1
  kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=ckad-task1
  # → Now just run commands without -n on every line!

  # Task 2: Switch to new namespace
  kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=ckad-task2
  # → No more accidentally deploying to the wrong namespace!

  ══════════ MULTIPLE CLUSTERS ══════════
  kubectl config get-contexts          # List all contexts
  kubectl config use-context kind-cka  # Switch clusters
  kubectl config current-context       # Show current

CKAD exam tip: The FIRST thing you should do for any task: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<given-ns>. This will save you dozens of -n flags and prevent deploying resources to the wrong namespace — a common CKAD fail reason!

Deploy 🟡 Q61 of 200
What is a ResourceQuota and how does it prevent a development team from consuming all cluster resources?
A) ResourceQuota is an advisory limit that sends warnings but doesn't actually prevent resource overuse
B) ResourceQuota only limits the NUMBER of objects (Pods, Services) — it cannot limit CPU or memory
C) ResourceQuota applies cluster-wide and cannot be scoped to individual namespaces
D) ResourceQuota limits TOTAL resource consumption per namespace — CPU, memory, storage, and object counts (max Pods, Services, PVCs, Secrets, ConfigMaps). If a namespace exceeds its quota, new resource creation is REJECTED. For easypj/jobpost: set quotas on dev/staging to prevent them from starving production
✅ Correct Answer: D

ResourceQuota is the hard limit per namespace. Create: kubectl create quota dev-quota --hard=cpu=10,memory=20Gi,pods=20 --namespace=easypj-dev. Check with kubectl describe quota -n easypj-dev. For easypj/jobpost: set dev quota to 2 CPU/4Gi/10 pods and prod quota to 20 CPU/40Gi/50 pods.

📝 ResourceQuota — Hard Limits Per Namespace
ResourceQuota in Action — easypj/jobpost
  ═══════════════ DEV NAMESPACE QUOTA ═══════════════
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ResourceQuota
  metadata:
    name: dev-quota
    namespace: easypj-dev
  spec:
    hard:
      requests.cpu: "2"        ← Total CPU requested by all pods
      requests.memory: "4Gi"    ← Total memory requested
      limits.cpu: "4"           ← Hard CPU cap (burst limit)
      limits.memory: "8Gi"      ← Hard memory cap
      pods: "10"                ← Max 10 pods
      services: "5"             ← Max 5 services
      persistentvolumeclaims: "3"  ← Max 3 PVCs
      configmaps: "10"          ← Max 10 ConfigMaps
      secrets: "10"             ← Max 10 Secrets

  ═══════════ WHAT HAPPENS WHEN QUOTA EXCEEDED ═══════════
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  kubectl create deploy new-app --image=nginx -n dev     │
  │  → Error from server (Forbidden):                       │
  │    "exceeded quota: dev-quota, requested: pods=1,       │
  │     used: pods=10, limited: pods=10"                    │
  │  → REQUEST DENIED — Pod NOT created!                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ══════════ CHECK QUOTA USAGE ══════════
  kubectl describe quota dev-quota -n easypj-dev
  Name:            dev-quota
  Namespace:       easypj-dev
  Resource         Used   Hard
  --------         ----   ----
  requests.cpu     800m   2       ← 40% used
  requests.memory   2Gi   4Gi     ← 50% used
  pods              4     10      ← 40% used

  ══════════ easypj/jobpost QUOTA STRATEGY ══════════
  ┌──────────────┬──────────┬───────────┬──────────┐
  │  NAMESPACE    │ CPU      │ MEMORY    │ PODS     │
  ├──────────────┼──────────┼───────────┼──────────┤
  │  dev          │ 2 cores  │ 4 Gi      │ 10       │
  │  staging      │ 4 cores  │ 8 Gi      │ 20       │
  │  prod         │ 20 cores │ 40 Gi     │ 50       │
  └──────────────┴──────────┴───────────┴──────────┘

CKAD exam tip: kubectl create quota is imperative! Use kubectl create quota my-quota --hard=cpu=2,memory=4Gi,pods=10 --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate the YAML, then edit and apply. Also: ResourceQuota requires ALL pods in the namespace to have resource requests/limits set — otherwise they're rejected. Combine with LimitRange to set defaults.

Deploy 🟡 Q62 of 200
What is a LimitRange and how does it work with ResourceQuota?
A) LimitRange is another name for ResourceQuota — they are identical resources
B) LimitRange sets DEFAULT, MIN, and MAX resource requests/limits for individual Pods/containers in a namespace. If a Pod doesn't specify resources, LimitRange provides defaults. If a Pod exceeds max, it's REJECTED. ResourceQuota limits TOTAL; LimitRange limits PER-POD. Together they provide complete resource governance
C) LimitRange works only on PersistentVolumes — it cannot set CPU or memory defaults
D) LimitRange is automatically created by Kubernetes — you cannot configure it
✅ Correct Answer: B

ResourceQuota = "this namespace can't use more than 10 CPU total." LimitRange = "each container must request between 100m and 2 CPU." Together they ensure fair resource distribution and prevent one Pod from hogging the namespace quota.

📝 LimitRange — Per-Pod/Container Resource Governance
LimitRange + ResourceQuota Together
  ═══════════════ LIMITRANGE YAML ═══════════════
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: LimitRange
  metadata:
    name: dev-limits
    namespace: easypj-dev
  spec:
    limits:
    - type: Container
      default:
        cpu: "500m"       ← If no limit specified, use 500m
        memory: "512Mi"
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: "200m"       ← If no request specified, use 200m
        memory: "256Mi"
      max:
        cpu: "2"          ← Single container CANNOT exceed 2 CPU
        memory: "2Gi"      ← Single container CANNOT exceed 2Gi
      min:
        cpu: "50m"        ← Must request at least 50m
        memory: "64Mi"     ← Must request at least 64Mi

  ══════════ HOW THEY WORK TOGETHER ══════════
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ResourceQuota: "10 CPU TOTAL for this namespace"   │
  │  LimitRange:    "Each pod: 50m-2 CPU, default 200m" │
  │                                                      │
  │  Pod A: 1 CPU    Pod B: 500m    Pod C: 200m         │
  │  Pod D: 800m     Pod E: 2 CPU   Pod F: 200m         │
  │                              ─────────────           │
  │  TOTAL: 4.7 CPU / 10  ← Quota OK                   │
  │                                                      │
  │  Pod G: 3 CPU  ← REJECTED by LimitRange (max: 2)   │
  │  Pod H: (empty) ← Gets default: 200m CPU, 256Mi     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ══════════ RESOURCEQUOTA vs LIMITRANGE ══════════
  ┌──────────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │  FEATURE      │ ResourceQuota       │ LimitRange       │
  ├──────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │  Scope        │ Namespace TOTAL     │ Per Pod/Container│
  │  Enforces     │ Sum of all requests │ Min/Max/Default  │
  │  Creates       │ kubectl create quota│ YAML only        │
  │  Blocks if    │ Total exceeds hard  │ Single exceeds   │
  │  Defaults     │ ❌ No               │ ✅ Yes           │
  │  Object counts│ ✅ pods, svc, pvc.. │ ❌ CPU/Mem only  │
  └──────────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: If a pod creation fails with "exceeded quota" but total usage is below quota, check if the pod is missing resource requests/limits. Without them, Kubernetes can't calculate quota usage. Use LimitRange defaults to solve this automatically.

Deploy 🟢 Q63 of 200
How do you create a namespace imperatively?
A) kubectl create ns easypj-dev — this creates the namespace immediately. For YAML: kubectl create ns easypj-dev --dry-run=client -o yaml > ns.yaml
B) Namespaces can only be created from YAML — there is no imperative command
C) kubectl new namespace easypj-dev — kubectl create ns does not exist
D) Namespaces are auto-created when you first deploy a resource that references them — no manual creation needed
✅ Correct Answer: A

kubectl create ns NAME (aliased to namespace, namespaces) is the fastest way. For the CKAD exam: create the namespace first, then deploy resources into it. Tip: kubectl get ns lists all namespaces.

📝 Namespace Management — Quick Reference
All Namespace Operations
  ═══════════════ CREATE ═══════════════
  # Imperative (fastest)
  kubectl create ns easypj-dev

  # Generate YAML (recommended for CKAD)
  kubectl create ns easypj-dev --dry-run=client -o yaml > ns.yaml
  kubectl apply -f ns.yaml

  ═══════════════ LIST & INSPECT ═══════════════
  kubectl get ns                          # All namespaces
  kubectl get ns easypj-dev -o yaml       # Full details
  kubectl describe ns easypj-dev          # Status, labels, annotations

  ═══════════════ DELETE ═══════════════
  kubectl delete ns easypj-dev
  ⚠️  WARNING: Deletes EVERYTHING in that namespace!
      → All Pods, Services, Deployments, ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs...
      → No undo! Namespace stays in "Terminating" until cleanup done.

  ═══════════════ LABEL & ANNOTATE ═══════════════
  kubectl label ns easypj-dev environment=development
  kubectl annotate ns easypj-dev owner=backend-team

  ══════════ NAMESPACE SHORTCUTS ══════════
  kubectl get pods -n easypj-dev    # Explicit namespace
  kubectl get pods -A               # All namespaces
  kubectl get pods --all-namespaces # Same as -A

CKAD exam tip: kubectl create ns is one of the simplest but most used commands. Create your namespace FIRST before doing anything else in a task. Namespaces cannot be nested — they are flat, top-level only.

Deploy 🟡 Q64 of 200
How do Pods in different namespaces communicate with each other?
A) Pods in different namespaces are completely isolated — no communication is possible between namespaces
B) Pods in different namespaces can only communicate through a NodePort or LoadBalancer Service — internal DNS does not work across namespaces
C) Pods use Service DNS with namespace: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. The shortened form <service>.<namespace> works for cross-namespace communication. Example: easypj-web pod in "default" namespace connects to easypj-api.easypj.svc.cluster.local to reach the API in the "easypj" namespace. NetworkPolicies can restrict this if needed
D) Cross-namespace communication requires a special ClusterRoleBinding — DNS does not work across namespaces
✅ Correct Answer: C

Kubernetes DNS is inherently cross-namespace. The full FQDN is <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. The short form <service>.<namespace> also works. Within the same namespace, you can use just <service>. This is how microservices in different namespaces discover each other.

📝 Cross-Namespace DNS Resolution
Service Discovery Across Namespaces
  ═══════════════ DNS NAME FORMAT ═══════════════
  <service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
       │              │          │      └── cluster domain (default)
       │              │          └── "svc" = Service (always)
       │              └── namespace where Service exists
       └── Service name

  ══════════ easypj/jobpost EXAMPLE ══════════
  ┌─ namespace: default ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  Pod: easypj-web                                    │
  │  Needs to call the API...                           │
  │                                                     │
  │  Connects to: easypj-api.easypj.svc.cluster.local  │
  │                  ─────────  ──────                  │
  │                  service    namespace               │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │
         │ DNS query
         ▼
  ┌─ namespace: easypj ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  Service: easypj-api (ClusterIP: 10.96.100.5)     │
  │  → Routes to: api-pod-1, api-pod-2, api-pod-3     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ══════════ RESOLUTION SHORTCUTS ══════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────┐
  │  DESTINATION                     │ FROM SAME NS       │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────┤
  │  Same namespace                  │ easypj-api         │
  │  Different namespace             │ easypj-api.easypj │
  │  Full FQDN (always works)        │ easypj-api.easypj │
  │                                  │ .svc.cluster.local│
  └──────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────┘

  ══════════ IMPORTANT NOTES ══════════
  • DNS is ALWAYS cross-namespace (unless NetworkPolicy blocks)
  • The "svc" subdomain is required — it's NOT the actual domain
  • Pod hostnames follow a different format (pod-ip.ns.pod.cluster.local)
  • Headless Services (clusterIP: None) return pod IPs directly
  • CoreDNS handles all cluster DNS resolution

CKAD exam tip: For cross-namespace communication in CKAD tasks, use the short form <svc>.<ns> — it's faster to type than the full FQDN. Remember: NetworkPolicies can BLOCK cross-namespace traffic even if DNS resolves correctly!
