2.4 Deployment Strategies — Canary, Blue/Green & A/BQ65-Q70

🟡→🔴 | LF Subtopic 1: Use Kubernetes primitives to implement common deployment strategies.

Deploy 🟡 Q65 of 200
In a Blue/Green deployment using two Deployments and a shared Service, how do you switch traffic from Blue to Green?
A) Delete the Blue Deployment — Kubernetes automatically sends traffic to the remaining Green pods
B) Change the Service selector from version: blue to version: green. Use: kubectl patch svc easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}'. Traffic switches INSTANTLY — no pod restarts, no image pulling. Rollback is just as fast: change the selector back to blue
C) Use kubectl switch-traffic easypj-api --from=blue --to=green — this is a built-in kubectl command for Blue/Green
D) You must delete and recreate the Service to switch traffic — Services cannot be updated imperatively
✅ Correct Answer: B

The Service selector is the "traffic switch." By patching it from version: blue to version: green, all traffic instantly moves to the Green pods. The Blue pods stay running (idle) for instant rollback. This is the core mechanism of Blue/Green on Kubernetes — no special tools needed, just standard Services and labels.

📝 Blue/Green Switch — One Command
Blue/Green Traffic Switch
  ═══════════════ BEFORE SWITCH ═══════════════
  Service selector: {app: easypj-api, version: blue}
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Traffic → Blue pods (v1.0) ✅  |  Green pods (v1.1)    │
  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐      ┌──────────┐           │
  │  │ blue-pod1│ │ blue-pod2│      │green-pod1│ (idle)    │
  │  │ (active) │ │ (active) │      │ (idle)   │           │
  │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘      └──────────┘           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ SWITCH (one command!) ═══════════════
  kubectl patch svc easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}'

  ═══════════════ AFTER SWITCH ═══════════════
  Service selector: {app: easypj-api, version: green}
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Blue pods (v1.0)         |  Traffic → Green pods (v1.1) │
  │  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐                │
  │  │ blue-pod1│ │ blue-pod2│ │green-pod1│ ✅              │
  │  │ (idle)   │ │ (idle)   │ │ (active) │                │
  │  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ ROLLBACK: Same command, swap back ═══════════
  kubectl patch svc easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"blue"}}}'
  → INSTANT rollback — Blue pods are still running!
Deploy 🔴 Q66 of 200
How do you implement a Canary deployment on CKAD using only standard Kubernetes resources?
A) Deploy two Deployments (stable and canary) with the SAME labels matching the Service selector but DIFFERENT replica counts. Traffic splits proportionally by pod count: 9 stable pods + 1 canary pod = 90/10 split. To promote: scale canary up, stable down. To rollback: scale canary to 0. No special controllers needed
B) Canary requires Istio, Linkerd, or some other service mesh — it's impossible with standard Kubernetes
C) Use the built-in canary strategy in Deployment spec: strategy.canary.percentage=10 — Kubernetes handles it automatically
D) Canary is deprecated — Blue/Green has replaced it as the recommended strategy
✅ Correct Answer: A

Proportional traffic splitting works because kube-proxy load-balances across ALL Service endpoints equally. With 9 stable pods and 1 canary pod, each pod gets ~10% of connections. This is the simplest canary implementation — no Ingress annotations, no service mesh, just math. More advanced tooling (Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Istio) provides precise percentage control, but the CKAD tests basic Kubernetes primitives.

📝 Pod-Count Canary — Pure Kubernetes, No Service Mesh
Canary Deployment via Proportional Pod Count
  ═══════════════ SETUP ═══════════════
  # Both Deployments share the SAME labels (match Service selector)
  ---
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: easypj-api-stable
  spec:
    replicas: 9
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        app: easypj-api        ← SAME label as canary!
    template:
      metadata:
        labels:
          app: easypj-api      ← SAME!
          version: stable      ← DIFFERENT (for identification)
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: api
          image: easypj/api:v1.0
  ---
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: easypj-api-canary
  spec:
    replicas: 1
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        app: easypj-api        ← SAME label!
    template:
      metadata:
        labels:
          app: easypj-api      ← SAME!
          version: canary      ← DIFFERENT
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: api
          image: easypj/api:v2.0

  ═══════════ HOW TRAFFIC SPLITS ═══════════
  Service selector: {app: easypj-api}
        │
        ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  kube-proxy iptables round-robin:        │
  │                                           │
  │  Endpoints (10 total):                    │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ S1 S2 S3 S4 S5 S6 S7 S8 S9 │ C1 │   │ │
  │  │ ←── 9 stable pods ──────→ │canary│   │ │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                           │
  │  Traffic split: ~90% stable / ~10% canary │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ PROMOTE CANARY ═══════════
  kubectl scale deploy easypj-api-stable --replicas=0
  kubectl scale deploy easypj-api-canary --replicas=10
  → Now 100% traffic to canary (new version)

  ═══════════ ROLLBACK ═══════════
  kubectl scale deploy easypj-api-canary --replicas=0
  kubectl scale deploy easypj-api-stable --replicas=10
  → Instant rollback!

CKAD exam tip: This is the simplest canary pattern for CKAD — two Deployments with same labels, different replica counts. No extra tools needed. But it's approximate (not exact 10%), because kube-proxy does simple round-robin, not weighted routing. For precise percentages, use Ingress annotations.

Deploy 🔴 Q67 of 200
What is A/B testing and how does it differ from Canary deployment?
A) A/B testing and Canary are identical — the terms are interchangeable
B) A/B testing is about infrastructure (testing Kubernetes versions A and B), while Canary is about application deployments
C) Canary routes a PERCENTAGE of ALL users to the new version indiscriminately (risk of exposing bugs to random users). A/B testing routes SPECIFIC users to the new version based on criteria (headers, cookies, geography, user ID) — useful for testing features with a controlled audience. A/B requires Ingress-level routing (headers/cookies), while basic Canary works with just pod counts
D) A/B testing is illegal under GDPR and cannot be used in production
✅ Correct Answer: C

A/B testing routes users intelligently: "beta testers see v2, everyone else sees v1." This requires Ingress-level routing based on headers or cookies. Canary is simpler: "10% of traffic goes to v2 regardless of who." For CKAD, understand the distinction but focus on Canary implementation.

📝 A/B Testing vs Canary — Key Differences
Deployment Strategies Comparison
  ═══════════════ CANARY ═══════════════
  "10% of ALL traffic → new version"
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Users → [Ingress] → Service             │
  │                        ├─ 90% → v1.0     │
  │                        └─ 10% → v2.0     │
  │                                           │
  │  Traffic split: RANDOM, any user may     │
  │  hit v2.0. If v2 has a bug, 10% of      │
  │  ALL users see errors.                    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ A/B TESTING ═══════════════
  "Beta users → v2.0, everyone else → v1.0"
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Users → [Ingress]                       │
  │    │                                      │
  │    ├─ Header: X-User-Group: beta        │
  │    │  → Route to v2.0 (A/B group)        │
  │    │                                      │
  │    └─ Everyone else                      │
  │       → Route to v1.0 (stable)           │
  │                                           │
  │  Traffic split: DETERMINISTIC. Only      │
  │  beta users see v2. Others safe.          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ══════════ COMPARISON TABLE ══════════
  ┌──────────────┬─────────────────┬────────────────────┐
  │  FEATURE      │ CANARY          │ A/B TESTING        │
  ├──────────────┼─────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │  Routing      │ Random %         │ Header/Cookie based│
  │  Who sees v2  │ Anyone (by %)    │ Specific users     │
  │  Requires     │ Pod count OR     │ Ingress annotations│
  │              │ Ingress          │ (header/cookie)    │
  │  Risk control │ Statistical      │ Targeted           │
  │  Rollback     │ Scale to 0       │ Change header rule │
  │  CKAD scope   │ ✅ Tested        │ ⚠️ Know concept    │
  └──────────────┴─────────────────┴────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: On the CKAD exam, you're more likely to be asked to implement a basic Canary (pod-count or Ingress-based) than A/B testing. A/B testing typically requires the nginx ingress controller with canary-by-header or canary-by-cookie annotations.

Deploy 🔴 Q68 of 200
How does traffic splitting with Ingress work for canary deployments?
A) Using Ingress annotations specific to your controller: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true" with canary-weight: "10" routes 10% of requests to the canary Service. This provides PRECISE percentage control compared to pod-count-based splitting. Different controllers (nginx, traefik, AWS ALB) have different annotation formats but the concept is the same
B) Ingress has a built-in spec.canary.percent field — no annotations needed
C) Traffic splitting only works with LoadBalancer type Services — Ingress cannot split traffic
D) Ingress traffic splitting requires at least 3 replicas of the Ingress controller for mathematical accuracy
✅ Correct Answer: A

Ingress-level canary provides precise percentage control using nginx-ingress annotations: nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true", nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "10", and nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-header: "X-Canary" for header-based routing. This is more accurate than pod-count splitting but requires an Ingress controller that supports canary annotations.

📝 Ingress Canary Annotations — Precise Traffic Control
nginx-ingress Canary Deployment Pattern
  ═══════════════ MAIN INGRESS (stable) ═══════════════
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Ingress
  metadata:
    name: easypj-api
  spec:
    rules:
    - host: api.easypj.com
      http:
        paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: Prefix
          backend:
            service:
              name: easypj-api-stable
              port:
                number: 80

  ═══════════════ CANARY INGRESS ═══════════════
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Ingress
  metadata:
    name: easypj-api-canary
    annotations:
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
      nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "10"
  spec:
    rules:
    - host: api.easypj.com
      http:
        paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: Prefix
          backend:
            service:
              name: easypj-api-canary
              port:
                number: 80

  ═══════════ HOW IT WORKS ═══════════
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Request → api.easypj.com                     │
  │         │                                      │
  │         ▼                                      │
  │  nginx-ingress checks canary annotations:     │
  │  canary-weight: "10"                           │
  │         │                                      │
  │         ├─ 90% → easypj-api-stable (v1.0)     │
  │         └─ 10% → easypj-api-canary (v2.0)     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ══════════ CANARY ANNOTATION REFERENCE ══════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
  │  ANNOTATION                       │ EFFECT                      │
  ├──────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
  │  canary: "true"                   │ Enable canary mode          │
  │  canary-weight: "0-100"           │ % traffic to canary         │
  │  canary-by-header: "X-Region"     │ Route by header VALUE       │
  │  canary-by-header-value: "us-east"│ Match specific header value │
  │  canary-by-cookie: "beta_flag"    │ Route by cookie presence    │
  └──────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: For Ingress canary, you need TWO Ingress resources: one for stable, one for canary. The canary Ingress MUST have the same host and path as the main Ingress. Different Ingress controllers (Traefik, Istio, AWS ALB) use different annotation formats — CKAD focuses on nginx-ingress.

Deploy 🟡 Q69 of 200
How do you choose between Recreate, RollingUpdate, Blue/Green, and Canary for easypj/jobpost?
A) Always use RollingUpdate — it's the only production-grade strategy
B) Always use Canary — it's the safest for every scenario
C) Pick randomly — the strategy doesn't matter as long as pods eventually run the new version
D) Decision matrix: Recreate for breaking schema changes (rare). RollingUpdate for routine updates (default, zero-downtime). Blue/Green for risky changes needing instant rollback (double resources during deploy). Canary for the most cautious rollouts (progressive % shift, monitors errors). For easypj/jobpost: RollingUpdate for API/web daily deploys, Blue/Green for major version bumps, Canary for risky performance changes
✅ Correct Answer: D

Each strategy has tradeoffs: Recreate = simple but downtime. RollingUpdate = zero-downtime but slower rollback. Blue/Green = instant rollback but double resources. Canary = safest but slowest to full deploy. The CKAD exam tests your ability to choose the RIGHT strategy for a given scenario.

📝 Deployment Strategy Decision Matrix
Strategy Selection Guide
  ┌──────────────┬───────┬──────────┬──────────┬────────────┐
  │  STRATEGY     │ DOWNTIME│ ROLLBACK │ RESOURCES│ BEST FOR    │
  ├──────────────┼───────┼──────────┼──────────┼────────────┤
  │  Recreate     │ YES    │ Slow      │ 1x       │ DB schema  │
  │  RollingUpdate│ NO     │ Medium    │ 1x+surge │ Daily deploys│
  │  Blue/Green   │ NO     │ INSTANT   │ 2x       │ Major bumps │
  │  Canary       │ NO     │ INSTANT   │ 1x+small │ Risky changes│
  └──────────────┴───────┴──────────┴──────────┴────────────┘
Deploy 🟢 Q70 of 200
What does kubectl run do, and what resource does it create by default?
A) kubectl run always creates a Deployment — it's the imperative way to deploy applications
B) kubectl run creates a standalone POD by default (not managed by a Deployment or ReplicaSet). For a Deployment: add --restart=Always. For a Job: --restart=OnFailure. For a CronJob: --restart=Never --schedule="*/5 * * * *". For interactive debugging: kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- sh
C) kubectl run is deprecated and removed — you must use kubectl create deploy instead
D) kubectl run creates a StatefulSet by default for stateful applications
✅ Correct Answer: B

kubectl run is the Swiss Army knife of quick Pod creation. By default it creates a standalone Pod. The --restart flag transforms it: --restart=Always → Deployment, --restart=OnFailure → Job, --restart=Never → Pod. The CKAD exam favors kubectl create deploy for clarity, but know kubectl run for quick debugging pods.

📝 kubectl run — The Shapeshifter Command
How --restart Transforms kubectl run
  ═══════════════ kubectl run RESOURCE DECISION TREE ═══════════════
  kubectl run NAME --image=IMG --restart=???
        │
        ├── --restart=Never (or omitted)
        │   └── Creates: STANDALONE POD
        │       Use: Quick test, one-off debug container
        │       Example: kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- sh
        │
        ├── --restart=Always
        │   └── Creates: DEPLOYMENT
        │       Use: Long-running web/api workers
        │       Example: kubectl run web --image=nginx --port=80
        │       ⚠️  Creates Deployment with 1 replica
        │
        └── --restart=OnFailure
            └── Creates: JOB
                Use: Batch processing, one-time tasks
                Example: kubectl run migrate --image=easypj/migrate
                Add --schedule for CronJob

  ═══════════ COMMON PATTERNS ═══════════
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  # Debug pod (auto-deleted on exit)                       │
  │  kubectl run debug --image=busybox --rm -it -- sh         │
  │                                                           │
  │  # Quick nginx test Deployment                            │
  │  kubectl run nginx-test --image=nginx --port=80           │
  │                                                           │
  │  # Generate Deployment YAML without creating              │
  │  kubectl run web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml   │
  │  > deploy.yaml                                            │
  │                                                           │
  │  # Run a Pod that sleeps (for network testing)            │
  │  kubectl run sleeper --image=busybox -- sleep 3600        │
  │                                                           │
  │  # One-off database migration Job                         │
  │  kubectl run db-migrate --image=easypj/migrate:v2         │
  │    --restart=OnFailure                                    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ══════════ kubectl run vs kubectl create deploy ══════════
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │  kubectl run      │ kubectl create   │ RECOMMENDATION   │
  │                   │ deploy           │                   │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │  Creates Pod by   │ Always creates   │ Use "create       │
  │  default (confus- │ Deployment       │ deploy" for       │
  │  ing behavior)    │ (explicit)       │ clarity on CKAD   │
  │  --restart flips  │ No surprise       │                   │
  │  resource type    │ behavior         │ Use "run" for     │
  │  Older syntax,    │ Modern syntax,    │ quick debug pods  │
  │  still common     │ CKAD preferred    │                   │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: For the exam, use kubectl create deploy for Deployments (it's unambiguous) and kubectl run ONLY for temporary debug pods with --rm -it. Know that kubectl run without --restart creates a Pod, not a Deployment — this is a common CKAD trick question!

2.5 Helm & KustomizeQ71-Q80

🟡→🔴 | LF Subtopic 3 & 4: Helm package manager and Kustomize.

Deploy 🟡 Q71 of 200
What is Helm and how does it simplify Kubernetes application deployment?
A) Helm is a Kubernetes container runtime that replaces containerd for faster image pulling
B) Helm is a monitoring tool that shows the health of your Deployments in a dashboard
C) Helm is the "package manager for Kubernetes" — it bundles Kubernetes YAML manifests into reusable, versioned, configurable packages called Charts. A Chart includes templates (parameterized YAML), default values, and metadata. Helm installs, upgrades, rolls back, and uninstalls releases (instances of Charts). Think: "apt-get for Kubernetes"
D) Helm is a Kubernetes security scanner that checks images for vulnerabilities before deployment
✅ Correct Answer: C

Helm v3 (no Tiller, client-only) uses Chart.yaml for metadata, values.yaml for defaults, and templates/ for parameterized YAML. Install: helm install myrelease ./chart. Key commands: helm install/upgrade/rollback/uninstall/list. Values priority: user --set > parent --values > child values.yaml > Chart.yaml defaults.

📝 Helm — The Kubernetes Package Manager
Helm Architecture (v3, Tiller-less)
  ═══════════════ HELM CONCEPTS ═══════════════
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CHART = Package (like .deb or .rpm)                    │
  │  ├── Chart.yaml    (metadata: name, version, appVersion)│
  │  ├── values.yaml   (default configuration)              │
  │  ├── templates/    (Go-templated K8s YAML)              │
  │  │   ├── deployment.yaml  ({{ .Values.replicas }})     │
  │  │   ├── service.yaml                                  │
  │  │   └── _helpers.tpl   (reusable template functions)  │
  │  └── charts/       (sub-chart dependencies)             │
  │                                                         │
  │  RELEASE = Installed instance of a Chart                │
  │  ├── Named: "easypj-prod", "easypj-dev"                │
  │  ├── Versioned: revision 1, 2, 3...                    │
  │  └── Stored in: Kubernetes Secret (release info)       │
  │                                                         │
  │  REPOSITORY = Chart storage (like Docker registry)      │
  │  ├── bitnami, stable, ingress-nginx                     │
  │  └── helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ HELM vs KUBECTL APPLY ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Without Helm:                                        │
  │  kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml -f svc.yaml -f cm.yaml │
  │  → 3 separate files, no versioning, no rollback      │
  │                                                       │
  │  With Helm:                                           │
  │  helm install easypj ./chart                          │
  │  → One command, versioned, rollback-able             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ══════════ easypj/jobpost HELM STRUCTURE ══════════
  easypj-chart/
  ├── Chart.yaml          # name: easypj, version: 1.0.0
  ├── values.yaml         # replicas: 3, image: easypj/api:v1
  ├── templates/
  │   ├── deployment.yaml
  │   ├── service.yaml
  │   ├── configmap.yaml
  │   └── ingress.yaml
  └── charts/
      ├── postgresql/     # Bitnami PostgreSQL sub-chart
      └── redis/          # Bitnami Redis sub-chart

CKAD exam tip: Helm v3 removed Tiller (server-side component). All Helm operations are now client-side using your kubeconfig — much simpler and more secure. The CKAD exam may ask you to install a chart from a repository or upgrade an existing release.

Deploy 🟡 Q72 of 200
How do you install, upgrade, and rollback a Helm release?
A) Helm releases are immutable — once installed, you must delete and reinstall to make any changes
B) Install: helm install easypj ./easypj-chart --set image.tag=v2.1. Upgrade: helm upgrade easypj ./easypj-chart --set replicas=5. Rollback: helm rollback easypj 1 (to revision 1). List: helm list. History: helm history easypj. Uninstall: helm uninstall easypj
C) Helm commands work only with remote chart repositories — local charts must be pushed to a registry first
D) Helm upgrade creates a completely new release — it does not preserve any configuration from the previous version
✅ Correct Answer: B

Helm tracks releases by name and revision number. helm history easypj shows all revisions. helm rollback easypj 2 reverts to revision 2. Each install/upgrade/rollback creates a new revision. Helm stores release info in Kubernetes Secrets (default) or ConfigMaps in the release namespace.

📝 Helm Release Lifecycle — Full Command Reference
Helm Release Lifecycle — Install → Upgrade → Rollback
  ═══════════════ INSTALL ═══════════════
  helm install easypj ./easypj-chart \
    --set image.tag=v2.1 \
    --set replicas=3 \
    --namespace easypj-prod \
    --create-namespace
  → NAME: easypj
  → LAST DEPLOYED: Mon Jun 10 14:30:00 2026
  → NAMESPACE: easypj-prod
  → STATUS: deployed
  → REVISION: 1

  ═══════════════ UPGRADE ═══════════════
  # Upgrade with new values
  helm upgrade easypj ./easypj-chart \
    --set replicas=5 \
    --set resources.limits.cpu=2
  → Release "easypj" has been upgraded. Happy Helming!
  → REVISION: 2

  # Upgrade with values file
  helm upgrade easypj ./easypj-chart -f prod-values.yaml
  → REVISION: 3

  ═══════════════ HISTORY & ROLLBACK ═══════════════
  helm history easypj
  ┌──────────┬────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────┐
  │ REVISION │ UPDATED     │ STATUS               │ CHART    │
  ├──────────┼────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ 1        │ Mon Jun 10  │ superseded            │ 1.0.0    │
  │ 2        │ Mon Jun 10  │ superseded            │ 1.0.0    │
  │ 3        │ Tue Jun 11  │ deployed              │ 1.0.0    │
  └──────────┴────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────┘

  # Rollback to revision 2
  helm rollback easypj 2
  → Rollback was a success! Happy Helming!
  → REVISION: 4  (rollback creates a NEW revision!)

  ═══════════════ INSPECT ═══════════════
  helm list -A                    # All releases across namespaces
  helm status easypj              # Current state
  helm get values easypj          # User-supplied values
  helm get values easypj --all    # All values (including defaults)
  helm get manifest easypj        # Generated K8s YAML

  ═══════════════ UNINSTALL ═══════════════
  helm uninstall easypj
  → Removes ALL resources created by this release
  → History is also deleted (unlike kubectl delete)

CKAD exam tip: helm rollback creates a NEW revision (doesn't delete the bad one). This means you can rollback a rollback! Also: helm upgrade --install creates the release if it doesn't exist and upgrades if it does — perfect for CI/CD pipelines.

Deploy 🟡 Q73 of 200
How does Helm value precedence work when multiple value sources conflict?
A) Highest to lowest priority: (1) --set flags (CLI overrides), (2) parent chart --values files, (3) child chart values.yaml, (4) Chart.yaml defaults. Multiple --values files are merged in order (later files override earlier ones). --set is the strongest and overrides everything else
B) All value sources have equal priority — Helm randomly selects which value to use
C) Chart.yaml defaults have the highest priority — they cannot be overridden by any other source
D) The LAST file specified wins, regardless of whether it's --set, --values, or Chart.yaml
✅ Correct Answer: A

Value precedence: --set key=val > --values file2.yaml > --values file1.yaml > child values.yaml > parent values.yaml > Chart.yaml. Use helm get values easypj to see all user-supplied values and helm get values easypj --all for all values including defaults.

📝 Helm Value Precedence — Ladder of Override
Which Value Wins? — Precedence Ladder (Highest First)
  ═══════════════ VALUE PRECEDENCE (STRONGEST → WEAKEST) ═══════════════

  🥇 --set replicas=5              ← CLI overrides (STRONGEST)
       │
  🥈 --values prod-overrides.yaml  ← 2nd values file (later overrides earlier)
       │
  🥉 --values base-config.yaml     ← 1st values file
       │
  4️⃣  Child chart values.yaml      ← Sub-chart defaults
       │
  5️⃣  Parent chart values.yaml     ← Main chart defaults
       │
  6️⃣  Chart.yaml defaults           ← Hardcoded chart metadata (WEAKEST)


  ═══════════ REAL EXAMPLE ═══════════
  Chart.yaml:        replicas: 1       ← Default
  values.yaml:       replicas: 3       ← Override default
  --values prod.yaml:  replicas: 5     ← Override values.yaml
  --set replicas=10                    ← OVERRIDES EVERYTHING!

  → Final value: replicas=10 ✓

  ═══════════ DEBUGGING ═══════════
  # What did the user actually pass?
  helm get values easypj
  → USER-SUPPLIED VALUES:
      replicas: 10
      image:
        tag: v2.1

  # What are ALL values (including defaults)?
  helm get values easypj --all
  → COMPUTED VALUES:
      replicas: 10
      image:
        repository: easypj/api
        tag: v2.1
        pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
      service:
        type: ClusterIP
        port: 80

  # Dry-run to see rendered templates without deploying
  helm install easypj ./chart --dry-run --debug
  → Shows ALL rendered YAML with final values

CKAD exam tip: When debugging Helm values, always use --dry-run --debug first. It renders the templates with your values without applying to the cluster. This catches template errors and shows you EXACTLY what will be deployed.

Deploy 🔴 Q74 of 200
What is the standard Helm chart directory structure?
A) A Helm chart is a single YAML file containing all templates, values, and metadata combined
B) Helm charts follow the same structure as Kubernetes manifests — there is no special directory layout
C) A Helm chart requires a Dockerfile to build the chart image before it can be deployed
D) Standard structure: Chart.yaml (metadata: name, version, appVersion), values.yaml (default configuration), templates/ (Go-templated YAML: Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, etc.), charts/ (sub-charts/dependencies), .helmignore (files to exclude). Optionally: templates/NOTES.txt (post-install instructions), templates/_helpers.tpl (reusable template functions), templates/tests/ (helm test files)
✅ Correct Answer: D

Create with helm create mychart for scaffolding. Key files: Chart.yaml (required), values.yaml (defaults), templates/ (required). Templates use Go template syntax with Sprig functions. Sub-charts go in charts/. Dependencies can also be managed in Chart.yaml with helm dependency update.

📝 Helm Chart Directory — Anatomy & Best Practices
Complete Helm Chart Structure
  ═══════════════ STANDARD CHART LAYOUT ═══════════════
  easypj-chart/
  │
  ├── Chart.yaml              ← REQUIRED: Chart metadata
  │   apiVersion: v2           (Helm v3 uses apiVersion: v2)
  │   name: easypj
  │   description: Job posting application
  │   type: application        (application | library)
  │   version: 1.2.3           (SemVer — Chart version)
  │   appVersion: "2.1.0"      (Version of the app being deployed)
  │   dependencies:            (Sub-charts defined here)
  │     - name: postgresql
  │       version: 12.x.x
  │       repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
  │
  ├── values.yaml              ← DEFAULT configuration
  │   replicas: 3
  │   image:
  │     repository: easypj/api
  │     tag: v2.1
  │   service:
  │     type: ClusterIP
  │     port: 80
  │
  ├── templates/               ← Go-templated K8s manifests
  │   ├── deployment.yaml      {{ .Values.replicas }}
  │   ├── service.yaml         {{ .Values.service.type }}
  │   ├── configmap.yaml
  │   ├── ingress.yaml
  │   ├── _helpers.tpl         ← Reusable template functions
  │   │   {{- define "easypj.fullname" -}}
  │   │   {{- .Release.Name }}-{{ .Chart.Name }}
  │   │   {{- end -}}
  │   ├── NOTES.txt            ← Post-install help text
  │   │   "Your app is running at..."
  │   └── tests/               ← helm test resources
  │       └── test-connection.yaml
  │
  ├── charts/                  ← Sub-chart dependencies
  │   ├── postgresql-12.1.0.tgz
  │   └── redis-17.0.0.tgz
  │
  ├── Chart.lock               ← Dependency lock file
  ├── .helmignore              ← Files to exclude from chart
  └── README.md                ← Chart documentation

  ══════════ GO TEMPLATE BASICS ══════════
  {{ .Values.replicas }}         → Simple value
  {{ .Release.Name }}            → Release name
  {{ .Chart.Name }}              → Chart name
  {{ include "easypj.fullname" . }} → Named template
  {{ .Values.image.tag | default "latest" }} → With default
  {{- if .Values.persistence.enabled }}...{{- end }} → Conditionals
  {{- range .Values.env }}...{{- end }} → Loops

CKAD exam tip: Use helm create mychart to scaffold a complete chart with best practices. It generates a working nginx chart you can modify. For the CKAD exam, you're more likely to USE existing charts than CREATE them from scratch.

Deploy 🟡 Q75 of 200
What is Kustomize and how does it differ from Helm?
A) Kustomize is Google's internal deployment tool — it is not available in standard Kubernetes
B) Kustomize is a TEMPLATE-FREE configuration management tool built into kubectl (kubectl apply -k). Unlike Helm (which uses Go templates with placeholder values), Kustomize works with PATCHES and OVERLAYS on top of BASE manifests. You create a base/ with original YAML, then overlays/ (dev, staging, prod) that patch specific fields. No templating language to learn — just YAML patches on YAML
C) Kustomize replaces kubectl — you use kustomize commands instead of kubectl for all cluster operations
D) Kustomize requires a separate binary installation — it cannot be used with kubectl directly
✅ Correct Answer: B

Kustomize is built into kubectl (since 1.14). Structure: base/kustomization.yaml + resources, overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml with patches. Use: kubectl apply -k ./overlays/prod/. Kustomize = patch-based (YAML patching YAML), Helm = template-based (Go templates with variables). Kustomize is simpler for multi-environment configs; Helm is better for distributing reusable packages.

📝 Kustomize — Template-Free Configuration Management
Kustomize Architecture — Base + Overlays
  ═══════════════ KUSTOMIZE DIRECTORY STRUCTURE ═══════════════
  kustomize/
  ├── base/
  │   ├── kustomization.yaml    ← Declares resources
  │   ├── deployment.yaml       ← Standard deployment
  │   ├── service.yaml          ← Standard service
  │   └── configmap.yaml        ← Standard configmap
  │
  └── overlays/
      ├── dev/
      │   ├── kustomization.yaml ← Patches + config
      │   ├── replica-patch.yaml ← Override replicas
      │   └── env-patch.yaml     ← Override env vars
      │
      ├── staging/
      │   ├── kustomization.yaml
      │   └── resource-patch.yaml
      │
      └── prod/
          ├── kustomization.yaml
          ├── replica-patch.yaml
          └── ingress-patch.yaml

  ═══════════ BASE kustomization.yaml ═══════════
  apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
  kind: Kustomization
  resources:
    - deployment.yaml
    - service.yaml
    - configmap.yaml

  ═══════════ DEV OVERLAY kustomization.yaml ═══════════
  apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
  kind: Kustomization
  resources:
    - ../../base           ← Point to base
  namePrefix: dev-          ← Add prefix to all names
  commonLabels:
    environment: dev       ← Add labels to all resources
  patchesStrategicMerge:
    - replica-patch.yaml   ← Patch the deployment
  images:
    - name: easypj/api
      newTag: dev-latest   ← Override image tag
  replicas:
    - name: easypj-api
      count: 1             ← Override replica count

  ═══════════ BUILD & APPLY ═══════════
  # Preview rendered YAML
  kubectl kustomize ./overlays/dev/

  # Apply directly
  kubectl apply -k ./overlays/dev/
  # -k = --kustomize (built into kubectl!)

CKAD exam tip: kubectl apply -k ./dir/ is the standard Kustomize command. The -k flag tells kubectl to process the kustomization.yaml. Kustomize is built into kubectl — no separate binary needed on the exam!

Deploy 🔴 Q76 of 200
How do Kustomize overlays work with patchesStrategicMerge and patchesJson6902?
A) patchesStrategicMerge: K8s-aware merge that knows about list semantics (e.g., merges containers by name, not position). patchesJson6902: RFC 6902 JSON Patch with explicit operations (add, remove, replace). Patches are applied in order specified in kustomization.yaml. Also: images: to override image tags, configMapGenerator: to create ConfigMaps from files, secretGenerator: for Secrets
B) Kustomize patches replace entire base files — you cannot modify individual fields
C) patchesStrategicMerge and patchesJson6902 are identical — they are two names for the same feature
D) Kustomize overlays require a special "Kustomize Controller" running in the cluster — they don't work client-side
✅ Correct Answer: A

Strategic merge understands K8s API semantics (containers merged by name). JSON patch is more explicit (operations list). Also powerful: commonLabels (add labels to all resources), namePrefix/nameSuffix, images (override image tags), configMapGenerator (auto-hash for rolling updates). For easypj/jobpost: base/ with standard config, overlays/prod/ with higher replicas and resource limits.

📝 Kustomize Patches & Transformers — Complete Reference
Patch Types & Built-in Transformers
  ═══════════ PATCH TYPES ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PATCH TYPE           │ BEHAVIOR                             │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  patchesStrategicMerge│ K8s-aware: merges containers by      │
  │                       │ NAME, not by array position.         │
  │                       │ Best for: Deployment/Service patches │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  patchesJson6902      │ RFC 6902 JSON Patch: explicit        │
  │                       │ operations (add, remove, replace,    │
  │                       │ copy, move, test).                   │
  │                       │ Best for: surgical field changes     │
  └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ STRATEGIC MERGE EXAMPLE ═══════════
  # patch.yaml (increase replicas + add env)
  apiVersion: apps/v1
  kind: Deployment
  metadata:
    name: easypj-api       ← Must match target name!
  spec:
    replicas: 5            ← Override replicas
    template:
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: django     ← Matched by NAME, not position!
          env:
          - name: DEBUG
            value: "false"

  ═══════════ JSON 6902 EXAMPLE ═══════════
  # patch.yaml (surgical operations)
  - op: replace
    path: /spec/replicas
    value: 5
  - op: add
    path: /spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources
    value:
      limits:
        cpu: "2"
        memory: "2Gi"

  ═══════════ BUILT-IN TRANSFORMERS ═══════════
  ┌─────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TRANSFORMER         │ WHAT IT DOES                      │
  ├─────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
  │  namePrefix          │ Add prefix to all resource names │
  │  nameSuffix          │ Add suffix to all resource names │
  │  commonLabels        │ Add labels to ALL resources      │
  │  commonAnnotations   │ Add annotations to ALL resources │
  │  images              │ Override image names/tags        │
  │  replicas            │ Override Deployment replicas     │
  │  configMapGenerator  │ Generate ConfigMap from files    │
  │  secretGenerator     │ Generate Secret from files/env   │
  └─────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ CONFIGMAPGENERATOR (auto-hash!) ═══════════
  configMapGenerator:
  - name: app-config
    files:
      - config.properties
    literals:
      - LOG_LEVEL=info
  → Creates ConfigMap with content hash in name:
    "app-config-7k8m2f" — Rolling update on change!

CKAD exam tip: configMapGenerator and secretGenerator append a content hash to the resource name. When the content changes, the name changes, which triggers a rolling update of Deployments that reference it. This is one of Kustomize's most powerful features!

Deploy 🔴 Q77 of 200
When should you choose Helm vs Kustomize for easypj/jobpost?
A) Always use Helm — Kustomize is deprecated and will be removed from kubectl
B) Always use Kustomize — Helm is too complex and requires a separate server component
C) Helm: when you need to distribute a reusable, versioned package (e.g., easypj/jobpost as a Helm chart shared across teams). Rich dependency management (PostgreSQL, Redis sub-charts). Kustomize: when you need to manage environment-specific variations (dev/staging/prod) of the SAME application. Built into kubectl — no extra tooling. Many teams use BOTH: Helm charts + Kustomize overlay for environment customization
D) Helm and Kustomize cannot be used together — you must choose one and stick with it
✅ Correct Answer: C

Hybrid approach: Use Helm for packaging (easypj chart with PostgreSQL + Redis dependencies), Kustomize for environment patches (dev: 1 replica, small DB; prod: 5 replicas, large DB). Command: helm template easypj ./chart | kubectl apply -f - or use helm install with --post-renderer for Kustomize integration. For CKAD exam: know both; you may be asked to use either.

📝 Helm vs Kustomize — Complete Comparison
Helm vs Kustomize — When to Use What
  ══════════ COMPARISON TABLE ══════════
  ┌────────────────┬─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┐
  │  FEATURE        │ HELM                │ KUSTOMIZE           │
  ├────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
  │  Approach       │ Template (Go tmpl)  │ Patch (overlay)     │
  │  Learning curve │ Steeper (Go tmpl)   │ Gentler (just YAML) │
  │  Reusability    │ ✅ Package + share  │ ⚠️  Workspace-only  │
  │  Dependencies   │ ✅ Sub-charts       │ ❌ No (manual)      │
  │  Versioning     │ ✅ Release history  │ ❌ No (git tracks)  │
  │  Rollback       │ ✅ helm rollback    │ ❌ git revert       │
  │  Templating     │ ✅ Go + Sprig       │ ❌ Pure YAML        │
  │  Built into     │ ❌ Separate binary  │ ✅ In kubectl       │
  │  Config mgmt    │ ⚠️  values.yaml     │ ✅ Overlays native  │
  │  Secret mgmt    │ ⚠️  Plain values    │ ✅ Encrypted (SOPS) │
  └────────────────┴─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┘

  ══════════ USE HELM WHEN ══════════
  ✅ Distributing reusable charts (Helm Hub, OCI registry)
  ✅ Complex deployments with many dependencies (DB, cache, queue)
  ✅ Need versioned releases with rollback capability
  ✅ Multi-tenant: same chart, different values per tenant
  ✅ CI/CD pipelines needing --set overrides

  ══════════ USE KUSTOMIZE WHEN ══════════
  ✅ Managing environment variations (dev/staging/prod)
  ✅ Want pure YAML (no template language to learn)
  ✅ Already using kubectl (no extra tooling)
  ✅ GitOps with ArgoCD (native Kustomize support)
  ✅ Simple label/annotation/replica overrides

  ══════════ HYBRID: HELM + KUSTOMIZE ══════════
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. Helm chart for packaging (with sub-charts):         │
  │     helm template easypj ./chart > base.yaml            │
  │                                                         │
  │  2. Kustomize for environment overlays:                 │
  │     kubectl kustomize ./overlays/prod/                  │
  │                                                         │
  │  3. Or use Helm --post-renderer:                        │
  │     helm install easypj ./chart                         │
  │       --post-renderer ./kustomize/render.sh             │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ══════════ easypj/jobpost RECOMMENDATION ══════════
  ├── Packaging: Helm chart (easypj + postgresql + redis)
  ├── Environments: Kustomize overlays (dev/staging/prod)
  └── GitOps: ArgoCD deploys Helm chart with Kustomize post-renderer

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam may ask you to use EITHER Helm or Kustomize. Know both but don't overthink it. For simple multi-environment configs, Kustomize is usually faster. For deploying a complex stack (like WordPress with MySQL), Helm is the clear winner.

Deploy 🟢 Q78 of 200
What command generates a valid Deployment YAML from scratch using imperative syntax?
A) kubectl generate deploy easypj-web --image=easypj/web:v2
B) kubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj/web:v2 --replicas=3 --port=8000 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml. This generates a complete, valid YAML with correct selectors, labels, and structure. Edit the output to add probes, resources, env vars, and volumes before applying
C) kubectl yaml deploy --name=easypj-web --image=easypj/web:v2
D) You cannot generate YAML imperatively — you must write it manually from scratch
✅ Correct Answer: B

The --dry-run=client -o yaml pattern is the #1 CKAD productivity hack. It generates YAML without contacting the API server. For server-side validation without applying: --dry-run=server. Always generate YAML first, edit it, then apply.

📝 CKAD Speed Hack — Generate YAML Imperatively
The CKAD Productivity Pattern
  ═══════════════ THE GOLDEN PATTERN ═══════════════
  kubectl create <RESOURCE> <NAME> [flags] \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml > resource.yaml
  #   ───────────── ──────────────────────
  #   Generate       Pipe to file
  #   locally only   for editing

  ═══════════════ ALL GENERATE COMMANDS ═══════════════
  # Deployment
  kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx --replicas=3 \
    --port=80 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml

  # Service (from Deployment)
  kubectl expose deploy web --port=80 --target-port=8080 \
    --type=ClusterIP --dry-run=client -o yaml > svc.yaml

  # Namespace
  kubectl create ns my-ns --dry-run=client -o yaml > ns.yaml

  # ConfigMap (from literal)
  kubectl create cm app-config \
    --from-literal=DB_HOST=postgres \
    --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=debug \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml > cm.yaml

  # ConfigMap (from file)
  kubectl create cm app-config \
    --from-file=config.properties \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml > cm.yaml

  # Secret
  kubectl create secret generic db-creds \
    --from-literal=username=admin \
    --from-literal=password=s3cr3t \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml > secret.yaml

  # Job (from cronjob!)
  kubectl create cronjob my-cron --image=busybox \
    --schedule="*/5 * * * *" -- /bin/sh -c "date" \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml > cronjob.yaml

  # ServiceAccount
  kubectl create sa build-robot \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml > sa.yaml

  ═══════════ CLIENT vs SERVER DRY-RUN ═══════════
  ┌─────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  --dry-run=client│ Pure local YAML gen (FAST)       │
  │                  │ No API server contact            │
  │                  │ Can't validate server-side rules │
  ├─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  --dry-run=server│ Sends to API server for validation│
  │                  │ REJECTED if invalid (but not     │
  │                  │ actually persisted)              │
  │                  │ Catches: quota, webhook, RBAC    │
  └─────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ CKAD WORKFLOW ═══════════
  1. kubectl create deploy ... --dry-run=client -o yaml > f.yaml
  2. vim f.yaml  (add probes, env, resources, volumes)
  3. kubectl apply -f f.yaml
  4. kubectl get pods, svc (verify)

CKAD exam tip: This is THE most important CKAD pattern. Memorize it: Generate → Edit → Apply → Verify. Never write YAML from scratch — always generate with --dry-run=client -o yaml first. This saves 20+ minutes on the exam and prevents YAML indentation errors.

How do you quickly create a Service to expose a Deployment using kubectl?
A) kubectl expose deploy easypj-api --port=80 --target-port=8000 --type=ClusterIP. This creates a Service with the correct selector (copied from the Deployment's pod labels). For YAML: add --dry-run=client -o yaml. Also works with pods, replicasets, and other resources
B) You must write a Service YAML from scratch — there is no imperative way to create Services
C) kubectl create service deploy/easypj-api --port=80

✅ Correct Answer: A

kubectl expose auto-detects the selector from the target resource. Default type is ClusterIP. For NodePort: --type=NodePort. For LoadBalancer: --type=LoadBalancer. Always use --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate the YAML first, then edit and apply.

📝 kubectl expose — Quick Service Creation
kubectl expose — All Service Types
  ═══════════════ SERVICE TYPE DECISION ═══════════════
  kubectl expose <RESOURCE> <NAME> --port=XX --target-port=YY --type=???
        │
        ├── --type=ClusterIP   (default)
        │   └── Internal cluster IP only
        │       Use: Pod-to-Pod communication, microservices
        │       Example: api ↔ database, api ↔ redis
        │
        ├── --type=NodePort
        │   └── Opens port 30000-32767 on EVERY node
        │       Use: External access during development
        │       Example: devs hitting nodeIP:30080 → app
        │
        └── --type=LoadBalancer
            └── Provisions cloud LB (AWS NLB, GCP LB)
                Use: Production external access
                ⚠️  Requires cloud provider support

  ═══════════════ COMMAND REFERENCE ═══════════════
  # ClusterIP (internal)
  kubectl expose deploy easypj-api \
    --port=80 --target-port=8000

  # ClusterIP with YAML output
  kubectl expose deploy easypj-api \
    --port=80 --target-port=8000 \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml > svc.yaml

  # NodePort
  kubectl expose deploy easypj-web \
    --port=80 --target-port=3000 \
    --type=NodePort
  → Service: easypj-web (NodePort: 30080)

  # Also works with Pods directly
  kubectl expose pod debug-pod --port=8080 --type=NodePort

  ══════════ PORT NAMING ══════════
  --port=80          Port the SERVICE listens on
  --target-port=8000 Port the CONTAINER listens on

  ┌──────────┬──────────────┬────────────────────┐
  │  SCENARIO │ --port        │ --target-port      │
  ├──────────┼──────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │  API      │ 80 (external) │ 8000 (django)      │
  │  Web      │ 443 (HTTPS)   │ 3000 (node/react)  │
  │  DB       │ 5432 (pg)     │ 5432 (postgres)    │
  └──────────┴──────────────┴────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: kubectl expose is one of the fastest ways to create a Service. It auto-copies the selector from the target resource's pod template labels. For the exam: expose → dry-run YAML → add any extra config → apply.

📝 CKAD Must-Know Imperative Commands — Cheat Sheet
Top 10 kubectl Commands for CKAD Speed
  ═══════════════ 1. CREATE DEPLOYMENT ═══════════════
  kubectl create deploy NAME --image=IMG --replicas=N \
    --port=P --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml
  → Generates complete Deployment YAML in seconds

  → CKAD usage: Quick image updates during exam tasks

    --rm -it -- curl http://easypj-api

    --dry-run=client -o yaml > cm.yaml

  kubectl describe pod/NAME
  kubectl logs pod/NAME

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Step 1: Generate YAML (imperative, --dry-run)        │
  │  Step 2: Edit YAML (vim/nano, add missing fields)     │

🚀 Beyond CKAD: In production, these imperative commands are NOT sufficient. Production deployments require: GitOps (ArgoCD/Flux) for declarative state, Helm/Kustomize for templating, CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, Jenkins) for automation, and observability (Prometheus/Grafana) for monitoring. But for the CKAD exam and rapid debugging, imperative commands are your best friend.

📊 Category 3: Application Observability & Maintenance (15%)Q81-Q110

🟢→🟡→🔴 Progressive: Monitoring & Maintaining Kubernetes Applications

This category is about SEEING what your application is doing — is it healthy? Is it using too much memory? Why did it crash? Think of it like the dashboard and diagnostics of your car — you need to monitor gauges (CPU/memory), read error codes (logs and events), and know how to fix things when they break (debugging). For easypj/jobpost, this means health checks for Django/PostgreSQL/Redis, log analysis, resource monitoring, and the debugging skills to diagnose a CrashLoopBackOff at 2 AM.
