3.1 API DeprecationsQ81-Q84

🟡→🔴 | LF Subtopic 1: Understand API deprecations and how to discover available APIs.

Observ 🟡 Q81 of 200
What are Kubernetes API deprecations and why do they matter for CKAD developers?
A) API deprecations are cosmetic warnings — deprecated APIs still work forever and never get removed from Kubernetes
B) API deprecations only affect cluster administrators — application developers don't need to worry about which API version they use in their YAML manifests
C) API deprecations are the formal process by which older Kubernetes API versions are marked for removal. When an API is deprecated, it still works but generates WARNINGS. After a deprecation period (typically 3 releases / ~12 months), the deprecated API is REMOVED — and any YAML manifest or Helm chart using it will FAIL with "no matches for kind". Example: extensions/v1beta1 Ingress was deprecated in v1.14 and removed in v1.22 — all Ingress resources had to be migrated to networking.k8s.io/v1
D) API deprecations happen automatically — Kubernetes automatically upgrades your YAML manifests from old API versions to new ones without any action needed
✅ Correct Answer: C

Kubernetes follows a strict API deprecation policy. APIs go through three phases: Alpha (disabled by default, may change), Beta (enabled by default, will be deprecated before removal), and GA/Stable (available for all releases of that major version). When a Beta API graduates to GA, the Beta version is deprecated and scheduled for removal. As a CKAD developer, you are responsible for ensuring your manifests use CURRENT API versions — an outdated apiVersion is one of the most common reasons for kubectl apply failures.

📝 Kubernetes API Deprecation Lifecycle
API Version Lifecycle — Alpha → Beta → GA → Deprecated → Removed
  ═══════════════ API VERSION LIFECYCLE ═══════════════
  Alpha          Beta             GA/Stable        Deprecated       REMOVED
    │              │                 │                 │                │
    ▼              ▼                 ▼                 ▼                ▼
  ┌──────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌────────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐
  │v1alpha1│→ │v1beta1    │→  │v1 (GA)     │→  │v1beta1   │→  │💀 GONE   │
  │Disabled│  │Enabled    │   │Stable      │   │WARNING!  │   │Manifests │
  │by def. │  │default    │   │forever     │   │3 releases│   │BREAK!    │
  └──────┘    └──────────┘    └────────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘
     ~N/A         ~9-12 months       FOREVER        ~12 months       ---

  ═══════════ REAL EXAMPLES (that BROKE production) ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────┬─────────────┬───────────┬──────────────────┐
  │  RESOURCE             │ DEPRECATED   │ REMOVED   │ MIGRATE TO       │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────────┼───────────┼──────────────────┤
  │  Ingress              │ v1beta1      │ v1.22     │ networking/v1    │
  │  (extensions/v1beta1) │ (v1.14)      │           │                  │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────────┼───────────┼──────────────────┤
  │  CronJob              │ v1beta1      │ v1.25     │ batch/v1         │
  │  (batch/v1beta1)      │ (v1.21)      │           │                  │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────────┼───────────┼──────────────────┤
  │  PodSecurityPolicy    │ v1beta1      │ v1.25     │ Pod Security     │
  │  (policy/v1beta1)     │ (v1.21)      │           │ Admission (PSA)  │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────────┼───────────┼──────────────────┤
  │  HorizontalPodAuto-   │ v2beta2      │ v1.26     │ autoscaling/v2   │
  │  scaler               │ (v1.23)      │           │                  │
  └──────────────────────┴─────────────┴───────────┴──────────────────┘

  ═══════════ HOW TO CHECK YOUR CLUSTER ═══════════
  # See all API versions available
  kubectl api-versions

  # See which API group a resource belongs to
  kubectl api-resources | grep -i ingress
  → ingresses   networking.k8s.io/v1   true   Ingress

  # Check if YOUR manifests use deprecated APIs
  kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f my-manifest.yaml
  → Warning: networking.k8s.io/v1beta1 Ingress is deprecated

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam cluster runs a specific Kubernetes version. ALWAYS check kubectl api-resources before writing YAML to confirm the correct apiVersion. The most common CKAD trap is using extensions/v1beta1 for Ingress instead of networking.k8s.io/v1. For easypj/jobpost, ensure all Ingress, CronJob, and HPA manifests use GA (v1) API versions.

Observ 🟡 Q82 of 200
How do you discover which API versions and resources are available on your Kubernetes cluster?
A) kubectl api-versions (lists ALL API group versions available on the server) and kubectl api-resources (lists all resource types with their API group, whether they're namespaced, and short names). Combine with --api-group to filter: kubectl api-resources --api-group=networking.k8s.io. These commands tell you EXACTLY what you can deploy on your cluster
B) You must read the Kubernetes documentation — there is no CLI command to discover available APIs dynamically from the cluster
C) kubectl get apis — this lists all endpoints and their supported HTTP methods
D) kubectl describe cluster — this command describes the cluster configuration including which APIs are enabled
✅ Correct Answer: A

kubectl api-versions and kubectl api-resources are your API discovery toolkit. api-versions shows every API group+version combination your cluster supports (e.g., networking.k8s.io/v1). api-resources shows every resource type with metadata including short names (aliases), whether the resource is namespaced, and which API group it belongs to. These commands are essential for CKAD because you need to know the correct apiVersion for every YAML manifest you write.

📝 API Discovery Commands — Complete Reference
kubectl api-versions vs api-resources
  ═══════════════ kubectl api-versions ═══════════════
  # Lists ALL API group versions available
  kubectl api-versions
  →
  admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
  apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
  apps/v1                          ← Deployments, StatefulSets
  autoscaling/v1                   ← HPAs
  autoscaling/v2
  batch/v1                         ← Jobs, CronJobs
  networking.k8s.io/v1             ← Ingress, NetworkPolicy
  policy/v1                        ← PodDisruptionBudget
  rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1    ← Roles, RoleBindings
  v1                               ← Pods, Services, ConfigMaps (core group)

  ═══════════════ kubectl api-resources ═══════════════
  kubectl api-resources
  →
  NAME         SHORTNAMES   APIVERSION     NAMESPACED   KIND
  pods         po           v1             true         Pod
  services     svc          v1             true         Service
  deployments  deploy       apps/v1        true         Deployment
  ingresses    ing          networking     true         Ingress
                            .k8s.io/v1
  cronjobs     cj           batch/v1       true         CronJob
  nodes        no           v1             false        Node
  namespaces   ns           v1             false        Namespace

  ═══════════ FILTER BY API GROUP ═══════════
  kubectl api-resources --api-group=networking.k8s.io
  → Ingress, IngressClass, NetworkPolicy

  kubectl api-resources --api-group=apps
  → Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, ReplicaSet

  ═══════════ CKAD WORKFLOW ═══════════
  1. kubectl api-resources | grep -i <resource>
     → Find the correct apiVersion and kind
  2. kubectl explain <resource> --recursive
     → See all available fields
  3. Write YAML with correct apiVersion
  4. kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f manifest.yaml
     → Validate before applying

CKAD exam tip: This is a CKAD essentials command. Before writing ANY YAML on the exam, verify the API version with kubectl api-resources. The exam cluster may have different API versions than your local practice cluster. Always check!

Observ 🟡 Q83 of 200
What does kubectl explain do, and how does it help you write correct YAML?
A) kubectl explain provides natural language explanations of Kubernetes concepts — it's like a built-in tutorial, not a field reference
B) kubectl explain <resource> shows the full field reference for any Kubernetes resource directly from the cluster's API documentation — including nested fields, required fields, field types, and descriptions. Example: kubectl explain deployment.spec.template.spec.containers shows every available field for container specs, including resources, ports, env, volumeMounts, livenessProbe, and more. This means you NEVER need to memorize YAML schemas
C) kubectl explain is only available for Pods and Services — it doesn't work for Deployments, Ingress, or other resources
D) kubectl explain requires an internet connection — it queries the remote Kubernetes documentation server, not the local cluster API
✅ Correct Answer: B

kubectl explain is the most underrated CKAD command. It reads the OpenAPI schema from your live cluster and shows you the exact field structure for any resource — what fields exist, what types they accept, which are required, and descriptions of what each field does. You can drill down with dot notation: kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate. This means you NEVER need to memorize YAML schemas — just kubectl explain it.

📝 kubectl explain — Your Built-In YAML Reference
How kubectl explain Works — Drill-Down Field Reference
  ═══════════════ BASIC USAGE ═══════════════
  kubectl explain pod
  →
  KIND:       Pod
  VERSION:    v1
  DESCRIPTION:
      Pod is a collection of containers that can run on a host.
  FIELDS:
    apiVersion   <string>
    kind         <string>
    metadata     <Object>
    spec         <Object>     ← Dig deeper!
    status       <Object>     ← Read-only, set by K8s

  ═══════════════ DRILL DOWN ═══════════════
  kubectl explain pod.spec
  →
  FIELDS:
    containers           <[]Object> -required-
    restartPolicy        <string>
    volumes              <[]Object>
    serviceAccountName   <string>

  kubectl explain pod.spec.containers
  →
  FIELDS:
    name         <string> -required-
    image        <string> -required-
    ports        <[]Object>
    resources    <Object>
    env          <[]Object>
    livenessProbe  <Object>      ← Found it!

  kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.livenessProbe
  →
  FIELDS:
    httpGet             <Object>
    exec                <Object>
    tcpSocket           <Object>
    initialDelaySeconds <integer>
    periodSeconds       <integer>
    failureThreshold    <integer>

  ═══════════ PRO TIP: --recursive ═══════════
  kubectl explain deployment --recursive
  → Shows EVERY field at ALL nesting levels!
  → Good for discovering fields you didn't know existed

  ═══════════ CKAD EXAM WORKFLOW ═══════════
  1. kubectl explain <resource> --recursive
     → See all available fields
  2. Copy the field path: resources.limits.cpu
  3. Write it in your YAML
  → No memorization needed!

CKAD exam tip: kubectl explain is available on the CKAD exam and it's your secret weapon. Stuck on what fields a resource accepts? kubectl explain deployment --recursive | grep -i <keyword>. Need to know what a probe field expects? kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.livenessProbe. Use it constantly — it's faster than searching docs.

Observ 🔴 Q84 of 200
You have YAML manifests using deprecated APIs (extensions/v1beta1 for Ingress). How do you migrate them?
A) Delete all resources and recreate them — there is no way to migrate from deprecated APIs to current versions without downtime
B) Simply change the apiVersion in the YAML and re-apply — the new apiVersion accepts the exact same field structure as the old one
C) The deprecated API will automatically redirect to the new API — no migration is needed, Kubernetes handles it transparently
D) Migration requires: (1) kubectl api-resources to find the current API version, (2) kubectl explain to understand NEW field structure (GA APIs often have different required fields — e.g., networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress requires pathType and uses service.name not serviceName), (3) Update apiVersion + adapt YAML fields, (4) kubectl apply --dry-run=server to validate, (5) kubectl apply -f to deploy. For Ingress specifically: networking.k8s.io/v1 requires pathType (Prefix/Exact/ImplementationSpecific) and changes the backend service reference format
✅ Correct Answer: D

Migrating from deprecated APIs requires more than just changing apiVersion — GA APIs often introduce new required fields and different field structures. For Ingress, the migration from extensions/v1beta1 to networking.k8s.io/v1 is the most common one you'll encounter: pathType becomes mandatory, the backend reference changes, and the IngressClass requirement was introduced. Always test with --dry-run=server before applying to avoid breaking production traffic.

📝 API Migration — Ingress v1beta1 → v1 (Real Example)
Migrating Ingress from extensions/v1beta1 to networking.k8s.io/v1
  ═══════════════ BEFORE (extensions/v1beta1 — DEPRECATED) ═══════════════
  apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1
  kind: Ingress
  metadata:
    name: easypj-ingress
  spec:
    rules:
    - host: api.easypj.com
      http:
        paths:
        - path: /
          backend:
            serviceName: easypj-api    ← OLD field name
            servicePort: 80            ← OLD field name

  ═══════════════ AFTER (networking.k8s.io/v1 — GA) ═══════════════
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1     ← CHANGED
  kind: Ingress
  metadata:
    name: easypj-ingress
  spec:
    ingressClassName: nginx            ← NEW: required in v1
    rules:
    - host: api.easypj.com
      http:
        paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: Prefix             ← NEW: REQUIRED in v1!
          backend:
            service:
              name: easypj-api        ← CHANGED structure
              port:
                number: 80            ← CHANGED structure

  ═══════════════ FIELD CHANGES SUMMARY ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
  │  FIELD               │ v1beta1 (OLD)        │ v1 (NEW)             │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │  apiVersion          │ extensions/v1beta1   │ networking.k8s.io/v1 │
  │  pathType            │ ❌ Not required      │ ✅ REQUIRED           │
  │  backend reference   │ serviceName +        │ service.name +       │
  │                      │ servicePort          │ port.number          │
  │  ingressClassName    │ ❌ Not required      │ ✅ Recommended        │
  └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ MIGRATION COMMANDS ═══════════
  # 1. Find current Ingress YAML
  kubectl get ingress easypj-ingress -o yaml > old.yaml

  # 2. Check current apiVersion
  kubectl api-resources | grep ingress
  → networking.k8s.io/v1

  # 3. Understand new fields
  kubectl explain ingress.spec.rules.http.paths

  # 4. Edit and validate
  kubectl apply -f new.yaml --dry-run=server
  → ingress.networking.k8s.io/easypj-ingress created (server dry run)

  # 5. Apply
  kubectl apply -f new.yaml

🚀 Beyond CKAD (CKA crossover): Before upgrading a cluster (e.g., v1.28 → v1.29), CKA admins use kubectl convert or the kubepug (Kubernetes Upgrade Planner) tool to scan all cluster resources for deprecated APIs. If deprecated APIs are found, the upgrade is BLOCKED. As a developer, proactively migrating your manifests prevents being the reason a cluster upgrade is delayed.

3.2 Implement Probes & Health ChecksQ85-Q92

🟢→🔴 | LF Subtopic 2: Implement probes and health checks. Liveness, readiness, startup probes — their types, parameters, and common mistakes.

Observ 🟢 Q85 of 200
What is a liveness probe and what happens when it fails?
A) A liveness probe checks if the application is ready to receive traffic — when it fails, the pod is removed from the Service endpoints but the container keeps running
B) A liveness probe sends an alert to the monitoring system — it does not affect the running container in any way
C) A liveness probe answers the question "Is my app alive or stuck?" Kubernetes periodically checks the probe. If it fails (after failureThreshold consecutive failures), the kubelet RESTARTS the container. This is like a watchdog timer — if your app deadlocks, runs out of memory, or enters an unrecoverable state, the liveness probe kills and restarts it. CRITICAL: a liveness probe should NOT depend on external services (databases, APIs) — otherwise a DB hiccup will kill all your pods
D) A liveness probe only works with HTTP endpoints — it cannot check TCP connections or execute commands inside the container
✅ Correct Answer: C

The liveness probe is your application's auto-restart mechanism. It's the Kubernetes equivalent of a watchdog timer — if your application freezes, deadlocks, or enters an unrecoverable state, the liveness probe detects it and restarts the container. This is fundamentally different from a readiness probe (which just removes the pod from the Service) — liveness actually KILLS and restarts the container. The golden rule: never make your liveness probe depend on external dependencies. If your liveness probe checks the database connection, a 5-second DB blip will trigger a cascade restart of all your application pods.

📝 Liveness Probe — Your App's Auto-Restart Mechanism
How a Liveness Probe Works — The Restart Cycle
  ═══════════════ LIVENESS PROBE TIMELINE ═══════════════
  Container Start
       │
       ├── initialDelaySeconds: 30s (wait for app to start)
       │
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PROBE CYCLE (repeats every periodSeconds: 10s)             │
  │                                                              │
  │  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐               │
  │  │ PROBE 1  │→  │ PROBE 2  │→  │ PROBE 3  │→ ...          │
  │  │ ✅ OK    │   │ ✅ OK    │   │ ❌ FAIL  │               │
  │  └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘               │
  │                                      │                      │
  │                         failureThreshold: 3                │
  │                                      │                      │
  │                    ┌─────────────────┘                      │
  │                    ▼                                        │
  │           ┌──────────────┐                                 │
  │           │ 3rd failure? │                                  │
  │           └──────────────┘                                 │
  │              │ Yes                                          │
  │              ▼                                              │
  │     🔄 CONTAINER RESTARTED by kubelet                       │
  │     • RestartCount incremented                              │
  │     • Backoff: 10s → 20s → 40s → 80s → ... (max 5min)     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ LIVENESS PROBE EXAMPLE (HTTP) ═══════════════
  livenessProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /healthz              ← App must respond 200-399
      port: 8000
    initialDelaySeconds: 30       ← Wait 30s after container start
    periodSeconds: 10             ← Check every 10 seconds
    timeoutSeconds: 5             ← Timeout after 5 seconds
    failureThreshold: 3           ← 3 consecutive failures = RESTART

  ═══════════════ GOLDEN RULES ═══════════════
  ✅ DO: Check internal app health (deadlocks, infinite loops)
  ✅ DO: Use a lightweight /healthz endpoint (no heavy DB queries)
  ❌ DON'T: Check external dependencies (DB, Redis, third-party APIs)
  ❌ DON'T: Set initialDelaySeconds too low (app needs time to start)
  ❌ DON'T: Set failureThreshold=1 (transient hiccups kill the pod)

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam frequently asks you to ADD probes to an existing Deployment. Use kubectl edit deploy or create a YAML patch. Remember: liveness = restart, readiness = traffic. For easypj/jobpost Django app, use an HTTP liveness probe at /healthz that returns 200 if Django's internal state is healthy (not checking PostgreSQL).

Observ 🟢 Q86 of 200
What is a readiness probe and how does it interact with Services?
A) A readiness probe restarts the container when it fails — it works the same way as a liveness probe
B) A readiness probe answers "Is my app ready to serve traffic?" When the probe FAILS, the pod's IP is REMOVED from ALL Service endpoints — no traffic is sent to it, but the container keeps running. When the probe succeeds again, the pod is re-added. This is critical for apps that need warm-up time (loading models, establishing DB connections, filling caches). Readiness probes prevent "the pod is running but returns 503s"
C) A readiness probe is only checked once at container startup — after the first success, it's never checked again
D) A readiness probe sends logs to an external system — it doesn't affect pod networking or Service endpoints
✅ Correct Answer: B

The readiness probe is your application's traffic control valve. It determines whether a pod should receive traffic through a Service. If the readiness probe fails, kube-proxy removes the pod's IP from the Service's Endpoints list — no new connections go to it. Unlike the liveness probe, a failed readiness probe does NOT restart the container. This is perfect for: (1) apps that need warm-up time, (2) temporarily overloaded pods that need to shed traffic, (3) pods that depend on external services not yet available.

📝 Readiness Probe — Traffic Control Valve
Readiness Probe + Service Integration
  ═══════════════ READINESS PROBE & SERVICE ENDPOINTS ═══════════════
  Service: easypj-api (selector: app=easypj-api)
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ENDPOINTS (kube-proxy maintains this list)                  │
  │                                                               │
  │  Pod A: 10.244.1.5   Readiness: ✅ Ready  → IN endpoints    │
  │  Pod B: 10.244.2.8   Readiness: ✅ Ready  → IN endpoints    │
  │  Pod C: 10.244.1.9   Readiness: ❌ FAIL   → OUT of endpoints │
  │  Pod D: 10.244.2.3   Readiness: ✅ Ready  → IN endpoints    │
  │                                                               │
  │  → Traffic flows to A, B, D only                             │
  │  → Pod C stays running but receives ZERO traffic             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ READINESS PROBE EXAMPLE ═══════════════
  readinessProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /ready
      port: 8000
    initialDelaySeconds: 5        ← Check quickly after start
    periodSeconds: 5              ← Check frequently
    failureThreshold: 3           ← 3 failures = remove from Service

  ═══════════════ LIVENESS vs READINESS ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────┬─────────────────────┬────────────────────────┐
  │  PROBE        │ QUESTION             │ ACTION ON FAILURE      │
  ├──────────────┼─────────────────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │  Liveness     │ "Is my app stuck?"   │ 🔄 RESTART container   │
  │  Readiness    │ "Can I serve?"       │ 🚫 Remove from Service │
  │  Startup      │ "Am I done booting?" │ 🔄 Restart (if fails)  │
  └──────────────┴─────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: For the easypj/jobpost Django API, the readiness probe should check that Django is loaded AND the database connection pool is ready. A good readiness endpoint responds 200 after django.setup() completes but returns 503 during migrations or when the DB connection pool is exhausted.

Observ 🟡 Q87 of 200
What is a startup probe and when should you use it instead of just liveness + readiness?
A) A startup probe answers "Has my app finished booting?" It runs FIRST, before liveness and readiness. While the startup probe is running, liveness and readiness are DISABLED. Once startup succeeds, liveness and readiness take over. This is essential for apps with SLOW startup (loading ML models, warming caches, database migrations) — without a startup probe, you'd have to set initialDelaySeconds very high on the liveness probe, which is imprecise and wastes time. With a startup probe, you can use aggressive liveness checks (periodSeconds=1) because they won't fire during startup
B) A startup probe is identical to a liveness probe — it's just a different name for the same mechanism
C) A startup probe replaces both liveness and readiness probes — once configured, you don't need the other two
D) A startup probe runs AFTER liveness and readiness probes succeed, not before — it verifies the app has successfully served its first request
✅ Correct Answer: A

The startup probe (introduced in Kubernetes 1.16, stable in 1.20) solves the slow-start problem. Before startup probes, you had to set initialDelaySeconds on the liveness probe to a worst-case startup time — which meant if your app started fast, you waited unnecessarily; if it started slower than expected, the liveness probe killed it prematurely. The startup probe gives slow apps time to boot without compromising on aggressive health checking after startup.

📝 Startup Probe — The Slow-Start Solution
Probe Sequence: Startup → Liveness + Readiness
  ═══════════════ PROBE SEQUENCE ═══════════════
  Container Starts
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STARTUP PROBE (runs first, blocks others)            │
  │                                                       │
  │  periodSeconds: 10    Check every 10s                │
  │  failureThreshold: 30  Max 30 checks                 │
  │  → Total patience: 10 × 30 = 300 seconds (5 min)    │
  │                                                       │
  │  ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐        ┌──────┐         │
  │  │Chk 1 │→│Chk 2 │→│Chk 3 │→ ... → │Chk 15│         │
  │  │ FAIL │ │ FAIL │ │ FAIL │        │ ✅ OK │         │
  │  └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘        └──────┘         │
  │                                               │       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┼───────┘
                                                   │
                                          Startup SUCCESS
                                                   │
                    ┌──────────────────────────────┘
                    ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LIVENESS + READINESS (take over after startup)       │
  │                                                       │
  │  Now you can use AGGRESSIVE settings:                 │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  livenessProbe:     periodSeconds: 5            │  │
  │  │  readinessProbe:    periodSeconds: 3            │  │
  │  │  → Fast detection of issues after startup!      │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ WITH vs WITHOUT STARTUP PROBE ═══════════
  ┌─────────────────┬─────────────────────┬────────────────────┐
  │                  │ WITHOUT Startup     │ WITH Startup       │
  ├─────────────────┼─────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │  Startup time   │ initialDelaySeconds │ Startup probe      │
  │  handled by     │ (worst-case guess)  │ (adaptive)         │
  │  Liveness during│ ⚠️ Can kill slow     │ ✅ Disabled until  │
  │  startup        │    starting apps     │    startup succeeds │
  │  Liveness after │ Same as during       │ ✅ Can be aggressive│
  │  startup        │ startup             │    (periodSecs=1)  │
  └─────────────────┴─────────────────────┴────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: If a CKAD task says "the application takes up to 2 minutes to start," use a startup probe with failureThreshold: 12 and periodSeconds: 10 (12 × 10 = 120 seconds of patience). For easypj/jobpost Django app that runs migrations on startup, a startup probe is perfect — wait for migrations to finish before liveness kicks in.

Observ 🟢 Q88 of 200
What are the four probe handler types and when should you use each?
A) All probes use HTTP GET requests — there is only one probe type in Kubernetes
B) The probe types are GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE — they correspond to HTTP methods
C) The probe types are ICMP ping, HTTP HEAD, UDP check, and file check — only network-level checks are supported
D) httpGet: HTTP GET to a path/port (best for web apps). tcpSocket: TCP connection check (best for databases, gRPC without health service). exec: run a command inside the container — exit 0 = success (best for custom logic, script-based checks). grpc: gRPC health check using standard health protocol (best for gRPC services, requires K8s 1.24+)
✅ Correct Answer: D

Kubernetes supports four probe handler types, each suited for different application architectures. httpGet is the most common for web applications (Django, Node.js). tcpSocket is ideal for databases and services that speak TCP but not HTTP (PostgreSQL, Redis). exec gives you complete flexibility — run any command inside the container. grpc (GA in 1.27) provides native gRPC health checking for microservices.

📝 Four Probe Handlers — Complete Reference
Probe Handler Types — When to Use Each
  ═══════════ 1. httpGet ═══════════
  livenessProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /healthz
      port: 8000
      httpHeaders:              ← Optional custom headers
      - name: X-Custom-Header
        value: probe-check
  ✅ Best for: Web apps (Django, Express, Spring Boot)
  📍 Use when: App has an HTTP health endpoint
  🎯 For easypj: Django /healthz endpoint

  ═══════════ 2. tcpSocket ═══════════
  livenessProbe:
    tcpSocket:
      port: 5432               ← Just checks if port is open
  ✅ Best for: Databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL), Redis, non-HTTP services
  📍 Use when: App listens on TCP but doesn't speak HTTP
  🎯 For easypj: PostgreSQL (5432), Redis (6379)

  ═══════════ 3. exec ═══════════
  livenessProbe:
    exec:
      command:
      - /bin/sh
      - -c
      - |
        pg_isready -h localhost -p 5432 &&
        redis-cli ping | grep PONG
  ✅ Best for: Custom health logic, scripted checks
  📍 Use when: Need to check multiple conditions or use CLI tools
  ⚠️  Requires the tool (pg_isready, redis-cli) in the container image!
  🎯 For easypj: Combined PostgreSQL + Redis + Celery worker check

  ═══════════ 4. grpc ═══════════
  livenessProbe:
    grpc:
      port: 50051
      service: health.Check     ← Optional: specific service
  ✅ Best for: gRPC microservices (requires K8s 1.24+)
  📍 Use when: Service uses gRPC with standard health protocol

  ═══════════ DECISION MATRIX ═══════════
  ┌─────────────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
  │  APP TYPE        │ httpGet  │ tcpSocket│ exec     │ grpc     │
  ├─────────────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
  │  Django / Flask  │ ✅ BEST  │ ⚠️ Basic │ ✅ Good  │ ❌ N/A   │
  │  PostgreSQL      │ ❌       │ ✅ BEST  │ ✅ Good  │ ❌       │
  │  Redis           │ ❌       │ ✅ BEST  │ ✅ Good  │ ❌       │
  │  gRPC Service    │ ❌       │ ⚠️ Basic │ ✅ Good  │ ✅ BEST  │
  │  Worker (Celery) │ ❌       │ ❌       │ ✅ BEST  │ ❌       │
  └─────────────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘

CKAD exam tip: For the exam, httpGet is tested most frequently. Know that tcpSocket only checks if a port is open — it can't verify the application logic. For exec probes, remember that the command runs INSIDE the container — you can't use tools that aren't installed in the image. For easypj/jobpost: use httpGet for Django, tcpSocket for PostgreSQL/Redis sidecars, and exec for Celery workers (check process list).

Observ 🟡 Q89 of 200
What do these probe parameters control: initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds, failureThreshold, successThreshold?
A) These parameters only affect the liveness probe — readiness and startup probes use different, incompatible parameter sets
B) initialDelaySeconds: seconds to wait before FIRST probe (app startup buffer). periodSeconds: how OFTEN to probe (e.g., every 10s). timeoutSeconds: how long to wait for a response before counting as failure. failureThreshold: consecutive failures needed to trigger action (restart for liveness, endpoint removal for readiness). successThreshold: consecutive successes needed after failure (for readiness: re-add to Service; for liveness: usually 1, just needs one success)
C) These are Kubernetes scheduling parameters — they control pod placement, not health checking
D) initialDelaySeconds sets the probe interval, periodSeconds sets the total probe timeout, and failureThreshold sets how many times the probe runs before stopping permanently
✅ Correct Answer: B

Understanding probe parameters is critical for setting realistic values. The most common CKAD mistake is setting initialDelaySeconds too low, causing the liveness probe to kill the container before the application finishes starting. Another common trap: setting failureThreshold: 1 means a single transient hiccup kills your pod. For production, use failureThreshold: 3 or higher.

CKAD exam tip: If the exam says "the application takes 45 seconds to start," set initialDelaySeconds: 45 on your liveness probe (or better, use a startup probe). Always add a safety margin — if the app takes ~45s, set initialDelaySeconds to 60. For easypj/jobpost Django: initialDelaySeconds=30, periodSeconds=10, failureThreshold=3.

Observ 🟡 Q90 of 200
How do you choose realistic probe thresholds for different application types?
A) Use the same probe thresholds for all applications — Kubernetes defaults are perfect for every scenario
B) Set all thresholds to 1 second for maximum responsiveness — faster failure detection is always better
C) Match thresholds to your application's characteristics: Django/Python apps need 30-60s initial delay (slow interpreter startup), Go/Rust binaries need 5-10s (near-instant), Java/Spring needs 60-90s (JVM warmup), ML model loading needs 120-300s. The periodSeconds should be 5-15s — shorter means faster detection but more CPU overhead. Always test with kubectl describe pod to see probe events
D) Probe thresholds are automatically determined by Kubernetes based on the container image size — no manual configuration is needed
✅ Correct Answer: C

Probe thresholds are not one-size-fits-all. They must be tuned to your specific application's startup characteristics and runtime behavior. Setting them too aggressively causes unnecessary restarts (flapping); setting them too leniently delays detection of real failures. The key insight: tighten liveness probes after startup, keep readiness probes responsive to traffic changes.

Observ 🟡 Q91 of 200
What exactly happens step by step when a liveness probe fails?
A) The pod is immediately deleted and a new pod is created — there is no delay or backoff between restarts
B) The container receives a SIGTERM, waits for terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30s), then the pod is deleted and recreated from scratch by the Deployment controller
C) The entire pod is evicted from the node and rescheduled to a different node — this is called pod eviction
D) Step 1: kubelet detects consecutive failures (reaching failureThreshold). Step 2: kubelet sends SIGTERM to the container (graceful shutdown). Step 3: If container doesn't exit within terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30s default), kubelet sends SIGKILL. Step 4: kubelet restarts the SAME container on the SAME node (NOT a new pod — same pod, restarted container). Step 5: restartCount increments. Step 6: kubelet applies exponential backoff (10s → 20s → 40s → 80s → ... max 5 min between restarts). The pod's IP, hostname, and volumes persist across restarts
✅ Correct Answer: D

When a liveness probe fails, the container is restarted, NOT the pod. This is a crucial distinction. The pod stays on the same node, keeps its IP, keeps its volumes, and keeps its hostname. Only the container process is killed and restarted. This is different from a pod restart (which loses the IP) and different from pod eviction (which moves to another node). The exponential backoff prevents "crash loops" from consuming excessive node resources.

📝 Liveness Probe Failure — Step-by-Step Timeline
What Happens When Liveness Fails — The Full Sequence
  ═══════════════ FAILURE SEQUENCE ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  STEP 1: Probe fails (reaches failureThreshold)              │
  │  kubelet: "Liveness probe failed 3 times consecutively"      │
  │  Event: Warning  Unhealthy  ... Liveness probe failed        │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  STEP 2: kubelet sends SIGTERM to PID 1 in container         │
  │  Container has terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30s) to exit   │
  │  Event: Normal   Killing     ... Container failed liveness   │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  STEP 3: If still running after 30s → SIGKILL (force kill)   │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  STEP 4: kubelet restarts container (same pod, same node!)   │
  │  • Pod IP: UNCHANGED (10.244.1.5 remains 10.244.1.5)        │
  │  • Volumes: RE-MOUNTED (data on volumes persists)            │
  │  • restartCount: incremented (kubectl get pods shows RESTARTS)│
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  STEP 5: Exponential backoff before accepting new probes     │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  Restart 1: wait 10s    Restart 4: wait 80s           │  │
  │  │  Restart 2: wait 20s    Restart 5: wait 160s          │  │
  │  │  Restart 3: wait 40s    Restart N: wait min(5min, ...)│  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ CONTAINER RESTART vs POD RESTART ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
  │                   │ CONTAINER RESTART│ POD RESTART/RECREATE │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │  Trigger          │ Liveness failure │ Pod deleted/evicted  │
  │  Pod IP           │ UNCHANGED        │ CHANGED              │
  │  Node             │ SAME             │ MAY CHANGE           │
  │  Volumes          │ RE-MOUNTED       │ NEW (unless PVC)     │
  │  restartCount     │ Incremented      │ Reset to 0 (new pod) │
  │  Init containers  │ NOT re-run       │ Re-run               │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: A common CKAD scenario: "Pod keeps restarting — what's wrong?" The answer is usually a failing liveness probe (wrong path, wrong port, too aggressive thresholds). Check with kubectl describe pod to see the "Liveness probe failed" event and kubectl logs --previous to see the previous container's logs before it was killed.

Observ 🔴 Q92 of 200
What are the most common probe configuration mistakes that cause production outages?
A) (1) Liveness probe depending on external services — a DB hiccup cascades to restart all app pods. (2) Using exec probes in distroless containers — there's no shell (/bin/sh) to run commands. (3) Probe pointing to wrong port (containerPort vs service port). (4) initialDelaySeconds too low — probe kills app before it finishes starting. (5) No startup probe for slow apps — liveness kills during legitimate startup. (6) periodSeconds too aggressive — excessive CPU from constant probing. (7) httpGet without scheme: HTTPS — probe fails on TLS endpoints. (8) Readiness probe identical to liveness — temporary overload removes ALL pods from Service
B) Probes are so simple that mistakes are impossible — Kubernetes validates all probe configurations automatically
C) The only mistake is forgetting to add a liveness probe — readiness and startup probes are optional and never cause issues
D) Probe mistakes only happen in development environments — production clusters have automatic probe optimization that prevents configuration errors
✅ Correct Answer: A

Probe misconfiguration is one of the most common causes of production incidents. The most dangerous mistake is having the liveness probe check external dependencies — this creates a cascading failure where a brief database slowdown causes ALL application pods to be restarted simultaneously, turning a minor hiccup into a full outage. The second most common mistake is using exec probes in distroless (shell-less) containers, which fail immediately because there's no /bin/sh to execute the command.

📝 Top 8 Probe Mistakes — And How to Avoid Them
Common Probe Mistakes & Their Fixes
  ═══════════════ TOP 8 PROBE MISTAKES ═══════════════
  ┌─────┬──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │  #  │ MISTAKE                       │ FIX                      │
  ├─────┼──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  1  │ Liveness checks DB/Redis      │ Liveness: internal only  │
  │     │ → DB blip kills ALL pods!     │ Readiness: can check DB  │
  ├─────┼──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  2  │ exec probe in distroless      │ Use httpGet or tcpSocket │
  │     │ → /bin/sh not found, fails   │ instead of exec command   │
  │     │   immediately!                │                          │
  ├─────┼──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  3  │ Wrong port (e.g., 80 not     │ Check containerPort, NOT │
  │     │ 8000) → probe hangs/refused  │ Service port!             │
  ├─────┼──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  4  │ initialDelaySeconds too low  │ Use startup probe or set │
  │     │ → kills during startup       │ generous initial delay    │
  ├─────┼──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  5  │ No startup probe for slow    │ Add startup probe with   │
  │     │ apps → liveness kills during │ failureThreshold ×       │
  │     │ legitimate boot process      │ periodSeconds = max boot  │
  ├─────┼──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  6  │ periodSeconds: 1             │ Use 5-10s for most apps   │
  │     │ → Too much CPU from probing │                          │
  ├─────┼──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  7  │ httpGet without scheme: HTTPS│ Add scheme: HTTPS for TLS │
  │     │ → probe tries HTTP on TLS   │ endpoints                 │
  ├─────┼──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  8  │ Readiness = Liveness         │ Differentiate: readiness  │
  │     │ → Temporary overload removes │ should be less sensitive  │
  │     │   ALL pods from Service      │ than liveness             │
  └─────┴──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ THE CASCADING FAILURE SCENARIO ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ❌ WRONG: Liveness checks DB                                │
  │                                                              │
  │  1. PostgreSQL has 3-second query spike                      │
  │  2. Django /healthz fails (can't reach DB)                  │
  │  3. Kubelet restarts ALL 10 Django pods simultaneously!     │
  │  4. Now 10 pods are restarting + DB is still busy            │
  │  5. New pods fail liveness (DB still slow)                  │
  │  6. 💥 FULL OUTAGE — Death spiral!                          │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  ✅ CORRECT: Liveness internal, Readiness checks DB          │
  │                                                              │
  │  1. PostgreSQL has 3-second query spike                      │
  │  2. Django /ready fails (can't reach DB)                    │
  │  3. Pods removed from Service — no traffic sent             │
  │  4. DB recovers after 3 seconds                             │
  │  5. /ready succeeds, pods re-added to Service               │
  │  6. ✅ No restart, no outage — graceful degradation!        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam loves testing probe misconfiguration scenarios. If you see "pod keeps restarting" or "pod not receiving traffic," think probe issues first. Always check the pod events with kubectl describe pod — probe failures are clearly logged there. For easypj/jobpost: keep liveness internal (/healthz checks only Django process health), put DB checks in readiness (/ready).

Observ 🟢 Q93 of 200
How do you view application logs from a running container using kubectl?
A) kubectl logs only works with cluster-level logging systems like Elasticsearch — it cannot show individual container logs directly
B) kubectl logs <pod-name> retrieves logs from the container's stdout/stderr streams. Key flags: --tail=N (last N lines), --since=5m (logs from last 5 minutes), --timestamps (show timestamp for each line), -f or --follow (stream logs in real-time like tail -f), --previous (logs from the PREVIOUS crashed container — essential for CrashLoopBackOff debugging). For multi-container pods: -c <container-name> to select which container
C) kubectl logs downloads log files from /var/log inside the container — it requires SSH access to the node
D) kubectl logs only shows the last 10 lines — there is no way to see more or stream logs in real-time
✅ Correct Answer: B

kubectl logs is your primary debugging tool on the CKAD exam. It reads container logs directly from the kubelet's log storage on the node. Understanding all its flags is essential — especially --previous (for CrashLoopBackOff debugging) and --tail (to avoid being overwhelmed by thousands of log lines). The -f (follow) flag is like tail -f — it streams new log entries in real time.

📝 kubectl logs — Complete Reference
kubectl logs — All Commands & Flags
  ═══════════════ BASIC USAGE ═══════════════
  kubectl logs easypj-web-9x7k2          # All logs
  kubectl logs easypj-web-9x7k2 --tail=50  # Last 50 lines
  kubectl logs easypj-web-9x7k2 -f         # Stream (follow)
  kubectl logs easypj-web-9x7k2 --since=10m # Last 10 minutes
  kubectl logs easypj-web-9x7k2 --timestamps # Show timestamps

  ═══════════════ MULTI-CONTAINER PODS ═══════════════
  kubectl logs easypj-pod -c django      # Specific container
  kubectl logs easypj-pod --all-containers # All containers

  ═══════════════ CRASHED CONTAINERS ═══════════════
  kubectl logs easypj-web-9x7k2 --previous
  → Shows logs from the PREVIOUS (crashed) container
  → ESSENTIAL for CrashLoopBackOff debugging!

  ═══════════════ DEPLOYMENT/REPLICASET ═══════════════
  kubectl logs deploy/easypj-web         # First pod in deploy
  kubectl logs deploy/easypj-web --tail=20
  kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api         # All pods matching label
  kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api --tail=10 --prefix
  → --prefix adds pod name prefix to each log line

  ═══════════ LOG FLOW ARCHITECTURE ═══════════
  Container (stdout/stderr)
       │
       ▼
  kubelet captures output
       │
       ▼
  /var/log/containers/<pod>_<ns>_<container>.log
       │
       ▼
  kubectl logs reads from here

CKAD exam tip: kubectl logs --previous is the #1 command for debugging CrashLoopBackOff pods. The current container's logs are empty (it crashed immediately), but the PREVIOUS container's logs show you exactly what went wrong. For easypj/jobpost: kubectl logs deploy/easypj-web --tail=50 -f to watch Django app logs during a deployment.

Observ 🟡 Q94 of 200
You have a pod with multiple containers. How do you view logs from a specific container?
A) kubectl logs merges all container logs together — you cannot view logs from a single container in a multi-container pod
B) You must SSH into the pod first, then check /var/log/ inside the specific container — kubectl logs doesn't support multi-container pods
C) kubectl logs <pod> -c <container-name> specifies which container to read logs from. Without -c, kubectl logs errors out on multi-container pods and asks you to specify a container. Use kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}' to list all container names first. For easypj/jobpost: a pod with django + redis sidecar requires -c django or -c redis
D) kubectl logs --container-name=<name> works but requires the full container ID, not the name from the pod spec
✅ Correct Answer: C

Multi-container pods are a key CKAD concept, and logging is one of the places where you must explicitly specify which container. Without -c, kubectl returns an error like "error: a container name must be specified for pod X, choose one of: [django, redis]". The --all-containers flag (K8s 1.18+) shows logs from all containers, prefixed with the container name.

📝 Multi-Container Logging — easypj/jobpost Example
Logging in Multi-Container Pods

      └── Logs: Redis connections, cache hits/misses

If you're not sure which containers are in the pod, kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}' is the fastest way to list them. For easypj/jobpost sidecar patterns (django + redis, web + nginx), always know which container's logs you need.

Observ 🟡 Q95 of 200
Your pod is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff. How do you see what error caused the previous crash?
A) kubectl logs <pod> --previous — this retrieves logs from the PREVIOUS instance of the container (the one that crashed). The current container's logs are empty because it starts and immediately crashes. This is the SINGLE most important command for CrashLoopBackOff debugging. Combine with --tail to limit output: kubectl logs <pod> --previous --tail=100
B) kubectl logs <pod> — the current running container's logs will show the error that caused the previous crash
C) CrashLoopBackOff means the logs are permanently deleted — you need to set up log aggregation BEFORE the crash to capture error messages
D) kubectl describe crash <pod> — there is a dedicated command for CrashLoopBackOff debugging that shows crash dumps
✅ Correct Answer: A

kubectl logs --previous is the #1 CrashLoopBackOff debugging command. When a container crashes and restarts, the new container starts fresh — its logs are empty (or show just the startup that's about to crash again). The --previous flag retrieves the logs from the immediately preceding crashed instance, which contains the error message that caused the crash. Without this flag, you're looking at the wrong container and will see nothing useful.

📝 CrashLoopBackOff — The Debugging Workflow
Debugging CrashLoopBackOff — Step by Step
  ═══════════════ CRASHLOOPBACKOFF DEBUG WORKFLOW ═══════════════
  kubectl get pods
  →
  NAME                    READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
  easypj-web-7x9k2        0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   5          3m

  Step 1: See the error (MOST IMPORTANT!)
  kubectl logs easypj-web-7x9k2 --previous
  →
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "/app/manage.py", line 10, in <module>
      from django.core.management import execute_from_command_line
  ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'django'
  → AHA! The Django package is not installed!

  Step 2: Check pod events for context
  kubectl describe pod easypj-web-7x9k2 | tail -20
  →
  Events:
    Type     Reason     Age   Message
    Warning  BackOff    2m    Back-off restarting failed container
    Normal   Pulled     3m    Container image "easypj/web:v2" present
    Warning  BackOff    30s   Back-off restarting failed container
    Normal   Created    3m    Created container django

  Step 3: Check pod status details
  kubectl get pod easypj-web-7x9k2 -o yaml | grep -A5 state
  →
  state:
    waiting:
      reason: CrashLoopBackOff
    lastState:
      terminated:
        reason: Error
        exitCode: 1

  ═══════════ COMMON CRASHLOOPBACKOFF CAUSES ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CAUSE               │ WHAT kubectl logs --previous SHOWS│
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Missing dependency  │ ModuleNotFoundError, ImportError │
  │  Wrong command       │ "executable file not found"      │
  │  Config error        │ "KeyError: DATABASE_URL"         │
  │  Permission denied   │ "PermissionError: [Errno 13]"    │
  │  Port already in use │ "Address already in use"         │
  │  OOMKilled           │ (logs empty — check status)      │
  └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: This is one of the most tested patterns on CKAD. If you see CrashLoopBackOff, your FIRST command should be kubectl logs <pod> --previous. 90% of the time, the previous container's logs will tell you exactly what's wrong. For easypj/jobpost, common CrashLoopBackOff causes: missing environment variables, database connection string errors, and missing migration files.

Observ 🟢 Q96 of 200
Why does the 12-Factor App methodology recommend logging to stdout instead of writing to log files?
A) stdout is faster than file I/O — logging to files causes a 50% performance penalty compared to stdout
B) Kubernetes does not allow containers to write to the filesystem — all writes must go to stdout or stderr
C) Writing to stdout is only recommended for development — production applications should always write to /var/log/app.log
D) Logging to stdout/stderr treats logs as EVENT STREAMS — the container runtime (containerd/CRI-O) automatically captures them and routes them to the logging driver (json-file, fluentd, Splunk, etc.). The application doesn't need to know WHERE logs go. If you write to files, you must manage log rotation, disk space, and collection yourself. stdout/stderr is the "universal log interface" — it works with any logging system without application changes
✅ Correct Answer: D

The 12-Factor App's log guideline is elegant in its simplicity: your application should write logs to stdout/stderr and let the platform handle the rest. In Kubernetes, the container runtime automatically captures stdout/stderr and writes it to /var/log/containers/ on the node. From there, you can use any log aggregation system (Fluentd, Filebeat, Loki, Datadog) without modifying your application code. This is the same pattern that makes kubectl logs work seamlessly.

📝 stdout/stderr — The Universal Log Interface
Log Flow from Container to Aggregation System
  ═══════════════ LOG FLOW IN KUBERNETES ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  YOUR APPLICATION                                            │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  print("GET /api/jobs 200")     → stdout (fd 1)        │  │
  │  │  sys.stderr.write("ERROR: ...") → stderr (fd 2)        │  │
  │  │                                                         │  │
  │  │  ✅ CORRECT: Log to stdout/stderr                       │  │
  │  │  ❌ WRONG:   Log to /var/log/app.log                    │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │                                   │
  │                           ▼                                   │
  │  CONTAINER RUNTIME (containerd / CRI-O)                      │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  Captures stdout/stderr streams                         │  │
  │  │  Writes to: /var/log/containers/<pod>_<ns>_<ctr>.log   │  │
  │  │  Rotates when log reaches max size (10MB default)      │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │                                   │
  │                           ▼                                   │
  │  LOG AGGREGATION (optional, via DaemonSet)                   │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  Fluentd / Filebeat / Vector / Loki Promtail            │  │
  │  │  │                                                      │  │
  │  │  ▼                                                      │  │
  │  │  Elasticsearch / Loki / Splunk / CloudWatch / Datadog   │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │                                   │
  │                           ▼                                   │
  │  kubectl logs <pod>  ← Reads directly from node's log dir  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ DJANGO LOGGING CONFIG ═══════════════
  # settings.py — 12-factor compliant logging
  import sys
  LOGGING = {
      'version': 1,
      'handlers': {
          'console': {
              'class': 'logging.StreamHandler',
              'stream': sys.stdout,      ← stdout!
          },
      },
      'root': {
          'handlers': ['console'],
          'level': 'INFO',
      },
  }

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam may ask you why an application's logs aren't showing up with kubectl logs. The answer is usually: the application is writing to a FILE instead of stdout/stderr. Fix this by configuring the app to log to stdout. For easypj/jobpost Django app, always use logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout) — never file-based handlers.

Observ 🟡 Q97 of 200
What information does kubectl describe provide that kubectl get doesn't?
A) kubectl describe and kubectl get show identical information — describe is just a more colorful version of get
B) kubectl describe shows the EVENTS section — a chronological log of everything that happened to the resource (scheduling, pulling, starting, probe failures, warnings). It also shows Conditions (PodScheduled, Initialized, ContainersReady, Ready), container states with exit codes and reasons, mount information, and annotations. Events are the most valuable part — they show the STORY of what happened to your pod. kubectl get shows current state only, not the history
C) kubectl describe only works on Pods — it cannot describe Deployments, Services, or other resource types
D) kubectl describe shows the full YAML manifest — it's equivalent to kubectl get -o yaml with better formatting
✅ Correct Answer: B

kubectl describe is your incident investigation tool. While kubectl get shows you the current state (like a snapshot), kubectl describe shows you the history — the Events section tells the chronological story of your resource. For debugging, always check Events first — they tell you about failed image pulls, scheduling issues, probe failures, OOM kills, and volume mount errors.

📝 kubectl describe — What Events Tell You
Reading kubectl describe Events for easypj/jobpost
  ═══════════════ WHAT DESCRIBE SHOWS (that get doesn't) ═══════════════
  kubectl describe pod easypj-web-failed
  →
  Name:         easypj-web-failed-7x9k2
  Namespace:    easypj-prod
  Node:         wk1/192.168.1.10
  Status:       Pending          ← Current state
  IP:           (none)
  Containers:
    django:
      Image:     easypj/web:v2.1.3
      State:     Waiting
        Reason:  ImagePullBackOff  ← WHY it's not running
  Conditions:
    Type              Status
    PodScheduled      True        ← Scheduled to a node ✅
    Initialized       True        ← Init containers ran ✅
    ContainersReady   False       ← Containers not ready ❌
    Ready             False       ← Pod not ready ❌

  ═══════════════ EVENTS — THE CHRONOLOGY ═══════════════
  Events:
    Type     Reason     Age    From               Message
    ────     ──────     ───    ────               ───────
    Normal   Scheduled  5m     default-scheduler   Successfully assigned easypj-prod/easypj-web-failed to wk1
    Normal   Pulling    5m     kubelet             Pulling image "easypj/web:v2.1.3"
    Warning  Failed     4m30s  kubelet             Failed to pull image: "rpc error: code = NotFound desc = failed to resolve image"
    Warning  Failed     4m     kubelet             Error: ErrImagePull
    Normal   BackOff    3m30s  kubelet             Back-off pulling image "easypj/web:v2.1.3"
    Warning  Failed     3m     kubelet             Error: ImagePullBackOff
  →
  DIAGNOSIS: Image tag "v2.1.3" doesn't exist in registry!
  Fix: Check correct tag and update Deployment with kubectl set image.

  ═══════════ DESCRIBE vs GET ═══════════
  ┌──────────────┬─────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┐
  │               │ kubectl get             │ kubectl describe        │
  ├──────────────┼─────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
  │  Shows        │ Current state (snapshot)│ History (Events)        │
  │  Events       │ ❌ No                   │ ✅ Yes — chronological  │
  │  Conditions   │ ❌ No (without -o yaml) │ ✅ Yes                  │
  │  Exit codes   │ ❌ No                   │ ✅ Yes (State.Reason)   │
  │  Volume info  │ ❌ No                   │ ✅ Yes (Mounts section) │
  │  Tolerations  │ ❌ No                   │ ✅ Yes                  │
  │  Best for     │ Listing, counting       │ Debugging, diagnosing   │
  └──────────────┴─────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: When debugging ANY pod issue, always run kubectl describe pod and scroll to the Events section FIRST. The Events tell you what Kubernetes tried to do and what went wrong. For easypj/jobpost: events like "Failed to pull image," "Liveness probe failed," or "0/3 nodes are available" immediately narrow down the problem.

Observ 🟡 Q98 of 200
How do you copy files to and from a running container using kubectl cp?
A) kubectl cp only copies files FROM containers — you cannot copy files INTO a running container
B) You must use SCP with the node's IP address — kubectl cp does not exist in Kubernetes
C) kubectl cp <source> <dest> works like Unix cp but across pod boundaries. Format: kubectl cp <namespace>/<pod>:<path> <local-path> (from pod) or kubectl cp <local-path> <namespace>/<pod>:<path> (to pod). For multi-container: -c <container>. Useful for: downloading debug logs, uploading config files, extracting data dumps
D) kubectl cp requires the pod to have SSH enabled — it uses SSH protocol for file transfer, not the Kubernetes API
✅ Correct Answer: C

kubectl cp is the file transfer tool for containers. It uses the tar command inside the container to package files and streams them over the Kubernetes API. Both the source and destination can be local or pod paths. For the CKAD exam, know the syntax: <pod>:<path> or <namespace>/<pod>:<path>. The -c flag specifies which container in a multi-container pod.

📝 kubectl cp — File Transfer Reference
kubectl cp — Copy Files To/From Containers
  ═══════════════ SYNTAX ═══════════════
  # FROM pod TO local
  kubectl cp <ns>/<pod>:<remote-path> <local-path>

  # FROM local TO pod
  kubectl cp <local-path> <ns>/<pod>:<remote-path>

  ═══════════════ COMMON USE CASES ═══════════════
  # Download debug logs from Django app
  kubectl cp easypj-prod/easypj-web-9x7k2:/app/debug.log ./debug.log

  # Download from specific container
  kubectl cp easypj-prod/easypj-web-9x7k2:/app/logs -c django ./logs/

  # Upload a config file
  kubectl cp ./config.yaml easypj-prod/easypj-web-9x7k2:/app/config.yaml

  # Extract database dump
  kubectl exec easypj-db-0 -- pg_dump -U postgres easypj > dump.sql
  # (or)
  kubectl cp easypj-prod/easypj-db-0:/tmp/dump.sql ./dump.sql

  ═══════════ LIMITATIONS ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  REQUIREMENT          │ NOTE                             │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  tar in container    │ kubectl cp uses tar internally   │
  │  Shell in container  │ Required for tar to work         │
  │  No symlinks         │ Symlinks are followed (not kept) │
  │  File ownership      │ Copied as root by default        │
  │  Distroless images   │ ❌ kubectl cp FAILS (no tar!)    │
  └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: kubectl cp is useful for the CKAD exam when you need to extract data from a pod for inspection. For easypj/jobpost: download Django debug logs when troubleshooting, or upload corrected configuration files to fix a misconfigured pod (though the proper CKAD way is to update the ConfigMap and restart).

3.4 Built-In CLI Monitoring ToolsQ99-Q104

🟢→🔴 | LF Subtopic 3: Use built-in CLI tools to monitor Kubernetes applications. kubectl top, metrics-server, resource requests/limits, QoS classes, OOM killer.

Observ 🟢 Q99 of 200
What does kubectl top show and what prerequisite must be installed for it to work?
A) kubectl top shows resource usage from the Kubernetes API server directly — no additional components are needed, it works out of the box on every cluster
B) kubectl top pod/node shows CURRENT CPU and memory usage of pods/nodes. It REQUIRES the metrics-server to be installed in the cluster — without it, you get "error: Metrics API not available." The metrics-server collects resource metrics from the kubelet's Summary API and exposes them through the metrics.k8s.io API. kubectl top pod --sort-by=cpu sorts pods by CPU usage; kubectl top node shows cluster-level resource utilization
C) kubectl top shows historical resource usage graphs — it's a built-in monitoring dashboard similar to Grafana
D) kubectl top is deprecated and replaced by kubectl metrics — you must use the newer command on Kubernetes 1.25+
✅ Correct Answer: B

kubectl top is the quickest way to check resource usage. If metrics-server isn't installed (common on CKAD exam clusters!), you'll get an error. The metrics-server is a cluster-wide aggregator that scrapes CPU/memory metrics from each kubelet every 15 seconds. On the CKAD exam, you may need to know that kubectl top requires metrics-server but you typically won't need to install it yourself.

📝 kubectl top — Resource Monitoring at a Glance
kubectl top — Pod & Node Resource Usage

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  kubectl top pod/node                                │
  │       │                                               │
  │       ▼                                               │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  metrics.k8s.io API (provided by metrics-server)│ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │       │                                               │
  │       ▼                                               │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  metrics-server (Deployment in kube-system)     │ │
  │  │  Scrapes kubelet /stats/summary every 15s       │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │       │                                               │
  │       ▼                                               │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  kubelet (on each node) — Summary API           │ │
  │  │  Has per-container CPU/memory from cAdvisor     │ │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ COMMANDS ═══════════════

  kubectl top pod
  →
  NAME               CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
  easypj-web-9x7k2   150m         256Mi

  ═══════════ WITHOUT METRICS-SERVER ═══════════
