CKAD exam tip: On the CKAD exam, kubectl top may or may not work depending on the cluster setup. If it works, use it to quickly check if a pod is consuming excessive resources. If it doesn't work, use kubectl describe node to see allocated resources. For easypj/jobpost: use kubectl top pod -l app=easypj-api to monitor the API tier's resource consumption.

Observ 🟡 Q100 of 200
How does the metrics-server collect and expose container resource metrics?
A) metrics-server runs as a Deployment in kube-system. It queries each kubelet's /stats/summary endpoint every 15 seconds (configurable). The kubelet gets metrics from cAdvisor (Container Advisor), which is built into the kubelet and monitors all containers on the node. metrics-server aggregates these metrics in memory (NOT persistent — restart = data loss) and exposes them via the metrics.k8s.io API. This is used by kubectl top, HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler), and VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler)
B) metrics-server stores all historical metrics in etcd — it provides a full time-series database similar to Prometheus
C) metrics-server is a cloud-only service — it only works on AWS EKS, GCP GKE, and Azure AKS
D) metrics-server collects metrics by running exec probes inside each container — it doesn't use the kubelet API
✅ Correct Answer: A

The metrics-server is simple but essential. It's NOT a full monitoring solution (it doesn't store historical data, show graphs, or send alerts). Its sole purpose is to provide the Resource Metrics API that kubectl top and the HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) depend on. For historical analysis, dashboards, and alerting, you need Prometheus + Grafana — but that's beyond CKAD scope.

📝 metrics-server — Architecture & Limitations
metrics-server Data Flow
  ═══════════════ METRICS-SERVER IN THE CLUSTER ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  kube-system namespace                                       │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  metrics-server Deployment (1 replica typically)       │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
  │  │  │  Every 15s:                                       │  │  │
  │  │  │  1. Discover all nodes via API server             │  │  │
  │  │  │  2. GET https://<node>:10250/stats/summary       │  │  │
  │  │  │  3. Parse CPU/memory per container                │  │  │
  │  │  │  4. Aggregate in memory (NO persistence!)         │  │  │
  │  │  │  5. Expose via metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1              │  │  │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ METRICS-SERVER vs PROMETHEUS ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────┬─────────────────────┬────────────────────┐
  │                   │ METRICS-SERVER      │ PROMETHEUS         │
  ├──────────────────┼─────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │  Purpose          │ HPA + kubectl top   │ Full monitoring    │
  │  Data retention   │ ❌ In-memory only   │ ✅ TSDB (days/mos) │
  │  Dashboards       │ ❌ None             │ ✅ Grafana          │
  │  Alerting         │ ❌ None             │ ✅ AlertManager     │
  │  Custom metrics   │ ❌ CPU/Mem only     │ ✅ Any metric       │
  │  Required for CKAD│ ⚠️  Not tested      │ ❌ Not tested      │
  └──────────────────┴─────────────────────┴────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: For the CKAD exam, you mainly need to know that kubectl top requires metrics-server and that HPA uses the same metrics API. You won't need to install or configure metrics-server on the exam. For easypj/jobpost: if you're setting up HPA for the Django API tier, metrics-server must be installed first.

Observ 🟡 Q101 of 200
What is the difference between resource requests and limits, and why do both matter?
A) Requests and limits are the same thing — they both specify the exact amount of CPU/memory a container will use
B) Requests are maximums and limits are minimums — the terms are intentionally opposite to confuse new users
C) Requests and limits are optional suggestions — Kubernetes ignores them during scheduling and only uses them for monitoring dashboards
D) Requests are the GUARANTEED minimum — the scheduler uses them to decide which node has enough resources (scheduling decision). Limits are the HARD MAXIMUM — the container cannot exceed them (CPU is throttled, memory over limit = OOMKilled). If Request < Limit: Burstable. If Request = Limit: Guaranteed. If neither set: BestEffort. For easypj/jobpost: API: request=200m/256Mi, limit=1/1Gi; DB: request=500m/1Gi, limit=2/2Gi
✅ Correct Answer: D

Resource requests and limits are the foundation of Kubernetes resource management. Requests = scheduling guarantee (the scheduler places pods based on requests). Limits = enforcement ceiling (the kubelet enforces limits with CPU throttling and OOM kills). A pod with no requests can be scheduled on an overcommitted node; a pod with no limits can consume all resources and starve neighbors.

📝 Requests vs Limits — Visual Explanation
How Requests & Limits Work on a Node
  ═══════════════ NODE CAPACITY: 4 CPU / 8Gi ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  Pod A: request=1 CPU  limit=2 CPU                     │  │
  │  │         [████████████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] │  │
  │  │          ◄─── guaranteed ──►◄── can burst ──►          │  │
  │  │                                                         │  │
  │  │  Pod B: request=500m  limit=1 CPU                      │  │
  │  │         [████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] │  │
  │  │                                                         │  │
  │  │  Pod C: request=1 CPU  limit=1 CPU  (Guaranteed QoS)   │  │
  │  │         [█████████████████████████████████████████████] │  │
  │  │                                                         │  │
  │  │  Pod D: NO request, NO limit  (BestEffort QoS) ⚠️       │  │
  │  │         [? (can use anything or be killed first)]       │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                               │
  │  SCHEDULABLE: 4 - (1+0.5+1) = 1.5 CPU remaining for requests│
  │  ACTUAL USAGE: A uses 1.8, B uses 0.3, C uses 0.5, D uses 0 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ CPU vs MEMORY ENFORCEMENT ═══════════
  ┌──────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
  │               │ CPU                   │ MEMORY               │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │  Over limit  │ THROTTLED (slowed)    │ OOMKILLED (killed!)  │
  │  Compressible?│ ✅ Yes               │ ❌ No                 │
  │  Enforcement │ CFS quota (kernel)   │ cgroup memory limit  │
  └──────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ easypj/jobpost RESOURCE RECOMMENDATIONS ═══════════
  ┌──────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │  COMPONENT    │ REQUESTS          │ LIMITS                   │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  Django API  │ 200m CPU, 256Mi   │ 1 CPU, 1Gi               │
  │  Web (nginx) │ 100m CPU, 128Mi   │ 500m CPU, 256Mi          │
  │  PostgreSQL  │ 500m CPU, 1Gi     │ 2 CPU, 2Gi (prod)        │
  │  Redis       │ 100m CPU, 128Mi   │ 500m CPU, 512Mi          │
  │  Celery      │ 200m CPU, 256Mi   │ 1 CPU, 1Gi               │
  └──────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam frequently asks you to set resource requests and limits. Use the imperative approach: kubectl set resources deploy/easypj-api --requests=cpu=200m,memory=256Mi --limits=cpu=1,memory=1Gi. Remember: requests are for SCHEDULING, limits are for ENFORCEMENT. Always set BOTH — missing limits is dangerous (no ceiling), missing requests is unpredictable (no scheduling guarantee).

Observ 🟡 Q102 of 200
What are the three QoS (Quality of Service) classes and how does Kubernetes assign them?
A) QoS classes are user-assigned labels — you manually set qos-class: gold/silver/bronze on each pod
B) Kubernetes AUTOMATICALLY assigns one of three QoS classes based on requests and limits: GUARANTEED (request=limit for all containers, and both CPU and memory are set — highest priority, last to be killed), BURSTABLE (at least one container has request≠limit or only one of CPU/memory is set — middle priority), BESTEFFORT (no requests or limits set on any container — lowest priority, FIRST to be evicted when node runs out of resources). QoS determines OOM kill order: BestEffort → Burstable (by usage relative to request) → Guaranteed
C) There are five QoS classes: Platinum, Gold, Silver, Bronze, and BestEffort
D) QoS classes are only relevant for cloud providers — on-premises clusters don't use QoS for resource management
✅ Correct Answer: B

QoS classes are Kubernetes' automatic priority system for deciding which pods to kill when a node runs out of resources. You don't set QoS directly — it's derived from your resource configuration. The key insight: Guaranteed pods are the last to be killed (they have the most predictable resource usage), while BestEffort pods are killed first (they have no resource contract with the scheduler).

📝 QoS Classes — Decision Tree & OOM Kill Order
QoS Class Assignment — Decision Tree
  ═══════════════ QoS CLASS DECISION TREE ═══════════════
  For EACH container in the pod:
       │
       ├── Does it have BOTH CPU AND MEMORY requests AND limits?
       │   │
       │   ├── YES → Are REQUEST == LIMIT for BOTH CPU and memory?
       │   │   │
       │   │   ├── YES for ALL containers → 🟢 GUARANTEED
       │   │   │   • Highest priority
       │   │   │   • Last to be OOMKilled
       │   │   │   • Most predictable
       │   │   │
       │   │   └── NO (request < limit for ANY) → 🟡 BURSTABLE
       │   │       • Middle priority
       │   │       • Killed after BestEffort
       │   │       • OOM score based on usage vs request
       │   │
       │   └── NO (missing CPU or memory request/limit) → 🟠 BESTEFFORT
       │       • Lowest priority
       │       • FIRST to be OOMKilled
       │       • No resource guarantees

  ═══════════ OOM KILL ORDER ═══════════
  When node memory is exhausted:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1️⃣  BESTEFFORT pods (no requests/limits)              │
  │      → Killed FIRST, regardless of actual usage         │
  │                                                         │
  │  2️⃣  BURSTABLE pods                                    │
  │      → Killed based on OOM score:                       │
  │        (memory_usage - memory_request) / memory_request │
  │      → Higher relative overcommit = killed first        │
  │                                                         │
  │  3️⃣  GUARANTEED pods (requests = limits)               │
  │      → Killed LAST, only if absolutely necessary        │
  │      → Only killed if exceeding their own limit         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ easypj/jobpost QoS ASSIGNMENTS ═══════════
  ┌────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │  COMPONENT      │ CONFIG                │ QoS CLASS        │
  ├────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │  Django API    │ req=200m,lim=1        │ 🟡 Burstable     │
  │  PostgreSQL    │ req=1Gi,lim=2Gi       │ 🟡 Burstable     │
  │  Redis         │ req=256Mi,lim=256Mi   │ 🟢 Guaranteed    │
  │  Debug pod     │ (no resources set)    │ 🟠 BestEffort    │
  └────────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: Check a pod's QoS class with kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'. For production easypj/jobpost deployments, always aim for Guaranteed or Burstable — never BestEffort. A BestEffort pod will be the first victim when the node runs out of memory.

Observ 🔴 Q103 of 200
How does the Linux OOM (Out of Memory) Killer decide which Kubernetes container to kill first?
A) OOM killer randomly selects a container — there is no priority system for OOM kills in Kubernetes
B) OOM killer always kills the container using the MOST absolute memory — the largest memory consumer dies first regardless of QoS class
C) OOM killer uses the OOM score (oom_score_adj) set by the kubelet based on QoS class and memory usage. BestEffort pods get highest OOM score (killed first). Burstable pods get a score proportional to (usage - request) / request — the more a pod exceeds its request, the higher the score. Guaranteed pods get a very negative score (killed last). The pod with the highest oom_score is killed. This means a BestEffort pod using 100Mi is killed BEFORE a Guaranteed pod using 2Gi
D) OOM killer kills the newest pod first — pod age is the only factor in OOM kill decisions
✅ Correct Answer: C

The OOM killer's decision is not random and not based on absolute usage — it's a calculated priority based on QoS class and relative memory overcommit. This is why a 100Mi BestEffort debug pod gets killed before a 2Gi Guaranteed PostgreSQL pod: QoS class matters MORE than absolute memory usage. Understanding this is critical for production: always set resource requests/limits on production pods to protect them from OOM kills.

📝 OOM Killer — How Kubernetes Protects Critical Pods
OOM Kill Decision — QoS-Based Priority
  ═══════════════ OOM KILL SCENARIO ═══════════════
  Node memory: 8Gi total, 7.8Gi used, 200Mi pressure
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Pod A: Django API (Burstable)                               │
  │    Request: 256Mi, Limit: 1Gi, USAGE: 800Mi                  │
  │    OOM Score: (800-256)/256 = 2.125                          │
  │                                                               │
  │  Pod B: PostgreSQL (Guaranteed) ← Will NOT be killed first!  │
  │    Request/Limit: 2Gi, USAGE: 2Gi                             │
  │    OOM Score: -998 (very negative, protected)                 │
  │                                                               │
  │  Pod C: Debug (BestEffort) ← KILLED FIRST!                   │
  │    No requests/limits, USAGE: 50Mi                            │
  │    OOM Score: 1000 (max, no protection)                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  KILL ORDER: Pod C (BestEffort) → Pod A (Burstable) → Pod B (Guaranteed)

  ═══════════ OOM_SCORE_ADJ VALUES ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │  QoS CLASS        │ oom_score_adj │ PRIORITY                 │
  ├──────────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  Guaranteed       │ -997          │ 🟢 Killed LAST           │
  │  Burstable        │ Based on usage│ 🟡 Middle priority       │
  │  (min=2, max=999) │ (request ratio)│ Higher usage → higher  │
  │  BestEffort       │ 1000           │ 🔴 Killed FIRST         │
  └──────────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ HOW TO CHECK ═══════════
  kubectl get pod easypj-db-0 -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
  → Guaranteed

  kubectl describe pod easypj-web | grep -A3 "State"
  → State: Terminated
  →   Reason: OOMKilled
  →   Exit Code: 137  (128 + 9 SIGKILL)

CKAD exam tip: If you see Exit Code: 137 or Reason: OOMKilled in pod status, the container was killed by the OOM killer — it used more memory than its limit (for Guaranteed/Burstable) or the node ran out of memory (for BestEffort). Fix: increase memory limit or reduce the application's memory footprint. For easypj/jobpost: the Django API and PostgreSQL must always have Guaranteed or Burstable QoS.

Observ 🔴 Q104 of 200
What is CPU throttling and how do you detect if your containers are being throttled?
A) CPU throttling happens when a container tries to use MORE CPU than its limit. The Linux CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) quota mechanism forces the container to wait — it can only use its limit's worth of CPU time per period (default: 100ms). Detect with: kubectl top pod (compare usage to limit), or check /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.stat for nr_throttled. Throttling doesn't KILL the container — it just SLOWS it down, which manifests as increased response latency. This is why CPU limits should be set carefully — too low = constant throttling = slow app
B) CPU throttling restarts the container when CPU usage exceeds the limit — it works exactly like memory OOMKill but for CPU
C) CPU throttling only happens on cloud providers — local clusters like kubeadm and kind don't enforce CPU limits
D) CPU throttling is a deprecated feature — Kubernetes 1.30 removed CPU limits entirely in favor of request-only resource management
✅ Correct Answer: A

CPU throttling is the silent performance killer. Unlike memory (where exceeding the limit causes OOMKill — visible and catastrophic), CPU throttling just makes your application slower — sometimes dramatically — without any obvious error message. A container limited to 200m CPU that needs 500m will have its CPU time forcibly limited, causing requests to queue up and latency to spike. This is why many organizations set generous CPU limits or even skip CPU limits entirely (relying on requests for scheduling fairness).

📝 CPU Throttling — The Silent Performance Killer
How CPU Throttling Works
  ═══════════════ CPU THROTTLING MECHANISM ═══════════════
  CFS Period: 100ms (default)
  CPU Limit: 200m (0.2 CPU = 20ms per 100ms period)

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  PERIOD 1 (0-100ms)     PERIOD 2 (100-200ms)             │
  │  ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐              │
  │  │█████████████████│    │█████████████████│              │
  │  │ 20ms running    │    │ 20ms running    │              │
  │  │ (quota used)    │    │ (quota used)    │              │
  │  └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘              │
  │  │░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░│    │░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░│              │
  │  │ 80ms THROTTLED! │    │ 80ms THROTTLED! │              │
  │  │ App is WAITING  │    │ App is WAITING  │              │
  │  └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Request takes 15ms CPU time → Only gets 20ms per period
  → Can process ~1.3 requests per 100ms
  → If 5 requests arrive in one period: 2 processed, 3 DELAYED
  → Response latency SPIKES!

  ═══════════ DETECTING CPU THROTTLING ═══════════
  # Check container CPU stats (inside container)
  cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.stat
  →
  nr_periods 1523          ← Total CFS periods
  nr_throttled 856         ← Periods where quota was exceeded!
  throttled_time 68432000  ← Total microseconds throttled

  → 856/1523 = 56% of periods throttled = SEVERE throttling!

  # Check from outside
  kubectl top pod easypj-api-5k3m8
  → CPU: 198m  (near 200m limit — likely throttled!)

  ═══════════ CPU THROTTLING SYMPTOMS ═══════════
  ┌───────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SYMPTOM              │ LIKELY CAUSE                     │
  ├───────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  High p99 latency     │ Requests waiting for CPU quota   │
  │  CPU usage flat at N  │ CPU limit = N (hard ceiling)     │
  │  No errors in logs    │ Throttling is silent!            │
  │  Variable latency     │ Some periods throttled, some not │
  └───────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam may ask about a pod that's "running but slow." If resource limits are too low, the app is likely being CPU-throttled. Fix with kubectl set resources deploy/name --limits=cpu=500m. For easypj/jobpost Django API: monitor CPU throttling with kubectl top pod -l app=easypj-api and if usage consistently hits the limit, increase it.

3.5 Debugging in KubernetesQ105-Q110

🟢→🔴 | LF Subtopic 5: Debugging in Kubernetes. CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, CreateContainerError, Pending pods, kubectl exec, ephemeral debug containers, kubelet logs.

Observ 🟡 Q105 of 200
Your pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. What is the complete debugging workflow step by step?
A) Immediately delete the pod and recreate it — CrashLoopBackOff is always caused by a temporary node issue that resolves on restart
B) Just wait — CrashLoopBackOff has an automatic recovery mechanism and the pod will fix itself after the backoff period
C) kubectl delete pod and kubectl apply the Deployment again — this is the only way to recover from CrashLoopBackOff
D) Step 1: kubectl logs <pod> --previous (THE most important — shows the error from the crashed container). Step 2: kubectl describe pod (check Events for clues about why it crashed). Step 3: kubectl get pod -o yaml (check command, args, env vars for misconfiguration). Step 4: Check if the image exists and is correct (ErrImagePull vs CrashLoopBackOff). Step 5: Fix the root cause (wrong command, missing config, bad env var) and the pod will automatically recover on next restart
✅ Correct Answer: D

CrashLoopBackOff is NOT a root cause — it's a symptom that means "the container keeps crashing and Kubernetes is spacing out restart attempts." The backoff is exponential (10s → 20s → 40s → ... → max 5 min) to prevent rapid crash-restart loops from consuming all node resources. Deleting the pod doesn't fix the underlying issue — the new pod will crash the same way. You must fix the root cause in the pod spec.

📝 CrashLoopBackOff — Complete Debugging Workflow
CrashLoopBackOff Debugging — easypj/jobpost Example
  ═══════════════ DEBUGGING WORKFLOW ═══════════════
  kubectl get pods
  →
  NAME                    READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
  easypj-web-9x7k2        0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   7

  Step 1: SEE THE ERROR (most important!)
  kubectl logs easypj-web-9x7k2 --previous
  →
  django.core.exceptions.ImproperlyConfigured:
  Set the DATABASE_URL environment variable

  Step 2: CHECK THE EVENTS
  kubectl describe pod easypj-web-9x7k2 | tail -15
  →
  Events:
    Warning  BackOff  3m  Back-off restarting failed container
    Normal   Created  3m  Created container django
    Normal   Started  3m  Started container django
    Warning  BackOff  1m  Back-off restarting failed container

  Step 3: INSPECT CONFIGURATION
  kubectl get pod easypj-web-9x7k2 -o yaml | grep -A5 env
  →
  env:              ← EMPTY! No DATABASE_URL set!
  (no environment variables)

  Step 4: FIX THE ROOT CAUSE
  kubectl set env deploy/easypj-web DATABASE_URL=postgres://...
  → deployment.apps/easypj-web env updated
  → New pod created with correct env → Running!

  ═══════════ CRASHLOOPBACKOFF vs OTHER STATES ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬────────────────────┐
  │  STATUS               │ MEANS               │ FIRST COMMAND      │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │  CrashLoopBackOff    │ App crashes on start│ logs --previous    │
  │  ImagePullBackOff    │ Can't pull image    │ describe pod       │
  │  ErrImagePull        │ Image pull error    │ Check image name   │
  │  CreateContainerError│ Invalid container   │ describe pod       │
  │                      │ config              │ (Mount/Command err)│
  │  Pending             │ Can't schedule      │ describe pod       │
  │                      │                     │ (Resources/Nodes)  │
  └──────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: CrashLoopBackOff is one of the most common CKAD debugging scenarios. The exam will give you a broken pod — your job is to diagnose and fix it. Your first command should ALWAYS be kubectl logs --previous. Don't waste time describing or getting YAML before you see the logs. For easypj/jobpost, common CrashLoopBackOff causes: missing DATABASE_URL, missing SECRET_KEY, or database migration errors.

Observ 🟢 Q106 of 200
Your pod shows ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull. What are the possible causes and fixes?
A) ImagePullBackOff always means the registry is down — just wait and it will resolve automatically when the registry comes back online
B) Three main causes: (1) WRONG IMAGE NAME/TAG — typo in the image field, or tag doesn't exist (check with docker pull locally). Fix: kubectl set image deploy/name container=correct:tag. (2) PRIVATE REGISTRY AUTH — image exists but cluster lacks credentials. Fix: kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=... --docker-username=... --docker-password=... and reference in pod spec. (3) NETWORK ISSUE — node can't reach the registry. Fix: check node network, proxy settings. Diagnose with: kubectl describe pod (Events show exact error)
C) ImagePullBackOff only happens with public images — private registries always work without authentication in Kubernetes
D) kubectl pull-image is the command to manually pull images and fix ImagePullBackOff errors
✅ Correct Answer: B

ImagePullBackOff is the second most common CKAD debugging scenario (after CrashLoopBackOff). The error is straightforward — Kubernetes can't pull the container image — but the ROOT CAUSE can vary. Always check kubectl describe pod for the exact error message in the Events section. It will tell you whether the issue is a missing tag, authentication failure, or network problem.

📝 ImagePullBackOff — Diagnostic Flowchart
ImagePullBackOff — Root Cause Analysis
  ═══════════════ DIAGNOSTIC FLOWCHART ═══════════════
  kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 Events
       │
       ├── "manifest unknown" or "not found"
       │   → Image name or tag is WRONG
       │   → Fix: Check registry, correct the image field
       │
       ├── "unauthorized: authentication required"
       │   → Private registry, no credentials
       │   → Fix: Create imagePullSecrets
       │       kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
       │         --docker-server=ghcr.io \
       │         --docker-username=easypj \
       │         --docker-password=$TOKEN \
       │         --docker-email=dev@easypj.com
       │
       └── "dial tcp: i/o timeout" or "no such host"
           → Network issue — node can't reach registry
           → Fix: Check DNS, proxy, firewall rules

  ═══════════════ CREATING IMAGEPULLSECRETS ═══════════════
  # 1. Create the secret
  kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-secret \
    --docker-server=ghcr.io \
    --docker-username=easypj \
    --docker-password=ghp_xxx \
    -n easypj-prod

  # 2. Reference in Pod spec (or add to ServiceAccount)
  spec:
    imagePullSecrets:
    - name: ghcr-secret
    containers:
    - name: django
      image: ghcr.io/easypj/jobpost:v2.1

  # 3. Or add to default ServiceAccount (all pods in namespace)
  kubectl patch serviceaccount default -n easypj-prod \
    -p '{"imagePullSecrets": [{"name": "ghcr-secret"}]}'

CKAD exam tip: On the CKAD exam, you'll typically use images already present in the cluster's registry. But if you encounter ImagePullBackOff, your diagnostic workflow is: (1) describe pod to see the error, (2) verify the image name and tag, (3) create imagePullSecrets if needed. For easypj/jobpost, all images should be pre-pushed to a registry accessible from all your 6-cluster lab nodes.

Observ 🟡 Q107 of 200
Your pod shows CreateContainerError. What causes this and how do you fix it?
A) CreateContainerError means the container runtime (containerd/CRI-O) couldn't create the container. Common causes: (1) INVALID COMMAND/ARGS — the specified command doesn't exist in the image (e.g., /bin/bash in a distroless image), (2) MISSING VOLUME MOUNT SOURCE — referenced ConfigMap/Secret/PVC doesn't exist, (3) INVALID SECURITY CONTEXT — impossible UID/GID or capability, (4) BROKEN HOOK — postStart/preStop hook command fails. Fix by checking kubectl describe pod for the exact error in Events, then correcting the pod spec
B) CreateContainerError means the cluster is full — you need to delete other pods to make room for new containers
C) CreateContainerError only happens with Windows containers — it's not applicable to Linux containers that run on standard Kubernetes clusters
D) CreateContainerError automatically resolves within 5 minutes — Kubernetes retries container creation with exponential backoff until it succeeds
✅ Correct Answer: A

CreateContainerError is different from CrashLoopBackOff — the container never started at all! The container runtime rejected the configuration before the process began. The most common cause on CKAD is a missing ConfigMap or Secret referenced in a volume mount, or an invalid command in a distroless container.

📝 CreateContainerError — Common Causes & Fixes
CreateContainerError Diagnostic Table
  ═══════════════ CAUSE → EVENT MESSAGE → FIX ═══════════════
  ┌─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
  │  CAUSE               │ EVENT MESSAGE       │ FIX                  │
  ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │  Missing ConfigMap   │ "MountVolume.SetUp  │ Create the ConfigMap │
  │  or Secret           │  failed: configmap  │ kubectl create cm    │
  │                      │  'app-config' not   │ app-config ...       │
  │                      │  found"             │                      │
  ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │  Invalid command     │ "exec: '/bin/bash': │ Change command to    │
  │  in distroless       │  stat /bin/bash: no │ something that exists│
  │                      │  such file or dir"  │ in the image         │
  ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │  Missing PVC         │ "MountVolume.SetUp  │ Create the PVC       │
  │                      │  failed: persistent │ kubectl apply -f     │
  │                      │  volumeclaim 'data' │ pvc.yaml             │
  │                      │  not found"         │                      │
  ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │  Invalid UID/GID     │ "container has      │ Fix securityContext  │
  │                      │  runAsNonRoot and   │ or use valid UID     │
  │                      │  image has UID 0"   │                      │
  ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │  postStart hook fail│ "PostStartHookError:│ Fix or remove the    │
  │                      │  command exited     │ postStart hook       │
  │                      │  with code 1"       │                      │
  └─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ DISTROLESS GOTCHA ═══════════
  ❌ Won't work:  command: ["/bin/bash", "-c", "echo hello"]
                  → /bin/bash doesn't exist in distroless!

  ✅ Use:         command: ["/app/server"]
                  → Direct binary execution (no shell needed)

CKAD exam tip: If the CKAD exam asks you to mount a ConfigMap/Secret as a volume and you get CreateContainerError, check that the ConfigMap/Secret EXISTS first with kubectl get cm or kubectl get secret. Create it if needed before the pod can start. For easypj/jobpost: ensure app-config ConfigMap and db-creds Secret exist before deploying pods that reference them.

Observ 🟡 Q108 of 200
Your pod is stuck in Pending state. What are the possible reasons and how do you diagnose each?
A) Pending always means the image is still downloading — just wait longer and the pod will eventually start
B) Pending means the pod was created but hasn't been acknowledged by the API server yet — it's a temporary state that resolves in seconds
C) Pending means the pod was ACCEPTED by the API server but NOT YET SCHEDULED to a node (or scheduled but containers not created). Diagnose with: kubectl describe pod and check Events — "0/N nodes are available" with reasons like: Insufficient cpu/memory (no node has enough), node selector/affinity mismatch (pod wants a label no node has), taint/toleration mismatch (pod doesn't tolerate node taints), PVC not bound (pod needs storage that's not available). Also check: kubectl get nodes (are nodes Ready?), kubectl top node (are nodes full?)
D) Pending pods are waiting for manual approval from a cluster administrator — this is a security feature for production clusters
✅ Correct Answer: C

A Pending pod is the Kubernetes equivalent of "waiting for a table at a restaurant." The reservation is made (API server accepted it), but there's no available table (node) yet. The Events section of kubectl describe pod tells you exactly WHY it can't be seated — not enough resources, wrong neighborhood (node selector), or the table isn't ready (node not Ready).

📝 Pod Stuck Pending — Diagnostic Guide
Why Is My Pod Pending? — Decision Tree
  ═══════════════ PENDING POD DIAGNOSIS ═══════════════
  kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A10 Events
       │
       ├── "0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu"
       │   → No node has enough CPU for the pod's requests
       │   → Fix: Reduce resource requests OR add nodes
       │
       ├── "0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) didn't match node selector"
       │   → Pod requires labels no node has
       │   → Fix: Check nodeSelector, add labels to nodes
       │
       ├── "0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) had taint {..}, that pod didn't tolerate"
       │   → Nodes have taints pod doesn't tolerate
       │   → Fix: Add toleration to pod OR remove taint from node
       │
       ├── "0/3 nodes are available: 3 persistentvolumeclaim 'data' not found"
       │   → PVC referenced but doesn't exist
       │   → Fix: Create the PVC first
       │
       └── "0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) were unschedulable"
           → All nodes are cordoned (kubectl cordon)
           → Fix: kubectl uncordon <node>

  ═══════════ QUICK CHECKS ═══════════
  kubectl get nodes                    # Are nodes Ready?
  kubectl describe node <node>         # Node conditions, capacity
  kubectl top node                     # Current resource usage
  kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -10

  ═══════════ COMMON CKAD PENDING SCENARIOS ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
  │  REASON               │ DIAGNOSTIC           │ FIX                  │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
  │  Insufficient CPU     │ Events + describe    │ Lower requests       │
  │  Node affinity/taints │ describe pod + node  │ Fix affinity/tolerate│
  │  PVC not found        │ Events shows PVC err │ Create PVC first     │
  │  Nodes NotReady       │ kubectl get nodes    │ Fix node issues      │
  └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: On the CKAD exam, if a pod is Pending, kubectl describe pod is your first command. The Events section will contain the exact scheduling failure reason. For easypj/jobpost: if the PostgreSQL pod is Pending, check that the PVC for data storage exists and has a matching PV available.

Observ 🟡 Q109 of 200
How do you get an interactive shell inside a running container using kubectl exec?
A) kubectl exec requires SSH access to the node — you cannot get a shell inside a container through kubectl directly
B) kubectl shell <pod> — this is the dedicated command for interactive container access, not kubectl exec
C) kubectl exec only works with containers that have SSH server running — it's not available for most application containers
D) kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/sh (or /bin/bash) gives you an interactive shell. Flags: -i (stdin, keep input open), -t (TTY, allocate a terminal), -- (separates kubectl flags from container command). For multi-container: -c <container>. Without -it you can run single commands: kubectl exec <pod> -- ls /app. Essential for: checking files, testing network connectivity (curl, ping), inspecting running processes (ps aux), and running database CLI tools (psql, redis-cli)
✅ Correct Answer: D

kubectl exec is your direct line into a running container. It's like SSH for containers — you get a shell or run any command. The -it flags are critical: -i keeps stdin open (so you can type), -t allocates a pseudo-TTY (so you get proper terminal formatting, colors, and interactive prompts). Without -it, kubectl exec runs a single command and returns the output — perfect for one-off checks.

📝 kubectl exec — Interactive Debugging Reference
kubectl exec — All Patterns
  ═══════════════ INTERACTIVE SHELL ═══════════════
  kubectl exec -it easypj-web-9x7k2 -- /bin/sh
  → Now inside the container!
  → /app $ ls
  → manage.py  requirements.txt  static/  templates/
  → /app $ env | grep DATABASE
  → DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@easypj-db:5432/easypj
  → /app $ exit

  ═══════════════ SINGLE COMMAND ═══════════════
  kubectl exec easypj-web-9x7k2 -- ls /app
  → manage.py requirements.txt static/ templates/

  kubectl exec easypj-web-9x7k2 -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
  → nameserver 10.96.0.10
  → search easypj-prod.svc.cluster.local

  kubectl exec easypj-web-9x7k2 -- python manage.py check
  → System check identified no issues (0 silenced).

  ═══════════════ MULTI-CONTAINER ═══════════════
  kubectl exec -it easypj-pod -c django -- /bin/sh
  kubectl exec -it easypj-pod -c redis -- redis-cli

  ═══════════════ NETWORK TESTING ═══════════════
  kubectl exec easypj-web-9x7k2 -- curl -s http://easypj-api:8000/healthz
  → {"status": "ok"}

  kubectl exec easypj-web-9x7k2 -- nslookup easypj-db
  → Name: easypj-db.easypj-prod.svc.cluster.local
  → Address: 10.96.50.15

  ═══════════ COMMON CKAD DEBUG COMMANDS ═══════════
  ┌─────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GOAL                │ COMMAND                          │
  ├─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Check processes    │ kubectl exec pod -- ps aux        │
  │  Check listening    │ kubectl exec pod -- netstat -tlnp │
  │  ports              │                                   │
  │  Test DNS           │ kubectl exec pod -- nslookup svc  │
  │  Test HTTP          │ kubectl exec pod -- curl svc:port │
  │  Check env vars     │ kubectl exec pod -- env           │
  │  Check mounts       │ kubectl exec pod -- df -h         │
  │  Check files        │ kubectl exec pod -- ls -la /path  │
  └─────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: kubectl exec is tested frequently on CKAD. Remember: (1) always use -it for interactive shells, (2) the -- separates kubectl flags from the container command, (3) the container must have a shell (/bin/sh or /bin/bash) for interactive access — distroless images won't work, (4) you can run ANY command available in the container image.

Observ 🔴 Q110 of 200
What are ephemeral debug containers (kubectl debug) and when are they essential?
A) Ephemeral debug containers are a logging plugin — they capture all container stdout/stderr to a persistent volume for later analysis
B) kubectl debug creates a TEMPORARY container alongside the existing pod containers — sharing the same process namespace (shareProcessNamespace), network, and volumes if needed. This is essential when: (1) the target container has NO SHELL (distroless images — you can't kubectl exec into it), (2) the target container keeps crashing (can't exec into a dead container), (3) you need debugging tools (tcpdump, strace, gdb) NOT available in the application image. The debug container gets its OWN image (e.g., busybox, alpine, nicolaka/netshoot) and can inspect the pod's processes, network, and filesystem from the outside
C) kubectl debug is deprecated — it was removed in Kubernetes 1.25 in favor of kubectl exec with extra flags
D) Ephemeral debug containers permanently modify the pod spec — they continue running even after debugging is complete and must be manually removed
✅ Correct Answer: B

Ephemeral debug containers (GA in Kubernetes 1.25, available since 1.18 as alpha) solve the "can't debug a distroless container" problem. Distroless images (like gcr.io/distroless/python3) contain only the application and its runtime — no shell, no debugging tools. You can't kubectl exec into them because there's no /bin/sh. Ephemeral containers let you attach a debugging sidecar with full tools that shares the target's process namespace, letting you inspect from outside what you can't enter from inside.

📝 Ephemeral Debug Containers — Debugging the Undebuggable
kubectl debug — Distroless & CrashLoopBackOff Debugging
  ═══════════════ USE CASE 1: DISTROLESS CONTAINER ═══════════════
  # Pod runs distroless Python image (NO /bin/sh!)
  kubectl exec -it easypj-distroless -- /bin/sh
  → error: Internal error occurred: error executing command
    in container: failed to exec in container: container
    does not have a shell

  # SOLUTION: Attach ephemeral debug container
  kubectl debug -it easypj-distroless \
    --image=busybox --target=django
  → Now in debug container!
  → / # ps aux            ← See target container's processes!
  → / # ls /proc/1/root   ← Access target's filesystem!
  → / # cat /proc/1/root/app/manage.py

  ═══════════════ USE CASE 2: CRASHING CONTAINER ═══════════════
  # Pod keeps crashing — can't exec because it's not running
  kubectl debug easypj-crashing --image=busybox \
    --copy-to=easypj-debug --share-processes
  → Creates COPY of pod with debug container added
  → Original pod unchanged
  → Inspect the copy to understand why original crashes

  ═══════════════ USE CASE 3: NETWORK DEBUGGING ═══════════════
  kubectl debug -it easypj-api-pod \
    --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=django
  → Full network debugging toolkit: tcpdump, netstat, curl, dig
  → # tcpdump -i eth0 port 8000
  → # dig easypj-db.easypj-prod.svc.cluster.local

  ═══════════════ DEBUG CONTAINER IMAGES ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  IMAGE            │ TOOLS INCLUDED                      │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  busybox          │ Basic: sh, cat, ls, ps, netstat     │
  │  alpine           │ apk add any tool you need           │
  │  nicolaka/netshoot│ Network pros: tcpdump, strace, dig, │
  │                   │ curl, nmap, iperf, socat            │
  │  ubuntu           │ Full OS: apt install anything       │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ KEY FLAGS ═══════════
  --target=<container>     Attach to specific container
  --image=<debug-image>   Image for debug container
  --copy-to=<name>        Create pod copy (don't modify original)
  --share-processes        Share process namespace
  -it                       Interactive TTY

🚀 Beyond CKAD (CKS crossover): Ephemeral debug containers have important security implications. In CKS, you learn that debug containers bypass normal pod security controls (they're added via the EphemeralContainers sub-resource). Attackers with pod/ephemeralcontainers RBAC can attach debug containers to any pod, gaining access to its processes, network, and filesystem. Always audit ephemeral container access in production clusters.

🔐 Category 4: Application Environment, Configuration & Security (25%)Q111-Q160

🟢→🟡→🔴→🚀 Progressive: Configuring & Securing Kubernetes Applications

This is the BIGGEST CKAD category (25%). It's about making your application configurable, secure, and well-integrated with its environment. Think of it like setting up a smart home — you need power (resources), keys (Secrets), settings (ConfigMaps), identity cards (ServiceAccounts), and security cameras (SecurityContexts). For easypj/jobpost, this means ConfigMaps for Django settings, Secrets for database passwords, RBAC for API access control, and SecurityContexts to run containers as non-root with read-only filesystems.

CKAD Weight: 25% | 50 Questions | 🟢 8 Qs · 🟡 24 Qs · 🔴 14 Qs · 🚀 4 Qs

⚠️ This category has the steepest learning curve. Master ConfigMaps/Secrets (🟡) first, then tackle RBAC (🔴), then CRD/Operators (🔴).

4.1 CRD & Operators — Extending KubernetesQ111-Q116

🟡→🔴 | LF Subtopic 1: Discover and use resources that extend Kubernetes (CRD, Operators).

Security 🔴 Q111 of 200
What is a Custom Resource Definition (CRD) and how does it extend the Kubernetes API?
A) A CRD is a plugin that modifies how kubectl displays existing resources — it's purely cosmetic and doesn't add new API functionality
B) A CRD is a security policy that defines custom RBAC roles for the cluster — it's part of the authorization system
C) A CRD allows you to DEFINE YOUR OWN RESOURCE TYPES that behave like native Kubernetes resources (Pods, Deployments). Once a CRD is created, you can create Custom Resources (CRs) of that type, use kubectl get/describe/delete on them, and controllers can watch them to automate application management. Example: defining a "JobPost" CRD for easypj that creates a Deployment + Service + ConfigMap from a single custom resource. CRD = schema definition; CR = instance of that schema; Operator = CRD + Controller that automates lifecycle
D) A CRD replaces the existing Kubernetes API — once installed, you must use custom resources instead of built-in resources like Pods and Deployments
✅ Correct Answer: C

A CRD is Kubernetes' extension mechanism — it allows you to teach Kubernetes about new resource types. Think of the Kubernetes API as a dictionary: Pod, Deployment, and Service are built-in words. A CRD lets you add YOUR OWN words to the dictionary — like "JobPost", "DatabaseBackup", or "Certificate". Once added, kubectl get jobposts works just like kubectl get pods. Combined with a custom controller (the Operator pattern), you get automated lifecycle management for complex applications.

📝 CRD Architecture — Extending the Kubernetes API
CRD → Custom Resource → Controller (Operator)
  ═══════════════ CRD = BLUEPRINT ═══════════════
  apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
  kind: CustomResourceDefinition
  metadata:
    name: jobposts.easypj.com        ← <plural>.<group>
  spec:
    group: easypj.com                 ← Your API group
    versions:
    - name: v1                        ← API version
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:                          ← OpenAPI v3 schema
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              properties:
                title: {type: string}
                company: {type: string}
                replicas: {type: integer, minimum: 1}
    scope: Namespaced                 ← Namespaced or Cluster
    names:
      plural: jobposts                ← kubectl get jobposts
      singular: jobpost               ← Singular form
      kind: JobPost                   ← PascalCase kind
      shortNames: ["jp"]              ← kubectl get jp

  ═══════════════ CR = INSTANCE ═══════════════
  apiVersion: easypj.com/v1
  kind: JobPost
  metadata:
    name: senior-backend-dev
  spec:
    title: "Senior Backend Developer"
    company: "easypj"
    replicas: 3

  ═══════════════ AFTER CRD CREATION ═══════════════
  kubectl apply -f crd.yaml           # Define the new type
  kubectl apply -f cr.yaml            # Create an instance
  kubectl get jobposts                # List all JobPosts
  kubectl describe jobpost senior-backend-dev
  kubectl get jp                      # Short name!

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam may ask you to create a CRD or interact with existing CRDs. Know that CRDs are cluster-scoped (even if the CRs they define are namespaced). Use kubectl get crds to see all installed CRDs and kubectl explain <custom-resource> to explore their schema. For easypj/jobpost: a CRD could automate deploying the entire job board stack from a single custom resource.

Security 🔴 Q112 of 200
How do you create a CRD and what are the key fields you must define?
A) Create a CRD YAML with apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1, kind: CustomResourceDefinition. Key required fields: metadata.name (must match <plural>.<group>), spec.group (API group), spec.versions (at least one with served/storage), spec.scope (Namespaced or Cluster), spec.names (plural, singular, kind). The spec.versions[].schema.openAPIV3Schema defines the structure of your custom resources using OpenAPI v3. Apply with kubectl apply -f crd.yaml
B) kubectl create crd jobpost —api-group=easypj.com — this imperative command creates CRDs without YAML
C) CRDs are defined in JSON format only — YAML is not supported for CRD definitions
D) CRDs must be approved by the cluster administrator before they can be applied — they require a ClusterRoleBinding to function
✅ Correct Answer: A

Creating a CRD is essentially defining a schema using the OpenAPI v3 specification. The key naming convention is critical: metadata.name MUST be <plural>.<group> (e.g., jobposts.easypj.com). The spec.names section defines how users interact with your resource: plural is the URL path, kind is the PascalCase type, and shortNames are kubectl aliases.

📝 CRD Creation — Field-by-Field Reference
Anatomy of a CRD
  ═══════════════ CRITICAL NAMING CONVENTION ═══════════════
  metadata.name = <plural>.<group>
  Example: jobposts.easypj.com
            ──────── ──────────
            plural   group (must match spec.group)

  ═══════════════ CRD KEY FIELDS ═══════════════
  ┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  FIELD                   │ PURPOSE                          │
  ├─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  spec.group              │ API group (e.g., easypj.com)    │
  │  spec.versions[].name    │ API version (v1, v1alpha1, etc) │
  │  spec.versions[].served  │ Is this version available?      │
  │  spec.versions[].storage │ Is this the storage version?    │
  │  spec.scope              │ Namespaced or Cluster           │
  │  spec.names.plural       │ URL path + kubectl plural       │
  │  spec.names.singular     │ Singular form                   │
  │  spec.names.kind         │ PascalCase kind                 │
  │  spec.names.shortNames   │ kubectl aliases (optional)      │
  │  spec.versions[].schema  │ OpenAPI v3 validation schema    │
  └─────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ CRD LIFECYCLE ═══════════
  kubectl apply -f crd.yaml
  → CRD created → New REST endpoint registered:
    /apis/easypj.com/v1/namespaces/{ns}/jobposts

  kubectl get crds | grep easypj
  → jobposts.easypj.com   2024-06-11T14:30:00Z

  kubectl api-resources --api-group=easypj.com
  → NAME       SHORTNAMES   APIVERSION       NAMESPACED
  → jobposts   jp           easypj.com/v1    true

CKAD exam tip: On the CKAD exam, CRD creation tasks usually provide a YAML snippet or ask you to complete one. The most common mistakes: (1) forgetting that name must be <plural>.<group>, (2) using wrong apiVersion for the CRD itself (apiextensions.k8s.io/v1), (3) schema validation errors. Always test with kubectl apply --dry-run=client first.

Security 🔴 Q113 of 200
What is a Kubernetes Operator and how does it differ from a simple CRD?
A) An Operator is just another name for a CRD — the terms are interchangeable with no functional difference
B) A CRD is just the DATA SCHEMA (defines what a custom resource looks like). An Operator = CRD + CUSTOM CONTROLLER — it's an application that watches custom resources and takes ACTION to reconcile the desired state with the actual state. Example: a PostgreSQL Operator watches PostgresCluster CRs and automatically creates StatefulSets, Services, PVCs, ConfigMaps, handles backups, and performs failovers. Without the controller, a CRD is just a data store — inert YAML with no automation
C) An Operator can only be written in Go — Python, Java, and other languages cannot be used to build Operators
D) Operators are only available on OpenShift — standard Kubernetes does not support the Operator pattern
✅ Correct Answer: B

The Operator pattern is Kubernetes' automation superpower. A CRD alone is like a form — you can fill it out and store it, but nothing happens. An Operator is the robot that reads the form and DOES the work. For easypj/jobpost, a custom Operator could watch for JobPost CRs and automatically create the Deployment for the job board, provision a PostgreSQL instance, set up monitoring, and handle upgrades — all from a single custom resource.

📝 Operator Pattern — CRD + Controller = Automation
How an Operator Works — The Reconciliation Loop
  ═══════════════ OPERATOR RECONCILIATION LOOP ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     OPERATOR (Controller)                    │
  │                                                              │
  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐              │
  │  │ OBSERVE  │ →  │ ANALYZE  │ →  │   ACT    │              │
  │  │          │    │          │    │          │              │
  │  │ Watch    │    │ Compare  │    │ Create/  │              │
  │  │ CR       │    │ desired  │    │ Update/  │              │
  │  │ changes  │    │ vs actual│    │ Delete   │              │
  │  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘              │
  │       │               │               │                     │
  │       └───────────────┴───────────────┘                     │
  │                       │                                     │
  │                       ▼                                     │
  │              ┌─────────────────┐                            │
  │              │ REPEAT FOREVER  │  ← Reconciliation Loop     │
  │              └─────────────────┘                            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ EXAMPLE: JOBPOST OPERATOR ═══════════════
  User creates JobPost CR:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  kind: JobPost                                           │
  │  spec:                                                   │
  │    title: "Job Board v2"                                 │
  │    replicas: 3                                           │
  │    database: postgresql                                  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │
         ▼ Operator's Reconciliation Loop
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. OBSERVE: "A new JobPost CR was created"             │
  │  2. ANALYZE: "No Deployment, Service, or DB exists yet" │
  │  3. ACT:                                                 │
  │     • Create Deployment (replicas: 3)                    │
  │     • Create Service (ClusterIP)                         │
  │     • Create PostgreSQL StatefulSet                      │
  │     • Create ConfigMap with DB connection string         │
  │     • Update JobPost status: "Ready"                     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ FRAMEWORKS FOR BUILDING OPERATORS ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  FRAMEWORK        │ LANGUAGE / NOTES                    │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Operator SDK     │ Go, Ansible, Helm (Red Hat)         │
  │  Kubebuilder      │ Go (CNCF, used by Operator SDK)    │
  │  Kopf             │ Python (lightweight)                │
  │  Metacontroller   │ Any language (JSON webhooks)        │
  │  KUDO             │ Declarative (YAML-based)            │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: For CKAD, you mainly need to understand what Operators ARE and how to USE them (install from OperatorHub, create custom resources). You won't be asked to write an Operator from scratch. Focus on: (1) knowing that CRD + Controller = Operator, (2) the reconciliation loop concept, (3) kubectl get crds to see what's available.

Security 🔴 Q114 of 200
How does the Operator reconciliation loop work — what are the steps from observing a change to acting on it?
A) Operators use cron jobs to periodically check resources — they don't react to real-time changes
B) The reconciliation loop is a simple if-else statement: if resource exists, create it; if not, do nothing — there is no state comparison
C) Operators use machine learning to predict what resources need to be created — the reconciliation loop is AI-driven
D) The reconciliation loop has 3 phases: OBSERVE (watch CR and related resources via the API), ANALYZE (compare DESIRED state from the CR spec vs ACTUAL state from cluster), ACT (create/update/delete resources to converge reality toward desire). This loop runs CONTINUOUSLY — if something drifts (a human deletes a managed Deployment), the Operator recreates it. This is the same pattern used by built-in controllers like Deployment and ReplicaSet
✅ Correct Answer: D

The reconciliation loop is the heart of Kubernetes itself. Every built-in controller (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Job, StatefulSet) uses this exact pattern. The Operator pattern simply extends this to custom resources. The beauty is that the loop is level-triggered, not edge-triggered — it doesn't matter WHY the state changed (user edit, node failure, manual deletion), only that the current state differs from the desired state.

📝 Reconciliation Loop — Deep Dive
Level-Triggered Reconciliation — Self-Healing in Action
  ═══════════════ RECONCILIATION LOOP IN PSEUDOCODE ═══════════════
  while True:
      # 1. OBSERVE
      desired = get_custom_resource("my-jobpost")
      actual_deployment = get_deployment("my-jobpost")
      actual_service = get_service("my-jobpost")
      actual_configmap = get_configmap("my-jobpost")

      # 2. ANALYZE
      if actual_deployment is None:
          # 3. ACT — Create
          create_deployment(desired.spec)
          update_status(desired, "Deploying")
      elif actual_deployment.spec.replicas != desired.spec.replicas:
          # 3. ACT — Update
          update_deployment(actual_deployment, desired.spec)
          update_status(desired, "Scaling")
      elif actual_service is None:
          create_service(desired.spec)
      else:
          # Everything matches — do nothing
          update_status(desired, "Ready")

      sleep(10)  # Requeue after 10 seconds

  ═══════════ LEVEL vs EDGE TRIGGERED ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LEVEL-TRIGGERED     │ EDGE-TRIGGERED                   │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  "The desired state  │ "User clicked SAVE → scale      │
  │   is 5 replicas"     │  up by 2"                        │
  │  Works EVEN IF the   │ If the event is MISSED (network │
  │  event was missed    │ blip), the change is lost        │
  │  ✅ Kubernetes uses  │ ❌ Kubernetes does NOT use this  │
  │  level-triggered!    │   for controllers               │
  └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: Understanding the reconciliation loop helps you debug why an Operator isn't working: (1) Check the CR's status field — does the Operator update it? (2) Check the Operator's logs — is it seeing the CR? (3) Check RBAC — does the Operator's ServiceAccount have permissions to create the resources it needs? For easypj/jobpost, an Operator would continuously reconcile the desired state of the job board application.

Security 🟡 Q115 of 200
What is OperatorHub and how do you discover and install community Operators?
A) OperatorHub is a GitHub repository that only lists Operators — you must manually clone, build, and deploy each Operator yourself
B) OperatorHub.io is a public registry of Kubernetes Operators. You can browse Operators by category (Database, Monitoring, Security, Storage). Popular examples: Prometheus Operator (automated Prometheus/Alertmanager/Grafana), cert-manager (automatic TLS certificates), PostgreSQL Operator (managed databases), Strimzi (Kafka on K8s). On OpenShift, OperatorHub is built into the console. On vanilla K8s, use OLM (Operator Lifecycle Manager) or install Operators manually via their Helm charts or YAML manifests
C) OperatorHub is a paid marketplace — all Operators require a commercial license to install and use
D) OperatorHub only works on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) — other Kubernetes distributions don't support it
✅ Correct Answer: B

OperatorHub is the app store for Kubernetes Operators. Instead of deploying raw YAML manifests and manually managing complex applications, you can install Operators that automate the entire lifecycle. For easypj/jobpost, you could use the PostgreSQL Operator from OperatorHub to automatically provision, back up, and scale the database tier without writing any database management code.

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam doesn't test OperatorHub directly, but you should know what it is and how Operators fit into the Kubernetes ecosystem. The exam may ask about CRDs and their relationship to Operators. For easypj/jobpost: the PostgreSQL Operator from OperatorHub would handle backups, scaling, and failover for the production database automatically.

Security 🔴 Q116 of 200
How do you list installed CRDs and explore the schema of a custom resource?
A) CRDs are hidden from regular users — only cluster administrators can list them with special privileges
B) kubectl get custom-resources lists all installed CRDs and their custom resource instances
C) kubectl get crds (list all CRDs). kubectl describe crd <name> (see full schema). kubectl explain <custom-resource> (interactive field reference — works with CRDs too!). kubectl api-resources --api-group=<group> (list resources in the custom API group). kubectl get <plural> (list instances of the custom resource, just like built-in resources)
D) kubectl crd list — this is a dedicated CRD management command separate from kubectl get
✅ Correct Answer: C

Once a CRD is installed, custom resources behave exactly like built-in resources. kubectl get, kubectl describe, kubectl explain, and kubectl delete all work with custom resources. This is the beauty of the Kubernetes API extension model — there's no special syntax for custom resources. The CKAD exam may test your ability to interact with pre-installed CRDs.

📝 Working with CRDs — Complete Command Reference
CRD Operations Cheat Sheet
  ═══════════════ CRD DISCOVERY ═══════════════
  # List all installed CRDs
  kubectl get crds
  →

  prometheuses.monitoring.coreos.com 2024-04-15T10:00:00Z

  # See full CRD schema

  → Shows versions, schema, accepted names, conditions

🚀 Beyond CKAD (CKA crossover): Cluster administrators need to understand how CRDs affect cluster performance (each CRD adds API server load), how to manage CRD lifecycle (versioning, deprecation, conversion), and how admission webhooks interact with custom resources. Tools like kubebuilder and operator-sdk are used to build production Operators with proper validation, status management, and testing.

4.2 Auth, RBAC & Admission ControlQ117-Q124

🟡→🔴 | LF Subtopic 2: Understand authentication, authorization, and admission control. RBAC, Pod Security Standards.

Security 🟡 Q117 of 200
What are the "3 A's" of Kubernetes security — Authentication, Authorization, and Admission Control?
A) All three terms mean the same thing — they're different names for checking if a user can access a resource
B) Authentication handles what you can do, Authorization handles who you are, and Admission Control handles logging — the order doesn't matter
C) Admission Control is the first step — it blocks requests before authentication or authorization are checked
D) Authentication (WHO are you? — verify identity via certs, tokens, OIDC), Authorization (WHAT can you do? — RBAC checks if the authenticated identity has permission for this action), Admission Control (SHOULD you do this? — mutating/validating webhooks can modify or reject requests based on custom policies, even if RBAC allows it). They execute in ORDER: AuthN → AuthZ → Admission → etcd
✅ Correct Answer: D

The 3 A's form a layered security pipeline. Every API request passes through all three before reaching etcd. If any layer rejects the request, it stops immediately. This layered approach means you can have defense in depth: even if RBAC allows an action, an admission webhook can block it based on custom business logic (e.g., "don't allow pods with latest tag in production").

📝 The 3 A's — API Request Security Pipeline
API Request Flow Through AuthN → AuthZ → Admission
  ═══════════════ API REQUEST SECURITY PIPELINE ═══════════════
  kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. AUTHENTICATION (AuthN) — "WHO are you?"                  │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  Check: X.509 cert, Bearer token, OIDC, Webhook        │  │
  │  │  Result: User "alice" or SA "easypj-api"               │  │
  │  │  ❌ Unknown identity → 401 Unauthorized                 │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │ PASS                             │
  │                           ▼                                   │
  │  2. AUTHORIZATION (AuthZ) — "WHAT can you do?"               │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  Check: RBAC (Role/ClusterRole + RoleBinding)          │  │
  │  │  Question: Can "alice" "create" "deployments" in "ns"? │  │
  │  │  ❌ Not allowed → 403 Forbidden                         │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │ PASS                             │
  │                           ▼                                   │
  │  3. ADMISSION CONTROL — "SHOULD you do this?"                │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  Mutating Webhooks: Can MODIFY the request              │  │
  │  │  (e.g., inject sidecar, add labels, set defaults)      │  │
  │  │  ↓                                                      │  │
  │  │  Validating Webhooks: Can REJECT the request            │  │
  │  │  (e.g., "no latest tag", "must have resource limits")  │  │
  │  │  ❌ Policy violation → Request denied                   │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │ PASS                             │
  │                           ▼                                   │
  │  4. ETCD — Request persisted! ✅                              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam focuses mostly on Authorization (RBAC) — creating Roles, RoleBindings, and testing permissions with kubectl auth can-i. Authentication and Admission Control are more relevant to CKA/CKS. For easypj/jobpost: use RBAC to give the API ServiceAccount read-only access to ConfigMaps in its namespace.

Security 🟡 Q118 of 200
What authentication methods does Kubernetes support for API server access?
A) Kubernetes only supports username/password authentication — all other methods require third-party plugins
B) X.509 Client Certificates (most common, used by kubectl), Bearer Tokens (ServiceAccount tokens, static tokens), OpenID Connect (OIDC — integrate with Google, Azure AD, Okta), Webhook Token Authentication (custom auth service), Authenticating Proxy (delegate to external proxy). ServiceAccounts use JWT tokens auto-mounted in pods. For easypj/jobpost: the API pod uses its ServiceAccount token to authenticate to the API server
C) Only X.509 certificates are supported — token-based authentication was deprecated in Kubernetes 1.24
D) Kubernetes doesn't have built-in authentication — it delegates all authentication to the cloud provider's IAM system
✅ Correct Answer: B

Kubernetes supports multiple authentication strategies simultaneously. The most common for CKAD is ServiceAccount tokens — when a pod needs to talk to the API server, it uses the token mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. This is why kubectl inside a pod works automatically.

📝 Kubernetes Authentication Methods
Authentication Strategies
  ═══════════════ AUTH METHODS ═══════════════
  ┌─────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  METHOD                  │ USE CASE                           │
  ├─────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  X.509 Client Certs     │ kubectl users, kubelet, etcd       │
  │  Bearer Tokens (SA)     │ Pods authenticating to API server  │
  │  Bearer Tokens (static) │ Simple static token auth (dev only)│
  │  OIDC (OpenID Connect)  │ Enterprise SSO (Google, Azure AD)  │
  │  Webhook Token          │ Custom auth service                │
  │  Authenticating Proxy   │ Delegate to external proxy         │
  └─────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ SERVICEACCOUNT TOKEN (Most CKAD-Relevant) ═══════════
  # Inside any pod:
  cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
  → eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6...

  # This token is automatically used by kubectl in the pod
  kubectl get pods
  → (works — authenticated as the pod's ServiceAccount)

  ═══════════ CHECK YOUR AUTH ═══════════
  kubectl auth whoami
  → (shows your current identity if supported by cluster)

CKAD exam tip: For the CKAD exam, focus on ServiceAccount tokens — they're how pods authenticate. You don't need to configure OIDC or webhook auth. Know that the token is auto-mounted unless automountServiceAccountToken: false is set. For easypj/jobpost: each pod component (web, API, worker) should use a dedicated ServiceAccount with minimal RBAC permissions.

Security 🟡 Q119 of 200
What is the difference between a Role and a ClusterRole in RBAC?
A) Role and ClusterRole are identical — the names are interchangeable with no functional difference in scope or usage
B) Role applies to a specific node, while ClusterRole applies to all nodes in the cluster
C) Role is NAMESPACE-SCOPED — permissions only apply within a single namespace (e.g., "can get pods in easypj-dev"). ClusterRole is CLUSTER-SCOPED — permissions apply across ALL namespaces or to cluster-scoped resources like Nodes, PVs, and Namespaces. Use Role for: per-namespace developer access. Use ClusterRole for: cluster-wide readers, node access, or reusing the same rules across multiple namespaces via ClusterRoleBinding
D) Role is for human users, ClusterRole is for ServiceAccounts — they target different types of subjects
✅ Correct Answer: C

The difference between Role and ClusterRole is purely about scope. A Role is tied to a specific namespace — if you create a Role in easypj-dev, it only grants permissions IN that namespace. A ClusterRole is cluster-wide and can grant access to both namespaced resources (across all namespaces) AND cluster-scoped resources (Nodes, PVs, Namespaces themselves).

📝 Role vs ClusterRole — Scope Comparison
Role (Namespaced) vs ClusterRole (Cluster-Wide)
  ═══════════════ ROLE (Namespaced) ═══════════════
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Role
  metadata:
    name: pod-reader
    namespace: easypj-dev       ← ONLY this namespace!
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  →
  Can: get pods in easypj-dev ✅
  Cannot: get pods in easypj-prod ❌
  Cannot: get nodes ❌ (cluster-scoped resource)

  ═══════════════ CLUSTEROLE (Cluster-Wide) ═══════════════
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: ClusterRole
  metadata:
    name: cluster-pod-reader     ← No namespace — cluster-wide!
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "nodes"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  →
  Can: get pods in ALL namespaces ✅
  Can: get nodes ✅ (cluster-scoped resource)

  ═══════════ BINDING DECISION TABLE ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────┬────────────────────┬────────────────────┐
  │                   │ RoleBinding        │ ClusterRoleBinding │
  ├──────────────────┼────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │  Role             │ Namespace access   │ ❌ Not valid       │
  │  ClusterRole      │ Namespace access   │ Cluster-wide access│
  │                   │ (common pattern!)  │ + cluster resources│
  └──────────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: A common CKAD pattern: create a ClusterRole (reusable rules), then bind it with a RoleBinding (namespace-scoped). This lets you reuse the same permission rules across multiple namespaces without duplicating the ClusterRole. For easypj/jobpost: create a ClusterRole "configmap-reader" and bind it in each namespace (dev, staging, prod).

Security 🟡 Q120 of 200
What is the difference between RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding?
A) RoleBinding grants permissions within a SINGLE namespace (even when referencing a ClusterRole). ClusterRoleBinding grants permissions across ALL namespaces (and can access cluster-scoped resources). Subjects: User (human), Group (team), or ServiceAccount (pod). Example: RoleBinding in "easypj-dev" binds the "edit" ClusterRole to ServiceAccount "easypj-api" — the SA can edit resources in easypj-dev ONLY
B) RoleBinding is for Roles, ClusterRoleBinding is for ClusterRoles — they must match the type they reference
C) RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding are identical — they're aliases for the same API resource that grant namespace-level access
D) RoleBinding can only bind human users, while ClusterRoleBinding can only bind ServiceAccounts
✅ Correct Answer: A

The binding is what connects subjects to rules. A common and powerful pattern is: ClusterRole (defines the WHAT) + RoleBinding (defines WHERE — a specific namespace). This means you can create ONE ClusterRole "pod-reader" and reuse it in every namespace via separate RoleBindings. The ClusterRoleBinding is for when you truly need cluster-wide access.

📝 RoleBinding vs ClusterRoleBinding
Binding Examples — easypj/jobpost RBAC
  ═══════════════ ROLEBINDING (Namespace-Scoped) ═══════════════
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: RoleBinding
  metadata:
    name: api-pod-reader
    namespace: easypj-dev
  subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: easypj-api           ← Who gets the permissions
    namespace: easypj-dev
  roleRef:
    kind: ClusterRole
    name: view                  ← Built-in ClusterRole
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  →
  SA "easypj-api" can VIEW resources in easypj-dev ONLY

  ═══════════════ CLUSTERROLEBINDING (Cluster-Wide) ═══════════════
  apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
  kind: ClusterRoleBinding
  metadata:
    name: cluster-admin-binding
  subjects:
  - kind: User
    name: alice@easypj.com
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  roleRef:
    kind: ClusterRole
    name: cluster-admin         ← Built-in superuser
    apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  →
  User "alice" is CLUSTER ADMIN — can do anything, anywhere

  ═══════════ BUILT-IN CLUSTERROLES ═══════════
  ┌─────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CLUSTERROLE     │ PERMISSIONS                              │
  ├─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  cluster-admin   │ 🚀 Everything (superuser)                │
  │  admin           │ Read/write in namespace (no resource     │
  │                  │ quota or namespace write)                │
  │  edit            │ Read/write most resources in namespace   │
  │  view            │ Read-only in namespace                   │
  └─────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: kubectl create rolebinding and kubectl create clusterrolebinding are imperative commands available on the CKAD exam. Use them for speed: kubectl create rolebinding pod-reader --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=easypj-dev:easypj-api -n easypj-dev. For easypj/jobpost: the API ServiceAccount needs "view" in its namespace, the CI/CD ServiceAccount needs "edit" in the deployment namespace.

Security 🟡 Q121 of 200
What RBAC verbs (actions) are available and what do they control?
A) RBAC only has three verbs: read, write, and delete — other operations don't require RBAC permissions
B) RBAC verbs are automatically generated from the HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) — you can't customize them
C) RBAC verbs only apply to kubectl commands — they don't affect API calls made by applications or controllers
D) Standard verbs: get (read a single resource), list (list all resources of a type), watch (stream changes), create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection (delete all). Special verbs: use (for PodSecurityPolicy), bind, escalate, impersonate. The wildcard * matches all verbs. For easypj/jobpost: the CI/CD pipeline needs get, list, create, update, patch on deployments; the monitoring SA needs get, list, watch on pods
✅ Correct Answer: D

RBAC verbs map directly to API operations. A common CKAD mistake is granting * (all verbs) when only specific verbs are needed. Follow the principle of least privilege: if a ServiceAccount only needs to READ pods, grant only get, list, watch — not create, update, delete. The watch verb is needed for controllers and monitoring tools that stream changes via the Kubernetes watch API.

📝 RBAC Verbs — Complete Reference
RBAC Verbs and Their kubectl Commands
  ═══════════════ STANDARD VERBS ═══════════════
  ┌─────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  VERB                │ kubectl COMMAND                      │
  ├─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  get                 │ kubectl get pod <name>              │
  │  list                │ kubectl get pods                     │
  │  watch               │ kubectl get pods -w (stream)        │
  │  create              │ kubectl create / kubectl apply      │
  │  update              │ kubectl replace / kubectl apply     │
  │  patch               │ kubectl patch                       │
  │  delete              │ kubectl delete pod <name>          │
  │  deletecollection    │ kubectl delete pods --all           │
  └─────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ SPECIAL VERBS ═══════════════
  ┌─────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  VERB                │ PURPOSE                              │
  ├─────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  *                   │ ALL verbs (wildcard — use carefully)│
  │  use                 │ PodSecurityPolicy (deprecated)      │
  │  bind                │ Create RoleBindings                 │
  │  escalate            │ Grant permissions you don't have    │
  │  impersonate         │ Act as another user/SA              │
  └─────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ LEAST PRIVILEGE FOR easypj/jobpost ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │  COMPONENT        │ RESOURCES            │ VERBS            │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │  API SA           │ configmaps, secrets  │ get, list, watch │
  │  CI/CD SA         │ deployments, svc     │ get,list,create, │
  │                   │                      │ update, patch    │
  │  Monitoring SA    │ pods, nodes          │ get, list, watch │
  │  Debug SA         │ pods, pods/log       │ get, list        │
  │  (read-only)      │ pods/exec            │ create           │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam often asks you to create RBAC resources with specific verbs. Memorize the standard set: get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection. Use kubectl create role imperatively for speed: kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n easypj-dev.

Security 🔴 Q122 of 200
How do you test if a ServiceAccount has permission to perform a specific action using kubectl auth can-i?
A) You must create the resource and check if it fails — there is no way to test permissions without actually performing the action
