B) kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa> -n <namespace>. This queries the SubjectAccessReview API WITHOUT making the actual change. Examples: kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-dev:easypj-api -n easypj-dev, kubectl auth can-i delete secrets --as=system:serviceaccount:default:default, kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-dev:easypj-api (check ALL permissions). Returns yes or no
C) kubectl check-permissions — this is a dedicated command for RBAC testing that replaces kubectl auth can-i in newer versions
D) kubectl auth can-i only works for your CURRENT user — you cannot test permissions as another ServiceAccount or user
✅ Correct Answer: B

kubectl auth can-i is the RBAC debugging essential. It performs a dry-run authorization check — it asks the API server "would this be allowed?" without actually doing it. The --as flag is critical: it lets you impersonate any user or ServiceAccount to test their permissions. This is how you verify that your RBAC configuration is correct BEFORE deploying applications that depend on those permissions.

📝 kubectl auth can-i — RBAC Testing Reference
Testing RBAC Permissions
  ═══════════════ BASIC SYNTAX ═══════════════
  kubectl auth can-i <VERB> <RESOURCE> [flags]
  → yes  (allowed)
  → no   (forbidden)

  ═══════════════ COMMON TESTS ═══════════════
  # Test YOUR permissions
  kubectl auth can-i create deployments
  kubectl auth can-i delete secrets -n easypj-dev
  kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' --all-namespaces

  # Test as a ServiceAccount
  kubectl auth can-i get pods \
    --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-dev:easypj-api \
    -n easypj-dev

  # Test as a User
  kubectl auth can-i create deployments \
    --as=alice@easypj.com

  # Test as part of a Group
  kubectl auth can-i list nodes \
    --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-dev:easypj-api \
    --as-group=system:serviceaccounts

  # List ALL permissions for a ServiceAccount
  kubectl auth can-i --list \
    --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-dev:easypj-api \
    -n easypj-dev

  ═══════════ SA FULL IDENTITY FORMAT ═══════════
  system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<serviceaccount-name>
  ───────────────────── ────────── ──────────────────
  Fixed prefix           Namespace   SA name

CKAD exam tip: kubectl auth can-i is one of the most useful CKAD debugging commands. After creating RBAC resources, ALWAYS test with --as to verify the ServiceAccount has exactly the permissions you intended — not more, not less. For easypj/jobpost: test that the CI/CD ServiceAccount can create deployments but CANNOT delete secrets.

Security 🔴 Q123 of 200
What are Admission Controllers and how do MutatingWebhook and ValidatingWebhook work?
A) Admission Controllers are plugins that only run at cluster startup — they cannot intercept API requests at runtime
B) MutatingWebhook and ValidatingWebhook do the same thing — they both reject requests that violate policies
C) Admission Controllers intercept API requests AFTER authentication and authorization. There are two types of dynamic admission webhooks: MUTATING webhooks run FIRST and can MODIFY resources (inject sidecars, add labels, set defaults). VALIDATING webhooks run AFTER mutations and can only ACCEPT or REJECT (enforce policies like "require resource limits" or "block latest tag"). Both call external HTTPS services (webhooks) that you deploy and register. Example: easypj validating webhook that rejects pods without securityContext.runAsNonRoot
D) Admission Controllers replace RBAC entirely — if you use admission webhooks, you don't need Roles or RoleBindings
✅ Correct Answer: C

Admission webhooks provide policy enforcement beyond RBAC. RBAC controls WHO can do WHAT — admission webhooks control WHAT KIND of resources can be created, regardless of who creates them. For example, even a cluster-admin can be blocked by a validating webhook from creating a pod with privileged: true. This is how organizations enforce security standards like "no pods without resource limits" or "all images must come from our private registry."

📝 Admission Webhooks — Policy Beyond RBAC
Mutating vs Validating Webhooks
  ═══════════════ WEBHOOK FLOW ═══════════════
  API Request (authenticated + authorized)
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  MUTATING WEBHOOKS (run first, can MODIFY)                   │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  kubectl apply -f pod.yaml                              │  │
  │  │  → API server calls https://mutate.easypj.com/mutate   │  │
  │  │  → Webhook ADDS sidecar container to pod spec          │  │
  │  │  → Webhook SETS default resource limits                │  │
  │  │  → Returns MODIFIED pod to API server                  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                           │ PASS                             │
  │                           ▼                                   │
  │  VALIDATING WEBHOOKS (run second, can only ACCEPT/REJECT)    │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  API server calls https://validate.easypj.com/validate │  │
  │  │  → Webhook CHECKS: "Does pod have resource limits?"   │  │
  │  │  → Webhook CHECKS: "Is image from allowed registry?"  │  │
  │  │  → ALLOW (200) or DENY (non-200 with reason)           │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ REGISTERING A WEBHOOK ═══════════
  apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
  kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
  metadata:
    name: easypj-security-policies
  webhooks:
  - name: require-nonroot.easypj.com
    clientConfig:
      service:
        name: admission-webhook
        namespace: easypj-system
        path: /validate
    rules:
    - operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
      apiGroups: [""]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      resources: ["pods"]
    failurePolicy: Fail         ← Block if webhook is down? Fail/Ignore

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam may mention admission webhooks but won't ask you to IMPLEMENT them (that's more CKA/CKS territory). Focus on understanding the concept: Mutating = can modify, Validating = can only approve/reject. Tools like Kyverno and OPA/Gatekeeper simplify admission control with policy-as-code.

Security 🟡 Q124 of 200
What are Pod Security Standards (PSS) and how do they compare to the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy?
A) Pod Security Standards (PSS) define three policy levels: PRIVILEGED (unrestricted — everything allowed), BASELINE (minimally restrictive — blocks known privilege escalations like hostPath, hostNetwork, privileged containers), RESTRICTED (heavily restricted — enforces pod hardening best practices like runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, seccomp, dropping ALL capabilities). PSS replaced PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) in Kubernetes 1.25 and is enforced via the built-in Pod Security Admission controller — no external webhook needed
B) Pod Security Standards are an external product by a third-party vendor — they're not built into Kubernetes
C) Privileged, Baseline, and Restricted are names of RBAC roles — they control user permissions, not pod security settings
D) Pod Security Standards only apply to Windows containers — Linux containers use a different security framework called AppArmor
✅ Correct Answer: A

Pod Security Standards (PSS) is the built-in replacement for PodSecurityPolicy, which was removed in Kubernetes 1.25. The big improvement: PSS doesn't require creating complex policy resources. Instead, you simply apply a NAMESPACE LABEL to set the enforcement level. This is dramatically simpler — one label vs hundreds of lines of PSP YAML.

📝 Pod Security Standards — Built-In Admission
PSS Levels — Privileged, Baseline, Restricted
  ═══════════════ THREE POLICY LEVELS ═══════════════
  ┌────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LEVEL          │ ALLOWS / BLOCKS                              │
  ├────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  PRIVILEGED    │ ✅ Everything allowed                         │
  │                │ ✅ hostPath, hostNetwork, privileged: true    │
  │                │ Use: System namespaces (kube-system)          │
  ├────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  BASELINE      │ ✅ Most workloads                            │
  │                │ ❌ hostPath volumes (unless allowed)         │
  │                │ ❌ hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC              │
  │                │ ❌ privileged containers                      │
  │                │ ❌ NET_RAW, SYS_ADMIN capabilities           │
  │                │ Use: Development and most production workloads│
  ├────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  RESTRICTED    │ ✅ Hardened, best-practice pods only         │
  │                │ ❌ Everything Baseline blocks, PLUS:          │
  │                │ ❌ Must runAsNonRoot (no UID 0)              │
  │                │ ❌ Must drop ALL capabilities                │
  │                │ ❌ Must use seccomp (RuntimeDefault/Local)   │
  │                │ ❌ readOnlyRootFilesystem recommended        │
  │                │ Use: Highly regulated production environments│
  └────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════ ENFORCING PSS ON A NAMESPACE ═══════════════
  # Apply Restricted policy with enforcement
  kubectl label ns easypj-prod \
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted

  # Modes: enforce (block), warn (warn but allow), audit (log only)

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam may ask you to apply PSS labels to a namespace. The label format is: pod-security.kubernetes.io/<mode>=<level>. Modes: enforce (block violating pods), warn (show warning), audit (log violation). Levels: privileged, baseline, restricted. For easypj/jobpost: use baseline for dev, restricted for production.

4.3 Requests, Limits & QuotasQ125-Q130

🟡→🔴 | LF Subtopic 3 & 5: Understand requests, limits, quotas. ResourceQuota, LimitRange.

Security 🟡 Q125 of 200
How do Kubernetes resource requests and limits work together to ensure fair resource distribution?
A) Requests are maximums that throttle the container, limits are minimums that guarantee resources — the terms are intentionally opposite
B) Requests and limits are independent — Kubernetes uses requests for scheduling and ignores limits, which are only for monitoring dashboards
C) Only limits matter — requests are optional suggestions that the scheduler ignores when placing pods on nodes
D) Requests = scheduling GUARANTEE (scheduler ensures the node has at least this much free capacity — think "reservation"). Limits = runtime ENFORCEMENT (container cannot exceed this — CPU is throttled, memory over limit triggers OOMKill). If request < limit, the container can BURST up to the limit. If request = limit, QoS is Guaranteed (highest priority). For easypj/jobpost: Django API request=256Mi, limit=1Gi means Django is guaranteed 256Mi at scheduling but can use up to 1Gi if available
✅ Correct Answer: D

Requests and limits serve two completely different purposes. Requests are for the scheduler: "I need at least this much to run." The scheduler places pods on nodes that have enough requested capacity remaining. Limits are for the kubelet: "Don't let me use more than this." The kubelet enforces limits at runtime. A pod with no requests can be scheduled on an overcommitted node (risky); a pod with no limits can consume all available resources (dangerous to neighbors).

📝 Requests vs Limits — Scheduling Guarantee vs Runtime Cap
How Requests & Limits Shape Pod Placement & Behavior
  ═══════════════ NODE: 4 CPU / 8Gi ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Pod A: req=1 CPU  lim=2 CPU   [████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░]  │
  │         ◄──── guaranteed ────►◄── can burst ──►            │
  │                                                              │
  │  Pod B: req=500m   lim=1 CPU   [██████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░] │
  │                                                              │
  │  Pod C: req=1 CPU  lim=1 CPU   [██████████████████████████] │
  │         Guaranteed QoS — reserved = limited                  │
  │                                                              │
  │  SCHEDULABLE: 4 - (1+0.5+1) = 1.5 CPU left for requests     │
  │  ACTUAL: A uses 1.8, B uses 0.3, C uses 0.5 = 2.6 total     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ ENFORCEMENT MECHANISMS ═══════════
  ┌──────────────┬─────────────────────┬────────────────────────┐
  │               │ CPU                  │ MEMORY                 │
  ├──────────────┼─────────────────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │  Over limit  │ THROTTLED (CFS quota)│ OOMKILLED (container  │
  │              │ Slowed, not killed   │ killed, exit code 137) │
  │  Compressible│ ✅ Yes               │ ❌ No — must free      │
  │  Can borrow? │ ✅ Yes (if idle)     │ ❌ No — allocated      │
  └──────────────┴─────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: ALWAYS set both requests and limits on production workloads. Missing limits = danger to neighbors. Missing requests = unpredictable scheduling. For easypj/jobpost: use kubectl set resources deploy/easypj-api --requests=cpu=200m,memory=256Mi --limits=cpu=1,memory=1Gi.

Security 🟡 Q126 of 200
How does Kubernetes assign QoS (Quality of Service) classes to pods?
A) QoS classes are assigned manually via labels — you set qos-class: guaranteed on each pod
B) QoS is automatically derived: GUARANTEED (every container has request==limit for BOTH CPU and memory), BURSTABLE (at least one container has request<limit or only one resource type set), BESTEFFORT (no requests or limits on any container). QoS determines OOM kill order: BestEffort (first) → Burstable (based on usage/request ratio) → Guaranteed (last). Check with kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
C) QoS classes are based on the container image's metadata — Kubernetes reads QOS labels from the Dockerfile
D) There are five QoS classes: Platinum, Gold, Silver, Bronze, and BestEffort — based on the total resources allocated
✅ Correct Answer: B

QoS is Kubernetes' automatic priority system. You don't set it — it's derived from your resource configuration. The key insight: Guaranteed pods are the LAST to be killed because they have the most predictable resource usage. BestEffort pods are killed FIRST because they made no resource contract with the scheduler. For easypj/jobpost, PostgreSQL should be Guaranteed (request=limit=2Gi), Django API can be Burstable (request=256Mi, limit=1Gi).

📝 QoS Class Assignment
QoS Decision Tree for Every Container in the Pod
  For EACH container:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Does it have BOTH CPU AND MEMORY requests AND limits?       │
  │  ├── NO → Pod is BESTEFFORT 🟠                               │
  │  │         Killed FIRST on memory pressure                   │
  │  │                                                           │
  │  └── YES → Are REQUEST == LIMIT for BOTH CPU and memory?     │
  │            ├── NO for ANY container → Pod is BURSTABLE 🟡    │
  │            │    Killed after BestEffort, by usage/request    │
  │            │                                                  │
  │            └── YES for ALL containers → GUARANTEED 🟢        │
  │                 Killed LAST, only if exceeding own limit     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ OOM KILL ORDER ═══════════
  1️⃣  BESTEFFORT    (no requests/limits)
  2️⃣  BURSTABLE     (higher usage/request ratio = killed sooner)
  3️⃣  GUARANTEED    (stable, predictable — last to go)

CKAD exam tip: Check QoS with kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'. Guaranteed QoS requires BOTH CPU AND MEMORY to have request==limit. Setting only one won't give you Guaranteed. For easypj/jobpost production: PostgreSQL = Guaranteed, Django = Burstable, debug pods = BestEffort (keep them temporary).

Security 🔴 Q127 of 200
When a node runs out of memory, how does the OOM killer decide which pod to kill first and why?
A) The OOM killer is random — it doesn't use any priority system and may kill critical production pods unpredictably
B) The pod using the most ABSOLUTE memory is killed first — a 2Gi Guaranteed pod dies before a 100Mi BestEffort pod
C) OOM priority: 1) BESTEFFORT pods killed FIRST (no resource guarantees). 2) BURSTABLE pods killed based on OOM score = (usage - request) / request — the pod most exceeding its request dies first. 3) GUARANTEED pods killed LAST — they have negative OOM scores (protected). This means a 100Mi BestEffort debug pod is killed BEFORE a 2Gi Guaranteed PostgreSQL pod — QoS class matters more than absolute usage
D) OOM killer uses pod age as the only criterion — the newest pods are killed first regardless of resource configuration
✅ Correct Answer: C

The OOM killer's decision is not random, not based on absolute usage, and not based on pod age. It's a calculated priority based on QoS class and relative overcommit. This is why you should always set resource requests and limits on production pods — it's not just about scheduling, it's about survival. A BestEffort pod will be the first victim when memory runs low, regardless of how little memory it's actually using.

📝 OOM Killer Priority — Survival of the Configured
OOM Kill Scenario — Node Memory Exhausted
  Node: 8Gi total, 7.9Gi used, 100Mi pressure
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Pod A: PostgreSQL (Guaranteed) — PROTECTED                  │
  │    req=2Gi, lim=2Gi, usage=1.9Gi                              │
  │    oom_score_adj: -997  ← Very negative = protected          │
  │                                                               │
  │  Pod B: Django API (Burstable) — AT RISK                     │
  │    req=256Mi, lim=1Gi, usage=900Mi                            │
  │    OOM score: (900-256)/256 = 2.5                             │
  │                                                               │
  │  Pod C: Debug (BestEffort) — DOOMED                          │
  │    No req/lim, usage=50Mi                                     │
  │    oom_score_adj: 1000  ← Very positive = first victim       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  KILL ORDER: Pod C (BestEffort, 50Mi) → Pod B (Burstable) → Pod A

  ═══════════ KEY INSIGHT ═══════════
  A 50Mi BestEffort pod dies BEFORE a 2Gi Guaranteed pod.
  Why? QoS class determines priority, not absolute memory usage.

CKAD exam tip: If you see Exit Code: 137 or Reason: OOMKilled, the container was OOM-killed. For production easypj/jobpost, ALWAYS set resource limits on critical pods. Never leave PostgreSQL or Redis as BestEffort — they'll be the first casualties during memory pressure.

Security 🟡 Q128 of 200
How do ResourceQuota and LimitRange work together to govern resource usage in a namespace?
A) ResourceQuota sets TOTAL limits per namespace (e.g., max 10 CPU, 20Gi memory, 20 pods). LimitRange sets PER-POD/CONTAINER defaults, mins, and maxes (e.g., each container must request between 100m-2 CPU, default 200m if not specified). Together: ResourceQuota prevents the NAMESPACE from consuming too much; LimitRange prevents individual PODS from being too large (or too small). If a namespace has a ResourceQuota of 10 CPU and a LimitRange max of 2 CPU per container, no single container can take more than 20% of the namespace quota
B) ResourceQuota and LimitRange are the same resource with different names — they're interchangeable
C) ResourceQuota sets per-pod limits, LimitRange sets per-namespace totals — their scopes are opposite of what the names suggest
D) ResourceQuota only limits object counts (number of pods, services), LimitRange only limits CPU/memory — they handle completely separate domains
✅ Correct Answer: A

ResourceQuota and LimitRange are complementary — one manages the collective, the other manages the individual. Think of a shopping mall: ResourceQuota is the fire code limit (max 500 people in the building), LimitRange is the rule that each store can hold 10-50 people. For easypj/jobpost: dev namespace gets 4 CPU total (Quota), each pod gets max 1 CPU (LimitRange).

📝 ResourceQuota + LimitRange Example
easypj/jobpost Namespace Governance
  ═══════════════ DEV NAMESPACE GOVERNANCE ═══════════════
  ResourceQuota:          LimitRange:
  ┌─────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │ cpu: 4              │ │ Container defaults:              │
  │ memory: 8Gi         │ │   cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi       │
  │ pods: 10            │ │ Container max:                   │
  │ services: 5         │ │   cpu: 1, memory: 2Gi           │
  │ configmaps: 10      │ │ Container min:                   │
  │ secrets: 10         │ │   cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi        │
  │ persistentvolume-   │ └──────────────────────────────────┘
  │   claims: 3          │
  └─────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ WHAT HAPPENS WHEN ═══════════
  kubectl create deploy big-app --image=nginx --replicas=5
  spec:
    containers:
    - resources:
        requests: {cpu: 2, memory: 4Gi}  ← 2 CPU per pod

  → REJECTED by LimitRange! "cpu request 2 exceeds max of 1"
  → Must reduce request to ≤ 1 CPU

  kubectl create deploy small-app --image=nginx --replicas=5
  → Allowed by LimitRange (1 CPU each)
  → 5 pods × 1 CPU = 5 CPU requested
  → REJECTED by ResourceQuota! "exceeded quota: cpu: used=3, requested=5, limited=4"

CKAD exam tip: Create quotas and limit ranges imperatively: kubectl create quota dev-quota --hard=cpu=4,memory=8Gi,pods=10 -n easypj-dev. LimitRanges can only be created from YAML. For easypj/jobpost: set quotas on dev and staging to prevent them from starving production resources.

Security 🟡 Q129 of 200
How does LimitRange set default, minimum, and maximum resource requests for pods in a namespace?
A) LimitRange is an annotation on the namespace object — it uses a simple key=value format without YAML
B) LimitRange is a YAML resource that defines: default (applied if no limit specified), defaultRequest (applied if no request specified), max (hard ceiling), min (hard floor) for CPU and memory. If a pod doesn't specify resources, defaults are applied automatically. If a pod exceeds max or falls below min, it's REJECTED at creation time. LimitRange applies per-container within the namespace
C) LimitRange only applies to Pods — it cannot set defaults for individual containers within a pod
D) kubectl create limitrange dev-limits --default-cpu=200m --default-memory=256Mi — this is the imperative command for creating LimitRanges
✅ Correct Answer: B

LimitRange is the default configuration enforcer for a namespace. Its most valuable feature is setting defaults — without it, pods without explicit resource requests get BestEffort QoS and are first in line for OOM kills. With LimitRange, every pod in the namespace automatically gets sensible defaults, protecting them from being BestEffort by accident.

📝 LimitRange YAML — Field Reference
LimitRange — Default Enforcement for easypj/jobpost
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: LimitRange
  metadata:
    name: dev-limits
    namespace: easypj-dev
  spec:
    limits:
    - type: Container
      default:              ← If no LIMIT specified
        cpu: "500m"
        memory: "512Mi"
      defaultRequest:       ← If no REQUEST specified
        cpu: "200m"
        memory: "256Mi"
      max:                  ← HARD CEILING — blocks creation
        cpu: "2"
        memory: "2Gi"
      min:                  ← HARD FLOOR — blocks creation
        cpu: "50m"
        memory: "64Mi"
      maxLimitRequestRatio: ← Limit/Request ratio cap (optional)
        cpu: "4"            ← limit can't be more than 4× request

  ═══════════ WHAT HAPPENS WITHOUT DEFAULTS ═══════════
  Pod created with NO resources specified:
  → Without LimitRange: BESTEFFORT QoS → first to be OOMKilled
  → With LimitRange: 200m/256Mi request, 500m/512Mi limit applied
    → BURSTABLE QoS → protected from being first victim!

CKAD exam tip: LimitRange is YAML-only (no imperative create command). The CKAD exam may ask you to apply a LimitRange to ensure pods have resource defaults. For easypj/jobpost: apply LimitRange in dev and staging namespaces to ensure all pods have at least basic resource protection.

Security 🔴 Q130 of 200
How do ResourceQuota and LimitRange interact with QoS classes to create complete resource governance?
A) They don't interact at all — ResourceQuota, LimitRange, and QoS are three independent and unrelated Kubernetes features
B) ResourceQuota overrides LimitRange — if they conflict, the quota wins and the limit range is ignored
C) QoS classes replace the need for ResourceQuota and LimitRange — if you use QoS, you don't need quotas or limit ranges
D) Together they form three-layer resource governance: (1) LimitRange ensures every pod has resource specs (no BestEffort by accident) through default/min/max, (2) ResourceQuota caps the namespace's TOTAL consumption preventing runaway usage, (3) QoS classes automatically assign priority (BestEffort first to die, Guaranteed last) based on the resources configured by the first two. Example: easypj-dev gets LimitRange defaults (200m/256Mi) → all pods are at least Burstable QoS → ResourceQuota caps total at 4 CPU/8Gi → when memory pressure hits, QoS determines kill order
✅ Correct Answer: D

These three mechanisms form a complete resource governance stack. LimitRange is the safety net (catches pods without resource specs), ResourceQuota is the boundary wall (prevents namespace from consuming too much), and QoS is the survival priority system (decides who dies when resources are scarce). Together they implement what cloud providers call "resource isolation" — completely within standard Kubernetes.

📝 Three-Layer Resource Governance
Complete Resource Governance for easypj/jobpost
  ═══════════════ THREE-LAYER RESOURCE GOVERNANCE ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LAYER 1: LimitRange — "Every pod gets protection"           │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────                       │
  │  Ensures all pods have CPU/memory specs:                     │
  │  • Defaults applied if pod doesn't specify                   │
  │  • Max/Min enforced at creation time                         │
  │  • Result: NO BestEffort pods (unless explicitly wanted)     │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  LAYER 2: ResourceQuota — "This namespace can't exceed N"    │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────                │
  │  Caps total resource consumption:                            │
  │  • Total CPU, memory, pods, services, PVCs                  │
  │  • Rejects new resources when quota is reached               │
  │  • Result: One namespace can't starve others                 │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  LAYER 3: QoS Classes — "Who dies first under pressure"      │
  │  ────────────────────────────────────────────                │
  │  Automatic priority based on resource config:                │
  │  • Guaranteed: request=limit → Last to be killed             │
  │  • Burstable: request<limit → Middle priority              │
  │  • BestEffort: no resources → First to be killed             │
  │  • Result: Predictable behavior under memory pressure        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ easypj/jobpost GOVERNANCE STRATEGY ═══════════
  ┌──────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │  NAMESPACE    │ LIMITRANGE       │ RESOURCEQUOTA            │
  ├──────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  dev          │ default: 200m/   │ cpu: 4, mem: 8Gi        │
  │              │ 256Mi, max: 1/2Gi│ pods: 10                │
  │  staging      │ default: 200m/   │ cpu: 8, mem: 16Gi       │
  │              │ 256Mi, max: 2/4Gi│ pods: 20                │
  │  prod         │ default: 500m/   │ cpu: 20, mem: 40Gi      │
  │              │ 512Mi, max: 4/8Gi│ pods: 50                │
  └──────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

🚀 Beyond CKAD (CKA crossover): Cluster administrators use these mechanisms to implement multi-tenant resource isolation. In CKA, you learn about node-pressure eviction (kubelet evicts pods when node resources are low) and how QoS classes determine eviction order — the same priority system applies. For production clusters, always combine all three layers.

4.4 ConfigMaps — Externalizing ConfigurationQ131-Q138

🟢→🔴 | LF Subtopic 4: Understand ConfigMaps. Create, consume as env vars or volume mounts, immutable, optional, and update strategies.

Security 🟢 Q131 of 200
What is a ConfigMap and why is it essential for 12-Factor applications on Kubernetes?
A) A ConfigMap is a Kubernetes resource that stores container images — it's an alternative to container registries
B) A ConfigMap is only used for storing large binary files (like ML models or database dumps) that are too big for container images
C) A ConfigMap decouples configuration from container images — it stores non-sensitive key-value pairs (app settings, feature flags, environment variables) that can be consumed by pods as environment variables or mounted as files. This follows the 12-Factor App principle: "Store config in the environment." Without ConfigMaps, you'd need to rebuild images every time a setting changes. For easypj/jobpost: ALLOWED_HOSTS, DEBUG, LOG_LEVEL, CACHE_TTL stored in ConfigMaps
D) A ConfigMap encrypts configuration data at rest — it's designed for storing passwords, API keys, and TLS certificates securely
✅ Correct Answer: C

ConfigMaps are the configuration layer of Kubernetes. They let you change application behavior WITHOUT rebuilding container images. This is a core 12-Factor App principle: config varies across deployments (dev, staging, prod), code doesn't. ConfigMaps store key-value pairs, configuration files, or even entire config directories — up to 1MiB total.

📝 ConfigMap — Decouple Config from Image
ConfigMap for easypj/jobpost Django Settings
  ═══════════════ WITHOUT CONFIGMAP ═══════════════
  # settings.py (hardcoded in image)
  DEBUG = True
  ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['localhost']
  LOG_LEVEL = 'DEBUG'
  → To change ANY setting: rebuild image, push, redeploy!
  → ❌ Slow, error-prone, violates 12-Factor

  ═══════════════ WITH CONFIGMAP ═══════════════
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ConfigMap
  metadata:
    name: django-config
    namespace: easypj-dev
  data:
    DEBUG: "false"
    ALLOWED_HOSTS: "easypj-dev.example.com"
    LOG_LEVEL: "info"
    CACHE_TTL: "300"
  →
  Pod reads config at RUNTIME from ConfigMap
  → Change a setting: kubectl edit cm django-config + restart pod
  → ✅ Fast, no image rebuild, 12-Factor compliant

  ═══════════ CONFIGMAP vs SECRET ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │                   │ CONFIGMAP        │ SECRET           │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │  Purpose          │ Non-sensitive    │ Sensitive data   │
  │  Encoding         │ Plain text       │ Base64 (not enc!)│
  │  Encryption       │ ❌ No            │ ⚠️  Not by default│
  │  Size limit       │ 1 MiB            │ 1 MiB            │
  │  Example          │ APP_SETTINGS     │ DB_PASSWORD      │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: ConfigMaps are heavily tested on CKAD. Key commands: kubectl create cm NAME --from-literal=KEY=VALUE, kubectl create cm NAME --from-file=config.properties. For easypj/jobpost: store ALL Django settings in a ConfigMap and read them via environment variables — never hardcode settings in the Dockerfile.

Security 🟢 Q132 of 200
How do you create ConfigMaps from literals, files, and environment files?
A) kubectl create cm NAME --from-literal=KEY=VALUE (single key), --from-literal=K2=V2 (multiple), --from-file=config.properties (file becomes key=filename, value=contents), --from-file=custom-key=config.properties (custom key name), --from-env-file=.env (reads KEY=VALUE pairs from env file). Generate YAML with --dry-run=client -o yaml. For easypj: kubectl create cm django-config --from-literal=DEBUG=false --from-literal=ALLOWED_HOSTS=easypj.com --from-file=settings.py --dry-run=client -o yaml > cm.yaml
B) ConfigMaps can only be created from YAML — there is no imperative kubectl create command for ConfigMaps
C) kubectl configmap create — this is the correct imperative command, not kubectl create cm
D) ConfigMaps are automatically created by Kubernetes when you deploy a pod with environment variables — no manual creation is needed
✅ Correct Answer: A

kubectl create cm is one of the most frequently used CKAD commands. The --from-literal flag is for simple key-value pairs (DEBUG=false), --from-file imports entire files as ConfigMap entries, and --from-env-file parses env-style files. Always generate YAML first with --dry-run=client -o yaml.

📝 ConfigMap Creation — All Methods
kubectl create configmap — Complete Reference
  ═══════════════ FROM LITERAL ═══════════════
  kubectl create cm app-settings \
    --from-literal=DEBUG=false \
    --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info \
    --from-literal=DB_HOST=postgres \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml
  →
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ConfigMap
  data:
    DEBUG: "false"
    LOG_LEVEL: "info"
    DB_HOST: "postgres"

  ═══════════════ FROM FILE ═══════════════
  kubectl create cm app-config \
    --from-file=settings.py \
    --from-file=nginx.conf \
    --from-file=custom-name=config.json
  →
  data:
    settings.py: |       ← Key = filename
      DEBUG = False...
    nginx.conf: |
      server { listen 80; }
    custom-name: |       ← Custom key name
      {"key": "value"}

  ═══════════════ FROM ENV FILE ═══════════════
  # .env file:
  # DB_HOST=postgres
  # DB_PORT=5432
  kubectl create cm db-config --from-env-file=.env

  ═══════════════ FROM DIRECTORY ═══════════════
  kubectl create cm full-config --from-file=config-dir/
  → Every file in config-dir/ becomes a key in the ConfigMap

CKAD exam tip: For the CKAD exam, kubectl create cm --from-literal is the fastest way to create ConfigMaps. Always generate YAML with --dry-run=client -o yaml first, then apply. For easypj/jobpost: store Django settings as literals and nginx config as files in the same ConfigMap.

Security 🟡 Q133 of 200
How do you consume ConfigMap values as environment variables in a pod?
A) ConfigMaps can only be mounted as files — they cannot be injected as environment variables into containers
B) Three methods: (1) envFrom with configMapRef (injects ALL ConfigMap keys as env vars — simplest), (2) valueFrom.configMapKeyRef (injects a SINGLE key with optional custom env var name), (3) env with individual valueFrom references for each key. Method 1 is best when you want all ConfigMap keys as env vars. Method 2 gives you fine-grained control over which keys become which env var names
C) kubectl inject cm django-config — this imperative command injects a ConfigMap into all pods in a namespace
D) Environment variables from ConfigMaps are read once at pod creation and never updated — even if the ConfigMap changes, the pod keeps old values
✅ Correct Answer: B

There are two patterns for consuming ConfigMaps as environment variables. envFrom is the "import all" approach — every key in the ConfigMap becomes an environment variable with the same name. valueFrom.configMapKeyRef is the "cherry-pick" approach — you select specific keys and can give them different environment variable names. The CKAD exam tests both patterns.

📝 ConfigMap as Environment Variables
Two Methods — envFrom vs valueFrom
  ═══════════════ METHOD 1: envFrom (ALL keys) ═══════════════
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: django
      envFrom:
      - configMapRef:
          name: django-config
  →
  All keys become env vars with SAME names:
  DEBUG=false, LOG_LEVEL=info, ALLOWED_HOSTS=easypj.com

  ═══════════════ METHOD 2: valueFrom (SELECTIVE) ═══════════════
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: django
      env:
      - name: DJANGO_DEBUG          ← Custom env var name!
        valueFrom:
          configMapKeyRef:
            name: django-config     ← ConfigMap name
            key: DEBUG              ← Key in ConfigMap
            optional: false         ← Pod fails if key missing
      - name: ALLOWED_HOSTS
        valueFrom:
          configMapKeyRef:
            name: django-config
            key: ALLOWED_HOSTS

  ═══════════ WHICH METHOD? ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  envFrom             │ valueFrom.configMapKeyRef        │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  All keys → env vars │ Selective keys → env vars        │
  │  Same names          │ Can RENAME keys (DJANGO_DEBUG)   │
  │  Simpler YAML        │ More explicit, safer              │
  │  Good for: dev envs  │ Good for: production, clarity    │
  │  Hidden dependency   │ Explicit dependency              │
  └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam often asks you to inject specific ConfigMap keys into a pod. Use valueFrom.configMapKeyRef for precision. Remember optional: true allows the pod to start even if the ConfigMap doesn't exist (useful for optional config). For easypj/jobpost: use envFrom for dev (simplicity) and valueFrom for prod (explicitness).

Security 🟡 Q134 of 200
How do you mount a ConfigMap as files in a pod, and why is this better for certain use cases?
A) ConfigMaps cannot be mounted as files — they only work as environment variables
B) Mounting ConfigMaps as files is deprecated — Kubernetes 1.30 requires all config to be consumed as environment variables
C) File mounts from ConfigMaps are read-write — pods can modify the config files and the changes are written back to the ConfigMap
D) Mount ConfigMap as a volume: each key becomes a FILE, value becomes file CONTENT. Files are read-only (by default) and UPDATED when the ConfigMap changes (with a delay of ~60s via kubelet sync). Use for: nginx.conf, application YAML configs, certificate bundles, any configuration that's file-based. For easypj/jobpost: mount nginx config as a file in the web pod; mount Django settings.py as a file in the API pod
✅ Correct Answer: D

Volume-mounted ConfigMaps are ideal for file-based configuration like nginx.conf, application YAML files, or certificate bundles. The key advantage over environment variables: the files are automatically updated when the ConfigMap changes (with a ~60-second symlink-based update). However, the application must watch for file changes and reload — Kubernetes doesn't restart the pod.

📝 ConfigMap as Volume Mount
ConfigMap → Volume → Pod Filesystem
  ═══════════════ VOLUME MOUNT EXAMPLE ═══════════════
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: Pod
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: web
      image: easypj/web
      volumeMounts:
      - name: nginx-config
        mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d    ← Where files appear
        readOnly: true                   ← Always true for CM
    volumes:
    - name: nginx-config
      configMap:
        name: nginx-config               ← ConfigMap name
        items:                            ← Optional: cherry-pick keys
        - key: nginx.conf
          path: default.conf             ← Rename key to this file
        - key: mime.types
          path: mime.types

  ═══════════ RESULT ═══════════
  Inside container:
  /etc/nginx/conf.d/
  ├── default.conf    ← Content of ConfigMap key "nginx.conf"
  └── mime.types      ← Content of ConfigMap key "mime.types"

  ═══════════ ENV VAR vs VOLUME MOUNT ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │                   │ ENV VAR           │ VOLUME MOUNT     │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │  Best for         │ Simple key=value │ Files, configs   │
  │  Auto-update      │ ❌ No (pod must  │ ✅ Yes (~60s lag)│
  │                   │   restart)       │                   │
  │  Large config     │ ⚠️  Awkward      │ ✅ Natural (files)│
  │  App needs reload │ N/A              │ Must watch files │
  └──────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: Volume-mounted ConfigMaps are updated automatically (~60 seconds) via symlink swaps. But your application must detect and reload the new config — Kubernetes won't restart the pod. Tools like stakater/Reloader can auto-restart pods on ConfigMap changes. For easypj/jobpost: mount nginx.conf as a file, use env vars for Django settings.

Security 🟡 Q135 of 200
When should you use ConfigMap as environment variables vs volume mounts?
A) Always use environment variables — volume mounts from ConfigMaps are deprecated and will be removed in a future release
B) Use ENV VAR for: simple key=value settings (DEBUG, LOG_LEVEL, DATABASE_URL) that your app reads from os.environ. Use VOLUME MOUNT for: configuration FILES (nginx.conf, app.yaml, cert.pem), large configs that are awkward as env vars, and configs that need auto-update without pod restart (app watches files and reloads). For easypj/jobpost: Django settings → env vars; Nginx config → volume mount; combined approach is common
C) Use volume mounts for everything — environment variables are less secure and should be avoided in production
D) ConfigMap consumption method is purely personal preference — there are no technical differences between env vars and volume mounts
✅ Correct Answer: B

The choice between env vars and volume mounts depends on what your application expects and whether you need auto-update. Environment variables are simpler for key-value pairs; volume mounts are natural for file-based config and support automatic updates without pod restarts.

📝 Env Var vs Volume Mount Decision Matrix
When to Use Which — easypj/jobpost Examples
  ═══════════ DECISION MATRIX ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
  │  SCENARIO             │ ENV VAR      │ VOLUME MOUNT │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤
  │  Simple key=value    │ ✅ BEST      │ ⚠️ Overkill  │
  │  File-based config   │ ❌ Impractical│ ✅ BEST      │
  │  Need auto-update    │ ❌ Must restart│ ✅ ~60s sync│
  │  Large config (>1KB)│ ⚠️ Awkward   │ ✅ Natural   │
  │  TLS certs/keys      │ ⚠️ Possible  │ ✅ Better    │
  │  App reads os.environ│ ✅ BEST      │ ❌ Must parse│
  └──────────────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: The exam may ask you to configure an application using a ConfigMap. Read the question carefully — does the app expect env vars or config files? Match your approach to what the application needs. For easypj/jobpost: Django uses env vars (os.environ), Nginx uses files.

Security 🔴 Q136 of 200
What happens when you update a ConfigMap — do pods automatically pick up the changes?
A) For ENV VAR consumers: pods DO NOT auto-update — you must restart the pod (rolling restart: kubectl rollout restart deploy). For VOLUME MOUNT consumers: files are auto-updated by the kubelet via symlink swap (delay: ~60s + TTL), but the application must detect and reload the new files — Kubernetes does NOT restart the pod. Common solutions: (1) kubectl rollout restart deploy (simplest), (2) stakater/Reloader (watches ConfigMap/Secret changes, triggers rolling restart), (3) app watches files and reloads config in-process
B) Pods automatically restart when ConfigMaps change — Kubernetes handles this natively without any additional tooling
C) ConfigMaps are immutable after creation — you cannot update them without deleting and recreating
D) ConfigMap updates propagate instantly to all pods — there is zero delay between updating a ConfigMap and all pods seeing the new values
✅ Correct Answer: A

ConfigMap updates are not instantaneous and not automatic for env vars. This is one of the most common CKAD gotchas. Volume-mounted ConfigMaps DO auto-update (with ~60s delay), but the application must reload. Environment variables from ConfigMaps are set ONCE at pod startup and never change until the pod restarts. The simplest solution for CKAD: kubectl rollout restart deploy/name.

📝 ConfigMap Update Behavior
What Happens When You Update a ConfigMap
  kubectl edit cm django-config  (change DEBUG=true → false)
       │
       ├── ENV VAR consumers: NO CHANGE in running pods!
       │   Pod reads env vars once at startup
       │   Fix: kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api
       │
       └── VOLUME MOUNT consumers: UPDATED after ~60s!
           kubelet syncs ConfigMap → updates symlink in pod
           App sees new files → must reload config itself
           Fix: App watches files, or use ReLoader to restart

CKAD exam tip: If a CKAD task asks you to update a ConfigMap and have pods use the new values, the answer is ALWAYS kubectl rollout restart deploy/name (for env var consumers). For easypj/jobpost: after updating django-config, run kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api.

Security 🟢 Q137 of 200
What is an immutable ConfigMap and why would you use it?
A) Immutable ConfigMaps are automatically created by Kubernetes for system components — users cannot create them manually
B) Immutable ConfigMaps encrypt all data at rest — they're a security feature for storing sensitive configuration
C) Set immutable: true in the ConfigMap manifest (K8s 1.21+). Once created, the ConfigMap CANNOT be modified — only deleted and recreated. Benefits: (1) prevents accidental changes to production config, (2) reduces kubelet API load (kubelet doesn't need to watch for changes), (3) ensures versioned, auditable configuration (delete old, create new with new name). For easypj/jobpost: production ConfigMaps with version in name (django-config-v2)
D) Immutable ConfigMaps are read-only inside the pod — containers cannot read them, only the kubelet can access the data
✅ Correct Answer: C

Immutable ConfigMaps and Secrets (K8s 1.21+) provide safety and performance. Safety: you can't accidentally edit production config. Performance: the kubelet doesn't need to continuously watch immutable resources for changes, reducing API server load at scale. The recommended pattern: version your ConfigMaps (django-config-v1, django-config-v2) and treat them as immutable artifacts.

📝 Immutable ConfigMap — Versioned & Protected
Immutable ConfigMap Pattern
  apiVersion: v1
  kind: ConfigMap
  metadata:
    name: django-config-v2    ← Versioned name
  immutable: true              ← Cannot be modified!
  data:
    DEBUG: "false"
    ALLOWED_HOSTS: "easypj.com"

  ═══════════ WORKFLOW ═══════════
  1. Create: kubectl apply -f cm-v1.yaml (immutable)
  2. Deploy app referencing django-config-v1
  3. Need config change? Create django-config-v2
  4. Update Deployment to reference v2 → rolling update
  5. Delete v1 (optional, after v2 is confirmed)

CKAD exam tip: Immutable ConfigMaps/Secrets can only be CREATED once — any attempt to update will fail. Use this pattern for production configs. For easypj/jobpost: version production ConfigMaps (django-config-v1, v2, v3) with immutable: true for audit trail and safety.

Security 🟡 Q138 of 200
What does optional: true do when referencing a ConfigMap or Secret?
A) optional: true makes the ConfigMap data editable inside the pod — containers can modify the mounted config files
B) optional: true is the default behavior — ConfigMaps are always optional and pods start without them
C) optional: true means the ConfigMap is not encrypted — it's a security setting for storing non-sensitive data
D) optional: true allows the pod to START even if the referenced ConfigMap/Secret DOES NOT EXIST. Without it (default: false), the pod stays Pending until the resource is created. Use for: truly optional configuration where the app has sensible defaults. Danger: if the ConfigMap is later created, the pod will mount it but will NOT automatically restart — you must restart manually
✅ Correct Answer: D

optional: true is a safety valve for non-critical configuration. Without it, a missing ConfigMap or Secret BLOCKS the pod from starting — the pod stays Pending forever. With optional: true, the pod starts anyway, and your application should have sensible defaults for missing configuration. For easypj/jobpost: core settings (DATABASE_URL in Secrets) should NOT be optional; optional configs (feature flags, debug settings in ConfigMaps) can be optional with defaults.

📝 optional — Graceful Degradation Without Config
optional: true Behavior & Decision Table
  ═══════════════ YAML EXAMPLE ═══════════════
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: django
      env:
      - name: FEATURE_FLAGS
        valueFrom:
          configMapKeyRef:
            name: feature-flags       ← May or may not exist
            key: flags
            optional: true            ← Pod starts anyway!

  ═══════════════ BEHAVIOR TABLE ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SCENARIO             │ RESULT                             │
  ├──────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  CM exists + key OK  │ FEATURE_FLAGS = value ✅            │
  │  CM exists + key bad │ FEATURE_FLAGS not set ⚠️            │
  │  CM missing          │ FEATURE_FLAGS not set (no error)   │
  │  (optional: true)    │ Pod STARTS anyway ✅                │
  ├──────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  CM missing          │ Pod STUCK in Pending ❌             │
  │  (optional: false)   │ Event: "configmap not found"       │
  └──────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ easypj/jobpost RECOMMENDATION ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────┬────────────────────────┐
  │  CONFIG               │ OPTIONAL │ REASON                 │
  ├──────────────────────┼──────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │  DATABASE_URL (Secret)│ ❌ false │ Must exist or app fails│
  │  SECRET_KEY (Secret)  │ ❌ false │ Django won't start     │
  │  DEBUG (ConfigMap)    │ ✅ true  │ Sensible default: False │
  │  LOG_LEVEL (ConfigMap)│ ✅ true  │ Sensible default: info │
  │  FEATURE_FLAGS (CM)   │ ✅ true  │ Default: all disabled  │
  └──────────────────────┴──────────┴────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: Use optional: true for non-critical configuration that has sensible defaults in the application code. Never make DATABASE_URL or SECRET_KEY optional — those should block pod startup if missing. For easypj/jobpost: DEBUG and FEATURE_FLAGS can be optional; DATABASE_URL must NOT be optional.

4.5 Secrets — Managing Sensitive DataQ139-Q146

🟢→🔴 | LF Subtopic 6: Create & consume Secrets. Types, env vars vs volume mounts, security considerations.

Security 🟢 Q139 of 200
What is a Kubernetes Secret and is it actually encrypted?
A) Secrets are fully encrypted at rest by default — Kubernetes automatically encrypts all Secret data using AES-256 before storing in etcd
B) Secrets are stored in a separate, encrypted database — they never touch etcd and are only accessible via a dedicated Secrets API
C) Secrets are stored as BASE64 ENCODED (NOT encrypted!) in etcd by default. Base64 is encoding, not encryption — anyone with etcd access can decode them. Encryption at rest requires EXPLICIT configuration (EncryptionConfiguration with a KMS provider or AES key). Secrets ARE automatically encrypted in transit (TLS). For production, you MUST enable etcd encryption or use external secret management (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, SealedSecrets)
D) Secrets are stored in plaintext in etcd with no encoding whatsoever — they're completely unprotected by default
✅ Correct Answer: C

This is one of the most misunderstood aspects of Kubernetes security. Secrets are NOT encrypted by default — they're base64-encoded, which is trivially reversible. Base64 protects against accidental exposure (e.g., someone glancing at your screen), not against attackers with etcd access. Encryption at rest is an opt-in feature requiring cluster-level configuration.

📝 Secret Security — Encoding vs Encryption
Base64 Encoding ≠ Encryption
  ═══════════════ BASE64 IS NOT ENCRYPTION ═══════════════
  Original:    s3cr3tP@ssw0rd
  Base64:      czNjcjN0UEBzc3cwcmQ=
  Decode:      echo czNjcjN0UEBzc3cwcmQ= | base64 -d
               → s3cr3tP@ssw0rd  (instantly recovered!)

  ═══════════ ENABLING ETCD ENCRYPTION (CKA territory) ═══════════
  apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
  kind: EncryptionConfiguration
  resources:
  - resources: [secrets]
    providers:
    - aescbc:
        keys:
        - name: key1
          secret: <base64-encoded-32-byte-key>
    - identity: {}  ← Fallback (plain text)

  ═══════════ SECRET SECURITY LAYERS ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  1. BASE64 (default) — protects against screen-glancing  │
  │  2. TLS (always) — protects data in transit              │
  │  3. ETCD ENCRYPTION (opt-in) — protects data at rest     │
  │  4. RBAC — controls who can READ secrets via API         │
  │  5. EXTERNAL (Vault, etc.) — secrets never touch etcd    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: For CKAD, focus on creating and consuming Secrets correctly. Know that they're base64-encoded (not encrypted). For easypj/jobpost production, consider using external secret management like SealedSecrets or External Secrets Operator to avoid storing raw secrets in etcd.

Security 🟡 Q140 of 200
What are the different Secret types and when should you use each?
A) There is only one Secret type (Opaque) — the other types are aliases that all store data the same way
B) Opaque (generic, default — arbitrary key-value pairs), kubernetes.io/tls (TLS cert + key — must have tls.crt and tls.key keys), kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson (~/.docker/config.json for imagePullSecrets), kubernetes.io/basic-auth (username + password), kubernetes.io/ssh-auth (SSH private key), kubernetes.io/service-account-token (auto-created SA tokens). For easypj/jobpost: Opaque for DB password and API keys, TLS for Ingress certificates, dockerconfigjson for private registry auth
C) Secret types are only used for documentation purposes — they don't affect how Kubernetes handles the data
D) Secret types determine the encryption algorithm used — TLS secrets use AES-256, Opaque uses Base64, etc.
✅ Correct Answer: B

Secret types provide structural validation — each type expects specific keys and formats. For example, a kubernetes.io/tls Secret must have tls.crt and tls.key keys with PEM-encoded data. This validation prevents misconfigurations where you accidentally use a password Secret where a TLS Secret is expected.

📝 Secret Types Reference
All Secret Types and Their Required Keys
  ═══════════════ SECRET TYPES ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  TYPE                     │ REQUIRED KEYS / USE CASE         │
  ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Opaque (default)        │ Arbitrary keys (DB_PASSWORD, etc)│
  ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubernetes.io/tls       │ tls.crt, tls.key (PEM format)    │
  │                          │ Used by: Ingress TLS             │
  ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubernetes.io/          │ .dockerconfigjson key            │
  │  dockerconfigjson        │ Used by: imagePullSecrets        │
  ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubernetes.io/basic-auth│ username, password               │
  ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubernetes.io/ssh-auth  │ ssh-privatekey                   │
  ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  kubernetes.io/          │ token (auto-generated JWT)       │
  │  service-account-token   │ Auto-created for each SA         │
  └──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: Most CKAD Secret tasks use Opaque (default). For TLS Secrets, remember the required keys are tls.crt and tls.key — misspelling these will cause Ingress to fail. For easypj/jobpost: Opaque for passwords, TLS for HTTPS Ingress.

Security 🟢 Q141 of 200
How do you create Secrets imperatively for passwords, TLS certificates, and Docker registry credentials?
A) Generic: kubectl create secret generic db-creds --from-literal=username=admin --from-literal=password=s3cr3t. TLS: kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls --cert=cert.pem --key=key.pem. Docker registry: kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=easypj --docker-password=token --docker-email=dev@easypj.com. ALWAYS use --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate YAML first
B) kubectl secret create — this is the only command for creating all types of secrets
C) Secrets can only be created from YAML files — there are no imperative kubectl commands for creating secrets
D) kubectl encrypt secret — secrets must be manually encrypted before they can be stored in Kubernetes
✅ Correct Answer: A

kubectl create secret has three subcommands for different Secret types. For CKAD, kubectl create secret generic is the most used. Always generate YAML with --dry-run=client -o yaml first to avoid storing plaintext passwords in your shell history.

📝 Secret Creation — All Methods
Imperative Secret Creation for easypj/jobpost
  ═══════════════ GENERIC (Opaque) ═══════════════
  kubectl create secret generic db-creds \
    --from-literal=POSTGRES_USER=easypj \
    --from-literal=POSTGRES_PASSWORD=s3cr3t \
    --from-literal=POSTGRES_DB=jobpost \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml > secret.yaml

  ═══════════════ TLS ═══════════════
  kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls \
    --cert=fullchain.pem \
    --key=privkey.pem

  ═══════════════ DOCKER REGISTRY ═══════════════
  kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-secret \
    --docker-server=ghcr.io \
    --docker-username=easypj \
    --docker-password=$GITHUB_TOKEN \
    --docker-email=dev@easypj.com

  ═══════════════ FROM FILE ═══════════════
  kubectl create secret generic app-keys \
    --from-file=api-key=./api-key.txt \
    --from-file=jwt-secret=./jwt-secret.txt

CKAD exam tip: Secret data is automatically base64-encoded when you use imperative commands. When writing Secret YAML manually, you MUST provide base64-encoded values: echo -n 's3cr3t' | base64. For easypj/jobpost: create a db-creds Secret for PostgreSQL credentials and a tls Secret for HTTPS.

Security 🟡 Q142 of 200
How do you inject Secrets as environment variables in a pod spec?
A) Secrets cannot be used as environment variables — they can only be mounted as files for security reasons
B) kubectl inject secret db-creds — this imperative command injects a Secret into all pods in the namespace
C) Secrets are automatically injected as environment variables in any pod that has a label matching the Secret name
D) Two methods: envFrom with secretRef (ALL Secret keys become env vars) and valueFrom.secretKeyRef (SELECTIVE — specific key with custom env var name). Example for easypj: envFrom: [secretRef: {name: db-creds}] injects POSTGRES_USER, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_DB as env vars. ⚠️ Security note: env vars are visible in /proc/<pid>/environ inside the container
✅ Correct Answer: D

Secrets as environment variables work identically to ConfigMaps — use envFrom for all keys or valueFrom.secretKeyRef for selective injection. However, environment variables have a security caveat: they're visible in /proc/<pid>/environ, which any process in the container can read. For highly sensitive secrets, consider volume mounts instead.

📝 Secrets as Environment Variables
Injecting Secrets into easypj/jobpost Pods
  ═══════════════ METHOD: envFrom ═══════════════
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: django
      envFrom:
      - secretRef:
          name: db-creds
  → All Secret keys become env vars:
    POSTGRES_USER=easypj
    POSTGRES_PASSWORD=s3cr3t
    POSTGRES_DB=jobpost

  ═══════════════ METHOD: valueFrom (SELECTIVE) ═══════════════
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: django
      env:
      - name: DATABASE_URL
        valueFrom:
          secretKeyRef:
            name: db-creds
            key: connection-string
  → Only connection-string key, renamed to DATABASE_URL

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam tests both envFrom and valueFrom patterns for Secrets. For database credentials, envFrom is usually what the application expects (Django reads DATABASE_URL from os.environ). For easypj/jobpost: use envFrom.secretRef for PostgreSQL credentials.

Security 🟡 Q143 of 200
How do you mount Secrets as files in a pod, and why is this more secure than environment variables?
A) Secrets cannot be mounted as files — they only work as environment variables due to Kubernetes security restrictions
B) Mount Secrets as a volume (tmpfs — stored in memory, NEVER written to disk). Each key becomes a file, each value becomes the file content. Volume mounts are MORE secure than env vars because: (1) env vars are visible in /proc/<pid>/environ, (2) env vars may appear in crash dumps, debug logs, and child process inheritance, (3) volume mounts are isolated to the mount path. For easypj/jobpost: mount TLS certs and JWT secrets as files; use env vars only for database connection strings where env vars are required by the framework
C) Volume-mounted Secrets are stored on the node's disk — they're less secure than environment variables which exist only in memory
D) Secret volume mounts require a special StorageClass — they don't work with default storage provisions
✅ Correct Answer: B

Secret volume mounts use tmpfs — an in-memory filesystem. The Secret data never touches the node's disk. This, combined with the isolation from /proc, makes volume mounts the recommended approach for highly sensitive secrets. Each key becomes a separate file, making it easy for applications that expect file-based configuration (TLS certs, JWT keys, CA bundles).

📝 Secrets as Volume Mounts (tmpfs)
Secret Volume Mount — In-Memory Only
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: django
      volumeMounts:
      - name: secrets
        mountPath: /etc/secrets
        readOnly: true
    volumes:
    - name: secrets
      secret:
        secretName: app-secrets

  Inside container:
  /etc/secrets/               ← tmpfs (in-memory!)
  ├── db-password             ← "s3cr3t"
  ├── api-key                 ← "sk-abc123"
  └── jwt-secret              ← "jwt-secret-value"

  ═══════════ ENV VAR vs VOLUME MOUNT SECURITY ═══════════
  ┌─────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │                  │ ENV VAR           │ VOLUME (tmpfs)   │
  ├─────────────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │  Visible in proc │ ✅ /proc/<pid>/environ│ ❌ Not in proc  │
  │  Child processes │ ✅ Inherited       │ ❌ Not inherited  │
  │  Crash dumps     │ ✅ May include     │ ❌ Not included   │
  │  Storage         │ In memory         │ tmpfs (memory)   │
  │  Disk exposure   │ ❌ No             │ ❌ No             │
  └─────────────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: For the CKAD exam, use whatever the task asks for. If given a choice, prefer volume mounts for TLS, JWT, and API keys. For easypj/jobpost: mount PostgreSQL password as a file if possible; use env vars only when the framework (Django + dj-database-url) expects them.

Security 🔴 Q144 of 200
How can malicious actors extract Secrets if they gain access to a container? What precautions should you take?
A) Secrets are completely safe inside containers — even with root access, attackers cannot read Secret data from Kubernetes
B) The only way to extract Secrets is through the Kubernetes API — processes inside the container cannot access Secret data at all
C) Attack vectors: (1) env vars visible in /proc/<pid>/environ (cat /proc/1/environ shows ALL env vars), (2) volume mounts readable at the mount path, (3) kubectl exec + SA token to query API server for more Secrets, (4) etcd access if encryption not enabled. Precautions: use volume mounts over env vars, set automountServiceAccountToken: false when not needed, use least privilege RBAC, enable etcd encryption, consider external secret management (Vault, SealedSecrets)
D) Secrets are encrypted inside the container — even the root user cannot read decrypted Secret data without the cluster's master key
✅ Correct Answer: C

Secrets inside a container are just data — there's no runtime encryption or access control beyond the Linux filesystem permissions. If an attacker gets code execution in your container (e.g., through an RCE vulnerability in your Django app), they can read all env vars from /proc/1/environ and all Secret volume mounts. This is why defense-in-depth matters: secure the container, the Secrets, the RBAC, AND the etcd.

📝 Secret Extraction Vectors — Defense in Depth
How Attackers Extract Secrets
  ═══════════════ ATTACK VECTORS ═══════════════
  # 1. Read env vars (trivial!)
  cat /proc/1/environ | tr '\0' '\n'
  → POSTGRES_PASSWORD=s3cr3t
  → API_KEY=sk-abc123
  → JWT_SECRET=super-secret-key

  # 2. Read volume mounts
  cat /etc/secrets/db-password
  → s3cr3t

  # 3. Use SA token to query API
  TOKEN=$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/easypj-prod/secrets
  → (if RBAC allows — lists all Secrets in namespace!)

  ═══════════ DEFENSE IN DEPTH ═══════════
  ✅ Volume mounts over env vars
  ✅ automountServiceAccountToken: false (when not needed)
  ✅ Least privilege RBAC (SA shouldn't list secrets!)
  ✅ etcd encryption at rest
  ✅ External secret management (Vault, SealedSecrets)
  ✅ NetworkPolicy to restrict egress
  ✅ Container security: readOnlyRootFilesystem, non-root user

🚀 Beyond CKAD (CKS crossover): CKS covers secret management in depth — etcd encryption, external secret stores, runtime security with Falco (detecting secret access from unexpected processes), and container escape techniques. For easypj/jobpost production: use SealedSecrets or External Secrets Operator to store secrets encrypted in git and decrypted only inside the cluster.

Security 🟢 Q145 of 200
What is an immutable Secret and when should you use it?
A) Set immutable: true (K8s 1.21+) — Secret cannot be edited after creation. Benefits: prevents accidental changes to production credentials, reduces kubelet watch load (performance), ensures credentials are versioned and auditable. Workflow: create secret-v1 (immutable), deploy app, rotate credentials → create secret-v2 → update Deployment → delete v1
B) Immutable Secrets are automatically encrypted with AES-256 — they provide stronger encryption than regular Secrets
C) Immutable Secrets are read-only inside the pod — containers can see the data but cannot modify the mounted files
D) Immutable Secrets cannot be deleted — once created, they persist for the lifetime of the Kubernetes cluster
✅ Correct Answer: A

Immutable Secrets are particularly important for credentials — you DON'T want anyone accidentally editing a production database password. Combined with versioned naming (db-creds-v1, db-creds-v2), immutable Secrets create an audit trail of credential rotations.

📝 Immutable Secret — Versioned Credential Rotation
Immutable Secret Rotation Pattern — Full Workflow
  ═══════════════ STEP 1: CREATE V1 (immutable) ═══════════════
  kubectl create secret generic db-creds-v1 \
    --from-literal=password=old-password \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml | \
    sed 's/^kind: Secret$/kind: Secret\nimmutable: true/' | \
    kubectl apply -f -
  → Secret "db-creds-v1" created (immutable — can't be edited!)

  ═══════════════ STEP 2: DEPLOY APP WITH V1 ═══════════════
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: django
      envFrom:
      - secretRef:
          name: db-creds-v1           ← References v1
  → App runs with old-password

  ═══════════════ STEP 3: ROTATE — CREATE V2 ═══════════════
  kubectl create secret generic db-creds-v2 \
    --from-literal=password=new-password \
    --dry-run=client -o yaml | \
    sed 's/^kind: Secret$/kind: Secret\nimmutable: true/' | \
    kubectl apply -f -
  → Secret "db-creds-v2" created (immutable)

  ═══════════════ STEP 4: UPDATE DEPLOYMENT → ROLLING RESTART ═══════════════
  kubectl set env deploy/easypj-api --from=secret/db-creds-v2
  → Rolling update starts → new pods use v2, old pods use v1
  → Zero-downtime credential rotation!

  ═══════════════ STEP 5: CLEANUP ═══════════════
  kubectl delete secret db-creds-v1   ← Remove old secret
  → Only after confirming v2 works in production

  ═══════════ IMMUTABLE vs MUTABLE SECRETS ═══════════
  ┌───────────────────┬───────────────────┬────────────────────┐
  │                    │ MUTABLE           │ IMMUTABLE          │
  ├───────────────────┼───────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │  Edit in-place    │ ✅ kubectl edit   │ ❌ Must replace    │
  │  Accidental change│ ⚠️  Possible      │ ✅ Impossible      │
  │  Audit trail      │ ❌ No versioning  │ ✅ Versioned names │
  │  kubelet watch    │ ✅ Watches changes│ ❌ No watch needed │
  │  Best for         │ Dev/Staging       │ Production         │
  └───────────────────┴───────────────────┴────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: Like immutable ConfigMaps, immutable Secrets can only be CREATED. Any update attempt fails. Use versioned naming for credential rotation. For easypj/jobpost: version production database credentials and use immutable Secrets.

Security 🟡 Q146 of 200
How do you authenticate to a private container registry using imagePullSecrets?
A) Private registries are automatically accessible if the cluster has outbound internet access — no authentication is needed
B) kubectl login registry ghcr.io — this authenticates the entire cluster to a private registry
C) imagePullSecrets are configured at the cluster level by the administrator — individual pods cannot specify their own registry credentials
D) Step 1: kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=USER --docker-password=TOKEN. Step 2: Reference in Pod spec via spec.imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}]. Or add to ServiceAccount (all pods using that SA get the secret): kubectl patch serviceaccount default -p '{"imagePullSecrets": [{"name": "regcred"}]}'
✅ Correct Answer: D

imagePullSecrets allow pods to pull images from private registries that require authentication. You create a special docker-registry type Secret containing registry credentials, then reference it in the pod spec. The ServiceAccount-level approach is preferred — every pod using that SA automatically gets registry access.

📝 imagePullSecrets — Private Registry Access
Authenticating to Private Registries
  ═══════════════ CREATE REGISTRY SECRET ═══════════════
  kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-secret \
    --docker-server=ghcr.io \
    --docker-username=easypj \
    --docker-password=$GITHUB_TOKEN \
    --docker-email=dev@easypj.com \
    -n easypj-prod

  ═══════════════ METHOD 1: POD-LEVEL ═══════════════
  spec:
    imagePullSecrets:
    - name: ghcr-secret
    containers:
    - name: django
      image: ghcr.io/easypj/jobpost:v2.1

  ═══════════════ METHOD 2: SERVICEACCOUNT-LEVEL ═══════════════
  kubectl patch sa default -n easypj-prod \
    -p '{"imagePullSecrets": [{"name": "ghcr-secret"}]}'
  → ALL pods using "default" SA automatically use ghcr-secret!

CKAD exam tip: On the CKAD exam, you may need to configure imagePullSecrets for a private registry. Remember: the Secret must be in the SAME namespace as the pod. For easypj/jobpost: if you push images to a private GitHub Container Registry, create an imagePullSecret and attach it to the default ServiceAccount.

4.6 ServiceAccounts — Pod IdentityQ147-Q150

🟢→🟡 | LF Subtopic 7: Understand ServiceAccounts. Default SA, custom SAs, token mounting, RBAC binding.

Security 🟢 Q147 of 200
What is a ServiceAccount and how does it provide identity to pods?
A) A ServiceAccount is a human user account for CI/CD pipelines — it's not used by pods or applications
B) A ServiceAccount is a KUBERNETES IDENTITY for pods (not humans). Every pod runs as exactly one ServiceAccount (default "default" if not specified). The SA's JWT token is auto-mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, which the pod can use to authenticate to the API server. RBAC binds permissions to SAs. For easypj/jobpost: the API pod runs as SA "easypj-api" which has read access to ConfigMaps; the CI/CD pod runs as SA "deployer" which can update Deployments
C) ServiceAccounts are only used by the control plane — application pods cannot use them for API authentication
D) ServiceAccounts are automatically created for each Deployment — the Deployment name becomes the ServiceAccount name
✅ Correct Answer: B

ServiceAccounts are the identity mechanism for pods. Just as human users authenticate with kubeconfig certificates, pods authenticate with ServiceAccount tokens. The token is a JWT that the API server validates. This is why kubectl works inside a pod — the pod's SA token is automatically used for authentication.

📝 ServiceAccount — Pod Identity System
ServiceAccount Token Authentication
  ═══════════════ POD IDENTITY ═══════════════
  Every pod has ONE ServiceAccount:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Pod: easypj-api-5k3m8                               │
  │  ServiceAccount: easypj-api                           │
  │                                                       │
  │  Auto-mounted at:                                     │
  │  /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/       │
  │  ├── token        ← JWT for API authentication       │
  │  ├── ca.crt       ← API server CA certificate        │
  │  └── namespace    ← Namespace name                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  kubectl get sa -n easypj-dev
  →
  NAME          SECRETS   AGE
  default       0         30d    ← Auto-created in every NS
  easypj-api    0         7d     ← Custom SA for API pods
  deployer      0         7d     ← Custom SA for CI/CD

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam frequently asks you to create a ServiceAccount, bind it to a Role, and use it in a pod. For easypj/jobpost: create dedicated SAs for the API, web, and worker components — never use the default SA for application pods.

Security 🟢 Q148 of 200
What is the default ServiceAccount and should you use it for application pods?
A) The default ServiceAccount has cluster-admin privileges — all pods get full API access by default for convenience
B) The default ServiceAccount must be explicitly created by the namespace administrator — namespaces don't have one by default
C) Every namespace has an auto-created "default" ServiceAccount. Every pod uses it UNLESS spec.serviceAccountName is set. The default SA has NO RBAC permissions by default (can't do anything with the API). Best practice: NEVER use the default SA for application pods — create dedicated SAs with least-privilege RBAC. If a pod doesn't need API access, set automountServiceAccountToken: false
D) The default ServiceAccount is deprecated — Kubernetes 1.30 removed it in favor of explicit ServiceAccount creation for every pod
✅ Correct Answer: C

The default ServiceAccount is a convenience that becomes a security risk if you rely on it. Every namespace has one, and every pod that doesn't specify a ServiceAccount uses it. If you accidentally bind permissions to the default SA, you've granted those permissions to EVERY pod in the namespace. Always create dedicated SAs and explicitly set serviceAccountName in your pod specs.

📝 Custom SAs — Dedicated Identity per Component
Custom SAs for easypj/jobpost
  ═══════════════ CREATE & USE DEDICATED SA ═══════════════
  # 1. Create SA
  kubectl create sa easypj-api -n easypj-dev

  # 2. Create Role with minimal permissions
  kubectl create role config-reader \
    --verb=get,list,watch \
    --resource=configmaps \
    -n easypj-dev

  # 3. Bind SA to Role
  kubectl create rolebinding api-config-access \
    --role=config-reader \
    --serviceaccount=easypj-dev:easypj-api \
    -n easypj-dev

  # 4. Use in Pod
  spec:
    serviceAccountName: easypj-api   ← Explicit SA!
    containers:
    - name: django
      image: easypj/api:v2.1

CKAD exam tip: On the CKAD exam, always create dedicated ServiceAccounts. If the task doesn't require API access, set automountServiceAccountToken: false for security. For easypj/jobpost: API SA needs ConfigMap/Secret read; CI/CD SA needs Deployment update; web SA needs nothing (automountServiceAccountToken: false).

Security 🟡 Q149 of 200
When should you set automountServiceAccountToken: false and what does it prevent?
A) Set automountServiceAccountToken: false in the Pod spec (or ServiceAccount) when the pod DOES NOT NEED to talk to the Kubernetes API. This prevents the SA token from being mounted at /var/run/secrets/... inside the pod. Benefits: reduces attack surface (if the container is compromised, there's no API token to steal), follows least privilege principle. For easypj/jobpost: the web frontend (nginx serving static files) doesn't need API access — set false. The API pod (needs ConfigMaps/Secrets) — keep enabled with minimal RBAC
B) automountServiceAccountToken is a performance setting — it speeds up pod startup by skipping the token mount process
C) automountServiceAccountToken: false disables the pod's ability to pull images — it should never be used in production
D) This setting only affects the default ServiceAccount — custom ServiceAccounts always mount tokens regardless of this setting
✅ Correct Answer: A

Disabling auto-mount is one of the simplest security hardening steps. If an attacker compromises your nginx container but there's no SA token to steal, they can't use it to access the Kubernetes API. This limits the blast radius of a container compromise. For many application pods (web servers, workers, databases), there's no legitimate reason to talk to the Kubernetes API.

📝 automountServiceAccountToken — Reduce Attack Surface
automountServiceAccountToken — easypj Decision Matrix
  ═══════════════ WHEN TO DISABLE ═══════════════
  spec:
    automountServiceAccountToken: false  ← No token mounted!
    serviceAccountName: easypj-web

  ✅ Disable for: web frontend (nginx), Celery workers,
     Redis, PostgreSQL, static file servers, any pod
     that doesn't call Kubernetes APIs

  ⚠️  Keep enabled for: API pods reading ConfigMaps,
     CI/CD pipelines, operators, ingress controllers,
     monitoring agents, any pod that NEEDS the API

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam may ask you to configure a pod that doesn't need API access. Always set automountServiceAccountToken: false if the pod doesn't call the Kubernetes API. This can be set at the pod level or the ServiceAccount level (affects all pods using that SA).

Security 🟡 Q150 of 200
How do you create a custom ServiceAccount and bind it to a Role for specific API access?
A) ServiceAccounts are automatically bound to the cluster-admin role — you cannot customize their permissions
B) kubectl create sa with --permissions flag — this imperatively creates a ServiceAccount with inline RBAC rules
C) ServiceAccounts are bound to Roles by naming convention only — the SA name must match the Role name exactly
D) Step 1: kubectl create sa easypj-api -n easypj-dev. Step 2: Create a Role (or use ClusterRole) with needed permissions. Step 3: kubectl create rolebinding api-binding --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=easypj-dev:easypj-api -n easypj-dev. Step 4: Use in pod: spec.serviceAccountName: easypj-api.
