But they only work if your CNI plugin supports them — the policy is defined in Kubernetes, but the CNI enforces it.

📝 NetworkPolicy — Pod Firewall Rules
NetworkPolicy Concept — Allow Specific Traffic
  ═══════════════ WITHOUT NETWORKPOLICY ═══════════════
  ALL pods can talk to ALL pods on ALL ports
  ┌─────────┐      ┌─────────┐      ┌─────────┐
  │ web-pod │ ←──→ │ api-pod │ ←──→ │ db-pod  │
  └─────────┘      └─────────┘      └─────────┘
       │                │                │
       └────────────────┴────────────────┘
         Anyone can talk to anyone!

  ═══════════════ WITH NETWORKPOLICY ═══════════════
  ┌─────────┐      ┌─────────┐      ┌─────────┐
  │ web-pod │ ───→ │ api-pod │ ───→ │ db-pod  │
  └─────────┘ ←─── └─────────┘ ←─── └─────────┘
       │                                    │
       └───────────── BLOCKED ──────────────┘
  web → api: ALLOWED (port 8000)
  api → db: ALLOWED (port 5432)
  web → db: DENIED (no direct access!)
  external → db: DENIED (no external access!)

CKAD exam tip: NetworkPolicy is a key CKAD topic. Remember: (1) default is allow-all, (2) NetworkPolicies are additive — multiple policies combine, (3) CNI must support it. For easypj/jobpost: web can only talk to API, API can only talk to DB and Redis — no cross-tier access.

Network 🟢 Q182 of 200
What is the difference between Ingress and Egress in NetworkPolicy terms?
A) Ingress and Egress mean the same thing in NetworkPolicies — they're different words for the same direction
B) Ingress = INCOMING traffic TO the selected pods (who can send traffic TO these pods?). Egress = OUTGOING traffic FROM the selected pods (where can these pods send traffic TO?). A NetworkPolicy can have ingress rules, egress rules, or both. For easypj/jobpost: API pod has ingress: from web pods on 8000 (allow web→API) and egress: to DB pods on 5432 (allow API→DB)
C) Ingress controls Kubernetes API access, Egress controls pod-to-pod traffic — they're completely different systems
D) Ingress rules are required, Egress rules are optional — you can't have a NetworkPolicy with only egress rules
✅ Correct Answer: B

Ingress and Egress are from the perspective of the SELECTED pods. Ingress = "who can talk to me?" Egress = "who can I talk to?" This is a common point of confusion — always think from the pod's perspective, not the network's.

📝 Ingress vs Egress — Pod Perspective
Ingress & Egress Directions
  ═══════════════ INGRESS (INCOMING TO POD) ═══════════════
  web-pod ──────────→ api-pod
           INGRESS to api-pod
  "I allow traffic FROM web-pod TO me on port 8000"

  ═══════════════ EGRESS (OUTGOING FROM POD) ═══════════════
  api-pod ──────────→ db-pod
           EGRESS from api-pod
  "I can send traffic TO db-pod on port 5432"

CKAD exam tip: For the CKAD exam, think: Ingress = "incoming" (who can reach my pod), Egress = "outgoing" (where can my pod reach). For easypj/jobpost: the DB pod has an ingress rule allowing API pods on port 5432; the API pod has an egress rule allowing outbound to DB on 5432 and DNS on 53.

Network 🟡 Q183 of 200
How does podSelector work in NetworkPolicies and how do you target specific pods?
A) spec.podSelector selects which pods the NetworkPolicy APPLIES TO (the target). spec.ingress[].from[].podSelector selects which pods are ALLOWED to send traffic (the source). Both use label selectors. For easypj/jobpost: podSelector: {app: easypj-api} targets the API pods; from[].podSelector: {app: easypj-web} allows web pods to send traffic to them
B) podSelector always selects ALL pods in the namespace — you cannot target individual pods with NetworkPolicies
C) podSelector uses pod names (not labels) — you must specify exact pod names like "easypj-web-9x7k2"
D) podSelector is optional — if omitted, the NetworkPolicy applies to all pods in all namespaces
✅ Correct Answer: A

There are TWO podSelectors in a NetworkPolicy: the top-level one (who the policy protects) and the from/to ones (who is allowed/denied). Empty podSelector {} means ALL pods. For easypj/jobpost: use podSelector to target specific components (API, DB, web) with different policies for each tier.

📝 podSelector — Target vs Source
Two podSelectors in NetworkPolicy
  ═══════════════ NETWORKPOLICY ANATOMY ═══════════════
  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: api-allow-from-web
  spec:
    podSelector:                    ← POLICY APPLIES TO these pods
      matchLabels:
        app: easypj-api
    policyTypes: [Ingress]
    ingress:
    - from:
      - podSelector:                ← ALLOW TRAFFIC FROM these pods
          matchLabels:
            app: easypj-web
      ports:
      - port: 8000
        protocol: TCP

  ═══════════ VISUAL ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  spec.podSelector = {app: easypj-api}                    │
  │  "THIS policy PROTECTS the API pods"                     │
  │                                                           │
  │  ingress.from[0].podSelector = {app: easypj-web}         │
  │  "ALLOW traffic FROM web pods"                           │
  │                                                           │
  │  web-pod ──── ALLOWED ────→ api-pod (port 8000)         │
  │  db-pod  ──── DENIED  ────→ api-pod                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam may ask you to write NetworkPolicies with specific podSelectors. Empty {} means all. For easypj/jobpost: create separate policies for each tier — API accepts from web, DB accepts from API, Redis accepts from API.

Network 🟡 Q184 of 200
How does namespaceSelector work for cross-namespace NetworkPolicy rules?
A) namespaceSelector selects pods by their namespace name — it works identically to podSelector
B) Cross-namespace traffic cannot be controlled by NetworkPolicies — policies only work within a single namespace
C) namespaceSelector is deprecated — you must use podSelector with namespace labels instead
D) namespaceSelector selects NAMESPACES (not pods) by their labels. It allows traffic from ALL pods in matching namespaces. Combined with podSelector, you can narrow to specific pods in specific namespaces. For easypj/jobpost: allow traffic from namespace: easypj-web (labeled env=production) to the API pods in easypj-api namespace
✅ Correct Answer: D

namespaceSelector is for cross-namespace policies. Since pods in different namespaces can't share labels that identify their namespace, you label the NAMESPACE itself and use namespaceSelector. Combined with podSelector (AND logic), you can precisely target pods in specific namespaces.

📝 namespaceSelector — Cross-Namespace Rules
Cross-Namespace NetworkPolicy for easypj/jobpost
  ═══════════════ STEP 1: LABEL NAMESPACE ═══════════════
  kubectl label ns easypj-web environment=production

  ═══════════════ STEP 2: POLICY IN EASYPJ-API NS ═══════════════
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-from-web-ns
    namespace: easypj-api
  spec:
    podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        app: easypj-api
    ingress:
    - from:
      - namespaceSelector:           ← Which NAMESPACE
          matchLabels:
            environment: production
        podSelector:                  ← Which PODS in that NS
          matchLabels:
            app: easypj-web
      ports:
      - port: 8000

  ═══════════ SELECTOR LOGIC ═══════════
  namespaceSelector AND podSelector = both must match
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  FROM namespace "easypj-web" (env=production)           │
  │  AND pods with app=easypj-web                            │
  │  → ALLOW on port 8000                                    │
  │                                                           │
  │  FROM namespace "easypj-web"                             │
  │  BUT pod with app=monitoring (doesn't match podSelector) │
  │  → DENIED                                                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: namespaceSelector + podSelector together work as AND — both must match. Empty podSelector {} means all pods in the matching namespace. For easypj/jobpost: use cross-namespace policies when the web pod is in a different namespace from the API.

Network 🟡 Q185 of 200
How does ipBlock work in NetworkPolicies for CIDR-based rules?
A) ipBlock replaces podSelector and namespaceSelector — you can only use one selector type per rule
B) ipBlock defines CIDR-based rules (IP ranges) independent of Kubernetes pods. Use for: allowing office VPN IPs, blocking external IPs, allowing cloud service IPs. ipBlock has cidr (network range) and except (excluded IPs within the range). ipBlock rules are OR'd with podSelector/namespaceSelector within the same from/to block. For easypj/jobpost: allow monitoring from office VPN CIDR 10.0.0.0/8 to API metrics port 9090
C) ipBlock only works for egress rules — it cannot be used for ingress traffic control
D) ipBlock requires a cloud provider — it doesn't work on local clusters like kubeadm or kind
✅ Correct Answer: B

ipBlock is for external traffic control — traffic from/to IPs outside the cluster. Within the same from block, multiple selectors (podSelector, namespaceSelector, ipBlock) are OR'd — traffic matching ANY of them is allowed.

📝 ipBlock — CIDR-Based Rules
ipBlock — CIDR-Based Rules
  ═══════════════ IPBLOCK EXAMPLE ═══════════════
  ingress:
  - from:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.0.0.0/8        ← Office VPN range
        except:
        - 10.0.0.5/32           ← EXCLUDE this specific IP
    ports:
    - port: 9090

  ═══════════════ RESULT ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  10.0.0.1  ──→ ALLOWED on port 9090 ✅                  │
  │  10.0.0.5  ──→ DENIED (in except list) ❌               │
  │  10.5.0.1  ──→ ALLOWED (in 10.0.0.0/8) ✅              │
  │  192.168.0.1 → DENIED (outside CIDR) ❌                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════ SELECTOR COMBINATION (OR logic) ═══════════
  Within one "from" block:
  podSelector OR namespaceSelector OR ipBlock = ANY match allows
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  from:                                                    │
  │  - podSelector: {app: web}        ← web pods            │
  │  - ipBlock: {cidr: 10.0.0.0/8}   ← VPN IPs             │
  │  → web pods OR VPN IPs → ALLOWED (either matches)       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: ipBlock is commonly used for allowing external monitoring (Prometheus) or blocking known bad IPs. For easypj/jobpost: allow the office VPN CIDR to access the Prometheus metrics endpoint on the API pods.

Network 🟡 Q186 of 200
How do you specify ports and protocols in a NetworkPolicy?
A) NetworkPolicies can only block/allow ALL ports — you cannot specify individual port numbers
B) Ports are specified by number only — named ports from pod specs cannot be used in NetworkPolicies
C) ports can specify port (number or named port), protocol (TCP, UDP, or SCTP), and optional endPort (port range). Named ports (matching containerPort name) are more maintainable than numbers. For easypj/jobpost: API accepts TCP on port 8000 from web, DB accepts TCP on port 5432 from API, Redis accepts TCP on 6379 from API
D) NetworkPolicy ports are always TCP — UDP and SCTP protocols are not supported for security reasons
✅ Correct Answer: C

Named ports are preferred for maintainability — if you change the container port number, the NetworkPolicy automatically follows. Only the CNI must support named ports (Calico, Cilium do; older Flannel may not).

📝 NetworkPolicy Port Specification
Port Specification in NetworkPolicies
  ═══════════════ PORT SPEC FORMATS ═══════════════
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 8000              ← Number (most common)
  - protocol: TCP
    port: http              ← Named port (matches containerPort name)
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 3000
    endPort: 4000           ← Port RANGE (3000-4000, K8s 1.22+)

  ═══════════ easypj/jobpost NETWORKPOLICY PORTS ═══════════
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │  POLICY           │ PORT     │ ALLOWS                   │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  web→api         │ TCP 8000 │ REST API traffic         │
  │  api→db          │ TCP 5432 │ PostgreSQL connections   │
  │  api→redis       │ TCP 6379 │ Redis cache              │
  │  monitoring→all  │ TCP 9090 │ Prometheus metrics       │
  │  all→dns         │ UDP 53   │ CoreDNS resolution       │
  └──────────────────┴──────────┴──────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: For the CKAD exam, TCP on numbered ports is the most common. For easypj/jobpost: use port numbers 8000 (API), 5432 (DB), 6379 (Redis) in NetworkPolicies.

Network 🟡 Q187 of 200
How do you create a default-deny-all-ingress NetworkPolicy?
A) Create a NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {} (all pods) and policyTypes: [Ingress] with NO ingress rules. This blocks ALL incoming traffic to all pods. Then create additional NetworkPolicies that ALLOW specific traffic (policies are additive). This implements "deny all by default, then explicitly allow" — the zero-trust model. For easypj/jobpost: start with default-deny in production, then add allow rules for web→API, API→DB
B) Default-deny requires a special annotation on the namespace — it cannot be done with a standard NetworkPolicy
C) Default-deny blocks all traffic including DNS — pods become completely isolated and unusable
D) Default-deny is the Kubernetes default — all pods start with no network access and you must explicitly allow everything
✅ Correct Answer: A

Default-deny is the foundation of zero-trust networking in Kubernetes. Create a "deny-all" policy first, then add specific "allow" policies. The key insight: policies are ADDITIVE — the deny-all blocks everything, and each allow policy opens specific holes.

📝 Default-Deny-All-Ingress Pattern
Zero-Trust NetworkPolicy for easypj/jobpost
  ═══════════ STEP 1: DENY ALL INGRESS ═══════════
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: default-deny-ingress
  spec:
    podSelector: {}            ← All pods
    policyTypes: [Ingress]
    # NO ingress rules → DENY ALL incoming traffic

  ═══════════ STEP 2: ALLOW SPECIFIC TRAFFIC ═══════════
  # Allow web → API on 8000
  # Allow API → DB on 5432
  # Allow API → Redis on 6379
  # Allow monitoring (namespace) → all on metrics port
  → Each allow policy ADDS to what's permitted

CKAD exam tip: The CKAD exam may ask you to "secure a namespace with NetworkPolicies." Start with default-deny, then add specific allow rules. For easypj/jobpost production: default-deny-ingress and default-deny-egress in all namespaces, with explicit allow rules for required communication paths.

Network 🔴 Q188 of 200
How do you create a default-deny-all-egress NetworkPolicy while still allowing DNS?
A) Default-deny-egress is not possible — Kubernetes always allows outbound traffic
B) DNS is automatically allowed even with default-deny-egress — no special rule is needed
C) Default-deny-egress prevents pods from starting — they can't pull images or register with the API server
D) Create a default-deny-egress policy (podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Egress], no egress rules). Then create a SEPARATE allow policy for DNS (egress to kube-system namespace on UDP 53, or to CoreDNS ClusterIP on TCP/UDP 53). DNS is NOT automatically allowed — without the DNS allow rule, pods can't resolve any names, including internal Services. For easypj/jobpost: allow DNS to kube-system, then allow API→DB, API→Redis
✅ Correct Answer: D

Default-deny-egress is the strictest NetworkPolicy — pods can't even resolve DNS unless you explicitly allow it. The #1 mistake with egress policies is forgetting the DNS allow rule, which breaks ALL pod communication (even internal). Always allow DNS to the CoreDNS service or kube-system namespace.

📝 Default-Deny-Egress + DNS Allow
Egress Lockdown with DNS Exception
  ═══════════ STEP 1: DENY ALL EGRESS ═══════════
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: default-deny-egress
  spec:
    podSelector: {}
    policyTypes: [Egress]
    # NO egress rules → DENY ALL outgoing traffic

  ═══════════ STEP 2: ALLOW DNS (CRITICAL!) ═══════════
  kind: NetworkPolicy
  metadata:
    name: allow-dns
  spec:
    podSelector: {}
    policyTypes: [Egress]
    egress:
    - to:
      - namespaceSelector:
          matchLabels:
            kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      ports:
      - protocol: UDP
        port: 53
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 53
  → Without this, pods can't resolve ANY names!

CKAD exam tip: Always add a DNS allow rule when creating default-deny-egress. The DNS service is typically CoreDNS running in kube-system. For easypj/jobpost production: default-deny-egress with DNS + specific outbound rules for required external services (API, payment gateway).

Network 🔴 Q189 of 200
How are multiple NetworkPolicies combined — is there a priority or ordering?
A) NetworkPolicies are evaluated in order — the first matching policy wins, like firewall rule chains
B) NetworkPolicies are ADDITIVE — ALL policies that match a pod are COMBINED (UNION of allowed traffic). There is NO priority or ordering. If ANY policy allows traffic, it's allowed. If NO policy allows it, it's denied (when at least one policy selects the pod). This means you can't have "allow A then deny B" ordering — you can only ADD allows. For easypj/jobpost: multiple policies (allow-web, allow-monitoring, allow-dns) combine to define the total allowed traffic
C) NetworkPolicies have explicit priority numbers — lower numbers are evaluated first, like iptables rules
D) Only the most recently created NetworkPolicy is active — new policies override older ones
✅ Correct Answer: B

NetworkPolicy additivity is a fundamental concept. Unlike traditional firewalls with ordered rules (first match wins), NetworkPolicies are UNION-based — all matching policies contribute their allowed traffic. There's no way to create a "block" rule that overrides an "allow" rule. This simplifies reasoning but limits expressiveness — for advanced policy, tools like OPA/Gatekeeper or CiliumNetworkPolicy are needed.

📝 Additive Policy Model
NetworkPolicy Combination — UNION of Allows
  Policy A: allow from namespace=web on port 8000
  Policy B: allow from namespace=monitoring on port 9090
  Policy C: deny-all-ingress (podSelector: {}, no ingress rules)

  Pod API is selected by ALL THREE policies:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Combined result:                                     │
  │  ✅ Allowed: web on 8000 (from Policy A)             │
  │  ✅ Allowed: monitoring on 9090 (from Policy B)      │
  │  ❌ Denied: everything else (from Policy C)          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  → Policy A + Policy B = UNION of allowed traffic
  → Policy C blocks everything NOT in the union

CKAD exam tip: You can't create a "deny" rule that overrides an "allow" — you can only add allows. The deny comes from having NO matching allow rule. For easypj/jobpost: create separate, focused policies (one per communication path) rather than one monolithic policy.

Network 🔴 Q190 of 200
What are the key limitations of NetworkPolicies that you should know?
A) (1) CNI DEPENDENCY — only works if CNI supports it (Calico, Cilium, Weave Net support; Flannel does NOT). (2) NO DENY RULES — policies are additive only, can't create explicit deny rules. (3) NO LOGGING — no built-in way to see what's being blocked. (4) NO L7 FILTERING — can't filter by HTTP method, URL path, or hostname (only IP:port). (5) NO ADVANCED MATCHING — no time-based rules, no user/identity-based rules. For advanced needs, use CiliumNetworkPolicy, Istio, or OPA/Gatekeeper
B) NetworkPolicies have no limitations — they provide enterprise-grade firewall capabilities out of the box
C) The only limitation is that NetworkPolicies can't be used with StatefulSets — they work only with Deployments
D) NetworkPolicies are limited to 10 rules per policy — beyond that, you must create additional policies
✅ Correct Answer: A

NetworkPolicies provide basic L3/L4 firewalling — IP, port, protocol. They don't understand HTTP, can't log, and critically depend on CNI support. For production easypj/jobpost, consider Cilium for eBPF-based networking with full L7 policies, or Istio for mTLS + HTTP-aware authorization.

📝 NetworkPolicy Limitations
What NetworkPolicies Can and Can't Do
  ═══════════════ NETWORKPOLICY LIMITATIONS ═══════════════
  ┌─────────────────────┬──────────┬──────────────────────────┐
  │  FEATURE             │ SUPPORTED│ ALTERNATIVE              │
  ├─────────────────────┼──────────┼──────────────────────────┤
  │  IP/port filtering   │ ✅       │                          │
  │  Pod/NS selectors    │ ✅       │                          │
  │  CIDR blocks         │ ✅       │                          │
  │  Explicit DENY rules │ ❌       │ CiliumNetworkPolicy      │
  │  L7 HTTP filtering   │ ❌       │ Istio, Cilium            │
  │  Traffic logging     │ ❌       │ Cilium Hubble, Falco     │
  │  Time-based rules    │ ❌       │ OPA/Gatekeeper           │
  │  DNAT/port remapping │ ❌       │ iptables directly        │
  └─────────────────────┴──────────┴──────────────────────────┘

🚀 Beyond CKAD (CKS crossover): CKS covers advanced network security — Cilium/eBPF for kernel-level enforcement, Tetragon for runtime network observability, and zero-trust architectures with mTLS everywhere. NetworkPolicies are the foundation; Cilium and Istio build on them for production-grade security.

5.4 Service Discovery & DNSQ191-Q194

🟢→🟡 | Supporting topic: CoreDNS, DNS naming convention, dnsPolicy, DNS debugging.

Network 🟢 Q191 of 200
What is CoreDNS and how does it provide service discovery in Kubernetes?
A) CoreDNS is an external DNS service that Kubernetes can optionally use — it's not built into the cluster
B) CoreDNS is a monitoring tool that tracks DNS query performance — it doesn't provide name resolution
C) CoreDNS is the DEFAULT DNS server for Kubernetes (replacing kube-dns since 1.11). It runs as a Deployment in kube-system, watches the API server for Services and Pods, and automatically creates DNS records. Every Service gets an A record (<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local → ClusterIP). Every pod (with hostname/subdomain) gets an A record. CoreDNS uses a flexible plugin architecture — the kubernetes plugin handles cluster DNS
D) CoreDNS only resolves external domain names — internal Kubernetes DNS is handled by kube-proxy
✅ Correct Answer: C

CoreDNS is the phone book of Kubernetes. Without it, pods would need to know IP addresses — impossible in a dynamic environment. CoreDNS watches the API server and auto-updates DNS records whenever Services or Pods change. Every pod's /etc/resolv.conf points to the CoreDNS Service IP.

📝 CoreDNS Architecture
CoreDNS — Automatic Service Discovery
  ═══════════════ COREDNS ARCHITECTURE ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  kube-system namespace                                    │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │  CoreDNS Deployment (2 replicas typically)         │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
  │  │  │  Watches API server for Services + Pods      │  │  │
  │  │  │  Auto-creates DNS records                    │  │  │
  │  │  │  Serves on UDP 53 (kube-dns ClusterIP)       │  │  │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                           │
  │  Every pod's /etc/resolv.conf:                            │
  │  nameserver 10.96.0.10  ← CoreDNS ClusterIP              │
  │  search easypj-prod.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: CoreDNS is automatically installed and managed. You rarely need to configure it for CKAD. Know that kubectl -n kube-system get pods | grep coredns shows the DNS pods. For easypj/jobpost: CoreDNS enables the Django API to resolve "easypj-db" to the PostgreSQL Service ClusterIP.

Network 🟡 Q192 of 200
What is the complete DNS naming convention for Services and Pods?
A) Services use <name>.<namespace> and pods use <name>.<node> — DNS naming is simple and flat
B) Service: <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local (FQDN), short forms: <svc>.<ns> or just <svc> (same namespace). Pod (with hostname+subdomain): <hostname>.<subdomain>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local. StatefulSet pod: <sts-name>-<ordinal>.<headless-svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local. For easypj/jobpost: easypj-api → easypj-api.easypj-prod.svc.cluster.local; postgresql-0.easypj-db-headless.easypj-prod.svc.cluster.local
C) DNS names are random hashes — there's no predictable naming convention in Kubernetes
D) Pods and Services share the same DNS format — both use <name>.pod.cluster.local regardless of type
✅ Correct Answer: B

Kubernetes DNS follows a hierarchical naming convention. The svc.cluster.local suffix is the cluster domain (configurable via kubelet). The short forms are resolved using the pod's DNS search domains from /etc/resolv.conf.

📝 DNS Naming Convention
Kubernetes DNS Name Hierarchy
  ═══════════════ SERVICE DNS ═══════════════
  Full:    easypj-api.easypj-prod.svc.cluster.local
           ────────── ─────────── ─── ────────────
           svc name   namespace   svc  cluster domain

  Short:   easypj-api.easypj-prod  (skip .svc.cluster.local)
  Shortest: easypj-api              (same namespace only)

  ═══════════════ STATEFULSET POD DNS ═══════════════
  Full:    postgresql-0.easypj-db-headless.easypj-prod.svc.cluster.local
           ──────────── ──────────────────
           pod hostname headless Service name

CKAD exam tip: For CKAD, use the shortest form that works: same namespace → just <svc>, cross-namespace → <svc>.<ns>. For easypj/jobpost: Django in easypj-prod resolves PostgreSQL as just "easypj-db" (same namespace).

Network 🟡 Q193 of 200
What does dnsPolicy control and what are the available options?
A) dnsPolicy controls how a pod's /etc/resolv.conf is configured. ClusterFirst (default): use cluster DNS first, fall back to node DNS. Default: inherit node's DNS config. ClusterFirstWithHostNet: use cluster DNS even with hostNetwork: true. None: custom DNS (must provide dnsConfig with nameservers). For easypj/jobpost: use ClusterFirst (default) for all pods; use None + dnsConfig for pods needing custom DNS (e.g., VPN-routed pods)
B) dnsPolicy controls which DNS server (CoreDNS vs kube-dns) is used — it's only relevant during cluster upgrades
C) dnsPolicy is automatically determined by the CNI plugin — you cannot set it manually in pod specs
D) dnsPolicy only affects Windows containers — Linux containers always use CoreDNS regardless of this setting
✅ Correct Answer: A

dnsPolicy is rarely changed from the default ClusterFirst, but it's important for special cases. The most common non-default use: None with dnsConfig when pods need custom DNS servers (e.g., enterprise VPN, custom DNS forwarding).

📝 dnsPolicy Options
DNS Policy Comparison
  ┌────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  POLICY                     │ POD /etc/resolv.conf             │
  ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  ClusterFirst (default)    │ nameserver <CoreDNS IP>         │
  │                            │ search <ns>.svc.cluster.local  │
  ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  Default                   │ Inherits node's /etc/resolv.conf │
  ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  ClusterFirstWithHostNet   │ Cluster DNS + hostNetwork        │
  │                            │ (hostNetwork pods need this)     │
  ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  None                       │ Custom: must provide dnsConfig  │
  │                            │ spec.dnsConfig.nameservers       │
  └────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: 99% of pods use ClusterFirst. The CKAD exam rarely tests dnsPolicy but know it exists. For easypj/jobpost: use ClusterFirst (default).

Network 🟡 Q194 of 200
How do you debug DNS issues from inside a Kubernetes pod?
A) DNS debugging requires cluster-admin access — regular users cannot troubleshoot DNS from inside pods
B) kubectl dns-check — this is the built-in command for diagnosing CoreDNS issues
C) DNS issues are always caused by the application code — Kubernetes DNS never fails
D) Step 1: Deploy a debug pod (kubectl run dnsutils --image=registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/jessie-dnsutils:1.3 --rm -it -- sh). Step 2: nslookup <service> (test resolution). Step 3: Check /etc/resolv.conf (nameserver, search domains, ndots). Step 4: Check CoreDNS pods (kubectl -n kube-system logs <coredns-pod>). Step 5: Check kube-dns Service (kubectl -n kube-system get svc kube-dns). Common issues: ndots causing too many queries, CoreDNS pod not running, kube-dns Service IP mismatch
✅ Correct Answer: D

DNS debugging is a key CKAD skill. The ndots setting in resolv.conf (default: 5) causes DNS to try absolute resolution for names with fewer than 5 dots before trying search domains — this can cause excessive DNS queries and slow resolution.

📝 DNS Debugging Workflow
DNS Debugging Commands
  ═══════════════ DEBUG POD ═══════════════
  kubectl run dnsutils --image=registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/jessie-dnsutils:1.3 --rm -it -- sh

  # Test resolution
  nslookup easypj-api
  nslookup easypj-api.easypj-prod.svc.cluster.local
  nslookup kubernetes.default

  # Check DNS config
  cat /etc/resolv.conf
  → nameserver 10.96.0.10
  → search easypj-prod.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
  → options ndots:5

  ═══════════ COREDNS HEALTH ═══════════
  kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns
  kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=20
  kubectl -n kube-system get svc kube-dns

CKAD exam tip: DNS debugging is a common CKAD task. Always deploy a dnsutils pod first when troubleshooting connectivity. For easypj/jobpost: if the API can't connect to PostgreSQL, check DNS first — nslookup easypj-db from a debug pod.

5.5 kubectl Networking CommandsQ195-Q200

🟢→🟡 | Supporting topic: port-forward, proxy, debug pods, connectivity testing, endpoint verification.

Network 🟢 Q195 of 200
How do you use kubectl port-forward to access a pod port locally?
A) kubectl port-forward creates a permanent Service — it modifies the cluster's networking configuration
B) kubectl port-forward pod/<name> <local-port>:<pod-port> creates a TEMPORARY TCP tunnel from your local machine to the pod via the API server. No Service needed. Use for: debugging (access pod directly), testing without exposing publicly, accessing admin UIs. Ctrl+C to stop. For easypj/jobpost: kubectl port-forward pod/easypj-api-5k3m8 8080:8000 → localhost:8080 reaches the Django API directly
C) kubectl port-forward requires a NodePort Service — it cannot forward to individual pods
D) kubectl port-forward only works on the control plane node — it's not available from remote machines
✅ Correct Answer: B

kubectl port-forward is the CKAD debugging essential. It creates a secure tunnel through the API server to a specific pod — no Service, no Ingress, no NodePort needed. Perfect for quick debugging when you don't want to expose a service publicly.

📝 kubectl port-forward Reference
kubectl port-forward — Direct Pod Access
  ═══════════════ PORT-FORWARD PATTERNS ═══════════════
  # Forward to a specific pod
  kubectl port-forward pod/easypj-api-5k3m8 8080:8000
  → localhost:8080 → pod:8000

  # Forward to a Deployment (random pod)
  kubectl port-forward deploy/easypj-api 8080:8000

  # Forward to a Service
  kubectl port-forward svc/easypj-api 8080:8000

  # Bind to specific address (not just localhost)
  kubectl port-forward --address 0.0.0.0 pod/easypj-web 8080:3000
  → Accessible from other machines on the network

  ═══════════ COMMON USES ═══════════
  ✅ Access Django admin panel locally
  ✅ Test API endpoints without Ingress
  ✅ Debug database directly (port-forward to PostgreSQL)
  ✅ Access Prometheus/Grafana UIs

CKAD exam tip: kubectl port-forward is your go-to for quick pod access during the exam. It works immediately — no need to create Services or Ingress. For easypj/jobpost: kubectl port-forward svc/easypj-api 8080:8000 to test the REST API locally.

Network 🟡 Q196 of 200
What does kubectl proxy do and how does it differ from port-forward?
A) kubectl proxy and kubectl port-forward are the same — they both create TCP tunnels to pods
B) kubectl proxy is deprecated — it was replaced by kubectl port-forward in Kubernetes 1.20
C) kubectl proxy creates a LOCAL HTTP PROXY to the KUBERNETES API SERVER (not to pods). It runs on localhost:8001 and forwards authenticated requests to the API server. Use for: accessing the API without tokens (proxy handles auth), exploring the API directly (curl localhost:8001/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods). port-forward goes to PODS; proxy goes to the API SERVER. For easypj/jobpost: use proxy to programmatically query pods, services, and deployments via the REST API
D) kubectl proxy requires cluster-admin privileges — regular users cannot start the proxy
✅ Correct Answer: C

kubectl proxy and kubectl port-forward serve completely different purposes. Proxy = API server access (no auth needed locally). Port-forward = pod access (direct TCP tunnel).

📝 kubectl proxy vs port-forward
Proxy vs Port-Forward
  ═══════════════ PROXY (to API SERVER) ═══════════════
  kubectl proxy --port=8001
  → curl localhost:8001/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods
  → Returns JSON list of pods (authenticated via kubeconfig)

  ═══════════════ PORT-FORWARD (to POD) ═══════════════
  kubectl port-forward pod/easypj-api-5k3m8 8080:8000
  → curl localhost:8080/api/jobs
  → Returns Django API response

  ┌───────────────┬────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │                │ PROXY              │ PORT-FORWARD     │
  ├───────────────┼────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │  Target        │ K8s API Server     │ Specific Pod     │
  │  Auth          │ Handled by proxy   │ Direct TCP       │
  │  Protocol      │ HTTP/HTTPS         │ Raw TCP          │
  └───────────────┴────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

CKAD exam tip: proxy is less tested on CKAD but useful for API exploration. For easypj/jobpost: use proxy when you need to query the Kubernetes API programmatically; use port-forward when you need to access a running application.

Network 🟢 Q197 of 200
How do you create a temporary debug pod for network testing?
A) kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- sh (creates pod, opens shell, auto-deletes on exit with --rm). For network-specific debugging, use images with built-in tools: nicolaka/netshoot (tcpdump, curl, dig, nmap, netstat, iperf), curlimages/curl (just curl), alpine/curl. For easypj/jobpost: kubectl run net-test --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it -- bash → then curl easypj-api:8000/healthz, dig easypj-db, etc.
B) Debug pods must be created from YAML — kubectl run cannot create interactive debugging pods
C) kubectl debug — this is the only way to create temporary pods for network testing
D) Network testing requires a Service — you cannot test connectivity directly from a pod without a Service
✅ Correct Answer: A

kubectl run --rm -it is the fastest way to get a shell in the cluster. The --rm flag is critical — it auto-deletes the pod when you exit, leaving no cleanup. This is your primary network debugging tool on CKAD.

📝 Debug Pod Patterns
Quick Network Debugging Pods
  ═══════════════ DEBUG PODS ═══════════════
  # Basic shell
  kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- sh

  # Full network toolkit (RECOMMENDED)
  kubectl run netshoot --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it -- bash
  → curl, dig, nslookup, netstat, tcpdump, nmap, iperf, socat

  # DNS testing
  kubectl run dnsutils --image=registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/jessie-dnsutils:1.3 --rm -it -- sh

  ═══════════ INSIDE THE DEBUG POD ═══════════
  # Test Service connectivity
  curl http://easypj-api:8000/healthz
  curl http://easypj-api.easypj-prod:8000/healthz

  # Test DNS
  nslookup easypj-db
  dig easypj-db.easypj-prod.svc.cluster.local

  # Test TCP
  nc -zv easypj-db 5432
  → Connection to easypj-db 5432 port [tcp/*] succeeded!

CKAD exam tip: Always use --rm to auto-cleanup debug pods. The nicolaka/netshoot image is the Swiss Army knife of network debugging. For easypj/jobpost: deploy a netshoot pod in the same namespace as the API to test all internal connectivity.

Network 🟡 Q198 of 200
How do you test Service connectivity from within the cluster?
A) Services can only be tested from outside the cluster — internal testing is not supported
B) kubectl test-service — this is the dedicated command for verifying Service connectivity
C) Use ping to test Service connectivity — ping <service-name> works for all Service types
D) Deploy a debug pod in the same namespace. Test DNS: nslookup <svc>. Test HTTP: curl http://<svc>:<port>/<path>. Test TCP: nc -zv <svc> <port>. Check Endpoints: kubectl get endpoints <svc>. Note: ClusterIP is virtual — ping does NOT work! Use application-level protocols (curl, nc, wget). For easypj/jobpost: curl http://easypj-api:8000/healthz from a debug pod
✅ Correct Answer: D

Testing Service connectivity requires understanding that ClusterIPs are virtual — they don't respond to ICMP ping. Always use application-level protocols (HTTP, TCP, DNS) for testing. The debug pod approach is the standard CKAD methodology.

📝 Service Connectivity Testing
Testing easypj/jobpost Services
  ═══════════════ TESTING FROM DEBUG POD ═══════════════
  kubectl run test --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it -- bash

  # Test API (HTTP)
  curl -v http://easypj-api:8000/healthz
  → HTTP/1.1 200 OK ✅

  # Test DB (TCP)
  nc -zv easypj-db 5432
  → Connection to easypj-db 5432 port succeeded ✅

  # Test Redis (TCP)
  nc -zv easypj-redis 6379
  → Connection succeeded ✅

  # FAILING TESTS
  ping easypj-api       ❌ ClusterIPs don't respond to ping!
  curl http://bad-svc   ❌ Could not resolve host → DNS or Service missing

CKAD exam tip: For CKAD connectivity testing: (1) deploy debug pod, (2) nslookup the Service, (3) curl/nc the endpoint, (4) if fails, check kubectl get endpoints. For easypj/jobpost: always verify API, DB, and Redis connectivity from a test pod before declaring a deployment complete.

Network 🟢 Q199 of 200
How do you verify a Service can reach its pods using kubectl?
A) kubectl test-service <name> — this is the built-in command for Service health verification
B) kubectl get endpoints <svc> shows the IP:port list of pods backing the Service. EMPTY = Service broken (selector mismatch, no ready pods, wrong port). Also check: kubectl describe svc (shows selector, type, ports, sessionAffinity). kubectl get pods -l <selector> (do pods matching the selector exist and are Ready?). For easypj/jobpost: kubectl get endpoints easypj-api should show pod IPs + port 8000
C) Services automatically report their status — kubectl get svc shows a HEALTHY column for each Service
D) kubectl get pods --show-service shows which Service each pod is backing — this is the only way to verify
✅ Correct Answer: B

kubectl get endpoints is the single most useful Service debugging command. It instantly tells you if a Service has working backends. Empty Endpoints = broken Service — the most common CKAD troubleshooting scenario.

📝 Service Health Verification
Verifying easypj/jobpost Service Health
  ═══════════════ CHECK ALL SERVICES ═══════════════
  kubectl get svc,endpoints -n easypj-prod
  →
  NAME                  TYPE        CLUSTER-IP     PORT(S)
  service/easypj-api    ClusterIP   10.96.100.50   8000/TCP
  service/easypj-db     ClusterIP   10.96.100.51   5432/TCP

  NAME                    ENDPOINTS
  endpoints/easypj-api    10.244.1.10:8000,10.244.2.15:8000 ✅
  endpoints/easypj-db     10.244.3.20:5432 ✅

  ═══════════ EMPTY ENDPOINTS — DIAGNOSIS ═══════════
  kubectl get endpoints easypj-web
  → NAME          ENDPOINTS
  → easypj-web    <none>              ← BROKEN!
  
  # Step 1: Check Service selector
  kubectl get svc easypj-web -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'
  → {"app":"easypj-web","tier":"frontend"}
  
  # Step 2: Do matching pods exist and are Ready?
  kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-web,tier=frontend
  → No resources found ← No pods match!

CKAD exam tip: kubectl get endpoints should be your FIRST command when a Service isn't working. For easypj/jobpost: after every deployment, verify all Services have Endpoints before considering the deployment complete.

Network 🟡 Q200 of 200
What is the complete network troubleshooting checklist from pod to external access?
A) Just check if the pod is running — if it's Running, networking always works automatically
B) Network troubleshooting is always a CNI plugin issue — just restart the CNI pods and everything fixes itself
C) Layer-by-layer checklist: (1) POD: is it Running? Ready? kubectl describe + logs. (2) DNS: can pods resolve Service names? nslookup from debug pod. (3) SERVICE: does it have Endpoints? kubectl get endpoints. (4) NETWORKPOLICY: is traffic blocked? Check if any policies select the pods. (5) INGRESS: rules, TLS, backend Service, controller logs. (6) EXTERNAL: NodePort open? LoadBalancer provisioned? Firewall rules? For easypj/jobpost: debug from the innermost layer outward — pod → DNS → Service → NetworkPolicy → Ingress → external
D) Network issues can only be debugged with tcpdump on the host — kubectl commands are insufficient for network troubleshooting
✅ Correct Answer: C

The inside-out debugging approach is the most efficient: start from the pod and work outward. Each layer must work before the next one can. This systematic approach prevents wild goose chases and ensures you find the actual root cause.

📝 Network Troubleshooting Checklist
Complete Network Debugging Flow — Inside Out
  ═══════════════ NETWORK DEBUGGING LAYERS ═══════════════
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  LAYER 1: POD — Is the process listening?                    │
  │  kubectl logs <pod> | kubectl exec <pod> -- netstat -tlnp │
  │  ✅ Process listening on :8000                               │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  LAYER 2: DNS — Can we resolve Service names?                │
  │  kubectl run dnsutils --rm -it -- nslookup easypj-api       │
  │  ✅ Name: easypj-api, Address: 10.96.100.50                  │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  LAYER 3: SERVICE — Does it have Endpoints?                  │
  │  kubectl get endpoints easypj-api                            │
  │  ✅ 10.244.1.10:8000,10.244.2.15:8000                       │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  LAYER 4: NETWORKPOLICY — Is traffic allowed?                │
  │  kubectl get networkpolicies -A                             │
  │  ✅ No blocking policies on these pods                       │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  LAYER 5: INGRESS — Are rules correct?                       │
  │  kubectl describe ingress <name>                            │
  │  ✅ Host + path match, TLS configured, backend valid         │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │  LAYER 6: EXTERNAL — Can outside reach inside?               │
  │  curl http://node-ip:nodePort/healthz                        │
  │  ✅ HTTP 200 OK                                              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🚀 Beyond CKAD (CKA crossover): CKA adds kube-proxy debugging (iptables vs IPVS mode), CNI plugin troubleshooting (Calico bird/confd, Cilium agents), and node-level networking (ip route, ip link, conntrack). The CKAD inside-out approach scales to CKA cluster-wide network debugging.

🔧 Part 2: 100 Troubleshooting Issues

Real-world Kubernetes application development failure scenarios — each with symptom, 15 categorized causes (5 most likely + 5 less likely + 5 new cluster), diagnostic commands, solutions, and personal advice. Patterned after the 5+5+5 cause-card format.

100Issues
5Categories
15Causes per Issue

🏗️ Category 1: App Design & Build (20 Issues)AB1-AB20

🟢→🟡 Application Design & Build Issues — Dockerfiles, Images, Pods, Volumes

These issues arise from misconfigured Dockerfiles, image builds, pod design patterns, init containers, Jobs, CronJobs, and volume mounting. Each issue follows the 5+5+5 cause-card pattern with diagnostic steps and solutions.

📌 AB1–AB3: Docker Build & Image Issues

AB1
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB1
Docker Build Fails — Missing requirements.txt in Build Context

🔍 Symptom: docker build fails with "COPY failed: file not found in build context or excluded by .dockerignore." The easypj/jobpost Docker image can't be built because a critical file is missing from the build context.

  docker build -t easypj/jobpost:v2.1 .
  [+] Building 15.2s (8/12)
  => [internal] load build definition from Dockerfile     0.0s
  => => transferring dockerfile: 842B                     0.0s
  => [internal] load .dockerignore                        0.0s
  => => transferring context: 2B                          0.0s
  => [internal] load metadata for python:3.12-slim       3.2s
  => [1/6] FROM python:3.12-slim@sha256:abc...            0.0s
  => [2/6] WORKDIR /app                                   0.0s
  => [3/6] COPY requirements.txt /app/                    0.0s
  ------                                                    
  > [3/6] COPY requirements.txt /app/:                     
  ------                                                    
  ERROR: failed to solve: failed to compute cache key:    
  failed to calculate checksum: "/requirements.txt":      
  not found                                               

  ls -la
  total 48
  drwxr-xr-x  6 dev dev  4096 Jun 11 14:30 .
  -rw-r--r--  1 dev dev   842 Jun 11 13:00 Dockerfile
  -rw-r--r--  1 dev dev   156 Jun 10 09:00 .dockerignore
  drwxr-xr-x  5 dev dev  4096 Jun 11 12:00 easypj
  drwxr-xr-x  2 dev dev  4096 Jun 11 11:00 static
  drwxr-xr-x  3 dev dev  4096 Jun 10 10:00 templates
  # ← requirements.txt is MISSING!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. requirements.txt not in project root: The developer created requirements.txt in a subdirectory (e.g., easypj/requirements.txt) but Dockerfile's COPY expects it in the build context root. ls -la — check the file's actual location.
  2. File listed in .dockerignore: requirements.txt is being excluded by .dockerignore rules. cat .dockerignore — check if requirements.txt or *.txt is listed.
  3. Wrong build context path: Running docker build from the wrong directory. The build context (the . at the end) must be the directory containing requirements.txt. pwd && ls — verify you're in the right directory.
  4. File not committed to git: Working in a cloned repo but requirements.txt is in .gitignore or was never committed. git status — check if the file is tracked.
  5. Case sensitivity mismatch: Dockerfile says COPY Requirements.txt (capital R) but the file is requirements.txt (lowercase). Linux filesystems are case-sensitive. ls -la | grep -i require — check exact filename.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Symlink to requirements.txt is broken — the symlink exists but the target file was deleted
  2. File permissions prevent Docker from reading requirements.txt (e.g., file owned by root with 000)
  3. Filesystem corruption or disk full — can't read the build context
  4. requirements.txt is a directory, not a file — COPY can't handle directories without trailing slash
  5. Docker daemon running in a VM (Docker Desktop) and the project directory is not shared/mounted
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Project was cloned but requirements.txt generation step skipped: If requirements.txt is generated (pip freeze, pip-compile), the generation command wasn't run. Run pip freeze > requirements.txt or pip-compile requirements.in first.
  2. Wrong Python version in Dockerfile: FROM python:3.13 but dependencies require python <3.13. The build may fail at pip install, not at COPY — confusing the error source.
  3. Multi-stage build referencing wrong stage: COPY --from=build-stage requirements.txt copies from a stage that never created the file.
  4. Docker not installed or daemon not running: docker info fails — the error message may be misleading about file not found.
  5. .dockerignore created by IDE template that excludes *.txt files unintentionally.
🔍 What to Look At:
ls -la and cat .dockerignore The two most common causes: file in wrong location or excluded by .dockerignore. Check both simultaneously.
docker build --no-cache -t easypj/jobpost . 2>&1 | head -30 Full build output with --no-cache to ensure you're seeing the real error, not a cached failure message.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: requirements.txt is not in the build context root. The developer created the file inside the easypj/ project directory but Dockerfile's COPY expects it at the context root. Solution: either move requirements.txt to the project root, or update the Dockerfile COPY path to match the actual location.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify file location relative to Dockerfile ls -la; cat Dockerfile | grep COPY Check what COPY expects and what actually exists in the build context.
2. Check .dockerignore cat .dockerignore Remove any rules that exclude requirements.txt. If *.txt is listed, add !requirements.txt to explicitly include it.
3. Move file to correct location or fix Dockerfile path mv easypj/requirements.txt . OR change Dockerfile: COPY easypj/requirements.txt /app/ Either move the file to where Dockerfile expects it, or update Dockerfile to find it.
4. Rebuild with --no-cache docker build --no-cache -t easypj/jobpost:v2.1 . Rebuild from scratch to ensure the fix works and no cached errors remain.
5. Verify the image works docker run --rm easypj/jobpost:v2.1 python -c "import django; print(django.VERSION)" Quick smoke test to confirm dependencies installed correctly.
💡 Personal Advice:
Always run `ls` before `docker build`. A 2-second check of your build context prevents 15 minutes of debugging. Make it a habit — ls before every build.
Use .dockerignore wisely. .dockerignore It speeds up builds by excluding unnecessary files, but overzealous rules (like *.txt) will break your build. Test with: tar -cf - . | docker build - to see exactly what's being sent.
Prefer pip-compile over pip freeze. pip freeze captures ALL installed packages including transitive dependencies with exact versions. pip-compile (from pip-tools) separates direct dependencies (requirements.in) from pinned transitive deps (requirements.txt), making updates safer.
Multi-stage builds need explicit COPY in each stage. If you have a build stage and a runtime stage, COPY requirements.txt separately in each. The runtime stage still needs it for --from=builder to work correctly.
AB2
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB2
Multi-Stage Build Fails — Artifact Not Copied from Build Stage

🔍 Symptom: The Docker image builds successfully but the container crashes on startup with "ModuleNotFoundError" or "file not found." The final image is missing compiled files or dependencies that were built in an earlier stage. The easypj/jobpost Django app can't start because static files or Python packages weren't carried over from the build stage.

  docker build -t easypj/jobpost:v2.1 .
  [+] Building 45.2s — FINISHED ✅ (build succeeded!)

  docker run easypj/jobpost:v2.1
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "/app/manage.py", line 10, in <module>
      from django.core.management import execute_from_command_line
  ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'django'

  docker run --entrypoint ls easypj/jobpost:v2.1 /app/
  manage.py  templates/  static/          ← NO site-packages!
  # The virtualenv from build stage was NOT copied!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Wrong COPY --from path: The build stage installs packages to /app/.venv but COPY --from=builder copies from /app/ (without .venv). Check the exact path: docker run --rm builder-stage ls /app/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages to verify the real location.
  2. FROM alias mismatch: The build stage is named "build-stage" but COPY --from references "builder" (wrong name). Docker silently copies from the LAST stage when the alias doesn't match — which may be the wrong stage.
  3. pip install outside virtualenv: Packages installed globally in the build stage but the runtime stage expects them in a virtualenv. Use python -m venv /opt/venv && /opt/venv/bin/pip install for explicit paths.
  4. Static files not collected: Django's collectstatic ran in the build stage but the STATIC_ROOT directory wasn't copied to the runtime stage. ls -la /app/staticfiles in the build stage to verify.
  5. COPY instruction in wrong order: COPY --from=builder happens BEFORE the WORKDIR is set, so files end up in the wrong directory. Always set WORKDIR before any COPY.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. BuildKit cache poisoning: Docker's BuildKit caches an old build stage and doesn't re-run pip install. Use --no-cache to force clean build.
  2. python:3.12-slim doesn't include gcc/build-essential: Some Python packages need compilation but the slim image lacks compilers — use python:3.12 for build stage.
  3. requirements.txt has platform-specific packages: Packages compiled for macOS (darwin) in the build stage won't work on Linux. Use --platform=linux/amd64.
  4. Virtualenv paths hardcoded with absolute paths: If /home/builder/.venv is used, the runtime stage's different user can't find it.
  5. Layer caching issue: Docker reused a cached layer from before the multi-stage COPY was added — the old layer has no artifacts.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Docker version doesn't support multi-stage builds: Multi-stage builds require Docker 17.05+. docker version — older Docker installations on fresh VMs may be outdated.
  2. BuildKit not enabled: Some multi-stage optimizations require BuildKit. Set DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 or add to daemon.json.
  3. Dockerfile syntax version mismatch: # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 at the top enables newer features but may not be supported on older Docker versions.
  4. Disk space exhausted during build: Multi-stage builds use more temporary space. docker system df — clean up with docker system prune -a.
  5. --squash not available: Some teams use --squash to reduce image size but it's an experimental feature not available in all Docker editions.
🔍 What to Look At:
docker run --rm builder-stage ls -la /app/ and docker run --rm --entrypoint ls easypj/jobpost:v2.1 /app/ Compare files in build stage vs runtime stage. Anything missing in the runtime stage means COPY --from didn't work.
docker history easypj/jobpost:v2.1 | head -20 See all layers. Verify the COPY --from layer exists and has a reasonable size (not 0B).
🎯 #1 Root Cause: COPY --from path doesn't match the actual directory structure in the build stage. The build stage installs packages to a specific path but the COPY command uses a different or incomplete path. Always verify with an ls command in the build stage first.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify the build stage's filesystem docker build --target=builder -t easypj-builder . && docker run --rm easypj-builder ls -la /app/ Build ONLY the build stage and inspect what's actually there.
2. Fix the COPY --from path COPY --from=builder /opt/venv /opt/venv and COPY --from=builder /app/staticfiles /app/staticfiles Use absolute paths that match the build stage's actual directory structure.
3. Verify stage alias names match FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder and COPY --from=builder /app /app Ensure the AS alias and --from reference use EXACTLY the same name.
4. Add verification to Dockerfile RUN ls -la /app/ && python -c "import django; print(django.VERSION)" Add a verification step in the runtime stage to fail the build if artifacts are missing.
5. Rebuild with no cache docker build --no-cache -t easypj/jobpost:v2.1 . && docker run --rm easypj/jobpost:v2.1 python -c "import django" Full clean rebuild and smoke test to confirm the fix.
💡 Personal Advice:
Always verify each stage independently. Use --target=stage-name to build and inspect each stage before combining them. This catches missing artifacts 10x faster than debugging the final image.
Use consistent, explicit paths. COPY --from=builder /opt/venv /opt/venv Avoid relative paths in multi-stage COPY. Absolute paths remove ambiguity about where files end up.
Consider using virtualenv in the build stage. python -m venv /opt/venv creates an isolated, relocatable Python environment. Copy the entire /opt/venv to the runtime stage for a clean, predictable setup.
Add a smoke test RUN in the final stage. A simple RUN python -c "import django" in the Dockerfile fails the build immediately if artifacts are missing — catching the problem before deployment.
AB3
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB3
Image Too Large — 2GB Docker Image in Production

🔍 Symptom: docker images shows the easypj/jobpost image is 2.1GB. Image pull takes 5+ minutes on new nodes, causing deployment timeouts and disk pressure. The production Django app image is bloated with development dependencies, build tools, and unnecessary files.

  docker images easypj/jobpost
  REPOSITORY        TAG       IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
  easypj/jobpost    v2.1      a1b2c3d4e5f6   2 hours ago    2.13GB

  docker history easypj/jobpost:v2.1 | head -10
  IMAGE          CREATED        CREATED BY                          SIZE
  a1b2c3d4e5f6   2 hours ago    CMD ["gunicorn" ...]                0B
  9f8e7d6c5b4a   2 hours ago    COPY . /app                          850MB ← HUGE!
  3a2b1c0d9e8f   2 hours ago    RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  620MB
  7f6e5d4c3b2a   2 hours ago    RUN apt-get update && apt-get install 350MB ← dev tools!
  1a9b8c7d6e5f   3 days ago     FROM ubuntu:22.04                    78MB
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Using full Ubuntu/Debian base image instead of slim/alpine: FROM ubuntu:22.04 adds 78MB of unnecessary OS. Use FROM python:3.12-slim (50MB) or FROM python:3.12-alpine (16MB) for production.
  2. Not using multi-stage builds: Build tools (gcc, make, git) are installed in the final image. Use multi-stage: install build deps in build stage, copy only runtime artifacts to the slim final stage.
  3. COPY . /app copies everything: The entire project directory including .git/, node_modules/, __pycache__/, and test files are copied into the image. Use .dockerignore and copy only what's needed.
  4. pip install includes dev dependencies: requirements.txt has pytest, black, debugpy, and other dev tools. Use separate requirements/prod.txt and requirements/dev.txt.
  5. apt-get cache not cleaned: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y gcc without && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* leaves 200MB+ of package cache.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Large static assets bundled in image: Images, videos, or ML models stored in the image. Use object storage (S3, MinIO) and load at runtime instead.
  2. Debug symbols included: Python packages compiled with debug symbols or .pyc files bloating the image. find /app -name "*.pyc" -delete in Dockerfile.
  3. Multiple Python versions installed: Both Python 3.11 and 3.12 installed. Use a base image with only the version you need.
  4. Log files accumulated during build: pip install logs, npm logs, or build artifacts not cleaned up. Add cleanup steps after each RUN.
  5. Docker layer duplication: Multiple COPY/RUN layers creating duplicate files. Combine related RUN commands with && to reduce layers.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No image registry caching: Images pulled fresh on every deployment instead of using a local registry cache or imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent.
  2. kind load / minikube cache not used: kind load docker-image or minikube image load avoids registry pulls on local clusters — use them during development.
  3. Registry bandwidth throttled: New cluster's network egress has bandwidth limits — 2GB images timeout. Push to a nearby registry or use image compression.
  4. Node disk pressure from large images: Multiple large images fill node disk. Set imageGCHighThresholdPercent in kubelet config.
  5. No image scanning or size gate in CI/CD: No pipeline check to reject images over 500MB before they reach the registry.
🔍 What to Look At:
docker history easypj/jobpost:v2.1 and dive easypj/jobpost:v2.1 docker history shows per-layer sizes. dive (tool) shows per-file sizes inside each layer — find the biggest files.
docker run --rm easypj/jobpost:v2.1 du -sh /app/* | sort -rh | head -10 See the largest directories inside the image. Identify what can be .dockerignored or moved to external storage.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No multi-stage build and wrong base image. The production image is built on a full Ubuntu base with development tools, test dependencies, and unnecessary files. Switching to a slim Python base with multi-stage build typically reduces image size by 80-90%.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Switch to slim base image and multi-stage build FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder and FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime Separate build from runtime. Install gcc/build-essential only in the builder stage.
2. Create .dockerignore .git/ __pycache__/ *.pyc .pytest_cache/ node_modules/ tests/ .env Exclude everything not needed at runtime. Test: tar -cf - . | wc -c to see context size before/after.
3. Use separate prod requirements pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements/prod.txt prod.txt has only gunicorn, django, psycopg2 — no pytest, black, or debug tools.
4. Clean apt cache in same RUN layer RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq-dev && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* Cache cleanup must be in the SAME RUN as the install, otherwise the cache is baked into its own layer.
5. Verify size improvement docker images easypj/jobpost Target: under 300MB for a Django production image. If still large, use dive to find remaining bloat.
💡 Personal Advice:
Target <300MB for production Python images. A well-optimized Django image with gunicorn, psycopg2, and no dev tools should be 150-300MB. If you're over 500MB, something is wrong.
Use dive to find bloat. dive easypj/jobpost:v2.1 This interactive tool shows every file in every layer. It reveals exactly which COPY or RUN added the big files.
distroless images for the truly minimal. Google's distroless Python image has no shell, no package manager — just Python and your app. ~50MB base. But debugging is harder (no apt, no sh).
Set image size gates in CI/CD. Add docker images --format '{{.Size}}' | awk '{if ($1+0 > 500000000) exit 1}' to your pipeline. Reject images over 500MB.

📌 AB4–AB6: Image Configuration & Security Issues

AB4
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB4
Wrong Base Image Tag — latest Pulls Unexpected Version

🔍 Symptom: The easypj/jobpost deployment was working yesterday but breaks today after a restart. The application crashes with "AttributeError" or "ImportError" because the base image tag python:latest pulled a NEW Python version (3.13) that's incompatible with Django or its dependencies.

  docker run python:latest python --version
  Python 3.13.0  ← Was 3.12.0 yesterday! The "latest" tag moved!

  kubectl logs easypj-web-9x7k2 --previous
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "/app/manage.py", line 5, in <module>
      from django.core.management import execute_from_command_line
    File "/usr/local/lib/python3.13/site-packages/django/__init__.py"
  AttributeError: module 'collections' has no attribute 'Callable'
  # Python 3.13 removed collections.Callable — Django <4.2 breaks!

  grep FROM Dockerfile
  FROM python:latest  ← ❌ NEVER use latest!
  FROM python:3.12-slim  ← ✅ Pin exact version
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Using :latest tag: FROM python:latest pulls whatever the current latest version is — which changes without warning. Always pin to a specific version like python:3.12.7-slim.
  2. Using :3 or :3.12 without minor version: python:3.12 gets the latest 3.12.x — security patches may introduce breaking changes. Pin to the patch version: python:3.12.7-slim.
  3. imagePullPolicy: Always with mutable tags: Kubernetes re-pulls the image on every restart, getting a different version. Use imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent for pinned tags.
  4. Dependencies not pinned: requirements.txt says django>=4.0 instead of django==4.2.15. A new Django version breaks compatibility.
  5. No CI/CD testing with version matrix: Only testing against latest Python. Add Python 3.12 and 3.13 to the test matrix to catch incompatibilities early.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Mirror/registry caching stale tags: A local registry mirror has an old cached "latest" that's actually newer than what you tested.
  2. Python standard library deprecations: Python 3.13 removed many deprecated modules (cgi, cgitb, smtpd) that older Django versions used.
  3. Alpine musl vs glibc issues: python:alpine uses musl libc which has subtle incompatibilities with packages compiled for glibc.
  4. Timezone data changes: The base image's tzdata package update changes timezone behavior in the app.
  5. Docker Hub rate limiting: Anonymous pulls of python:latest hit Docker Hub rate limits, causing ImagePullBackOff.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No image cache on new cluster nodes: Fresh nodes pull the latest tag from the registry — getting a different version than existing nodes running cached images.
  2. Air-gapped environment with stale images: Images imported into a private registry months ago have different :latest than current Docker Hub.
  3. kind/minikube using different architecture: Apple Silicon (arm64) vs Intel (amd64) — latest tag resolves to different architectures.
  4. Digest not used: python@sha256:abc123... is immutable — always reference by digest for guaranteed reproducibility.
  5. No image vulnerability scanning: Latest tag may include known CVEs that a pinned, scanned version would avoid.
🔍 What to Look At:
docker run python:latest python --version and cat Dockerfile | grep FROM Compare what version "latest" currently resolves to vs what your Dockerfile specifies.
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 "Image:" and kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].image}' Check the exact image reference in the running pod — is it a mutable tag?
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Mutable tags (latest, :3.12) in FROM and Deployment specs. These tags silently change over time as new versions are released. Always pin to a specific digest or full semver version (python:3.12.7-slim@sha256:...).
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Pin base image to exact version FROM python:3.12.7-slim@sha256:abc123def456... Use BOTH the version tag AND the digest for maximum reproducibility.
2. Pin all Python dependencies pip freeze > requirements.txt or pip-compile requirements.in Every dependency should have an exact version. No >=, no ~= in production requirements.
3. Use imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent For pinned tags, don't re-pull on every restart. Node cache is used first.
4. Add version matrix to CI/CD python-version: ["3.11", "3.12", "3.13"] Test against multiple Python versions to catch incompatibilities before they reach production.
5. Set up Dependabot/Renovate Automated PRs for base image and dependency updates — you review and merge when ready, not surprised by silent changes.
💡 Personal Advice:
Never use :latest in production. Ever. This is the #1 Docker anti-pattern. :latest means "I accept whatever the registry gives me today" — which is never what you want.
Digest + tag for defense in depth. python:3.12.7-slim@sha256:abc... The tag helps humans, the digest guarantees immutability. Even if someone force-pushes a new :3.12.7-slim, the digest protects you.
Lock files are your friend. requirements.txt with pinned versions + pip freeze > constraints.txt. Commit both. Your CI should fail if they're out of sync.
Schedule regular base image updates. Pinning prevents surprises but you still need security patches. Set a monthly task to update base images and dependency versions.
AB5
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB5
Container Runs as Root — Security Vulnerability

🔍 Symptom: Security scanner (Trivy, Snyk, AWS Inspector) flags the easypj/jobpost container running as UID 0 (root). The pod's kubectl exec whoami returns "root." This violates security policies and fails compliance audits. An attacker who escapes the container would have root access on the host.

  kubectl exec easypj-web-9x7k2 -- whoami
  root  ← ❌ Container is running as UID 0!

  kubectl exec easypj-web-9x7k2 -- id
  uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

  docker history easypj/jobpost:v2.1 | grep USER
  (empty — no USER directive in Dockerfile!)

  cat Dockerfile | grep -i user
  # No USER directive found — defaults to root!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No USER directive in Dockerfile: Docker defaults to USER root (UID 0) if no USER is specified. Every Dockerfile should end with USER 1000 or a named user.
  2. USER at wrong position: USER is set at the beginning but subsequent COPY/RUN instructions change file ownership to root. Put USER as the LAST instruction (or just before CMD/ENTRYPOINT).
  3. COPY --chown not used: Files copied as root can't be read by the non-root user. Use COPY --chown=1000:1000 . /app to set correct ownership.
  4. Port <1024 requires root: Django app binds to port 80 which requires root. Use port 8000 (non-privileged) or add CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE capability instead of running as root.
  5. No securityContext in pod spec: Even if the Dockerfile sets USER, the pod spec can override it. Add securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true as defense in depth.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Init container runs as root: The main container has USER 1000 but an init container that sets up files runs as root — scanner flags the pod.
  2. Entrypoint script uses sudo: A custom entrypoint.sh calls sudo or su to switch users — unnecessary in containers.
  3. Base image configured for root: Some base images (nvidia/cuda) are designed to run as root. Check the base image's default user.
  4. Volume permissions require root: Persistent volumes mounted with root ownership require root to write — use fsGroup instead.
  5. Legacy app hardcoded for root: The Django management commands or entrypoint scripts assume root access for file operations.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Pod Security Standards not enforced: New cluster doesn't have Restricted PSS enabled — privileged and root containers are allowed by default. kubectl label ns easypj-prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted
  2. No admission webhook for security: Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper not installed — no policy to block root containers at admission time.
  3. Image scanning not configured: No Trivy/Grype scan in CI/CD — root containers reach production undetected.
  4. Default ServiceAccount has excessive RBAC: Running as root combined with cluster-admin RBAC is catastrophic — limit SA permissions.
  5. Compliance framework not applied: CIS Benchmark checks for "containers should not run as root" not configured.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pod -o json | jq '.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, user: .spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsUser}' Check all running pods — are any missing runAsUser or running as 0?
docker inspect easypj/jobpost:v2.1 | jq '.[].Config.User' and cat Dockerfile | grep USER Check both the image's default user and the Dockerfile's USER instruction.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No USER directive in the Dockerfile. Docker defaults to root, and without an explicit USER instruction, the container runs with full root privileges. Combined with no securityContext in the pod spec, there's no defense in depth.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create a non-root user in the Dockerfile RUN groupadd -r django && useradd -r -g django django and USER django Create a dedicated system user and group. Put USER as the second-to-last instruction (before CMD).
2. Fix file ownership with COPY --chown COPY --chown=django:django . /app All application files must be owned by the non-root user, otherwise the app can't read/write them.
3. Add securityContext to pod spec securityContext: {runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000} Pod-level security as defense in depth. runAsNonRoot: true BLOCKS the pod from starting if the image defaults to root.
4. Use port >1024 or add capability --port=8000 or capabilities.add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"] Django should run on port 8000 (non-privileged). If port 80 is required, add NET_BIND_SERVICE instead of root.
5. Enforce with Pod Security Standards kubectl label ns easypj-prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted Restricted PSS blocks root containers at the namespace level — last line of defense.
💡 Personal Advice:
Make non-root the default for EVERY image. Start every Dockerfile with the assumption that USER 1000 is mandatory. Treat root containers as bugs to be fixed, not options.
Use runAsNonRoot as safety net. securityContext: {runAsNonRoot: true} This one line in your pod spec prevents root containers from starting, even if the Dockerfile is misconfigured. The kubelet will refuse to start the container.
Test with Restricted PSS locally. Label your dev namespace with restricted PSS. If your pod doesn't start, you know it has security issues before it reaches production.
Root in a container IS root on the host. Linux UID 0 is UID 0 — there's no "container root vs host root." A container escape vulnerability gives an attacker host root access if the container runs as root.
AB6
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB6
Secrets in Dockerfile — API Key Hardcoded in Image Layer

🔍 Symptom: docker history easypj/jobpost:v2.1 reveals sensitive environment variables baked into image layers. AWS credentials, API keys, and database passwords are visible to anyone with access to the image. Security scanner flags the image as CRITICAL risk.

  docker history easypj/jobpost:v2.1 --no-trunc
  IMAGE          CREATED BY
  a1b2c3d4e5f6   ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
                  ENV AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
                  ENV DATABASE_URL=postgres://easypj:s3cr3tP@ss@db:5432/jobpost
                  ENV SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-abc123def456ghi789
  # ← ALL SECRETS VISIBLE IN PLAINTEXT! Anyone with image access can see them!

  docker inspect easypj/jobpost:v2.1 | jq '.[].Config.Env'
  [
    "AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE",
    "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY",
    "DATABASE_URL=postgres://easypj:s3cr3tP@ss@db:5432/jobpost",
    "SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-abc123def456ghi789"
  ]
  # docker inspect reveals ALL ENV vars — including secrets!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. ENV for secrets in Dockerfile: ENV DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@host/db bakes the secret into the image layer forever. Use Kubernetes Secrets mounted at runtime, never ENV in Dockerfile.
  2. ARG used for secrets without cleanup: ARG AWS_KEY passed via --build-arg AWS_KEY=xxx persists in image history. Use --secret with BuildKit instead.
  3. COPY of .env file into image: COPY .env /app/.env copies the local .env file with all secrets into the image. Add .env to .dockerignore.
  4. No .dockerignore excluding sensitive files: .env, credentials.json, service-account-key.json, id_rsa — all copied into the image by accident.
  5. Hardcoded secrets in source code: SECRET_KEY = "my-hardcoded-key" in settings.py. Use os.environ.get() and provide at runtime via Kubernetes Secrets.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Multi-stage build copies secrets from build stage: COPY --from=builder also copies .env files from the build stage.
  2. Git credentials baked into image: RUN git clone with username:password@repo embedded in the URL — visible in docker history.
  3. pip install from private repo with token: pip install git+https://token@github.com/org/repo.git — token exposed in layer.
  4. SSH keys copied for private dependencies: COPY id_rsa /root/.ssh/ — private key permanently in the image.
  5. Image pushed to public registry: Even with secrets in ENV, if the image is in a PUBLIC Docker Hub repo, anyone can pull and inspect it.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No image scanning in CI/CD: Trivy/Grype not configured — secrets in images reach production undetected.
  2. Kubernetes Secrets not created yet: Pods reference Secrets that don't exist — developer used ENV as workaround.
  3. etcd encryption not enabled: Even if using K8s Secrets, they're stored as base64 (not encrypted) in etcd by default.
  4. No private registry: Images pushed to Docker Hub because no internal registry is set up — secrets exposed publicly.
  5. RBAC too permissive: Any cluster user can docker pull the image and docker inspect to extract secrets.
🔍 What to Look At:
docker history --no-trunc <image> | grep -iE "(ENV|ARG|key|secret|password|token)" Scan image history for any instruction that sets secrets. ENV and ARG lines are permanently recorded.
docker run --rm --entrypoint cat <image> /app/.env /app/settings.py Check if sensitive files were accidentally copied into the image. Also check /root/.ssh/ and /home/.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: ENV instructions for secrets in the Dockerfile. Every ENV creates a permanent layer visible in docker history. Secrets should NEVER be in the Dockerfile — provide them at runtime via Kubernetes Secrets, environment variable injection, or external secret stores (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager).
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Remove ALL ENV secrets from Dockerfile Delete every ENV line that contains credentials, keys, or tokens. The app should read these from the environment at runtime, not from the image.
2. Use BuildKit --secret for build-time secrets docker build --secret id=aws_key,src=$HOME/.aws/credentials -t easypj/jobpost . BuildKit secrets are mounted temporarily during build and NEVER appear in image history.
3. Create Kubernetes Secrets for runtime kubectl create secret generic db-creds --from-literal=DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@host/db Inject at runtime via envFrom.secretRef or valueFrom.secretKeyRef in the pod spec.
4. Add sensitive files to .dockerignore .env .env.* credentials.json *.pem id_rsa service-account.json .secrets/ Prevent accidental COPY of sensitive files. Test: docker build outputs should show small context size.
5. Rotate all exposed credentials If secrets were in a pushed image, they're compromised. Rotate ALL exposed keys, passwords, and tokens immediately.
💡 Personal Advice:
Treat Docker images as PUBLIC artifacts. Even in private registries, assume any image could be leaked. Never put anything in an image that you wouldn't publish on GitHub.
Use docker history as a security audit. docker history --no-trunc <image> Run this on every image before pushing. If you see any ENV with a secret, stop and fix it immediately.
BuildKit --secret is your friend. For private pip repos, private git clones, or AWS credentials during build — use --secret. The secret exists only during the RUN instruction, never in a layer.
Scan images before pushing. trivy image --severity CRITICAL easypj/jobpost:v2.1 Trivy detects exposed secrets in image layers. Add to CI/CD to block pushes containing credentials.

📌 AB7–AB9: Build Cache, Init Containers & Sidecar Issues

AB7
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB7
Build Cache Not Working — Full Rebuild Every Time

🔍 Symptom: Every docker build takes 10+ minutes even when only a single Python file changed. The layer cache is completely invalidated because COPY . . runs before RUN pip install, causing dependencies to reinstall on every code change.

  docker build -t easypj/jobpost .
