  => [1/5] FROM python:3.12-slim        0.0s (cached)
  => [2/5] WORKDIR /app                  0.0s (cached)
  => [3/5] COPY . .                      2.3s ← CACHE MISS (any file change!)
  => [4/5] RUN pip install -r requirements.txt  420s ← REINSTALLS EVERY TIME!
  => [5/5] CMD ["gunicorn", "..."]       0.0s
  # Every code edit → cache miss at COPY → full pip install → 7+ minute build!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. COPY . . before COPY requirements.txt: The broad COPY invalidates the cache before pip install runs. Move COPY requirements.txt and RUN pip install BEFORE COPY . .
  2. No .dockerignore file: Every temporary file (.pyc, __pycache__, .git) changes the COPY checksum. Create .dockerignore to exclude non-essential files.
  3. RUN apt-get update without version pinning: apt-get update changes every build because package lists change. Pin to specific versions or use a base image with pre-installed deps.
  4. RUN pip install without --no-cache-dir: pip cache is rebuilt every layer. Use --no-cache-dir to avoid caching pip packages in the image layer itself.
  5. Build context too large: Sending gigabytes of unnecessary files. docker build shows "Sending build context to Docker daemon: 2.5GB" — add large files to .dockerignore.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Docker cache cleared by CI/CD: CI systems often use --no-cache or clean environments that don't preserve layers between builds.
  2. Docker layer cache size limit reached: Docker Desktop has a max cache size — old layers evicted.
  3. RUN timestamp-dependent commands: RUN date > /build-time.txt invalidates cache every build.
  4. BuildKit not enabled: BuildKit provides smarter cache invalidation — DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build ..
  5. Network-dependent RUN commands: RUN curl/wget with changing URLs invalidate cache. Pin to specific versions.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No Docker layer cache in CI/CD: New pipeline has no cache configuration — every build from scratch. Use docker/build-push-action with cache-from/cache-to.
  2. Registry cache not configured: --cache-from=registry.example.com/easypj/cache:latest not set — pulls full base images every build.
  3. Base image frequently updated: python:3.12-slim has daily updates — cache invalidated from the first layer. Pin to digest.
  4. Different build hosts: Cache is local to each build host — new CI workers have no cache. Use distributed cache or registry cache.
  5. BuildKit daemon not running: Some CI images ship without BuildKit — falls back to legacy builder with poorer caching.
🔍 What to Look At:
docker build -t easypj/jobpost . 2>&1 | grep -E "(CACHED|RUN|COPY)" Watch which layers say CACHED vs which rebuild. The FIRST non-CACHED layer in the output is where cache breaks.
wc -c requirements.txt and docker build --no-cache . 2>&1 | grep "Sending build context" Compare: if build context is 500MB but requirements.txt is 2KB, ordering COPY . before pip install is the problem.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: COPY . . is placed BEFORE RUN pip install. Since source code changes frequently, the cache breaks at the COPY layer, forcing pip install (the slowest step) to re-run every time. Move the dependency installation BEFORE the application code COPY.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Reorder: dependencies FIRST, code LAST COPY requirements.txt . && RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt && COPY . . Dependencies install once and cache. Only code changes trigger the final COPY.
2. Create .dockerignore .git/ __pycache__/ *.pyc .env .pytest_cache/ node_modules/ tests/ Reduce build context size. Fewer changing files = better cache hit rate.
3. Pin base image to digest FROM python:3.12.7-slim@sha256:abc... Prevent cache invalidation from base image updates. Update intentionally, not accidentally.
4. Use BuildKit cache mounts RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt BuildKit cache mounts persist pip cache across builds without baking it into the image layer.
5. Measure improvement time docker build -t easypj/jobpost . Before: 10+ minutes. After fix + code-only change: should be under 30 seconds.
💡 Personal Advice:
Order matters. Least-changing at the top. FROM → apt-get → pip install → COPY code. This is the golden Dockerfile ordering. Every Dockerfile should follow it.
docker build output tells you everything. Look for "[CACHED]" vs the step that re-runs. The first non-cached step is where your cache breaks. Fix that layer.
Separate requirements.txt from requirements-dev.txt. Dev dependencies (pytest, black) change more often than production deps. Separate files = better caching.
BuildKit cache mounts are game-changing. They persist package caches (apt, pip, npm) between builds without baking them into layers. Build times drop 50-80%.
AB8
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB8
initContainer Fails — Database Migration Dependency Not Ready

🔍 Symptom: Pod stuck in Init:0/1 or Init:CrashLoopBackOff. The Django migration initContainer keeps failing because it tries to connect to PostgreSQL before the database pod is ready. kubectl logs <pod> -c django-migrate --previous shows connection refused errors.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME                           READY   STATUS              RESTARTS
  easypj-web-9x7k2               0/1     Init:CrashLoopBackOff  5

  kubectl logs easypj-web-9x7k2 -c django-migrate --previous
  Running migrations...
  Traceback (most recent call last):
  django.db.utils.OperationalError: could not connect to server: Connection refused
      Is the server running on host "easypj-db" (10.96.100.50) and accepting
      TCP/IP connections on port 5432?
  # Init container tried to migrate before PostgreSQL was ready!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No retry logic in init container: The init container runs python manage.py migrate once and exits. Add a loop with sleep and retry: while ! pg_isready -h easypj-db; do sleep 2; done.
  2. PostgreSQL pod not Ready yet: The web pod starts before the DB pod's readiness probe passes. DB startup (with WAL recovery) can take 30-60 seconds.
  3. initContainer restartPolicy not respected: Init containers always restart on failure regardless of the pod's restartPolicy. The backoff increases (10s, 20s, 40s...) causing long delays.
  4. Wrong DB hostname in init container: initContainer uses "localhost" but PostgreSQL is in a different pod. Use the Service name: easypj-db.
  5. NetworkPolicy blocking initContainer: A deny-all NetworkPolicy blocks the init container from reaching the DB Service. Init containers use the same network as the pod.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. initContainer image missing psql client: The init container uses python:3.12-slim which doesn't have pg_isready. Use a DB-aware image or install postgresql-client.
  2. DB credentials wrong in initContainer: Migration init container uses different env vars than the main container — missing DATABASE_URL.
  3. PostgreSQL requiring SSL connection: pg_isready succeeds but migrate fails because SSL is required and not configured in the init container.
  4. initContainer resource limits too low: Django migrate needs 500MB+ memory for large migrations — OOMKilled before connecting.
  5. DNS not ready when initContainer starts: On brand-new clusters, CoreDNS may not be ready when the first pods start.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. PostgreSQL not deployed yet: Web Deployment created before DB StatefulSet — init container has nothing to connect to. Use Helm hooks or deploy in order.
  2. DB Service not created: The Service that init container references doesn't exist. kubectl get svc easypj-db returns not found.
  3. PVC for PostgreSQL not bound: DB pod can't start because PVC is Pending — init container waits forever for a DB that can't start.
  4. kind/minikube network not ready: CNI plugin (Calico/Flannel) still initializing — pod-to-pod networking not functional.
  5. CoreDNS pods not running: On fresh cluster, CoreDNS might be Pending — DNS resolution fails, init container can't resolve easypj-db.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl logs <pod> -c <init-container> --previous Init containers store logs from previous runs. Use --previous to see why the last attempt failed.
kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-db and kubectl get svc easypj-db Verify the dependency exists and is Ready before the init container can succeed.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No retry/wait logic in the init container. The migration command runs immediately without checking if the database is ready. Add a wait loop using pg_isready or a simple TCP check: while ! nc -z easypj-db 5432; do sleep 2; done before running migrations.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add database wait loop to init container command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while ! pg_isready -h $DB_HOST; do sleep 2; done && python manage.py migrate"] Wait for DB to be ready before attempting migration. pg_isready is the standard PostgreSQL readiness check.
2. Use an init container image with pg_isready The python:3.12-slim image lacks postgresql-client. Either install it or use a dedicated migration image with the client tools.
3. Set restartPolicy for init container restartPolicy: OnFailure Init containers restart on failure by default. Set appropriate restart policy for the pod.
4. Deploy in order or use Helm hooks Deploy DB first, wait for Ready, then deploy web. Or use Helm chart hooks: post-install for migrations.
5. Increase failureThreshold to handle slow DB startup If the DB takes 60s to start, the init container needs enough retries. Set a reasonable timeout (e.g., 30 retries × 2s = 60s).
💡 Personal Advice:
Always add a wait loop to dependency-dependent init containers. Never assume a dependency is ready when the init container starts. A 5-line while/sleep loop saves hours of debugging.
Use kubectl logs --previous for init containers. Init containers log to stdout like regular containers. If the pod is in Init:CrashLoopBackOff, the previous run's logs tell you exactly what failed.
Consider migration Jobs instead of initContainers. For large migrations, a separate Job (not initContainer) is better — you can monitor it, retry it independently, and it won't block pod startup forever.
Test with the DB actually down. Delete the DB pod and watch your init container. If it crashes immediately instead of waiting, your retry logic is broken.
AB9
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB9
Sidecar Container CrashLoopBackOff — Shared Volume Permissions

🔍 Symptom: The nginx sidecar container keeps restarting with "Permission denied" errors. The main Django container writes static files to a shared emptyDir volume as UID 0 (root), but the nginx sidecar runs as UID 101 (nginx user) and can't read the files. Static assets are not served.

  kubectl logs easypj-web -c nginx --previous
  2024/06/11 14:30:22 [error] 7#7: *1 open() "/usr/share/nginx/html/static/css/main.css" failed (13: Permission denied)
  # nginx can't read files written by Django's collectstatic!

  kubectl exec easypj-web -c django -- ls -la /shared/static/css/
  -rw-r--r-- 1 root root 4521 Jun 11 14:30 main.css
  # Django writes as root (UID 0)...

  kubectl exec easypj-web -c nginx -- id
  uid=101(nginx) gid=101(nginx) groups=101(nginx)
  # ...but nginx runs as UID 101 and can't read root's files!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. UID/GID mismatch between containers: Django container runs as root (UID 0) and creates files owned by root. nginx container runs as UID 101. Without matching GID, nginx gets Permission denied.
  2. fsGroup not set on pod: securityContext.fsGroup: 101 is not set. This would make all files on shared volumes group-owned by GID 101, which nginx can access.
  3. Django container not running as matching user: The Django container should run as the same UID/GID as nginx, or at least share the same GID via supplemental groups.
  4. emptyDir default permissions: emptyDir volumes default to 0777 but files created inside inherit the container's umask (typically 022 → 0644/0755, owned by the container's UID).
  5. No initContainer to pre-set permissions: An init container running as root could chown the shared volume before the main containers start, ensuring correct ownership.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. SELinux/AppArmor blocking cross-container file access: SELinux contexts prevent nginx from reading files created by Django despite correct Unix permissions.
  2. readOnlyRootFilesystem on nginx: nginx needs to write temp files but readOnlyRootFilesystem is set — mount emptyDir for /var/cache/nginx.
  3. Django collectstatic runs as postStart hook: Hook runs after nginx starts — nginx checks for files before they exist, not permission denied.
  4. Shared volume is a hostPath with restricted permissions: hostPath volumes inherit host directory permissions which may be more restrictive than expected.
  5. Container runs with no_new_privs: Security option prevents setuid/setgid — can't elevate to access files even with group membership.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Pod Security Standards (Restricted) enforced: Restricted PSS requires runAsNonRoot — Django can't run as root, write as root, or chown files. Must use fsGroup.
  2. Different container runtimes: containerd vs CRI-O handle supplemental groups differently — test on your actual runtime.
  3. Node filesystem mount options: noexec/nosuid mount options on /var/lib/kubelet affect volume permissions.
  4. User namespace remapping enabled: UID 0 inside container may map to a different host UID — file ownership doesn't match.
  5. CSI volume instead of emptyDir: CSI volumes may have different default permission models than emptyDir.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl exec <pod> -c <container> -- id and ls -la /shared/ Compare the UID/GID of each container with the file ownership on the shared volume. They must match or share a group.
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -A10 securityContext Check if fsGroup, runAsUser, runAsGroup, and supplementalGroups are configured correctly.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: UID/GID mismatch and missing fsGroup. The Django container creates files as UID 0 (root), but the nginx sidecar runs as UID 101. Set fsGroup: 101 at the pod level and run Django as UID 1000 with supplemental group 101 to ensure all files on shared volumes are readable by nginx.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set fsGroup at pod level securityContext: {fsGroup: 101} All files on shared volumes will have group ownership set to 101. Both containers can read/write if they're in group 101.
2. Run both containers with matching GID Django: runAsUser: 1000, runAsGroup: 101. Nginx: runs as UID 101 by default. Both share GID 101.
3. Use initContainer to fix permissions initContainers: [{command: ["chown", "-R", "1000:101", "/shared"]}] An init container (running as root) can pre-set permissions before the main containers start.
4. Set umask in Django container umask 0002 Files created by Django will be group-writable. Combined with fsGroup, nginx can read them.
5. Verify with ls -la inside each container kubectl exec <pod> -c django -- ls -la /shared/ && kubectl exec <pod> -c nginx -- cat /shared/static/css/main.css Confirm nginx can read the files after fixes are applied.
💡 Personal Advice:
fsGroup is the simplest fix for shared volume permissions. One line in the pod securityContext solves 90% of multi-container file sharing issues. Always set it when using shared volumes.
Test with non-root from day one. Start all containers as non-root users. If your app works as root but not as non-root, you have permission bugs — find them early.
Consider init containers for one-time setup. Instead of running Django as root to chown files, use an init container. It runs once, does the setup as root, and exits — main containers stay non-root.
EmptyDir is tmpfs-compatible. For better security, use emptyDir.medium: Memory for shared volumes — files never touch disk and are wiped on pod restart.

📌 AB10–AB12: CronJobs, Jobs & Lifecycle Hooks

AB10
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB10
CronJob Misses Schedule — Timezone Mismatch

🔍 Symptom: The nightly database backup CronJob runs at 2 PM instead of 2 AM. Kubernetes CronJobs use UTC timezone by default, but the developer wrote the schedule for their local timezone. Backups run during peak traffic instead of off-peak.

  kubectl get cronjob easypj-db-backup -o yaml | grep schedule
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"     ← 2:00 AM UTC = 3:00 AM local (CET)

  kubectl get jobs --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
  NAME                       COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
  easypj-db-backup-28901234   1/1           45s        2h
  # Ran at 2:00 UTC (4:00 local!) — wrong timezone!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Kubernetes CronJobs use UTC always: There's no timezone field in CronJob spec (before K8s 1.25 beta). All schedules are interpreted as UTC. "0 2 * * *" means 2 AM UTC, not local time.
  2. Developer wrote schedule in local timezone: Schedule written as "midnight EST" but CronJob interprets as midnight UTC. Always convert to UTC.
  3. No timeZone field set (K8s 1.25+): K8s 1.25+ supports spec.timeZone: "America/New_York" but it's beta and not set. Use it if available.
  4. Daylight Saving Time not accounted for: 2 AM UTC may become 3 AM or 1 AM local depending on DST. CronJobs don't auto-adjust.
  5. startingDeadlineSeconds too low: If the CronJob controller is down when a schedule fires, the job is skipped. Set startingDeadlineSeconds to allow catch-up.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CronJob controller not running: kube-controller-manager CronJob controller is disabled — jobs never fire regardless of schedule.
  2. concurrencyPolicy: Forbid blocking new jobs: Previous job still running when next schedule fires — new job skipped.
  3. suspend: true accidentally set: CronJob was suspended for maintenance and never re-enabled.
  4. successfulJobsHistoryLimit too low: Old jobs deleted, making it hard to verify when the CronJob last ran.
  5. Node clock skew: If node clocks are off by hours (NTP not configured), CronJob schedules are wrong relative to real time.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. NTP not configured on nodes: Fresh VMs without NTP have wrong system clocks — CronJob fires at completely wrong times.
  2. CronJob controller disabled in kube-controller-manager: Some minimal kubeadm installs disable optional controllers. Check controller-manager args.
  3. RBAC missing for CronJob: ServiceAccount used by CronJob doesn't have permission to create Jobs/Pods.
  4. Cluster in different geographic region: Cluster nodes in us-east but developers in Europe — UTC schedule confusion.
  5. No monitoring on CronJob execution: No alert if CronJob hasn't run in expected window. Set up cronjob monitoring.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get cronjob -o yaml | grep -E "schedule|timeZone|lastScheduleTime|suspend" Check the schedule, timezone setting, last execution time, and whether the CronJob is suspended.
date -u and kubectl get jobs --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -5 Compare current UTC time with actual CronJob execution times. Are they aligned?
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Kubernetes CronJob schedules are ALWAYS in UTC. A schedule of "0 2 * * *" means 2 AM UTC regardless of where the cluster or developer is located. Convert all schedules to UTC and document the conversion clearly.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Convert schedule to UTC If backup should run at 2 AM local (EST = UTC-5), schedule should be "0 7 * * *" (UTC). Always calculate: local_time - offset = UTC.
2. Use timeZone field (K8s 1.25+) spec.timeZone: "America/New_York" If your cluster supports it, set the timezone explicitly. CronJob handles DST automatically.
3. Set concurrencyPolicy and history limits concurrencyPolicy: Forbid and successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3 Prevent overlapping jobs and keep history for debugging.
4. Add startingDeadlineSeconds startingDeadlineSeconds: 300 Allow the CronJob to start up to 5 minutes late if the controller was temporarily unavailable.
5. Verify with a test schedule schedule: "*/5 * * * *" Temporarily set to every 5 minutes, verify jobs fire at expected UTC times, then set the production schedule.
💡 Personal Advice:
Always document CronJob schedules in BOTH UTC and local. In comments or runbooks: "# Runs at 2 AM EST (7 AM UTC)". Future you (and your teammates) will thank you.
Test CronJobs with high-frequency schedules first. Set to every 5 minutes for testing, verify execution times, then switch to the real schedule. Never deploy an untested CronJob schedule.
Monitor CronJob execution. Set up alerts if a CronJob hasn't run in its expected window. A silent CronJob failure can go unnoticed for weeks.
Consider CronJob alternative for critical tasks. For mission-critical scheduled tasks, external schedulers (Airflow, Argo Workflows) offer better timezone handling and monitoring.
AB11
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB11
Job Never Completes — Infinite Loop or Missing Exit Condition

🔍 Symptom: A data migration Job runs forever without completing. kubectl get jobs shows completions: 0/1 even after hours. The Job's pod keeps running a Django management command that has an infinite loop or never reaches its exit condition.

  kubectl get jobs
  NAME              COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
  easypj-data-migrate   0/1        6h23m      6h23m

  kubectl logs job/easypj-data-migrate --tail=5
  Processing record 1847 of 1850...
  Processing record 1847 of 1850...  ← Same record, infinite loop!
  Processing record 1847 of 1850...

  kubectl describe job easypj-data-migrate
  Active Deadline:  <unset>     ← No deadline — runs forever!
  Backoff Limit:    6            ← Will retry 6 times but never completes
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Application bug: infinite loop or retry: The Django management command has while True: without a proper exit condition, or a retry loop that never gives up.
  2. No activeDeadlineSeconds set: Without activeDeadlineSeconds, a stuck Job runs forever. Set to a reasonable maximum: activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600 (1 hour).
  3. backoffLimit too high for retryable errors: A transient error causes restarts, and with backoffLimit=6, it retries 6 times — each taking hours.
  4. Data dependency not met: The migration waits for data that never arrives — waiting on an API, a file, or a database condition that never becomes true.
  5. Resource starvation causing extreme slowness: The Job pod has CPU limit set too low (50m) — processing takes 100x longer than expected.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Deadlock in database transactions: Two migration jobs running concurrently create a deadlock — each waiting for the other.
  2. Network partition: Job pod loses network connectivity mid-execution and hangs on a network call with no timeout.
  3. Memory leak in migration script: Each record processed leaks memory — eventually OOMKilled after hours.
  4. Concurrency issue with CronJob: CronJob creates new Job before previous one finishes — multiple Jobs processing same data.
  5. ttlSecondsAfterFinished not set: Completed (or failed) Jobs are never cleaned up — clutter makes it hard to see which are still running.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Job controller not running: kube-controller-manager Job controller is disabled — Jobs are created but never managed.
  2. RBAC preventing Job from listing/completing: ServiceAccount doesn't have permission to update Job status — can't mark as complete.
  3. ResourceQuota preventing pod creation: Namespace quota reached — Job can't create pods but doesn't report failure clearly.
  4. NodeSelector with no matching nodes: Job's pod requires a node label that no node has — stays Pending forever.
  5. Default storage class not set: Job pod references a PVC that can't bind — pod stays Pending, Job never runs.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe job <name> and kubectl logs job/<name> --tail=20 Check Active Deadline, Backoff Limit, and the actual log output. Is it making progress or repeating the same operation?
kubectl get pod -l job-name=<name> -o yaml | grep -A5 "state:" Check if the pod is actually Running (stuck) vs Terminated (restarting) vs Pending (not scheduled).
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No activeDeadlineSeconds set AND an application-level infinite loop. Always set activeDeadlineSeconds on Jobs as a safety net. The application should also have internal timeouts for any I/O operations.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set activeDeadlineSeconds spec.activeDeadlineSeconds: 3600 The Job is automatically terminated after 1 hour — prevents infinite runs. All terminated pods are deleted.
2. Fix the application bug Add exit condition, timeout, or progress tracking to the management command. Verify locally before deploying as a Job.
3. Set appropriate backoffLimit spec.backoffLimit: 3 Limit retries. After 3 failures, the Job is marked as Failed — visible and actionable.
4. Add ttlSecondsAfterFinished spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 3600 Auto-cleanup completed/failed Jobs after 1 hour. Keeps the cluster clean.
5. Monitor long-running Jobs kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/easypj-data-migrate --timeout=3600s Wait for completion with a timeout. Integrate into CI/CD pipelines to catch stuck Jobs.
💡 Personal Advice:
Every Job needs activeDeadlineSeconds. This is the #1 Job best practice. Without it, a bug can consume resources forever. Set it to 2-3× the expected runtime.
Test Jobs locally before deploying. Run the exact command in a local container. If it hangs locally, it will hang in Kubernetes. Fix the code, not the infrastructure.
Use kubectl wait in CI/CD. After kubectl apply -f job.yaml, immediately run kubectl wait. If the Job doesn't complete in time, the pipeline fails — catching stuck Jobs before they waste hours.
Jobs are for finite tasks. If your "Job" runs forever, it should be a Deployment. Jobs have an expected end — design them that way.
AB12
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB12
Pod Stuck in Init:CrashLoopBackOff — Init Container Missing Script

🔍 Symptom: Pod stuck at Init:CrashLoopBackOff. The init container references a shell script /scripts/wait-for-db.sh that doesn't exist in the container image. The init container exits immediately with "no such file or directory."

  kubectl get pods
  NAME              READY   STATUS                  RESTARTS
  easypj-web-9x7k2  0/1     Init:CrashLoopBackOff    8

  kubectl logs easypj-web-9x7k2 -c init-db-check --previous
  /bin/sh: 1: /scripts/wait-for-db.sh: not found

  kubectl describe pod easypj-web-9x7k2 | grep -A10 "Init Containers"
  Init Containers:
    init-db-check:
      Command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "/scripts/wait-for-db.sh"]
      # Script doesn't exist in the image!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Script not included in the image: The init container uses the same application image which doesn't have /scripts/wait-for-db.sh. The script was added to a different image or not COPY'd.
  2. Wrong image for init container: Init container uses the runtime image (python:3.12-slim) but the script expects bash — slim images don't have bash, only sh.
  3. COPY path mismatch in Dockerfile: Script was copied to /app/scripts/ but init container command references /scripts/. Check the Dockerfile COPY paths.
  4. Script not executable: The file exists but doesn't have execute permission (chmod +x missing). Error is "Permission denied" not "not found" but still fails.
  5. Init container uses different image than main: Main container has the script at /scripts/ but init container uses busybox which doesn't have it. Specify image explicitly.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Script has Windows line endings (CRLF): Script edited on Windows — #!/bin/sh^M causes "not found" because the shebang includes a carriage return.
  2. Script uses non-existent interpreter: #!/usr/bin/python3 but the image has python at /usr/local/bin/python3.
  3. Image pull error for init container: Different imagePullPolicy or registry for init container image — not pulled successfully.
  4. Init container overwritten by mutating webhook: Admission webhook modifies the init container command and breaks it.
  5. Filesystem mounted read-only: Script exists but readOnlyRootFilesystem prevents execution.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Image not available in cluster registry: Init container image not pushed to the registry the cluster uses. ImagePullBackOff on init container.
  2. Dockerfile COPY fails silently: COPY scripts/ /scripts/ — if scripts/ doesn't exist in build context, Docker creates an empty directory.
  3. .dockerignore excluding scripts/: The scripts directory is in .dockerignore — not included in the image.
  4. Multi-stage build: scripts only in builder stage: COPY --from=builder copied app files but forgot to copy scripts/.
  5. SecurityContext blocking execution: noexec on the volume or AppArmor profile preventing script execution.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl exec <pod> -c <init-container> -- ls -la /scripts/ (if pod is still in init phase, use kubectl debug) Verify the script file exists at the expected path. If the init container already failed, inspect the image locally with docker run.
docker run --rm --entrypoint ls <image> /scripts/ Check the actual filesystem of the image. Does the script exist? Is it executable?
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The init container uses the application image, but the required script was never added to the Dockerfile. The Dockerfile needs COPY scripts/wait-for-db.sh /scripts/ and RUN chmod +x /scripts/wait-for-db.sh.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add script to Dockerfile COPY scripts/ /scripts/ && RUN chmod +x /scripts/*.sh Copy the scripts directory into the image and make all .sh files executable.
2. Rebuild and push the image docker build -t easypj/jobpost:v2.1 . && docker push easypj/jobpost:v2.1 Rebuild with the script included. Verify with docker run --rm --entrypoint ls easypj/jobpost:v2.1 /scripts/.
3. Use a dedicated init container image Instead of the app image, use busybox or alpine with a simple command: until nc -z easypj-db 5432; do sleep 2; done. No script needed.
4. Add Dockerfile validation step RUN test -x /scripts/wait-for-db.sh || (echo "Script missing!" && exit 1) Fail the build if required scripts don't exist or aren't executable.
5. Delete and recreate the pod After fixing the image, delete the stuck pod. The Deployment will create a new one with the updated image.
💡 Personal Advice:
Validate init container commands locally first. docker run --rm --entrypoint /bin/sh <image> -c "/scripts/wait-for-db.sh". If it fails locally, it will fail in Kubernetes.
Prefer inline commands over scripts for simple checks. while ! nc -z easypj-db 5432; do sleep 2; done — no script file needed, works in any image with nc (or use /dev/tcp in bash).
Use the same image for init and main containers. If init uses the same image as main, scripts and tools are guaranteed to be available. Different images = surprises.
Check .dockerignore before debugging. If docker build succeeds but files are missing, .dockerignore is the #1 suspect. Test: docker run --rm <image> ls /scripts/.

📌 AB13–AB15: Pod Lifecycle & Termination Issues

AB13
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB13
postStart Hook Timeout — Pod Never Reaches Ready

🔍 Symptom: Pod stays in ContainerCreating or NotReady state for a long time. The postStart hook makes an HTTP call to /api/health but the application startup takes longer than the hook timeout, causing the pod to get stuck in an initialization loop.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME              READY   STATUS              RESTARTS
  easypj-web-9x7k2  0/1     ContainerCreating   0         ← Stuck!

  kubectl describe pod easypj-web-9x7k2 | grep -A5 postStart
  postStart:
    exec:
      command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while ! curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/health; do sleep 1; done"]
  # Hook runs BEFORE the main process is considered "started"!
  # If the hook never completes, the container never reaches Running state.
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. postStart hook blocks container startup: postStart runs AFTER the container starts but BEFORE it's marked Running. If the hook never returns, the container is stuck in ContainerCreating forever.
  2. Hook depends on the application being ready: A postStart HTTP call to the app endpoint creates a deadlock — the hook waits for the app, but the app can't be Ready until the hook completes.
  3. No timeout set on the hook: postStart hooks have no default timeout. A hung hook blocks the container indefinitely. The hook should always have a timeout.
  4. Hook command has a bug: curl to localhost:8000 but Django binds to 0.0.0.0:8080 — the hook will loop forever waiting for port 8000.
  5. postStart used for startup logic instead of startupProbe: postStart should be a quick one-shot task. Long-running startup checks belong in a startupProbe, which doesn't block the container state.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Network policy blocks localhost access in hook: Rare but possible — container network restricted, localhost not accessible in hook context.
  2. Hook runs as wrong user: postStart hook inherits container's securityContext — if it tries to write to a protected directory, it fails.
  3. Django migration in postStart hook: Heavy migration runs as postStart — takes 5+ minutes, pod stays ContainerCreating.
  4. postStart hook interferes with readiness probe: Hook modifies files that readiness probe checks — probe fails because hook isn't done.
  5. Container restart due to liveness probe during hook: Liveness probe starts counting from container start — if the hook delays startup, liveness kills it.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. CNI plugin not ready: Container starts but networking isn't available — localhost curl fails, hook loops forever.
  2. Container runtime bug: Specific CRI versions have bugs with postStart hook lifecycle. Check runtime version.
  3. Resource starvation: Node CPU/memory exhausted — hook command runs extremely slowly, appears hung.
  4. Mutating webhook adding broken postStart: Admission controller adds a postStart hook that conflicts with the app's startup.
  5. PVC not mounted yet when hook runs: postStart tries to write to a volume that isn't mounted yet — hangs on filesystem operation.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A20 "Events:" Look for "FailedPostStartHook" events. The event message tells you if the hook timed out or errored.
kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml | grep -A10 postStart Review the hook command. Does it have a timeout? Does it depend on the app being ready? Does it have an exit condition?
🎯 #1 Root Cause: postStart hook has no timeout AND it waits for the application health endpoint — creating a deadlock. The hook blocks until the app is ready, but the container can't be Ready until the hook completes. Use a startupProbe for readiness checks, not postStart.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Replace postStart wait loop with startupProbe startupProbe: {httpGet: {path: /api/health, port: 8000}, initialDelaySeconds: 5, periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 30} startupProbe checks readiness WITHOUT blocking container state transition. Use postStart only for one-time quick tasks.
2. Add timeout to postStart hook timeout 30 /bin/sh -c "while ! curl -s http://localhost:8000/api/health; do sleep 1; done" The timeout command ensures the hook exits after 30 seconds instead of hanging forever.
3. Use postStart for fire-and-forget tasks only postStart is ideal for: creating directories, setting permissions, sending a startup notification. Not for: waiting for app readiness.
4. Set initialDelaySeconds on liveness probe livenessProbe: {initialDelaySeconds: 60, ...} If postStart takes time, liveness probe needs enough delay to not kill the container during startup.
5. Delete and recreate the stuck pod kubectl delete pod and let the Deployment recreate it. The postStart deadlock can only be resolved by restart.
💡 Personal Advice:
postStart is NOT for readiness checks. This is the most common lifecycle hook mistake. postStart blocks the container state — use startupProbe for health checks.
Every postStart hook should complete in under 5 seconds. If your hook takes longer, it's doing too much. Move long-running setup to an init container or startupProbe.
Test hooks independently. Run the hook command manually inside the container: kubectl exec <pod> -- /bin/sh -c "your-hook-command".
postStart + liveness combo is dangerous. If postStart takes 30s but liveness initialDelaySeconds is 15s, the container is killed before postStart finishes. Always tune initialDelaySeconds.
AB14
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB14
preStop Hook Not Executing — Dirty Shutdown Causing Data Loss

🔍 Symptom: Django pods lose in-flight requests and Celery tasks are abandoned during pod termination. The preStop hook that should drain connections and stop receiving new tasks never executes because the pod is force-killed before the hook can run. SIGTERM arrives and the container exits before hook completion.

  kubectl logs easypj-web-9x7k2 --previous | tail -10
  [2024-06-11 14:30:22] SIGTERM received
  [2024-06-11 14:30:22] Shutting down... (no graceful drain!)
  [2024-06-11 14:30:23] Connection closed (abandoned 5 in-flight requests!)

  kubectl describe pod easypj-web-9x7k2 | grep -A5 preStop
  preStop:
    exec:
      command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 30 && kill -QUIT 1"]
  # 30s sleep but terminationGracePeriodSeconds is only 15s!
  # SIGKILL arrives before the hook finishes!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. terminationGracePeriodSeconds too short for preStop: preStop hook needs 30 seconds but terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 30 (default). Hook starts → 30s passes → SIGKILL kills hook mid-execution.
  2. Application doesn't handle SIGTERM properly: preStop sends SIGTERM to the main process, but Django ignores it or takes too long. The app must have a proper signal handler.
  3. preStop hook runs in parallel with SIGTERM: When pod deletion starts, SIGTERM is sent to the main process IMMEDIATELY. preStop runs concurrently, not before SIGTERM.
  4. Hook command fails silently: The hook script errors out (wrong path, permission denied) but the pod continues terminating without the drain logic.
  5. preStop command depends on network: Hook tries to call an external service to deregister, but the pod is already being removed from Service endpoints — network call fails.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Container runtime ignores preStop: Very rare — specific CRI versions might skip lifecycle hooks under certain conditions.
  2. preStop not defined at all: Pod manifest doesn't have lifecycle.preStop — container receives SIGTERM directly with no drain period.
  3. Hook uses postStart instead of preStop: YAML typo: lifecycle.postStart instead of lifecycle.preStop — wrong hook in wrong place.
  4. Pod force-deleted with --grace-period=0: kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0 skips preStop entirely. SIGKILL immediately.
  5. Node drain during maintenance: Node is drained with --grace-period=0 or --force, skipping preStop for all pods.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. PodDisruptionBudget not set: During node drain, all pods are terminated simultaneously — preStop hooks may be skipped if resources are tight.
  2. Cluster autoscaler eviction: Autoscaler evicts pods aggressively — may not respect full grace periods on scale-down.
  3. kubelet restart during termination: If kubelet restarts while a pod is terminating, the preStop hook state may be lost.
  4. OOM condition on node: Node memory exhausted — OOM killer might kill the container before preStop can run.
  5. CRI socket timeout: Container runtime communication timeout causes hook execution to fail silently.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -E "terminationGracePeriod|preStop|PreStop" Compare terminationGracePeriodSeconds with preStop expected duration. Grace period MUST exceed hook runtime.
kubectl logs <pod> --previous | grep -iE "sigterm|shutdown|graceful|drain|prestop" Check if the application logged SIGTERM receipt, whether it attempted graceful shutdown, and how far it got.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30s default) is less than or equal to the preStop hook duration. preStop and SIGTERM run CONCURRENTLY, not sequentially. The grace period must be: preStop_duration + app_shutdown_time + buffer (e.g., 30 + 30 + 10 = 70s).
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds longer than preStop spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 90 Formula: preStop_duration (30s) + app_shutdown_time (30s) + safety_buffer (30s) = 90s minimum.
2. Fix the preStop command to actually drain command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "kill -TERM 1 && sleep 30"] Send SIGTERM to main process (PID 1), then wait for it to finish gracefully. The 30s gives the app time to drain.
3. Implement graceful shutdown in the application Django should catch SIGTERM, stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests, close DB connections, then exit 0.
4. Add sleep as preStop's last action command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 15"] The simplest preStop: just sleep to allow in-flight requests to complete. Kubernetes removes the pod from Service endpoints BEFORE preStop starts.
5. Test with kubectl delete pod kubectl delete pod <name> && kubectl logs <name> -f Watch the logs during deletion. You should see the preStop hook executing and the app shutting down gracefully.
💡 Personal Advice:
preStop and SIGTERM run concurrently, not sequentially. This is the most misunderstood lifecycle behavior. preStop starts, then SIGTERM is sent to PID 1 — they overlap. Design your shutdown accordingly.
The simplest preStop: sleep 10. Kubernetes removes the pod from Service endpoints BEFORE preStop runs. A 10-second sleep ensures no new requests arrive while existing ones drain.
Always set terminationGracePeriodSeconds explicitly. The default 30s is rarely enough for apps with database connections or in-flight requests. Set it to 60-90s.
Never use kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0 in production. This skips preStop entirely and sends SIGKILL immediately. It's useful for stuck pods but causes data loss in production.
AB15
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB15
Pod Stuck in Terminating State — Finalizers Not Released

🔍 Symptom: Pod deletion hangs in Terminating state for 5+ minutes. kubectl delete pod doesn't return. The pod has a finalizer that blocks deletion until some external controller processes it, but the controller is stuck or not running.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME              READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
  easypj-web-9x7k2  0/1     Terminating   0          5m      ← Stuck 5 minutes!

  kubectl get pod easypj-web-9x7k2 -o yaml | grep finalizers -A5
  finalizers:
  - kubernetes.io/pod
  - custom.example.com/backup-before-delete   ← Custom finalizer stuck!

  kubectl describe pod easypj-web-9x7k2 | grep -i finalizer
  Finalizers:  custom.example.com/backup-before-delete
  # The backup-before-delete controller isn't running!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Custom finalizer controller not running: A mutating webhook or operator added a finalizer but the controller that processes it is down — the finalizer is never removed.
  2. Finalizer controller stuck processing: The controller that handles the finalizer is running but stuck in a loop or waiting for an external resource that's unavailable.
  3. PVC with retain reclaimPolicy blocking deletion: StatefulSet pods may be stuck because the PVC has retain policy and the finalizer prevents the PV from being released.
  4. Service endpoint finalizer not cleaned: The pod is in a Service's endpoints list and the endpoints controller hasn't removed it — blocks pod deletion.
  5. Foreground cascading deletion hanging: kubectl delete pod --cascade=foreground — waits for all dependents to be deleted first. A stuck dependent blocks everything.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. kubelet not responding: Node is NotReady or kubelet process is hung — can't process pod deletion.
  2. Network partition between kubelet and API server: Kubelet can't report container termination status to the API server.
  3. Container runtime hung: Docker/containerd process is stuck — can't kill the container.
  4. NFS volume stuck: Pod has an NFS mount and the NFS server is unreachable — unmount hangs indefinitely.
  5. Huge pages or GPU resources not released: Special hardware resources held by the container are not released properly.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. API server slow or overloaded: High request latency causes finalizer removal to time out repeatedly.
  2. etcd performance issues: Slow etcd writes — finalizer removal patches take too long.
  3. Mutating webhook adds unintended finalizer: Admission webhook adds a custom finalizer to every pod — cleanup logic missing.
  4. Storage class finalizer on PVC: PVC has kubernetes.io/pvc-protection finalizer — pod can't be deleted until PVC is unbound.
  5. ServiceAccount token finalizer: Token request finalizer blocks pod deletion until token is revoked.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pod <name> -o json | jq '.metadata.finalizers' List ALL finalizers on the stuck pod. Any non-standard finalizer is a suspect. Standard finalizer: kubernetes.io/pod.
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<pod> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -10 Check events for errors related to finalizer processing or volume unmount failures.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: A custom finalizer (custom.example.com/backup-before-delete) is blocking pod deletion. The controller that should process this finalizer is not running, so the finalizer is never removed from the metadata. The pod stays in Terminating forever.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Patch the pod to remove the finalizer kubectl patch pod <name> -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":[]}}' --type=merge Remove ALL finalizers from the pod. Use [] to clear the entire finalizers list. Pod deletion proceeds immediately.
2. Remove only the problematic finalizer kubectl patch pod <name> -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}' Setting finalizers to null removes all. Or use JSON patch to remove a specific finalizer.
3. Restart the controller that manages the finalizer kubectl rollout restart deployment <controller-deployment> If the finalizer controller exists, restart it. It should reprocess all pods with pending finalizers.
4. Force delete as last resort kubectl delete pod <name> --force --grace-period=0 This removes the pod from etcd immediately WITHOUT waiting for finalizers. Use only when finalizer removal doesn't work.
5. Check and fix the finalizer controller logic Ensure the controller handles errors gracefully and uses timeouts. A finalizer that blocks indefinitely is a design flaw.
💡 Personal Advice:
Finalizers are a promise, not a suggestion. If you add a finalizer, you MUST have a controller that will remove it. An orphaned finalizer = stuck resources forever.
Always set timeouts in finalizer controllers. A finalizer cleanup should complete in seconds, not minutes. If it can't, fail fast and log the error — don't block deletion.
kubectl patch ... finalizers:null is your emergency tool. When a pod is stuck in Terminating and you can't figure out why, clearing finalizers almost always works. Know this command.
Check for stuck PVCs when pods won't terminate. StatefulSet pods are often stuck because of PVC finalizers. Patch the PVC, not just the pod.

📌 AB16–AB20: Deployment & Multi-Container Issues

AB16
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB16
Wrong Image in Production — latest Tag Deployed

🔍 Symptom: kubectl describe pod shows the image is easypj/jobpost:latest instead of a specific version tag. A new push to latest accidentally triggered a rollout restart and broke production. The image running is completely different from what was tested in staging.

  kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.containers[*].image}'
  easypj/jobpost:latest    ← DANGER! Not a specific version!

  kubectl describe pod easypj-web-9x7k2 | grep Image:
  Image:          easypj/jobpost:latest
  Image ID:       docker.io/easypj/jobpost@sha256:abc123...

  kubectl rollout history deployment/easypj-web
  REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
  4         <none>             ← No idea why it changed!
  3         <none>
  2         Update to v2.0
  1         Initial deploy v1.0
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Using latest tag in Deployment spec: image: easypj/jobpost:latest — latest is mutable. Any new push to latest can trigger a rollout if imagePullPolicy is Always.
  2. imagePullPolicy: Always + latest tag: Every pod restart pulls latest again, potentially getting a different image. Combine with imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent or use specific tags.
  3. CI/CD pushes to latest tag: CI pipeline tags every build as latest, overwriting the previous image. A pod restart picks up an untested build.
  4. No version tagging strategy: Images are only tagged as latest with no semantic versioning. Cannot identify which version is running in any environment.
  5. Deployment not pinned to digest: Even with a version tag, image: easypj/jobpost:v2.0 can be overwritten. Pin to digest: easypj/jobpost@sha256:abc....
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Accidental kubectl set image with wrong tag: kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web *=easypj/jobpost:latest was run in the wrong cluster context.
  2. GitOps auto-sync from wrong branch: ArgoCD/Flux syncing from a feature branch that has latest tag in its manifests.
  3. Helm upgrade with wrong values: Helm chart values.yaml has latest tag — deploying to production without overriding image.tag.
  4. Admission webhook mutating image: A mutating webhook changes image tags on admission — replaces v2.1 with latest for some reason.
  5. Image garbage collection on node: Node ran out of disk space, kubelet GC'd the correct image, pulled latest as fallback.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No private registry: Images pulled from Docker Hub — latest tag could be compromised or changed externally.
  2. Registry mirror not configured: Pulls go to public registry instead of internal mirror with pinned images.
  3. No image signing/verification: No cosign/notation verification — can't confirm the image digest matches what was approved.
  4. No admission policy blocking latest: Kyverno/OPA not configured to block :latest tag — any deployment can use it.
  5. No image pull secret configured: Cluster can't pull from private registry — someone changed image to public latest as workaround.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get deploy -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.template.spec.containers[*].image}' Check ALL deployments for :latest tags. Also check imagePullPolicy — Always + latest = unpredictable.
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -E "Image:|Image ID:" Compare Image: (tag) with Image ID: (digest). They should match. If Image is latest but ID is a specific digest, find out why.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Deployment specifies image: easypj/jobpost:latest with imagePullPolicy: Always. Every time a pod restarts, it pulls whatever is currently tagged as latest — which may be a completely untested build pushed by CI minutes ago.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Use specific semantic version tags image: easypj/jobpost:v2.1.3 or even better, pin to digest: image: easypj/jobpost@sha256:abc123... Specific tags are immutable (by policy, not by registry enforcement). Digests are cryptographically immutable.
2. Change imagePullPolicy to IfNotPresent imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent If the tag exists locally, don't pull a new version. This prevents unexpected image changes on pod restart.
3. Block :latest with admission policy (Kyverno) Create a Kyverno ClusterPolicy that rejects any Pod/Deployment using :latest tag. Enforce at admission time.
4. Add CHANGE-CAUSE to rollouts kubectl annotate deployment/easypj-web kubernetes.io/change-cause="Deploy v2.1.3 - Fix DB timeout" Every rollout has a documented reason. kubectl rollout history shows exactly what changed and why.
5. Rollback to the last known good version kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj-web --to-revision=3 Immediately rollback to the previous revision while you fix the image tag issue.
💡 Personal Advice:
Never use :latest in production. Ever. It's the number one rule of container deployments. latest means "I don't know what's running." You should always know.
Pin to digest for true immutability. Tags are mutable pointers. Digests are immutable content hashes. image: easypj/jobpost@sha256:abc... guarantees the exact image you tested.
Enforce with policy, not convention. Team conventions fail. A Kyverno policy that rejects :latest tags at admission NEVER fails. Automate the enforcement.
Always annotate rollouts with CHANGE-CAUSE. Days later, "kubectl rollout history" should tell you exactly who deployed what and why. No more mystery image changes.
AB17
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB17
Multi-Container Pod — localhost Communication Fails

🔍 Symptom: Django app container can't reach Redis sidecar on localhost:6379. The two containers are in the same pod and should share the network namespace, but the Redis container is crashing because it's also trying to bind to port 6379 which conflicts with something else, or the Redis sidecar hasn't started yet.

  kubectl logs easypj-web -c django | grep -i redis
  redis.exceptions.ConnectionError: Error 111 connecting to localhost:6379. Connection refused.

  kubectl logs easypj-web -c redis-sidecar --previous
  Could not create server TCP listening socket 127.0.0.1:6379: bind: Address already in use

  kubectl get pod easypj-web -o yaml | grep -A3 "ports:"
  ports:
  - containerPort: 8000   # Django
  - containerPort: 6379   # Redis sidecar
  - containerPort: 6379   # OOPS — duplicate port in another container!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Port conflict between containers: Two containers in the same pod declare the same containerPort. Containers in a pod share the network namespace — port conflicts are real.
  2. Redis sidecar binding to wrong interface: Redis binds to 127.0.0.1:6379 but another process already has it, or Redis defaults to 0.0.0.0 but is restricted to localhost.
  3. Sidecar container not Ready yet: Django starts before Redis is ready. localhost:6379 is available immediately (same pod) but Redis hasn't finished loading data.
  4. Django configured with wrong Redis host: CELERY_BROKER_URL=redis://redis-service:6379 but Redis is a sidecar on localhost. Should be redis://localhost:6379.
  5. Startup ordering not guaranteed: Containers in a pod start in parallel — Django may try Redis before it's listening. No built-in ordering.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. NetworkPolicy blocking pod-local traffic: Rare — but a NetworkPolicy could restrict localhost communication within a pod.
  2. Redis protected mode: Redis protected mode rejects connections from non-localhost. If Django connects via pod IP instead of 127.0.0.1, Redis rejects.
  3. Container restarting (CrashLoopBackOff): Redis sidecar crashes and restarts — Django gets connection refused during restart window.
  4. SELinux blocking port access: SELinux context prevents Django container from accessing port opened by Redis container.
  5. Resource limits starving Redis: Redis has CPU limit 100m and can't keep up with connection requests.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. CNI plugin issue: Pod network namespace not properly shared — localhost traffic doesn't work between containers.
  2. Container runtime bug: Specific containerd/CRI-O versions have bugs with network namespace sharing.
  3. Istio/Envoy sidecar injection: Istio injects a sidecar that intercepts ALL traffic — localhost may be routed through Envoy unexpectedly.
  4. IPv6/IPv4 mismatch: Django connects via ::1 (IPv6 localhost) but Redis only listens on 127.0.0.1 (IPv4).
  5. DNS override via /etc/hosts: Mutating webhook or hostAliases overrides localhost resolution.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl exec <pod> -c django -- ss -tlnp and kubectl exec <pod> -c redis-sidecar -- ss -tlnp Inspect all listening ports from each container's perspective. Since they share the network namespace, both see the same ports.
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -A2 "containerPort" Check for duplicate containerPort declarations. Duplicate ports will prevent the second container from starting.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Two containers in the same pod declare the same containerPort (6379). Since containers in a pod share the network namespace, ports must be unique. Also, containers start in parallel with no ordering guarantee — Django may try Redis before it's ready. Add a startup check in Django or configure a proper init container.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Ensure unique containerPort per pod No two containers in the same pod can use the same containerPort. Remove duplicates. containerPort is informational but duplicates cause issues.
2. Add Redis readiness check in Django Django should retry the Redis connection with a timeout: retry for 10 seconds before giving up. Use django-redis retry settings.
3. Use init container to verify sidecar initContainers: [{command: ["sh", "-c", "until nc -z localhost 6379; do sleep 1; done"]}] Wait for Redis to be available before starting Django. Runs once before main containers.
4. Consider separate pod for Redis Sidecar pattern is for tightly coupled helpers (log shippers, proxies). A cache like Redis is often better as an independent Service.
5. Bind Redis to 0.0.0.0 in sidecar redis-server --bind 0.0.0.0 Inside a pod, binding to 0.0.0.0 is fine — only containers in the same pod can reach it (shared network namespace).
💡 Personal Advice:
Containers in a pod share localhost. This is the most powerful feature of pods. nginx → Django, Django → Redis, all on localhost. But it also means ports CANNOT overlap.
Sidecar = tightly coupled helper. If the helper container can run independently (like a Redis cache), it's probably NOT a good sidecar. Use a separate pod + Service.
Test multi-container pods locally with docker-compose. docker-compose with network_mode: "service:main" simulates pod networking. Test your multi-container setup before deploying to K8s.
Use kubectl exec to troubleshoot shared network. kubectl exec into any container in the pod and run netstat/ss. Since they share the network namespace, you'll see all ports from all containers.
AB18
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB18
StatefulSet Pods Out of Order — Pod Management Policy Conflict

🔍 Symptom: StatefulSet for easypj-db has 3 replicas, but pod-2 started before pod-1, and pod-1 is stuck in Pending. The StatefulSet is supposed to start pods in order (0→1→2) but they're starting randomly, causing data inconsistency and cluster formation issues for PostgreSQL.

  kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-db
  NAME           READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
  easypj-db-0    1/1     Running   0          10m  ← Started first (expected)
  easypj-db-2    1/1     Running   0          8m   ← Started BEFORE db-1! (unexpected)
  easypj-db-1    0/1     Pending   0          0s   ← Stuck because PVC not ready?

  kubectl get sts easypj-db -o yaml | grep podManagementPolicy
  podManagementPolicy: Parallel    ← Set to Parallel, not OrderedReady!

  kubectl describe pod easypj-db-1 | grep -A5 Events
  Events:
    Warning  FailedScheduling  2m  pod has unbound PVC: data-easypj-db-1
  # PVC for db-1 can't bind — but db-2 already started!
  # With OrderedReady, db-2 would have waited for db-1.
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. podManagementPolicy: Parallel set instead of OrderedReady: Parallel starts all pods simultaneously — no ordering guarantees. Use OrderedReady for databases so pods start 0→1→2.
  2. PVC not pre-provisioned for sequential pods: With volumeClaimTemplates, PVCs are created per pod. If PVC for pod-1 can't bind (storage class issue, quota), pod-1 stays Pending while pod-2 starts.
  3. Node anti-affinity not configured: Without anti-affinity, StatefulSet pods might schedule on a node that doesn't have enough storage or resources.
  4. RollingUpdate partition set wrong: spec.updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.partition: 1 blocks updates to pod-0 only — can cause ordering confusion.
  5. StatefulSet controller confusion after force delete: Pod was force-deleted (--force --grace-period=0) — controller loses track of pod order.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. StorageClass with volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer: PVC is created but not bound until pod schedules. Pod can't schedule because PVC isn't bound — deadlock solved by WaitForFirstConsumer.
  2. Node failure during ordered startup: pod-0 runs on node-1, node-1 fails, pod-0 reschedules — pod-1 and pod-2 startup delayed.
  3. Topology spread constraints conflict: maxSkew: 1 across zones but only 2 zones for 3 pods — pod-3 can't schedule at all.
  4. Revision history limit causing controller confusion: Too many revisions — controller slows down, ordering becomes inconsistent.
  5. ServiceName not set on StatefulSet: Without serviceName, StatefulSet doesn't create DNS entries — pods can't find each other by ordinal.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default StorageClass not set: StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates can't create PVCs because no default StorageClass exists — all pods stuck.
  2. CSINode driver not registered: CSI driver not installed on node — PVC provisioner can't create volumes.
  3. ResourceQuota limiting PVC count: Namespace has a ResourceQuota that limits PVCs to 2 — pod-2's PVC creation fails.
  4. Topology-aware scheduling: volume topology constraints prevent scheduling in certain zones — some pods can't place.
  5. kube-controller-manager StatefulSet controller not running: StatefulSet controller is one of many controllers — if disabled, StatefulSet doesn't manage pods at all.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get sts <name> -o yaml | grep -E "podManagementPolicy|serviceName|replicas|partition" podManagementPolicy should be OrderedReady for databases. Check if serviceName is set (required for StatefulSet).
kubectl get pvc -l app=easypj-db and kubectl get pv Check that PVCs are bound in order. If data-easypj-db-1 is Pending, check StorageClass and provisioner logs.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: podManagementPolicy is set to Parallel. With Parallel, all pods start simultaneously with no ordering guarantees. For database clusters (PostgreSQL, MySQL), use OrderedReady so pods start 0→1→2, and each pod is Ready before the next starts.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Change podManagementPolicy to OrderedReady kubectl patch sts easypj-db -p '{"spec":{"podManagementPolicy":"OrderedReady"}}' OrderedReady ensures pod-0 starts and becomes Ready before pod-1 starts, and pod-1 before pod-2.
2. Check PVC binding kubectl get pvc -l app=easypj-db Ensure all PVCs are Bound. If PVC for pod-1 is Pending, investigate the StorageClass and provisioner.
3. Add podAntiAffinity for StatefulSet podAntiAffinity: {requiredDuringScheduling: [{labelSelector: {...}, topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname}]} Ensure each StatefulSet pod runs on a different node — prevents single node failure from taking down the whole cluster.
4. Set serviceName (required for StatefulSet) spec.serviceName: easypj-db-headless StatefulSet requires a headless Service for stable network identity. Without it, DNS entries don't work.
5. Delete stuck pods to trigger ordered restart kubectl delete pod easypj-db-1 easypj-db-2 After fixing podManagementPolicy, delete pods to force the controller to recreate them in order.
💡 Personal Advice:
OrderedReady is the default — don't change it without a good reason. Parallel is for stateless, distributed systems like Cassandra where any pod can start anytime. For PostgreSQL, MySQL, etcd — OrderedReady only.
StatefulSet = OrderedReady + stable identities + persistent storage. If you don't need all three, you probably don't need a StatefulSet. Deployment might be simpler.
Test PVC provisioning BEFORE deploying StatefulSet. Create a test PVC with the same StorageClass first. If it binds, your StatefulSet will work. If not, fix storage first.
Headless Service is mandatory for StatefulSet. Without serviceName pointing to a headless Service (clusterIP: None), pods get no DNS names and inter-pod discovery fails.
AB19
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB19
DaemonSet Not Scheduling on New Node — NodeSelector/Taints Mismatch

🔍 Symptom: A new worker node joined the cluster but the log-collector DaemonSet pod is not scheduled on it. The node has a taint node-role.kubernetes.io/worker:NoSchedule but the DaemonSet doesn't have the corresponding toleration, or the node's label doesn't match the DaemonSet's nodeSelector.

  kubectl get nodes
  NAME        STATUS   ROLES           AGE
  easy        Ready    control-plane   90d
  worker-1    Ready    worker          30d
  worker-2    Ready    worker          5m    ← New node!

  kubectl get ds -n kube-system log-collector -o yaml | grep -A5 nodeSelector
  nodeSelector:
    node-role.kubernetes.io/worker: ""   ← Missing on worker-2?

  kubectl describe node worker-2 | grep -E "Labels|Taints"
  Labels:  kubernetes.io/hostname=worker-2
  Taints:  node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=true:NoSchedule  ← Has taint, missing label!
  # worker-2 has TAINT but no LABEL — DaemonSet requires the label!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. NodeSelector label missing on new node: The DaemonSet requires node-role.kubernetes.io/worker: "" but worker-2 was joined without this label. Add it: kubectl label node worker-2 node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=.
  2. Taint without matching toleration: worker-2 has a taint that the DaemonSet doesn't tolerate. Add the toleration to the DaemonSet or remove the taint from the node.
  3. Node affinity not matching: DaemonSet uses nodeAffinity for a specific zone/region that worker-2 is not part of.
  4. Node resources exhausted: DaemonSet pod has resource requests that worker-2 can't satisfy — node is "full" even though it's new.
  5. DaemonSet updateStrategy: OnDelete: If OnDelete is set, existing nodes get updates only when pods are manually deleted — but new nodes should still get pods.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CNI not ready on new node: Node joined but CNI pod (Calico/Flannel) not running yet — DaemonSet pod can't start without networking.
  2. Node NotReady: New node shows NotReady — DaemonSet controller won't schedule on unhealthy nodes.
  3. Pod Security admission blocking: New node enforces Restricted PSS — DaemonSet pod runs as root, rejected by admission.
  4. DaemonSet controller not running: kube-controller-manager DaemonSet controller disabled or crashed.
  5. NetworkPolicy blocking DaemonSet pod: Global NetworkPolicy blocks DaemonSet pod traffic — pod starts but is immediately terminated.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. kubeadm join without --node-labels: Node joined with kubeadm but no labels set — missing the labels DaemonSet requires.
  2. Node not part of cluster DNS: CoreDNS not deployed on new node yet — DaemonSet pod requires DNS.
  3. Different architecture (arm64 vs amd64): New node is ARM64 but DaemonSet image is amd64 only — scheduling fails silently.
  4. CRI runtime mismatch: New node uses containerd but DaemonSet mounts Docker socket — fails on node without Docker.
  5. Cloud provider taint: Cloud controller adds taints like node.cloudprovider.kubernetes.io/uninitialized — cleared only after cloud-init completes.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe node <new-node> | grep -E "Labels:|Taints:" Compare labels and taints on the new node with existing nodes where DaemonSet is running.
kubectl get ds <name> -o yaml | grep -A20 "nodeSelector\|tolerations\|affinity" Review all scheduling constraints. Does the new node satisfy ALL of them?
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The new node is missing the label used by the DaemonSet's nodeSelector. The node was joined without the required node-role.kubernetes.io/worker label. DaemonSet uses nodeSelector to constrain which nodes get pods — if the label isn't there, pods won't schedule.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add missing label to the node kubectl label node worker-2 node-role.kubernetes.io/worker= The empty value (just the key) matches the nodeSelector node-role.kubernetes.io/worker: "". Pod schedules immediately.
2. Add missing toleration to DaemonSet kubectl patch ds log-collector -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"tolerations":[{"key":"node-role.kubernetes.io/worker","operator":"Exists","effect":"NoSchedule"}]}}}}' If the taint is intentional, add the corresponding toleration to the DaemonSet.
3. Remove the taint from the node kubectl taint node worker-2 node-role.kubernetes.io/worker:NoSchedule- If the taint was added accidentally or is no longer needed, remove it. The - at the end removes the taint.
4. Standardize node join process Use kubeadm join --node-labels or a post-join script that applies required labels. Document node requirements.
5. Verify with kubectl get ds kubectl get ds log-collector DESIRED should match CURRENT and READY for all nodes. If counts match the number of nodes, scheduling is working.
💡 Personal Advice:
DaemonSet scheduling is ALL about labels and taints. New node doesn't have DaemonSet pod? Check: 1) Labels match nodeSelector, 2) Tolerations cover taints, 3) Node is Ready.
Document node requirements in your runbook. "New worker nodes must have label X and taint Y." Without documentation, every new node is a troubleshooting mystery.
Use tolerations for ALL common taints. A good DaemonSet tolerates: node-role.kubernetes.io/master, node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane, and any custom taints.
DaemonSet should run on ALL nodes by default. Unless you have a specific reason to exclude nodes (GPUs, special hardware), don't use nodeSelector on DaemonSets.
AB20
🏗️ CATEGORY 1: APP DESIGN & BUILD — Issue AB20
Can't Debug Container — Distroless Image Missing Tools

🔍 Symptom: Django app is failing in production but the container runs a distroless image with no shell, no debugging tools. kubectl exec fails: "unable to upgrade connection: container has no shell." Need to inspect files, check network connectivity, and view environment but can't get into the container.

  kubectl exec -it easypj-web-9x7k2 -- /bin/sh
  error: Internal error occurred: error executing command in container:
  failed to exec in container: container has no shell: unknown

  kubectl exec -it easypj-web-9x7k2 -- /bin/bash
  error: Internal error occurred: error executing command in container:
  failed to exec in container: container has no shell: unknown

  kubectl exec -it easypj-web-9x7k2 -- ls /app/
  error: ... container has no shell
  # Distroless image — no shell, no tools, NO WAY IN!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Distroless image has no shell: Google's distroless images contain ONLY the application and its runtime dependencies. No bash, sh, ls, curl, or any debugging tools.
  2. Image stripped for security/minimalism: The Dockerfile uses a minimal base (scratch, distroless, alpine-slim) intentionally — no debugging tools by design.
  3. No debug sidecar defined: The application was deployed without considering debugging needs. No ephemeral container or debug sidecar configured.
  4. Restricted security context: readOnlyRootFilesystem, no_new_privs, and runAsNonRoot prevent installing tools or running with privileges.
  5. Ephemeral containers feature not known: Team doesn't know about kubectl debug with ephemeral containers — trying to exec into a distroless image instead.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Container restarting too fast: CrashLoopBackOff — container exits before kubectl exec can attach.
  2. NetworkPolicy blocking kubectl exec: Very rare — but WebSocket connection to kubelet could be blocked.
  3. kubelet not responding: Node is NotReady or kubelet is overloaded — exec times out.
  4. RBAC not allowing exec: User doesn't have create permission on pods/exec subresource.
  5. Container runtime exec timeout: CRI runtime has a short exec timeout — connection drops before shell starts.
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Ephemeral containers feature gate disabled: EphemeralContainers feature gate not enabled on older clusters. K8s 1.25+ enables it by default.
  2. No debug tools image available: Cluster can't pull busybox or alpine for ephemeral container — air-gapped environment.
  3. PodSecurityPolicy/PSS blocking ephemeral containers: Admission controller rejects ephemeral containers that don't meet security standards.
  4. kubectl version too old: kubectl older than 1.18 doesn't support kubectl debug. Update kubectl.
  5. CNI not supporting ephemeral container networking: Certain CNI plugins have issues with ephemeral container network setup.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> Use kubectl debug with --target to create an ephemeral container that shares the target container's process namespace.
kubectl version --short and kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml | grep ephemeralContainers Check kubectl version supports kubectl debug (1.18+) and if ephemeral containers are already attached.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The container uses a distroless image which intentionally has no shell or debugging tools. kubectl exec requires a shell in the container (either sh or bash). The correct approach is to use kubectl debug with an ephemeral container that shares the target container's namespaces.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Use kubectl debug for distroless containers kubectl debug -it easypj-web-9x7k2 --image=busybox --target=django Creates an ephemeral container with busybox (has shell/tools) that shares the target container's process namespace.
2. Copy target container's filesystem kubectl debug easypj-web-9x7k2 --image=busybox --target=django --copy-to=debug-web -- sh --copy-to creates a copy of the pod with a debug container. You can explore all files, processes, and network.
3. Share process namespace for process inspection kubectl debug -it easypj-web-9x7k2 --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=django --share-processes Share the target container's process namespace. Use tools like strace, tcpdump, and netstat inside the ephemeral container.
4. Add debug tools to image for future builds Create a separate debug image tag: easypj/jobpost:v2.1-debug that includes busybox tools. Switch to this image for debugging.
5. Check logs and events without exec kubectl logs easypj-web-9x7k2 --previous && kubectl describe pod easypj-web-9x7k2 Even without exec, logs, events, and describe provide valuable debugging information.
💡 Personal Advice:
Distroless images are great for security, terrible for debugging. Always have a debug strategy BEFORE you need it. Know kubectl debug. Know your debug image. Practice once on a test pod.
kubectl debug is the most underrated K8s command. It creates ephemeral containers that share namespaces with your target container. --target and --share-processes are game-changers.
Build a parallel debug image tag. easypj/jobpost:v2.1 (distroless) and easypj/jobpost:v2.1-debug (alpine with tools). Same app, different base, ready for emergencies.
netshoot is the ultimate debug image. nicolaka/netshoot contains: curl, dig, nmap, tcpdump, strace, iperf, and more. Keep it in your cluster. docker pull nicolaka/netshoot.

🚀 Category 2: App Deployment (20 Issues)AD1-AD20

🟡→🔴 Deployment Issues — Deployments, Rollouts, Helm, Kustomize, Strategies

Issues from Deployment rollouts, canary/blue-green strategies, Helm chart failures, Kustomize overlay misconfigurations, and scaling problems.

📌 AD1–AD5: Deployment & Rolling Update Failures

AD1
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD1
Deployment Stuck in Progressing — Wrong Image Tag

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get deploy shows READY: 0/3 and AVAILABLE: 0. The Deployment is stuck in a Progressing state. kubectl describe deploy shows "ReplicaSet has timed out progressing." New pods are CrashLoopBackOff because the image tag easypj/jobpost:v3.0 doesn't exist.

  kubectl get deploy easypj-web
  NAME          READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
  easypj-web    0/3     3            0           15m

  kubectl describe deploy easypj-web | grep -A5 Conditions
  Conditions:
    Available      False    MinimumReplicasUnavailable
    Progressing    False    ReplicaSet "easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e" has timed out progressing

  kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-web
  NAME                            READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
  easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde    0/1     ImagePullBackOff   0       5m
  easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e-fghij    0/1     ImagePullBackOff   0       5m
  easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e-klmno    0/1     ErrImagePull       0       5m

  kubectl describe pod easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde | grep -i image
  Image:       easypj/jobpost:v3.0     ← This tag doesn't exist!
  Error:       ErrImagePull
  Message:     failed to pull and unpack image "docker.io/easypj/jobpost:v3.0":
               not found
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Image tag doesn't exist in registry: The Deployment references easypj/jobpost:v3.0 but the tag was never pushed. docker pull easypj/jobpost:v3.0 locally to verify the tag exists before deploying.
  2. Typo in image tag: kubectl set image used v3.0 instead of v2.3.0. Always copy-paste image tags, never type them manually.
  3. Wrong registry referenced: Image exists at ghcr.io/easypj/jobpost:v3.0 but Deployment references docker.io/easypj/jobpost:v3.0. Check the full registry path.
  4. imagePullPolicy: Always combined with missing tag: Pod can't fall back to a cached version because Always forces a pull attempt.
  5. Image built but not pushed before deploy: docker build -t easypj/jobpost:v3.0 . succeeded locally but docker push was forgotten. The image exists on the dev machine, not in registry.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Registry authentication expired — imagePullSecrets token has expired and can't pull private images
  2. Network proxy blocking registry access — HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY not configured for container runtime
  3. Docker rate limit hit on Docker Hub — anonymous pulls exhausted, need authenticated pull
  4. Image manifest list architecture mismatch — deploying amd64 image to arm64 node (or vice versa)
  5. Registry down or unreachable from cluster nodes — nodes can't reach the registry due to network policy or firewall
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No imagePullSecrets configured: Private registry requires imagePullSecrets in Pod spec or ServiceAccount. New cluster has no registry credentials.
  2. Container runtime not configured for registry mirrors: containerd/config.toml doesn't have mirror endpoint — pulls go directly to internet.
  3. Air-gapped cluster has no local registry: Offline environment — images must be pre-loaded with kind load docker-image or ctr image import.
  4. DNS resolution for registry failing: CoreDNS not resolving registry hostname — nodes can't reach the registry.
  5. kind/minikube image cache not populated: kind load docker-image or minikube image load not run after build — image exists locally but not in cluster.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 "Events:" The Events section shows exactly why the image can't be pulled — "not found", "unauthorized", "connection refused".
docker pull <image> locally and kubectl get deploy -o yaml | grep image: Can you pull the image from your local machine? Does the tag in the Deployment match exactly?
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The image tag v3.0 doesn't exist in the registry. The Deployment was updated with kubectl set image to a tag that was never pushed. Always verify docker pull <image> succeeds before updating any Deployment.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Verify the image exists docker pull easypj/jobpost:v3.0 If this fails locally, it will fail in Kubernetes. Push the image first: docker push easypj/jobpost:v3.0.
2. Rollback to the previous working version kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-web Immediately rollback to the last known good revision while you fix the image issue.
3. Fix the image and do a new rollout kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web easypj-web=easypj/jobpost:v2.1 Point to a verified-good image. Monitor with kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web.
4. Add imagePullSecrets for private registries kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=<user> --docker-password=<token> Reference in Deployment: spec.template.spec.imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}].
5. Check rollout history and verify kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-web && kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web Verify the Deployment recovered and all pods are READY.
💡 Personal Advice:
