Always docker pull before kubectl apply. If you can't pull the image, Kubernetes can't either. A 2-second verification saves 15 minutes of debugging a stuck Deployment.
Use kubectl rollout undo as your emergency brake. Don't debug a broken image in production. Rollback first, then investigate. kubectl rollout undo is the fastest recovery.
Pin images to digest for guaranteed immutability. image: easypj/jobpost@sha256:abc123... Tags are pointers. Digests are cryptographic hashes. If you deploy by digest, the image ALWAYS exists.
On kind, use kind load docker-image. Instead of pushing to a registry, kind load docker-image easypj/jobpost:v3.0 --name kind-cka-lab loads directly into the cluster.
AD2
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD2
Rolling Update Stalled — maxSurge Zero Blocks Progress

🔍 Symptom: A rolling update starts but stalls after replacing only 1 pod. The Deployment shows 2/3 READY for 10+ minutes. kubectl describe deploy reveals maxSurge: 0 and maxUnavailable: 1, but the node has no capacity for the new pod — the old pod can't be removed until the new one is running, and the new one can't be created.

  kubectl get deploy easypj-api
  NAME          READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
  easypj-api    2/3     1            2           10m     ← Stuck for 10 minutes!

  kubectl describe deploy easypj-api | grep -A5 Strategy
  RollingUpdateStrategy:  1 max unavailable, 0 max surge
  # OLD pod can go down (maxUnavailable=1) but NO new pod can start (maxSurge=0)!

  kubectl describe rs easypj-api-9f8e7d6c5b | grep -A5 Conditions
  Conditions:
    ReplicaFailure  True  Deployment does not have minimum availability
  # New ReplicaSet can't create its pod → stall!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Node has insufficient CPU/memory for new pod: maxSurge=0 means no extra capacity is created. If the node is full, the new pod can't schedule — deadlock. Increase maxSurge or free node resources.
  2. maxSurge: 0 combined with maxUnavailable: 0: This configuration makes rolling updates IMPOSSIBLE. No new pods can be created AND no old pods can be removed. The deployment is frozen.
  3. PodDisruptionBudget blocking eviction: PDB requires minAvailable: 3 but maxUnavailable=1 — removing 1 pod would violate the PDB. Increase maxUnavailable or adjust PDB.
  4. NodeSelector/Affinity changed in new revision: New pod spec has a nodeSelector that no node matches, but old pods are on nodes that don't match either. New pods can't schedule anywhere.
  5. PVC with ReadWriteOnce blocking pod reschedule: Old pod uses an RWO PVC on node-A. New pod can only be scheduled on node-A (PVC affinity), but node-A is full.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Anti-affinity rules blocking co-location — new pod and old pod can't run on the same node
  2. Taints added to nodes after initial deployment — new pods can't tolerate taints that old pods inherited
  3. ResourceQuota reached in namespace — Deployment can't scale up beyond quota limits for the rollout
  4. Readiness gate blocking new pods — custom readiness condition never becomes True, stalls rollout
  5. Admission webhook rejecting new pods — mutating/validating webhook blocks pod creation for the new ReplicaSet
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. All nodes cordoned/unschedulable: Cluster maintenance — all worker nodes are cordoned. No pods can be scheduled until nodes are uncordoned.
  2. Cluster Autoscaler not adding nodes fast enough: Pending pods trigger scale-up but new nodes take 3-5 minutes to join — rollout stalls during this window.
  3. Topology spread constraints too restrictive: maxSkew=1 across 3 zones with 3 replicas — can't place the new pod without violating skew.
  4. Default StorageClass not set for new PVC: New pod template references a PVC that can't bind — pod stays Pending forever.
  5. kube-scheduler not running: Scheduler pod is down — no pods can be scheduled, rollout stalls indefinitely.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe deploy <name> | grep -E "Strategy|Conditions|Replicas" Check maxSurge, maxUnavailable, and the deployment conditions. Progressing: False with a reason tells you why.
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | grep <deployment> | tail -10 Events reveal scheduling failures, quota exceeded, or PDB violations blocking the rollout.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: maxSurge: 0 combined with insufficient node capacity. With no surge allowed, the new pod must fit into existing capacity. If nodes are full, the rollout deadlocks. The fix: increase maxSurge to at least 1, or scale down before updating.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Increase maxSurge to at least 1 kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"maxSurge":1}}}}' Allow one extra pod to be created during the rollout. This requires cluster capacity for N+1 pods temporarily.
2. Scale down before upgrading if capacity is tight kubectl scale deploy easypj-api --replicas=2 && kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api *=easypj/jobpost:v2.1 Reduce replicas temporarily, upgrade, then scale back up. Simpler than fighting capacity.
3. Use Recreate strategy for capacity-constrained clusters spec.strategy.type: Recreate Kills all old pods first, then creates new ones. Downtime but guaranteed to work when capacity is tight.
4. Check and fix scheduling constraints kubectl describe rs <new-rs> | grep -A10 "Events:" If pods can't schedule, the ReplicaSet events tell you why — node affinity, taints, resources.
5. Rollback if stuck too long kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api If the rollout is fundamentally broken, rollback to the previous version while you fix the issue.
💡 Personal Advice:
Always set maxSurge >= 1 for production Deployments. The default (25% rounded up) is usually fine. Setting it to 0 only makes sense when you have NO extra capacity — and that's a capacity problem, not a deployment strategy.
PDB + RollingUpdate = potential stall. A PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable: 3 AND maxUnavailable: 1 creates a conflict. Always ensure maxUnavailable is high enough to satisfy the PDB.
Monitor rollout with kubectl rollout status. kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api --timeout=300s Use in CI/CD pipelines. If the rollout doesn't complete in 5 minutes, fail the pipeline and alert.
maxSurge=0 + maxUnavailable=0 = impossible rollout. This combination mathematically prevents any rolling update. Kubernetes won't warn you — it'll just silently stall forever.
AD3
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD3
Orphaned ReplicaSet — Deployment Selector Changed

🔍 Symptom: After editing a Deployment's labels, kubectl shows TWO ReplicaSets managing different sets of pods. The old ReplicaSet wasn't scaled down, and the new one creates additional pods. Now 6 pods are running instead of 3 — both old and new versions serving traffic simultaneously.

  kubectl get deploy,rs,pods -l app=easypj-web
  NAME                          READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
  deployment.apps/easypj-web    6/3     3            6        ← 6/3 READY!

  NAME                                     DESIRED   CURRENT   READY
  replicaset.apps/easypj-web-5g4h3j2k1l    3         3         3    ← OLD RS (v2.0)
  replicaset.apps/easypj-web-9f8e7d6c5b    3         3         3    ← NEW RS (v2.1)

  NAME                                  READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
  pod/easypj-web-5g4h3j2k1l-abcde      1/1     Running   0        ← OLD pod (v2.0)
  pod/easypj-web-9f8e7d6c5b-fghij      1/1     Running   0        ← NEW pod (v2.1)
  # Both old AND new pods are running — 6 pods total instead of 3!

  kubectl describe deploy easypj-web | grep -A10 "Pod Template"
  Labels:  app=easypj-web-v2    ← Changed from "app=easypj-web"!
  # Old RS has selector app=easypj-web — doesn't match new labels!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Deployment selector or template labels changed: kubectl edit deploy modified the matchLabels selector or pod template labels. The old ReplicaSet's selector no longer matches the new labels — Deployment loses track of the old RS.
  2. kubectl apply with incorrect YAML: A manually edited YAML changed the selector fields. Deployment selector is IMMUTABLE after creation — the API should reject this, but template labels can change.
  3. Deployment templates diverged across revisions: Different revisions have different label selectors — rollout history shows incompatible revisions.
  4. Labels patched directly on pods: Someone ran kubectl label pod on individual pods, breaking the match between pods and their ReplicaSet.
  5. Service selector changed to match new labels only: The Service was updated to match only v2 labels while v1 pods still run — traffic goes only to v2, but v1 pods consume resources.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Multiple Deployments with overlapping selectors — two Deployments fighting over the same pods
  2. kubectl replace instead of apply — replace with wrong YAML creates a new ReplicaSet without cleaning up old ones
  3. ReplicaSet manually created with matching labels — someone created an RS outside the Deployment controller
  4. Deployment revision history limit hides the mismatch — old RS was kept but revision was pruned
  5. Helm upgrade with changed selector — Helm templates changed selectors between releases without cleanup
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. ArgoCD auto-sync causing label drift: GitOps tool syncs a Deployment with changed labels — auto-creates new RS without pruning old one.
  2. Git branch merge conflict in Deployment YAML: Two branches changed labels differently — merged YAML has conflicting selectors.
  3. CI/CD pipeline deploying to wrong namespace: Staging Deployment with staging labels deployed to production namespace — mismatched.
  4. Mutating webhook adding labels inconsistently: Admission webhook adds different labels to pods vs ReplicaSet — selector mismatch.
  5. Kustomize overlay with different commonLabels: Base and overlay have different commonLabels — selectors don't align.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get rs -l app=easypj-web --show-labels Check how many ReplicaSets exist and whether their selectors differ. More than 1 active RS = likely selector mismatch.
kubectl get deploy easypj-web -o yaml | grep -A5 "selector:" Verify the selector matches the pod template labels. They should be identical.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Deployment's pod template labels were changed, creating a new ReplicaSet with a different selector. The old ReplicaSet is now orphaned — the Deployment controller no longer manages it, so old pods keep running independently. The fix: scale down old RS manually, then align labels.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Identify and scale down the orphaned ReplicaSet kubectl scale rs easypj-web-5g4h3j2k1l --replicas=0 Manually scale down the old ReplicaSet to 0. The Deployment won't do this since it lost track of it.
2. Delete the orphaned ReplicaSet kubectl delete rs easypj-web-5g4h3j2k1l Once scaled to 0, delete the orphaned ReplicaSet entirely to clean up.
3. Never change Deployment selectors after creation Deployment selector is effectively immutable. If you need different labels, create a NEW Deployment and migrate traffic.
4. Use kubectl rollout undo if caught early kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-web --to-revision=1 If you just made the change, rollback to the previous revision before old pods multiply.
5. Align Service selectors with Deployment labels kubectl get svc easypj-web -o yaml | grep selector Ensure the Service selector matches the CURRENT pod labels so traffic routes correctly.
💡 Personal Advice:
Deployment selectors are effectively immutable. You CAN change pod template labels, but you SHOULDN'T. If you need new labels, create a new Deployment and migrate with a Service switch.
Always check kubectl get rs after editing a Deployment. If you see more ReplicaSets than expected (especially with non-zero replicas), something went wrong. Investigate immediately.
Orphaned ReplicaSets waste resources silently. They don't show up in typical kubectl get pods (if labels differ). Use kubectl get rs -A periodically to find zombie ReplicaSets.
Use revisionHistoryLimit to control RS count. spec.revisionHistoryLimit: 3 Keeps only the last 3 ReplicaSets. Prevents RS clutter but doesn't help with selector-mismatched orphans.
AD4
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD4
Rollback Fails — Revision History Pruned

🔍 Symptom: kubectl rollout undo fails with "no rollout history found" or rolls back to the WRONG revision. The Deployment has revisionHistoryLimit: 1 and the only saved revision is the broken one. The known-good revision was pruned — rolling back now rolls back to nothing or a different broken version.

  kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-web
  REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
  5         kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web *=easypj/jobpost:v3.0
  # Only ONE revision exists! revisionHistoryLimit is 1!

  kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-web --to-revision=4
  error: unable to find revision 4 for Deployment easypj-web

  kubectl get deploy easypj-web -o yaml | grep revisionHistoryLimit
  revisionHistoryLimit: 1     ← Only keeps the LATEST revision!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. revisionHistoryLimit set too low: revisionHistoryLimit: 1 keeps ONLY the current revision. Previous revisions are deleted — rollback is impossible. Default is 10, which is usually adequate.
  2. Multiple deployments since the known-good revision: Even with limit=10, if you've done 15 deployments, revision 1 is pruned. The oldest revisions are removed first.
  3. Deployment was deleted and recreated: kubectl delete deploy followed by kubectl create deploy resets revision history to 1. Rollback target is gone.
  4. --to-revision references a non-existent revision: The revision number you specified never existed or was already pruned. Use kubectl rollout history to see available revisions.
  5. CHANGE-CAUSE annotations missing: Without kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation, you can't identify which revision was good — rolling back is a blind guess.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. ReplicaSet for target revision was manually deleted — the RS that holds the old pod spec is gone
  2. Deployment paused during rollout — history shows paused state, not completed revisions
  3. Rollout undo without --to-revision — rolls back to the previous revision, which may also be broken
  4. Image tag overwritten — the tag you want to roll back to was overwritten in the registry (e.g., :latest)
  5. Helm release rollback instead of kubectl — Helm manages revision history differently, kubectl history may be empty
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. ArgoCD/Flux sync pruning history: GitOps tools auto-sync and may prune old ReplicaSets aggressively — revision history lost.
  2. Cluster backup doesn't include Deployment history: etcd backup restores current state only — old ReplicaSets are not restored, revision history lost.
  3. Namespace-wide resource cleanup: Cluster admin ran cleanup script that deleted "old" ReplicaSets across all namespaces.
  4. Admission webhook rejecting ReplicaSets: Webhook rejects ReplicaSet creation — history can't be saved, new revisions fail silently.
  5. Deployment controller crashed during rollout: Controller-manager crash corrupted revision tracking — history inconsistent.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl rollout history deploy/<name> Shows all available revisions. If the target revision isn't listed, it's been pruned. Increase revisionHistoryLimit for the future.
kubectl get rs -l app=<label> --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp Check which ReplicaSets still exist. Each revision corresponds to an RS — if the RS is gone, rollback to that revision is impossible.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: revisionHistoryLimit is set to 1, keeping only the current Revision. All previous revisions and their ReplicaSets were pruned. The fix: increase revisionHistoryLimit to at least 5, redeploy the known-good image with a new revision, and always annotate with CHANGE-CAUSE.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Increase revisionHistoryLimit immediately kubectl patch deploy easypj-web -p '{"spec":{"revisionHistoryLimit":10}}' Set to at least 5-10 to keep a meaningful history. Future rollbacks will have targets.
2. Redeploy the known-good image as a NEW revision kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web easypj-web=easypj/jobpost:v2.1 --record Since the old revision is gone, create a new revision pointing to the known-good image. Use --record to annotate.
3. Annotate every rollout with CHANGE-CAUSE kubectl annotate deploy/easypj-web kubernetes.io/change-cause="Rollback to v2.1 — fixed DB timeout" Without annotations, kubectl rollout history shows <none> — you can't identify which revision is good.
4. Keep a separate audit log of deployments Git commits, CI/CD logs, or external tools (ArgoCD history) provide fallback when K8s revision history is pruned.
5. Set default revisionHistoryLimit in CI/CD templates Ensure all Deployment YAMLs generated by CI/CD have revisionHistoryLimit >= 10. Never use 1 or 2.
💡 Personal Advice:
Never set revisionHistoryLimit below 5. ReplicaSets are lightweight (they don't consume CPU/memory, just etcd storage). The default of 10 is good. Setting it to 1 or 2 is premature optimization that WILL bite you.
Always use --record or annotate with CHANGE-CAUSE. Without it, kubectl rollout history shows <none>. You'll waste precious minutes guessing which revision is which during an incident.
Revision history is your safety net. Don't delete it. Each old ReplicaSet is a snapshot of a working (or broken) configuration. They cost almost nothing and are invaluable during debugging.
Git is your ultimate revision history. If K8s history is pruned, git log --oneline deploy/easypj-web.yaml tells you every change ever made. Use Git as your source of truth.
AD5
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD5
Deployment Scaled to Zero — HPA with Zero MinReplicas

🔍 Symptom: The easypj-api Deployment was scaled to 0 replicas unexpectedly. kubectl get hpa shows minReplicas: 0, and the HPA scaled down to 0 when traffic dropped to zero overnight. Morning traffic can't reach the API because there are no pods to receive it.

  kubectl get deploy easypj-api
  NAME          READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
  easypj-api    0/0     0            0           12h     ← Scaled to ZERO!

  kubectl get hpa easypj-api-hpa -o yaml | grep -A5 spec
  spec:
    minReplicas: 0          ← ZERO minimum!
    maxReplicas: 10
    metrics:
    - resource: {name: cpu, target: {averageUtilization: 70, type: Utilization}}
  # Overnight CPU dropped → HPA scaled to 0!

  kubectl describe hpa easypj-api-hpa | grep -A5 "Conditions:"
  Conditions:
    AbleToScale   True    SucceededRescale
    ScalingActive False   FailedGetResourceMetric: the HPA was unable to compute the replica count
    ScalingLimited False  desired within acceptable range
  # No metrics → scaled to minReplicas = 0!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. minReplicas set to 0 in HPA: The HPA was configured with minReplicas: 0. When metrics are unavailable or traffic is zero, HPA scales to the minimum — which is 0 pods. Set minReplicas to at least 1.
  2. HPA competing with manual scaling: Someone ran kubectl scale deploy easypj-api --replicas=0 and the HPA didn't override it because 0 is within the HPA's range.
  3. Metrics server not returning data: If the metrics server is down, HPA can't compute desired replicas. It may scale to minReplicas as a safety measure.
  4. ResourceQuota preventing scale-up: Namespace CPU quota is exhausted. HPA tries to scale up but can't create pods — appears to stay at 0.
  5. HPA targeting wrong resource: HPA is configured to scale on a metric that never has data (e.g., custom metric not implemented). Falls back to minReplicas.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Multiple HPAs targeting the same Deployment — conflicting scale decisions, one set to 0 min
  2. HPA status shows AbleToScale: False — HPA can't communicate with the scale subresource
  3. Stabilization window too short — HPA scaled down too quickly during a brief traffic dip
  4. External metrics adapter not running — custom metrics unavailable, HPA defaults to min
  5. Cluster autoscaler removed nodes that had the pods — pods lost, HPA not yet triggered to recreate
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Metrics server not deployed: New cluster has no metrics-server — HPA can't get CPU/memory metrics. Stays at minReplicas or fails.
  2. RBAC for HPA not configured: HPA's ServiceAccount doesn't have permission to read metrics or update scale subresource.
  3. HPA API version mismatch: Using autoscaling/v1 (CPU only) when you need autoscaling/v2 (custom metrics) — missing metric causes fallback to min.
  4. Cold start on new cluster — no historical metrics: HPA needs at least 1-2 data points before making scaling decisions. New cluster = no data = stays at min.
  5. Prometheus adapter not installed: HPA configured for custom Prometheus metrics but prometheus-adapter not deployed — metrics permanently unavailable.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get hpa <name> -o yaml | grep -E "minReplicas|currentReplicas|desiredReplicas" Check if minReplicas is 0, if current replicas match desired, and if desired is 0.
kubectl top pods -l app=<label> and kubectl describe hpa <name> Check if metrics are available. If kubectl top works but HPA shows unknown metrics, the HPA configuration is wrong.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: HPA minReplicas is set to 0. When metrics are unavailable or traffic drops to zero, HPA scales the Deployment to the configured minimum — which is 0. Always set minReplicas to at least 1 for any workload that must be always available.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Immediately scale back to minimum kubectl scale deploy easypj-api --replicas=3 Override the HPA temporarily to restore service. The HPA will take over again once it has metrics.
2. Fix HPA minReplicas kubectl patch hpa easypj-api-hpa -p '{"spec":{"minReplicas":2}}' Set minReplicas to at least 2 for high availability. Never use 0 unless you explicitly want scale-to-zero.
3. Verify metrics-server is running kubectl get deploy -n kube-system metrics-server && kubectl top nodes If metrics-server is down, HPA can't make decisions. Install: kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml.
4. Set appropriate stabilization window behavior: {scaleDown: {stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300}} Wait 5 minutes before scaling down. Prevents HPA from scaling to 0 during brief traffic dips.
5. Add readiness probe delays to prevent premature scale-down readinessProbe: {initialDelaySeconds: 30, periodSeconds: 10} Ensures pods are truly ready before HPA considers them in scaling calculations.
💡 Personal Advice:
Never set minReplicas to 0 for production workloads. Scale-to-zero is a pattern for dev/test environments or event-driven functions (Knative). For always-on APIs, minReplicas >= 2 is the standard.
HPA needs metrics-server. Always verify it's running. kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep metrics-server Without metrics-server, HPA is blind. It either does nothing or scales to min — both are dangerous.
Set scaleDown stabilization to at least 300 seconds. Without stabilization, a 30-second traffic dip can trigger a scale-down. The pods are terminated, and a scale-up 30 seconds later causes unnecessary churn.
Use kubectl scale to manually override HPA in emergencies. HPA will eventually reconcile, but manual scaling is faster when your service is at 0 replicas. Fix the HPA config AFTER restoring service.

📌 AD6–AD10: Deployment Operations & Debugging

AD6
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD6
kubectl apply Rejected — Immutable Selector Field Changed

🔍 Symptom: kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml fails with "field is immutable". The Deployment YAML was updated with new spec.selector.matchLabels, but Deployment selectors are immutable after creation. The apply is rejected and the Deployment is not updated.

  kubectl apply -f easypj-web-deploy.yaml
  The Deployment "easypj-web" is invalid:
  * spec.selector: Invalid value: v1.LabelSelector{...}: field is immutable

  diff easypj-web-deploy.yaml easypj-web-deploy-v2.yaml
  <     app: easypj-web
  ---
  >     app: easypj-web-v2    ← Selector changed — IMMUTABLE!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. selector.matchLabels changed in YAML: Someone edited the Deployment YAML and changed the selector labels. Deployment selectors are immutable — you must DELETE and RECREATE the Deployment to change selectors.
  2. New version of YAML template changed labels: CI/CD updated the Deployment template generator and changed labels — old Deployments can't be patched to match.
  3. Helm chart upgrade changes selectors: Chart template changed matchLabels — Helm upgrade fails with immutable field error.
  4. Kustomize commonLabels changes selectors: Adding commonLabels to an existing Deployment overlay changes the selector — apply fails.
  5. Manual kubectl edit changed selector: Someone ran kubectl edit deploy and changed matchLabels — API server rejects the edit.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Conflicting YAML files in Git repo — two versions of the same Deployment with different selectors
  2. kubectl replace used instead of apply — replace deletes and recreates, which would work but causes downtime
  3. Multiple environments sharing the same Deployment name — staging YAML applied to production namespace
  4. Auto-generated YAML from kubectl create changed selectors — dry-run output modified incorrectly
  5. Admission webhook mutating labels inconsistently — different labels on Deploy vs ReplicaSet
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. ArgoCD auto-sync with changed selectors: Git repo changed selector labels — ArgoCD tries to sync and fails with immutable field error.
  2. Migration from apps/v1beta1 to apps/v1: Old beta API allowed mutable selectors — upgrading to v1 rejects existing Deployments with mismatched selectors.
  3. New team member unaware of immutability: Fresh engineer edits selector labels in YAML — didn't know Deployment selectors can't change.
  4. Template library updated with new label standards: Organization changed label conventions — all Deployments need recreation to adopt new labels.
  5. Cluster upgrade from K8s 1.15 to 1.25+: Older versions were more lenient — new version strictly enforces selector immutability.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get deploy <name> -o yaml | grep -A5 "selector:" Compare the current selector in the cluster with the selector in your YAML. They must match exactly.
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f deploy.yaml Server-side dry-run catches immutable field errors BEFORE applying. Use this in CI/CD to validate.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Deployment YAML changed spec.selector.matchLabels, which is immutable after creation. To change labels, you must delete the Deployment and recreate it. Alternative: keep the same selector but change only pod template labels (the selector stays the same but selects different pods).
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Delete and recreate the Deployment (with downtime) kubectl delete deploy easypj-web && kubectl apply -f easypj-web-deploy.yaml Only option if you MUST change selectors. Expect downtime — pods are deleted before new ones start.
2. Create new Deployment and migrate with Service switch kubectl apply -f easypj-web-v2-deploy.yaml && kubectl patch svc easypj-web -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"easypj-web-v2"}}}' Zero-downtime approach: create new Deployment with new labels, then switch Service selector atomically.
3. Keep same selector, change only template labels Pod template labels can change. As long as matchLabels still matches the new pod labels, the Deployment accepts the change.
4. Use --dry-run=server before every apply kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f deploy.yaml Catches immutable field errors in CI/CD before they reach production.
5. Revert the YAML change if accidental git checkout -- deploy.yaml If the selector change was unintended, revert the YAML and apply the original version.
💡 Personal Advice:
Treat Deployment selectors as permanent. Once created, they can NEVER change. Plan your labeling strategy carefully before creating your first Deployment.
Service selector switch = zero-downtime migration. Instead of deleting and recreating (downtime), create a new Deployment and switch the Service selector. Users never notice.
Always use server-side dry-run. kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f deploy.yaml Client-side dry-run (--dry-run=client) won't catch immutable field errors. Always use server-side in CI/CD.
Design labels for longevity, not current needs. app.kubernetes.io/name and app.kubernetes.io/component are designed to be stable. Use these recommended labels from day one.
AD7
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD7
Manual Scale vs HPA — Replicas Immediately Reverted

🔍 Symptom: You run kubectl scale deploy easypj-api --replicas=10 to handle a traffic spike. Seconds later, the Deployment is back to 3 replicas. The HPA overrides the manual scale because 10 is outside the HPA's range (min: 2, max: 5). The scale command "succeeds" but is immediately reverted.

  kubectl scale deploy easypj-api --replicas=10
  deployment.apps/easypj-api scaled
  # Seems successful!

  kubectl get deploy easypj-api -w
  NAME          READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
  easypj-api    10/10   10           10        ← Brief moment at 10
  easypj-api    5/5     5            5         ← HPA scaled back to 5!

  kubectl get hpa easypj-api-hpa -o yaml | grep -A3 spec
  spec:
    maxReplicas: 5          ← Manual scale to 10 is OUTSIDE HPA range!
    minReplicas: 2
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. HPA overrides manual scale outside its range: HPA continuously monitors and adjusts replicas. Any manual scale outside [minReplicas, maxReplicas] is immediately corrected by HPA.
  2. HPA reconciliation loop detected the change: HPA reconciles every 15 seconds by default. Your manual scale was reverted within 15 seconds.
  3. Scaling above maxReplicas not possible with active HPA: The HPA enforces its maxReplicas as an absolute ceiling. kubectl scale to 10 is accepted but immediately reverted to ≤5.
  4. HPA minReplicas is too high: You tried to scale down to 1 but HPA minReplicas is 2 — HPA scales back up to 2 immediately.
  5. Multiple controllers managing replicas: Both HPA and an external controller (KEDA, custom operator) are adjusting replicas — they fight each other.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Cluster autoscaler interaction — HPA scales pods, CA scales nodes, timing mismatch causes oscillation
  2. Metrics spike/drop causing HPA action — your manual scale happened to coincide with an HPA metric-based scale event
  3. HPA behavior settings causing rapid scale-down — scaleDown behavior with very short stabilization window
  4. VPA (Vertical Pod Autoscaler) conflicting with HPA — VPA adjusts resource requests, HPA adjusts replica count
  5. Argo Rollouts or similar controller managing replicas — additional controller overrides both manual and HPA scaling
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. HPA configured on wrong metric: New cluster set up HPA on external metric that doesn't exist — HPA constantly adjusts replicas based on invalid data.
  2. CronJob scaling script fighting HPA: Nightly scaling script changes replicas — HPA corrects it every morning, causing daily oscillations.
  3. kubectl scale in CI/CD pipeline: CI/CD job scales deploy after deployment — HPA immediately reverts, pipeline thinks it succeeded.
  4. Prometheus adapter returning stale metrics: HPA makes decisions on 5-minute-old data — over-scales based on outdated metrics.
  5. Lack of HPA monitoring: No alerts on HPA capping at maxReplicas — team doesn't know pods are at ceiling during traffic spikes.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get hpa <name> --watch Watch the HPA in real-time. You'll see it detect the manual scale and correct it within 15 seconds.
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<hpa> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -5 HPA events show every scale decision — "New size: 5; reason: Current number of replicas above Spec.MaxReplicas".
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The HPA reconciliation loop continuously enforces replicas within [minReplicas, maxReplicas]. Manual scaling outside this range is accepted by the API but immediately corrected by the HPA controller. To scale beyond max, you must update the HPA maxReplicas first.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Update HPA maxReplicas before manual scale kubectl patch hpa easypj-api-hpa -p '{"spec":{"maxReplicas":10}}' && kubectl scale deploy easypj-api --replicas=10 Increase HPA ceiling FIRST, then scale. The HPA won't revert changes within its range.
2. Temporarily disable HPA for manual control kubectl delete hpa easypj-api-hpa Remove HPA temporarily. Scale manually. Recreate HPA when done. Use with caution — no auto-scaling during this period.
3. Use HPA behavior to respect manual scaling behavior: {scaleUp: {policies: [{type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 15}]}} Configure HPA behavior to be less aggressive. Longer stabilization windows prevent rapid corrections.
4. Plan for capacity in advance If you regularly need more replicas than maxReplicas, your HPA limits are too low. Increase them proactively.
5. Monitor HPA limits kubectl describe hpa easypj-api-hpa | grep -A5 "Conditions:" Check if ScalingLimited condition is True — this means the HPA is at its limit and can't scale further.
💡 Personal Advice:
HPA always wins over manual scaling. The HPA controller runs every 15 seconds. Any manual scale outside its range is reverted before you can even check kubectl get deploy again.
Patch HPA first, then scale. If you need to manually override, update HPA limits FIRST. The sequence is: patch HPA → scale deploy. Not the other way around.
kubectl scale "succeeds" even when HPA overrides. The API accepts your scale request immediately. The revert happens asynchronously — don't trust that a successful scale command means the replicas stayed.
Set HPA maxReplicas with headroom. Your maxReplicas should be at least 2× normal load. If you normally run at 5, set max to 15-20. The HPA won't use them unless needed.
AD8
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD8
Deployment Paused — kubectl rollout pause Forgotten

🔍 Symptom: You update a Deployment with a new image, but nothing happens. Pods remain at the old version. kubectl rollout status shows "waiting for deployment rollout to finish: 0 out of 3 new replicas have been updated." The Deployment was paused days ago and nobody remembered to resume it.

  kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web easypj-web=easypj/jobpost:v2.1
  deployment.apps/easypj-web image updated

  kubectl get deploy easypj-web
  NAME          READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
  easypj-web    3/3     0            3           5d     ← 0 UP-TO-DATE!

  kubectl describe deploy easypj-web | grep -i pause
  Paused:  true     ← Deployment is PAUSED!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Deployment was paused and never resumed: Someone ran kubectl rollout pause deploy/easypj-web for maintenance and forgot to resume. The Deployment stops processing any changes.
  2. Pause used for debugging and left active: Developer paused to inspect a failing rollout, debugged, but never ran kubectl rollout resume.
  3. Multiple team members unaware of paused state: Team member A paused, team member B tried to deploy — B doesn't know the Deployment is paused.
  4. CI/CD pipeline doesn't check paused state: Pipeline runs kubectl apply/set image and reports success — doesn't verify the rollout actually progressed.
  5. Goldilocks rollout pattern misused: Developer paused mid-rollout to monitor, then the weekend came — Deployment stayed paused for days.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Canary deployment paused indefinitely — canary Deployment was paused and never promoted to full rollout
  2. Helm hooks pausing Deployment — custom Helm hooks call kubectl rollout pause without corresponding resume
  3. Admission webhook pausing Deployments — webhook adds paused annotation to all new Deployments
  4. ResourceQuota preventing new pod creation — appears "paused" but actually quota is blocking
  5. Multiple paused states across namespaces — audit shows 5+ paused Deployments across the cluster
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. ArgoCD sync window misconfiguration: ArgoCD pauses Deployment during maintenance window — window ended but Deployment not resumed.
  2. Disaster recovery exercise left Deployments paused: DR drill paused all Deployments — only critical ones were resumed after.
  3. Automation script error: Nightly script pauses for backup, resumes after — but error handling is missing; if script crashes, Deployments stay paused.
  4. New cluster with security policy: Policy requires paused state for all deployments until security review — review backlog means Deployments stay paused.
  5. Monitoring alert on paused Deployments not set up: No alert exists to detect paused Deployments older than N hours — they stay paused until someone notices.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get deploy -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.paused}{"\n"}{end}' Check ALL Deployments in a namespace for paused status. Look for "true" in the output.
kubectl describe deploy <name> | grep -i paused The describe output clearly shows "Paused: true" near the top of the Deployment status.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Deployment was paused with kubectl rollout pause and never resumed. Paused Deployments stop all rollouts — new changes are queued but not applied. The fix is kubectl rollout resume deploy/<name> to process all pending changes.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Resume the paused Deployment kubectl rollout resume deploy/easypj-web All pending changes are immediately applied. The Deployment processes the queued revision.
2. Check pending changes are correct before resuming kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-web && kubectl describe deploy easypj-web | grep Image: Verify the pending image/change is what you intend. Resuming applies ALL queued changes at once.
3. Monitor rollout after resume kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web --timeout=300s Watch the rollout complete. If it was paused due to a known issue, that issue may still exist.
4. Add CI/CD check for paused state kubectl get deploy <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.paused}' | grep -q false Block deployments if the Deployment is paused. Fail the pipeline instead of silently queuing changes.
5. Set up monitoring for paused Deployments kubectl get deploy -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.paused == true) | .metadata.name' Alert if any Deployment has been paused for more than 1 hour. Prevent forgotten pauses.
💡 Personal Advice:
Always resume after pause — set a timer. If you pause a Deployment for maintenance, set a 30-minute reminder. Paused Deployments are silent deployment blockers.
Check .spec.paused before every deployment. Add a pre-deployment check in CI/CD: if Deployment is paused, fail the pipeline and alert. Don't silently queue changes.
Pause is for short-term debugging only. Don't pause a Deployment and leave for the weekend. If you need long-term freeze, scale to 0 or use a different strategy.
Audit paused Deployments weekly. kubectl get deploy -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.paused==true) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"' Run this weekly. Any Deployment paused > 24h is a bug — resume it or investigate why it's paused.
AD9
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD9
ImagePullBackOff on New Nodes — Missing imagePullSecrets

🔍 Symptom: After a cluster autoscaler adds new nodes, some pods fail with ImagePullBackOff on the new nodes. Old nodes work fine. The Deployment has imagePullSecrets configured, but the new nodes can't authenticate to the private registry because the secret isn't propagated to the new nodes.

  kubectl get pods -o wide -l app=easypj-web
  NAME                            READY   STATUS              NODE
  easypj-web-9f8e7d6c5b-abcde    1/1     Running             wk1     ← Old node OK
  easypj-web-9f8e7d6c5b-fghij    1/1     Running             wk2     ← Old node OK
  easypj-web-9f8e7d6c5b-klmno    0/1     ImagePullBackOff    wk3     ← NEW node FAIL!

  kubectl describe pod easypj-web-9f8e7d6c5b-klmno | grep -A3 "Failed"
  Failed to pull image "ghcr.io/easypj/jobpost:v2.1": failed to pull and unpack
  image "ghcr.io/easypj/jobpost:v2.1": failed to resolve reference
  "ghcr.io/easypj/jobpost:v2.1": pull access denied, repository does not exist
  or may require 'docker login': denied: Your request could not be authenticated.
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. imagePullSecrets not in pod spec: Deployment specifies a private registry image (ghcr.io/easypj/jobpost) but imagePullSecrets is missing from the pod template. Add the secret reference.
  2. imagePullSecrets secret doesn't exist in namespace: The Deployment references imagePullSecrets: [{name: ghcr-secret}] but the Secret was never created.
  3. Secret created but in wrong namespace: The Secret exists in namespace "default" but the Deployment is in "easypj-prod". Secrets are namespace-scoped.
  4. Registry credentials expired: The dockerconfigjson in the Secret contains an expired token or password. Generate a new token.
  5. ServiceAccount without imagePullSecrets: imagePullSecrets can be attached to a ServiceAccount. If the SA doesn't have them and the pod doesn't specify them, pulls fail.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. New node has different container runtime — containerd vs Docker, different auth config paths
  2. NetworkPolicy blocking registry access from new node IP range — egress rules not updated for new CIDR
  3. Registry IP allowlist not updated — new node IPs not in registry's allowed list
  4. dockerconfigjson format error — extra whitespace or incorrect JSON breaks parsing on new node
  5. kubelet image credential provider not configured — new nodes don't have the credential provider plugin
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Air-gapped cluster — no internet access: New nodes can't reach external registries at all. Need local registry mirror or pre-loaded images.
  2. Private registry not accessible from new node subnet: New nodes created in a different subnet/VPC — registry firewall rules not updated.
  3. containerd registry config missing on new node: Node was provisioned without /etc/containerd/config.toml registry mirror/credentials setup.
  4. kind/minikube cluster — image not loaded: kind load docker-image not run after adding new kind node — image exists on control-plane but not worker.
  5. Cloud IAM role for node pool missing registry permissions: New node pool uses different IAM role without ECR/GCR/ACR pull permissions.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -A3 imagePullSecrets and kubectl get sa <sa> -o yaml | grep -A3 imagePullSecrets Check both pod-level and SA-level imagePullSecrets. If both are empty, private registry pulls will fail.
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A10 "Events:" The Events section tells you WHY the pull failed — authentication, not found, or network error.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The pod template doesn't have imagePullSecrets configured. Private registry images (ghcr.io, ECR, etc.) require authentication that public images don't. Create a docker-registry Secret and reference it in the pod spec or ServiceAccount.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create the registry secret kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-secret --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=<user> --docker-password=<token> -n easypj-prod Creates a kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret with registry credentials.
2. Add imagePullSecrets to pod template kubectl patch deploy easypj-web -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"ghcr-secret"}]}}}}' Add the secret reference to the Deployment's pod template. Triggers a rolling update.
3. Attach to ServiceAccount for all pods kubectl patch sa default -n easypj-prod -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"ghcr-secret"}]}' All pods using this SA automatically get the pull secret. No per-Deployment changes needed.
4. Verify secret is valid kubectl get secret ghcr-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.\.dockerconfigjson}' | base64 -d | jq . Decode the secret and check the auth URL, username, and that auth is base64(user:token).
5. Delete failing pods to force re-pull kubectl delete pod easypj-web-9f8e7d6c5b-klmno After fixing the secret, delete stuck pods. New pods will use the pull secret and pull successfully.
💡 Personal Advice:
Attach imagePullSecrets to ServiceAccount, not every pod. One patch to the default SA propagates to ALL pods. Much cleaner than adding imagePullSecrets to every Deployment.
Test image pulls on new nodes before production traffic. After adding nodes, deploy a test pod that pulls from your private registry. If it fails, your production pods will too.
Docker Hub rate limits apply per IP. New nodes get new IPs — but your pull quota may be exhausted. Use authenticated pulls (dockerconfigjson) to get higher limits.
On kind, use kind load docker-image for private images. kind load docker-image ghcr.io/easypj/jobpost:v2.1 --name kind-cka-lab No registry authentication needed — the image is pre-loaded directly into the node's containerd.
AD10
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD10
Deployment Not Adopting Pods — Orphaned ReplicaSet Chaos

🔍 Symptom: After deleting and recreating a Deployment, there are now double the expected pods. The old ReplicaSet (from before deletion) is still running pods, and the new Deployment created its own pods. The old pods are not managed by any Deployment — they're orphaned but still serving traffic.

  kubectl get deploy,rs,pods -l app=easypj-api
  NAME                          READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
  deployment.apps/easypj-api    3/3     3            3

  NAME                                     DESIRED   CURRENT   READY
  replicaset.apps/easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e    3         3         3    ← NEW RS (managed)
  replicaset.apps/easypj-api-abc123def4     2         2         2    ← OLD RS (ORPHANED!)

  NAME                                  READY   STATUS
  pod/easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde      1/1     Running   ← NEW pod
  pod/easypj-api-abc123def4-pqrst       1/1     Running   ← ORPHANED!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Deployment deleted with --cascade=orphan: kubectl delete deploy easypj-api --cascade=orphan deletes the Deployment but leaves ReplicaSets and pods running.
  2. Deployment recreated with different selector: New Deployment has different matchLabels than the old one. Old RS pods don't match new selector — not adopted.
  3. ReplicaSet manually created with same labels: Someone created a standalone RS that matches the Deployment's selector — Deployment can't adopt it.
  4. Deployment YAML applied over existing resources: kubectl apply with --force replaced objects but didn't clean up old ReplicaSets.
  5. Helm uninstall without --cascade: Helm delete removed the Deployment but left ReplicaSets — they keep running until manually cleaned.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. kubectl replace instead of apply — replaces Deployment object but doesn't clean up old RS ownership chain
  2. API server crash during deletion — Deployment deleted but cleanup of dependent resources failed
  3. Garbage collection delay — RS is in terminating state but pods still running during grace period
  4. Manual label removal breaking ownership — someone removed ownerReferences from pods, orphaning them
  5. Two Deployments with overlapping selectors — both claim the same pods, causing ownership conflict
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. ArgoCD pruning disabled: Auto-sync creates new resources but pruning is off — old ReplicaSets from previous sync remain.
  2. Multi-cluster sync lag: Deployment deleted on cluster A, but sync to cluster B hasn't propagated — cluster B still has old RS.
  3. Namespace stuck in Terminating: Namespace deletion initiated but stuck — deployments deleted, RS/pods linger in terminating namespace.
  4. etcd backup restore: Restored from backup — Deployment restored but old RS wasn't in backup, creating orphaned pods.
  5. Garbage collection controller not running: kube-controller-manager GC controller disabled — orphaned resources never cleaned up.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get rs -l app=<label> -o yaml | grep -A5 ownerReferences ReplicaSets owned by a Deployment have ownerReferences. Orphaned RS have no ownerReferences or reference a deleted UID.
kubectl get pods -l app=<label> -o yaml | grep -B2 -A5 ownerReferences Pods should be owned by a ReplicaSet. If ownerReferences points to a non-existent RS, the pod is orphaned.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The old Deployment was deleted with --cascade=orphan, which intentionally leaves ReplicaSets and pods running. When a new Deployment was created with a different selector, it couldn't adopt the old resources. The fix: manually scale down and delete orphaned ReplicaSets.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Identify orphaned ReplicaSets kubectl get rs -l app=easypj-api -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.ownerReferences == null) | .metadata.name' Orphaned ReplicaSets have no ownerReferences. These are the ones to clean up.
2. Scale down orphaned ReplicaSet kubectl scale rs easypj-api-abc123def4 --replicas=0 Gradually reduce orphaned pods. Monitor the new Deployment to ensure it has enough capacity.
3. Delete the orphaned ReplicaSet kubectl delete rs easypj-api-abc123def4 Once scaled to 0, delete the orphaned ReplicaSet. Its pods are already gone.
4. Use --cascade=background for normal deletions kubectl delete deploy easypj-api (default is background cascading) Background cascading deletes the Deployment AND all its ReplicaSets and pods. Use this unless you specifically need to preserve pods.
5. Audit for other orphaned resources kubectl get rs -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.metadata.ownerReferences == null) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"' Find ALL orphaned ReplicaSets across the cluster and clean them up.
💡 Personal Advice:
Never use --cascade=orphan unless you explicitly need it. It's the nuclear option for debugging — you preserve pods to inspect them. Always clean up afterward, or they'll run forever.
Orphaned pods consume resources and serve traffic. They don't show up in typical monitoring (Deployment replicas = 3). Your Service load-balances to them, but you can't manage them.
ownerReferences tells the adoption story. kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml | grep -A10 ownerReferences Every managed pod has ownerReferences pointing to its ReplicaSet. No ownerReferences = orphaned.
Audit for orphaned resources monthly. Orphaned ReplicaSets, pods, and PVCs accumulate over time. A monthly cleanup script saves cluster resources and prevents confusion.

📌 AD11–AD15: Blue/Green, Canary & Advanced Strategies

AD11
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD11
Blue/Green Deployment — Service Selector Never Switched to Green

🔍 Symptom: A "green" (new) Deployment of easypj-web v2.1 was created alongside the "blue" (old) v2.0 Deployment. Both are running, but the Service selector still points to the blue pods. The green ones are healthy but receiving zero traffic because the Service was never updated.

  kubectl get deploy -l app=easypj-web
  NAME              READY   AGE   VERSION
  easypj-web-blue   3/3     2d    v2.0    ← Old (BLUE) — receiving traffic
  easypj-web-green  3/3     1h    v2.1    ← New (GREEN) — ZERO traffic!

  kubectl get svc easypj-web -o yaml | grep selector -A3
  selector:
    app: easypj-web
    version: blue         ← STILL pointing to BLUE!

  kubectl get endpoints easypj-web
  NAME          ENDPOINTS
  easypj-web    10.244.1.5:3000,10.244.2.8:3000,10.244.3.9:3000
  # All endpoints are BLUE pods — green pods are invisible!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Service selector not updated after green deploy: The green Deployment was created successfully, but the critical final step — switching the Service selector — was forgotten. The blue pods still receive all traffic.
  2. Service selector uses generic labels: If the Service selects app: easypj-web without a version label, BOTH blue and green pods receive traffic — confusing but not zero. Adding version: blue locks traffic to blue.
  3. Green pods use different port name: The Service references targetPort: http but green pods name their port web. Port name mismatch = no endpoints.
  4. Green pods not Ready: Green Deployment exists but pods are in CrashLoopBackOff or readiness probe failing. Service has no green endpoints to route to.
  5. Service switch automation failed silently: CI/CD script that patches the Service selector errored out but didn't report failure — deploy marked as "successful".
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Multiple Services with same name in different namespaces — patched the wrong Service in the wrong namespace
  2. kubectl context wrong — patched staging Service thinking it was production
  3. Blue and green in different namespaces — Service can only select pods in its own namespace
  4. NetworkPolicy blocking traffic to green pods — Service selects them but traffic blocked by policy
  5. Green pods on different node with taint — scheduled but not receiving traffic due to node issue
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. ArgoCD sync not updating Service selector: Blue/Green controlled via Git — Service selector change committed but ArgoCD sync failed.
  2. Canary vs Blue/Green confusion: Team set up canary (weighted Ingress) instead of Blue/Green (selector switch) — green gets 0% weight.
  3. New team unfamiliar with Blue/Green pattern: Junior engineer deployed green but didn't know the final step of switching the Service.
  4. Runbook step missed during deployment: Production deployment runbook has 5 steps — step 5 (switch selector) was accidentally skipped.
  5. Green pods use different containerPort than blue: Green uses port 8080, blue uses 3000 — Service targetPort doesn't match green.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get svc <name> -o yaml | grep -A5 selector and kubectl get pods -l <selector> Verify the Service selector matches the green pod labels exactly. If green has version=green but selector has version=blue, traffic goes to blue.
kubectl get endpoints <svc> -o json | jq '.subsets[].addresses[].targetRef.name' List which pods are actually receiving traffic through the Service. Blue or green?
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Service selector was never switched from blue to green. Blue/Green deployment requires an explicit final step: kubectl patch svc easypj-web -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}'. Without this, the green Deployment runs but serves no traffic.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Switch the Service selector to green kubectl patch svc easypj-web -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"easypj-web","version":"green"}}}' Atomically switches ALL traffic from blue to green. Instant cutover — no gradual shift.
2. Verify green pods are receiving traffic kubectl get endpoints easypj-web and kubectl logs -l version=green --tail=5 Endpoints should now show green pod IPs. Logs should show new requests arriving.
3. Keep blue as instant rollback Don't delete the blue Deployment yet. If green has issues, switch the Service selector back to blue in seconds.
4. Scale down blue after verification period kubectl scale deploy easypj-web-blue --replicas=0 After confirming green is stable (hours, not minutes), scale down or delete the blue Deployment.
5. Automate the selector switch in CI/CD Add the Service patch as the final step in your deployment pipeline. Never rely on manual steps for production cutover.
💡 Personal Advice:
Blue/Green = two Deployments + one Service switch. The Service selector is the traffic switch. Never create a second Service — one Service with a changeable selector is the correct pattern.
Always verify endpoints after switching. kubectl get endpoints <svc> If endpoints are empty after switching, the selector doesn't match any pods. Check labels immediately.
Blue/Green gives instant rollback. Switch the Service selector back to blue and you're done. No waiting for rollouts, no pod restarts. This is the biggest advantage of Blue/Green.
Use labels: version=blue, version=green. Simple, clear, and the Service selector changes from one to the other atomically. Don't overcomplicate with multiple selectors.
AD12
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD12
Canary Deployment — 100% Traffic Still Going to Stable

🔍 Symptom: A canary Deployment with 1 replica was created alongside the stable Deployment with 9 replicas. The goal is 10% canary traffic, but the canary pod receives ZERO requests. All traffic continues to the stable pods because the Ingress canary annotations are misconfigured.

  kubectl get deploy -l app=easypj-api
  NAME                   READY   AGE   TRAFFIC
  easypj-api-stable      9/9     3d    100%    ← ALL traffic!
  easypj-api-canary      1/1     1h    0%      ← ZERO traffic!

  kubectl get ingress easypj-api-canary -o yaml | grep nginx
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "10"
  # Canary Ingress created but canary-by-header ALSO set — conflicts!
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-header: "X-Canary"
  # With canary-by-header, canary-weight is IGNORED!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. canary-by-header overrides canary-weight: When both annotations exist, header-based routing takes priority. Traffic goes to canary ONLY when the X-Canary header is present — weight is ignored.
  2. Canary Ingress not created in correct namespace: The canary Ingress was created in a different namespace than the stable Ingress — canary rules never apply.
  3. Canary Ingress host doesn't match stable Ingress: The stable Ingress handles api.easypj.com, but the canary Ingress uses canary.api.easypj.com — different host, no traffic routed to canary.
  4. Canary service name wrong: The canary Ingress backend references easypj-api-canary-svc but the actual Service is named easypj-api-canary. Backend not found.
  5. Ingress Controller doesn't support canary: The cluster uses an Ingress controller that doesn't support canary annotations (e.g., AWS ALB Ingress Controller).
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Canary Ingress created AFTER stable Ingress — ordering matters for some controllers, canary must be created second
  2. Canary pods in different namespace — canary Ingress can only route to Services in the same namespace
  3. Default backend catching canary traffic — default backend rule in stable Ingress intercepts before canary
  4. TLS misconfiguration on canary Ingress — TLS secret not available for canary host, requests fail
  5. Cookie stickiness interference — session affinity on stable Service prevents traffic from reaching canary
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Argo Rollouts not configured correctly: Canary steps defined in Rollout but the argo-rollouts controller not installed — canary never progresses.
  2. Istio VirtualService vs Ingress conflict: Both Istio and nginx-ingress are installed — canary rules in one are overridden by the other.
  3. Flagger not installed: Team attempted Flagger canary without installing the Flagger controller — canary resources created but ignored.
  4. Service mesh (Linkerd) mTLS blocking canary: mTLS between ingress and canary pods fails — traffic dropped silently.
  5. Cloud load balancer health checks failing for canary: LB health check path different on canary pods — pods marked unhealthy, no traffic routed.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe ingress <canary-ingress> Verify all canary annotations are correct. Check for conflicting annotations (canary-by-header + canary-weight).
kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx deploy/ingress-nginx-controller --tail=20 | grep canary Ingress controller logs show whether canary rules are being processed and applied.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Both canary-by-header and canary-weight annotations are set. When canary-by-header is present, the Ingress controller routes to canary ONLY when the specified header exists — weight-based routing is disabled. Remove canary-by-header to enable weight-based canary.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Remove conflicting canary-by-header annotation kubectl annotate ingress easypj-api-canary nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-header- The trailing - removes the annotation. Now canary-weight takes effect.
2. Verify canary Ingress host matches stable kubectl get ingress easypj-api-stable -o yaml | grep host: and compare with canary Both Ingresses must use the SAME host. Canary Ingress adds rules to the existing host — it doesn't create a new one.
3. Test canary with header-based routing first curl -H "X-Canary: always" https://api.easypj.com/healthz Use header-based canary for testing. Remove the header annotation only when ready for weight-based rollout.
4. Gradually increase canary weight kubectl annotate ingress easypj-api-canary nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight="25" --overwrite Start at 5%, monitor, increase to 25%, 50%, 100%. Each step is a kubectl annotate command.
5. Promote canary to stable kubectl scale deploy easypj-api-stable --replicas=10 && kubectl delete deploy easypj-api-canary After canary is validated at 100%, update the stable image and remove canary resources.
💡 Personal Advice:
Canary by weight AND by header are mutually exclusive. Pick ONE method. canary-by-header is for testing (internal users). canary-weight is for gradual rollout to all users. Don't set both.
Canary Ingress MUST use the same host as stable. If hosts differ, the canary Ingress creates a completely separate routing rule — not a canary of the stable rule.
Test canary with curl -H "X-Canary: always". Before going to weight-based canary, verify the canary pod works by sending traffic directly with the header. Fix bugs first, then roll out.
Canary is about risk reduction, not zero risk. Even 1% canary traffic hitting a bug can be catastrophic at scale. Always have monitoring on canary pods and a rollback plan.
AD13
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD13
A/B Testing — Cookie/Header Routing Not Working

🔍 Symptom: A/B testing is configured to route users with X-Experiment: new-ui header to the experimental Deployment. But ALL users — regardless of the header — are seeing the experimental UI. The canary-by-header annotation is set but the canary Ingress is capturing all traffic.

  kubectl get ingress easypj-web-experiment -o yaml | grep nginx
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-header: "X-Experiment"
  nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-header-value: "new-ui"
  # Looks correct — but experiment is getting ALL traffic!

  curl -H "X-Experiment: new-ui" https://easypj.com/
  (returns experimental UI) ✅ Expected

  curl https://easypj.com/
  (returns experimental UI) ❌ Should return stable UI!
  # Stable users are seeing the experiment!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Stable Ingress missing or misconfigured: The canary Ingress exists but the stable Ingress was deleted or not created. Canary Ingress alone routes ALL traffic — it needs a stable Ingress to split with.
  2. Canary weight also set to 100: canary-weight: "100" was accidentally left on the canary Ingress — routes all traffic regardless of header.
  3. Stable Service backend broken: The stable Service has no endpoints. nginx-ingress falls back to canary when stable is unavailable.
  4. Canary Ingress created BEFORE stable Ingress: The canary Ingress was created first and became the "stable" route. The stable Ingress created later is treated as the canary.
  5. Stable Ingress in different namespace: Canary Ingress is in easypj-prod, stable Ingress is in easypj-staging — different namespace, controller doesn't link them.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Ingress controller version doesn't support canary-by-header-value — older nginx-ingress only supports canary-by-header
  2. Header name case sensitivity — Ingress expects "X-Experiment" but client sends "x-experiment"
  3. CDN or proxy stripping custom headers — CloudFront/Cloudflare removes X-Experiment header before reaching Ingress
  4. Stable pods crashed — all stable pods are CrashLoopBackOff, controller routes everything to canary
  5. Default backend captures traffic — Ingress default backend overrides canary routing
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Multiple Ingress controllers installed: nginx-ingress AND Traefik both processing Ingress resources — canary annotations ignored by one.
  2. IngressClass not set on canary Ingress: Multiple Ingress controllers — canary Ingress not assigned to the controller that supports canary annotations.
  3. Service type LoadBalancer bypassing Ingress: External traffic goes directly to LoadBalancer Service, not through Ingress — canary annotations never applied.
  4. DNS pointing directly to canary Service: External DNS record for easypj.com points to canary Service's external IP — bypasses Ingress entirely.
  5. kind/minikube — Ingress not working: Local cluster doesn't have Ingress controller or port mappings — all testing done via port-forward which bypasses Ingress.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get ingress -A and verify BOTH stable and canary Ingresses exist in the SAME namespace Canary only works when a stable Ingress exists in the same namespace with the same host.
kubectl get svc,endpoints <stable-svc> Verify the stable Service has healthy endpoints. If stable has no endpoints, all traffic falls through to canary.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The canary Ingress is the ONLY Ingress for this host. Canary annotations only split traffic from an existing stable Ingress. Without a stable Ingress, the canary Ingress becomes the default route and receives ALL traffic. Create the stable Ingress first, then add the canary Ingress.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Ensure stable Ingress exists WITH the same host kubectl get ingress easypj-web-stable The stable Ingress must exist, have the same host, and have healthy backends. Create it if missing.
2. Delete and recreate canary Ingress AFTER stable kubectl delete ingress easypj-web-experiment && kubectl apply -f canary-ingress.yaml Order matters for some controllers. Delete and recreate canary to ensure it's recognized as secondary.
3. Verify canary annotations are correct kubectl get ingress canary -o yaml | grep "canary-" Only canary-by-header OR canary-weight should be set, not both. Remove the unused one.
4. Test with explicit header curl -H "X-Experiment: new-ui" https://easypj.com/ and curl https://easypj.com/ First should return experimental. Second should return stable. If both return the same, routing is broken.
5. Use cookie-based routing for persistent A/B nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-cookie: "experiment" Cookie-based routing keeps users in the same group across requests. Better UX than header-based.
💡 Personal Advice:
Stable Ingress must exist for canary to work. Canary is a modifier on the stable route, not an independent route. Always create the stable Ingress FIRST, canary SECOND.
Test canary routing with curl before deploying to users. Three curl tests: (1) no header → stable, (2) canary header → canary, (3) wrong header value → stable. All three must work.
Cookie-based A/B is better than header-based. Users can't modify cookies as easily as headers. Use canary-by-cookie for production A/B tests to ensure consistent user experience.
Canary Ingress in the same namespace as stable Ingress. Cross-namespace canary doesn't work with nginx-ingress. Both Ingresses must be in the same namespace.
AD14
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD14
Rolling Update Too Fast — Pods Receiving Traffic Before Ready

🔍 Symptom: During a rolling update, new pods start receiving traffic immediately after starting, before Django finishes loading. Users see 502/503 errors because the pods haven't completed startup — the readiness probe isn't configured, so kube-proxy considers them "ready" as soon as the container process starts.

  kubectl logs easypj-api-9f8e7d6c5b-newpod --tail=5
  [2024-06-11 14:30:22] Starting Django 4.2 development server...
  [2024-06-11 14:30:25] Performing system checks...
  [2024-06-11 14:30:40] 502 Bad Gateway ← User request BEFORE Django ready!
  [2024-06-11 14:30:50] Django is ready. Listening on 0.0.0.0:8000

  kubectl get deploy easypj-api -o yaml | grep -A10 readinessProbe
  (empty — NO readinessProbe configured!)

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api-9f8e7d6c5b-newpod | grep Ready
  Ready: True  ← Marked ready IMMEDIATELY (no probe!)
  # Container started but Django wasn't ready — 502 errors!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No readinessProbe configured: The Deployment has no readiness probe. Kubernetes considers the pod ready as soon as the container process starts — even if Django takes 20 more seconds to be ready.
  2. readinessProbe initialDelaySeconds too low: Probe starts checking after 0 seconds, but Django needs 30 seconds. The probe fails, and the pod is marked Not Ready — but by then traffic already hit it.
  3. Probe endpoint doesn't check real readiness: httpGet: {path: /} returns 200 immediately from nginx, but Django behind it isn't ready. Probe should hit a dedicated health endpoint.
  4. maxSurge too high relative to readiness: maxSurge: 5 replaces 5 pods at once. If none are ready, you lose 5 pods of capacity — cascading 502s.
  5. Container starts quickly but app initialization is slow: The container process (gunicorn) starts in 1 second but Django model loading takes 15 seconds — probe passes on the process, not the app.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Readiness probe timeout too short — probe gives up before Django finishes startup, pod never becomes ready
  2. Probe hitting wrong port — httpGet targets port 8080 but Django listens on 8000
  3. Database connection slow — readiness probe depends on DB query, but DB connection pool not initialized yet
  4. minReadySeconds not set — new pod considered "available" immediately after Ready, before traffic stabilizes
  5. Readiness probe removed during debugging and never restored — developer commented it out and committed the change
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Helm chart template missing readinessProbe: Default chart values have probes disabled — new deployment has no probes.
  2. Kustomize overlay removing probes: Production overlay accidentally patches out readiness probes from the base — all pods deployed without them.
  3. Gateway timeout in front of Ingress: Cloud LB has 5-second timeout — slow Django startup (15s) causes LB to mark nodes unhealthy before Django is ready.
  4. Startup probe not configured for slow-starting apps: Django with large migrations needs 60+ seconds — readiness probe fails repeatedly, pod never becomes ready without startupProbe.
  5. New cluster with different hardware: App starts in 5s on fast SSDs, but new cluster uses slower storage — startup takes 40s, probes configured for 5s fail.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -A15 readinessProbe Check if readinessProbe exists, its path, port, initialDelaySeconds, and failureThreshold.
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 "Conditions:" and kubectl get endpoints <svc> If the pod is Ready but not in Endpoints, the readiness probe is passing but there's another issue.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No readinessProbe configured. Without it, pods are marked Ready instantly and start receiving traffic before the application is actually ready to serve requests. Always add a readinessProbe that hits a real health endpoint (/healthz) with appropriate initialDelaySeconds.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add readinessProbe to Deployment readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000}, initialDelaySeconds: 10, periodSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3} Probe waits 10s before first check, checks every 5s, allows 3 failures before marking Not Ready.
2. Add a proper health check endpoint in Django path('healthz/', lambda r: JsonResponse({'status': 'ok', 'db': check_db()})) The endpoint should verify DB connectivity AND app readiness, not just return 200. If DB is down, probe fails.
3. Add startupProbe for slow-starting apps startupProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000}, initialDelaySeconds: 0, failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 2} Gives Django up to 60 seconds (30×2) to start. Readiness and liveness probes wait until startup probe succeeds.
4. Set minReadySeconds to allow stabilization spec.minReadySeconds: 10 Pod must be Ready for 10 seconds before considered Available. Prevents traffic from hitting a just-barely-ready pod.
5. Test rollout with traffic simulation while true; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://easypj-api/healthz; sleep 0.5; done During a rolling update, watch for non-200 responses. If you see 502s, probes need tuning.
💡 Personal Advice:
Every production Deployment needs a readinessProbe. This is non-negotiable. Without it, you're routing traffic to pods that aren't ready to serve. The 502 errors are inevitable.
StartupProbe + ReadinessProbe + LivenessProbe = the holy trinity. Startup: "Is it alive yet?" Readiness: "Can it serve traffic?" Liveness: "Has it crashed?" Three probes, three purposes.
Health check endpoints must check real dependencies. Returning 200 without checking the database is a false positive. Your health check should ping the DB, Redis, and any critical dependency.
Test rolling updates with traffic before production. Run a continuous curl loop during a staging rollout. If you see ANY non-200 responses, your probe configuration needs work.
AD15
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD15
Recreate Strategy Kills All Pods — Production Downtime

🔍 Symptom: A Deployment update causes a complete service outage. All old pods are terminated BEFORE new pods start. kubectl describe deploy shows Strategy: Recreate. The team expected a rolling update but got total downtime because the strategy was accidentally set to Recreate instead of RollingUpdate.

  kubectl get deploy easypj-api -o yaml | grep -A5 strategy
  strategy:
    type: Recreate       ← KILLS ALL pods before creating new ones!

  kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api
  Waiting for deployment "easypj-api" rollout to finish: 0 of 3 updated replicas...
  # Complete outage during this period — all pods are terminated!

  kubectl get pods -l app=easypj-api -w
  easypj-api-old-abcde   Terminating   0         10m
  easypj-api-old-fghij   Terminating   0         10m
  easypj-api-old-klmno   Terminating   0         10m
  # ALL old pods terminated — 30 seconds of ZERO pods!
  easypj-api-new-12345   ContainerCreating   0         0s
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Strategy accidentally set to Recreate: The Deployment YAML was copied from an example or template that used Recreate. RollingUpdate is the default, but someone explicitly set Recreate.
  2. Recreate used for StatefulSet-like behavior: Team thought Recreate was needed because "the app can't have two versions running" — but rolling update with proper DB migrations handles this.
  3. CI/CD template incorrectly set Recreate: The deployment pipeline template has strategy: Recreate hardcoded — all Deployments inherit it.
  4. Helm chart default is Recreate: A third-party Helm chart or custom chart defaults to Recreate — team didn't override in values.yaml.
  5. Intentional Recreate for DB migrations but left on app: Recreate was set for a one-time migration, then forgotten. Subsequent deploys caused unexpected downtime.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Kustomize overlay changing strategy — production overlay sets Recreate while base has RollingUpdate
  2. RollingUpdate configured with impossible parameters — maxSurge=0 + maxUnavailable=100%, effectively Recreate
  3. Readiness probe missing — with RollingUpdate, new pods marked ready instantly but not actually ready, same effect
  4. PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable=3 — prevents ANY pod from being removed, rollout can't proceed
  5. ResourceQuota preventing new pod creation — old pods terminate but new ones can't start due to quota
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New cluster with different defaults: Older K8s versions had different default strategies — cluster upgrade changed behavior.
  2. Operator or controller overriding strategy: Custom operator modifies Deployment strategies based on labels — unexpected Recreate applied.
  3. Disaster recovery runbook mistake: DR procedure documented "kubectl patch strategy=Recreate" for fast recovery — applied to wrong Deployment.
  4. Intern following outdated wiki: Company wiki recommends Recreate "to be safe" — intern applies it to all new Deployments.
  5. Single-replica Deployment: With only 1 replica, even RollingUpdate causes downtime — need at least 2 for zero-downtime rolling updates.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get deploy <name> -o yaml | grep -A10 strategy: Check the strategy type. RollingUpdate is the default. Recreate is explicitly set and should be flagged.
kubectl get deploy -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.strategy.type=="Recreate") | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"' Find ALL Deployments using Recreate strategy across the cluster. Audit and justify each one.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Deployment strategy is explicitly set to Recreate. This causes Kubernetes to terminate ALL old pods before creating any new pods, resulting in complete downtime. RollingUpdate (the default) should be used unless there's a specific reason (e.g., incompatible schema changes).
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Change strategy to RollingUpdate immediately kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"RollingUpdate","rollingUpdate":{"maxSurge":1,"maxUnavailable":0}}}}' maxUnavailable: 0 ensures ZERO downtime — new pods are created and ready before old ones are terminated.
2. Increase replicas before applying the fix kubectl scale deploy easypj-api --replicas=3 Ensure enough capacity for the next rollout. With 1 replica, even RollingUpdate causes brief downtime.
3. Audit all Deployments for Recreate strategy kubectl get deploy -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.strategy.type=="Recreate") | .metadata.name' Identify every Recreate Deployment. Document why each uses Recreate — most should be RollingUpdate.
4. Add validation in CI/CD Block deployments with Recreate strategy in production. Require explicit approval or an exception ticket.
5. Use Blue/Green for truly incompatible updates If RollingUpdate doesn't work (incompatible schema), use Blue/Green instead of Recreate — switch traffic with zero downtime.
💡 Personal Advice:
Recreate = planned downtime. Never a surprise. If you see Recreate in a Deployment strategy, someone intended for downtime. Verify that intention and document it.
RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable: 0 = zero downtime. With maxSurge >= 1 and proper readiness probes, RollingUpdate can deploy without dropping a single request.
Single-replica Deployments can't do zero-downtime. Even with RollingUpdate, if you have only 1 replica, there will be a gap. Always run at least 2 replicas for production.
Audit Recreate usage quarterly. Recreate is a valid strategy for specific cases (incompatible upgrades, single-worker consumers). But it should never be the default.

📌 AD16–AD20: Helm & Kustomize Deployment Issues

AD16
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD16
Helm Install Fails — Chart Repository Not Added

🔍 Symptom: helm install easypj-web bitnami/django fails with "Error: failed to download bitnami/django." The Bitnami chart repository was never added to Helm. The developer assumed the chart was available by default, but Helm requires explicit repo registration.

  helm install easypj-web bitnami/django
  Error: failed to download "bitnami/django" (hint: running `helm repo update` may help)

  helm repo list
  Error: no repositories to show

  helm search repo django
  Error: no repositories found. Add a repo with "helm repo add"
  # No repos configured — Helm can't find any charts!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Chart repository never added: helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami was never run. Helm has NO default repositories — every repo must be explicitly added.
  2. repo add ran but repo update not run: helm repo add was executed but helm repo update was forgotten — local cache is empty, chart index not downloaded.
  3. Helm repo cache is stale: The repo was added months ago but never updated. The chart version being requested was released after the last helm repo update.
  4. Repo URL has changed: Bitnami moved their chart repo URL — old URL in Helm config returns 404. Run helm repo list and verify URLs.
