  5. Chart name is wrong or doesn't exist: bitnami/django might not exist — the correct name is bitnami/nginx or the chart was renamed. Search with helm search repo.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Network proxy blocking Helm — HTTP_PROXY not set, Helm can't reach chart repo URL
  2. Helm version too old for chart — chart requires Helm 3.12+ but system has Helm 3.8
  3. Chart repo requires authentication — private repo (Harbor, Artifactory) needs helm repo add --username --password
  4. OCI-based chart — trying to pull OCI chart with classic repo commands, need helm pull oci://
  5. Air-gapped environment — no internet access, need to download chart .tgz and use local path
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New machine — Helm just installed: Fresh Helm installation has zero repos. Every developer must add repos on each new machine.
  2. CI/CD runner has no Helm repos: Pipeline runs in ephemeral container — repos must be added in pipeline setup step.
  3. ArgoCD manages Helm repos differently: ArgoCD needs repository credentials in its own config, not in local Helm — team confused about where to add repos.
  4. Corporate chart repo not documented: Internal chart repo URL not in onboarding docs — new team members don't know it exists.
  5. kind cluster — no Helm installed: Some lightweight cluster setups don't pre-install Helm. Must install separately.
🔍 What to Look At:
helm repo list and helm search repo <chart> Verify repos are added and the chart exists. If repo list is empty, add repos first.
helm env and curl -I <repo-url>/index.yaml Check Helm environment and network connectivity to the repo. If curl fails, Helm will too.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The chart repository was never added to Helm. Unlike apt or yum, Helm starts with ZERO repositories. Every repo must be explicitly added with helm repo add <name> <url> followed by helm repo update.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add the chart repository helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami && helm repo update Registers the Bitnami chart repository and downloads the latest chart index.
2. Search for available charts helm search repo bitnami/django or helm search repo bitnami/ | grep -i django Verify the chart exists. If not, search for alternatives or use a custom chart.
3. Install the chart helm install easypj-web bitnami/django --namespace easypj-prod --create-namespace Install with explicit namespace. --create-namespace creates the namespace if it doesn't exist.
4. For private repos, add credentials helm repo add myrepo https://charts.internal.com --username <user> --password <token> Private chart repositories (Harbor, Artifactory) require authentication credentials.
5. Add repo setup to CI/CD and onboarding Document required repos in team runbook. Add helm repo add commands to CI/CD pipeline setup and developer onboarding scripts.
💡 Personal Advice:
Helm starts with zero repos. Always. New machine, new CI/CD runner, new Docker container — you must add repos before any helm install or search works.
helm repo update is as important as apt update. Without it, Helm uses stale cached index. Run helm repo update before any helm install or helm search.
Store Helm repo config in your dev setup script. Add `helm repo add` commands to your .bashrc, Makefile, or onboarding script. Every developer hits this on their first day.
OCI registries are replacing classic Helm repos. helm pull oci://ghcr.io/org/chart --version 1.0.0 — no repo add needed. OCI is the future of Helm chart distribution.
AD17
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD17
Helm Upgrade Breaks App — Custom Values Overwritten

🔍 Symptom: After helm upgrade easypj-web bitnami/django --version 2.0.0, the Django app breaks. Custom values like database host, replica count, and resource limits were reset to chart defaults because --reuse-values or --values was not specified. The app loses its production configuration.

  helm get values easypj-web
  USER-SUPPLIED VALUES:
  (empty — all values reset to chart defaults!)

  kubectl get deploy -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=easypj-web
  NAME              READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE
  easypj-web        1/1     1            1          ← Was 3 replicas!

  kubectl describe deploy easypj-web | grep -A3 Resources
  Resources:
    Limits:    cpu: 500m, memory: 512Mi     ← Was 2 CPU, 4Gi!
    Requests:  cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi     ← Defaults applied!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. helm upgrade without --reuse-values or --values: Running helm upgrade without any value flags resets ALL values to chart defaults. Always use --reuse-values to keep existing customizations.
  2. Upgrade command omitted the values file: CI/CD pipeline uses helm upgrade --values values-prod.yaml but the file path was wrong or the flag was forgotten.
  3. --reset-values used accidentally: --reset-values explicitly drops all previously set values and uses only values from the current command — very dangerous if unintended.
  4. New chart version has renamed values: The chart changed value key names (e.g., replicaCount → replicas). Old values file has the old key — silently ignored, defaults applied.
  5. --set overrides conflicting with values file: CI/CD uses --set image.tag=v2.1 but also --values values.yaml — the command-line --set from a different pipeline overwrites.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Helm release secrets corrupted — previous values stored in release Secret can't be read, defaults applied
  2. Multiple values files with conflicting precedence — file2.yaml overwrites file1.yaml unexpectedly
  3. CI/CD deploying to wrong Helm release name — upgrade applied to "easypj-web-staging" instead of "easypj-web"
  4. Helm hooks modifying resources after upgrade — post-upgrade hook changes the Deployment after Helm applies defaults
  5. GitOps auto-sync overwriting manual helm upgrade — ArgoCD detects drift and reverts to Git state
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New team member unfamiliar with Helm: Junior dev runs helm upgrade like it's kubectl apply — doesn't understand values persistence.
  2. Migration from Helm 2 to Helm 3: Helm 2 stored release info in Tiller. Helm 3 uses Secrets — migration lost values.
  3. Values file not in version control: Production values exist only on one engineer's laptop — CI/CD can't access them.
  4. Kubernetes Secret size limit (1MB): Helm stores values in a Secret — very large values files exceed the limit, values truncated.
  5. Namespace-scoped values confusion: Team deploys same chart to multiple namespaces with different values — wrong values file applied.
🔍 What to Look At:
helm get values <release> --all and helm history <release> Shows all values (user-supplied + defaults) for the current revision. Compare with previous revision.
helm diff upgrade <release> <chart> --values values.yaml (requires helm-diff plugin) Preview what will change BEFORE upgrading. Catches value resets before they happen.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: helm upgrade was run without --reuse-values or --values. Helm resets ALL previously set custom values to chart defaults. Always use helm upgrade --reuse-values or specify --values values.yaml to preserve customizations.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Always use --reuse-values or --values on upgrade helm upgrade easypj-web bitnami/django --reuse-values --version 2.0.0 Keeps all previously set custom values. Only chart template changes are applied.
2. Store values in version-controlled files helm upgrade easypj-web bitnami/django --values values-prod.yaml --version 2.0.0 Always use a values file. Version control it. Never rely on --reuse-values alone for production.
3. Use helm diff before every upgrade helm diff upgrade easypj-web bitnami/django --values values-prod.yaml Install the helm-diff plugin. Review changes BEFORE applying — catches value resets.
4. Rollback if upgrade broke configuration helm rollback easypj-web 3 Rollback to the last known-good revision. Helm stores up to 10 revisions by default.
5. Use GitOps to make Helm upgrades declarative ArgoCD or Flux syncs chart + values from Git. No manual helm upgrade commands — values always come from Git.
💡 Personal Advice:
Never helm upgrade without values. Missing values = reset to defaults. Always provide values via --values, --reuse-values, or both. This is the #1 Helm mistake.
helm get values --all is your post-upgrade check. After every upgrade, verify values are correct. Compare with the previous revision's values.
Install helm-diff. Use it every time. helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff Shows exactly what will change. Like terraform plan for Helm. Non-negotiable for production upgrades.
Values in Git, not in heads. Store values-prod.yaml in Git. Review value changes in PRs. Never set production values from memory or the CLI.
AD18
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD18
Kustomize Overlay — Wrong Image Tag in Production

🔍 Symptom: After deploying with kubectl apply -k overlays/production, the production Deployment runs easypj/jobpost:latest instead of easypj/jobpost:v2.1.3. The production overlay's kustomization.yaml doesn't override the image tag from the base — the base's :latest tag leaks into production.

  kubectl get deploy easypj-web -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'
  easypj/jobpost:latest     ← Wrong! Should be v2.1.3!

  cat base/kustomization.yaml
  images:
  - name: easypj/jobpost
    newTag: latest           ← Base uses :latest!

  cat overlays/production/kustomization.yaml
  bases:
  - ../../base
  # NO images: override! Production inherits :latest from base!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Production overlay missing images: override: The base kustomization.yaml has images: [{name: easypj/jobpost, newTag: latest}] but the production overlay doesn't override newTag. Production inherits latest.
  2. Wrong overlay applied: kubectl apply -k overlays/staging was run instead of overlays/production. The staging image tag (latest) deployed to production.
  3. Image tag override has incorrect syntax: The production overlay has newName: easypj/jobpost but newTag: latest was accidentally copied from base.
  4. Kustomize build not tested before apply: Team ran kubectl apply -k without first running kubectl kustomize to preview the rendered YAML.
  5. CI/CD using wrong kustomization path: Pipeline kubectl apply -k ./ resolves to the base directory, not the production overlay.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Base kustomization.yaml accidentally committed with :latest — developer tested locally and forgot to revert
  2. Strategic merge patch not matching — patch targets wrong container name, image override not applied
  3. Multiple overlays chained — dev → staging → production, and production inherits staging's :latest
  4. Kustomize version mismatch — CI uses older Kustomize that doesn't support images: field
  5. kubectl kustomize output not validated — CI applies generated YAML without checking image tag
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New team setting up Kustomize from scratch: Overlay structure created but image overrides not understood — base images used everywhere.
  2. Git branch merge conflict in kustomization.yaml: Production overlay's images: override lost during merge — reverted to base.
  3. ArgoCD sync from wrong path: ArgoCD Application points to base/ instead of overlays/production — serves base config in production.
  4. Kustomize vs Helm confusion: Team used to Helm values, new to Kustomize overlays — didn't realize overlays must override images explicitly.
  5. Monorepo Kustomize structure too complex: 10+ overlays with shared bases — hard to trace which image each environment uses.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl kustomize overlays/production | grep "image:" Build the Kustomize output and check what image tag is rendered. This is what gets applied.
cat overlays/production/kustomization.yaml and verify images: overrides exist Each overlay MUST override the image tag for its environment. Check that newTag is specific and not :latest.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The production overlay's kustomization.yaml doesn't override the image tag. Kustomize overlays INHERIT from the base — any field not explicitly overridden in the overlay uses the base value. Production inherited :latest from the base instead of having its own newTag: v2.1.3.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add images: override to production overlay images: [{name: easypj/jobpost, newTag: v2.1.3}] in overlays/production/kustomization.yaml Overrides the base image tag. Every overlay should have its own images: section.
2. Always preview with kubectl kustomize before apply kubectl kustomize overlays/production | grep "image:" | head -5 Check the rendered output. If you see :latest in production manifests, the overlay isn't overriding.
3. Use digest instead of tag in production overlay images: [{name: easypj/jobpost, digest: sha256:abc123...}] Digest is cryptographically immutable. No tag movement can change what production runs.
4. Add CI validation for production image tags kubectl kustomize overlays/production | grep -q "latest" && echo "ERROR: latest tag in production!" && exit 1 Block deployments with :latest tag. CI/CD should reject any production manifest containing :latest.
5. Remove images from base if all overlays override If every overlay sets its own image, remove images: from the base. The base should have placeholders that overlays must specify.
💡 Personal Advice:
Every overlay must override the image tag. No exceptions. Production overlay → specific version. Staging overlay → specific version. Dev overlay → specific version. Never let :latest leak through.
kubectl kustomize is your preview tool. Run it before every kubectl apply -k. It shows exactly what Kubernetes will receive. Catch image tag mistakes before they hit the cluster.
Base Kustomization should be minimal. Put common configuration in base. Put environment-specific overrides (images, replicas, resources) in overlays. Never put environment-specific values in base.
Use CI to block :latest in production. A simple grep in CI catches this before deployment. The cost of the check is zero. The cost of :latest in production is catastrophic.
AD19
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD19
Kustomize ConfigMap Generator — Unnecessary Pod Restarts

🔍 Symptom: Every kubectl apply -k causes a rolling restart of all pods, even when no application configuration changed. The ConfigMap generator appends a content hash to the ConfigMap name, creating a new ConfigMap each time. The Deployment references it by the new name, triggering a rolling update — even for whitespace-only changes.

  kubectl get configmap | grep django
  django-config-7f8d9c6b5e   1      2h    ← Previous
  django-config-9a8b7c6d5e   1      1m    ← NEW (whitespace change!)
  django-config-8e7f6d5c4b   1      3d    ← Old

  kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-web
  REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
  15        ConfigMap hash changed    ← Whitespace-only!
  14        ConfigMap hash changed    ← Comment change!
  13        ConfigMap hash changed    ← Actual config change
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. ConfigMapGenerator always creates new ConfigMaps: Kustomize's configMapGenerator appends a content hash to the name. ANY change — even whitespace or comments — creates a new ConfigMap and triggers a Deployment rollout.
  2. ConfigMap used as envFrom or volume mount: If the Deployment references ConfigMap by generated name, each new ConfigMap changes the pod spec — triggering a rolling update of ALL pods.
  3. No disableNameSuffixHash configured: Without disableNameSuffixHash: true, Kustomize ALWAYS generates a new ConfigMap name. Use this to keep a stable name.
  4. Whitespace or formatting changes in config files: Editor auto-formatting changes trailing spaces or line endings — ConfigMap content hash changes even though the actual config is the same.
  5. Multiple config files in generatorLiterals: Kustomize hashes the combined content of ALL files. Changing one comment in one file changes the hash for everything.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Editor adding newline at end of file — trailing newline changes hash but not application behavior
  2. Git merge conflict markers in config file — merge artifacts in file, ConfigMap created with garbage content
  3. ConfigMap size approaching 1MB limit — Kustomize generates hash from truncated content, hash unstable
  4. Helm upgrade triggering Kustomize rebuild — Helm post-renderer runs Kustomize, double-generation issue
  5. Immutable ConfigMaps with different hash — immutable ConfigMap can't be updated in place, new one created each time
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. ArgoCD auto-sync triggering frequent restarts: ArgoCD syncs every 3 minutes — ConfigMap hash changes detected by diff, new ConfigMap applied, pods restart.
  2. CI/CD pipeline applying Kustomize on every commit: Even README changes trigger pipeline — Kustomize generates new ConfigMap, pods restart unnecessarily.
  3. Old ConfigMaps never cleaned up: 50+ ConfigMaps with different hashes accumulated — confusing, wastes etcd space.
  4. Multiple teams editing same config files: Team A and Team B edit different files in same ConfigMap — hash changes from either team cause restarts for both.
  5. Lack of understanding of Kustomize hash behavior: New team doesn't know that configMapGenerator creates new ConfigMaps — surprised by rolling restarts.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get configmap -l app=<label> --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp Check how many ConfigMaps exist. If you see dozens with different hashes, the generator is creating new ones on every apply.
kubectl kustomize overlays/production | grep "configMap" Preview the generated ConfigMap name. Compare with what's currently in the cluster.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Kustomize's configMapGenerator creates a new ConfigMap with a content hash suffix on every build. The Deployment references this generated name, so every apply triggers a pod restart. Use disableNameSuffixHash: true for stable names, or use generatorOptions: {labels: {...}} to manage lifecycle.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Disable hash suffix for stable ConfigMap names configMapGenerator: [{name: django-config, disableNameSuffixHash: true, files: [config.ini]}] No hash appended — ConfigMap name stays constant. But: pods won't automatically restart on config changes.
2. Use immutable ConfigMaps with versioned names configMapGenerator: [{name: django-config-v2, files: [config.ini]}] Manually version the ConfigMap name. Update the Deployment reference when you want a restart — not automatically.
3. Clean up old ConfigMaps kubectl get cm -l app=easypj-web | grep "django-config-" | tail -n +4 | awk '{print $1}' | xargs kubectl delete cm Keep only the last 3 ConfigMaps. Delete older ones to prevent etcd bloat.
4. Use --prune with kubectl apply kubectl apply -k overlays/production --prune -l app=easypj-web Prune old resources that are no longer in the Kustomize output. Automatically cleans up old ConfigMaps.
5. Separate configs that change frequently Put stable configs in one ConfigMap (disableNameSuffixHash) and dynamic configs in another (with hash). Only dynamic changes trigger restarts.
💡 Personal Advice:
The hash is a feature, not a bug. ConfigMap hash suffix ensures pods restart when config changes. But if you're getting 15 restarts a day, you need to separate configs or disable the hash.
disableNameSuffixHash = stable name, no auto-restart. Use it when config changes should NOT trigger pod restarts (e.g., feature flags). Pods read the updated ConfigMap via volume mount auto-refresh.
Clean up old ConfigMaps regularly. Without pruning, you'll accumulate hundreds of ConfigMaps. Set up a CronJob or use --prune with kubectl apply.
Use .gitattributes to prevent whitespace changes. * text=auto Prevents line ending changes when multiple OS developers edit the same config files. Reduces hash changes from formatting.
AD20
🚀 CATEGORY 2: APP DEPLOYMENT — Issue AD20
Helm vs Kustomize — Wrong Tool Chosen for Simple Deployment

🔍 Symptom: A simple 3-replica Django Deployment with a Service requires a 25-line Helm chart with templates, values, and helpers. But the team only needs to change the image tag per environment. Using Helm for this simple case creates unnecessary complexity — Kustomize would do the same job with 5 lines in an overlay.

  tree helm-chart/
  helm-chart/
  ├── Chart.yaml           ← 10 lines of metadata
  ├── values.yaml          ← 50 lines of defaults
  ├── templates/
  │   ├── _helpers.tpl     ← 30 lines of template functions
  │   ├── deployment.yaml  ← 60 lines (mostly Go template syntax)
  │   ├── service.yaml     ← 25 lines
  │   └── NOTES.txt        ← 10 lines
  └── charts/              ← Sub-charts (empty)

  tree kustomize/overlays/production/
  kustomize/overlays/production/
  └── kustomization.yaml   ← 8 lines
      bases: [../../base]
      images: [{name: easypj/jobpost, newTag: v2.1.3}]
      replicas: [{name: easypj-web, count: 3}]
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Helm chosen for simple environment overrides: The only variation between environments is image tag and replica count. Helm's templating is overkill — Kustomize overlays are purpose-built for this.
  2. Team only knows Helm, unaware of Kustomize: Helm was the first tool learned. Kustomize exists but team hasn't invested time to learn it — defaulting to Helm for everything.
  3. Organization standardized on Helm globally: Company mandate: "all deployments must use Helm." Simple apps suffer from the complexity of templating when overlays would suffice.
  4. Go template complexity causing bugs: Helm templates use Go templating with whitespace control ({{- -}}). Simple YAML errors from incorrect indentation are common.
  5. Over-engineering from the start: "We might need complex templating later" — but the app never needed it. The complexity was paid upfront and never amortized.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Helm chart from artifact hub — team uses full chart when they only need deployment + service
  2. Both Helm and Kustomize used together — kubectl apply -k with helm template as base, double complexity
  3. Helm hooks not needed but configured — pre-install/post-upgrade hooks add complexity without value
  4. Kustomize not installed in CI/CD — team uses Helm because it's pre-installed, Kustomize requires setup
  5. Helm release management needed for rollback — but kubectl rollout undo does the same for Deployments
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New project, no established tooling: Greenfield project — team picks Helm because "everyone uses Helm" without evaluating if it fits the use case.
  2. ArgoCD can use both — team confused: ArgoCD supports Helm, Kustomize, and plain YAML. New team doesn't know which to choose.
  3. Helm chart written by previous team: Inherited infrastructure — chart is too complex to refactor, team maintains complexity they didn't create.
  4. No decision framework for tool selection: Organization has no guidelines for when to use Helm vs Kustomize vs plain YAML — every team decides independently.
  5. kind/kubeadm environments — Kustomize built into kubectl: kubectl apply -k works with no installation — team doesn't know Kustomize is already available.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl kustomize and helm version Kustomize is built into kubectl (since 1.14). No installation needed. kubectl apply -k ./overlays/production works immediately.
Ask: "Do I need conditional logic in my YAML?" If NO → Kustomize. If YES → Helm. Kustomize = patch-based configuration. Helm = template-based generation. Different tools for different jobs.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Helm was chosen for a use case where Kustomize is the better tool. Helm excels at packaging complex apps with conditional logic and dependencies. Kustomize excels at managing configuration variants across environments. For simple environment overrides (image, replicas, resources), Kustomize requires 90% less code.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Choose the right tool for the job Kustomize: environment variants, simple patches. Helm: packaging, conditional logic, dependencies, distribution. Plain YAML: single environment, no variants.
2. Migrate simple apps from Helm to Kustomize helm template mychart | kubectl kustomize as a migration path Render the Helm chart once, use the output as a Kustomize base. Then create overlays for environments.
3. Use Helm for complex, distributable apps If your app has 10+ templates, sub-charts, hooks, and conditional features — Helm is the right tool. Don't reinvent Helm in Kustomize.
4. Use Kustomize for environment management Base + overlays (dev/staging/prod) with minimal YAML. Kustomize is built into kubectl — no extra tooling needed.
5. Create a team decision framework Document: "Kustomize for config variants, Helm for packaging and distribution, plain YAML for one-offs." Prevents tool choice paralysis.
💡 Personal Advice:
Kustomize is built into kubectl. You already have it. kubectl apply -k ./overlays/production No installation, no plugin, no package manager. If you have kubectl (and you do), you have Kustomize.
Helm for packaging. Kustomize for configuration. They're complementary, not competitors. Use Helm charts to package complex apps. Use Kustomize to customize them for each environment.
If your all your templates do is {{ .Values.image }}, you don't need Helm. Kustomize's images: and replicas: fields handle 80% of environment customization. Don't write Go templates for simple variable substitution.
Start simple, add complexity only when needed. Plain YAML → Kustomize → Helm → ArgoCD. Add each layer only when the previous one no longer meets your needs. Don't jump to Helm on day one.

📊 Category 3: Observability & Maintenance (15 Issues)OM1-OM15

🟡 Intermediate — Probe, Logging, and Monitoring Issues

Issues from misconfigured liveness/readiness/startup probes, logging configuration, kubectl debugging, and metrics collection.

📌 OM1–OM5: Probes & Health Check Failures

OM1
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM1
Liveness Probe Too Aggressive — Container Restarts Endlessly

🔍 Symptom: The Django container restarts every 30 seconds despite serving traffic normally. kubectl get pods shows RESTARTS: 47. The liveness probe has initialDelaySeconds: 5 and periodSeconds: 5 with failureThreshold: 3, giving Django only 15 seconds to respond before being killed — but Django takes 20 seconds to process some API requests under load.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME                            READY   STATUS    RESTARTS     AGE
  easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde    1/1     Running   47           2h
  # 47 restarts in 2 hours — liveness probe is killing healthy pods!

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde | grep -A10 Liveness
  Liveness:  http-get http://:8000/healthz delay=5s timeout=3s period=5s #success=1 #failure=3
  # 5s delay + (3 failures × 5s) = 20s max — too short for Django under load!

  kubectl logs easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde --previous | tail -3
  [14:30:20] GET /api/jobs?page=5 — Processing...
  [14:30:22] Liveness probe timeout — request took 8 seconds!
  [14:30:23] SIGTERM received — container killed by kubelet!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. initialDelaySeconds too low: The probe starts checking 5 seconds after container start. Django takes 15-20 seconds to load models and connect to PostgreSQL. The probe fails 3 times before Django is even ready — container restarts.
  2. timeoutSeconds too short for app under load: Default timeout is 1 second. Under load, /healthz takes 3-5 seconds to respond. Probe times out, counts as failure. Set timeoutSeconds to 5-10.
  3. failureThreshold too low combined with short periodSeconds: 3 failures × 5 seconds = 15 seconds of grace. A temporary DB connection blip or GC pause exceeding 15 seconds kills the container.
  4. Liveness probe endpoint does real work: The /healthz endpoint runs DB queries and checks Redis connectivity. Under load, these checks compete with real traffic — making the probe slower and increasing failure risk.
  5. periodSeconds too frequent: Checking every 5 seconds adds unnecessary load. For most web apps, 10-20 seconds is sufficient. Frequent checks waste resources and increase false-positive failure risk.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Probe uses exec instead of httpGet — exec opens a new process per check, slow under load
  2. Health endpoint not optimized — runs complex computation instead of simple status check
  3. Database connection pool exhausted — health check waits for a connection, probe times out
  4. Resource limits too low — CPU throttling causes health check response to lag beyond timeout
  5. Node overloaded — kubelet itself slow, probe requests queued behind other kubelet tasks
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Probe defaults from Helm chart too aggressive: Default chart values set for lightweight Go apps, not heavyweight Django — never tuned for the actual application.
  2. New cluster with slower storage: App starts in 10s on SSDs, but new cluster uses HDDs — startup takes 60s, probe configured for 10s kills it.
  3. Metrics-server not installed: No resource usage data — team can't see that CPU throttling is causing probe timeouts.
  4. CI/CD pipeline copied probe config from staging: Staging has no load — probes work fine. Production under load reveals the misconfiguration.
  5. No startup probe configured: Without startupProbe, liveness and readiness compete during startup — liveness kills the container before readiness can signal it's ready.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -E "Liveness|Readiness|Startup" Check ALL probe configurations at once. Look for short delays, short timeouts, and low failure thresholds.
kubectl logs <pod> --previous | tail -20 The last log entries of the killed container. Look for long-running requests or "SIGTERM received" messages.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The liveness probe is configured too aggressively for a Django application. initialDelaySeconds: 5 doesn't account for Django's model loading time, and periodSeconds: 5 with failureThreshold: 3 gives only 15 seconds of grace — too short for a database-backed app under load. Increase initialDelaySeconds to 30, periodSeconds to 10, and failureThreshold to 5.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Increase initialDelaySeconds for app startup livenessProbe: {initialDelaySeconds: 30, ...} Give Django 30 seconds before the first liveness check. Measure actual startup time and add 50% buffer.
2. Increase failureThreshold and periodSeconds failureThreshold: 5, periodSeconds: 10 5 failures × 10 seconds = 50 seconds of grace before restart. Enough for most temporary slowdowns.
3. Add timeoutSeconds explicitly timeoutSeconds: 5 Default is 1 second — way too short. Set to 5-10 seconds to allow for slow health check responses under load.
4. Add a startupProbe for slow-starting apps startupProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000}, failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 2} Gives Django 60 seconds to start. Liveness and readiness wait until startup probe succeeds.
5. Make the health endpoint lightweight Don't run DB queries in the liveness endpoint — liveness should only check if the process is alive. Use readiness for dependency checks. Separate the two concerns.
💡 Personal Advice:
Liveness probe = "Is the process stuck?" Not "Is the app healthy?" Liveness should be a lightweight check — just return 200 if the process is alive. Save dependency checks (DB, Redis) for the readiness probe.
Use startupProbe for ANY app that takes >10 seconds to start. Django, Spring Boot, Rails — all need startups. Without startupProbe, liveness kills the container during startup. Always add it.
Formula: failureThreshold × periodSeconds = total grace period. If your grace period is 15 seconds, your app dies during ANY 15-second slowdown. Set the grace period to at least 60 seconds for DB-backed apps.
Test probes under load in staging first. Probes that work at idle may fail under 1000 req/s. Run load tests against your staging cluster before deploying probe configs to production.
OM2
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM2
Readiness Probe Fails — Pod Running but Not in Service Endpoints

🔍 Symptom: Pod is Running and looks healthy, but receives zero traffic. kubectl get endpoints shows the pod IP is missing from the Service endpoints. The readiness probe is failing because it checks /healthz on port 8080, but Django listens on port 8000. The pod is perfectly healthy but invisible to the Service.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME                            READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
  easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde    0/1     Running   0          5m

  kubectl get endpoints easypj-api
  NAME          ENDPOINTS   AGE
  easypj-api    <none>      2d     ← No pod IPs in endpoints!

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde | grep -A5 Readiness
  Readiness:  http-get http://:8080/healthz delay=0s timeout=1s
  Warning  Unhealthy  5m    Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 500
  # Probe hitting port 8080 — Django is on port 8000!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Wrong port in readiness probe: Probe targets port 8080 but the app listens on 8000. Port mismatch = probe always fails. kubectl describe pod shows the port — compare with the actual containerPort.
  2. Wrong path in readiness probe: Probe hits /health but the app exposes /healthz. Returns 404 — probe considers this a failure. Always verify the exact health endpoint path.
  3. Readiness probe checks unavailable dependency: The /ready endpoint checks DB connectivity, but the DB pod isn't ready yet. Probe keeps failing — pod never added to Service, creating a circular dependency.
  4. initialDelaySeconds not set for readiness: Probe starts immediately (delay=0s). App hasn't finished loading — first few checks fail. If failureThreshold is reached before the app is ready, pod stays NotReady.
  5. Readiness probe uses exec with wrong command: exec: {command: ["cat", "/tmp/ready"]} but the file is never created. Probe always fails.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Probe protocol mismatch — httpGet used but app only serves HTTPS, connection refused
  2. NetworkPolicy blocking kubelet probe traffic — kubelet IP not in allowed ingress rules
  3. Readiness probe and liveness probe swapped — readiness checks return 500, liveness checks return 200
  4. Pod security context blocking probe — non-root user can't bind to the probe port
  5. Container runtime issue — specific CRI version has bug with HTTP probe handling
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Helm chart values.yaml has wrong default port: Chart defaults to port 8080 (Java standard) but easypj uses 8000 (Python/Django standard).
  2. Base image changed port between versions: Django 4.2 used port 8000, Django 5.0 changed default to 8080 — probe config not updated.
  3. Kustomize overlay missing probe overrides: Base has correct probe, but production overlay doesn't override — uses staging port which differs.
  4. Multiple containers in pod — probe targets wrong container name: Probe configured for container "django" but the container is named "api" in the Deployment.
  5. kubelet version mismatch with probe API: Older kubelet doesn't support certain probe fields — silently ignores them, defaults applied.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A10 "Readiness:" and kubectl get endpoints <svc> Compare the probe port/path with the actual container port. Empty endpoints = readiness probe failing.
kubectl exec <pod> -- curl -v localhost:<actual-port>/<probe-path> Manually test the probe from inside the container. If curl works but the probe fails, the probe configuration is wrong.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The readiness probe targets the wrong port (8080 vs 8000). The pod runs fine, but the probe always fails because there's nothing listening on port 8080. The pod is never added to the Service endpoints — it's invisible to traffic. Fix: change port: 8080 to port: 8000.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Fix the probe port kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"django","readinessProbe":{"httpGet":{"port":8000}}}]}}}}' Change the probe port to match the actual container port. The pod will immediately become Ready.
2. Add initialDelaySeconds to readiness probe readinessProbe: {initialDelaySeconds: 10, ...} Give the app time to initialize before the first probe check. Prevents false failures during startup.
3. Verify probe path returns 200 kubectl exec <pod> -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" localhost:8000/healthz Manually test the health endpoint. If it returns non-200, fix the endpoint before fixing the probe.
4. Match port names, not just numbers ports: [{name: http, containerPort: 8000}] and httpGet: {port: http} Use named ports for probes. If the port number changes, the probe follows the name automatically.
5. Verify endpoints after fix kubectl get endpoints easypj-api --watch Watch endpoints populate with pod IPs as the readiness probe starts succeeding.
💡 Personal Advice:
0/1 READY but Running = readiness probe failing. If the pod is Running but not Ready, the readiness probe is the issue. Check port, path, and manual curl from inside the pod.
Always use named ports in probe definitions. httpGet: {port: http} Named ports decouple probe config from port numbers. If you change the port, update it in one place (containerPort), not five.
Readiness = traffic switch. Liveness = restart switch. Readiness controls whether the pod is in Service endpoints. Liveness controls whether the pod stays alive. Different purposes, different tuning.
Empty endpoints are always a probe or selector problem. No endpoints = either readiness probe failing OR Service selector doesn't match pod labels. Check both with kubectl describe.
OM3
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM3
Slow-Starting App Killed Before Ready — No Startup Probe

🔍 Symptom: Django with large database migrations takes 90 seconds to start. The liveness probe is configured with initialDelaySeconds: 30 and failureThreshold: 3 — giving only 30 + (3×10) = 60 seconds total. Django is killed by liveness probe at 60 seconds, never reaching Ready. Pod restarts, cycle repeats forever.

  kubectl get pods -w
  easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde   0/1   Running             0     0s
  easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde   0/1   Running             1     60s  ← Killed!
  easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde   0/1   Running             1     65s
  easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff    1     70s

  kubectl logs easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde --previous | tail -5
  [14:30:20] Applying database migrations...
  [14:30:50] Migration 12/25: adding index to users table...
  [14:30:55] Liveness probe failed: timeout
  [14:31:00] SIGTERM — killed by kubelet (liveness probe failure)
  # Killed at migration 12/25 — never finished starting!

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api | grep -i startup
  (empty — no startupProbe configured!)
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No startupProbe configured: Without a startup probe, liveness and readiness probes compete during startup. Liveness kills the container before the app finishes initializing. Always add a startupProbe for apps that take >10 seconds to start.
  2. Liveness initialDelaySeconds too short for migrations: initialDelaySeconds: 30 doesn't account for database migrations. Django with 25 migrations takes 90-120 seconds — probe starts checking at 30s, kills at 60s.
  3. Large database migration slows startup: Each migration adds time. 5 migrations = 15s. 50 migrations = 150s. Liveness probe timing must scale with migration count.
  4. CPU limit throttling slows migrations: Migrations are CPU-intensive (index creation, data transformation). If CPU limit is 500m, migrations take 3× longer than on unlimited CPU.
  5. Readiness probe checking during startup: Without startupProbe, readiness starts immediately. If it checks DB connectivity and DB isn't ready, it fails — but liveness is also checking and kills the pod.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Database migration stuck waiting for lock — migration competes with another instance, blocks indefinitely
  2. initContainer for migrations would solve this — migrations should run in an initContainer, not at app startup
  3. Persistent volume slow I/O — migrations writing to slow NFS/CIFS storage, taking much longer than expected
  4. Python dependency imports slow on first load — Django loads all models, each import takes time on cold start
  5. DNS resolution slow during startup — Django resolves DB hostname, DNS timeout causes startup delay
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Fresh database with no migrations applied: New environment — all 25 migrations run for the first time (slow). Production runs only 1 (fast) — startupProbe tuned for production kills staging pods.
  2. ResourceQuota limiting CPU during startup: Namespace has low CPU quota — pod gets minimal CPU during migration, startup takes 5× longer.
  3. Cluster node under memory pressure: Node swapping — all processes slow down, including Django migrations and health check responses.
  4. Helm chart defaults without startupProbe: Community chart doesn't include startupProbe — every deployment suffers from this issue.
  5. Different K8s versions handle probes differently: Older kubelet (pre-1.20) doesn't support startupProbe — only option is to increase initialDelaySeconds massively.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -E "Startup|Liveness|Restart Count" Check if startupProbe exists. If not, and the pod restarts before becoming Ready, this is likely the issue.
kubectl logs <pod> --previous | grep -iE "migration|starting|ready|killed|sigterm" Look for evidence that the app was still initializing when killed. Migration progress logs confirm this.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: No startupProbe is configured for a slow-starting Django application. Without startupProbe, the liveness probe starts checking at initialDelaySeconds (30s) and kills the container after failureThreshold × periodSeconds (30s more) — 60 seconds total. Django needs 90+ seconds for migrations. The fix: add a startupProbe with failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 5 giving 150 seconds of startup grace.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add a startupProbe with generous failureThreshold startupProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000}, failureThreshold: 30, periodSeconds: 5} Gives Django 150 seconds (30×5) to complete startup. Liveness and readiness wait until startup succeeds.
2. Move migrations to initContainer Run python manage.py migrate in an initContainer. The main container starts with migrations already applied — fast startup.
3. Increase liveness initialDelaySeconds as fallback livenessProbe: {initialDelaySeconds: 120, ...} Even with startupProbe, set a reasonable initialDelaySeconds. If startupProbe succeeds at 90s, liveness starts at 120s.
4. Run migrations in CI/CD or as a Job Apply migrations BEFORE deploying the new version. Use a Kubernetes Job or CI/CD pipeline step — app starts instantly.
5. Monitor startup probe success rate kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep "Started container" Verify the startup probe succeeded. If it still fails, increase failureThreshold further.
💡 Personal Advice:
Every Django/Rails/Spring app needs a startupProbe. These frameworks are slow to boot. Without startupProbe, you're in a race between liveness and startup — and liveness always wins.
Migrations in initContainers, not in the app. Separate concerns: initContainer runs migrations (one-time), main container serves traffic. App startup becomes predictable and fast.
startupProbe failureThreshold × periodSeconds = total startup window. 30 × 5 = 150 seconds. Measure your app's maximum startup time and double it for safety.
K8s 1.18+ supports startupProbe. Use it. It was added specifically to solve this problem. If your cluster is older than 1.18, upgrade — or massively increase liveness initialDelaySeconds.
OM4
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM4
TCP Probe Fails — Container Port and Probe Port Mismatch

🔍 Symptom: A TCP socket probe is configured for PostgreSQL to check port 5432, but the probe always fails. The pod stays in Not Ready state. kubectl describe pod shows "Liveness probe failed: dial tcp :5432: connect: connection refused." PostgreSQL is running and accepting connections — but on a different port (5433) due to a custom configuration.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
  easypj-db-0       0/1     Running   0          5m    ← Running but NOT Ready!

  kubectl describe pod easypj-db-0 | grep -A5 "Liveness:"
  Liveness:  tcp-socket :5432 delay=30s timeout=5s
  Warning  Unhealthy  Liveness probe failed: dial tcp :5432: connect: connection refused

  kubectl exec easypj-db-0 -- pg_isready -p 5433
  /var/run/postgresql:5433 - accepting connections  ← PostgreSQL on 5433!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. TCP probe port doesn't match container port: Probe checks port 5432 (default) but PostgreSQL was configured to listen on port 5433. The probe dials the wrong port — connection refused.
  2. Container hasn't started listening yet: TCP probe starts before PostgreSQL finishes its startup sequence (WAL recovery, checkpoint). Probe should have initialDelaySeconds set.
  3. Probe targets wrong host: TCP probe defaults to pod IP, but the probe configuration explicitly sets host: 127.0.0.1 — PostgreSQL is bound to 0.0.0.0 only. Remove the host field or set to pod IP.
  4. PostgreSQL configured to listen on Unix socket only: listen_addresses = '' in postgresql.conf — no TCP listener at all. Probe will always fail.
  5. Container port name mismatch: Probe references port by name port: pgsql but containerPort name is postgresql. Named port lookup fails, probe defaults to port 0.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. TCP probe timeout too short — PostgreSQL under load takes >1s to accept new connections, default timeout kills it
  2. IPv6 vs IPv4 mismatch — probe tries ::1 but PostgreSQL only listens on 0.0.0.0 (IPv4)
  3. Container security context blocking port — seccomp or AppArmor profile prevents binding to the probe port
  4. Kubelet network issue — kubelet can't reach pod network namespace, TCP probe fails even though port is open
  5. probe port set to 0 — port field missing or misconfigured, defaults to 0 which always fails
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. StatefulSet uses different port than standalone: PostgreSQL StatefulSet chart defaults to 5432, but custom Docker image uses 5433 — probe misconfiguration.
  2. CNI plugin delay on new cluster: Pod starts but networking isn't fully ready — TCP probe fails in the first few seconds, pod marked unhealthy.
  3. Cluster with dual-stack networking: IPv4 and IPv6 — probe binds to wrong IP version, connection refused on the other.
  4. Kind/minikube port forwarding interference: Host-level port forwarding conflicts with pod-level TCP probe — probe hits wrong process.
  5. Container restart changes port: ConfigMap mount changes port on restart — probe still uses old port, fails after first restart.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A3 "Liveness:\|Readiness:" and kubectl exec <pod> -- ss -tlnp Compare the probe port with the actual listening ports inside the container. They must match.
kubectl exec <pod> -- nc -zv localhost <probe-port> Manually test the TCP connection from inside the container. If nc fails, the probe will too.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The TCP socket probe is configured for port 5432 but PostgreSQL is listening on port 5433. The probe can't establish a connection — always fails. Fix: change the probe port to match the actual PostgreSQL listening port, or reconfigure PostgreSQL to listen on the expected port.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Fix the probe port to match the container kubectl patch sts easypj-db -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"postgres","livenessProbe":{"tcpSocket":{"port":5433}}}]}}}}' Change the probe port to the actual PostgreSQL listening port.
2. Use named ports for consistency ports: [{name: pgsql, containerPort: 5433}] and tcpSocket: {port: pgsql} Reference ports by name. If PostgreSQL is reconfigured to a different port, update only the containerPort.
3. Add initialDelaySeconds for database startup livenessProbe: {tcpSocket: {port: pgsql}, initialDelaySeconds: 30, ...} PostgreSQL needs 10-30 seconds for WAL recovery and checkpoint. Give it time before probing.
4. Verify with pg_isready inside the container kubectl exec easypj-db-0 -- pg_isready -p <port> If pg_isready accepts connections but the probe fails, the probe configuration is wrong — not PostgreSQL.
5. Use exec probe with pg_isready for accurate health check exec: {command: ["pg_isready", "-U", "postgres"]} For databases, an exec probe running pg_isready is more reliable than a raw TCP check — it verifies the DB is actually accepting queries.
💡 Personal Advice:
TCP probes check connectivity, not application health. A TCP probe succeeding only means the port is open — not that PostgreSQL is ready to serve queries. Use exec probes with pg_isready for databases.
Always test probes manually from inside the container. kubectl exec <pod> -- nc -zv localhost <port> If your manual test works and the probe fails, the probe config is wrong. Debug from the inside out.
Named ports prevent configuration drift. If every probe and Service references port "pgsql" by name, changing the number only requires updating the containerPort definition.
Default PostgreSQL port is 5432 — but verify. Custom Docker images, ConfigMaps, or startup scripts can change the port. Never assume — always check with ss -tlnp inside the container.
OM5
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM5
exec Probe Fails — Distroless Image Has No Shell

🔍 Symptom: A liveness probe using exec: {command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "curl -f http://localhost:8000/healthz"]} fails immediately with "exec format error" or "no such file or directory." The container uses a distroless Python image — it has no shell (/bin/sh), no curl, and no debugging tools. The exec probe can't run.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME              READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
  easypj-api-abcde  0/1     Running   12         10m    ← 12 restarts!

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api-abcde | grep -A5 Liveness
  Liveness:  exec [/bin/sh -c curl -f http://localhost:8000/healthz] delay=10s
  Warning  Unhealthy  Liveness probe failed: 
    OCI runtime exec failed: exec: "/bin/sh": stat /bin/sh: no such file or directory
  # Distroless images have NO SHELL — exec probe can't run!

  kubectl exec easypj-api-abcde -- ls /bin/sh
  error: failed to exec in container: container has no shell: unknown
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Distroless image has no shell: Google's distroless images contain ONLY the runtime (Python) and its dependencies. No bash, sh, curl, wget, or any tools. exec probes that invoke /bin/sh or /bin/bash will always fail.
  2. Probe command references missing binary: command: ["curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8000/healthz"] — curl is not in the distroless image. Probe fails with "executable file not found."
  3. Probe written for a different base image: Developer tested probe on python:3.12-slim (has bash + curl), but production uses gcr.io/distroless/python3 (has neither). Probe works in dev, fails in prod.
  4. Probe uses shell features (pipes, redirects): command: ["sh", "-c", "curl ... | grep OK"] — pipes require a shell. Without /bin/sh, the probe can't parse the command.
  5. Wrong probe type for distroless: exec probes are inherently incompatible with distroless images. Use httpGet or tcpSocket probes instead — they don't require binaries inside the container.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Probe references absolute path that doesn't exist — /usr/bin/curl vs /usr/local/bin/curl in different base images
  2. Probe command is a script that depends on environment — script uses env vars that aren't set in the distroless image
  3. Probe uses Python but Python path differs — /usr/bin/python vs /usr/local/bin/python3 in distroless
  4. Image built FROM scratch — even fewer tools than distroless, no libc, no dynamic linker
  5. Multi-arch image — probe binary compiled for amd64 but running on arm64, exec format error
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Security team mandated distroless images: All production images switched to distroless — all existing exec probes broke. Need to convert to httpGet probes.
  2. CI/CD pipeline doesn't test probes against distroless: Integration tests use debug images (with shell) — probes pass in CI but fail in production with distroless.
  3. Helm chart probe defaults use exec: Community chart has default exec probes — deploying with distroless images breaks silently.
  4. New cluster with strict Pod Security Standards: Restricted PSS blocks certain exec probe patterns — probes that worked in Baseline fail in Restricted.
  5. Distroless images updated, tools removed: Image v1 had busybox for debugging — v2 removed it for security. Probes that relied on it break.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A10 "Liveness:" and check the error message "no such file or directory" = binary missing. "exec format error" = wrong architecture. Check which image you're using.
docker run --rm --entrypoint ls <image> /bin/sh /usr/bin/curl Verify what tools exist in the image. If /bin/sh doesn't exist, you can't use shell-based exec probes.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The container uses a distroless image that has no shell and no command-line tools. exec probes that invoke /bin/sh or curl will always fail. The fix: switch to httpGet probes which don't require any binaries inside the container — they're performed by the kubelet from outside.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Switch from exec probe to httpGet probe livenessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000}, ...} httpGet probes are performed by kubelet — no tools needed inside the container. Works with ANY image.
2. If you MUST use exec, add a minimal shell to the image COPY --from=busybox /bin/sh /bin/sh Add just /bin/sh from busybox (a few KB). Enough for exec probes. Compromise between security and functionality.
3. Use a dedicated health check binary in the app Build a small Go binary that checks app health — include it in your distroless image. Probe runs the binary directly, no shell needed.
4. Use tcpSocket probe for port-only checks tcpSocket: {port: 8000} Simplest probe — just checks if port is open. No tools, no shell, no HTTP parsing needed.
5. Test probes against the production image in CI docker run --rm <prod-image> <probe-command> Run the exact probe command against the production image. If it fails in CI, it will fail in Kubernetes.
💡 Personal Advice:
Use httpGet probes for distroless images. Always. httpGet probes are performed by the kubelet from the node, not inside the container. They work with scratch, distroless, and any other minimal image.
Test probes against the EXACT image you deploy. Dev images have shells and tools. Production images don't. Test probes against the production image in CI, not the dev image.
exec probes are powerful but fragile. They let you run any command, but that command must exist in the image. httpGet and tcpSocket probes are safer and more portable across base images.
distroless = secure but hard to debug. Plan ahead. Have a plan for debugging distroless containers before you need it. Know about kubectl debug, ephemeral containers, and httpGet probes before your first incident.

📌 OM6–OM10: Logging & Debugging Failures

OM6
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM6
kubectl logs Returns Empty — App Writes Logs to File Not stdout

🔍 Symptom: kubectl logs easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e returns nothing — empty output. The Django app is running and serving traffic, but all logs are written to /var/log/app/django.log inside the container instead of stdout/stderr. kubectl logs only captures stdout/stderr — file-based logs are invisible.

  kubectl logs easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e
  (no output — empty!)

  kubectl exec easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e -- tail -5 /var/log/app/django.log
  [14:30:20] GET /api/jobs 200 45ms
  [14:30:22] POST /api/jobs 201 120ms
  [14:30:25] GET /api/jobs/42 200 15ms
  # All logs are in the file — stdout is empty!

  cat Dockerfile | grep -i log
  LOG_FILE=/var/log/app/django.log    ← App configured to log to FILE!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. App configured to log to file instead of stdout: Django's LOGGING config has a FileHandler writing to /var/log/app/django.log. kubectl logs only captures stdout/stderr. Change to StreamHandler with stream: sys.stdout.
  2. Gunicorn logging to file: Gunicorn's --error-logfile /var/log/gunicorn-error.log and --access-logfile /var/log/gunicorn-access.log redirect logs away from stdout. Use - for stdout: --access-logfile -.
  3. Log file path not on a volume: Logs written to the container filesystem disappear when the pod restarts. Even if you exec in, old logs are lost after a restart.
  4. Log rotation filling disk: Log file grows without rotation — container disk fills up, app crashes. stdout logging avoids this because kubelet handles rotation.
  5. Multi-line logs broken in kubectl logs: File logging preserves multi-line stack traces. stdout logging may split them — but this is the 12-factor app standard.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Logging sidecar reading files — sidecar container tails the log file and outputs to its own stdout, adding complexity
  2. Python buffering stdout — logs in memory, not flushed until buffer fills. Set PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
  3. Log level set too high — INFO logs written to file but stdout only gets WARNING/ERROR
  4. Fluentd/Fluent Bit DaemonSet reading files from host — works but requires hostPath volumes, adds operational complexity
  5. Multiple log files for different Django apps — scattered across the filesystem, hard to correlate in kubectl logs
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Legacy app migrated from VMs: App originally ran on VMs with log files on disk. Containerizing without changing the logging config — kubectl logs shows nothing.
  2. No centralized logging stack: Without EFK/Loki/Datadog, kubectl logs is the only debugging tool. File-based logs = zero visibility.
  3. Django DEBUG=False silences console output: Production settings disable console logging while enabling file logging — kubectl logs becomes useless.
  4. New team unfamiliar with 12-factor app: Developers don't know that containers should log to stdout. File logging is "how we've always done it."
  5. Cloud provider log collector expects files: AWS CloudWatch agent or GCP ops agent configured to scrape files — team configured files for the collector, forgot kubectl logs.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl logs <pod> --tail=10 and kubectl exec <pod> -- ls /var/log/ If kubectl logs is empty but log files exist inside the container, the app is logging to files. Fix the logging config.
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/fd/1 and kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/fd/2 Check if anything is writing to stdout (fd 1) or stderr (fd 2). If both are empty, all output is going elsewhere.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Django application is configured to log to a file (/var/log/app/django.log) instead of stdout. This violates the 12-factor app principle. kubectl logs only captures container stdout/stderr — file-based logs require exec into the container. Fix: configure Django's LOGGING to use StreamHandler with sys.stdout.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Change Django logging to stdout 'handlers': {'console': {'class': 'logging.StreamHandler', 'stream': sys.stdout}} Use StreamHandler with sys.stdout. All Django logs now appear in kubectl logs.
2. Configure Gunicorn to log to stdout CMD ["gunicorn", "--access-logfile", "-", "--error-logfile", "-", "easypj.wsgi"] The - argument redirects gunicorn logs to stdout. Now gunicorn access/error logs appear in kubectl logs.
3. Set PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 Ensures Python doesn't buffer stdout. Logs appear immediately in kubectl logs, not in delayed batches.
4. Use logging sidecar ONLY if necessary If you MUST keep file logging (legacy app), use a sidecar container that tails the log file and outputs to its own stdout.
5. Verify with kubectl logs after fix kubectl logs -f deploy/easypj-api Stream logs to confirm they appear in real-time. Generate some traffic to trigger log output.
💡 Personal Advice:
Containers MUST log to stdout/stderr. This is the 12-factor app rule #11. kubectl logs, Loki, Fluentd, Datadog — they all expect stdout. File logging in containers is an anti-pattern.
PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 in every Python Dockerfile. Without it, Python buffers stdout and logs appear in chunks. Set it as an ENV in your Dockerfile so logs are always real-time.
kubectl logs is your first debug tool. Make it work. If kubectl logs shows nothing, you're flying blind. Fix logging to stdout before anything else — it's the foundation of all debugging.
Sidecar logging is a workaround, not a solution. It adds complexity (two containers, shared volume, coordination). Fix the app to log to stdout instead. Only use sidecars for apps you can't modify.
OM7
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM7
Multi-Container Pod — Checking Wrong Container Logs

🔍 Symptom: kubectl logs easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e shows nginx access logs, but the developer needs Django error logs. The pod has two containers — nginx and django. Without -c django, kubectl logs defaults to the first container defined in the pod spec (nginx), showing the wrong logs.

  kubectl logs easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e
  10.244.1.5 - - [11/Jun/2026:14:30:22] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 4521
  10.244.2.8 - - [11/Jun/2026:14:30:25] "POST /api/jobs HTTP/1.1" 201 120
  # This is NGINX access log — NOT Django error log!

  kubectl get pod easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'
  nginx django   ← Two containers — kubectl logs defaults to FIRST (nginx)!

  kubectl logs easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e -c django
  [ERROR] django.db.utils.OperationalError: could not connect to server
  # THIS is the error log we needed!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. -c flag omitted for multi-container pod: kubectl logs defaults to the FIRST container in the pod spec. If nginx is defined before django, kubectl logs shows nginx logs. Always use -c <container>.
  2. Pod has initContainers that ran previously: kubectl logs shows the first regular container, but --previous shows the first initContainer logs — confusion about which container's logs are shown.
  3. Sidecar container generates most logs: nginx sidecar has high traffic — its access logs flood kubectl logs output. Django error logs are buried or missed.
  4. --all-containers flag not used: kubectl logs --all-containers=true shows logs from ALL containers. Without it, only one container's logs appear.
  5. Container ordering changes between deployments: CI/CD changes container order in the pod spec — kubectl logs (without -c) shows different containers after each deploy.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Ephemeral containers — kubectl logs doesn't show ephemeral container logs by default, need specific flags
  2. Container restarting — logs from previous instance overwritten, need --previous to see crash logs
  3. Log rotation by kubelet — old logs rotated away, only recent logs available from specific container
  4. kubectl stern or kubetail tool — third-party tool shows merged logs but may filter out errors
  5. Container names too similar — "django" and "django-init" — easy to specify wrong container name with -c
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New pod with additional sidecar added: Istio/envoy sidecar injected — now there are 3 containers. Default container shifted, logs confusing.
  2. Pod presets or mutating webhooks adding containers: Admission controller adds containers — unexpected additional containers change which is "first."
  3. Helm chart adding sidecars conditionally: Chart adds monitoring sidecar in production but not staging — container list differs between environments.
  4. Team unfamiliar with multi-container debugging: New developers don't know about -c flag — waste time reading wrong container logs.
  5. kind/minikube — logs from pause container: Local cluster shows pause container logs when container name not specified — confusing for beginners.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}' List ALL container names. Then query each with kubectl logs <pod> -c <name>. The first name is the default.
kubectl logs <pod> --all-containers=true --tail=5 Show logs from ALL containers at once. Useful for quick overview — find which container has the error.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: kubectl logs defaults to the first container defined in the pod spec. In a multi-container pod, this may not be the container you want. Always specify the container with -c <container-name> or use --all-containers=true to see all logs.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Always specify -c for multi-container pods kubectl logs easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e -c django --tail=50 Explicitly name the container. Makes your intent clear and avoids confusion.
2. Use --all-containers for broad debugging kubectl logs deploy/easypj-web --all-containers=true -f Streams logs from ALL containers in the pod. Labels each line with the container name.
3. Use kubectl stern for multi-pod, multi-container log streaming stern easypj-web -c django --since 5m Stern shows logs from all pods matching a pattern. Color-coded by pod. Better than kubectl logs for multi-pod debugging.
4. Create aliases for frequently accessed containers alias klog-django='kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api -c django --tail=100 -f' Save time during incidents. Pre-configure aliases for each service's primary container.
5. Use kubectl logs deploy/... for Deployment-level logging kubectl logs deploy/easypj-web -c django Automatically picks a pod from the Deployment. No need to copy-paste pod names.
💡 Personal Advice:
kubectl logs without -c is a gamble in multi-container pods. It picks the first container — which changes if your pod spec changes. Always be explicit. Always use -c.
Know your containers before debugging. kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}' Run this first. Surprises about which containers exist waste time during incidents.
stern is worth the install. Color-coded, regex-filtered, multi-pod log streaming. Once you use stern, you'll never go back to plain kubectl logs for multi-pod debugging.
Istio/Envoy injection adds containers silently. Your 2-container pod becomes 3-container with envoy. kubectl logs defaults may change. Always check with -o jsonpath first.
OM8
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM8
CrashLoopBackOff — Developer Doesn't Check --previous Logs

🔍 Symptom: Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. kubectl logs easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e shows only the latest (crashing) instance's startup messages — not the actual error that caused the crash. The error is in the PREVIOUS instance's logs, but the developer doesn't use --previous. Hours wasted guessing the cause.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME                            READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
  easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde    0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   14

  kubectl logs easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde
  [14:30:55] Starting Django 4.2...
  [14:30:56] Loading models...
  (container crashed — no error shown in CURRENT logs!)

  kubectl logs easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde --previous
  [14:30:20] Starting Django 4.2...
  [14:30:22] Applying database migrations...
  [14:30:50] django.db.utils.ProgrammingError: column "new_field" does not exist
  [14:30:51] SIGTERM — container exited with code 1
  # ← THIS is the actual error! Only visible in --previous logs!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Developer doesn't know about --previous: kubectl logs --previous shows logs from the PREVIOUS container instance — the one that crashed. Without it, you only see the current (restarting) instance, which hasn't failed yet.
  2. CrashLoopBackOff restarts too fast for current logs: Container crashes in 3 seconds. Current logs show only startup messages — the crash happens after kubectl logs captures the output.
  3. Error logged just before crash — not in current logs: The error message is the LAST thing the crashed instance logged. The current instance hasn't reached that point yet — error is invisible.
  4. Container restarts reset log stream: Each restart = new log stream. kubectl logs without --previous shows the new stream — empty or incomplete.
  5. --previous not documented in team runbooks: Team debugging guides don't mention --previous. Developers use kubectl logs, see nothing useful, and guess.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. kubelet log rotation deleted previous logs — too many restarts, kubelet rotated away the crashed instance's logs
  2. Container outputs to stderr but developer checks stdout — error on stderr, kubectl logs shows stdout by default
  3. Crash reason in Events, not logs — kubectl describe shows "OOMKilled" but developer only checks logs
  4. Application crashes before logging framework initializes — error not captured by logging, only visible via exec or describe
  5. --since flag used with --previous — time filter excludes the actual crash time, previous logs filtered out
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New team, no K8s training: Developers come from Docker Compose — don't know about kubectl logs --previous. This is a training gap.
  2. Logging aggregator delay: Loki/EFK stack ingests logs with 2-minute delay — previous instance logs not yet visible in centralized logging.
  3. Pod restart count exceeds kubelet log retention: After 50+ restarts, kubelet has rotated away the first crash's logs — root cause lost forever.
  4. Production incident pressure: During an outage, developer panics and forgets --previous flag — extends outage by minutes.
  5. Monitoring doesn't alert on CrashLoopBackOff: Pod crashes for hours before anyone notices — --previous logs rotated away by then.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl logs <pod> --previous --tail=50 ALWAYS check previous logs for CrashLoopBackOff pods. The error is almost always in the previous instance, not the current one.
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A10 "Last State:" The Last State section shows the previous container's exit code and reason (Error, OOMKilled). Correlate with logs.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The developer doesn't use --previous when checking CrashLoopBackOff pod logs. kubectl logs without --previous shows the CURRENT container instance — which is still starting up and hasn't crashed yet. The error is in the PREVIOUS instance's logs. Always use kubectl logs --previous for crashed pods.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Always use --previous for CrashLoopBackOff pods kubectl logs <pod> --previous --tail=100 This should be muscle memory. CrashLoopBackOff = always check --previous first.
2. Check both current AND previous logs kubectl logs <pod> --tail=20 && echo "---PREVIOUS---" && kubectl logs <pod> --previous --tail=20 Sometimes the current instance has useful context. Compare both to understand the crash timeline.
3. Use kubectl describe for the exit reason kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 "Last State:" Exit Code 137 = OOMKilled (SIGKILL). Exit Code 1 = application error. Exit Code 0 = completed normally.
4. Add logging to centralized system Loki, ELK, or Datadog captures all logs — including previous instances. No kubectl logs needed for crash investigation.
5. Document this in the team runbook First line of the "Pod CrashLoopBackOff" runbook: "Run kubectl logs <pod> --previous". Save future developers hours.
💡 Personal Advice:
--previous is the most underused kubectl flag. It's the difference between seeing the crash error and guessing. For CrashLoopBackOff pods, it should be your FIRST command.
Exit codes tell the story before logs do. 137 = OOM (memory), 1 = app error, 0 = completed normally. Check kubectl describe for the exit code — it narrows your investigation.
Centralized logging saves --previous debugging. With Loki or ELK, you can query all logs — current, previous, and historical — without kubectl. Worth the investment.
If --previous is empty, kubelet rotated the logs. Too many restarts → logs gone. Increase container log retention or ship logs externally. Don't rely on kubectl logs for long-term debugging.
OM9
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM9
kubectl describe Events Ignored — Developer Misses Root Cause

🔍 Symptom: Pod is stuck in Pending for 30 minutes. Developer checks kubectl logs (empty), checks the Deployment YAML, checks the image — all look fine. The Events section of kubectl describe pod clearly states "0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory" — but the developer never reads the Events section, wasting 30 minutes on unrelated investigations.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME                            READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
  easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde    0/1     Pending   0          30m

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde | grep -A5 Events
  Events:
    Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
    ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
    Warning  FailedScheduling  30m   default-scheduler  0/3 nodes available: 
             3 Insufficient memory. preemption: 0/3 nodes available
  # ← Events section tells you EXACTLY why! 3 nodes, all out of memory!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Developer doesn't read describe output fully: kubectl describe output is long — the Events section is at the bottom and often overlooked. Developer checks the top section (container specs) and misses the critical Events.
  2. Events scrolled off screen: kubectl describe output is 100+ lines. Events are at the very end — terminal scrollback may not show them without piping to less.
  3. Developer checks only kubectl logs: Pod is Pending — has no running container, so kubectl logs returns empty. Developer assumes "no information available" instead of checking describe.
  4. Events provide the exact reason: "Insufficient memory" — the scheduler tells you precisely why the pod can't be placed. No need to guess about resource requests, node capacity, or taints.
  5. Describe includes ALL pod state transitions: Image pull success/failure, volume mount errors, scheduling decisions — all recorded as Events. Missing this section = missing the investigation's starting point.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Events expired — default event TTL is 1 hour. Old events may be gone, only recent ones visible
  2. kubectl describe pod vs kubectl describe deploy — different Events, developer checks the wrong resource
  3. Events in different namespace — developer checks default namespace but pod is in easypj-prod
  4. kubectl get events not used — kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp shows cluster-wide events
  5. Too many events — 200+ events for the pod, the important one is buried in noise
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New developers from non-K8s background: Used to docker logs, docker ps. kubectl describe is unfamiliar — they don't know Events exist.
  2. Monitoring dashboards don't surface events: Grafana shows pod status but not events. Developers rely on dashboards, miss the Events section.
  3. Cluster with 100+ pods crashing simultaneously: Events flood — node pressure events mixed with pod-specific events, hard to find the right one.
  4. No event-based alerting: "FailedScheduling" event exists but no alert fires — pod stays Pending for hours with no notification.
  5. kubectl describe output format unfamiliar: New team doesn't know that Events are the last section — stops reading halfway through.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A20 "Events:" The Events section is THE most important part of kubectl describe for troubleshooting. Always read it first.
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<pod> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp Shows only events for a specific pod, sorted by time. Cleaner than the full describe output.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The developer doesn't read the Events section of kubectl describe. The Events section contains scheduler decisions, image pull results, volume mount errors, and probe failures — it tells you exactly what's wrong. The fix is a habit change: always grep for Events first.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Always grep Events first from describe kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A20 "Events:" Make this your first command for any pod issue. The Events section gives you the root cause in seconds.
2. Use kubectl get events for focused output kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<pod> -n <ns> --sort-by=.lastTimestamp More focused than describe. Shows ONLY events for the target pod, sorted by time.
3. Check events at the Deployment level too kubectl describe deploy <name> | grep -A10 "Events:" Deployment-level events show ReplicaSet creation, scaling decisions, and rollout status.
4. Watch events in real-time during deployments kubectl get events -w --all-namespaces Watch events stream as they happen. See scheduling failures, image pulls, and probe results in real-time.
5. Add event-based alerts to monitoring Configure alerts for Warning-type events: FailedScheduling, FailedMount, BackOff, Unhealthy. Catch issues before developers notice.
💡 Personal Advice:
Events are Kubernetes telling you what's wrong in plain English. The scheduler, kubelet, and controllers write Events specifically to help you. Ignoring them is like ignoring error messages from your compiler.
kubectl describe → grep Events. Every time. Burn this into muscle memory. Before checking logs, before checking YAML, before ANYTHING else — read the Events.
kubectl get events is faster than describe for focused debugging. Use --field-selector to filter events for a specific pod. It's cleaner, faster, and easier to read than the full describe output.
Events have a TTL — they disappear after 1 hour. If a pod has been stuck for hours, old events may be gone. Check events early in your investigation, not as an afterthought.
OM10
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM10
kubectl apply Fails — Deprecated API Version Removed

🔍 Symptom: kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml fails with "no matches for kind Deployment in version extensions/v1beta1." The YAML uses apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1 which was removed in Kubernetes 1.16. The cluster is running 1.30 — this API hasn't existed for years. Old YAML templates are incompatible with the current cluster.

  kubectl apply -f easypj-web-deploy.yaml
  error: unable to recognize "easypj-web-deploy.yaml":
  no matches for kind "Deployment" in version "extensions/v1beta1"

  head -3 easypj-web-deploy.yaml
  apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1    ← REMOVED in K8s 1.16!
  kind: Deployment

  kubectl api-resources | grep -i deploy
  deployments  deploy  apps/v1  true  Deployment
  # Current API is apps/v1 — extensions/v1beta1 was deprecated years ago!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Old YAML template with deprecated apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1 was removed in K8s 1.16. The YAML was copied from a pre-2019 tutorial or blog post. Must use apps/v1.
  2. Cluster upgraded — old APIs removed: Cluster was upgraded from 1.15 to 1.30. APIs that were deprecated (but functional) in 1.15 are now REMOVED. Existing YAML files break.
  3. kubectl convert not used: kubectl convert -f old.yaml --output-version apps/v1 automatically converts deprecated API versions. Developer manually edits instead — introduces errors.
  4. Helm chart uses deprecated API version: Old chart template has apiVersion: extensions/v1beta1 in deployment.yaml. Chart needs updating.
  5. apiVersion mismatch between environments: Dev cluster is K8s 1.20 (still supports beta), production is 1.30 (removed). YAML works in dev, fails in prod.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Other common deprecations — networking.k8s.io/v1beta1 Ingress (removed 1.22), rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1beta1 (removed 1.22)
  2. kubectl explain not used to check available versions — kubectl explain deployment shows apps/v1 as the only version
  3. CI/CD pipeline has old kubectl — older kubectl generates YAML with deprecated apiVersions via --dry-run
  4. Custom Resource Definition removed — CRD apiVersion changed, old manifests reference removed version
  5. kubectl apply --validate=false bypasses API checks — manifests with wrong apiVersion accepted silently, then fail later
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New cluster with latest K8s: Fresh kubeadm 1.30 install — old YAML files from previous 1.15 cluster don't work. All deprecated APIs are gone.
