  2. kind cluster version mismatch with production: kind runs 1.30, YAML developed for 1.20 — deprecated APIs break immediately on kind.
  3. Old training materials used by junior devs: Team uses 2019 CKAD study materials with extensions/v1beta1 examples — need updated templates.
  4. kubeadm upgrade plan not checked: Cluster upgraded without running kubeadm upgrade plan — removed APIs were a surprise.
  5. Operator or controller still using deprecated APIs: Third-party operator watches extensions/v1beta1 — stops working after cluster upgrade.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl api-resources and kubectl explain <resource> Check which API versions are available. kubectl explain deployment shows the current apiVersion (apps/v1).
kubectl convert -f old.yaml --output-version apps/v1 --dry-run=client Automatically converts deprecated API versions. Preview the result with --dry-run before applying.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The YAML manifest uses a deprecated and removed API version (extensions/v1beta1). This API was removed in Kubernetes 1.16. The current cluster (1.30) doesn't serve it. Fix: change apiVersion to apps/v1 and update the spec to match the current schema.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Change apiVersion to the current version apiVersion: apps/v1 (for Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, ReplicaSets) Also add spec.selector.matchLabels — required in apps/v1 but not in extensions/v1beta1.
2. Use kubectl convert for automatic migration kubectl convert -f old-deploy.yaml --output-version apps/v1 > new-deploy.yaml kubectl convert handles the schema migration. Review the output, then apply.
3. Check all YAML files for deprecated APIs grep -r "extensions/v1beta1\|apps/v1beta1\|networking.k8s.io/v1beta1" *.yaml Audit all manifests before a cluster upgrade. Find and fix deprecated API versions proactively.
4. Use kubectl explain to check available versions kubectl explain deployment Shows the current API version and schema. Always check before writing YAML.
5. Add API version validation to CI/CD kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f deploy.yaml Server-side dry-run catches deprecated API errors before deployment. Fail the pipeline if the API version is rejected.
💡 Personal Advice:
extensions/v1beta1 is dead since K8s 1.16. If you see it in any YAML file, it was written before 2019. Replace with apps/v1 immediately. The spec structure is different — don't just change the version string.
Always run kubectl api-resources before writing YAML. It shows every available API and version. If your desired apiVersion isn't listed, find the replacement.
kubectl convert is the fastest migration tool. One command converts all deprecated fields and versions. Always review the output — it may add fields you didn't have before.
Check API deprecations BEFORE upgrading your cluster. Kubernetes documentation publishes a deprecation guide for each version. Run kubectl convert on all manifests before upgrading.

📌 OM11–OM15: Monitoring & CLI Debugging Tools

OM11
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM11
kubectl top Fails — metrics-server Not Installed

🔍 Symptom: kubectl top pods returns "error: Metrics API not available." The metrics-server is not installed on the cluster. Developers can't see pod CPU/memory usage and can't use HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) because HPA depends on metrics-server for resource metrics.

  kubectl top pods
  error: Metrics API not available

  kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep metrics
  (no output — metrics-server not deployed!)

  kubectl get apiservices | grep metrics
  v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io   kube-system/metrics-server   False (MissingEndpoints)
  # API service exists but has no backend — metrics-server not running!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. metrics-server not installed: metrics-server is NOT included in a default Kubernetes installation. It must be installed separately: kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml.
  2. metrics-server installed but pods not running: The Deployment exists but pods are CrashLoopBackOff — check logs for TLS certificate errors (common in kind/kubeadm).
  3. --kubelet-insecure-tls not set on kind/kubeadm: metrics-server needs --kubelet-insecure-tls flag on clusters without proper kubelet TLS certificates (kind, kubeadm). Without it, metrics-server can't scrape kubelet.
  4. NetworkPolicy blocking metrics-server: A deny-all NetworkPolicy blocks metrics-server from reaching kubelet (port 10250). Metrics-server pods show "unable to fully collect metrics."
  5. HPA configured but metrics-server missing: Team created HPA objects expecting autoscaling — HPA status shows "unable to get metrics" because metrics-server isn't running.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. metrics-server in different namespace — deployed to custom namespace, API service can't find it
  2. Resource limits on metrics-server too low — metrics-server OOMKilled under load, metrics gaps
  3. Kubelet read-only port (10255) disabled — newer K8s versions disable it, metrics-server must use authenticated port 10250
  4. Prometheus adapter used instead — team installed prometheus-adapter but not metrics-server, kubectl top still fails
  5. Cluster behind proxy — metrics-server can't reach kubelet through corporate proxy
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Fresh kubeadm cluster: kubeadm doesn't install metrics-server by default. Every new cluster needs manual installation.
  2. kind cluster without metrics-server: kind clusters are minimal — no metrics-server, no dashboard. Must install separately.
  3. New team assumes metrics-server is built-in: Coming from managed K8s (GKE, EKS) where metrics-server is pre-installed — don't realize it's optional.
  4. Air-gapped cluster can't pull metrics-server image: No internet access — need to download and side-load the metrics-server image.
  5. Monitoring stack not yet set up: New cluster without Prometheus/Grafana — metrics-server is the first step, but hasn't been installed yet.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep metrics and kubectl top nodes If no metrics-server pods, it's not installed. kubectl top nodes works if metrics-server is healthy.
kubectl get apiservices v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io Shows if the metrics API is registered and whether its backend (metrics-server) is Available.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: metrics-server is not installed on the cluster. It's an optional add-on that must be explicitly deployed. Without it, kubectl top fails and HPA can't scale based on CPU/memory. Install with: kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Install metrics-server kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml Deploys metrics-server in kube-system. Wait 1-2 minutes for metrics to start collecting.
2. Add --kubelet-insecure-tls for kind/kubeadm kubectl patch deploy metrics-server -n kube-system --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]' Required on kind and kubeadm clusters where kubelet TLS certs aren't trusted.
3. Verify metrics are available kubectl top nodes && kubectl top pods -A If nodes show metrics but pods don't, wait another minute for pod metrics to be collected.
4. Check HPA is working after metrics-server install kubectl describe hpa <name> | grep -A5 "Metrics:" HPA should now show current CPU/memory utilization values. Scaling decisions resume.
5. For air-gapped clusters, side-load the image docker pull registry.k8s.io/metrics-server/metrics-server:v0.7.0 && kind load docker-image registry.k8s.io/metrics-server/metrics-server:v0.7.0 --name kind-cka-lab Pull on a connected machine, transfer and load into air-gapped cluster.
💡 Personal Advice:
metrics-server is NOT installed by default on kubeadm or kind. Managed K8s (EKS, GKE, AKS) pre-installs it. kubeadm and kind do not. Always install it as part of cluster setup.
--kubelet-insecure-tls is required for dev clusters. On kind, kubeadm, and minikube, kubelet certificates are self-signed. Without this flag, metrics-server can't scrape metrics.
No metrics-server = no HPA based on CPU/memory. HPA relies on metrics-server for resource metrics. Without it, HPA stays at minReplicas or reports "unable to get metrics."
kubectl top is your quick health check. If kubectl top nodes works, metrics-server is running. If not, it's either not installed or misconfigured.
OM12
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM12
OOMKilled — Container Memory Limit Too Low for Django

🔍 Symptom: Django pod restarts randomly with Exit Code 137. kubectl describe pod shows "OOMKilled" — the container exceeded its memory limit. The limit is set to 256Mi, but Django with PostgreSQL connections and template rendering needs ~512Mi under load. The container is killed by the OOM killer during traffic spikes.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME                            READY   STATUS    RESTARTS     AGE
  easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde    1/1     Running   8            2h

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api | grep -A5 "Last State:"
  Last State:    Terminated
    Reason:      OOMKilled
    Exit Code:   137         ← 128 + 9 (SIGKILL) = OOMKilled!

  kubectl get pod easypj-api -o yaml | grep -A3 "limits:"
  limits:
    cpu: "1"
    memory: 256Mi           ← Way too low for Django!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Memory limit set too low for the workload: Django needs 300-500Mi baseline. 256Mi limit is exceeded under any real load — OOM killer terminates the container. Increase to 512Mi or 1Gi.
  2. Memory leak in the application: Django process grows over time — each request adds memory that isn't freed. Eventually hits the limit. Check for query result caching, template caching, or unclosed DB connections.
  3. No memory request set — QoS class is BestEffort: Without a memory request, the pod is BestEffort QoS — first to be killed under memory pressure. Set requests == limits for Guaranteed QoS.
  4. Traffic spike causes temporary memory surge: 100 concurrent requests each allocating 2Mi = 200Mi surge. If baseline is 300Mi, total exceeds 500Mi limit. Need higher limit or lower concurrency.
  5. Worker process count too high: Gunicorn configured with 4 workers × 128Mi each = 512Mi. With 256Mi limit, even idle usage exceeds the limit. Reduce workers or increase limit.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Database connection pool too large — each connection uses memory, pooled connections accumulate
  2. DEBUG=True in production — Django debug toolbar and SQL logging consume extra 100-200Mi
  3. Large file uploads in memory — Django reads uploaded files into memory, 100MB file = 100MB RAM usage
  4. Python garbage collector not running — memory fragmentation, GC threshold not reached
  5. Third-party library memory leak — ORM, image processing, or PDF generation library leaking
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default Helm chart limits too low: Chart values.yaml has conservative defaults (256Mi/512Mi) — never adjusted for the actual workload.
  2. ResourceQuota limiting namespace memory: Namespace has 2Gi total quota — 4 pods × 512Mi would exceed it. Limits kept artificially low.
  3. No vertical scaling monitoring: Team doesn't use kubectl top or Prometheus to track memory usage — unaware the pod is at 95% memory constantly.
  4. Staging vs production resource divergence: Staging has 1Gi limit (no issues), production has 256Mi (cost cutting) — OOM only in production.
  5. New Django version uses more memory: Django 5.0 uses 20% more memory than 4.2 — existing limits no longer sufficient after upgrade.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -E "State:|Reason:|Exit Code:" and kubectl top pod <pod> Exit Code 137 = OOMKilled. Compare kubectl top memory usage with the configured limit.
kubectl logs <pod> --previous | grep -iE "memory|oom|killed|out of memory" The previous instance may have logged memory warnings before being killed.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The memory limit (256Mi) is set below the application's actual memory requirements. Django with multiple workers, database connections, and template rendering needs at least 512Mi. Under traffic load, memory spikes above 256Mi and the OOM killer terminates the container. Fix: increase memory: 512Mi (or 1Gi for safety) and set requests == limits for Guaranteed QoS.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Increase memory limit based on actual usage kubectl set resources deploy easypj-api --limits=memory=1Gi --requests=memory=1Gi Set to at least 2× observed peak usage. Use kubectl top to measure baseline and peak.
2. Set requests == limits for Guaranteed QoS resources: {requests: {memory: "1Gi"}, limits: {memory: "1Gi"}} Guaranteed QoS pods are the LAST to be killed under memory pressure. Production databases and APIs should use Guaranteed.
3. Reduce Gunicorn worker count CMD ["gunicorn", "--workers", "2", "--threads", "2", "easypj.wsgi"] Fewer workers = less memory per pod. Use --threads to handle more concurrent requests per worker.
4. Monitor memory with Prometheus + Grafana container_memory_working_set_bytes{pod="easypj-api-.*"} Set up dashboards and alerts. Alert when memory usage exceeds 80% of limit for >5 minutes.
5. Use HPA based on memory to scale out Scale pods out BEFORE memory becomes critical. Combined with proper limits, prevents OOMKilled entirely.
💡 Personal Advice:
Exit Code 137 = killed by OOM killer. Period. 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). Always means memory limit exceeded. Increase the limit or reduce memory usage. No other fix exists.
Always set memory requests == limits for production. Guaranteed QoS protects your pods from being killed under node memory pressure. BestEffort pods die first — don't let that be your API.
Measure, don't guess memory limits. Run load tests. Watch kubectl top. Use Prometheus. Know your app's memory profile before setting limits. Guessing 256Mi is a recipe for OOMKilled.
Django DEBUG=True in production = memory disaster. SQL query logging stores every query in memory. Debug toolbar adds overhead. Always set DEBUG=False in production — it saves memory AND improves security.
OM13
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM13
CPU Throttling — App Responds Slowly Under Load

🔍 Symptom: Django API response times increase from 50ms to 2000ms under load. The pod doesn't crash, doesn't restart — it's just slow. CPU limit is set to 200m (0.2 cores), but Django needs 500m+ to process concurrent requests. The kernel throttles CPU usage, causing request queuing and timeout-like behavior without actual errors.

  kubectl top pod easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde
  NAME                            CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
  easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde    200m          512Mi
  # CPU at limit (200m) — being throttled!

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api | grep -A3 "limits:"
  limits:
    cpu: 200m              ← 0.2 cores — too low for Django!
    memory: 512Mi

  curl -w "@curl-format.txt" -o /dev/null -s http://easypj-api/healthz
  time_total: 2.345s       ← Response time 2+ seconds on health check!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. CPU limit set too low for the workload: 200m (0.2 cores) is insufficient for Django processing concurrent API requests. The kernel throttles CPU usage — requests queue up, response times skyrocket. Increase to 500m-1 CPU.
  2. CPU throttling is silent: Unlike OOMKilled (which kills the container), CPU throttling just slows everything down. No error messages, no logs — just poor performance. Harder to detect.
  3. Gunicorn workers competing for limited CPU: 4 workers sharing 200m CPU = 50m each. Each request needs 100m+ for processing. Workers starve, requests pile up.
  4. No CPU request set: Without a CPU request, the pod is Burstable QoS. Under CPU contention, the pod's CPU can be taken by Guaranteed pods — throttling becomes worse.
  5. CPU limit = CPU request (no burst allowed): Setting both to 200m means the pod can NEVER use more than 200m — even if the node has idle CPU. Allow bursting with higher limit.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) period too short — default 100ms period causes micro-throttling even at moderate usage
  2. Node CPU contention — multiple pods competing for the same physical cores, all throttled simultaneously
  3. Python GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) — single Python process can only use 1 CPU core, tuning workers vs threads matters
  4. Database connection pooling not configured — every request opens a new DB connection, CPU spent on TCP handshakes
  5. Template rendering on every request — Django re-renders templates without caching, CPU-bound rendering slows responses
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Default LimitRange sets low CPU ceiling: Namespace LimitRange defaults to 200m max CPU — all pods get throttled. Adjust LimitRange.
  2. Cost optimization gone wrong: Team reduced CPU limits to save cloud costs — app performance degraded but nobody correlated it.
  3. New feature increased CPU usage: New PDF generation or image processing feature doubles CPU usage — existing limits no longer sufficient.
  4. HPA not configured for CPU scaling: App needs more replicas under load, but HPA is based on memory or not configured at all.
  5. kind/minikube — CPU limits enforced differently: Local clusters may not enforce CPU limits strictly — app works in dev but throttles in production.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl top pod <pod> and compare CPU(cores) with the configured limit If CPU usage is at or near the limit, throttling is occurring. The pod CAN'T use more CPU even if the node is idle.
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.stat and look for nr_throttled and throttled_time Non-zero throttled_time confirms CPU throttling is happening. This is the definitive evidence.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The CPU limit (200m) is set too low. Django needs more CPU to process concurrent requests. The kernel enforces the limit via CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) — when the pod exceeds 200m in a scheduling period, CPU access is throttled. Requests queue up, response times increase. Fix: increase CPU limit to at least 500m-1 and set requests < limits to allow bursting.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Increase CPU limit based on observed usage kubectl set resources deploy easypj-api --limits=cpu=1 --requests=cpu=500m Set limit higher than request to allow bursting. 500m baseline + burst to 1 CPU when needed.
2. Check throttling metrics directly kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.stat If nr_throttled > 0 and throttled_time is increasing, the pod is being throttled. Raise the limit.
3. Configure HPA based on CPU usage kubectl autoscale deploy easypj-api --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70 Scale out before CPU reaches the limit. More replicas = more aggregate CPU capacity.
4. Add response time monitoring Set up Prometheus alerts for p99 response time >1000ms. CPU throttling shows up as latency, not errors.
5. Tune workers and threads for CPU allocation --workers 2 --threads 4 Threads share CPU better than processes. 2 workers × 4 threads = handle 8 concurrent requests with less CPU overhead.
💡 Personal Advice:
CPU throttling is silent — monitor latency, not errors. Your app won't crash. It won't log errors. It'll just get slower. Monitor response time percentiles (p50, p95, p99) to detect throttling.
requests < limits for CPU is the best practice. Requests guarantee baseline. Limits allow bursting during traffic spikes. If requests == limits, you can't burst — every CPU cycle above baseline is throttled.
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/cpu.stat proves throttling. If throttled_time is >0, your pod has been throttled. No guessing, no correlation — definitive proof.
200m CPU is enough for Go/Rust, not for Python/Ruby. Language matters. Python's GIL and Django's ORM overhead need more CPU per request. 200m might work for a Go API but chokes Django.
OM14
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM14
Can't Debug Container — kubectl debug Ephemeral Container

🔍 Symptom: Django is returning 500 errors in production. Developer tries kubectl exec -it easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e -- /bin/sh but fails — the distroless image has no shell. Needs to inspect files, check environment variables, and test network connectivity but can't get into the container.

  kubectl exec -it easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e -- /bin/sh
  error: Internal error: container has no shell: unknown

  kubectl exec easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e -- ls /app/
  error: ... container has no shell
  # Distroless image — no shell, no tools, no way in!

  kubectl debug -it easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e --image=busybox --target=django
  If you don't see a command prompt, try pressing enter.
  / # ps aux
  PID   USER     TIME  COMMAND
  1     root      0:00 python manage.py runserver
  / # ls /app/
  manage.py  easypj/  static/  templates/
  / # cat /proc/1/environ | tr '\0' '\n' | grep DATABASE_URL
  DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@easypj-db:5432/jobpost
  # NOW we can debug! Ephemeral container saves the day!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Distroless/scratch image has no debugging tools: The production image is built for security and minimalism — no shell, no ls, no curl. kubectl exec requires a shell inside the container.
  2. kubectl debug with ephemeral containers not known: kubectl debug (K8s 1.18+) creates ephemeral containers that share the target container's namespaces. The developer doesn't know this command exists.
  3. Team relies on kubectl exec for all debugging: Habit from non-distroless days — exec into container, run tools, debug. Distroless breaks this workflow completely.
  4. --target flag not used with kubectl debug: Without --target, the ephemeral container is separate — can't see the target container's processes or filesystem. Must use --target=<container>.
  5. No debug image available in cluster: kubectl debug needs an image (busybox, alpine, netshoot). If the cluster can't pull images or is air-gapped, debug fails.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Ephemeral containers feature gate disabled — older clusters (pre-1.23) need EphemeralContainers=true feature gate
  2. --share-processes not used — can't see target container's processes from ephemeral container
  3. PodSecurityPolicy/PSS blocking ephemeral containers — restricted policy prevents ephemeral container creation
  4. CrashLoopBackOff — container exits too fast for kubectl debug to attach, need --copy-to
  5. RBAC not allowing pods/ephemeralcontainers — user doesn't have permission to create ephemeral containers
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Security team mandated distroless without training: All images switched to distroless — developers lost kubectl exec access. No training on kubectl debug.
  2. kind cluster — EphemeralContainers enabled by default: Kind 1.25+ supports ephemeral containers. Team doesn't know the feature exists on their own cluster.
  3. Debug image not cached locally: kubectl debug --image=busybox pulls from Docker Hub — slow on first use, times out during incidents.
  4. Air-gapped cluster — no debug images available: No internet access. Need to pre-load busybox or netshoot into the cluster registry.
  5. kubectl version too old for debug: kubectl 1.17 or older doesn't support kubectl debug. Cluster is 1.30 but developer has old kubectl binary.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> The primary command for debugging distroless containers. Creates an ephemeral container that shares the target's process namespace.
kubectl version --short and kubectl alpha debug (older versions) kubectl debug requires kubectl 1.18+. Older versions use kubectl alpha debug.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The container uses a distroless image with no shell or debugging tools. kubectl exec requires a shell. The fix: use kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> to create an ephemeral container that shares the target container's namespaces and provides debugging tools.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Use kubectl debug with ephemeral container kubectl debug -it easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e --image=busybox --target=django Creates ephemeral container with shell. Shares process, network, and filesystem namespaces with the target.
2. Use --copy-to for CrashLoopBackOff pods kubectl debug easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e --image=busybox --target=django --copy-to=debug-api -- sh Creates a COPY of the pod with a debug container. Original pod is untouched. Good for pods that restart rapidly.
3. Use --share-processes to see target processes kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=django --share-processes Enables process namespace sharing. ps aux shows the target container's processes.
4. Pre-pull debug images to all nodes kubectl create ds preload-debug --image=busybox as a DaemonSet Ensures busybox is cached on every node. kubectl debug starts instantly — no pull delay during incidents.
5. Add a debug image tag to your application easypj/jobpost:v2.1-debug (same app, with shell and tools) Build a parallel debug image. Switch to it temporarily for debugging, then switch back to distroless.
💡 Personal Advice:
kubectl debug is the distroless survival tool. Learn it before you need it. --target, --copy-to, and --share-processes are the three flags you need to know.
Practice kubectl debug on a healthy pod first. During an incident is the worst time to learn a new command. Debug a running pod today so you know the workflow.
Pre-pull busybox and netshoot to your nodes. During an outage, waiting 30 seconds for an image pull feels like an eternity. Pre-cache debug images.
netshoot is the ultimate debug image. kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container> Contains curl, dig, nmap, tcpdump, strace, iperf, netstat — every network and process debugging tool you'll ever need.
OM15
📊 CATEGORY 3: OBSERVABILITY — Issue OM15
kubectl exec Fails — RBAC Denies pods/exec Permission

🔍 Symptom: kubectl exec -it easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e -- /bin/sh fails with "Unable to upgrade connection: pods 'easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e' is forbidden: User cannot create resource 'pods/exec' in API group '' in the namespace 'easypj-prod'." The user's RBAC role doesn't include the pods/exec subresource. Can't get a shell into any pod.

  kubectl exec -it easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e -- /bin/sh
  Error from server (Forbidden): pods "easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e" is forbidden: 
  User "developer@easypj.com" cannot create resource "pods/exec" in API 
  group "" in the namespace "easypj-prod"

  kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n easypj-prod
  no     ← User doesn't have pods/exec permission!

  kubectl get role developer -n easypj-prod -o yaml | grep -A10 rules
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
  # Missing: pods/exec subresource!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. RBAC role doesn't include pods/exec subresource: kubectl exec requires the pods/exec subresource permission — separate from pods. The role has pods: get, list, watch — but not pods/exec: create.
  2. Developer role is read-only: The role follows least privilege — only get/list/watch. Exec requires create on pods/exec, which is a write operation. Read-only roles can't exec into pods.
  3. ClusterRole vs Role scoping: Role is namespace-scoped (easypj-prod). Developer trying to exec in easypj-dev where no RoleBinding exists.
  4. Wrong verb for pods/exec: pods/exec requires the create verb (creating a connection), not get or list. Common mistake: adding "exec" to the verbs list.
  5. kubectl exec also needs pods/log implicitly: Some setups require both pods/exec AND pods/log permissions. Missing either blocks kubectl exec.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Kubeconfig context has wrong user — using a different ServiceAccount than expected, with fewer permissions
  2. PodSecurityPolicy blocking exec — legacy PSP prevents exec into pods regardless of RBAC
  3. NetworkPolicy blocking kubelet API — exec traffic uses kubelet port 10250, blocked by network policy
  4. API server flag disabling exec — --enable-debugging-handlers=false disables kubectl exec entirely
  5. Mutating webhook stripping exec permissions — admission controller removes pods/exec from all bindings
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New cluster with strict RBAC: Security team locked down all permissions — developers have minimal access. pods/exec was forgotten.
  2. Production namespace has tighter RBAC: Dev namespace allows exec (for debugging), production doesn't (security policy). Developer tries production.
  3. kubectl debug used as exec workaround: kubectl debug creates ephemeral containers — requires pods/ephemeralcontainers permission, which may also be missing.
  4. AWS EKS — aws-auth ConfigMap not updated: New IAM user added to cluster but not mapped to a Kubernetes role — falls back to system:unauthenticated.
  5. kind/minikube — running as cluster-admin: Local clusters give full access — developer never encounters RBAC issues until production.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n <ns> and kubectl auth can-i --list -n <ns> Check what permissions you have. If pods/exec returns "no", you need a role update.
kubectl get role,rolebinding -n <ns> -o yaml | grep -A10 "pods/exec\|rules:" Check existing role definitions. Look for pods/exec in the resources list with create verb.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The user's RBAC role doesn't include the pods/exec subresource with create verb. kubectl exec requires a special subresource permission that's separate from basic pod access. The role needs: resources: ["pods/exec"], verbs: ["create"].
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add pods/exec to the user's Role kubectl patch role developer -n easypj-prod --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/rules/-","value":{"apiGroups":[""],"resources":["pods/exec"],"verbs":["create"]}}]' Adds pods/exec create permission to the existing role. User can now exec into pods.
2. Create a dedicated debug Role kubectl create role pod-debugger --verb=create --resource=pods/exec,pods/log -n easypj-prod Separate role for debugging. Bind to specific users or SAs who need exec access.
3. Verify with kubectl auth can-i kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n easypj-prod Should return "yes" after the role update. Test before trying kubectl exec again.
4. Use ephemeral containers as alternative kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container> Requires pods/ephemeralcontainers permission. May be allowed when pods/exec is blocked.
5. Audit existing RBAC for exec permissions kubectl get clusterrole,role -A -o yaml | grep -B5 "pods/exec" Find all roles with exec permission. Verify they're assigned to the right users.
💡 Personal Advice:
pods/exec is a SUBRESOURCE — not part of "pods". Granting "pods" with all verbs does NOT include pods/exec. Subresources must be explicitly listed in the resources array.
kubectl auth can-i is your RBAC debugger. Before filing a ticket, run kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n <ns>. It tells you immediately if RBAC is the issue.
create verb on pods/exec — not get, not list. kubectl exec creates a connection to the container. RBAC verb must be "create". This is the most common RBAC mistake for exec.
Production exec access should be tightly controlled. Exec into a production pod gives access to secrets, environment variables, and the filesystem. Grant sparingly and audit regularly.

🔐 Category 4: Config & Security (25 Issues)ES1-ES25

🟡→🔴 Intermediate to Advanced — ConfigMaps, Secrets, RBAC, SecurityContext, CRDs

The LARGEST category (25% of CKAD). Issues from ConfigMap/Secret misconfigurations, RBAC permission errors, SecurityContext hardening, resource limits, and CRD/Operator problems.

📌 ES1–ES5: ConfigMap Misconfigurations

ES1
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES1
ConfigMap Not Found — Pod Stuck in Pending Forever

🔍 Symptom: Pod stuck in ContainerCreating or Pending state indefinitely. kubectl describe pod shows "configmap 'django-config' not found." The Deployment references a ConfigMap via envFrom but the ConfigMap was never created — and optional: false (the default) blocks the pod from starting.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME                            READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
  easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde    0/1     ContainerCreating   0       10m

  kubectl describe pod easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde | grep -A5 Events
  Events:
    Warning  FailedMount  10m  MountVolume.SetUp failed: 
    configmap "django-config" not found

  kubectl get configmap django-config -n easypj-prod
  Error from server (NotFound): configmaps "django-config" not found
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. ConfigMap never created: The Deployment manifest references django-config but kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml was forgotten. kubectl get cm shows nothing.
  2. ConfigMap created in wrong namespace: ConfigMap exists in easypj-dev but the pod is in easypj-prod. ConfigMaps are namespace-scoped — each namespace must have its own.
  3. ConfigMap name typo in pod spec: Pod references django-config but the actual ConfigMap is django-conf. Single character difference — pod can't find it.
  4. optional: false is the default: Without optional: true, the pod BLOCKS on missing ConfigMap. Set optional: true for non-critical configs that have sensible defaults.
  5. ConfigMap deleted after pod was running: If a pod is running and its ConfigMap is deleted, the pod continues running — but any new pods can't start. Rollout after ConfigMap deletion fails.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Helm chart deployed without ConfigMap template — chart expects pre-created ConfigMap, but docs weren't followed
  2. ArgoCD sync ordering — ConfigMap created AFTER Deployment, pod starts before ConfigMap exists
  3. Git branch merge deleted ConfigMap YAML — merge conflict resolution accidentally removed the ConfigMap file from Git
  4. Namespace deletion/recreation — old namespace with ConfigMap deleted, new namespace without ConfigMap created
  5. ConfigMap created via kubectl create --dry-run=client — developer ran dry-run, saw output, forgot to remove --dry-run
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New namespace — no resources exist yet: Fresh namespace, Deployment applied before ConfigMap. Apply ConfigMap first, then Deployment.
  2. CI/CD pipeline ordering incorrect: Pipeline deploys Deployment before ConfigMap — race condition. Always deploy configs before workloads.
  3. Kustomize overlay missing configMapGenerator: Base has ConfigMap reference, but production overlay doesn't generate it — reference to non-existent ConfigMap.
  4. kind cluster — ConfigMap not synced between nodes: Rare — ConfigMap propagation delayed, new pod on different node can't find it.
  5. etcd backup restore incomplete: Restored from backup — ConfigMaps not included in backup scope, Deployments reference missing ConfigMaps.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get cm -n <ns> | grep <name> and kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep "not found" Verify the ConfigMap exists in the pod's namespace. The Events section tells you exactly which ConfigMap is missing.
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -A5 "configMapRef\|configMapKeyRef" Check which ConfigMaps the pod references. Compare names and namespaces with actual ConfigMaps.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The ConfigMap django-config doesn't exist in the pod's namespace. The pod references it with envFrom.configMapRef and the default optional: false prevents the pod from starting. Fix: create the ConfigMap in the correct namespace or set optional: true for non-critical configuration.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create the missing ConfigMap kubectl create cm django-config --from-literal=DEBUG=false --from-literal=ALLOWED_HOSTS=easypj.com -n easypj-prod Pod should immediately start mounting the ConfigMap and transition to Running.
2. Set optional: true for non-critical ConfigMaps envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: django-config, optional: true}}] Pod starts even if ConfigMap doesn't exist. Use for feature flags and optional settings.
3. Verify ConfigMap exists before deploying the Deployment kubectl get cm django-config -n easypj-prod || kubectl create cm ... Add existence check to CI/CD. Deploy ConfigMaps BEFORE Deployments that reference them.
4. Check across all namespaces kubectl get cm -A | grep django-config If found in the wrong namespace, copy it: kubectl get cm django-config -n easypj-dev -o yaml | sed 's/namespace: easypj-dev/namespace: easypj-prod/' | kubectl apply -f -.
5. Delete the stuck pod kubectl delete pod easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde After fixing the ConfigMap, delete the stuck pod. The Deployment creates a new one that mounts the ConfigMap.
💡 Personal Advice:
ConfigMap before Deployment. Always. Deploy configs first, then workloads. In CI/CD, order your apply commands: ConfigMaps → Secrets → Deployments. This prevents the "not found" deadlock.
optional: true saves you during partial deployments. For feature flags and non-critical settings, use optional: true. The pod starts with default values and picks up the ConfigMap when it's created.
Events tell you exactly which ConfigMap is missing. kubectl describe pod shows "configmap 'X' not found" — the name is right there. Don't guess, read the Events.
Namespaces isolate ConfigMaps. A ConfigMap in easypj-dev is invisible to pods in easypj-prod. Each namespace needs its own copy. Use Kustomize overlays to manage namespace-specific configs.
ES2
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES2
ConfigMap Volume Mount Overwrites Entire Directory

🔍 Symptom: Django can't find /app/easypj/wsgi.py after a ConfigMap is mounted. The ConfigMap was mounted at /app using mountPath: /app, which OVERWROTE the entire /app directory that contained the Django source code. The app crashes because all its Python files are gone — replaced by ConfigMap entries.

  kubectl logs easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde --previous
  python: can't open file '/app/manage.py': [Errno 2] No such file or directory

  kubectl exec easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde -- ls /app/
  DEBUG        ← ConfigMap key, not a Django file!
  ALLOWED_HOSTS  ← ConfigMap key!
  LOG_LEVEL    ← ConfigMap key!
  # WHERE IS manage.py, easypj/, static/?!

  kubectl get pod easypj-web -o yaml | grep -A5 "mountPath: /app"
  - mountPath: /app        ← OVERWROTE the entire /app directory!
    name: django-config
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. ConfigMap mounted at application root directory: mountPath: /app replaces the ENTIRE /app directory with ConfigMap contents. All application files (manage.py, easypj/, static/) are hidden. Use a subdirectory: mountPath: /app/config.
  2. subPath not used for individual files: Without subPath, mounting a ConfigMap key replaces the directory. With subPath, individual files can be mounted without deleting existing directory contents.
  3. Confusion between file mount and directory mount: Developer expected ConfigMap keys to be "added" to the directory. Actually, volume mounts REPLACE the directory — it's an overlay, not a merge.
  4. Multiple ConfigMaps mounted to same path: Two ConfigMaps with overlapping mount paths — the later one overwrites the earlier one. Only one volume can occupy a mountPath.
  5. ConfigMap with too many keys: 50+ keys in a ConfigMap mounted at /app/config — cluttered, hard to find the right file.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. subPath with ConfigMap key that doesn't exist — empty file created, app reads empty config
  2. defaultMode permissions too restrictive — ConfigMap files mounted with 000, app can't read them
  3. ConfigMap mounted as read-write (not possible) — developer confused about why changes to mounted files don't persist
  4. Symlinks in the original directory broken — mount replaces the directory, symlinks in the ConfigMap reference non-existent targets
  5. Mount propagation setting — HostToContainer or Bidirectional propagation causes unexpected behavior
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Helm chart with default mountPath at /app: Community chart uses /app as default mount path — incompatible with Django app that also uses /app.
  2. Kustomize overlay adding ConfigMap volume: Overlay adds ConfigMap mount at /app, unaware that base Deployment already has app at /app.
  3. New developer unfamiliar with volume mounts: Assumes ConfigMap "merges" with existing files — doesn't know volume mounts are replacements.
  4. Multi-container pod with shared volumes: ConfigMap mounted at /app for sidecar container — overwrites app files for main container sharing the volume.
  5. Migration from Docker Compose: Compose uses bind mounts which merge — Kubernetes volume mounts replace. Behavior difference surprises new users.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -A10 "volumeMounts:" and kubectl exec <pod> -- ls <mountPath> Compare the mountPath with the expected directory contents. If only ConfigMap keys appear, the mount overwrote the original files.
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -B5 "mountPath:" Check mountPath values — if any point to /app, /usr/share, or other app directories, investigate.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The ConfigMap is mounted at /app, overwriting the entire application directory. Volume mounts REPLACE the target directory — they don't merge. Fix: mount the ConfigMap at a subdirectory (/app/config) or use subPath to mount individual files without overwriting the directory.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Mount ConfigMap to a subdirectory mountPath: /app/config Creates /app/config/ directory with ConfigMap files. Original /app/ contents remain untouched.
2. Use subPath for individual file mounts mountPath: /app/settings.py, subPath: settings.py Mounts ONE file without replacing the directory. The rest of /app remains intact.
3. Use envFrom or valueFrom instead of volume mount envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: django-config}}] Inject config as environment variables — no directory overwrite risk.
4. Use items to selectively mount ConfigMap keys items: [{key: settings.py, path: settings.py}] Mount only specific keys from the ConfigMap. Other files in the directory are preserved.
5. Verify with kubectl exec after fixing kubectl exec <pod> -- ls /app/ Confirm manage.py, easypj/, static/, AND config files all exist in /app after the fix.
💡 Personal Advice:
Never mount a ConfigMap at /app, /usr, /etc, or /var. These directories contain your application. Mount ConfigMaps at dedicated paths: /app/config, /etc/app-settings, /secrets. Keep them separate.
Volume mounts REPLACE, they don't MERGE. Unlike Docker Compose bind mounts, K8s volume mounts completely replace the target directory. Every file that was there becomes invisible.
subPath is your friend for individual file mounts. Need to mount settings.py but not overwrite /app? Use subPath. It's the difference between replacing a directory and adding a single file.
Prefer envFrom for simple key-value configs. ConfigMap → env vars is simpler and safer than ConfigMap → volume mount. No directory overwrite risk. Use volume mounts only for file-based configs.
ES3
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES3
ConfigMap Too Large — 1MB Limit Exceeded

🔍 Symptom: kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml fails with "Too long: must have at most 1048576 bytes." The ConfigMap contains a large nginx configuration file or TLS certificate that exceeds the 1MB etcd limit. The entire ConfigMap is rejected — none of it is stored.

  kubectl apply -f nginx-config.yaml
  The ConfigMap "nginx-config" is invalid: 
  metadata.annotations: Too long: must have at most 1048576 bytes

  wc -c nginx.conf
  1204567 nginx.conf    ← 1.2 MB — exceeds 1 MB etcd limit!

  kubectl get cm nginx-config
  Error from server (NotFound): configmaps "nginx-config" not found
  # ConfigMap was never created — rejected by API server!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Single key in ConfigMap exceeds 1MB: A ConfigMap key (e.g., nginx.conf) is 1.2MB. etcd has a 1MB per-object limit. The entire ConfigMap is rejected. Split into multiple ConfigMaps or use smaller files.
  2. Large binary file stored in ConfigMap: TLS certificates, Java keystores, or binary config files stored in ConfigMap. ConfigMaps are for text — not binaries. Use Secrets for binary data.
  3. ConfigMap with hundreds of keys: 200+ small keys adding up to >1MB total. Combined size of ALL keys + metadata exceeds the limit.
  4. Large JSON/YAML config stored as single key: Entire application config (all environments, all settings) in one massive JSON file. Split per environment or per feature.
  5. annotations pushing it over the limit: Large last-applied-configuration annotation added by kubectl apply — combined with the data, exceeds 1MB.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. ConfigMap with embedded base64 data — base64 increases size by 33%, turning 800KB into >1MB
  2. Repeated config sections — same config replicated for 10 environments, bloating a single ConfigMap
  3. kubectl create cm --from-file=large-dir/ — directory with many files adds up beyond 1MB
  4. ConfigMap generated by script — script output containing debug data or logs accidentally included
  5. Compression not used — large text config could be compressed but is stored uncompressed
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. etcd size limit differs by provider: Some managed K8s have lower limits than 1MB — check your provider's documentation for actual limits.
  2. Nginx ingress controller with large config: Default nginx config grows as routes are added — eventually exceeds 1MB in ConfigMap.
  3. Migration from file-based config: App migrated from VM with 5MB config file — expected ConfigMap to handle it. Needs splitting.
  4. Kustomize configMapGenerator with large directory: Generator includes all files in a directory — some large, unexpected files push beyond the limit.
  5. No validation in CI/CD: ConfigMap size not checked before deploy — rejected at apply time, pipeline fails silently.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl create cm test --from-file=config.yaml --dry-run=server -o yaml | wc -c Server-side dry-run reveals if the ConfigMap would exceed the 1MB limit BEFORE applying.
kubectl get cm <name> -o json | jq '.data | to_entries | .[] | "\(.key): \(.value | length) bytes"' Check each key's size in an existing ConfigMap. Find the largest keys to split off.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The ConfigMap data exceeds the 1MB etcd object limit. A single key (nginx.conf) is 1.2MB — the entire ConfigMap is rejected by the API server. Fix: split the large config into multiple ConfigMaps, use smaller files, or store large configs as separate files on a PersistentVolume.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Split into multiple ConfigMaps nginx-config-part1 and nginx-config-part2. Mount both as separate volumes or combine in an initContainer.
2. Store large files on a PersistentVolume Mount a PVC and store large config files there. ConfigMaps are for small (<1MB) text-based configuration.
3. Use a separate container image with baked-in config Build a custom nginx image with the large config file baked in. Image layers have no 1MB limit.
4. Compress and decompress at runtime Store gzip-compressed config in ConfigMap. Decompress in an initContainer before the app starts.
5. Use binaryData for binary files binaryData: {keystore.jks: <base64>} Use binaryData field (not data) for binary content. Still subject to 1MB limit but avoids encoding issues.
💡 Personal Advice:
ConfigMap is for configuration, not for data. If your "config" is >1MB, it's probably not configuration — it's data. Store large files in PVs, object storage, or baked into images.
Always test with server-side dry-run for large ConfigMaps. kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f configmap.yaml Client-side dry-run doesn't check etcd limits. Always use server-side for size validation.
Split configs by feature, not by environment. One ConfigMap for Django settings, one for nginx config, one for logging — each smaller and easier to manage.
1MB includes metadata and annotations. The limit applies to the ENTIRE object, not just the data field. Large annotations (kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration) count toward the limit.
ES4
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES4
ConfigMap Updated — Pod Still Using Old Values

🔍 Symptom: You updated a ConfigMap with kubectl edit cm django-config and changed LOG_LEVEL: DEBUG to LOG_LEVEL: ERROR. Hours later, the Django pod is still logging at DEBUG level. The ConfigMap was updated, but the pod only reads ConfigMap values at startup — it doesn't auto-reload. The pod must be restarted.

  kubectl edit cm django-config
  configmap/django-config edited
  # Changed LOG_LEVEL from DEBUG to ERROR

  kubectl logs easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde --tail=3
  [14:30:20] DEBUG: SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE status='open'
  [14:30:22] DEBUG: Rendering template job_list.html
  # STILL logging DEBUG — 2 hours after ConfigMap edit!

  kubectl exec easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde -- env | grep LOG_LEVEL
  LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG      ← Pod still has OLD value!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Pod only reads env vars at startup: ConfigMap changes injected via envFrom are read once when the container starts. Updates to the ConfigMap don't update running pods. Must restart the pod.
  2. Volume-mounted ConfigMaps auto-update but app doesn't reload: ConfigMaps mounted as volumes update in the pod's filesystem within ~60 seconds. But the app must watch for file changes — Django doesn't auto-reload in production.
  3. Developer doesn't know pods must restart: "I edited the ConfigMap, why isn't it working?" — common misunderstanding. ConfigMaps are not live configuration servers.
  4. kubectl rollout restart needed but not run: kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-web triggers a rolling restart — all pods get the new ConfigMap values. Without it, old pods keep running.
  5. Kustomize ConfigMap hash triggers restart automatically: If using configMapGenerator, the hash suffix changes, triggering a rollout. But manual ConfigMap edits don't change hashes — no automatic restart.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Stale file handle — volume-mounted ConfigMap symlink not refreshed, pod reads old version despite update
  2. subPath mounts don't auto-update — unlike directory mounts, subPath-mounted files are NOT updated when ConfigMap changes
  3. Multiple replicas — only one pod restarted, others still on old config
  4. kubelet sync delay — ConfigMap update takes up to 60 seconds to propagate to the pod's filesystem
  5. ConfigMap edited with wrong editor — changes not actually saved, developer thought they edited it
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Reloader/Stakater not installed: Tools that auto-restart pods on ConfigMap changes are not installed — manual restarts always required.
  2. No CI/CD for ConfigMap changes: ConfigMaps edited directly (kubectl edit) without pipeline — no automatic rollout restart triggered.
  3. Team new to K8s: Expects ConfigMap updates to be "live" like a configuration server (Consul, etcd watch). Kubernetes doesn't work this way.
  4. Immutable ConfigMaps used: ConfigMap created with immutable: true — can't be edited in place at all. Must delete and recreate.
  5. kind cluster — kubelet sync slower: ConfigMap mount propagation may be slower on local clusters — takes >90 seconds to appear in pods.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl exec <pod> -- env | grep <key> and kubectl get cm <name> -o yaml | grep <key> Compare the ConfigMap value with the pod's environment. If they differ, the pod needs a restart.
kubectl rollout status deploy/<name> after kubectl rollout restart deploy/<name> Verify the restart completed and all pods are running the new configuration.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The ConfigMap was updated but the running pods still have the old values. Pods read environment variables from ConfigMaps ONLY at startup. Volume-mounted ConfigMaps update automatically (~60s) but the application must reload the file. Fix: run kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-web to restart all pods with the new ConfigMap.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Restart the Deployment kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-web Triggers a rolling restart. All pods restart and pick up the new ConfigMap values.
2. Install Reloader for automatic restarts kubectl apply -f https://github.com/stakater/Reloader/releases/latest/download/reloader.yaml Watches ConfigMaps/Secrets and auto-restarts Deployments when they change. Annotation: reloader.stakater.com/auto: "true".
3. Use Kustomize configMapGenerator with hash Kustomize appends a hash to the ConfigMap name. When the content changes, the name changes — Deployment rollout triggers automatically.
4. For volume mounts, implement file watching in the app Watch the mounted ConfigMap directory for changes. On change, reload configuration without restarting (if your framework supports it).
5. Verify with a canary test kubectl exec <new-pod> -- env | grep LOG_LEVEL After restart, confirm the new pods have the updated value. Old pods should be terminated.
💡 Personal Advice:
ConfigMap edits don't restart pods. YOU must restart them. This is the #1 ConfigMap misconception. Kubernetes doesn't have a built-in mechanism to restart pods on ConfigMap changes. Use rollout restart or Reloader.
Volume-mounted ConfigMaps update automatically (60s delay). But the app still needs to RELOAD the file. Most apps read config once at startup. File system notification or periodic reload is required.
kubectl rollout restart is the simplest fix. One command, rolling restart, zero downtime. Use it whenever you change a ConfigMap or Secret that's injected via envFrom.
subPath mounts do NOT auto-update. If you used subPath to mount individual ConfigMap keys, those files are STATIC — they never update. Only full directory mounts auto-refresh.
ES5
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES5
ConfigMap envFrom — Key Collision Overwrites Existing Env Vars

🔍 Symptom: Django can't connect to PostgreSQL — DATABASE_URL is set to sqlite:///db.sqlite3 instead of the correct PostgreSQL connection string. The Deployment has both a Secret (DATABASE_URL) and a ConfigMap (DATABASE_URL) — the ConfigMap key OVERWRITES the Secret key because ConfigMaps are listed AFTER Secrets in envFrom. Order matters.

  kubectl exec easypj-web-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde -- env | grep DATABASE_URL
  DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///db.sqlite3     ← Wrong! Should be postgres://...

  kubectl get pod easypj-web -o yaml | grep -A20 "envFrom:"
  envFrom:
  - secretRef: {name: db-creds}          ← Contains DATABASE_URL=postgres://...
  - configMapRef: {name: django-config}  ← Contains DATABASE_URL=sqlite://...
  # ConfigMap comes AFTER — overwrites Secret's DATABASE_URL!

  kubectl get cm django-config -o yaml | grep DATABASE_URL
  DATABASE_URL: sqlite:///db.sqlite3    ← Dev default leaked into production!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Same key name in Secret and ConfigMap: Both db-creds Secret and django-config ConfigMap have DATABASE_URL. The LAST one in envFrom wins — overwrites earlier values.
  2. envFrom ordering determines priority: Kubernetes processes envFrom top-to-bottom. Later entries overwrite earlier entries with the same key name. Secret first, ConfigMap second = ConfigMap wins.
  3. Dev defaults in ConfigMap leaked to production: The ConfigMap has DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///db.sqlite3 as a "safe default" for development. In production, this default overwrites the Secret's real database URL.
  4. No key naming convention: Both Secret and ConfigMap use the generic DATABASE_URL. Different prefixes would prevent collision: PROD_DATABASE_URL in Secret, DEV_DATABASE_URL in ConfigMap.
  5. valueFrom with explicit key ignores collisions: Using valueFrom.secretKeyRef for the Secret and valueFrom.configMapKeyRef for the ConfigMap with different env var names would avoid the conflict entirely.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Helm values merging accidentally — values.yaml has same key in both Secret and ConfigMap sections
  2. Kustomize overlay not overriding dev defaults — production overlay doesn't remove the dev DATABASE_URL from ConfigMap
  3. Multiple envFrom with overlapping keys — 3+ ConfigMaps/Secrets all have overlapping keys, hard to trace which wins
  4. Application itself has a default — DATABASE_URL set in Dockerfile ENV, then ConfigMap overwrites, then Secret doesn't apply
  5. CI/CD merging environment variables — pipeline merges env vars from multiple sources, collision undetected
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No namespace separation for dev vs prod ConfigMaps: Same ConfigMap template used for both — dev default values present in production.
  2. New team member added DATABASE_URL to ConfigMap: "Just a default" — didn't know Secret already had it. The default became the override.
  3. Schema validation not enforced: No OPA/Kyverno policy to prevent DATABASE_URL from appearing in ConfigMaps in production namespaces.
  4. Git repository has dev-focused ConfigMap: ConfigMap commited with dev defaults — applied to production without modification.
  5. No environment parity testing: Production env vars never compared with dev — collision goes unnoticed until app breaks in production.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl exec <pod> -- env | sort and compare with kubectl get cm,secret -o yaml Check for duplicate keys across Secret and ConfigMap. The LAST one in envFrom wins.
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -A30 "envFrom:" Check the order of envFrom entries. Later entries overwrite earlier ones with the same key name.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The ConfigMap (django-config) contains DATABASE_URL which overwrites the Secret's (db-creds) DATABASE_URL because the ConfigMap is listed AFTER the Secret in envFrom. The dev default value (sqlite) overwrites the production value (postgres). Fix: remove DATABASE_URL from the ConfigMap or reorder envFrom so Secrets come last.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Remove the duplicate key from ConfigMap kubectl edit cm django-config — delete the DATABASE_URL key DATABASE_URL belongs in Secrets, not ConfigMaps. ConfigMaps are for non-sensitive settings.
2. Reorder envFrom — Secrets LAST envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: django-config}}, {secretRef: {name: db-creds}}] Secrets listed last will overwrite ConfigMap keys with the same name. Sensitive values take priority.
3. Use valueFrom for explicit, collision-free mapping env: [{name: DB_URL, valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: db-creds, key: DATABASE_URL}}}] Explicitly map each env var to a specific source. No ambiguity about which source provides which value.
4. Use distinct key names CM_DATABASE_URL for ConfigMap defaults, DATABASE_URL for Secret. Different names = no collision possible.
5. Restart pods after fixing kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-web Pods must restart to pick up the corrected env vars. Verify with kubectl exec env | grep DATABASE_URL.
💡 Personal Advice:
Secrets last in envFrom. Always. If a Secret and ConfigMap share a key name, the LAST one wins. List Secrets after ConfigMaps so sensitive values take priority.
Never put credentials in ConfigMaps. Ever. DATABASE_URL, API keys, passwords — these belong in Secrets. ConfigMaps are for non-sensitive settings like LOG_LEVEL, DEBUG, FEATURE_FLAGS.
Prefer valueFrom over envFrom for production. Explicit mapping tells you exactly where each env var comes from. envFrom is convenient but hides collisions and makes debugging harder.
Production ConfigMaps should not have dev defaults. Use Kustomize overlays or separate ConfigMaps per environment. A ConfigMap with "sqlite:///db.sqlite3" should never exist in production.

📌 ES6–ES10: Secret Misconfigurations

ES6
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES6
Secret Base64 Double-Encoded — App Gets Garbage Value

🔍 Symptom: Django can't connect to PostgreSQL — authentication fails. The password is wrong. Developer manually base64-encoded the password before putting it in the Secret YAML, but kubectl create secret ALSO base64-encodes the value. Result: double-encoding — the app receives the base64 string, not the original password.

  echo -n "s3cr3tP@ss" | base64
  czNjcjN0UEBzcw==

  cat secret.yaml
  data:
    DB_PASSWORD: czNjcjN0UEBzcw==  ← Developer pre-encoded it!

  kubectl create -f secret.yaml
  secret/db-creds created
  # kubectl ALSO base64-encodes the value!

  kubectl exec easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e -- env | grep DB_PASSWORD
  DB_PASSWORD=Y3pOamNqTjBVRUJ6Y3c9PQ==   ← DOUBLE-ENCODED!
  # App receives: "czNjcjN0UEBzcw==" — NOT the password!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Developer manually base64-encoded the value: echo "s3cr3t" | base64 then put the base64 output in Secret YAML. kubectl apply auto-encodes it AGAIN. Use stringData with plain text, or let kubectl encode once from literal.
  2. stringData vs data confusion: data field requires base64-encoded values. stringData field accepts plain text and auto-encodes. Using data with plain text causes issues.
  3. kubectl create secret from literal is safe: kubectl create secret generic db-creds --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3tP@ss — kubectl handles base64 encoding correctly, no double-encoding.
  4. Copy-paste from base64 output directly into data: Developer ran base64, copied the output, pasted into data: field. kubectl encode it again — double-encoded.
  5. Misunderstanding of Secret encoding: "Secrets are base64 encoded" — Yes, but KUBERNETES does the encoding. You provide plain text (via stringData or --from-literal), Kubernetes stores as base64. You do NOT pre-encode.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Helm template double-encoding — values.yaml has pre-encoded value AND template uses b64enc function
  2. CI/CD pipeline encoding — pipeline encrypts/encodes before passing to kubectl, which encodes again
  3. Secret imported from another cluster — previously encoded, then kubectl apply encodes again on new cluster
  4. Multiple layers of encoding — base64 → base64 → base64 from repeated copy-paste cycles
  5. External secrets operator encoding — Vault/SealedSecrets already encoded, kubectl encodes again
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New developer unfamiliar with Secrets: Comes from Docker where you manually encode. Kubernetes does it automatically — double-encoding is the most common Secret mistake.
  2. Documentation copied from old wiki: Internal docs show "base64 first then apply" — outdated instructions from pre-1.14 era.
  3. Secrets created via dashboard/UI: Some K8s dashboards auto-encode — developer pre-encodes, dashboard encodes again.
  4. No CI validation for Secret values: Pipeline doesn't decode and validate Secret values — double-encoded garbage deployed to production.
  5. Air-gapped cluster — secrets created manually: No external secret management, all secrets created by hand — double-encoding inevitable at scale.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get secret db-creds -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d | base64 -d Double-decode the Secret value. If the second decode produces the actual password, the value was double-encoded.
Compare the decoded length: original password is 10 chars, decoded should be ~10. If decoded is 7 chars (base64 length), it's double-encoded.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The developer manually base64-encoded the password before putting it in the Secret YAML data field. Kubernetes ALSO base64-encodes the data field, resulting in double-encoding. Fix: use stringData with plain text values, or use kubectl create secret --from-literal which handles encoding correctly.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Use stringData instead of data stringData: {DB_PASSWORD: s3cr3tP@ss} stringData accepts plain text. Kubernetes encodes to base64 automatically. No double-encoding.
2. Use kubectl create secret --from-literal kubectl create secret generic db-creds --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3tP@ss kubectl handles encoding. The safest way to create Secrets from the CLI.
3. Delete and recreate the double-encoded Secret kubectl delete secret db-creds && kubectl create secret generic db-creds --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cr3tP@ss Delete the broken Secret, recreate with correct encoding. Pods referencing it must restart.
4. Verify encoding with decode kubectl get secret db-creds -o jsonpath='{.data.DB_PASSWORD}' | base64 -d Should print the original password. If it prints another base64 string, it's double-encoded.
5. Restart pods after fixing the Secret kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-web Pods must restart to pick up the corrected Secret value.
💡 Personal Advice:
Never manually base64-encode Secret values. Kubernetes does it for you. Use stringData or --from-literal. Manually encoding is the #1 Secret mistake and it's 100% preventable.
stringData is your friend in YAML. Write plain text in stringData. Kubernetes converts to base64 in data automatically. Cleaner YAML, no encoding errors.
Double-decode to verify. kubectl get secret X -o jsonpath='{.data.Y}' | base64 -d | base64 -d If second decode produces readable text, the original was double-encoded. Fix it immediately.
base64 is encoding, NOT encryption. Anyone with kubectl access can decode Secrets. Use etcd encryption, external secret stores (Vault), or SealedSecrets for real security.
ES7
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES7
Secret Exposed via Environment Variable — Visible in /proc

🔍 Symptom: Security audit reveals that database passwords and API keys are visible in /proc/1/environ inside the container. Anyone with kubectl exec access (or a compromised container) can read all environment variables — including Secrets. Secrets injected via envFrom or valueFrom are exposed in plain text.

  kubectl exec easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e -- cat /proc/1/environ | tr '\0' '\n'
  PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
  DATABASE_URL=postgres://easypj:s3cr3tP@ss@easypj-db:5432/jobpost
  SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-abc123def456ghi789
  AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
  AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
  # ALL secrets visible in plain text in /proc!

  kubectl get pod easypj-api -o yaml | grep -A10 "envFrom:"
  envFrom:
  - secretRef: {name: db-creds}      ← Secrets as env vars — visible in /proc!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Secrets injected as environment variables: envFrom.secretRef makes all Secret keys environment variables. Env vars are visible in /proc/<pid>/environ to anyone with container access — and to child processes.
  2. Environment variables inherited by all child processes: Any process spawned by Django (subprocess, shell, debugging tool) inherits all env vars — including secrets. Volume mounts don't have this problem.
  3. Crash dumps and error reports include env vars: Django DEBUG error pages show environment variables. Sentry/Airbrake crash reports may capture env vars. Secrets leak through error reporting.
  4. Volume-mounted Secrets are NOT visible in /proc: Mounting Secrets as files stores them in tmpfs. They're only accessible by reading the file. Much safer than env vars. Use mountPath: /etc/secrets.
  5. Process listing tools can read /proc: ps aux, top, and monitoring agents can read /proc/pid/environ — exposing secrets to any tool that lists processes.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Debug logging prints environment — app logs all env vars on startup for "debugging", including secrets
  2. Sidecar container has access — logging sidecar can read /proc of the main container's processes
  3. Kubernetes dashboard showing env vars — dashboard users can view pod environment variables including secrets
  4. RBAC too permissive — too many users have pods/exec permission, all can read secrets from /proc
  5. readOnlyRootFilesystem prevents env var access — but most containers don't use this, making /proc readable
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Security audit finds env var secrets: First security review of the cluster reveals all secrets in /proc — needs immediate remediation.
  2. Compliance requirement (SOC2, PCI): Secrets must not be in environment variables — volume mounts are mandatory for compliance.
  3. No security hardening guide: Team doesn't know env vars are less secure — no documented best practice for Secret consumption.
  4. Helm chart defaults to envFrom: Popular charts use envFrom for simplicity — teams inherit insecure defaults.
  5. External secret operator (Vault/SealedSecrets): Even with external secrets, injecting as env vars still exposes them in /proc. Volume mounts are still safer.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/environ | tr '\0' '\n' | grep -iE "password|secret|key|token" Check if secrets are visible in /proc. Any environment variable with "password", "secret", "key", "token" is a concern.
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -E "envFrom|secretRef|secretKeyRef" Identify which Secrets are injected as env vars. These are the ones exposed in /proc.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: Secrets are injected as environment variables (envFrom.secretRef), making them visible in /proc/<pid>/environ. Anyone with container access (or compromised process) can read all secrets. Fix: mount Secrets as files using volume mounts — they're stored in tmpfs and not exposed in /proc.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Switch from envFrom to volume mount volumes: [{name: secrets, secret: {secretName: db-creds}}], volumeMounts: [{name: secrets, mountPath: /etc/secrets, readOnly: true}] Each Secret key becomes a file in /etc/secrets. Read by the app at runtime — not visible in /proc.
2. Update app to read secrets from files Instead of os.environ.get('DB_PASSWORD'), use open('/etc/secrets/DB_PASSWORD').read().strip(). Minor code change, major security improvement.
3. Set defaultMode to restrict file permissions defaultMode: 0400 Only the container user can read the secret files. Other processes on the same node can't access them.
4. Disable service account token automount if not needed automountServiceAccountToken: false Prevents the SA token from being mounted — one less secret to leak.
5. Audit all pods for env var secrets kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].envFrom[].secretRef != null) | .metadata.name' Find all pods using envFrom with Secrets. Migrate each to volume mounts.
💡 Personal Advice:
Volume mounts are ALWAYS more secure than env vars for secrets. tmpfs, not in /proc, not inherited by child processes, not in crash dumps. Use volume mounts for any secret that would be catastrophic if leaked.
Don't print env vars in error pages or logs. Django DEBUG pages and Sentry crash reports can capture all env vars. Configure error reporting to filter out sensitive keys.
/proc/1/environ is the first place an attacker checks. If someone gets exec access to your container, this is their first command. Don't leave secrets there.
PCI/SOC2 auditors WILL check for this. Secrets in environment variables is a common audit finding. Fix it before the audit, not after.
ES8
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES8
imagePullSecrets — Secret in Wrong Namespace

🔍 Symptom: Pods in easypj-prod fail with ImagePullBackOff because the private registry secret exists in default namespace but not in easypj-prod. Secrets are namespace-scoped — a Secret in one namespace is INVISIBLE to pods in another namespace. The pod can't authenticate to the private registry.

  kubectl get pods -n easypj-prod
  NAME                            READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
  easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde    0/1     ImagePullBackOff   0       5m

  kubectl get secret ghcr-secret
  NAME           TYPE                             DATA   AGE
  ghcr-secret    kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson   1      2d

  kubectl get secret ghcr-secret -n easypj-prod
  Error from server (NotFound): secrets "ghcr-secret" not found
  # Secret exists in DEFAULT namespace but NOT in easypj-prod!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Secret created in wrong namespace: kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-secret --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=X --docker-password=Y was run without -n easypj-prod. Secret went to default namespace.
  2. imagePullSecrets reference correct but Secret missing: Pod spec references imagePullSecrets: [{name: ghcr-secret}] — but the Secret doesn't exist in the pod's namespace.
  3. Secret created in namespace A, pod in namespace B: Different teams create resources in different namespaces. Ops creates Secret in kube-system, dev creates pods in easypj-prod — mismatch.
  4. ServiceAccount with imagePullSecrets in wrong namespace: SA in easypj-prod references imagePullSecrets: [{name: ghcr-secret}] but the Secret is in default.
  5. Namespace created after Secret: Secret was created before the easypj-prod namespace existed. New namespace doesn't automatically get Secrets.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Secret copied with kubectl get secret -o yaml but namespace not updated — YAML still says default namespace
  2. Helm chart creates Secret in release namespace — ServiceAccount in different namespace doesn't have it
  3. GitOps sync (ArgoCD) — Secret synced to cluster-A namespace but pods run in cluster-A/different-ns
  4. Multiple clusters — Secret propagated to cluster A but pods run in cluster B
  5. Secret deleted by namespace cleanup job — cron cleanup deleted Secrets in easypj-prod but not in default
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New namespace created without Secrets: Every new namespace needs its own copy of imagePullSecrets. Automation didn't include this step.
  2. Namespace-per-team architecture: Each team gets a namespace — registry secret must be replicated to all of them.
  3. No namespace bootstrap automation: New namespaces manually created — Secrets creation forgotten in the process.
  4. kind/minikube — no private registry: Local clusters use kind load / minikube image load — imagePullSecrets not needed, never tested in production.
  5. Cluster autoscaler creating new nodes: New nodes pull images — but Secret must be in the namespace, not on the node.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get secret -n <pod-ns> <secret-name> and kubectl get secret -A | grep <secret-name> Check if the Secret exists in the pod's namespace. If not, which namespace has it?
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 "Events:" Events may show "Failed to pull image" with authentication details — confirms imagePullSecrets issue.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The ghcr-secret docker-registry Secret exists in the default namespace but the pod is in easypj-prod. Secrets are namespace-scoped — a pod can only reference Secrets in its own namespace. Fix: copy the Secret to easypj-prod.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Copy the Secret to the correct namespace kubectl get secret ghcr-secret -o yaml | sed 's/namespace: default/namespace: easypj-prod/' | kubectl apply -f - Copy the Secret from default to easypj-prod. Pods in easypj-prod can now pull images.
2. Attach imagePullSecrets to ServiceAccount kubectl patch sa default -n easypj-prod -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"ghcr-secret"}]}' All pods using the default SA automatically get the pull secret. One patch, all pods covered.
3. Create Secret with explicit namespace kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-secret --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=X --docker-password=Y -n easypj-prod Always specify -n when creating Secrets. Prevents the "wrong namespace" problem.
4. Bootstrap new namespaces with required Secrets Create a script/operator that copies registry Secrets to new namespaces automatically. Never rely on manual steps.
5. Delete stuck pods to re-pull images kubectl delete pod -n easypj-prod -l app=easypj-api After fixing the Secret, delete stuck pods. New pods will use the pull secret and succeed.
💡 Personal Advice:
Secrets are namespace-scoped. Always. A Secret in "default" doesn't exist in "easypj-prod". Copy it. This is the #1 cause of ImagePullBackOff in multi-namespace clusters.
Attach imagePullSecrets to the ServiceAccount, not every pod. One kubectl patch sa default covers all pods. Much cleaner than adding imagePullSecrets to every Deployment.
Bootstrap namespaces with required Secrets. Registry credentials, TLS certs, API tokens — every new namespace needs them. Automate the copying.
Always use -n with kubectl create secret. Without -n, the Secret goes to the current context namespace — which may not be where your pods are. Be explicit.
ES9
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES9
TLS Secret Wrong Key Names — Ingress Doesn't Use It

🔍 Symptom: Ingress is configured with TLS but browsers show "NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID" or the default fake certificate. kubectl describe ingress shows the TLS section references a Secret, but the Secret has wrong key names (cert.pem instead of tls.crt, key.pem instead of tls.key). The Ingress controller ignores the Secret — uses the default fake certificate.

  kubectl get secret easypj-tls -o yaml | grep -E "  [a-z].*:"
  cert.pem: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi...    ← Should be tls.crt!
  key.pem: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi...     ← Should be tls.key!

  kubectl describe ingress easypj-ingress | grep -A5 TLS
  TLS:
    easypj-tls terminates api.easypj.com
  # Secret exists but Ingress controller ignores it — wrong key names!

  curl -v https://api.easypj.com 2>&1 | grep "subject:"
  * subject: CN=Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate
  # Fake cert — TLS Secret not being used!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Wrong key names in TLS Secret: Kubernetes requires EXACTLY tls.crt and tls.key. Using cert.pem, certificate, tls.cert, or any other name — Secret is ignored silently.
  2. Secret type is Opaque instead of kubernetes.io/tls: kubectl create secret generic creates an Opaque Secret. Ingress TLS requires type: kubernetes.io/tls. Use kubectl create secret tls.
  3. Certificate and key content swapped: tls.crt contains the private key, tls.key contains the certificate — Ingress controller can't use it.
  4. Certificate not PEM-encoded: Certificate is in DER or PKCS#12 format. Kubernetes requires PEM (base64 with BEGIN/END markers). Must convert first.
  5. Certificate chain incomplete: tls.crt has only the server certificate — missing intermediate CA certificates. Some browsers reject the incomplete chain.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. TLS Secret in wrong namespace — Ingress references tls.secretName but Secret is in a different namespace
  2. Certificate expired — TLS Secret exists with correct keys but certificate validity period has ended
  3. Host mismatch — certificate CN/SAN doesn't match the Ingress host, browser shows warning
  4. cert-manager not renewing — certificate auto-renewal failed, Secret contains expired certificate
  5. Ingress controller restart needed — some controllers cache TLS config, need restart to pick up new Secret
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Self-signed certificate created manually: Developer generated cert with openssl, named keys differently — cert.pem and key.pem instead of tls.crt and tls.key.
  2. cert-manager not installed: No automatic TLS — all certificates created manually with inconsistent key names.
  3. kind cluster — local TLS: Using self-signed certs for local development — key naming conventions not followed.
  4. Migration from other platform: Certificates imported from AWS ACM/Heroku — key naming conventions differ from Kubernetes.
  5. No TLS Secret validation in CI/CD: Pipeline deploys any Secret — doesn't validate tls.crt and tls.key exist and are valid PEM.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get secret easypj-tls -o jsonpath='{.data}' | jq 'keys' Check the key names. Must be exactly tls.crt and tls.key. Any other names = Secret ignored.
kubectl get secret easypj-tls -o jsonpath='{.type}' Must be kubernetes.io/tls. If it's Opaque, the Ingress controller won't use it for TLS.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The TLS Secret has wrong key names (cert.pem and key.pem instead of tls.crt and tls.key). Kubernetes requires these EXACT key names. When the Ingress controller can't find tls.crt and tls.key, it silently falls back to its default fake certificate.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Use kubectl create secret tls (correct way) kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls --cert=fullchain.pem --key=privkey.pem -n easypj-prod Creates Secret with correct type (kubernetes.io/tls) and correct key names (tls.crt, tls.key) automatically.
2. Fix existing Secret by recreating it kubectl delete secret easypj-tls && kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls --cert=cert.pem --key=key.pem Delete the broken Secret, recreate with the correct command. Key names will be correct.
3. Verify the Ingress uses the Secret curl -sv --insecure https://api.easypj.com 2>&1 | grep "subject=" Should show your certificate's subject, not "Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate."
