4. Use cert-manager for automated TLS kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/latest/download/cert-manager.yaml cert-manager automatically creates and renews TLS Secrets with correct key names. No manual errors possible.
5. Validate Secrets in CI/CD kubectl get secret easypj-tls -o json | jq -e '.data."tls.crt" and .data."tls.key"' Block deployment if tls.crt or tls.key are missing from the Secret.
💡 Personal Advice:
Always use kubectl create secret tls. It guarantees the correct type AND correct key names. Never create TLS Secrets with kubectl create secret generic — you'll get the key names wrong.
tls.crt and tls.key are case-sensitive and hyphenated. Not tls.cert, not TLS.CRT, not tls_crt. Exactly tls.crt and tls.key. Any deviation = Secret ignored silently.
"Fake Certificate" = Secret not being used. If you see the Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate, your TLS Secret is not being recognized. Check key names and type.
cert-manager eliminates this entire class of errors. It creates properly formatted TLS Secrets automatically. No manual key naming, no type errors, automatic renewal. Install it on every cluster.
ES10
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES10
Immutable Secret — Can't Edit, Must Delete and Recreate

🔍 Symptom: kubectl edit secret db-creds fails with "Secret 'db-creds' is invalid: data: Forbidden: field is immutable." The Secret was created with immutable: true. The database password changed and needs updating, but the Secret can't be modified — the entire Secret must be deleted and recreated.

  kubectl edit secret db-creds -n easypj-prod
  error: secrets "db-creds" is invalid
  A value must be specified for field data

  kubectl patch secret db-creds -p '{"data":{"DB_PASSWORD":"bmV3cGFzcw=="}}'
  The Secret "db-creds" is invalid: data: Forbidden: field is immutable

  kubectl get secret db-creds -o yaml | grep immutable
  immutable: true     ← Can't modify this Secret!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Secret created with immutable: true: Immutable Secrets can't be modified after creation — data AND metadata are locked. This is a security best practice but requires delete-and-recreate for updates.
  2. Developer doesn't know about immutable Secrets: Tried kubectl edit, got "Forbidden" error — doesn't understand why. immutable: true is a deliberate security choice, not a bug.
  3. No versioned naming strategy: With immutable Secrets, you need a naming strategy: db-creds-v1, db-creds-v2. Without it, updating requires the same name — which is impossible with immutable.
  4. Helm chart sets immutable: true by default: Chart has immutable: true in the Secret template. Team doesn't know, expects to edit Secrets directly.
  5. Rotating credentials workflow broken: Password rotation requires updating the Secret — but immutable blocks it. Workflow must be: create new Secret → update Deployment references → delete old Secret.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Kustomize sets immutable on all Secrets — security policy applied cluster-wide without team awareness
  2. Kyverno/OPA policy enforcing immutable — admission controller adds immutable: true to all Secrets, overriding user intent
  3. cert-manager creates immutable Secrets — TLS certificates managed by cert-manager are immutable, manual edits rejected
  4. GitOps tool (ArgoCD) recreating Secret — editing directly gets overwritten by Git state, appears as "immutable"
  5. Multiple pods reference same Secret by name — can't delete Secret without breaking all pods, need coordinated rollout
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Security policy mandates immutable Secrets: New cluster has policy: all Secrets must be immutable. Team unfamiliar with the workflow.
  2. Credential rotation tool expects mutable Secrets: Automated password rotation script uses kubectl edit — breaks when Secrets are immutable.
  3. No documented credential rotation process: Team doesn't know how to update credentials on an immutable Secret — no runbook exists.
  4. External secret operator creates immutable Secrets: Vault/SealedSecrets creates Secrets with immutable: true — managed externally, can't be edited locally.
  5. kind cluster — immutable Secrets behave same: Testing rotation workflow on kind reveals immutable issue before production.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get secret <name> -o yaml | grep immutable Check if the Secret is immutable. If true, you can't modify it — delete and recreate is the only option.
kubectl get secret -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.immutable == true) | .metadata.name' Find ALL immutable Secrets in the cluster. Know which ones can't be edited before you need to update them.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Secret was created with immutable: true, which prevents ANY modification after creation. This is a security best practice to prevent accidental or malicious changes — but it requires a delete-and-recreate workflow. Fix: delete the old Secret, create a new one with updated values, and restart pods referencing it.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Delete and recreate with updated values kubectl delete secret db-creds -n easypj-prod && kubectl create secret generic db-creds --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=newpass -n easypj-prod Delete the old immutable Secret, create a new one with updated values. Pods must restart.
2. Use versioned Secret names for rotation kubectl create secret generic db-creds-v2 --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=newpass -n easypj-prod Create db-creds-v2 (immutable). Update Deployment to reference v2. Delete db-creds-v1 after rollout. Zero-downtime rotation.
3. Update Deployment references after creating new Secret kubectl set env deploy/easypj-api --from=secret/db-creds-v2 Point the Deployment to the new Secret. Triggers a rolling restart with the new credentials.
4. Use external secret management for rotation Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or SealedSecrets handle rotation automatically. Secrets update without manual delete-and-recreate.
5. Document the immutable Secret workflow Create runbook: "To update credentials: 1. Create vN+1 Secret, 2. Update Deployment, 3. Verify, 4. Delete vN Secret."
💡 Personal Advice:
Immutable Secrets are a feature, not a bug. They prevent accidental changes and make credential rotation explicit. Versioned names are the correct pattern: db-creds-v1, db-creds-v2, etc.
Versioned Secret names = zero-downtime rotation. Create v2, update Deployment → rolling restart. Keep v1 until all pods are on v2. Then delete v1. No downtime, no errors.
Don't fight immutability — work with it. Instead of trying to patch immutable Secrets, build your workflow around versioned names and rolling updates. Your security auditors will thank you.
External secret operators handle rotation for you. If manual Secret rotation is painful, invest in SealedSecrets, External Secrets Operator, or Vault. They handle versioning automatically.

📌 ES11–ES15: SecurityContext Misconfigurations

ES11
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES11
runAsNonRoot Blocks Container — Image Defaults to Root

🔍 Symptom: Pod fails with "Error: container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root." The Deployment has runAsNonRoot: true, but the Django image was built without a USER directive — it defaults to root (UID 0). Kubernetes blocks the pod from starting because the image's default user is root, violating the runAsNonRoot policy.

  kubectl get pods
  NAME                            READY   STATUS                       RESTARTS
  easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde    0/1     CreateContainerConfigError   0

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde | grep -i error
  Error: container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root
  (image "easypj/jobpost:v2.1" cannot run as root when runAsNonRoot is true)

  docker run --rm easypj/jobpost:v2.1 whoami
  root                ← Image defaults to root!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No USER directive in Dockerfile: Docker defaults to root (UID 0). Without USER 1000 in the Dockerfile, the image runs as root. runAsNonRoot: true blocks it.
  2. runAsNonRoot added without fixing the image: Security team added runAsNonRoot: true to all pods via policy — but images weren't updated. Pods can't start.
  3. Wrong UID specified: runAsUser: 0 conflicts with runAsNonRoot: true. runAsNonRoot checks the final UID — 0 is always blocked.
  4. Distroless image has no USER but has no shell either: Distroless images run as root by default. Need explicit USER in the Dockerfile — distroless doesn't set it automatically.
  5. Base image changed — new version defaults to root: Old base image had USER 1000 built-in. New version removed it. Image now defaults to root.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. PodSecurityStandard Restricted applied — namespace-level policy blocks root, overriding pod-level settings
  2. Mutating webhook adding runAsNonRoot — admission controller adds it, developer didn't know image runs as root
  3. Multi-stage build — USER set in build stage but not in runtime stage
  4. runAsUser set but not applied — securityContext at wrong level (pod vs container), runAsNonRoot still blocks
  5. Helm chart securityContext defaults — chart adds runAsNonRoot but image is third-party (e.g., nginx) that defaults to root
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Security hardening initiative: New policy: all pods must have runAsNonRoot. Legacy images built as root — mass pod failures.
  2. Pod Security Standards enforced cluster-wide: Restricted PSS mandates runAsNonRoot — all root images blocked until fixed.
  3. New K8s version enforces previously ignored settings: Earlier version tolerated runAsNonRoot with root image — upgrade now enforces it strictly.
  4. Third-party Helm chart with root image: Community chart uses nginx:latest (root) — runAsNonRoot policy blocks it from starting.
  5. No container image scanning: Security team doesn't know which images run as root — runAsNonRoot added blindly, causing mass failures.
🔍 What to Look At:
docker run --rm <image> whoami or docker inspect <image> | jq '.[].Config.User' Check the image's default user. If empty or "root", the image runs as root. Fix the Dockerfile or add runAsUser.
kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep "runAsNonRoot" The error message tells you exactly why the pod was blocked: image runs as root but runAsNonRoot is true.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The image was built without a USER directive, defaulting to root (UID 0). The pod spec has runAsNonRoot: true which blocks any container running as UID 0. Fix: add USER 1000 to the Dockerfile, OR add runAsUser: 1000 to the pod spec (which overrides the image's default user).
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add USER to Dockerfile (best practice) USER 1000 at the end of the Dockerfile Image now runs as UID 1000. Rebuild and push. runAsNonRoot: true allows the pod to start.
2. Add runAsUser to pod spec (quick fix) securityContext: {runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000} Overrides the image's default user to UID 1000. Pod starts even if image defaults to root.
3. For third-party images, always set runAsUser Nginx, Redis, PostgreSQL images often default to root. Set runAsUser to their expected non-root UID.
4. Scan images before deploying docker inspect <image> | jq '.[].Config.User' Know which images run as root BEFORE deploying. Fix images or add runAsUser to pod specs.
5. Delete and recreate the pod After fixing the Dockerfile or pod spec, delete the stuck pod. New pod starts successfully.
💡 Personal Advice:
Every Dockerfile should end with USER 1000. This is the #1 container security practice. Non-root containers are required by Pod Security Standards (Restricted). Build it in from day one.
runAsNonRoot + runAsUser together are defense in depth. runAsUser forces a specific UID. runAsNonRoot ensures that UID is never 0. Use both.
Third-party images often default to root. Don't assume nginx, Redis, or PostgreSQL images run as non-root. Check with docker inspect before deploying with runAsNonRoot.
Fix the image, not just the pod spec. Adding runAsUser to the pod spec works, but fixing the Dockerfile works for EVERY pod that uses the image. Fix the source.
ES12
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES12
readOnlyRootFilesystem — App Can't Write to /tmp

🔍 Symptom: Django pod restarts immediately with "Permission denied" errors. The pod has readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, but Django needs to write temporary files to /tmp for file uploads, session storage, and cache. The root filesystem is read-only — every write attempt fails with "Read-only file system."

  kubectl logs easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde --previous | tail -5
  OSError: [Errno 30] Read-only file system: '/tmp/tmpfile123'
  During handling: Failed to write session data to /tmp/django_sessions

  kubectl exec easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e-abcde -- touch /tmp/test
  touch: /tmp/test: Read-only file system

  kubectl get pod easypj-api -o yaml | grep readOnlyRootFilesystem
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true     ← No writable volumes for /tmp!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. No writable volume mounted for /tmp: readOnlyRootFilesystem makes ALL directories read-only — including /tmp. Must mount an emptyDir volume at /tmp for temporary writes.
  2. Application writes to unexpected paths: Django writes to /tmp, /var/cache, /app/media for uploads. Each writable path needs its own emptyDir volume mount.
  3. readOnlyRootFilesystem added without testing: Security team enabled it cluster-wide. Apps that write to filesystem weren't tested — mass failures.
  4. Log files written to /var/log: App configured to log to files — /var/log is now read-only. Must log to stdout or mount emptyDir at /var/log.
  5. Python bytecode cache (.pyc) can't be written: Python tries to create __pycache__/ directories — fails on read-only filesystem. Set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. emptyDir with sizeLimit too small — /tmp volume fills up, writes start failing even with writable volume
  2. Memory-backed emptyDir (medium: Memory) fills up — node memory exhausted, /tmp writes fail
  3. NFS/CIFS volume mounted as read-only — shared volume for uploads mounted ro instead of rw
  4. PodSecurityPolicy restricts volume types — policy blocks emptyDir, can't create writable volumes
  5. initContainer creates files on ephemeral volume — main container can't read/write due to UID mismatch
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Pod Security Standard Restricted requires readOnlyRootFilesystem: New cluster enforced it — all existing apps break. Need to add emptyDir mounts.
  2. Security audit finding: "Containers should have read-only root filesystems" — enabled globally without testing.
  3. Helm chart doesn't include emptyDir mounts: Chart sets readOnlyRootFilesystem but doesn't provide writable volumes — apps fail.
  4. Migration from VMs: App writes to /opt, /var, /tmp on VMs — container with readOnlyRootFilesystem needs volumes for all of them.
  5. kind/minikube testing: readOnlyRootFilesystem works differently — local tests pass, production fails due to different storage driver.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl exec <pod> -- find / -type d -writable 2>/dev/null List all writable directories inside the container. If /tmp is not writable, mount an emptyDir.
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -A20 "volumeMounts:" Check which volumes are mounted and where. Identify missing mounts for writable paths.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true makes the entire container filesystem read-only. The app needs to write to /tmp (Django sessions, uploads) but no writable volume is mounted there. Fix: mount an emptyDir volume at /tmp and any other paths the app writes to.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Mount emptyDir at /tmp volumes: [{name: tmp, emptyDir: {}}], volumeMounts: [{name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}] Provides writable temporary storage. Deleted when pod restarts — use PVC for persistent data.
2. Mount emptyDir for all writable paths /tmp, /var/run, /var/cache, /app/media — every path the app writes to needs a writable volume.
3. Set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 Prevents Python from trying to write .pyc files. Eliminates the __pycache__ write error.
4. Use memory-backed emptyDir for performance emptyDir: {medium: Memory} Stores /tmp in memory — faster, but consumes node memory. Set sizeLimit to prevent OOM.
5. Test write access after mounting kubectl exec <pod> -- touch /tmp/test && echo "writable" Confirm the volume is mounted and writable before deploying to production.
💡 Personal Advice:
readOnlyRootFilesystem without emptyDir = guaranteed crash. Every app writes to /tmp. Django, Node, Java — they all need /tmp. Always mount an emptyDir at /tmp when using readOnlyRootFilesystem.
Find writable paths before hardening. kubectl exec <pod> -- find / -type d -writable Know what your app writes to. Mount emptyDir for each path. Don't guess — measure.
PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 in production. Bytecode caching helps in development but causes write errors in read-only containers. Disable it in production Dockerfiles.
Test readOnlyRootFilesystem in CI before production. Add a CI step that runs the app container with --read-only and verifies it starts. Catch missing volumes before they cause an outage.
ES13
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES13
capabilities drop ALL Breaks App — NET_BIND_SERVICE Needed

🔍 Symptom: Nginx fails to start with "bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (13: Permission denied)." The pod has capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}, but binding to port 80 (below 1024) requires the NET_BIND_SERVICE capability. All capabilities were dropped without adding back the needed one — nginx can't bind to privileged ports.

  kubectl logs easypj-web-nginx-7f8d9c6b5e --previous | tail -3
  nginx: [emerg] bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (13: Permission denied)

  kubectl get pod easypj-web -o yaml | grep -A5 capabilities
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]              ← ALL capabilities dropped!
    # add: []  — nothing added back!

  kubectl exec easypj-web-nginx-7f8d9c6b5e -- cat /proc/1/status | grep Cap
  CapEff: 0000000000000000     ← ZERO effective capabilities!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. drop: ALL without adding needed capabilities: drop: ["ALL"] removes every Linux capability. Nginx needs NET_BIND_SERVICE to bind to port 80. Add it back: add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"].
  2. App binding to privileged port (<1024): Ports below 1024 require CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE or root. Without it, bind() fails with Permission denied.
  3. Security team applied drop: ALL broadly: Policy added drop: ALL to all containers without analyzing what each container actually needs — mass failures.
  4. Use non-privileged port instead: Nginx can listen on port 8080 without any capabilities. If the Service maps 80→8080, no NET_BIND_SERVICE needed.
  5. Other capabilities commonly needed after drop ALL: CHOWN (PostgreSQL), DAC_OVERRIDE (file access), SETUID/SETGID (some runtimes). Test each app.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. App needs SYS_PTRACE for debugging — dropped by ALL, debug tools (strace) fail
  2. App needs NET_RAW for ping/ICMP — monitoring agent can't ping external hosts
  3. App needs SYS_TIME for time sync — chrony/ntp client can't adjust clock
  4. Runtime (Java, Node) needs specific caps — JVM needs certain capabilities for thread management
  5. seccomp profile also blocking — both capabilities AND seccomp restricting the syscall, harder to diagnose
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Pod Security Standard Restricted requires drop: ALL: New cluster enforces it — all containers need individual capability additions.
  2. Security policy without capability analysis: drop: ALL applied cluster-wide without auditing what each container needs.
  3. Third-party Helm charts without capabilities: Community charts don't set add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE] — nginx containers fail under Restricted PSS.
  4. New K8s version enforcing capabilities differently: Older versions were lenient — new version strictly enforces capability drops.
  5. kind/minikube: capabilities not enforced: Local clusters may not enforce capabilities — app works in dev, fails in production.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -A10 "capabilities:" Check if drop: ALL is set AND if the needed capabilities are added back.
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/status | grep -E "^Cap" CapEff (effective capabilities) shows what the process actually has. 0000000000000000 = nothing.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]} removed every Linux capability, including NET_BIND_SERVICE which is required to bind to ports below 1024 (like port 80). Fix: add NET_BIND_SERVICE back, or change nginx to listen on an unprivileged port (>1024).
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add NET_BIND_SERVICE to the add list capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"], add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]} Allows binding to privileged ports. All other capabilities remain dropped.
2. Switch to unprivileged port (no caps needed) Configure nginx to listen on 8080. Service maps 80→8080. No capabilities required at all.
3. Audit what capabilities each container needs kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff Run the container, check effective capabilities. Add back only what was actually used.
4. Use securityContext at the right level Pod-level securityContext sets defaults. Container-level can override. Put capabilities at the container level for granularity.
5. Test with Restricted Pod Security Standard kubectl label ns easypj-prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted If the pod can't start under Restricted PSS, your capabilities configuration needs work.
💡 Personal Advice:
drop: ALL is best practice — but always add back what's needed. Start with ALL, then add the minimum. NET_BIND_SERVICE for web servers, CHOWN for databases. One capability at a time.
Unprivileged ports (>1024) are safer and simpler. If your app can run on 8080 instead of 80, you don't need NET_BIND_SERVICE at all. Fewer capabilities = smaller attack surface.
Test capabilities in CI with the EXACT same security context. If production has drop: ALL, test with drop: ALL. Don't discover missing capabilities during a production incident.
capabilities + seccomp + AppArmor = defense in depth. Capabilities are one layer. Combine with seccomp profiles and AppArmor/SELinux for comprehensive container security.
ES14
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES14
privileged: true — Container Has Full Host Access

🔍 Symptom: Security scanner flags the Django pod as CRITICAL risk — it's running with privileged: true. This gives the container FULL access to all host devices, all Linux capabilities, and disables seccomp/AppArmor restrictions. The container essentially has root access to the host node — a container escape would be catastrophic.

  kubectl get pod easypj-api -o yaml | grep privileged
  privileged: true     ← WHY?! This is a Django web app!

  kubectl exec easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e -- cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff
  CapEff: 000001ffffffffff   ← ALL Linux capabilities enabled!

  kubectl exec easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e -- ls /dev/
  sda  sda1  sda2  ...       ← Access to ALL host devices!
  # Django web app does NOT need access to host disk devices!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. privileged: true used for debugging and never removed: Developer added privileged to test something, fixed the issue, forgot to remove it. The flag stayed in the Deployment YAML.
  2. Copy-paste from a debugging guide: Online tutorial said "add privileged: true to fix permission issue." Developer copied it, never reverted.
  3. "It works, don't touch it" mentality: privileged fixed a problem months ago. No one wants to risk removing it and breaking things — technical debt accumulates.
  4. No security review of pod specs: CI/CD doesn't block privileged containers. No one reviews security contexts before deployment.
  5. Misunderstanding of what privileged does: Developer thought privileged was needed for volume mounts or network access — it's not. privileged is a nuclear option.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Helm chart defaults to privileged — third-party chart sets privileged: true for all containers
  2. Docker-in-Docker (DinD) use case — CI/CD pod needs privileged, but the flag leaked to app pods
  3. HostPath volume requires privileged — developer needed hostPath, thought privileged was required (it's not)
  4. Mutating webhook adding privileged — admission controller adds privileged to pods matching certain criteria
  5. PodSecurityPolicy migration — old PSP allowed privileged, new PSS blocks it but migration incomplete
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No Pod Security Standards enforced: New cluster without Restricted PSS — privileged containers deploy without warnings.
  2. Security scanning tool (Trivy/Falco) just installed: First scan reveals privileged containers — remediation backlog created.
  3. New security policy: no privileged containers: Organization bans privileged containers — all existing privileged pods must be fixed.
  4. Dev environment allows privileged (kind/minikube): No restrictions locally — privileged flag leaks to production manifests.
  5. Runbook for debugging says "add privileged: true": Outdated runbook tells developers to use privileged for debugging — never says to remove it.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged == true) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"' Find ALL privileged pods across the cluster. Every one needs justification or remediation.
kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /proc/1/status | grep CapEff Check effective capabilities. Full capability set = privileged or CAP_SYS_ADMIN.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: privileged: true was added for debugging and never removed. This gives the Django container full root access to the host — all devices, all capabilities, no security restrictions. A web application should NEVER run as privileged. Fix: remove privileged: true and replace with specific capabilities if needed.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Remove privileged: true immediately kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"django","securityContext":{"privileged":false}}]}}}}' Setting to false or removing the field entirely. The pod runs without host-level access.
2. Add only needed capabilities (if any) capabilities: {add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]} Almost no web app needs capabilities beyond NET_BIND_SERVICE. Start minimal.
3. Block privileged containers with Pod Security Standards kubectl label ns easypj-prod pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted Restricted PSS rejects any pod with privileged: true. Technical enforcement, not convention.
4. Add CI/CD validation kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f deploy.yaml 2>&1 | grep -q privileged && echo "BLOCKED: privileged container" && exit 1 Block any deployment that contains privileged: true. Catch it before it reaches the cluster.
5. Audit and justify remaining privileged pods System components (CNI, CSI, kube-proxy) may need privileged. Application pods never do. Document every exception.
💡 Personal Advice:
privileged: true on a web app = security emergency. A compromised Django container with privileged access can escape to the host, access all pods, steal all secrets. Remove it NOW.
privileged is for system components, not applications. CNI plugins, CSI drivers, kube-proxy — these NEED privileged. Your Django app does not. Never.
Pod Security Standards (Restricted) = automatic blocking. One label on the namespace prevents ALL privileged containers. No one can accidentally deploy one. Use it.
If you added privileged for debugging, add a comment and a TODO. # TODO: Remove privileged: true after fixing volume permissions (JIRA-1234) Temporary privileged access should be tracked as a ticket. It should never survive to production.
ES15
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES15
fsGroup Not Set — PostgreSQL Can't Write to PVC

🔍 Symptom: PostgreSQL StatefulSet pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. The logs show "Permission denied" when trying to write to /var/lib/postgresql/data. The PVC is mounted but owned by root:root, while PostgreSQL runs as user postgres (UID 999). Without fsGroup: 999, PostgreSQL can't write to the volume.

  kubectl logs easypj-db-0 --previous | tail -3
  FATAL: could not create lock file "/var/lib/postgresql/data/postmaster.pid": Permission denied

  kubectl exec easypj-db-0 -- ls -la /var/lib/postgresql/data/
  drwx------  3 root root 4096 Jun 11 14:30 .
  # Owned by root:root — PostgreSQL (UID 999) can't write!

  kubectl get pod easypj-db-0 -o yaml | grep -A5 securityContext
  securityContext:
    runAsUser: 999
    # NO fsGroup set!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. fsGroup not set in pod securityContext: fsGroup: 999 changes the group ownership of ALL mounted volumes to GID 999. Without it, volumes are owned by root:root — non-root processes can't write.
  2. runAsUser set but fsGroup missing: runAsUser: 999 sets the process UID but doesn't change volume ownership. The volume is still owned by root — PostgreSQL can't write.
  3. PVC provisioned with root ownership: Storage provisioners create volumes owned by root by default. fsGroup is the mechanism to grant non-root containers access.
  4. StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplate doesn't inherit fsGroup: fsGroup must be set at the pod level in the StatefulSet template. It isn't automatically inherited from the PVC.
  5. Wrong fsGroup value: fsGroup: 1000 but PostgreSQL runs as GID 999. Must match the container's expected GID — check the image documentation.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. initContainer ran as root and changed permissions — initContainer no longer runs as root, permissions not set
  2. Volume already has data with wrong permissions — existing data owned by different UID, fsGroup only affects new files
  3. NFS volume doesn't support fsGroup — some volume types (NFS, hostPath) don't support fsGroup-based permission changes
  4. SELinux context blocking — even with correct fsGroup, SELinux prevents write access to the volume
  5. fsGroup only applies at mount time — changing fsGroup after PVC is mounted doesn't retroactively fix permissions
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New cluster with different StorageClass: Provisioner sets different default permissions — volume is writable on old cluster, not on new one.
  2. kind/kubeadm with hostPath volumes: HostPath provisioner doesn't support fsGroup — permissions must be set manually on the node.
  3. Helm chart without fsGroup in values: PostgreSQL Helm chart doesn't set fsGroup by default — needs manual override in values.yaml.
  4. Security policy (restricted PSS) requires non-root: Policy forces runAsNonRoot — without fsGroup, non-root processes can't write to volumes.
  5. CSI driver doesn't support fsGroup: Some CSI drivers (older versions) don't implement the fsGroup volume ownership change — volumes stay root-owned.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -A5 "securityContext:" and kubectl exec <pod> -- ls -la <mountPath> Check if fsGroup is set. Check the volume ownership. If owned by root and app runs as non-root, fsGroup is the fix.
kubectl exec <pod> -- id Confirm the container user's UID and GID. fsGroup should match the GID.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: fsGroup is not set in the pod's securityContext. PostgreSQL runs as UID/GID 999, but the PVC is owned by root:root. fsGroup changes the group ownership of all volumes to the specified GID, allowing the container process to read/write. Fix: add fsGroup: 999 to the pod securityContext.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Add fsGroup to pod securityContext securityContext: {fsGroup: 999, runAsUser: 999, runAsGroup: 999} All volumes are recursively chowned to GID 999 at mount time. PostgreSQL can now write.
2. Recreate the pod (or StatefulSet) kubectl delete pod easypj-db-0 fsGroup only applies at volume mount time. The pod must restart for the ownership change to take effect.
3. Verify volume ownership after restart kubectl exec <pod> -- ls -la <mountPath> Volume should now show group ownership matching fsGroup. PostgreSQL can write successfully.
4. Use initContainer for manual permission fix (alternative) initContainers: [{command: ["chown", "-R", "999:999", "/var/lib/postgresql/data"]}] Works even for volume types that don't support fsGroup (hostPath, NFS).
5. Set fsGroup in StatefulSet template for all pods Apply fsGroup at the StatefulSet pod template level. All pods in the StatefulSet inherit it automatically.
💡 Personal Advice:
fsGroup is mandatory for any StatefulSet with non-root containers. PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB — they all run as non-root and need fsGroup to write to their data volumes. Set it every time.
fsGroup + runAsUser + runAsGroup = the holy trinity. Set all three at the pod level for stateful workloads. UID for the process, GID for the process, fsGroup for volume ownership.
Not all volume types support fsGroup. hostPath and some NFS implementations don't support fsGroup. Use initContainers with chown for these cases.
Check the image documentation for the expected UID/GID. PostgreSQL uses 999, nginx uses 101, Redis uses 1000. Don't guess — the image docs tell you the expected user.

📌 ES16–ES20: RBAC & ServiceAccount Issues

ES16
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES16
ServiceAccount Token Not Mounted — App Can't Access API

🔍 Symptom: Django app makes requests to the Kubernetes API to list pods, but gets "403 Forbidden." The app uses the ServiceAccount token from /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, but the token file doesn't exist. automountServiceAccountToken: false was set on the pod — the token was never mounted.

  kubectl exec easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/
  ls: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/: No such file or directory

  kubectl get pod easypj-api -o yaml | grep automountServiceAccountToken
  automountServiceAccountToken: false     ← Token not mounted!

  kubectl exec easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e -- curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/easypj-prod/pods
  cat: /var/run/secrets/.../token: No such file or directory
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. automountServiceAccountToken set to false: This is a security best practice — disable the token for pods that don't need API access. But if the app needs it, the token won't be there.
  2. ServiceAccount doesn't exist: The pod references serviceAccountName: easypj-api but the SA was never created. Falls back to default SA — which may also have automount disabled.
  3. Default ServiceAccount has automount disabled: Someone set automountServiceAccountToken: false on the default SA in the namespace — all pods affected.
  4. ServiceAccount token projection misconfigured: Using projected volumes for tokens but the projection is set up incorrectly — token path wrong.
  5. RBAC permissions missing even with token: Token exists but the SA doesn't have RoleBindings — still gets 403 Forbidden, confused with missing token.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Token expired — projected tokens have expiration (default 1 hour), app doesn't reload the token
  2. Bind service account not enabled — kube-apiserver --disable-service-account-bind=true disables SA binding
  3. Mutating webhook removing automount — admission controller strips SA token from all production pods
  4. Pod spec has serviceAccountName: "" — empty string means "no SA", not "default"
  5. Token path mount overwritten — another volume mounted at /var/run/secrets overwrites the SA token mount
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Security policy disables token automount cluster-wide: All SAs have automount disabled — apps that need API access must explicitly enable it.
  2. Kyverno/OPA policy blocking automount: Admission controller rejects pods with automountServiceAccountToken: true — overzealous security policy.
  3. New developer unaware of SA tokens: Doesn't know that /var/run/secrets contains the SA token — can't debug API authentication issues.
  4. Migration from cloud-managed K8s: EKS/GKE use IAM/Workload Identity instead of SA tokens — on-prem cluster uses SA tokens, app not configured.
  5. kind/minikube: full admin access: Local cluster gives admin access — app doesn't need SA token for API calls, production does.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -E "serviceAccount|automountServiceAccountToken" Check which SA is assigned and whether token automount is enabled.
kubectl exec <pod> -- ls /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ If directory doesn't exist or is empty, the token wasn't mounted.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: automountServiceAccountToken: false prevents the SA token from being mounted. This is a security best practice for pods that don't need API access, but if the app needs to call the Kubernetes API, the token must be mounted. Fix: set automountServiceAccountToken: true or use a projected volume for the token.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Enable automountServiceAccountToken for API-accessing pods automountServiceAccountToken: true The token will be mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token.
2. Create a dedicated ServiceAccount kubectl create sa easypj-api -n easypj-prod Don't use the default SA. Create a dedicated SA with minimal RBAC permissions.
3. Bind the SA to a Role with minimal permissions kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods -n easypj-prod && kubectl create rolebinding api-pod-reader --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=easypj-prod:easypj-api Grant exactly what the app needs — not cluster-admin. Least privilege principle.
4. Use projected token volumes for better security Projected tokens have expiration and are audience-specific. More secure than the legacy SA token in /var/run/secrets.
5. Verify token works kubectl exec <pod> -- curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://kubernetes.default.svc/api/v1/namespaces/easypj-prod/pods Should return pod list (200 OK). If 403, the SA has no RBAC permissions.
💡 Personal Advice:
Disable automount for pods that don't need API access. Most web apps don't need to call the K8s API. Set automountServiceAccountToken: false for all pods except those that explicitly need it.
Create dedicated SAs for each app. easypj-api SA, easypj-web SA, easypj-worker SA. Each with its own minimal RBAC. Never use the default SA for applications.
Projected tokens > Legacy tokens. Projected tokens expire (configurable, default 1h), are audience-specific, and don't require a Secret. Use them for all new deployments.
If /var/run/secrets/... doesn't exist, check automountServiceAccountToken. This is always the first thing to check. The directory is only created when the token is mounted.
ES17
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES17
RoleBinding Wrong Namespace — RBAC Not Taking Effect

🔍 Symptom: Django app gets "403 Forbidden" when trying to read ConfigMaps. kubectl auth can-i get configmaps --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-prod:easypj-api -n easypj-prod returns "no." The Role and RoleBinding exist — but the RoleBinding is in the WRONG namespace. RoleBindings are namespace-scoped — a RoleBinding in easypj-dev doesn't grant permissions in easypj-prod.

  kubectl auth can-i get configmaps --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-prod:easypj-api -n easypj-prod
  no     ← SA can't read ConfigMaps in easypj-prod!

  kubectl get rolebinding -n easypj-prod | grep api
  (no output — no RoleBinding in easypj-prod!)

  kubectl get rolebinding -n easypj-dev | grep api
  api-config-reader   Role/config-reader   30m   ← RoleBinding is in easypj-DEV!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. RoleBinding created in wrong namespace: kubectl create rolebinding without -n creates the binding in the default namespace. Pods in easypj-prod don't get the permissions.
  2. SA and RoleBinding in different namespaces: The SA is in easypj-prod, but the RoleBinding is in easypj-dev. A RoleBinding only grants permissions within its own namespace — and can only bind SAs from its own namespace.
  3. Role (namespaced) vs ClusterRole (cluster-wide): Developer created a Role (namespace-scoped) but needed a ClusterRole because the resource is cluster-scoped (e.g., nodes, PVs).
  4. RoleBinding references wrong SA name: subjects: [{kind: ServiceAccount, name: easypj-api}] — but the SA is named api-sa. Name mismatch = no binding.
  5. CI/CD applied YAML to wrong namespace: Pipeline script applies RBAC YAML to staging namespace, but pods run in production namespace.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. RoleBinding references a Group instead of SA — SA is part of system:authenticated group but that group wasn't bound
  2. ArgoCD sync applies RoleBinding to wrong namespace — Application destination namespace mismatch
  3. RoleBinding YAML generated with wrong namespace — kubectl create --dry-run captured the current context namespace
  4. Helm chart creates RoleBinding in release namespace — SA in different namespace not covered
  5. RoleBinding was accidentally deleted — cleanup script removed RBAC that looked unused
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Multiple environments in same cluster: easypj-dev, easypj-staging, easypj-prod namespaces — RBAC must be replicated to each.
  2. New namespace created without RBAC: Namespace provisioning script creates the namespace but doesn't copy RBAC from dev namespace.
  3. Team uses default namespace for RBAC testing: Tests pass in default namespace — RBAC never tested in the actual app namespace.
  4. No RBAC auditing: No tool to verify that SAs have the expected permissions across all namespaces.
  5. kind cluster: all namespaces share same RBAC: On local cluster, RBAC is loose — namespace-scoping issues only appear in production.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa> -n <ns> The definitive test for RBAC. Shows whether a specific SA has a specific permission in a specific namespace.
kubectl get rolebinding,clusterrolebinding -A | grep <sa-name> Find ALL bindings for a ServiceAccount across all namespaces.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The RoleBinding was created in the wrong namespace (easypj-dev instead of easypj-prod). RoleBindings are namespace-scoped — a binding in namespace A grants permissions only within namespace A. The RoleBinding must be in the same namespace as the pod and the resources.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create RoleBinding in the correct namespace kubectl create rolebinding api-config-reader --role=config-reader --serviceaccount=easypj-prod:easypj-api -n easypj-prod Always specify -n with the namespace where the pod and resources are.
2. Copy existing RoleBinding to correct namespace kubectl get rolebinding api-config-reader -n easypj-dev -o yaml | sed 's/namespace: easypj-dev/namespace: easypj-prod/' | kubectl apply -f - Copy the binding from dev to prod. Adjust namespace in the YAML.
3. Verify with kubectl auth can-i kubectl auth can-i get configmaps --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-prod:easypj-api -n easypj-prod Should now return "yes." Test every permission the app needs.
4. Use ClusterRoleBinding for cluster-wide access If the SA needs access to resources across ALL namespaces (or cluster-scoped resources), use ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding.
5. Automate RBAC deployment per namespace Create a script/operator that creates the necessary RoleBindings in every new namespace automatically.
💡 Personal Advice:
RoleBinding namespace must match the pod namespace. If your pod is in easypj-prod, the RoleBinding MUST be in easypj-prod. A RoleBinding in default namespace is invisible to the pod.
kubectl auth can-i --as is your RBAC unit test. Test every permission before deploying. "Why isn't RBAC working?" → kubectl auth can-i gives you the answer.
ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding for cross-namespace access. If one SA needs to read pods in ALL namespaces, use ClusterRole. If it only needs access in its own namespace, use Role.
Automate RBAC bootstrapping per namespace. Every namespace should get the same set of RoleBindings for standard SAs. Automate this — manual copying is error-prone.
ES18
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES18
ClusterRole vs Role — Wrong Scope for Resource

🔍 Symptom: Django app needs to list PersistentVolumes (cluster-scoped resource). The SA has a Role (namespace-scoped) granting access to PVs, but kubectl auth can-i get pv returns "no." PersistentVolumes are cluster-scoped — a namespace Role CANNOT grant access to cluster-scoped resources. Must use ClusterRole.

  kubectl auth can-i get persistentvolumes --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-prod:easypj-api
  no

  kubectl get role pv-reader -n easypj-prod -o yaml | grep -A5 rules
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["persistentvolumes"]     ← PV is cluster-scoped!
    verbs: ["get", "list"]
  # Role can't grant cluster-scoped permissions!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Role used for cluster-scoped resource: PersistentVolumes, Nodes, Namespaces, ClusterRoles are cluster-scoped. A namespace Role can't grant access — must use ClusterRole.
  2. ClusterRole used for namespace-scoped resource: Creating a ClusterRole for Pods, Services, ConfigMaps — over-privileged. Use Role for namespace-scoped resources, ClusterRole only for cluster-scoped.
  3. RoleBinding to ClusterRole in wrong namespace: ClusterRoleBinding grants cluster-wide access. RoleBinding to ClusterRole grants access only in that namespace — often the desired pattern.
  4. Not knowing which resources are cluster-scoped: Developer assumes all resources work with Role. PVs, Nodes, Namespaces, StorageClasses are cluster-scoped.
  5. apiGroups mismatch: apiGroups: [""] (core) vs apiGroups: ["apps"] vs apiGroups: ["*"]. Wrong group = permission not granted.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CRD scope mismatch — custom resource defined as cluster-scoped, but Role trying to access it
  2. Aggregated ClusterRoles not propagated — labels not matching, permissions not aggregated
  3. kubectl explain <resource> shows scope — developer didn't check, assumed namespace-scoped
  4. ClusterRole has node restriction — some ClusterRoles restricted to specific nodes via nodeSelector
  5. Admission webhook rejecting ClusterRole — policy blocks ClusterRole creation for security reasons
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New developer unfamiliar with K8s RBAC scoping: "Role" and "ClusterRole" sound similar — doesn't understand namespace vs cluster scope.
  2. RBAC copied from tutorial without understanding: Tutorial example uses ClusterRole — developer uses it for everything, including namespace resources.
  3. No RBAC linting in CI/CD: kubectl apply accepts Role with cluster-scoped resources — no validation that permissions will work.
  4. Cluster upgrade changes resource scope: Resource moved from namespace-scoped to cluster-scoped in new API version — existing Role breaks.
  5. kind cluster: cluster-admin permissions: Everything works locally as cluster-admin — RBAC scoping issues only discovered in production.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false and kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true List cluster-scoped vs namespace-scoped resources. Cluster-scoped resources require ClusterRole.
kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=<sa> -n <ns> Test the exact permission. If "no" and the resource is cluster-scoped, you need ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: A Role (namespace-scoped) was used for a cluster-scoped resource (PersistentVolume). Namespace Roles CANNOT grant access to cluster-scoped resources — the API server ignores those rules. Fix: use a ClusterRole with ClusterRoleBinding to grant cluster-scoped permissions.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Create a ClusterRole for cluster-scoped resources kubectl create clusterrole pv-reader --verb=get,list --resource=persistentvolumes ClusterRole for PV access. Bind with ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-wide) or RoleBinding (namespace-specific).
2. Bind with ClusterRoleBinding for cluster-wide access kubectl create clusterrolebinding api-pv-reader --clusterrole=pv-reader --serviceaccount=easypj-prod:easypj-api Grants the SA access to PVs across the entire cluster.
3. Or bind with RoleBinding for namespace-restricted access kubectl create rolebinding api-pv-reader --clusterrole=pv-reader --serviceaccount=easypj-prod:easypj-api -n easypj-prod Grants ClusterRole permissions but ONLY within easypj-prod namespace.
4. Check resource scope before creating RBAC kubectl api-resources | grep -E "^NAME|persistentvolume" NAMESPACED column: true = namespaced (use Role), false = cluster-scoped (use ClusterRole).
5. Verify with kubectl auth can-i kubectl auth can-i get pv --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-prod:easypj-api Should now return "yes" after ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding are created.
💡 Personal Advice:
kubectl api-resources tells you scope. Use it. NAMESPACED column: true = Role, false = ClusterRole. Never guess — check before creating RBAC.
ClusterRole + RoleBinding = best of both worlds. Define permission in ClusterRole (reusable). Scope with RoleBinding (namespace-restricted). This is the recommended pattern.
ClusterRoleBinding is cluster-wide — use sparingly. Only for system components and cross-namespace controllers. Most apps should use RoleBinding to a ClusterRole.
RBAC is additive — no deny rules. You can only ADD permissions. If a ClusterRole grants access and a RoleBinding scopes it to a namespace, there's no way to "subtract" from it.
ES19
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES19
kubectl auth can-i — Inconsistent with Actual Access

🔍 Symptom: kubectl auth can-i create pods returns "yes" but kubectl run test --image=nginx fails with "Forbidden." The user can list and get pods (verbs), but creating a pod from the CLI requires pods AND deployments (kubectl run creates a Deployment by default). The auth can-i check was incomplete — didn't check the actual subcommand.

  kubectl auth can-i create pods -n easypj-prod
  yes     ← Can create pods!

  kubectl run test --image=nginx -n easypj-prod
  Error from server (Forbidden): deployments.apps "test" is forbidden: 
  User cannot create resource "deployments" in the namespace "easypj-prod"

  kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n easypj-prod
  no     ← kubectl run creates a Deployment, not a Pod!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. kubectl run creates a Deployment, not a Pod: kubectl run generates a Deployment (since K8s 1.18). kubectl auth can-i create pods returns "yes" but the actual operation requires create deployments.
  2. --subresource not checked: kubectl auth can-i create pods returns "yes" but kubectl exec requires pods/exec subresource. The check was for the wrong subresource.
  3. Impersonation flags missing: kubectl auth can-i uses the current user by default. To check a ServiceAccount's permissions, must use --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>.
  4. Wrong namespace in auth can-i: kubectl auth can-i create pods checks in the current context namespace — but the pod was being created in a different namespace.
  5. Cluster-scoped vs namespace-scoped confusion: kubectl auth can-i get namespaces needs ClusterRole. -n flag is ignored for cluster-scoped resources.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. RBAC changes not propagated yet — RoleBinding created seconds ago, not yet reflected in authorization
  2. Webhook authorizer overriding RBAC — custom webhook allows/denies based on different logic than RBAC
  3. Node authorizer restricting access — system:node RBAC only works from specific nodes
  4. kubeconfig context switching — auth can-i uses different context than the kubectl command
  5. Attribute-based access control (ABAC) also configured — ABAC policy file conflicts with RBAC
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. New developer misunderstanding kubectl run: Thinks kubectl run creates a Pod — it creates a Deployment. auth can-i for pods returns wrong answer for the real action.
  2. Multiple auth modes configured: RBAC + Webhook + ABAC — authorization result depends on which mode responds first.
  3. OIDC authentication with group claim issues: OIDC token missing group claim — user is system:authenticated but not in expected groups.
  4. kind cluster: auth can-i always yes: Local cluster runs as cluster-admin — RBAC tests always pass, production reveals real restrictions.
  5. No RBAC test suite: Organization doesn't test RBAC as part of deployment — permissions assumed, not verified.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl auth can-i --list -n <ns> Lists ALL permissions for the current user/SA. Compare with what the app actually needs.
kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --subresource=<sub> --as=<sa> -n <ns> Check the EXACT permission including subresource. pods/exec, pods/log, etc.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The kubectl auth can-i check was for the wrong resource. kubectl run creates a Deployment (not a Pod), so the check should have been kubectl auth can-i create deployments. Always check the EXACT resource and subresource that the command/application will use.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Check the exact resource the command uses kubectl run test --dry-run=client -o yaml | head -5 shows what resource is created kubectl run creates deployments.apps. Check for that, not pods.
2. Use --list to see all permissions kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-prod:easypj-api -n easypj-prod Shows every permission the SA has. Identify gaps in the resource-verb matrix.
3. Add missing RBAC permissions kubectl create role deploy-creator --verb=create --resource=deployments -n easypj-prod Grant the exact missing permission. Bind to the SA with a RoleBinding.
4. Test the actual command as the SA kubectl run test --dry-run=server --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-prod:easypj-api Server-side dry-run with impersonation catches RBAC errors before real execution.
5. Create an RBAC test suite Automated tests that verify each SA has exactly the permissions it needs — and no more. Run in CI/CD.
💡 Personal Advice:
kubectl run creates a Deployment, not a Pod. Since K8s 1.18. If you auth can-i create pods, you'll think you have permission — but the command uses deployments. Know what your tools actually do.
Always use --as when testing SA permissions. Without --as, you're testing YOUR permissions, not the SA's. Your cluster-admin access always returns "yes" — masking the real issue.
kubectl auth can-i --list is the RBAC diagnostic. It shows everything the SA can do. Compare with what the app actually does. Find gaps before the app breaks.
Server-side dry-run with --as catches RBAC errors. kubectl apply --dry-run=server --as=<sa> This is the closest you can get to "what will happen when the SA does this" without actually doing it.
ES20
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES20
Default ServiceAccount Too Powerful — Every Pod Is Admin

🔍 Symptom: Security audit reveals that EVERY pod in the namespace can list all Secrets. The default ServiceAccount was accidentally bound to the edit ClusterRole via a ClusterRoleBinding. Any pod that doesn't specify a ServiceAccount inherits the default SA — which now has write access to almost everything in the namespace.

  kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-prod:default -n easypj-prod | head -20
  Resources  Non-Resource URLs  Resource Names  Verbs
  pods       []                 []              [create delete get list patch update watch]
  secrets    []                 []              [create delete get list patch update watch]
  services   []                 []              [create delete get list patch update watch]
  # DEFAULT SA has FULL write access to everything!

  kubectl get clusterrolebinding | grep default
  default-edit-binding   ClusterRole/edit   30d   ← Bound default SA to edit!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. ClusterRoleBinding bound to default SA: Someone created a ClusterRoleBinding that binds the edit ClusterRole to the default ServiceAccount in every namespace — every pod inherits edit access.
  2. Default SA used for all deployments: No serviceAccountName specified in Deployment YAML. All pods use the default SA — if default SA has elevated permissions, all pods do.
  3. Temporary debugging permission never revoked: Developer bound admin to default SA to debug an issue — never removed it. Every pod is now admin.
  4. "It works" mentality: App needed Secret access — developer bound the edit role to the default SA because it was the fastest fix. Never created a dedicated SA.
  5. No RBAC review process: No periodic audit of who has what permissions. Default SA over-privileged for months undetected.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Helm chart creates ClusterRoleBinding for default SA — chart designed for ease-of-use, not security
  2. namespace-level edit RoleBinding — each namespace has default SA bound to edit Role via namespace provisioning
  3. system:serviceaccount:<ns>:default group binding — all default SAs in all namespaces share a group, bound to admin role
  4. ArgoCD sync applies old RBAC — Git has ClusterRoleBinding that was supposed to be removed but wasn't
  5. OIDC group mapping — users get default SA's elevated permissions through group inheritance
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. No RBAC hardening after cluster creation: Fresh cluster has relaxed RBAC — never tightened before production workloads deployed.
  2. No security scanning for RBAC: Tools like kube-bench, Popeye, or rbac-lookup not installed — over-privileged SAs undetected.
  3. New team unaware of least privilege: "Just give it admin access" is the culture — no one questions RBAC permissions.
  4. Migration from non-RBAC cluster: Cluster was migrated from K8s 1.5 (pre-RBAC) — all permissions carried over as cluster-admin bindings.
  5. kind cluster: default SA has no restrictions: Local cluster doesn't reflect production RBAC — app works locally with default SA, breaks in production.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:default -n <ns> Check what the default SA can do. If it's more than get/list/watch on a few resources, it's over-privileged.
kubectl get clusterrolebinding,rolebinding -A | grep "default" Find all bindings that reference the default ServiceAccount or the system:serviceaccounts group.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The default ServiceAccount is over-privileged due to a ClusterRoleBinding granting edit access to all default SAs. Since pods that don't specify a serviceAccountName inherit the default SA, every pod in the namespace has write access to almost all resources. Fix: remove the over-privileged binding and create dedicated SAs with minimal RBAC.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Remove over-privileged bindings from default SA kubectl delete clusterrolebinding default-edit-binding Revokes edit access from all default SAs. Pods will lose permissions — create dedicated SAs first.
2. Create dedicated SAs for each app kubectl create sa easypj-api && kubectl create sa easypj-web && kubectl create sa easypj-worker -n easypj-prod Each app gets its own SA. No app uses the default SA.
3. Create minimal Roles for each SA kubectl create role api-role --verb=get,list --resource=configmaps,secrets -n easypj-prod && kubectl create rolebinding api-binding --role=api-role --serviceaccount=easypj-prod:easypj-api Grant ONLY what each app needs. api needs ConfigMaps, Secrets. web needs nothing. worker needs pods/log.
4. Update Deployments to use dedicated SAs serviceAccountName: easypj-api in pod spec Explicitly assign the dedicated SA. Pods no longer inherit the default SA.
5. Audit RBAC monthly kubectl get clusterrolebinding,rolebinding -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.subjects[]?.name == "default")' Find any binding still referencing the default SA. Alert on new bindings to default SA.
💡 Personal Advice:
Never bind roles to the default ServiceAccount. The default SA is used by every pod that doesn't specify one. Binding privileges to it gives privileges to everything. This is the #1 RBAC mistake.
Every app deserves its own ServiceAccount. easypj-api, easypj-web, easypj-worker — each with exactly the permissions it needs. No more, no less. Least privilege.
Default SA should have ZERO permissions beyond the defaults. No RoleBindings, no ClusterRoleBindings. The default SA should only have the auto-generated token access — nothing more.
Audit default SA permissions monthly. Use rbac-lookup, kube-bench, or a simple kubectl command to check. Over-privileged default SAs are a ticking security bomb.

📌 ES21–ES25: Resource Management & CRD Issues

ES21
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES21
ResourceQuota Blocks New Deployments — Namespace Over Limit

🔍 Symptom: kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml fails with "exceeded quota." The namespace has a ResourceQuota limiting CPU to 4 cores and memory to 8Gi. Existing Deployments already use 3.5 CPU — the new Deployment requesting 1 CPU pushes the total to 4.5, exceeding the quota. The Deployment is rejected by the API server.

  kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
  Error from server (Forbidden): deployments.apps "easypj-worker" is forbidden: 
  exceeded quota: easypj-resource-quota, requested: cpu=1, used: cpu=3500m, 
  limited: cpu=4

  kubectl describe resourcequota easypj-resource-quota -n easypj-prod
  Name:       easypj-resource-quota
  Resource    Used    Hard
  --------    ----    ----
  cpu         3500m   4        ← 3.5 used of 4 limit!
  memory      6Gi     8Gi
  pods        8       10
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. New Deployment pushes total requests over quota: Existing resources consume 3.5 CPU. New Deployment needs 1 CPU. Total 4.5 > 4 limit. Deployment rejected.
  2. ResourceQuota too restrictive for the namespace: The quota was set months ago when the namespace had fewer workloads. Growth wasn't planned for.
  3. No resource requests set on existing Deployments: Without requests, pods count as 0 toward quota — but when new pods add requests, quota is suddenly exceeded.
  4. ResourceQuota counts ALL resources — not just CPU/memory: Also limits pods count, services, ConfigMaps, PVCs — any of these can block deployments.
  5. Rolling update temporarily needs extra resources: maxSurge creates an extra pod during rollout — pushes requests temporarily above quota. Rollout blocked.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Multiple ResourceQuotas in same namespace — multiple quotas combine, total limit is the sum
  2. LimitRange adding default requests — pod didn't specify requests, LimitRange adds defaults that push over quota
  3. HPA scaling out — HPA tries to add pods but ResourceQuota blocks new pods, scaling fails silently
  4. Orphaned resources consuming quota — old ReplicaSets or completed Jobs still count against quota
  5. Quota scope selector mismatch — ResourceQuota targets specific priority classes or SAs
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Namespace created with default restrictive quota: New namespace template has low default limits — pods can't fit within them.
  2. Multi-tenant cluster — quotas enforced strictly: Each team gets a fixed quota. Expanding requires approval — deployment blocked until then.
  3. No monitoring on quota usage: Team doesn't know they're at 90% quota — deployment fails as a surprise.
  4. Resource requests inflated "to be safe": Developer set 1 CPU request for a pod that uses 100m — wastes quota, blocks other deployments.
  5. kind cluster: no quotas: Local cluster has no ResourceQuotas — deployment always works, production reveals the restriction.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe resourcequota -n <ns> Shows Used vs Hard for every resource. If any resource is near Hard, quota is blocking deployments.
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -o json | jq '[.items[].spec.containers[].resources.requests.cpu // "0" | tonumber] | add' Calculate total CPU requests in the namespace. Compare with ResourceQuota Hard limit.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The ResourceQuota limits CPU to 4 cores but existing workloads already consume 3.5 cores. The new Deployment requests 1 CPU, pushing total to 4.5 — exceeding the quota. Fix: increase the ResourceQuota limit, reduce existing requests, or reduce the new Deployment's requests.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Increase the ResourceQuota limit kubectl patch resourcequota easypj-resource-quota -n easypj-prod -p '{"spec":{"hard":{"cpu":"8","memory":"16Gi"}}}' Double the CPU/memory quota. Make sure the cluster has the actual capacity.
2. Reduce existing Deployment requests kubectl set resources deploy easypj-api --requests=cpu=200m Many pods request more than they use. Reduce to actual usage + 20% buffer.
3. Reduce new Deployment requests Set CPU request to 200m instead of 1. Use HPA to scale out when needed, not over-provision upfront.
4. Clean up orphaned resources consuming quota kubectl get rs -n easypj-prod | grep "0 .*0 .*0" Delete old ReplicaSets (kubectl delete rs <name>). They count toward pod quota.
5. Set up quota monitoring and alerts Alert when namespace resource usage exceeds 80% of quota. Proactive scaling before deployments fail.
💡 Personal Advice:
ResourceQuota is a hard stop — plan capacity ahead. If you're at 80% quota, the next deployment WILL fail. Monitor quota usage and increase proactively, not reactively.
Don't over-provision requests "to be safe." Requesting 1 CPU for a pod that uses 100m wastes 900m of quota. Set requests to actual usage — limits can be higher for bursting.
RollingUpdate needs extra capacity within quota. maxSurge=1 means one extra pod during rollout — counts against ResourceQuota. Ensure quota has headroom for rollouts.
kubectl describe quota is your first check when deploy fails. "exceeded quota" error = check used vs hard immediately. The error message tells you exactly which resource is over.
ES22
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES22
LimitRange Defaults Not Applied — Pod Has No Resource Limits

🔍 Symptom: A pod was created without any resource requests or limits — it's BestEffort QoS and will be the first killed under memory pressure. The namespace has a LimitRange configured with defaults, but the pod was created before the LimitRange existed. LimitRange only applies to NEW pods — existing pods are not updated.

  kubectl describe pod easypj-api-7f8d9c6b5e | grep -A5 "QoS Class"
  QoS Class: BestEffort     ← NO resources specified!

  kubectl describe limitrange easypj-limits -n easypj-prod
  Type        Resource  Min   Max   Default Request  Default Limit
  Container   cpu       -     -     200m             500m
  Container   memory    -     -     256Mi            512Mi
  # LimitRange exists — but was created AFTER the pod!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. LimitRange created after pods already running: LimitRange only applies to pods created AFTER the LimitRange. Existing pods keep their configuration — need to restart to get defaults.
  2. LimitRange has max limit below pod's request: Pod requests 1 CPU but LimitRange max is 500m. Pod is REJECTED — not limited. Must reduce request.
  3. LimitRange defaults not used because pod specified SOME resources: If pod specifies CPU request but not memory request, only the missing one gets default. Partial spec = partial defaults.
  4. LimitRange scoped to specific container type: LimitRange applies to Containers, but the pod uses initContainers — different scope, defaults not applied.
  5. Multiple LimitRanges with overlapping scopes: Two LimitRanges target the same container — conflict, one of them ignored.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. LimitRange created in wrong namespace — defaults in easypj-dev, pod in easypj-prod
  2. Pod created by controller that overrides defaults — StatefulSet/Job sets its own resource requests
  3. LimitRange updated but only applies to new pods — existing pods not retroactively updated
  4. Default values too low — defaults applied but pod OOMs because 256Mi is insufficient
  5. HPA adjusting replicas — pod count changes but individual pod resources unchanged
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Namespace created without LimitRange: Bootstrap script creates namespace and deploys apps — LimitRange added later, existing pods have no limits.
  2. LimitRange added as part of security hardening: New security policy requires limits — LimitRange created after apps deployed.
  3. CI/CD deploys before LimitRange: Pipeline ordering: Deployment first, LimitRange second — pods created without defaults.
  4. kind cluster: no LimitRange: Local testing doesn't enforce defaults — pods with no resources work fine locally, fail in production.
  5. Team unaware of LimitRange existence: LimitRange was set up by platform team — app developers don't know it exists or how it works.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl describe limitrange -n <ns> and kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml | grep -A10 resources: Compare LimitRange defaults with the pod's actual resource spec. If pod has no resources, it was created before the LimitRange.
kubectl get pods -n <ns> -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].resources.requests == null) | .metadata.name' Find all pods without resource requests. Every one is BestEffort QoS — at risk of OOM.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The LimitRange was created AFTER the pods were already running. LimitRange defaults only apply at pod creation time — existing pods are not updated. Fix: restart pods after creating a LimitRange, or delete and recreate them so they pick up the defaults.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Restart pods to pick up LimitRange defaults kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api -n easypj-prod New pods will have LimitRange defaults applied. Old pods without limits are terminated.
2. Create LimitRange BEFORE deploying workloads Deploy LimitRange as the FIRST resource in a namespace. Then deploy Deployments — all pods inherit defaults.
3. Verify defaults applied after restart kubectl get pod <new-pod> -o yaml | grep -A5 resources: Should show default request/limit values from the LimitRange.
4. Set explicit resources in Deployment YAML (best practice) Don't rely on LimitRange defaults. Set resources explicitly in every Deployment for clarity and predictability.
5. Audit pods without resources kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq '.items[] | select(.spec.containers[].resources.requests == null) | "\(.metadata.namespace)/\(.metadata.name)"' Find and fix all BestEffort pods. Every production pod should have explicit resource requests and limits.
💡 Personal Advice:
LimitRange is a safety net, not a primary resource strategy. Always set resources explicitly in Deployment YAML. Use LimitRange to catch pods that forgot — not as the only source of resource configuration.
Existing pods don't get LimitRange defaults. Only NEW pods created after the LimitRange benefit from defaults. If you add a LimitRange later, YOU must restart pods.
No resources = BestEffort QoS = first to die. A pod without resource requests is the OOM killer's primary target. Every production pod should have requests and limits set.
Deploy LimitRange first, then everything else. Namespace provisioning order: LimitRange → ResourceQuota → Secrets → ConfigMaps → Deployments. This ensures every pod has resources.
ES23
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES23
CRD Schema Validation Rejects Custom Resource

🔍 Symptom: kubectl apply -f jobpost.yaml fails with "Invalid value: jobposts.easypj.com 'my-post' is invalid: spec.priority: Invalid value: 'string': spec.priority in body must be of type integer." The Custom Resource Definition has schema validation that enforces field types, and the submitted YAML has a string where an integer is expected.

  kubectl apply -f jobpost.yaml
  The JobPost "my-post" is invalid: 
  * spec.priority: Invalid value: "string": spec.priority in body must be of type integer

  cat jobpost.yaml | grep priority
    priority: "high"        ← String! Schema says integer!

  kubectl get crd jobposts.easypj.com -o yaml | grep -A10 "priority:"
    priority:
      type: integer          ← Schema requires integer!
      minimum: 1
      maximum: 5
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Wrong data type in custom resource YAML: CRD schema defines priority: integer but YAML has priority: "high" (string). Schema validation rejects the resource.
  2. Required field missing: CRD schema has required: [name, email] but the submitted YAML is missing email. Resource rejected with field-level error.
  3. Enum value not allowed: CRD schema has enum: [low, medium, high] but YAML has status: critical. Not in the allowed values list.
  4. API version mismatch: CRD defines versions: [v1] but YAML uses apiVersion: easypj.com/v1beta1. Version not served.
  5. CRD schema updated — existing resources now invalid: Schema was changed from type: string to type: integer. Existing resources with string values are now invalid on update.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. CRD scope mismatch — Namespaced vs Cluster, resource created in wrong scope
  2. Schema uses OpenAPI v3 features not supported — certain validation keywords not implemented in K8s
  3. Conversion webhook failing — stored version different from served version, conversion error
  4. Printer columns misconfigured — resource created but kubectl get shows wrong data
  5. Subresources not enabled — trying to use /status or /scale subresource but not defined in CRD
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. CRD installed by operator — developer doesn't know the schema: Operator installed the CRD with strict schema — developer writes YAML without reading CRD spec.
  2. New CRD version added — v1alpha1 → v1beta1 → v1: Schema tightened at each stage. v1alpha1 was lenient, v1 is strict — old YAML breaks.
  3. CRD created by another team: Platform team creates CRD — app team writes custom resources without knowing the schema.
  4. No CRD documentation: Schema exists only in the CRD definition — no human-readable docs for what fields require.
  5. kind cluster: CRD without validation schema: Local CRD has no schema — any YAML accepted. Production CRD has strict schema — surprises.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl explain <crd> --recursive Shows the full schema with field types and descriptions. Your YAML must match exactly.
kubectl get crd <name> -o yaml | grep -A50 "openAPIV3Schema:" View the raw validation schema. Check types, required fields, and enum values.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The custom resource YAML has a field with the wrong data type (priority: "high" string instead of integer). The CRD schema enforces type: integer with min/max constraints. Fix: change the field to match the schema type, or update the CRD schema to accept the desired type.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Fix the YAML to match the CRD schema priority: 3 (integer, not "high") Match the field type, enum values, and constraints defined in the CRD schema.
2. Use kubectl explain to see expected schema kubectl explain jobposts.spec.priority Shows the field type, description, and constraints. Write YAML based on this output.
3. Update CRD schema if validation is too strict kubectl edit crd jobposts.easypj.com and adjust the openAPIV3Schema Be careful — loosening validation may break controllers that expect specific types.
4. Use --validate=false to bypass (temporary, not recommended) kubectl apply -f jobpost.yaml --validate=false Bypasses schema validation. Resource stored but may cause controller errors. Use only for migration.
5. Test with server-side dry-run kubectl apply -f jobpost.yaml --dry-run=server Catches schema validation errors BEFORE applying. Always dry-run custom resources.
💡 Personal Advice:
kubectl explain is your CRD API documentation. Every CRD publishes its schema through kubectl explain. Use it before writing custom resource YAML — it tells you exactly what fields and types are expected.
CRD schemas are enforced at admission time. The API server validates custom resources against the CRD schema BEFORE storing them. Invalid resources never reach etcd.
Start with loose validation, tighten over time. CRD v1alpha1: minimal validation. v1beta1: add required fields. v1: full strict schema. This gives users time to adapt.
--dry-run=server catches schema errors without side effects. Always dry-run custom resources. Schema errors are caught before the resource is stored — saving you from partial failures.
ES24
🔐 CATEGORY 4: CONFIG & SECURITY — Issue ES24
Operator Not Reconciling — Missing RBAC Permissions

🔍 Symptom: A custom PostgreSQL Operator is deployed but doesn't create any database pods. Custom resources are created successfully, but the Operator controller logs show "403 Forbidden: cannot create pods." The Operator's ServiceAccount doesn't have RBAC permissions to manage the resources it needs — pods, services, PVCs. The Operator is running but can't do its job.

  kubectl logs -n easypj-system deploy/postgres-operator --tail=5
  ERROR  reconciling PostgresDB "easypj-db": 
  pods is forbidden: User "system:serviceaccount:easypj-system:postgres-operator"
  cannot create resource "pods" in API group "" in the namespace "easypj-prod"

  kubectl auth can-i create pods --as=system:serviceaccount:easypj-system:postgres-operator -n easypj-prod
  no     ← Operator can't create pods!
🔴5 Most Likely Causes
  1. Operator SA doesn't have required RBAC: The Operator creates pods, services, PVCs, ConfigMaps — but its SA only has permissions for its own CRD. Missing RBAC for managed resources.
  2. ClusterRole only in Operator's namespace: Operator SA has a Role (namespace-scoped) but needs a ClusterRole to manage resources across all namespaces where custom resources are deployed.
  3. RBAC YAML not applied with Operator deployment: The Operator Deployment was applied, but the accompanying ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding YAML files were forgotten.
  4. Operator watches wrong namespace: Operator is configured to watch namespace "easypj-prod" but its RBAC only covers "easypj-system" — can't manage resources outside its own namespace.
  5. Helm chart RBAC creation disabled: Chart has rbac.create: false by default — expected user to create RBAC manually. RBAC was never created.
🟡5 Less Likely Causes
  1. Operator RBAC scoped to specific resource names — resourceNames field restricts which resources the Operator can manage
  2. Operator uses webhooks — needs additional RBAC for MutatingWebhookConfiguration and ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
  3. CRD subresources not accessible — Operator needs /status subresource but RBAC doesn't include it
  4. Leader election requires additional RBAC — Operator uses ConfigMap or Endpoint for leader election, needs read/write on those
  5. Aggregated ClusterRole labels wrong — Operator's ClusterRole uses aggregation labels but doesn't match
🟣5 New Cluster Causes
  1. Operator installed from OperatorHub without reading docs: OLM installs Operator but RBAC requirements weren't reviewed — Operator can't manage anything.
  2. New namespace for Operator-managed resources: Operator works in namespace A but custom resources created in namespace B — Operator has no access to B.
  3. Cluster upgraded — RBAC API changed: RBAC API version changed (rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1beta1 removed). Old ClusterRole definitions no longer valid.
  4. kind cluster: cluster-admin avoids RBAC issues: Everything runs as cluster-admin locally — Operator RBAC gaps only visible in production.
  5. Security team tightened RBAC: Audit found Operators had too many permissions — reduced to minimum, broke reconciliation for edge cases.
🔍 What to Look At:
kubectl logs deploy/<operator> | grep -i "forbidden\|unauthorized\|403" Operator logs contain RBAC errors. The error message tells you exactly which resource and verb is missing.
kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa> -n <target-ns> Check what the Operator SA can actually do in the target namespace.
🎯 #1 Root Cause: The Operator's ServiceAccount doesn't have RBAC permissions to create/manage the resources it's responsible for (pods, services, PVCs). The Operator was deployed without the required ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding. Fix: create a ClusterRole with all needed permissions and bind it to the Operator's SA.
🔧 How to Solve:
1. Identify all permissions the Operator needs Check Operator documentation or logs for all resources it manages. Typically: pods, services, pvc, configmaps, secrets, deployments, statefulsets.
