🧪 SCENARIO S5 — Category 1: App Design & Build Image Size

Image Too Large (1.2 GB) — Missing Multi-Stage Build

The Problem: The easypj/jobpost Docker image is 1.2 GB — way too large for production. It pulls slowly, wastes disk space, and includes compilers and dev headers that are a security risk. The Dockerfile uses a single stage with all build tools baked into the final image. Your job: convert the Dockerfile to a multi-stage build, keeping only the runtime artifacts in the final image.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Build on Ubuntu, compare image sizes
1

📋 Build the Bloated Single-Stage Image (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The dev team's CI/CD pipeline takes 3 minutes just to pull the easypj/jobpost image. Deployments are slow, nodes run out of disk space, and the security scanner flagged 87 CVEs — most of them in gcc, make, and dev headers that shouldn't be in production. The single-stage Dockerfile leaves all build tools in the final image. Converting to multi-stage will shrink it from 1.2 GB to ~200 MB.
📁 PROJECT for S5: 
~/jobpost-s5/
├── Dockerfile              ← Single-stage with gcc, dev headers — BUG!
├── requirements.txt
├── Dockerfile.fixed        ← Multi-stage (not yet created — your job!)
└── easypj/
    ├── settings.py
    ├── urls.py
    └── wsgi.py
BASH — Create the bloated single-stage Dockerfile and build it 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S5: Single-Stage Build — Image Too Large
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE PROJECT
mkdir -p ~/jobpost-s5/easypj && cd ~/jobpost-s5

# 2. CREATE THE BLOATED SINGLE-STAGE DOCKERFILE
cat << 'EOF' > Dockerfile
# ❌ BUG! Single-stage keeps ALL build tools in the final image
FROM python:3.12
WORKDIR /app
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc g++ make python3-dev libpq-dev postgresql-client curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput 2>/dev/null || true
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind=0.0.0.0:8000", "easypj.wsgi:application"]
EOF

# 3. CREATE requirements.txt
cat << 'EOF' > requirements.txt
Django==4.2.11
djangorestframework==3.14.0
psycopg2-binary==2.9.9
gunicorn==21.2.0
EOF

# 4. CREATE DJANGO PROJECT FILES
echo "" > easypj/__init__.py
cat << 'EOF' > easypj/settings.py
SECRET_KEY='s5-test-key'
DEBUG=False
ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*']
INSTALLED_APPS=['django.contrib.admin','django.contrib.auth','django.contrib.contenttypes']
ROOT_URLCONF='easypj.urls'
STATIC_URL='/static/'
STATIC_ROOT='/app/staticfiles'
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > easypj/urls.py
from django.urls import path
urlpatterns=[]
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > easypj/wsgi.py
import os
from django.core.wsgi import get_wsgi_application
os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE','easypj.settings')
application=get_wsgi_application()
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > manage.py
#!/usr/bin/env python
import os, sys
if __name__=="__main__":
    os.environ.setdefault("DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE","easypj.settings")
    from django.core.management import execute_from_command_line
    execute_from_command_line(sys.argv)
EOF

# 5. BUILD THE BLOATED IMAGE
docker build -t easypj/jobpost:s5-bloated .

# 6. CHECK THE IMAGE SIZE — IT'S HUGE!
docker images easypj/jobpost:s5-bloated
# → easypj/jobpost   s5-bloated   abc123   1.15GB  ← WAY too big!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check image size: docker images easypj/jobpost:s5-bloated → 1.15 GB — production images should be <300 MB
✗2. Check layers: docker history easypj/jobpost:s5-bloated → gcc, g++, python3-dev all present
✗3. The image contains build tools (gcc, make) that are NEVER used at runtime
✗4. 87 CVEs flagged by security scanner — most in build-only dependencies!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1List installed packages: docker run --rm easypj/jobpost:s5-bloated dpkg -l | grep -E "gcc|g\+\+|make|python3-dev"
→ gcc, g++, make, python3-dev, libpq-dev — ALL present in final image!
2Check pip cache: docker run --rm easypj/jobpost:s5-bloated ls -la /root/.cache/pip
→ pip cache still exists — wasted space
3Identify the fix: Multi-stage build — compile in builder stage, copy only runtime artifacts to final
→ Builder stage: install gcc + dev headers + compile. Final stage: COPY --from=builder only Python packages
4The current Dockerfile has ONE FROM: Everything ends up in one image — no separation of build vs runtime
5Root cause: Single-stage Dockerfile — build tools (gcc, g++, dev headers) are baked into the production image
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Image is 1.2 GB → Too large for production
②
docker history → gcc, dev headers present
③
These are BUILD-ONLY dependencies
④
Multi-stage: build in stage 1, copy to stage 2
⑤
Result: 1.2 GB → ~200 MB (83% reduction!)

Tenet: Multi-stage builds are the #1 technique for reducing Docker image size. The first stage (builder) has all compilers and dev tools — it compiles your app. The second stage (runtime) starts fresh from a minimal base and copies ONLY the compiled artifacts using COPY --from=builder. Build tools never enter the final image. For Python apps, use pip install --user in the builder and copy /root/.local to the runtime. This single technique reduces image size by 70-90% and eliminates most CVEs.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ docker images easypj/jobpost:s5-bloated REPOSITORY TAG IMAGE ID SIZE easypj/jobpost s5-bloated abc123def456 1.15GB ← HUGE!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ docker images easypj/jobpost:s5-optimized REPOSITORY TAG IMAGE ID SIZE easypj/jobpost s5-optimized xyz789abc012 195MB ← 83% smaller! ✅
🔧
Dockerfile — Multi-Stage Build (replace the old Dockerfile) 
# ═══════════ STAGE 1: BUILDER (all dev tools here) ═══════════
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc g++ make python3-dev libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# ═══════════ STAGE 2: RUNTIME (minimal, no build tools) ═══════════
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
# Install ONLY runtime dependencies (no compilers!)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \
    && useradd -m -u 1000 django
# Copy ONLY Python packages from builder (no gcc, no dev headers!)
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /usr/local
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput 2>/dev/null || true
USER django
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind=0.0.0.0:8000", "easypj.wsgi:application"]
BASH — Replace Dockerfile and rebuild 
# Save the multi-stage Dockerfile (overwrite the old one)
cd ~/jobpost-s5
# Copy the multi-stage Dockerfile content above into Dockerfile

# Rebuild
docker build --no-cache -t easypj/jobpost:s5-optimized .

# Compare sizes!
docker images | grep "s5"
# easypj/jobpost   s5-optimized   xyz789   195MB  ✅ FAST & SMALL!
# easypj/jobpost   s5-bloated     abc123   1.15GB ❌ HUGE & DANGEROUS!
✓

✅ Verify — Image Shrunk from 1.15 GB to 195 MB

The multi-stage build reduces the image by 83% (from 1.15 GB to 195 MB). The final image contains only Python packages and the application code — no gcc, no g++, no dev headers, no pip cache. This means faster pulls, faster deploys, less disk usage, and dramatically fewer CVEs. The image still runs the same application — the key difference is WHERE the build tools exist (only in the builder stage, which is discarded).

💡 Key takeaway: Multi-stage builds are the standard for ALL production Dockerfiles. Use pip install --user in the builder stage and COPY --from=builder /root/.local /usr/local in the runtime stage. The builder stage is never pushed to registries — it only exists during docker build. Every production Dockerfile should be multi-stage.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Remove both images
docker rmi easypj/jobpost:s5-bloated
docker rmi easypj/jobpost:s5-optimized

# Remove project
rm -rf ~/jobpost-s5

# Verify
docker images | grep "s5"
S6
🧪 SCENARIO S6 — Category 1: App Design & Build CronJob

CronJob Never Fires — Invalid Cron Schedule (4 Fields)

The Problem: The easypj team created a CronJob to run nightly database backups at 2 AM. The CronJob was applied successfully — no errors — but it never fires. No jobs are created, no pods run, the backup directory stays empty. The schedule looks correct at first glance: 0 2 * *. But Kubernetes cron syntax requires 5 fields (minute hour day month weekday) — this schedule only has 4. Your job: find why the CronJob never triggers and fix the schedule.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node cluster for CronJob testing
1

📋 Create CronJob with Invalid Schedule (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj operations team set up automated PostgreSQL backups for the job board database. The CronJob manifest was reviewed in a PR and merged — no syntax errors, kubectl accepted it. But after 3 days, the SRE noticed the backup directory was empty. The cron schedule has only 4 fields (0 2 * *) instead of the required 5 (0 2 * * *). Kubernetes accepted the YAML but silently ignored the schedule — the CronJob controller can't parse it. Every night without backups is a data loss risk.
📁 MANIFESTS for S6: 
s6-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml        ← kubectl create ns s6-jobpost
├── 01-cronjob.yaml          ← CronJob with BUG: schedule "0 2 * *"
│                              ❌ 4 fields instead of 5 — never fires!
└── 02-pvc.yaml              ← PVC for backup storage
BASH — Create namespace, PVC, and CronJob with invalid schedule 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S6: CronJob — Invalid 4-Field Cron Schedule
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create ns s6-jobpost

# 2. CREATE PVC FOR BACKUP STORAGE
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: backup-pvc
  namespace: s6-jobpost
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
EOF

# 3. CREATE CRONJOB WITH THE BUG
#    ❌ BUG! Schedule "0 2 * *" has only 4 fields!
#    Kubernetes cron requires 5: minute hour day month weekday
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: db-backup
  namespace: s6-jobpost
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * *"         # ❌ BUG! 4 fields — should be "0 2 * * *"
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 1
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
          - name: backup
            image: postgres:15-alpine
            command:
            - /bin/sh
            - -c
            - |
              echo "Backup started at $(date)"
              pg_dump -h easypj-db -U easypj -d jobpost > /backups/backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).sql
              echo "Backup completed"
            env:
            - name: PGPASSWORD
              value: secret123
            volumeMounts:
            - name: backup-storage
              mountPath: /backups
          volumes:
          - name: backup-storage
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: backup-pvc
EOF

# 4. CHECK THE CRONJOB — It was created but will NEVER fire!
kubectl get cj -n s6-jobpost
kubectl describe cj db-backup -n s6-jobpost | grep -A5 Schedule
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check CronJob: kubectl get cj -n s6-jobpost → LAST SCHEDULE: None — never fired!
✗2. Check Jobs: kubectl get jobs -n s6-jobpost → No resources found
✗3. Check Pods: kubectl get pods -n s6-jobpost → No backup pods ever created
✗4. Backup directory is EMPTY — data loss risk growing every night!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check CronJob details: kubectl get cj db-backup -n s6-jobpost -o yaml | grep schedule
→ schedule: 0 2 * * — Only 4 fields!
2Count the fields: Kubernetes cron format is MINUTE HOUR DAY MONTH WEEKDAY (5 fields)
→ "0 2 * *" has: minute=0, hour=2, day=*, month=*, weekday=MISSING!
3Check controller logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/coredns — No, check CronJob controller events
→ kubectl get events -n s6-jobpost --field-selector involvedObject.name=db-backup — No events at all. The controller silently ignores invalid schedules.
4Compare with valid cron: Standard Linux cron uses 5 fields: 0 2 * * * (minute=0, hour=2, every day, every month, every weekday)
→ Missing the 5th field (weekday)!
5Root cause: CronJob schedule has 4 fields instead of 5 — Kubernetes CronJob controller silently ignores invalid cron expressions, never scheduling any jobs
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
CronJob exists but LAST SCHEDULE = None
②
No Jobs or Pods ever created
③
Check schedule field → "0 2 * *"
④
Count: 4 fields. K8s needs 5!
⑤
Fix to "0 2 * * *" → Jobs fire!

Tenet: Kubernetes CronJob uses the standard 5-field cron format: MINUTE HOUR DAY MONTH WEEKDAY. A 4-field schedule is silently accepted by the API (no validation error) but the CronJob controller cannot parse it and will NEVER create jobs. Always verify with kubectl get cj — if LAST SCHEDULE stays None after the scheduled time passes, your cron expression is invalid. This is one of the most common CronJob bugs because it fails silently.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get cj -n s6-jobpost NAME SCHEDULE SUSPEND ACTIVE LAST SCHEDULE AGE db-backup 0 2 * * False 0 <none> 5m ← Never fires!
$ kubectl get jobs -n s6-jobpost No resources found in s6-jobpost namespace. ← No jobs created!
$ kubectl get cj db-backup -n s6-jobpost -o yaml | grep schedule schedule: 0 2 * * ← Only 4 fields! Should be "0 2 * * *"
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get cj -n s6-jobpost NAME SCHEDULE SUSPEND ACTIVE LAST SCHEDULE AGE db-backup 0 2 * * * False 0 2m ago 10m ✅ Firing!
$ kubectl get jobs -n s6-jobpost NAME COMPLETIONS DURATION AGE db-backup-28901234 1/1 12s 2m ✅ Job ran!
🔧
BASH — Patch the CronJob with correct 5-field schedule 
# Method 1: Patch the schedule (RECOMMENDED)
kubectl patch cj db-backup -n s6-jobpost -p '{"spec":{"schedule":"0 2 * * *"}}'

# Method 2: Edit directly
kubectl edit cj db-backup -n s6-jobpost
# Change: schedule: "0 2 * *"  →  schedule: "0 2 * * *"

# Verify the fix
kubectl get cj db-backup -n s6-jobpost
# → SCHEDULE should now show "0 2 * * *" (5 fields)

# OPTIONAL: Manually trigger a test job to verify it works
kubectl create job --from=cronjob/db-backup test-backup -n s6-jobpost
kubectl logs -l job-name=test-backup -n s6-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — CronJob Schedule Corrected to 5 Fields

After patching the schedule to the correct 5-field format 0 2 * * *, the CronJob controller can now parse the expression and will create Jobs at the scheduled time. kubectl get cj -n s6-jobpost shows the correct 5-field schedule. The backup system is now properly configured — nightly backups at 2 AM UTC are ensured.

💡 Key takeaway: Kubernetes CronJob schedule uses standard 5-field cron: MINUTE(0-59) HOUR(0-23) DAY(1-31) MONTH(1-12) WEEKDAY(0-6). Always verify with kubectl get cj -o yaml | grep schedule. If LAST SCHEDULE stays None, your cron syntax is invalid. The API does NOT validate cron expressions — it silently accepts and ignores invalid ones.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything
kubectl delete ns s6-jobpost

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get ns s6-jobpost 2>&1
# → Error from server (NotFound): namespaces "s6-jobpost" not found
S7
🧪 SCENARIO S7 — Category 1: App Design & Build Sidecar

Redis Ambassador Sidecar — Wrong Hostname (localhost vs Service DNS)

The Problem: The easypj API pod has a Redis ambassador sidecar that manages connection pooling to the Redis cache. The pod starts, both containers run — but the API can't reach Redis. The ambassador connects to localhost:6379 instead of the Kubernetes Service DNS name redis-svc:6379. localhost inside each container is its own network namespace — not the Redis Service. Your job: find the misconfigured hostname and fix the sidecar.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-container pod debugging
1

📋 Deploy Redis Service + API Pod with Sidecar (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj job board uses Redis for caching job listings and Celery task queues. The platform team decided to use a sidecar ambassador pattern: each API pod gets a lightweight Redis proxy that handles connection pooling. The sidecar was configured by a new engineer who tested it with redis-cli -h localhost during development (where Redis was on the same machine). In Kubernetes, localhost means the container itself — not the Redis Service. The ambassador connects to itself, finds no Redis, and the API gets connection errors.
📁 MANIFESTS for S7: 
s7-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml        ← kubectl create ns s7-jobpost
├── 01-redis-deploy.yaml     ← Redis Deployment + Service (correct)
├── 02-api-pod.yaml          ← API Pod with Redis ambassador sidecar
│                              ❌ BUG: REDIS_HOST=localhost instead of redis-svc
└── 03-api-service.yaml      ← ClusterIP Service for API (port 8000)
BASH — Deploy Redis, then API pod with broken sidecar 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S7: Sidecar — Wrong Redis Host (localhost)
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create ns s7-jobpost

# 2. DEPLOY REDIS (correct — no bugs here)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: redis
  namespace: s7-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: redis
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: redis
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: redis
        image: redis:7-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 6379
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: redis-svc
  namespace: s7-jobpost
spec:
  selector:
    app: redis
  ports:
  - port: 6379
    targetPort: 6379
EOF

# 3. WAIT FOR REDIS TO BE READY
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app=redis -n s7-jobpost --timeout=60s

# 4. DEPLOY API POD WITH SIDECAR — THE BUG IS HERE!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s7-jobpost
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
spec:
  containers:
  # Main container: Django API
  - name: django-api
    image: python:3.12-slim
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
    - |
      pip install django djangorestframework redis 2>/dev/null
      echo "Starting API — connecting to Redis via sidecar at localhost:16379..."
      python -c "
import redis, time, os
redis_host = os.environ.get('REDIS_HOST', 'localhost')
print(f'API: Trying Redis at {redis_host}:6379 via sidecar proxy...')
time.sleep(5)
try:
    r = redis.Redis(host=redis_host, port=6379, socket_timeout=2)
    r.ping()
    print('API: Connected to Redis successfully!')
except Exception as e:
    print(f'API: FAILED to connect to Redis: {e}')
    print('API: Job board cache is DOWN!')
"
      while true; do sleep 3600; done
    env:
    - name: REDIS_HOST
      value: "localhost"
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
  # Sidecar: Redis Ambassador (BROKEN — wrong host!)
  - name: redis-ambassador
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
    - |
      echo "Redis Ambassador starting..."
      # ❌ BUG! Connecting to localhost:6379 instead of redis-svc:6379
      REDIS_TARGET="localhost:6379"
      echo "Ambassador: Forwarding to $REDIS_TARGET"
      # Simulate connection failure by trying to connect
      while true; do
        if redis-cli -h localhost -p 6379 PING 2>/dev/null; then
          echo "Ambassador: Connected to Redis"
        else
          echo "Ambassador: ERROR — Cannot connect to Redis at localhost:6379"
          echo "Ambassador: The Redis Service is at redis-svc:6379, NOT localhost!"
        fi
        sleep 10
      done
EOF

# 5. CHECK LOGS — Ambassador will show connection errors!
kubectl logs easypj-api -c redis-ambassador -n s7-jobpost --tail=10
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check ambassador logs: kubectl logs easypj-api -c redis-ambassador -n s7-jobpost → "Cannot connect to Redis at localhost:6379"
✗2. Check API logs: kubectl logs easypj-api -c django-api -n s7-jobpost → "FAILED to connect to Redis"
✗3. Redis IS running: kubectl get pods -l app=redis -n s7-jobpost → Running ✅ — the problem is connectivity, not availability
✗4. Job board cache is DOWN — search results and listing pages are slow/unavailable
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check the ambassador's target: kubectl logs easypj-api -c redis-ambassador -n s7-jobpost | grep Forwarding
→ "Ambassador: Forwarding to localhost:6379" — localhost is the CONTAINER, not Redis!
2Verify Redis Service exists: kubectl get svc -n s7-jobpost
→ redis-svc ClusterIP 10.96.x.x 6379/TCP — Redis Service IS available!
3Test Redis from the API pod (bypass ambassador): kubectl exec easypj-api -c django-api -n s7-jobpost -- python -c "import redis; r=redis.Redis(host='redis-svc',port=6379); print(r.ping())"
→ Works when using redis-svc! The problem is the ambassador using localhost.
4Understand Kubernetes networking: Each container has its own network namespace. localhost:6379 in the ambassador = the ambassador container itself. The Redis Service is at redis-svc:6379 (cluster DNS).
5Root cause: Sidecar ambassador connects to localhost:6379 (itself) instead of the Redis Service at redis-svc:6379
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Ambassador logs: "Cannot connect to localhost"
②
Redis Service exists → Not a deployment issue
③
Ambassador uses "localhost" → Wrong target
④
Each container has own network namespace
⑤
Change to redis-svc → Ambassador connects!

Tenet: In Kubernetes, localhost inside a container refers to THAT container only — not the pod, not the node, and definitely not a Service. Multi-container pods share the same network namespace, so localhost CAN reach another container in the SAME pod. But a Service is a separate pod — you MUST use the Service DNS name (<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local or just <service>). On CKAD, "can't connect to localhost" in a sidecar is a classic sign of this misconfiguration.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs easypj-api -c redis-ambassador -n s7-jobpost --tail=5 Redis Ambassador starting... Ambassador: Forwarding to localhost:6379 Ambassador: ERROR — Cannot connect to Redis at localhost:6379 Ambassador: ERROR — Cannot connect to Redis at localhost:6379 Ambassador: The Redis Service is at redis-svc:6379, NOT localhost!
$ kubectl get svc -n s7-jobpost NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP PORT(S) AGE redis-svc ClusterIP 10.96.100.50 6379/TCP 10m ← Redis IS available!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl logs easypj-api -c redis-ambassador -n s7-jobpost --tail=3 Ambassador: Forwarding to redis-svc:6379 Ambassador: Connected to Redis ✅ Ambassador: Proxying requests on port 16379...
🔧
BASH — Patch the Pod with correct Redis host 
# Since Pod specs are mostly immutable, delete and recreate
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s7-jobpost

# Recreate with FIXED ambassador config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s7-jobpost
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
spec:
  containers:
  - name: django-api
    image: python:3.12-slim
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
    - |
      pip install django djangorestframework redis 2>/dev/null
      echo "API: Connected to Redis via sidecar!"
      while true; do sleep 3600; done
    env:
    - name: REDIS_HOST
      value: "localhost"
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
  - name: redis-ambassador
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
    - |
      # ✅ FIXED! Using redis-svc instead of localhost
      REDIS_TARGET="redis-svc:6379"
      echo "Ambassador: Forwarding to $REDIS_TARGET"
      while true; do
        redis-cli -h redis-svc -p 6379 PING && echo "Ambassador: Connected to Redis"
        sleep 10
      done
EOF

# Verify the fix
kubectl logs easypj-api -c redis-ambassador -n s7-jobpost --tail=5
✓

✅ Verify — Ambassador Connects to Redis via Service DNS

After changing the ambassador's target from localhost:6379 to redis-svc:6379, the sidecar successfully connects to the Redis Service. The API can now cache job listings via Redis. The job board search is fast again. The key insight: in Kubernetes, Service DNS names replace localhost for inter-pod communication. Always use <service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local for reliable connectivity.

💡 Key takeaway: localhost in a container = that container only. For pod-to-pod communication, use Service DNS. For container-to-container in the SAME pod, localhost DOES work (shared network namespace). For sidecars that proxy external services, use environment variables or ConfigMaps for the target host — never hardcode localhost.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything
kubectl delete ns s7-jobpost

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get ns s7-jobpost 2>&1
# → Error from server (NotFound): namespaces "s7-jobpost" not found
S8
🧪 SCENARIO S8 — Category 1: App Design & Build Adapter

Log Adapter Sidecar — Shared Volume Mount Path Mismatch

The Problem: The easypj Django app writes application logs to a shared emptyDir volume. A Fluentd adapter sidecar is supposed to read those logs, convert them to JSON, and forward them to the logging system. Both containers mount the same volume — but at different paths. Django writes to /var/log/app/app.log while Fluentd watches /logs/app.log. The adapter never sees any log files. Your job: find the mount path mismatch and align them.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-container volume debugging
1

📋 Deploy Pod with Log Adapter — Misaligned Volume Mounts (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj observability team set up centralized logging with EFK (Elasticsearch, Fluentd, Kibana). Each app pod writes logs to a shared volume, and a Fluentd adapter sidecar tails the log file and ships JSON to Elasticsearch. The junior DevOps engineer configured the volume mounts — but used different mount paths in each container. Django writes to /var/log/app/app.log but Fluentd is watching /logs/app.log. Same volume, different paths inside each container — the adapter sees an empty directory. No logs are being shipped to Elasticsearch.
📁 MANIFESTS for S8: 
s8-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml        ← kubectl create ns s8-jobpost
└── 01-app-pod.yaml          ← Pod with Django + Fluentd sidecar
│                              ❌ BUG: Volume mounts at different paths!
│                              Django: mountPath /var/log/app
│                              Fluentd: mountPath /logs  (WRONG!)
BASH — Deploy pod with mismatched volume mounts 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S8: Adapter — Volume Mount Path Mismatch
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create ns s8-jobpost

# 2. DEPLOY POD WITH MISMATCHED VOLUME MOUNTS
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-app
  namespace: s8-jobpost
  labels:
    app: easypj-app
spec:
  volumes:
  - name: app-logs
    emptyDir: {}
  containers:
  # Django app — writes logs to /var/log/app/app.log
  - name: django-app
    image: python:3.12-slim
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
    - |
      mkdir -p /var/log/app
      while true; do
        echo "[$(date -Iseconds)] INFO Request processed: 200 OK" >> /var/log/app/app.log
        echo "[$(date -Iseconds)] DEBUG Query: SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE status='active'" >> /var/log/app/app.log
        echo "App: Wrote 2 log lines to /var/log/app/app.log"
        sleep 5
      done
    volumeMounts:
    - name: app-logs
      mountPath: /var/log/app      # Django writes here
  # Fluentd adapter — watches /logs/app.log (WRONG PATH!)
  - name: fluentd-adapter
    image: alpine:3.19
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
    - |
      echo "Fluentd Adapter: Watching /logs/app.log for new entries..."
      sleep 3
      if [ -f /logs/app.log ]; then
        echo "Fluentd Adapter: Found log file, starting tail..."
        tail -f /logs/app.log | while read line; do
          echo "Fluentd: Shipping to ES: {\"msg\": \"$line\"}"
        done
      else
        echo "Fluentd Adapter: ❌ ERROR — /logs/app.log NOT FOUND!"
        echo "Fluentd Adapter: Contents of /logs/: $(ls -la /logs/ 2>&1 || echo 'EMPTY')"
        echo "Fluentd Adapter: Django writes to /var/log/app/ — I'm watching /logs/!"
        echo "Fluentd Adapter: VOLUME MOUNT PATH MISMATCH DETECTED!"
        while true; do sleep 60; done
      fi
    volumeMounts:
    - name: app-logs
      mountPath: /logs             # ❌ BUG! Fluentd watches /logs — Django writes to /var/log/app!
EOF

# 3. CHECK LOGS — Fluentd will report the mismatch!
kubectl logs easypj-app -c fluentd-adapter -n s8-jobpost
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Fluentd adapter logs: kubectl logs easypj-app -c fluentd-adapter -n s8-jobpost → "/logs/app.log NOT FOUND"
✗2. Fluentd sees EMPTY directory at /logs/ — no log files present
✗3. Django IS writing logs: kubectl logs easypj-app -c django-app -n s8-jobpost → "Wrote 2 log lines to /var/log/app/app.log"
✗4. No logs are being shipped to Elasticsearch — observability is BLIND!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Django's mount path: kubectl get pod easypj-app -n s8-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A3 "name: django-app" | grep mountPath
→ mountPath: /var/log/app
2Check Fluentd's mount path: kubectl get pod easypj-app -n s8-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A3 "name: fluentd-adapter" | grep mountPath
→ mountPath: /logs — DIFFERENT from Django's /var/log/app!
3Verify the volume is the same: Both containers mount name: app-logs — same volume, BUT at different paths inside each container
→ The volume data lives at /var/log/app inside django-app but at /logs inside fluentd-adapter. They're looking at DIFFERENT directories on the same volume!
4Root cause: Both containers mount the same emptyDir volume but at different mountPath values — Django writes to /var/log/app/app.log but Fluentd watches /logs/app.log (empty directory)
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Fluentd: "app.log NOT FOUND"
②
Django IS writing logs → File exists somewhere
③
Check mountPath of each container
④
/var/log/app ≠ /logs → PATH MISMATCH!
⑤
Align mountPath → Fluentd sees logs!

Tenet: When two containers share a volume via emptyDir or persistentVolumeClaim, the volume data is the SAME — but each container sees it at its own mountPath. If mountPath differs between containers, files written to /path/A/file.log in container 1 will appear at /path/B/file.log in container 2 — or NOT at all if the subdirectory doesn't match. Always align mountPath across containers that need to read each other's files. On CKAD, volume path mismatches are a common sidecar debugging scenario.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs easypj-app -c fluentd-adapter -n s8-jobpost Fluentd Adapter: Watching /logs/app.log for new entries... Fluentd Adapter: ❌ ERROR — /logs/app.log NOT FOUND! Fluentd Adapter: Contents of /logs/: (empty) Fluentd Adapter: Django writes to /var/log/app/ — I'm watching /logs/! Fluentd Adapter: VOLUME MOUNT PATH MISMATCH DETECTED!
$ kubectl logs easypj-app -c django-app -n s8-jobpost --tail=3 App: Wrote 2 log lines to /var/log/app/app.log App: Wrote 2 log lines to /var/log/app/app.log App: Wrote 2 log lines to /var/log/app/app.log ← Django IS writing!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl logs easypj-app -c fluentd-adapter -n s8-jobpost --tail=3 Fluentd Adapter: Found log file, starting tail... Fluentd: Shipping to ES: {"msg": "[2024-06-12] INFO Request processed: 200 OK"} Fluentd: Shipping to ES: {"msg": "[2024-06-12] DEBUG Query: SELECT..."} ✅
🔧
BASH — Delete and recreate pod with aligned mountPath 
# Delete the broken pod
kubectl delete pod easypj-app -n s8-jobpost

# Recreate with ALIGNED mountPath in Fluentd
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-app
  namespace: s8-jobpost
  labels:
    app: easypj-app
spec:
  volumes:
  - name: app-logs
    emptyDir: {}
  containers:
  - name: django-app
    image: python:3.12-slim
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
    - |
      mkdir -p /var/log/app
      while true; do
        echo "[$(date -Iseconds)] INFO Request processed: 200 OK" >> /var/log/app/app.log
        sleep 5
      done
    volumeMounts:
    - name: app-logs
      mountPath: /var/log/app
  - name: fluentd-adapter
    image: alpine:3.19
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
    - |
      sleep 3
      tail -f /var/log/app/app.log | while read line; do
        echo "Fluentd: Shipping to ES: {\"msg\": \"$line\"}"
      done
    volumeMounts:
    - name: app-logs
      mountPath: /var/log/app       # ✅ FIXED! Now matches Django's mountPath
EOF

# Verify Fluentd can now read the logs
kubectl logs easypj-app -c fluentd-adapter -n s8-jobpost --tail=5
✓

✅ Verify — Fluentd Reads Logs via Aligned Mount Path

After aligning the mountPath in both containers to /var/log/app, Fluentd can now see and tail the Django application logs. The adapter ships JSON-formatted logs to Elasticsearch. The logging pipeline is operational. The fix was simple: both containers must mount the shared volume at the same path if they access the same files.

💡 Key takeaway: Shared volumes in Kubernetes use the same underlying storage, but each container has its own filesystem namespace. If container A writes to /data/file.log and container B reads from /logs/file.log, they won't match unless both mountPath values resolve to the same directory on the volume. Always verify volume mount consistency when debugging sidecar adapters.

Multi-Stage Build Fails — Typo in COPY --from Stage Name

The Problem: You converted the easypj/jobpost Dockerfile to a multi-stage build. The builder stage compiles dependencies, the runtime stage copies only the artifacts. But the build fails at the COPY --from step with "stage not found." You used COPY --from=buildr but the builder stage is named builder. One missing letter — and Docker can't find the stage. Your job: find the typo in the stage name and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Build on Ubuntu host. Docker scenario only.
1

📋 Create Multi-Stage Dockerfile with Typo & Attempt Build (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: After the SRE flagged the 1.2 GB single-stage image, the dev team rewrote the Dockerfile as a proper multi-stage build. Stage 1 (named builder) installs all compilers and builds the Python dependencies. Stage 2 (runtime) copies only the compiled packages. But during the YAML review, a reviewer suggested renaming the stage — and the COPY --from line was updated incorrectly. The stage is named builder but the COPY references buildr — one letter missing. Docker can't find a stage named "buildr" and the build fails.
📁 PROJECT for S9: 
~/jobpost-s9/
├── Dockerfile              ← Multi-stage with BUG: COPY --from=buildr
│                              Stage is named "builder" — typo in reference!
├── requirements.txt
└── easypj/                 ← Minimal Django project
BASH — Create multi-stage Dockerfile with stage name typo 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S9: Multi-Stage — Wrong COPY --from Stage Name
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE PROJECT
mkdir -p ~/jobpost-s9/easypj && cd ~/jobpost-s9

# 2. CREATE MULTI-STAGE DOCKERFILE WITH THE BUG
cat << 'EOF' > Dockerfile
# ═══ Stage 1: Builder (named "builder") ═══
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc python3-dev libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# ═══ Stage 2: Runtime ═══
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \
    && useradd -m -u 1000 django
# ❌ BUG! "buildr" is not the stage name — it's "builder"!
COPY --from=buildr /root/.local /usr/local
COPY . .
USER django
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind=0.0.0.0:8000", "easypj.wsgi:application"]
EOF

# 3. CREATE requirements.txt
cat << 'EOF' > requirements.txt
Django==4.2.11
djangorestframework==3.14.0
gunicorn==21.2.0
EOF

# 4. CREATE MINIMAL DJANGO PROJECT
echo "" > easypj/__init__.py
cat << 'EOF' > easypj/settings.py
SECRET_KEY='s9-key'
DEBUG=True
ALLOWED_HOSTS=['*']
INSTALLED_APPS=['django.contrib.admin','django.contrib.auth','django.contrib.contenttypes']
ROOT_URLCONF='easypj.urls'
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > easypj/urls.py
from django.urls import path
urlpatterns=[]
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > easypj/wsgi.py
import os
from django.core.wsgi import get_wsgi_application
os.environ.setdefault('DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE','easypj.settings')
application=get_wsgi_application()
EOF

# 5. ATTEMPT THE BUILD — THIS WILL FAIL!
docker build -t easypj/jobpost:s9 .

# EXPECTED OUTPUT:
# ERROR: failed to solve: buildr not found
# The stage name in "COPY --from" must match an AS name
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Build fails at Stage 2: COPY --from=buildr → "buildr not found"
✗2. Check the stage name: grep "AS " Dockerfile → Stage is named builder, not buildr!
✗3. Stage 1 (builder) builds fine — Stage 2 fails at the COPY step
✗4. Cannot deploy without a built image — CI/CD pipeline is BLOCKED!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Read the error message: ERROR: failed to solve: buildr not found
→ Docker is looking for a stage named "buildr"
2List defined stages: grep "^FROM" Dockerfile
→ FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder — Stage is named builder (with "e")!
3Find all COPY --from lines: grep "COPY --from" Dockerfile
→ COPY --from=buildr — MISSING the "e"! Should be builder!
4Compare: Stage name = builder (7 letters). COPY --from = buildr (6 letters). One letter dropped.
5Root cause: Typo in COPY --from=buildr — stage is named builder but COPY references the non-existent buildr
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Build fails: "buildr not found"
②
Check FROM lines → Stage is "builder"
③
Check COPY --from → "buildr" (typo!)
④
builder ≠ buildr → One letter missing
⑤
Fix typo → Rebuild → SUCCESS

Tenet: In multi-stage Dockerfiles, COPY --from=<stage> and FROM <image> AS <stage> must use the EXACT same stage name — including case. A single character typo ("buildr" vs "builder") breaks the entire build. Docker does NOT do fuzzy matching on stage names. On CKAD, always verify that every COPY --from reference matches an AS name exactly.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ docker build -t easypj/jobpost:s9 . [+] Building 15.2s (8/10) => [builder 1/4] FROM python:3.12-slim 0.0s => [builder 2/4] RUN apt-get update && apt-get... 12.1s => [builder 3/4] COPY requirements.txt . 0.1s => [builder 4/4] RUN pip install --user -r... 3.0s => [stage-1 1/5] FROM python:3.12-slim 0.0s => ERROR [stage-1 2/5] COPY --from=buildr /root/.local /usr/local 0.0s ------ > [stage-1 2/5] COPY --from=buildr /root/.local /usr/local: ------ ERROR: failed to solve: failed to prepare stage "buildr": stage not found
$ grep -E "(^FROM|COPY --from)" Dockerfile FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder ← Stage name is "builder" FROM python:3.12-slim COPY --from=buildr /root/.local /usr/local ← TYPO! "buildr" ≠ "builder"
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ sed -i 's/--from=buildr/--from=builder/' Dockerfile && docker build -t easypj/jobpost:s9 . [+] Building 28.5s (13/13) FINISHED => [stage-1 2/5] COPY --from=builder /root/.local /usr/local 2.1s ✅ => naming to easypj/jobpost:s9 0.0s ✅ BUILD SUCCESS!
🔧
BASH — Fix the typo and rebuild 
# Fix the typo: buildr → builder
cd ~/jobpost-s9
sed -i 's/--from=buildr/--from=builder/' Dockerfile

# Verify the fix
grep "COPY --from" Dockerfile
# → COPY --from=builder /root/.local /usr/local  ✅

# Rebuild
docker build -t easypj/jobpost:s9 .

# Verify image
docker images | grep jobpost
# → easypj/jobpost   s9   def456   200MB  ✅
✓

✅ Verify — Multi-Stage Build Completes

After correcting buildr to builder, the multi-stage Docker build completes successfully. The runtime stage correctly copies only the compiled Python packages from the builder stage — no compilers, no dev headers in the final image. The image size is optimized at ~200 MB instead of 1+ GB.

💡 Key takeaway: COPY --from=<name> references a stage by its AS name. You can also use numeric indices (--from=0 for the first stage). Always double-check that the name in COPY --from exactly matches the AS name — Docker does case-sensitive, exact matching with no fuzzy search.

🧪 SCENARIO S10 — Category 1: App Design & Build Lifecycle

Pod 502 Errors on Rollout — Missing preStop Hook

The Problem: During rolling updates, the easypj API pods are deleted and recreated. Users report intermittent 502 Bad Gateway errors during deploys. The Deployment has terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 5 and NO preStop hook. Gunicorn receives SIGTERM and immediately kills all workers — even ones mid-request. Your job: add a preStop hook to gracefully drain connections before the pod terminates.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-node cluster for rollout testing
1

📋 Deploy API Without Graceful Shutdown (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Every time the easypj team deploys a new API version, the monitoring dashboard lights up with 502 errors for ~10 seconds. Users refreshing the job board during deploys see "Bad Gateway." The root cause: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM to the pod, and Gunicorn immediately kills all worker processes — even those handling active HTTP requests. With only 5 seconds of terminationGracePeriod and no preStop hook, there's no time for graceful connection draining. The fix is a preStop hook that gives Gunicorn time to finish in-flight requests.
📁 MANIFESTS for S10: 
s10-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml        ← kubectl create ns s10-jobpost
├── 01-deployment.yaml       ← Deployment with BUG: no preStop hook
│                              terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 5 (too short!)
└── 02-service.yaml          ← ClusterIP Service (port 8000)
BASH — Deploy API with no graceful shutdown 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S10: Missing preStop Hook — 502 Errors
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create ns s10-jobpost

# 2. DEPLOY API WITH NO PRESTOP HOOK
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s10-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      # ❌ BUG! No preStop hook — SIGTERM kills active connections!
      # ❌ BUG! 5 seconds is too short for graceful connection draining
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 5
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-slim
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
        args:
        - |
          echo "API: Simulating Gunicorn server..."
          echo "API: Registering SIGTERM handler for graceful shutdown..."
          trap 'echo "API: Received SIGTERM — would start draining connections..."; sleep 3; echo "API: Drain complete (3s)"; exit 0' TERM
          echo "API: Server ready on port 8000"
          while true; do
            echo "API: Processing request..."
            sleep 10 &
            wait $!
          done
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        # No lifecycle.preStop configured!
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s10-jobpost
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api
  ports:
  - port: 8000
    targetPort: 8000
EOF

# 3. CHECK — Pods are Running but vulnerable to 502s on rollout
kubectl get pods -n s10-jobpost
kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s10-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A2 terminationGrace
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pod spec: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s10-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A5 lifecycle → No lifecycle hooks configured!
✗2. Check terminationGracePeriod: kubectl get deploy -o yaml | grep terminationGrace → 5 seconds — far too short!
✗3. During rollout: existing pods receive SIGTERM and immediately stop — active requests are DROPPED
✗4. Users see 502 errors during every deployment — ~10s of downtime per rollout!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check lifecycle hooks: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s10-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].lifecycle}'
→ EMPTY — No preStop or postStart hooks configured!
2Check terminationGracePeriodSeconds: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s10-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds}'
→ 5 — Default is 30. 5 seconds is not enough for graceful drain!
3Understand the termination flow: SIGTERM → container stops → if preStop exists, it runs first. Without preStop, the container gets SIGTERM immediately and stops accepting connections.
→ Gunicorn needs ~15-20 seconds to finish in-flight requests. 5 seconds guarantees data loss and 502 errors.
4Root cause: No preStop hook configured + terminationGracePeriodSeconds too short (5s) → Gunicorn workers killed immediately during rollout → 502 errors
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
502 errors during rollout → Pods dying mid-request
②
Check lifecycle → No preStop hook
③
Check terminationGracePeriod → 5s (too short!)
④
Add preStop: sleep 20 + drain connections
⑤
Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 → No more 502s!

Tenet: The Kubernetes pod termination flow is: (1) Pod set to Terminating, removed from Service endpoints, (2) preStop hook executes (if defined), (3) SIGTERM sent to all containers, (4) Kubernetes waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds, (5) SIGKILL sent if still running. A preStop hook is your chance to drain connections gracefully BEFORE SIGTERM. Without it, active requests are dropped. On CKAD, preStop + terminationGracePeriodSeconds is a common lifecycle question.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s10-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].lifecycle}' ← EMPTY! No lifecycle hooks at all!
$ kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s10-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds}' 5 ← Too short! Gunicorn needs at least 15-20s for graceful drain.
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s10-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].lifecycle.preStop}' {"exec":{"command":["/bin/sh","-c","sleep 20"]}} ✅ preStop hook configured!
$ kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s10-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.terminationGracePeriodSeconds}' 30 ✅ Enough time for graceful shutdown + drain!
🔧
BASH — Patch Deployment with preStop and longer grace period 
# Step 1: Increase terminationGracePeriodSeconds to 30
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s10-jobpost \
  -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"terminationGracePeriodSeconds":30}}}}'

# Step 2: Add preStop hook to drain connections for 20 seconds
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s10-jobpost \
  -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"api","lifecycle":{"preStop":{"exec":{"command":["/bin/sh","-c","echo Draining connections...; sleep 20; echo Drain complete"]}}}}]}}}}'

# Step 3: Verify the fix
kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s10-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A10 lifecycle

# Step 4: Watch rollout — no more 502 errors!
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s10-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Graceful Shutdown Configured

After adding a preStop hook with a 20-second sleep and increasing terminationGracePeriodSeconds to 30, the deployment now drains connections gracefully during rollouts. When a pod is terminated: (1) it's removed from the Service endpoints, (2) preStop hook runs for 20 seconds, allowing Gunicorn to finish in-flight requests, (3) SIGTERM is sent, (4) the pod exits cleanly. No more 502 errors during deploys.

💡 Key takeaway: preStop runs BEFORE SIGTERM — use it for graceful connection draining. terminationGracePeriodSeconds must be LONGER than your preStop sleep time (otherwise SIGKILL cuts it short). Rule of thumb: preStop sleep = estimated max request time, gracePeriod = preStop + 10s buffer.

S11
🧪 SCENARIO S11 — Category 1: App Design & Build Lifecycle

postStart Hook Fails — Command Runs Before App Is Ready

The Problem: The easypj API needs to warm up the Django cache and run database migrations on startup. A postStart hook was added to run python manage.py migrate && python manage.py warm_cache. But the postStart hook runs in parallel with the ENTRYPOINT — the migration runs while Gunicorn is still starting, causing a race condition where the database isn't ready. Your job: redesign the startup sequence to ensure migrations complete before the app starts serving traffic.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Pod lifecycle debugging
1

📋 Deploy Pod with Racy postStart Hook (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj backend team added a postStart hook to automate migrations and cache warming. The idea: when a new API pod starts, run migrations first, then warm the cache. But postStart runs concurrently with the main container process — there's no ordering guarantee. Gunicorn starts accepting requests BEFORE the migration finishes. The first API requests hit a database with missing tables, causing 500 errors. postStart is for side-effects (notifications, health checks), NOT for blocking startup tasks.
📁 MANIFESTS for S11:
s11-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── 01-deployment.yaml  ← BUG: postStart runs migration in parallel with app!
BASH — Deploy with racy postStart
kubectl create ns s11-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s11-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-slim
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          echo "Gunicorn: Starting on port 8000..."
          sleep 2
          echo "Gunicorn: NOW accepting requests!"
          while true; do sleep 60; done
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
        lifecycle:
          postStart:
            exec:
              command:
              - /bin/sh
              - -c
              - |
                echo "postStart: Running migrations..."
                sleep 5
                echo "postStart: Migrations complete!"
                echo "postStart: Warming cache..."
                sleep 3
                echo "postStart: Cache warm!"
EOF
echo "Observe: Gunicorn starts BEFORE postStart finishes → RACE!"
kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api -n s11-jobpost
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check logs: kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api -n s11-jobpost → "Gunicorn: NOW accepting requests!" appears BEFORE "Migrations complete!"
✗2. postStart and main process run CONCURRENTLY — no ordering guarantee
✗3. First API requests arrive while migrations are still running → 500 errors!
✗4. Users see "table not found" errors for the first 5 seconds of pod startup
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check postStart definition: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s11-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A8 postStart
→ postStart configured correctly, but it runs IN PARALLEL with the main container process
2K8s docs: "The postStart handler runs asynchronously with the container's main process"
→ Kubernetes does NOT wait for postStart to complete before considering the container "Running"
3Correct approach: Use an initContainer for migrations (runs BEFORE main container) + readiness probe for cache warm check
4Root cause: postStart runs asynchronously — migrations and app startup race each other. Use initContainers for sequential startup tasks.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
500 errors on pod startup → Migration not ready
②
Check postStart → migrations run there
③
postStart is ASYNC → races with main process
④
Move to initContainer → Runs BEFORE app
⑤
Add readiness probe → Traffic only after warm

Tenet: postStart hooks run asynchronously with the container's ENTRYPOINT. Kubernetes does NOT wait for postStart to finish before marking the container as Running. For blocking startup tasks (migrations, cache warming, data seeding), use initContainers — they run to completion BEFORE the main container starts. Use readinessProbe to delay traffic until the app is truly ready.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api -n s11-jobpost Gunicorn: Starting on port 8000... postStart: Running migrations... Gunicorn: NOW accepting requests! ← READY before migration done! postStart: Migrations complete! ← Too late! postStart: Warming cache...
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api -n s11-jobpost Init: Running migrations... complete ✅ (initContainer) Init: Warming cache... complete ✅ (initContainer) Gunicorn: Starting on port 8000... ✅ (now safe to start) Gunicorn: NOW accepting requests!
🔧
BASH — Replace postStart with initContainer
kubectl delete deploy easypj-api -n s11-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s11-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: db-migrate
        image: python:3.12-slim
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - "echo 'Init: Running migrations...'; sleep 3; echo 'Init: Migrations complete!'"
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-slim
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - "echo 'Gunicorn: Starting...'; sleep 1; echo 'Gunicorn: NOW accepting!'; while true; do sleep 60; done"
        readinessProbe:
          exec:
            command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'Readiness check passed'"]
          initialDelaySeconds: 2
          periodSeconds: 5
EOF
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s11-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Sequential Startup with initContainer

After replacing postStart with an initContainer, migrations run to completion BEFORE the main container starts. The readiness probe ensures traffic only reaches the pod after it's truly ready.

💡 Key takeaway: initContainers run sequentially to completion before main containers. postStart runs asynchronously. Use initContainers for blocking startup tasks, postStart for non-blocking side-effects only.

🧹

kubectl delete ns s11-jobpost
kubectl get ns s11-jobpost 2>&1
S12
🧪 SCENARIO S12 — Category 1: App Design & Build Lifecycle

Pod Ignores SIGTERM — Shell Form CMD Blocks Signal

The Problem: The easypj API pod takes 30+ seconds to terminate during rollouts. Logs show the app never received SIGTERM — Kubernetes had to SIGKILL it. The Dockerfile uses shell form CMD (CMD python manage.py runserver) instead of exec form (CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi"]). In shell form, the command runs inside /bin/sh -c — SIGTERM goes to sh, not Python. sh doesn't forward the signal. Your job: convert to exec form so Gunicorn receives SIGTERM directly.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Signal handling debugging
1

📋 Deploy Pod with Shell Form CMD (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Every rollout takes 35+ seconds because pods ignore SIGTERM and get SIGKILLed after the grace period. The developer used CMD python app.py (shell form) in the Dockerfile. In shell form, Docker wraps the command in /bin/sh -c "python app.py". sh is PID 1, and sh does NOT forward signals to child processes. Gunicorn never sees SIGTERM — Kubernetes has to wait 30 seconds and then force-kill with SIGKILL. This causes slow rollouts and dropped connections.
📁 MANIFESTS for S12:
s12-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── 01-deployment.yaml  ← BUG: Shell form CMD — SIGTERM lost!
BASH — Deploy pod with shell form CMD
kubectl create ns s12-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s12-jobpost
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: python:3.12-slim
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
    args:
    - |
      # ❌ BUG! Shell form: sh is PID 1, python is child
      # SIGTERM goes to sh, NOT forwarded to python!
      echo "PID 1 is: $$ (this is sh, not Python!)"
      python -c "
import signal, sys, time
def handle(sig, frame):
    print('Python: Received signal, shutting down...')
    sys.exit(0)
signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, handle)
print('Python: Waiting for SIGTERM... (PID:', __import__('os').getpid(), ')')
while True:
    time.sleep(5)
    print('Python: Still running...')
"
EOF
kubectl get pod easypj-api -n s12-jobpost
# Simulate SIGTERM by deleting — watch it take 30s!
echo "Deleting pod — observe it takes full 30s (SIGKILL, not graceful)..."
time kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s12-jobpost
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Delete pod: time kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s12-jobpost → Takes FULL 30 seconds!
✗2. Python never logs "Received signal" — SIGTERM went to sh, not Python
✗3. PID 1 is /bin/sh — not the application. sh doesn't forward signals.
✗4. Slow rollouts, dropped connections, poor user experience!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check PID 1: kubectl exec easypj-api -n s12-jobpost -- ps aux
→ PID 1 is /bin/sh -c ... — sh is the init process!
2Check Dockerfile CMD format: Shell form (CMD command arg) vs exec form (CMD ["command","arg"])
→ Shell form wraps in /bin/sh -c — sh becomes PID 1 and doesn't forward signals
3Root cause: Shell form CMD makes /bin/sh PID 1 — sh doesn't forward SIGTERM to child processes. Gunicorn never receives the termination signal.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod takes 30s to terminate → SIGKILL, not SIGTERM
②
Check PID 1 → /bin/sh, not the app
③
Shell form CMD → sh wraps the command
④
sh doesn't forward signals → SIGTERM lost
⑤
Convert to exec form → App is PID 1 → Receives SIGTERM!

Tenet: Docker supports two CMD forms: shell form (CMD command arg) and exec form (CMD ["command","arg"]). Shell form runs inside /bin/sh -c — sh is PID 1 and does NOT forward signals to child processes. Exec form runs the command directly as PID 1 — signals go straight to the app. On CKAD, always use exec form for production containers that need graceful shutdown.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s12-jobpost -- ps aux PID USER COMMAND 1 root /bin/sh -c python -c "..." ← SH is PID 1! 7 root python -c "..." ← Python is child
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s12-jobpost -- ps aux PID USER COMMAND 1 root python -c "..." ← Python is PID 1! ✅ Receives SIGTERM directly
🔧
BASH — Use exec form CMD
# Exec form: CMD ["executable","arg1","arg2"]
# The command runs as PID 1 — receives SIGTERM directly
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s12-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s12-jobpost
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: python:3.12-slim
    command: ["python"]
    args: ["-c", "import signal,sys,time; signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, lambda s,f: (print('Graceful shutdown!'), sys.exit(0))); print('PID 1 is Python — ready for SIGTERM'); [time.sleep(10) or print('Working...') for _ in iter(int,1)]"]
EOF
kubectl get pod easypj-api -n s12-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Exec Form — App Receives SIGTERM Directly

With exec form, the application is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly. Pods terminate gracefully in seconds, not 30. Rollouts are fast and connections drain cleanly.

💡 Key takeaway: Always use exec form: CMD ["gunicorn", "app.wsgi"] NOT CMD gunicorn app.wsgi. The brackets make all the difference for signal handling.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s12-jobpost
kubectl get ns s12-jobpost 2>&1
S13
🧪 SCENARIO S13 — Category 1: App Design & Build Labels

Service Targets No Pods — Inconsistent Label Selectors

The Problem: The easypj API Service has no endpoints — it targets zero pods. You deployed 2 API pods and a Service, but kubectl get endpoints shows empty. The Service selector says app: easypj-api but one pod has app: easypj and the other has app: api. Inconsistent labeling means the Service can't find any pods. Your job: standardize the labels so the Service can route traffic.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Label selector debugging
1

📋 Deploy Pods and Service with Mismatched Labels (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Two different developers created the API pods using slightly different naming conventions. Dev A used app: easypj, Dev B used app: api. The Service was configured with app: easypj-api — matching NEITHER. The Service has an empty endpoint list — no traffic reaches any pod. The job board API returns "connection refused" for all users.
📁 MANIFESTS for S13:
s13-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
├── 01-pod-a.yaml       ← label app: easypj    ❌
├── 02-pod-b.yaml       ← label app: api       ❌
└── 03-service.yaml     ← selector app: easypj-api (matches nothing!)
BASH — Deploy mismatched labels
kubectl create ns s13-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api-pod-a
  namespace: s13-jobpost
  labels:
    app: easypj       # ❌ Wrong label!
    tier: backend
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: api-pod-b
  namespace: s13-jobpost
  labels:
    app: api          # ❌ Different wrong label!
    tier: backend
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s13-jobpost
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api   # Matches NEITHER pod!
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF
echo "Check endpoints — will be EMPTY!"
kubectl get endpoints easypj-api -n s13-jobpost
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check endpoints: kubectl get ep easypj-api -n s13-jobpost → ENDPOINTS: <none>
✗2. Check pod labels: kubectl get pods -n s13-jobpost --show-labels → Two different app labels!
✗3. Check Service selector: kubectl get svc easypj-api -n s13-jobpost -o yaml | grep selector -A2 → app: easypj-api
✗4. API unreachable — users get "connection refused" or 503!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check endpoints: kubectl get ep -n s13-jobpost
→ easypj-api has NO endpoints — Service matches zero pods!
2List pod labels: kubectl get pods -n s13-jobpost -L app
→ api-pod-a: app=easypj, api-pod-b: app=api — neither is "easypj-api"!
3Service selector: kubectl get svc easypj-api -n s13-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'
→ {"app":"easypj-api"} — matches none of the running pods
4Root cause: Pod labels (easypj, api) don't match Service selector (easypj-api) — Service has empty endpoints
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Service unreachable → Check endpoints
②
Endpoints EMPTY → Service has no targets
③
Check pod labels vs Service selector
④
Mismatch! Labels ≠ Selector
⑤
Fix labels → Endpoints populated → Traffic flows!

Tenet: Empty endpoints = label mismatch. kubectl get endpoints is the most underrated debugging command — it instantly tells you if the Service-to-Pod connection works. The Service selector must match EXACTLY with pod labels. Even a one-character difference ("easypj" vs "easypj-api") breaks everything. On CKAD, empty endpoints is one of the most common Service debugging scenarios.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get ep -n s13-jobpost NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-api <none> 5m ← Empty!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get ep -n s13-jobpost NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-api 10.244.1.5:80,10.244.2.3:80 5m ✅
🔧
BASH — Relabel pods to match Service selector
# Fix pod A: change label from "easypj" to "easypj-api"
kubectl label pod api-pod-a -n s13-jobpost app=easypj-api --overwrite

# Fix pod B: change label from "api" to "easypj-api"
kubectl label pod api-pod-b -n s13-jobpost app=easypj-api --overwrite

# Verify endpoints are now populated
kubectl get ep easypj-api -n s13-jobpost
# → Should show 2 endpoints now!

# Best practice: Use recommended Kubernetes labels
kubectl label pod api-pod-a -n s13-jobpost app.kubernetes.io/name=easypj app.kubernetes.io/component=api
✓

✅ Verify — Endpoints Populated

After standardizing pod labels to match the Service selector (app: easypj-api), the endpoints are populated and traffic flows to both pods. The API is reachable again.

💡 Key takeaway: kubectl get endpoints is the first command to run when a Service isn't working. Empty endpoints = label mismatch 90% of the time. Use kubectl label --overwrite to fix labels on running pods.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s13-jobpost
kubectl get ns s13-jobpost 2>&1
S14
🧪 SCENARIO S14 — Category 1: App Design & Build DaemonSet

DaemonSet Skips Control-Plane Node — Missing Toleration

The Problem: You deployed a Fluentd log collector as a DaemonSet to run on EVERY node. But the control-plane node has no Fluentd pod — its logs are not being collected. The control-plane node has a taint node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule that blocks regular pods. The DaemonSet has no toleration for this taint. Your job: add the toleration so Fluentd runs on ALL nodes.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-node cluster with tainted control-plane
1

📋 Deploy DaemonSet Without Control-Plane Toleration (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj SRE team deployed Fluentd as a DaemonSet to collect logs from all nodes for the EFK stack. After a week, they noticed the Elasticsearch index was missing control-plane logs — critical for auditing API server activity. The control-plane node has a taint that prevents regular pods from scheduling. The DaemonSet doesn't tolerate this taint, so no Fluentd pod runs on the control-plane. Audit logs are not being collected — a compliance violation.
📁 MANIFESTS for S14:
s14-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── 01-daemonset.yaml   ← BUG: No toleration for control-plane taint!
BASH — Deploy DaemonSet without toleration
kubectl create ns s14-jobpost
# First check the taint on control-plane node
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.spec.taints}{"\n"}{end}'
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: fluentd
  namespace: s14-jobpost
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: fluentd
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: fluentd
    spec:
      # ❌ BUG! No tolerations — won't schedule on tainted nodes!
      containers:
      - name: fluentd
        image: alpine:3.19
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - "echo 'Fluentd running on node:' $(cat /etc/hostname); while true; do echo 'Collecting logs...'; sleep 30; done"
EOF
echo "Check DaemonSet pods — one per WORKER node only!"
kubectl get pods -n s14-jobpost -o wide
kubectl get nodes --show-labels | grep control-plane
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Count pods: kubectl get pods -n s14-jobpost -o wide → 2 pods on 2 workers, NONE on control-plane!
✗2. Check node count: 3 nodes (cp, wk1, wk2) but only 2 DaemonSet pods
✗3. Check taint on cp: kubectl describe node cp | grep Taint → NoSchedule taint present
✗4. Control-plane logs are NOT collected — compliance audit failure!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check DaemonSet status: kubectl get ds fluentd -n s14-jobpost
→ DESIRED: 2, CURRENT: 2, READY: 2 — but there are 3 NODES!
2Check node taints: kubectl get nodes -o json | jq '.items[].spec.taints'
→ control-plane node has taint: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule
3Check DaemonSet tolerations: kubectl get ds fluentd -n s14-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A5 tolerations
→ EMPTY — No tolerations configured! DaemonSet skips tainted nodes.
4Root cause: DaemonSet has no toleration for control-plane taint — cannot schedule on the master node
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
DaemonSet has fewer pods than nodes → Some nodes skipped
②
Check node taints → control-plane has NoSchedule
③
Check DaemonSet tolerations → None configured
④
Toleration required to schedule on tainted node
⑤
Add toleration → DaemonSet runs on ALL nodes!

Tenet: Taints and tolerations work together: taints REPEL pods, tolerations ALLOW pods onto tainted nodes. DaemonSets are designed to run on all nodes by default — but they still respect taints. To run a DaemonSet on the control-plane, you must add a toleration for node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule. On CKAD, DaemonSet tolerations are a frequently tested concept.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES AGE cp Ready control-plane 7d ← Has taint! wk1 Ready <none> 7d wk2 Ready <none> 7d
$ kubectl get pods -n s14-jobpost -o wide NAME NODE fluentd-abc1 wk1 ← Only 2 pods, none on cp! fluentd-def2 wk2
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n s14-jobpost -o wide NAME NODE fluentd-abc1 wk1 fluentd-def2 wk2 fluentd-ghi3 cp ✅ Now on control-plane too!
🔧
BASH — Patch DaemonSet with toleration
kubectl patch ds fluentd -n s14-jobpost -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"tolerations":[{"key":"node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane","operator":"Exists","effect":"NoSchedule"}]}}}}'
kubectl rollout status ds/fluentd -n s14-jobpost
kubectl get pods -n s14-jobpost -o wide
# → Should now show 3 pods: one per node including control-plane!
✓

✅ Verify — DaemonSet Runs on All Nodes

After adding the control-plane toleration, the DaemonSet schedules a pod on EVERY node — including the tainted control-plane. All logs are now collected.

💡 Key takeaway: DaemonSets automatically add tolerations for some default taints, but NOT for node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane. You must add this toleration explicitly if you need DaemonSet pods on the control-plane.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s14-jobpost
kubectl get ns s14-jobpost 2>&1
S15
🧪 SCENARIO S15 — Category 1: App Design & Build StatefulSet

Database Corruption Risk — Deployment with Shared PVC vs StatefulSet

The Problem: The easypj PostgreSQL database was deployed as a Deployment with replicas: 2, both pods sharing a single PVC via ReadWriteMany. Two PostgreSQL instances writing to the SAME data directory causes database corruption. The correct approach is a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates — each pod gets its own PVC. Your job: convert the Deployment to a StatefulSet with per-pod storage.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Single-node, good for StatefulSet demos
1

📋 Deploy PostgreSQL as Deployment with Shared PVC (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: An intern deployed PostgreSQL using a Deployment with 2 replicas and a single shared PVC. Everything seemed fine for a week — then the database started returning inconsistent query results. Two independent PostgreSQL processes were writing to the same data files on the shared volume. WAL logs conflicted, tables got corrupted, and the job board started losing data. The correct design is a StatefulSet where each pod has its OWN PVC via volumeClaimTemplates.
📁 MANIFESTS for S15:
s15-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
├── 01-pvc.yaml          ← Shared PVC (RWO — can only mount on ONE pod!)
└── 02-deployment.yaml   ← ❌ BUG: Deployment with replicas:2 + shared PVC
BASH — Deploy broken shared-PVC PostgreSQL
kubectl create ns s15-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: db-data
  namespace: s15-jobpost
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: s15-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 2    # ❌ BUG! Multiple pods sharing ONE PVC = CORRUPTION!
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        volumeMounts:
        - name: db-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
      volumes:
      - name: db-data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: db-data
EOF
echo "Check pods — second pod will be Pending (PVC is RWO, can't mount twice)!"
kubectl get pods -n s15-jobpost -o wide
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pods: kubectl get pods -n s15-jobpost → Second pod stuck Pending or crashes
✗2. RWO PVC can only mount on ONE node at a time — second pod can't start!
✗3. Even if both ran (RWX), two PostgreSQL instances sharing data = DATA CORRUPTION!
✗4. Job board data integrity at risk — inconsistent query results!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check pod status: One pod Running, one Pending — PVC can only attach once (RWO)
→ Deployment is the wrong workload resource for stateful databases!
2Check PVC accessMode: ReadWriteOnce — only ONE node can mount it
→ Even with RWX, two Postgres instances sharing data = corruption
3Correct pattern: StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates — each pod gets its OWN PVC
→ StatefulSet creates PVCs named db-data-easypj-db-0, db-data-easypj-db-1, etc.
4Root cause: Using Deployment with shared PVC for a stateful database — need StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates for per-pod storage
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Second pod Pending → PVC mount conflict
②
RWO PVC + replicas:2 → Can't work
③
Deployment is stateless → Wrong for databases
④
StatefulSet + volumeClaimTemplates → Per-pod PVC
⑤
Each pod gets own stable storage → No corruption!

Tenet: StatefulSets provide stable network identity (pod-0, pod-1) and per-pod persistent storage via volumeClaimTemplates. Deployments are for stateless apps — all replicas are identical and interchangeable. Databases, message queues, and any app requiring stable identity + dedicated storage should use StatefulSets. On CKAD, knowing when to use Deployment vs StatefulSet is a core competency.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n s15-jobpost NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-db-6f8b9c5d4-abc12 1/1 Running 0 5m easypj-db-6f8b9c5d4-def34 0/1 Pending 0 5m ← Can't mount shared PVC!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods,pvc -n s15-jobpost NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-db-0 1/1 Running 0 2m ✅ easypj-db-1 1/1 Running 0 2m ✅ PVC: db-data-easypj-db-0 Bound 1Gi ← Per-pod storage! PVC: db-data-easypj-db-1 Bound 1Gi ← Per-pod storage!
🔧
BASH — Replace Deployment with StatefulSet
kubectl delete deploy easypj-db -n s15-jobpost
kubectl delete pvc db-data -n s15-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: s15-jobpost
spec:
  serviceName: easypj-db
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        volumeMounts:
        - name: db-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: db-data
    spec:
      accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: s15-jobpost
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: easypj-db
  ports:
  - port: 5432
EOF
kubectl get pods,pvc -n s15-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — StatefulSet with Per-Pod PVCs

After converting to a StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates, each PostgreSQL pod gets its own dedicated PVC. Pods are named easypj-db-0 and easypj-db-1 with stable identities. No more shared storage conflicts.

💡 Key takeaway: StatefulSet + volumeClaimTemplates = each pod gets its own PVC automatically. PVCs persist even if the pod is deleted/rescheduled. Use a headless Service (clusterIP: None) for stable DNS: easypj-db-0.easypj-db.s15-jobpost.svc.cluster.local.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s15-jobpost
kubectl get ns s15-jobpost 2>&1
S16
🧪 SCENARIO S16 — Category 1: App Design & Build Resources

Pod OOMKilled — No Resource Limits Set

The Problem: The easypj API pod keeps getting OOMKilled in production. The Deployment has resources: {} — no requests or limits. The pod consumes unlimited memory, the node runs out, and the kubelet kills it. Other pods on the same node also suffer. Your job: set appropriate resource requests and limits based on the app's actual usage.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Resource management debugging
1

📋 Deploy Pod Without Resource Limits (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj API was deployed without resource limits — the team wanted to "optimize later." Under load, the Django process ballooned to 800MB, starving neighboring pods. The kubelet OOMKilled the API pod, causing cascading failures. Without resource limits, a single misbehaving pod can take down an entire node. The fix: profile actual usage with kubectl top and set appropriate requests/limits.
📁 MANIFESTS for S16:
s16-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── 01-deployment.yaml  ← BUG: resources: {} (no limits!)
BASH — Deploy with no resource limits
kubectl create ns s16-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s16-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-slim
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          echo "API: No resource limits set — can consume unlimited memory!"
          echo "API: Simulating memory leak..."
          python -c "
import time
data = []
for i in range(100):
    data.append('x' * (10*1024*1024))  # 10MB per iteration
    print(f'Allocated {(i+1)*10}MB...')
    time.sleep(0.3)
print('Memory leak simulation complete')
" 2>&1 || echo "Pod was OOMKilled!"
          while true; do sleep 60; done
        # ❌ BUG! No resources field — unlimited memory!
EOF
echo "Watch pod get OOMKilled..."
kubectl get pods -n s16-jobpost -w
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pod status: kubectl get pods -n s16-jobpost → RESTARTS increasing, REASON: OOMKilled
✗2. Check pod details: kubectl describe pod -n s16-jobpost <pod> | grep -A3 State → "Reason: OOMKilled"
✗3. Check resources: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s16-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A5 resources → resources: {}
✗4. Neighboring pods are affected — node memory pressure!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check OOMKilled reason: kubectl describe pod -n s16-jobpost <pod>
→ Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137
2Check resource config: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s16-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'
→ {} or empty — No limits or requests configured!
3Profile actual usage: kubectl top pod -n s16-jobpost (if metrics-server is available)
→ Pod using 600+ MB before crash — needs at least 256Mi request, 512Mi limit
4Root cause: No resource limits → pod uses unlimited memory → node OOM → kubelet kills pod
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod OOMKilled → Exit code 137 (SIGKILL)
②
Check resources → Empty (no limits)
③
Profile with kubectl top → 600MB+ usage
④
Set requests: 256Mi, limits: 512Mi
⑤
Pod stays within limits → No more OOMKills!

Tenet: OOMKilled (exit code 137) means the container exceeded its memory limit — or the node ran out of memory because no limit was set.
