Always set resources.requests (what the scheduler reserves) and resources.limits (hard cap). If requests=limits, the pod gets a Guaranteed QoS class — last to be killed under memory pressure. On CKAD, setting resource limits is a core task.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe pod -n s16-jobpost easypj-api-xxx | grep -A5 "Last State" Last State: Terminated Reason: OOMKilled Exit Code: 137 ← SIGKILL: memory limit exceeded!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n s16-jobpost NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-9g3f4d5h6-xyz 1/1 Running 0 5m ✅ No OOMKills!
🔧
BASH — Patch Deployment with resource limits
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s16-jobpost -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"api","resources":{"requests":{"memory":"128Mi","cpu":"100m"},"limits":{"memory":"512Mi","cpu":"500m"}}}]}}}}'
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s16-jobpost
kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s16-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources}'
✓

✅ Verify — Resource Limits Enforced

With requests: 128Mi/100m and limits: 512Mi/500m, the pod is protected from memory leaks and the node is protected from resource starvation. The pod gets a Burstable QoS class.

💡 Key takeaway: Always set resource limits. Requests help the scheduler place pods correctly; limits prevent runaway resource consumption. Exit code 137 = OOMKilled = check your limits.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s16-jobpost
kubectl get ns s16-jobpost 2>&1
S17
🧪 SCENARIO S17 — Category 1: App Design & Build Annotations

Annotations Not Visible on Pods — Added to Deployment, Not Template

The Problem: The team added git commit SHA, CI pipeline URL, and build timestamp as annotations — but they appear on the Deployment object, not the Pods. When debugging, kubectl describe pod shows no build info. Annotations must be in spec.template.metadata.annotations to propagate to pods. Your job: move annotations to the pod template so they're visible during debugging.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Single-node production cluster on node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy with Annotations on Wrong Object (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: After a production incident, the SRE team mandated that every pod must carry git commit and build info as annotations for rapid debugging. The dev team added the annotations to the Deployment YAML — but on metadata.annotations (the Deployment itself), not spec.template.metadata.annotations (the pod template). When troubleshooting, engineers run kubectl describe pod and see NO build info — they can't tell which commit is running.
📁 MANIFESTS for S17:
s17-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── 01-deployment.yaml  ← BUG: annotations on Deployment metadata,
                           NOT on spec.template.metadata!
BASH — Deploy with wrong annotation placement
kubectl create ns s17-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s17-jobpost
  annotations:
    # ❌ BUG! These are on the Deployment, NOT the pods!
    git-commit: "abc123def456"
    ci-pipeline: "https://ci.easypj.com/build/1234"
    build-timestamp: "2024-06-12T10:30:00Z"
    team: "backend-sre"
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
      # Annotations SHOULD be here to propagate to pods!
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
EOF
echo "Check Deployment annotations — they're there..."
kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s17-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations}'
echo ""
echo "But check Pod annotations — EMPTY!"
kubectl get pod -n s17-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.annotations}'
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Deployment has annotations: kubectl describe deploy easypj-api -n s17-jobpost | grep Annotations → Shows git-commit, ci-pipeline
✗2. Pod has NO annotations: kubectl describe pod -n s17-jobpost <pod> | grep Annotations → Only default annotations!
✗3. During incident response, engineers run kubectl describe pod — they see NO build info!
✗4. Nobody knows which git commit is running in production!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Deployment annotations: Present ✅
→ Annotations exist but on the WRONG object (Deployment, not Pod)
2Check Pod annotations: Empty ❌
→ Not propagated — annotations must be in spec.template.metadata.annotations
3Root cause: Annotations placed on Deployment metadata.annotations instead of spec.template.metadata.annotations — not propagated to pods
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Need build info on pods → Check pod annotations
②
Pod annotations empty → Where are they?
③
Deployment has annotations → Wrong level!
④
Move to spec.template.metadata.annotations
⑤
Pods now show build info → Debugging works!

Tenet: metadata.annotations on a Deployment applies to the Deployment object itself. To propagate annotations to pods, put them in spec.template.metadata.annotations. This is a common mistake — the Deployment template is the pod blueprint, and only template-level metadata flows to the pods. On CKAD, knowing the difference between Deployment metadata and pod template metadata is essential.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe deploy easypj-api -n s17-jobpost | grep -A4 Annotations Annotations: git-commit: abc123def456 ← On Deployment only! ci-pipeline: https://ci.easypj.com/build/1234
$ kubectl describe pod -n s17-jobpost easypj-api-xxx | grep -A2 Annotations Annotations: <none> ← Pod has NO build info!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl describe pod -n s17-jobpost easypj-api-xxx | grep -A4 Annotations Annotations: git-commit: abc123def456 ✅ On pod now! ci-pipeline: https://ci.easypj.com/build/1234 build-timestamp: 2024-06-12T10:30:00Z team: backend-sre
🔧
BASH — Patch template metadata
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s17-jobpost -p '{"spec":{"template":{"metadata":{"annotations":{"git-commit":"abc123def456","ci-pipeline":"https://ci.easypj.com/build/1234","build-timestamp":"2024-06-12T10:30:00Z","team":"backend-sre"}}}}}'
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s17-jobpost
kubectl describe pod -n s17-jobpost -l app=easypj-api | grep -A4 Annotations
✓

✅ Verify — Annotations Visible on Pods

After moving annotations to spec.template.metadata.annotations, every pod created by the Deployment carries the build info. Engineers can now identify the running git commit with a single kubectl describe pod.

💡 Key takeaway: Deployment metadata.annotations apply to the Deployment object. To propagate annotations to pods, put them in spec.template.metadata.annotations — the pod template is the blueprint for all created pods.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s17-jobpost
kubectl get ns s17-jobpost 2>&1
S18
🧪 SCENARIO S18 — Category 1: App Design & Build Debug

Debug Running Pod Without Restart — kubectl debug with Ephemeral Container

The Problem: A production easypj API pod has high CPU but you can't restart it — it's serving live traffic. The pod's container image is distroless (no shell, no tools). You need to inspect the running process. Use kubectl debug with an ephemeral container to attach a debugging toolkit. But first you need to fix the pod spec: shareProcessNamespace must be enabled to see the target process.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Advanced debugging
1

📋 Deploy Pod WITHOUT shareProcessNamespace (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The on-call engineer gets paged: easypj API pod CPU is at 95%. The pod is serving production traffic — no restart allowed. The container image is distroless (no shell). The engineer tries kubectl debug with an ephemeral container but can't see the target process — the pod doesn't have shareProcessNamespace: true. Without process namespace sharing, the debug container is isolated and can't inspect the app process.
📁 MANIFESTS for S18:
s18-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── 01-pod.yaml  ← BUG: No shareProcessNamespace — can't debug!
BASH — Deploy pod without shared process namespace
kubectl create ns s18-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s18-jobpost
spec:
  # ❌ BUG! No shareProcessNamespace — ephemeral container can't see app process!
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: python:3.12-slim
    command: ["python", "-c"]
    args:
    - |
      import time, os
      print(f"API running with PID {os.getpid()}")
      while True:
          time.sleep(30)
          print("API: Processing requests...")
EOF
echo "Try to debug — but ephemeral container can't see the Python process!"
kubectl debug -it easypj-api -n s18-jobpost --image=alpine:3.19 --target=api -- ps aux 2>&1 || echo "Failed: need shareProcessNamespace!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Attempt debug: kubectl debug easypj-api -n s18-jobpost --image=alpine --target=api -- ps aux → Can't see target process!
✗2. Ephemeral container runs but is ISOLATED — different PID namespace
✗3. Can't inspect the running Python process — no shareProcessNamespace
✗4. On-call engineer can't diagnose the CPU issue without restarting!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check pod spec: kubectl get pod easypj-api -n s18-jobpost -o yaml | grep shareProcessNamespace
→ Not present or false — process namespaces are isolated per container!
2Root cause: Pod doesn't have shareProcessNamespace: true — ephemeral debug container runs in a separate PID namespace and cannot see the main container's processes
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Need to debug running pod → kubectl debug
②
Ephemeral container can't see target process
③
Check shareProcessNamespace → false/missing
④
PID namespaces are isolated → Can't inspect
⑤
Recreate pod with shareProcessNamespace: true

Tenet: By default, each container in a pod has its own PID namespace — processes in container A are invisible to container B. shareProcessNamespace: true makes all containers share a single PID namespace, enabling kubectl debug --target to attach to and inspect the target container's processes. This is essential for debugging distroless containers. On CKAD, ephemeral containers and kubectl debug are advanced debugging topics.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl debug easypj-api -n s18-jobpost --image=alpine --target=api -- ps aux error: ephemeral container cannot be added because pod does not have shareProcessNamespace enabled
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl debug easypj-api -n s18-jobpost --image=alpine --target=api -- ps aux PID USER COMMAND 1 root python -c ... ← Can see the app process! ✅
🔧
BASH — Recreate with shared PID namespace
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s18-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s18-jobpost
spec:
  shareProcessNamespace: true  # ✅ FIXED!
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: python:3.12-slim
    command: ["python","-c"]
    args:
    - "import time,os; print(f'API PID: {os.getpid()}'); [time.sleep(30) or print('Working...') for _ in iter(int,1)]"
EOF
kubectl debug -it easypj-api -n s18-jobpost --image=alpine:3.19 --target=api -- ps aux
✓

✅ Verify — Ephemeral Container Can See Target Process

With shareProcessNamespace: true, the ephemeral debug container shares the PID namespace and can inspect the API process. On-call engineers can now profile, trace, and diagnose without restarting.

💡 Key takeaway: shareProcessNamespace: true is required for kubectl debug --target to work. Set this on pods you expect to debug in production. Consider security implications — all containers see each other's processes.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s18-jobpost
kubectl get ns s18-jobpost 2>&1
S19
🧪 SCENARIO S19 — Category 1: App Design & Build CronJob

CronJob Overlapping Runs — Missing concurrencyPolicy

The Problem: The nightly database backup CronJob sometimes runs for 3+ hours on large datasets. When the next scheduled run starts before the previous one finishes, two backup jobs run simultaneously — competing for database resources and doubling the load. The CronJob has no concurrencyPolicy set, defaulting to Allow. Your job: set concurrencyPolicy: Forbid to prevent overlapping executions.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — CronJob scheduling on production node "easy"
1

📋 Create CronJob Without concurrencyPolicy (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj DB backup CronJob runs every hour and normally takes 20 minutes. But after the job board grew to 5 million listings, backups started taking 70+ minutes. The CronJob default concurrencyPolicy: Allow means the next hourly run starts even if the previous is still running. Two pg_dump processes hammer the database simultaneously — query performance drops 50% for end users during the overlap.
📁 MANIFESTS for S19:
s19-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── 01-cronjob.yaml  ← BUG: No concurrencyPolicy set (defaults to Allow!)
BASH — Deploy CronJob with default Allow policy
kubectl create ns s19-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: db-backup
  namespace: s19-jobpost
spec:
  schedule: "*/30 * * * *"
  # ❌ BUG! No concurrencyPolicy — defaults to Allow!
  # If a job runs >30min, the next will overlap it.
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
          - name: backup
            image: alpine:3.19
            command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
            args:
            - |
              echo "Backup started at $(date)"
              echo "Simulating long backup (60s)..."
              sleep 60
              echo "Backup completed at $(date)"
EOF
echo "Check CronJob — concurrencyPolicy defaults to Allow!"
kubectl get cj db-backup -n s19-jobpost -o yaml | grep concurrencyPolicy
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check CronJob: kubectl get cj -n s19-jobpost → ACTIVE: 2 (two jobs running at once!)
✗2. Check Jobs: kubectl get jobs -n s19-jobpost → Two backup jobs running simultaneously
✗3. concurrencyPolicy not set → defaults to Allow → overlapping executions!
✗4. Database under DOUBLE load during overlap — users experience slow queries!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check active jobs: kubectl get jobs -n s19-jobpost
→ Two jobs with status Running — overlapping!
2Check concurrencyPolicy: kubectl get cj db-backup -n s19-jobpost -o yaml | grep concurrencyPolicy
→ Not set — defaults to Allow!
3Root cause: Missing concurrencyPolicy — defaults to Allow, causing overlapping backup jobs that compete for database resources
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Two backup jobs running → Overlap detected
②
Check concurrencyPolicy → Not set (Allow)
③
Allow = new job starts even if old running
④
Set to Forbid → Skip if previous still running
⑤
No more overlap → Database load normal!

Tenet: CronJob concurrencyPolicy has three values: Allow (default — overlapping jobs allowed), Forbid (skip next run if previous still running), Replace (kill previous job and start new). For database backups, always use Forbid to prevent double load. On CKAD, CronJob configuration including concurrencyPolicy is a tested topic.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get cj db-backup -n s19-jobpost -o yaml | grep concurrency concurrencyPolicy: Allow ← BUG! (or absent, same default)
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get cj db-backup -n s19-jobpost -o yaml | grep concurrency concurrencyPolicy: Forbid ✅ No more overlaps!
🔧
BASH — Patch CronJob
kubectl patch cj db-backup -n s19-jobpost -p '{"spec":{"concurrencyPolicy":"Forbid"}}'
kubectl get cj db-backup -n s19-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A1 concurrencyPolicy
✓

✅ Verify — No More Overlapping Jobs

With concurrencyPolicy: Forbid, if a backup job is still running when the next schedule triggers, the CronJob controller skips that execution. No more double-load on the database.

💡 Key takeaway: concurrencyPolicy: Allow (default, overlapping OK), Forbid (skip if running), Replace (kill old, start new). For resource-intensive jobs, always use Forbid.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s19-jobpost
kubectl get ns s19-jobpost 2>&1
S20
🧪 SCENARIO S20 — Category 1: App Design & Build Job

Job Completes Too Early — completions Conflicts with Work Queue

The Problem: The easypj team created a Job to process 1000 job applications from a Redis work queue. The Job runs 5 parallel workers, each fetching one item, processing it, and fetching the next. But the Job completes after only 10 completions — even though 990 items remain in the queue. The completions: 10 field tells Kubernetes to mark the Job done after 10 successful pods — but a work queue pattern needs NO completions limit. Your job: remove the completions field so workers process the entire queue.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Job work queue pattern
1

📋 Create Job with Wrong completions Setting (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj data team needs to re-process 1000 job applications (resume parsing, scoring). They created a Job with 5 parallel workers that pull from a Redis queue. The Job was configured with completions: 10 — the engineer thought this meant "10 parallel workers." completions actually means "total successful pod completions across the entire Job." After 10 workers finish, Kubernetes marks the Job complete — even if 990 items are still unprocessed.
📁 MANIFESTS for S20:
s20-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── 01-job.yaml  ← BUG: completions:10 stops job too early!
BASH — Deploy Job with wrong completions
kubectl create ns s20-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: process-applications
  namespace: s20-jobpost
spec:
  completions: 10    # ❌ BUG! Job stops after 10 successful pods!
  parallelism: 3     # Run 3 workers at a time
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: OnFailure
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: alpine:3.19
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          echo "Worker started — simulating processing 1 item..."
          sleep 5
          echo "Worker: Item processed!"
EOF
echo "Watch Job — it will stop after 10 completions, even though more work could be done!"
kubectl get jobs -n s20-jobpost -w
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check Job: kubectl get job process-applications -n s20-jobpost → COMPLETIONS: 10/10, DURATION: 25s — Too short!
✗2. Job marked Complete but 990 items still unprocessed in the queue!
✗3. completions: 10 means "stop after 10 successful pods" — not "10 workers"
✗4. Job board applications not processed — hiring pipeline STALLED!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Job spec: kubectl get job process-applications -n s20-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A2 completions
→ completions: 10 — This is the TOTAL completions, not parallelism!
2Work queue pattern: For a work queue where each pod processes items until the queue is empty, DO NOT set completions
→ Omit completions entirely — workers exit only when the queue is empty
3Root cause: completions: 10 limits the total number of successful pods — Job stops early, leaving work in the queue unprocessed
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Job completes with work remaining → Check spec
②
completions: 10 → Fixed limit
③
Work queue = no fixed completions
④
Remove completions → Workers run until queue empty
⑤
All 1000 items processed!

Tenet: completions sets the TOTAL successful pod count. parallelism sets how many pods run at once. For a work queue pattern where workers pull items until the queue is empty, omit completions entirely. Workers should exit when the queue is drained. Use activeDeadlineSeconds as a safety timeout. On CKAD, Job configuration is a core topic.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get job process-applications -n s20-jobpost NAME COMPLETIONS DURATION AGE process-applications 10/10 25s 2m ← Stopped at 10!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get job process-applications -n s20-jobpost NAME COMPLETIONS DURATION AGE process-applications 100/100 8m 10m ✅ All processed!
🔧
BASH — Recreate Job without completions limit
kubectl delete job process-applications -n s20-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: process-applications
  namespace: s20-jobpost
spec:
  # ✅ No completions! Workers run until queue is empty
  parallelism: 3
  backoffLimit: 3
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 600
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: OnFailure
      containers:
      - name: worker
        image: alpine:3.19
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - "for i in $(seq 1 10); do echo \"Worker processed item $i\"; sleep 2; done; echo 'Worker done — queue empty!'"
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Complete job/process-applications -n s20-jobpost --timeout=120s
✓

✅ Verify — Work Queue Processes All Items

Without the completions field, workers run until they determine the queue is empty and exit. All 1000 applications get processed. The Job is protected by activeDeadlineSeconds as a safety timeout.

💡 Key takeaway: completions = total successful pods (fixed count). parallelism = concurrent pods. For work queues, omit completions and let workers decide when to exit. Use activeDeadlineSeconds as a circuit breaker.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s20-jobpost
kubectl get ns s20-jobpost 2>&1

🚀 Category 2: App Deployment (S21–S40)20 Scenarios

🟡 easypj/jobpost — Deployment Strategies & Rollouts

What you'll master: Deployments, rolling updates, rollbacks, canary deployments, Blue/Green, Helm charts, Kustomize overlays, imperative commands, scaling, namespace isolation, DaemonSet updates, StatefulSet headless services, revision history, and multi-cluster deployment. Each scenario has an intentional bug you must find and fix. ⚠️ IMPORTANT: Check the cluster requirement at the top of each scenario before applying!

S21
🧪 SCENARIO S21 — Category 2: App Deployment ConfigMap

Deployment Pods CrashLoopBackOff — Referencing Non-Existent ConfigMap

The Problem: You deploy the easypj web frontend with 3 replicas. All pods immediately crash with CrashLoopBackOff. The Deployment references configMapRef: easypj-config but the actual ConfigMap is named easypj-web-config. Django can't load its settings, Gunicorn exits immediately, and the pods keep restarting. Your job: find the misnamed ConfigMap reference and fix it.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production-like cluster for deployment practice
1

📋 Deploy easypj-web with Wrong ConfigMap Name (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj platform team created a standard Deployment manifest for the web frontend. The manifest references a ConfigMap for Django settings (database URL, allowed hosts, debug flag). But the DevOps engineer who created the ConfigMap named it easypj-web-config while the Deployment template references easypj-config. Every pod starts, tries to load the missing ConfigMap, and crashes immediately. The job board is completely down.
📁 MANIFESTS for S21:
s21-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
├── 01-configmap.yaml     ← ConfigMap named "easypj-web-config" (correct)
└── 02-deployment.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: references "easypj-config" (WRONG!)
BASH — Deploy with ConfigMap name mismatch
kubectl create ns s21-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: easypj-web-config
  namespace: s21-jobpost
data:
  DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: "easypj.settings"
  ALLOWED_HOSTS: "*"
  DEBUG: "false"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: s21-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: python:3.12-slim
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - "echo 'Loading config...'; sleep 2; echo 'ERROR: ConfigMap easypj-config not found!'; exit 1"
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: easypj-config    # ❌ BUG! Should be "easypj-web-config"!
EOF
kubectl get pods -n s21-jobpost
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pods: kubectl get pods -n s21-jobpost → STATUS: CrashLoopBackOff, 3/3 crashing
✗2. Check logs: kubectl logs -l app=easypj-web -n s21-jobpost → "ConfigMap easypj-config not found"
✗3. Check ConfigMaps: kubectl get cm -n s21-jobpost → "easypj-web-config" exists, but "easypj-config" does NOT!
✗4. Job board web frontend completely DOWN — 3 replicas all crashing!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Deployment envFrom: kubectl get deploy easypj-web -n s21-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A3 configMapRef
→ name: easypj-config — This ConfigMap does NOT exist!
2List ConfigMaps: kubectl get cm -n s21-jobpost
→ easypj-web-config exists — the Deployment has a NAME MISMATCH!
3Root cause: Deployment references ConfigMap "easypj-config" but the actual ConfigMap is named "easypj-web-config"
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pods crashing → Check logs for error
②
Logs: "ConfigMap not found" → Name mismatch
③
kubectl get cm → "easypj-web-config" exists
④
Deployment references "easypj-config" → TYPO!
⑤
Fix name in Deployment → Pods run!

Tenet: When pods crash on startup with "ConfigMap not found" or "Secret not found", check the Deployment's envFrom or env.valueFrom references. A single character difference in the ConfigMap/Secret name breaks everything. On CKAD, ConfigMap/Secret name mismatches are one of the most common intentional bugs.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n s21-jobpost NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-web-6f8b9c5d4-abc 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 3 2m easypj-web-6f8b9c5d4-def 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 3 2m easypj-web-6f8b9c5d4-ghi 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 3 2m
$ kubectl get cm -n s21-jobpost NAME DATA AGE easypj-web-config 3 5m ← This is the CORRECT name!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n s21-jobpost NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-web-9g3f4d5h6-jkl 1/1 Running 0 30s ✅ easypj-web-9g3f4d5h6-mno 1/1 Running 0 28s ✅ easypj-web-9g3f4d5h6-pqr 1/1 Running 0 25s ✅
🔧
BASH — Patch the ConfigMap reference
kubectl set env deploy/easypj-web -n s21-jobpost --from=configmap/easypj-web-config
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web -n s21-jobpost
kubectl get pods -n s21-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Pods Running with Correct ConfigMap

After pointing the Deployment to the correct ConfigMap name, all 3 replicas start successfully. The web frontend is back online serving the job board.

💡 Key takeaway: ConfigMap and Secret names must match EXACTLY between the resource and the Deployment reference. Use kubectl get cm,secret to verify names before troubleshooting pod crashes.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s21-jobpost
kubectl get ns s21-jobpost 2>&1
S22
🧪 SCENARIO S22 — Category 2: App Deployment Rollout

Rolling Update Causes 503 Errors — maxUnavailable: 50% Too Aggressive

The Problem: The easypj API is being updated from v1 to v2 with a rolling update. During the rollout, users report intermittent 503 errors. The Deployment strategy has maxUnavailable: 50% — on a 4-replica deployment, 2 pods go down simultaneously. With only 2 pods serving traffic, the remaining pods can't handle the load. Your job: adjust the rolling update parameters for zero-downtime deploys.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-node for rollout testing
1

📋 Deploy API v1 with Aggressive Rolling Update Strategy (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team is rolling out API v2 with improved search. The Deployment has 4 replicas. The rolling update strategy was configured by an intern who set maxUnavailable: 50% — meaning up to 2 pods can be down during the update. With only 2 pods serving traffic, the load balancer overwhelms them. Response times spike to 5+ seconds and users get 503 errors. The correct setting is maxUnavailable: 1 (25%) so at least 3 pods always serve traffic.
📁 MANIFESTS for S22:
s22-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── 01-deployment.yaml  ← BUG: maxUnavailable: 50% (too aggressive!)
BASH — Deploy with aggressive rolling update
kubectl create ns s22-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s22-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 50%    # ❌ BUG! 2 of 4 pods down simultaneously!
      maxSurge: 25%
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s22-jobpost
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
EOF
kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s22-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A5 rollingUpdate
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check strategy: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s22-jobpost -o yaml | grep maxUnavailable → 50% — too high!
✗2. 50% of 4 = 2 pods down during rollout → only 2 pods serving traffic
✗3. During traffic spikes, 2 pods can't handle the load → 503 errors!
✗4. Users experience slow responses and intermittent failures during every deploy
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check rolling update params: kubectl describe deploy easypj-api -n s22-jobpost | grep -A3 RollingUpdate
→ maxUnavailable: 50% — allows HALF the pods to be unavailable!
2Safe defaults: maxUnavailable: 25% (1 pod for every 4), maxSurge: 25%
→ Standard safe config: maxUnavailable: 1 (absolute) or 25%
3Root cause: maxUnavailable: 50% is too aggressive — too many pods are down simultaneously during rolling updates, causing capacity issues
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
503 errors during rollout → Capacity issue
②
Check rolling update strategy → 50% unavailable
③
50% of 4 = 2 pods → Only 2 serving
④
Set maxUnavailable: 1 → Always 3+ pods serving
⑤
Zero-downtime rollouts achieved!

Tenet: maxUnavailable controls how many pods can be unavailable during a rolling update. Setting it too high (50%+) risks capacity loss during deploys. For production, use maxUnavailable: 1 (absolute) or 25% for larger deployments. Combined with maxSurge: 1, this ensures at most 1 pod is down and 1 extra is created during the rollout.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s22-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable}' 50% ← ❌ Too aggressive!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s22-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable}' 1 ← ✅ Safe: only 1 pod down at a time
🔧
BASH — Patch with safe defaults
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s22-jobpost -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"maxUnavailable":1,"maxSurge":1}}}}'
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s22-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Safe Rolling Update Configured

With maxUnavailable: 1 and maxSurge: 1, rolling updates now maintain at least 3 pods serving traffic at all times. Zero-downtime deploys achieved.

💡 Key takeaway: maxUnavailable=1, maxSurge=1 is the safest rolling update config for deployments with 3-10 replicas. For larger deployments, use 25%.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s22-jobpost
kubectl get ns s22-jobpost 2>&1
S23
🧪 SCENARIO S23 — Category 2: App Deployment Rollback

Rollback Goes Too Far — Undo Without --to-revision

The Problem: The easypj API was updated to v3, but a bug was discovered. You run kubectl rollout undo to rollback. Instead of going back to v2 (revision 2), it rolls back to revision 1. rollout undo without --to-revision goes back ONE revision from current — but the team expected it to go to the "last known good" version. Your job: learn how to rollback to a specific revision using rollout history.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Rollback practice on production node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy Multiple Revisions to Practice Rollback (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team deployed v1 (working), updated to v2 (working), then updated to v3 (broken). Panicking, they ran kubectl rollout undo. Instead of going back to v2, it went to v1 — the undo command goes back ONE revision from the current, and since v3 was deployed twice (once normally, once as a fix attempt that also failed), the revision history got confusing. The correct approach: use kubectl rollout history to find the right revision, then undo --to-revision=N.
📁 for S23:
s23-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── Deploy v1 → update v2 → update v3 → undo (BUG: wrong revision!)
BASH — Simulate multiple revisions and observe rollback
kubectl create ns s23-jobpost
# Deploy v1
kubectl create deploy easypj-api -n s23-jobpost --image=nginx:1.25 --replicas=1
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api nginx=nginx:1.26 -n s23-jobpost --record
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api nginx=nginx:1.27 -n s23-jobpost --record
# ❌ BUG! Undo goes back ONE revision (to 1.26), but team wanted 1.25!
kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api -n s23-jobpost
kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-api -n s23-jobpost
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check history: kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-api -n s23-jobpost → Multiple revisions
✗2. rollout undo goes back ONE — not to the specific version you expected!
✗3. Without --to-revision, you can't target a specific known-good version
✗4. Rollback went to wrong version — bug is still in production!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check rollout history: kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-api -n s23-jobpost
→ Shows all revisions with CHANGE-CAUSE if --record was used
2Undo to specific revision: kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api -n s23-jobpost --to-revision=1
→ Use --to-revision to target exactly which version to restore
3Root cause: kubectl rollout undo without --to-revision goes back only 1 revision — not necessarily to the intended known-good version
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Need to rollback → Check rollout history
②
Identify correct revision from history
③
Use --to-revision=N to target exactly
④
Undo without --to-revision goes 1 back only!
⑤
Always specify --to-revision for precision

Tenet: kubectl rollout undo without flags rolls back ONE revision. To target a specific revision, use --to-revision=N. Always check kubectl rollout history first to find the correct revision number. Use --record on kubectl commands to add CHANGE-CAUSE annotations for easier identification. On CKAD, rollout undo --to-revision is a tested command.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api -n s23-jobpost deployment.apps/easypj-api rolled back ← But to WHICH revision?
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-api -n s23-jobpost kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api -n s23-jobpost --to-revision=1 deployment.apps/easypj-api rolled back to revision 1 ✅ Precise!
🔧
BASH — Targeted rollback
# Step 1: Find the correct revision
kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-api -n s23-jobpost
# Step 2: Undo to specific revision
kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api -n s23-jobpost --to-revision=1
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s23-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Rolled Back to Correct Revision

Using --to-revision=N, you can precisely target which version to rollback to. Always check rollout history first.

💡 Key takeaway: rollout undo = one revision back. rollout undo --to-revision=N = exactly revision N. Use --record for human-readable history.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s23-jobpost
kubectl get ns s23-jobpost 2>&1
S24
🧪 SCENARIO S24 — Category 2: App Deployment Canary

Canary Deployment Gets 50/50 Traffic — Labels Not Versioned

The Problem: You deploy a canary version of the API (v3) alongside the stable version (v2). The Service uses a single label selector app: easypj-api which matches BOTH versions. Instead of 90/10 split, traffic distributes evenly. Your job: add version-specific labels and create weighted routing for proper canary deployment.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Canary deployment practice
1

📋 Deploy Stable + Canary with Same Labels (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team wants to test API v3 with 10% of production traffic. They deploy 9 stable v2 pods and 1 canary v3 pod. But both use app: easypj-api as the only label. The Service selector matches ALL pods with this label — 10 pods total. Traffic distributes roughly 50/50 between the two Deployments (not 90/10) because the Service sees them as identical. Canary users get v3 50% of the time instead of 10%.
📁 MANIFESTS for S24:
s24-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
├── 01-stable-deploy.yaml   ← 9 replicas, label app: easypj-api (version: v2)
├── 02-canary-deploy.yaml   ← 1 replica,  label app: easypj-api (version: v3)
└── 03-service.yaml         ← ❌ BUG: selector matches BOTH versions!
BASH — Deploy with unversioned labels causing 50/50 split
kubectl create ns s24-jobpost
# Stable v2: 9 replicas
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api-stable
  namespace: s24-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 9
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
      version: v2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        env:
        - name: VERSION
          value: "v2-stable"
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF
# Canary v3: 1 replica
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api-canary
  namespace: s24-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
      version: v3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
        version: v3
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        env:
        - name: VERSION
          value: "v3-canary"
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
EOF
# Service — ❌ BUG! Selector matches ALL app=easypj-api pods!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s24-jobpost
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api     # ❌ Matches all 10 pods equally!
  ports:
  - port: 80
EOF
kubectl get ep easypj-api -n s24-jobpost
# Shows 10 endpoints — traffic splits ~50/50 not 90/10!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check endpoints: kubectl get ep easypj-api -n s24-jobpost → 10 endpoints (9 stable + 1 canary)
✗2. Service selector app: easypj-api matches BOTH Deployments equally
✗3. Traffic distributes ~50/50 between the two Deployment objects (not 90/10)!
✗4. Canary users get v3 MUCH more often than intended — risky!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Count endpoints per version: kubectl get pods -n s24-jobpost -L version
→ 9 pods with version=v2, 1 pod with version=v3 — but Service sees ALL of them
2Fix: Service should use version-specific selector OR use two Services with weighted routing
→ For native K8s canary: create stable-svc (selector: version=v2) and canary-svc (selector: version=v3)
3Root cause: Service selector uses only app=easypj-api without version differentiation — all pods treated equally
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Canary getting too much traffic → Check Service
②
Service selector matches all pods equally
③
Need version-specific labels for weighted routing
④
Create separate Services per version
⑤
Use Ingress for true weighted canary routing

Tenet: Native Kubernetes Services do round-robin across all matching pods — there's no built-in weighted routing. For canary deployments, use separate version labels + separate Services, or use an Ingress controller (nginx, Istio) for true percentage-based traffic splitting. On CKAD, understanding Service selector matching is essential.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get ep easypj-api -n s24-jobpost NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-api 10.244.1.5:80,10.244.1.6:80,...,10.244.2.9:80 5m ← 10 endpoints!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get ep easypj-api-stable -n s24-jobpost NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-api-stable 10.244.1.5:80,...,(9 total) 2m ✅ Only v2!
🔧
BASH — Create versioned Services
kubectl delete svc easypj-api -n s24-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api-stable
  namespace: s24-jobpost
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api
    version: v2      # ✅ Only matches stable pods!
  ports:
  - port: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api-canary
  namespace: s24-jobpost
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api
    version: v3      # ✅ Only matches canary pods!
  ports:
  - port: 80
EOF
kubectl get ep -n s24-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Traffic Split by Version

With version-specific Service selectors, stable traffic goes only to v2 pods and canary traffic goes only to v3 pods. Use an Ingress controller for percentage-based canary routing in production.

💡 Key takeaway: Native K8s Services do round-robin across all matching pods. For canary, add version labels and create separate Services. For true weighted routing, use an Ingress controller like nginx or Istio.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s24-jobpost
kubectl get ns s24-jobpost 2>&1
S25
🧪 SCENARIO S25 — Category 2: App Deployment BlueGreen

Blue/Green Switch Breaks User Sessions — No External Session Store

The Problem: The easypj team performs a Blue/Green deployment: deploy the new v4 stack (green) alongside the current v3 stack (blue), test, then switch the Service selector. The switch is instant — but all logged-in users are kicked out. User sessions are stored in the pod's local memory (Django's default). When the Service switches from blue to green pods, sessions don't transfer. Your job: fix this by externalizing sessions to Redis.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Blue/Green deployment on node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy Blue + Green with Local Sessions (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The platform team perfected the Blue/Green switch — v3 (blue) and v4 (green) running side by side. QA validated v4, the Service selector was updated from version: v3 to version: v4. Traffic switched instantly to green. But the support desk exploded — all users were logged out. Django's default session backend stores sessions in the database or local memory. Blue pods had the sessions, green pods don't. The fix: store sessions in Redis, accessible to both blue and green pods.
📁 MANIFESTS for S25:
s25-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
├── 01-blue-deploy.yaml    ← v3 stack with local sessions
├── 02-green-deploy.yaml   ← v4 stack with local sessions
├── 03-service.yaml        ← Switch selector from v3 → v4
└── 04-redis-deploy.yaml   ← ✅ FIX: Redis for shared sessions
BASH — Deploy Blue/Green with session problem
kubectl create ns s25-jobpost
# Blue (v3) — serving production traffic
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web-blue
  namespace: s25-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
      version: v3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
        version: v3
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:alpine
        env:
        - name: SESSION_ENGINE
          value: "django.contrib.sessions.backends.cache" # ❌ BUG! Sessions in local cache!
EOF
# Green (v4) — new version, no sessions
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web-green
  namespace: s25-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
      version: v4
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
        version: v4
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:alpine
EOF
# Service — currently pointing to v3 (blue)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: s25-jobpost
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-web
    version: v3   # Switching this to v4 will lose all sessions!
  ports:
  - port: 80
EOF
kubectl get deploy,svc -n s25-jobpost
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Switch Service to v4: kubectl patch svc easypj-web -n s25-jobpost -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"v4"}}}'
✗2. All users logged out — sessions were in blue pods' local memory!
✗3. Django's default cache-based sessions are NOT shared across pods
✗4. Blue/Green switch is technically successful but user experience is BROKEN!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check session backend: SESSION_ENGINE=django.contrib.sessions.backends.cache → stored in local memory per pod
→ Each pod has its own session cache — not shared between blue and green!
2Fix: Use Redis as the session backend — accessible to ALL pods regardless of version
→ SESSION_ENGINE=django.contrib.sessions.backends.cached_db with REDIS_URL pointing to shared Redis
3Root cause: User sessions stored in pod-local cache — Blue/Green switch moves traffic to pods that don't have the session data
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Users logged out after Blue/Green switch
②
Sessions in local cache → Not shared
③
Green pods have no session data
④
Move sessions to Redis → Shared across all pods
⑤
Blue/Green switch now seamless!

Tenet: Blue/Green deployment requires externalized state. Sessions, file uploads, and cache must live OUTSIDE the pods — in Redis, a shared database, or object storage. If state is pod-local, switching from blue to green pods loses all that state. This applies to ANY deployment strategy where pods are replaced. On CKAD, understanding state externalization is crucial for deployment scenarios.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n s25-jobpost -L version NAME VERSION easypj-web-blue-xxx v3 ← Has sessions! easypj-web-green-yyy v4 ← No sessions!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n s25-jobpost NAME READY STATUS easypj-web-blue-xxx 1/1 Running ← Session in Redis easypj-web-green-yyy 1/1 Running ← Session in Redis ✅ Shared!
🔧
BASH — Add Redis and update ConfigMap
# Deploy Redis for shared sessions
kubectl create deploy redis -n s25-jobpost --image=redis:7-alpine
kubectl expose deploy redis -n s25-jobpost --port=6379
# Update ConfigMap with Redis-backed sessions
kubectl create cm session-config -n s25-jobpost \
  --from-literal=SESSION_ENGINE=django.contrib.sessions.backends.cache \
  --from-literal=REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/1
# Now Blue/Green switch preserves sessions via Redis!
✓

✅ Verify — Sessions Survive Blue/Green Switch

With Redis as the shared session store, switching the Service from blue (v3) to green (v4) no longer logs out users. Sessions persist across pod replacements.

💡 Key takeaway: Externalize all state (sessions, uploads, cache) before implementing Blue/Green deployment. Redis, S3, or shared databases make state portable across pod versions.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s25-jobpost
kubectl get ns s25-jobpost 2>&1
S26
🧪 SCENARIO S26 — Category 2: App Deployment Imperative

kubectl run Creates Pod Instead of Deployment — Missing --restart Flag

The Problem: You need to quickly deploy easypj-api using imperative commands. You run kubectl run easypj-api --image=nginx:alpine --port=80. It creates a Pod, not a Deployment. Without --restart=Always (or using kubectl create deploy), the pod won't be managed by a controller — no self-healing, no scaling. Your job: learn the correct imperative commands for creating Deployments.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Quick imperative practice
1

📋 Run Imperative Commands — Creates Pod Not Deployment (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: During an incident, the SRE needs to quickly spin up an API instance. They run kubectl run easypj-api --image=nginx:alpine. It works — the pod is running. But when they try to scale it with kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api --replicas=3, they get "deployment not found." kubectl run creates a standalone Pod by default. To create a Deployment imperatively, you need kubectl create deploy.
📁 for S26:
s26-jobpost namespace/ (all done via imperative commands)
BASH — Try imperative commands
kubectl create ns s26-jobpost
# ❌ BUG! Creates a Pod, NOT a Deployment!
kubectl run easypj-api -n s26-jobpost --image=nginx:alpine --port=80
kubectl get pods -n s26-jobpost
kubectl get deploy -n s26-jobpost  # → No resources found! It's a Pod, not a Deployment
# Try to scale — fails!
kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api -n s26-jobpost --replicas=3
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. kubectl get deploy -n s26-jobpost → No resources found — not a Deployment!
✗2. kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api -n s26-jobpost --replicas=3 → "deployment not found"
✗3. Created a bare Pod — no controller, no self-healing, no scaling!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1kubectl run default behavior: Creates a Pod (not a Deployment) since Kubernetes 1.18+
→ Use kubectl create deploy for Deployments, kubectl run for quick test Pods
2Root cause: kubectl run creates a Pod by default — must use kubectl create deploy for Deployments
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Need Deployment → Run kubectl run
②
Get Pod, not Deployment → Wrong command
③
kubectl run = Pod (since K8s 1.18)
④
kubectl create deploy = Deployment
⑤
Use correct command → Deployment + scaling works!

Tenet: Since Kubernetes 1.18, kubectl run creates Pods by default. For Deployments, use kubectl create deploy NAME --image=IMG --replicas=N. For CronJobs, use kubectl create cj. For Jobs, use kubectl create job. On CKAD, knowing the correct imperative commands saves valuable exam time.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get deploy -n s26-jobpost No resources found in s26-jobpost namespace. ← Not a Deployment!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl create deploy easypj-api -n s26-jobpost --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=3 deployment.apps/easypj-api created ✅
🔧
BASH — Correct imperative commands
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s26-jobpost
kubectl create deploy easypj-api -n s26-jobpost --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=3 --port=80
kubectl expose deploy easypj-api -n s26-jobpost --port=80
kubectl scale deploy easypj-api -n s26-jobpost --replicas=5
kubectl get deploy,svc -n s26-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Deployment Created Imperatively

Using kubectl create deploy creates a proper Deployment with a ReplicaSet controller. Now scaling, rolling updates, and self-healing all work.

💡 Key takeaway: kubectl run creates a Pod by default. Use kubectl create deploy for Deployments. Or add --restart=Always to kubectl run to create a Deployment. Always verify with kubectl get deploy after imperative creation.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s26-jobpost
kubectl get ns s26-jobpost 2>&1
S27
🧪 SCENARIO S27 — Category 2: App Deployment Imperative

kubectl set image Updates Wrong Container — Multi-Container Pod

The Problem: You run kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web nginx=nginx:1.27 but the Deployment has TWO containers (django and nginx). Without specifying the container name, kubectl updates the WRONG one. Django now runs on nginx:1.27 instead of the Python image. Your job: understand container targeting in kubectl set commands.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-container imperative practice
1

📋 Deploy Multi-Container Pod, Then Update Wrong Container (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj-web Deployment has two containers: django (Python app) and nginx (static file server). The SRE needed to update nginx from 1.25 to 1.27. They ran kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web *=nginx:1.27 — using * to update ALL containers. Django was replaced with the nginx image! The app crashes because there's no Python runtime.
📁 MANIFESTS for S27:
s27-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── 01-deployment.yaml  ← Two containers: django + nginx
BASH — Deploy multi-container, then update wrong container
kubectl create ns s27-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: s27-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: python:3.12-slim
        command: ["sleep","3600"]
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.25
EOF
# ❌ BUG! Updates ALL containers to nginx:1.27!
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web -n s27-jobpost *=nginx:1.27
kubectl get pods -n s27-jobpost  # → CrashLoopBackOff! Django is now nginx!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Pod crashes: kubectl get pods -n s27-jobpost → STATUS: CrashLoopBackOff
✗2. Check images: kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.containers[*].image}' → Both show nginx:1.27!
✗3. *= updates ALL containers — django replaced with nginx image!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check container images: kubectl describe pod -n s27-jobpost | grep Image:
→ django container has image nginx:1.27 — WRONG! Should be python:3.12-slim
2Correct syntax: kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web nginx=nginx:1.27 (specify container name)
→ Never use *= unless you intentionally want to update ALL containers
3Root cause: kubectl set image with *= updates all containers — must specify the target container name explicitly
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod crashes after set image → Wrong image?
②
Check container images → django=nginx?!
③
*= updated ALL containers → Bug!
④
Use specific container name → Safe update
⑤
Rollback to fix → Then update correctly

Tenet: kubectl set image DEPLOY CONTAINER=IMAGE — always specify the container name! Using *= or omitting the container name updates ALL containers, which can break multi-container pods. On CKAD, container name targeting in imperative commands is a key skill.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n s27-jobpost -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}' nginx:1.27 nginx:1.27 ← Both containers are nginx! Django was replaced!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n s27-jobpost -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}' python:3.12-slim nginx:1.27 ✅ Correct: django=python, nginx=nginx!
🔧
BASH — Rollback and update correctly
kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-web -n s27-jobpost
kubectl set image deploy/easypj-web -n s27-jobpost nginx=nginx:1.27
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web -n s27-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Only nginx Container Updated

By specifying the container name, only the nginx container is updated. Django continues running on the Python image.

💡 Key takeaway: kubectl set image without a container name updates ALL containers. In multi-container pods, always specify the container name: kubectl set image deploy/NAME CONTAINER=IMAGE.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s27-jobpost
kubectl get ns s27-jobpost 2>&1
S28
🧪 SCENARIO S28 — Category 2: App Deployment Config

Deployment References Wrong ConfigMap — Pods Fail to Start

The Problem: The complete easypj-web stack is deployed: Deployment (2 replicas), ConfigMap (Django settings), Secret (DB password), and Service. But pods crash because the Deployment volume mount references configMap: easypj-config while the actual ConfigMap is easypj-web-config. Your job: find and fix the name mismatch in the full stack.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Full stack deployment on node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy Full Stack with ConfigMap Name Typo (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj platform team deployed the full web stack: ConfigMap for settings, Secret for DB credentials, Deployment for the app, and Service for networking. The ConfigMap was created as easypj-web-config but the Deployment references it as easypj-config. A one-word difference — "web" — and the entire stack fails. The pods can't mount the ConfigMap volume and crash.
📁 MANIFESTS for S28:
s28-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
├── 01-configmap.yaml     ← named "easypj-web-config"
├── 02-secret.yaml        ← DB password
├── 03-deployment.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: references "easypj-config"
└── 04-service.yaml       ← ClusterIP (port 80)
BASH — Deploy full stack with name mismatch
kubectl create ns s28-jobpost
kubectl create cm easypj-web-config -n s28-jobpost --from-literal=DEBUG=false --from-literal=ALLOWED_HOSTS=*
kubectl create secret generic db-secret -n s28-jobpost --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=secret123
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: s28-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: nginx:alpine
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/config
      volumes:
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: easypj-config   # ❌ BUG! Should be "easypj-web-config"!
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: s28-jobpost
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-web
  ports:
  - port: 80
EOF
kubectl get pods -n s28-jobpost
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pods: kubectl get pods -n s28-jobpost → STATUS: ContainerCreating stuck or CrashLoopBackOff
✗2. Check events: kubectl describe pod -n s28-jobpost → "configmap easypj-config not found"
✗3. ConfigMap exists as easypj-web-config — name mismatch!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check volume config: kubectl get deploy easypj-web -n s28-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A2 configMap
→ name: easypj-config — wrong name!
2List ConfigMaps: kubectl get cm -n s28-jobpost
→ easypj-web-config — with "web" in the name!
3Root cause: Deployment volume references "easypj-config" but the ConfigMap is named "easypj-web-config"
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pods stuck → Check events
②
"configmap not found" → Name mismatch
③
kubectl get cm → Find correct name
④
Patch deployment → Fix name reference
⑤
Pods start → Full stack operational!

Tenet: ConfigMap and Secret name mismatches in volume mounts or envFrom cause pods to fail at creation time. kubectl describe pod will show exactly which resource is missing. Always cross-reference names between the resource and the Deployment spec.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe pod -n s28-jobpost easypj-web-xxx | grep -A3 Events Warning FailedMount MountVolume.SetUp failed: configmap "easypj-config" not found
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n s28-jobpost NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-web-xxx 1/1 Running 0 30s ✅ easypj-web-yyy 1/1 Running 0 28s ✅
🔧
BASH — Correct the ConfigMap reference
kubectl patch deploy easypj-web -n s28-jobpost -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"volumes":[{"name":"config","configMap":{"name":"easypj-web-config"}}]}}}}'
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web -n s28-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — ConfigMap Mounted Correctly

After fixing the ConfigMap name, the volume mounts successfully and all pods start. The full stack is operational.

💡 Key takeaway: ConfigMap and Secret names must match EXACTLY between the resource definition and the Deployment reference. A single character typo breaks the entire deployment. Always verify with kubectl get cm,secret before troubleshooting pod crashes.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s28-jobpost
kubectl get ns s28-jobpost 2>&1
S29
🧪 SCENARIO S29 — Category 2: App Deployment Helm

Helm Upgrade Fails — Changing Immutable Selector Field

The Problem: You install easypj as a Helm chart, then try to upgrade it with a changed matchLabels selector. Helm upgrade fails because spec.selector is immutable on a Deployment after creation. You must either use --force (recreates the resource) or delete and recreate. Your job: understand immutable fields in Helm upgrades.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Helm practice
1

📋 Install Helm Chart, Then Attempt Immutable Field Change (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team created a Helm chart for the web app. The initial install used label app: easypj. Later, the platform team standardized on app: easypj-web and updated values.yaml. The helm upgrade failed because the Deployment's matchLabels selector is immutable — you can't change it on a running Deployment. The team didn't know about --force or the need to delete first.
📁 HELM CHART for S29:
~/easypj-chart/
├── Chart.yaml
├── values.yaml
└── templates/
    └── deployment.yaml  ← matchLabels changed → upgrade fails!
BASH — Create chart, install, then fail upgrade
kubectl create ns s29-jobpost
mkdir -p ~/easypj-chart/templates
cat << 'EOF' > ~/easypj-chart/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: easypj-web
version: 1.0.0
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > ~/easypj-chart/values.yaml
label: easypj
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > ~/easypj-chart/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Values.label }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Values.label }}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:alpine
EOF
helm install easypj ~/easypj-chart -n s29-jobpost
# ❌ BUG! Change immutable field → upgrade fails!
helm upgrade easypj ~/easypj-chart -n s29-jobpost --set label=easypj-web
# Error: Deployment.apps "easypj-web" is invalid: spec.selector: field is immutable
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Helm upgrade fails: "field is immutable" — can't change selector after creation
✗2. Deployment stuck with old label, helm release in failed state
✗3. Without knowing about --force, the team is blocked from upgrading!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Immutable Deployment fields: spec.selector, spec.template.metadata.labels (if selector changes)
→ matchLabels is immutable after creation — must recreate the Deployment
2Root cause: Helm upgrade tries to patch immutable field (selector) — must use --force to delete and recreate
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Helm upgrade fails → Check error
②
"field is immutable" → Selector changed
③
Use --force to recreate → Deployment replaced
④
Or: helm uninstall + helm install
⑤
Upgrade succeeds with new selector!

Tenet: Helm upgrade patches resources in place. Some Kubernetes fields are immutable after creation (Deployment selector, StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates, Service clusterIP). Use helm upgrade --force to delete and recreate immutable resources, or manually uninstall/reinstall. On CKAD, understanding Helm's limitations is important.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ helm upgrade easypj ~/easypj-chart -n s29-jobpost --set label=easypj-web Error: UPGRADE FAILED: Deployment.apps "easypj-web" is invalid: spec.selector: Invalid value: field is immutable
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ helm upgrade easypj ~/easypj-chart -n s29-jobpost --set label=easypj-web --force Release "easypj" has been upgraded. Happy Helming! ✅
🔧
BASH — Helm upgrade with --force
# Option 1: --force deletes and recreates immutable resources
helm upgrade easypj ~/easypj-chart -n s29-jobpost --set label=easypj-web --force
# Option 2: Uninstall and reinstall
# helm uninstall easypj -n s29-jobpost
# helm install easypj ~/easypj-chart -n s29-jobpost --set label=easypj-web
helm list -n s29-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Helm Upgrade Succeeds

Using --force, Helm deletes and recreates the Deployment with the new selector. The upgrade succeeds without manual intervention.

💡 Key takeaway: Helm cannot change immutable fields (like selector) on existing resources. Use helm upgrade --force to delete and recreate resources, or better yet, plan selector changes as part of a new major chart version with helm install instead of upgrade.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
helm uninstall easypj -n s29-jobpost
kubectl delete ns s29-jobpost
rm -rf ~/easypj-chart
kubectl get ns s29-jobpost 2>&1
S30
🧪 SCENARIO S30 — Category 2: App Deployment Kustomize

Kustomize Staging Overlay Inherits Production Resource Limits

The Problem: You create a Kustomize base and overlays for dev, staging, and prod. The staging overlay deploys — but pods are Pending because it inherited resources.limits.memory: 4Gi from the base, and the staging cluster nodes only have 2Gi. The staging overlay didn't override the base's production resource limits. Your job: add a patch to staging that overrides resources.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Kustomize overlays on production node "easy"
1

📋 Create Kustomize Base with Prod Limits, Staging Doesn't Override (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj DevOps team adopted Kustomize for environment-specific configurations. The base/ directory has production resource limits (4Gi memory, 2 CPU). The staging/ overlay changes replica count but forgets to override resources. When deploying to staging, pods request 4Gi memory — but the staging nodes only have 2Gi. Every pod stays Pending with "insufficient memory."
📁 KUSTOMIZE STRUCTURE for S30:
~/easypj-kustomize/
├── base/
│   ├── deployment.yaml    ← resources: {limits: {memory: 4Gi}}
│   └── kustomization.yaml
├── staging/
│   └── kustomization.yaml  ← ❌ BUG: No resource override!
BASH — Create Kustomize with inherited prod limits
kubectl create ns s30-jobpost
mkdir -p ~/easypj-kustomize/{base,staging}
cat << 'EOF' > ~/easypj-kustomize/base/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:alpine
        resources:
          limits:
            memory: "4Gi"    # Prod-level limit!
            cpu: "2"
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > ~/easypj-kustomize/base/kustomization.yaml
resources:
- deployment.yaml
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > ~/easypj-kustomize/staging/kustomization.yaml
resources:
- ../base
# ❌ BUG! No patches to override resources — inherits 4Gi from base!
EOF
kubectl apply -k ~/easypj-kustomize/staging -n s30-jobpost
kubectl get pods -n s30-jobpost
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Pod Pending: kubectl get pods -n s30-jobpost → STATUS: Pending
✗2. Reason: "Insufficient memory" — requesting 4Gi but nodes have 2Gi
✗3. Staging overlay didn't override prod's resource limits!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check pod resources: kubectl describe pod -n s30-jobpost | grep -A3 Requests
→ memory: 4Gi — inherited from base!
2Root cause: Staging overlay doesn't override base resources — inherits production limits that don't fit staging nodes
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod Pending → Insufficient resources
②
Check resource requests → 4Gi (prod level!)
③
Check Kustomize overlay → No resource patch
④
Add patchStrategicMerge for staging resources
⑤
Pods schedule with staging-appropriate limits!

Tenet: Kustomize overlays inherit everything from the base unless explicitly overridden. Always check that staging/dev overlays override resource limits, replica counts, and other environment-specific settings. Use kubectl kustomize to preview the rendered output before applying.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe pod -n s30-jobpost | grep -A5 Events Warning FailedScheduling 0/3 nodes available: insufficient memory
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n s30-jobpost NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-web-xxx 1/1 Running 0 30s ✅
🔧
BASH — Add staging resource patch
cat << 'EOF' > ~/easypj-kustomize/staging/resource-patch.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        resources:
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
EOF
cat << 'EOF' > ~/easypj-kustomize/staging/kustomization.yaml
resources:
- ../base
patchesStrategicMerge:
- resource-patch.yaml
EOF
kubectl delete -k ~/easypj-kustomize/staging -n s30-jobpost
kubectl apply -k ~/easypj-kustomize/staging -n s30-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Staging Gets Appropriate Resources

With a patchStrategicMerge in the staging overlay, the Deployment now requests 512Mi instead of 4Gi. Pods schedule successfully on staging nodes.

💡 Key takeaway: Kustomize overlays inherit from the base by default. Use patchesStrategicMerge to override specific fields per environment. Always verify overlay output with kubectl kustomize before applying. Dev/staging/prod should each have different resource limits.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s30-jobpost
rm -rf ~/easypj-kustomize
kubectl get ns s30-jobpost 2>&1
S31
🧪 SCENARIO S31 — Category 2: App Deployment Scale

Scale Beyond Node Capacity — Pods Stuck Pending

The Problem: The easypj API goes viral — a new job posting hits the front page. You quickly scale from 2 to 10 replicas with kubectl scale. But 4 pods stay Pending — the cluster only has capacity for 6. You didn't check available resources before scaling. Your job: learn to check node capacity before scaling and use resource requests appropriately.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Single-node capacity limits
1

📋 Scale Beyond Capacity Without Checking (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Traffic spiked 5x after a viral job posting. The SRE ran kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api --replicas=20 without checking node capacity. 14 pods are Pending — the cluster can only fit 6 pods with the current resource requests. Users hitting the Pending pods get nothing. The viral moment is wasted because the infrastructure can't scale.
📁 for S31:
s31-jobpost namespace/ (imperative scaling)
BASH — Scale without checking capacity
kubectl create ns s31-jobpost
kubectl create deploy easypj-api -n s31-jobpost --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=2
kubectl set resources deploy/easypj-api -n s31-jobpost -c=nginx --requests=cpu=500m,memory=256Mi
# ❌ BUG! Scale to 10 without checking available capacity!
kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api -n s31-jobpost --replicas=10
kubectl get pods -n s31-jobpost -o wide
# → Multiple pods stuck Pending: "Insufficient cpu"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pods: kubectl get pods -n s31-jobpost → Some Pending with "Insufficient cpu/memory"
✗2. Didn't check kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 Allocated before scaling!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check node capacity: kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 "Allocated resources"
→ CPU/Memory nearly fully allocated!
2Root cause: Scaled beyond cluster capacity without checking available resources first
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pods Pending → Check events
②
"Insufficient cpu" → Capacity issue
③
Check node allocated resources
④
Scale down to fit → Or add nodes
⑤
Always check capacity before scaling!

Tenet: kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 Allocated shows the percentage of CPU/memory already allocated. Always check this before scaling. If pods are Pending with "Insufficient" errors, either scale down, reduce resource requests, or add nodes. On CKAD, understanding cluster capacity is essential for troubleshooting.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n s31-jobpost NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-xxx 1/1 Running 0 5m easypj-api-yyy 0/1 Pending 0 1m ← Insufficient cpu!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api -n s31-jobpost --replicas=4 kubectl get pods -n s31-jobpost All pods Running ✅ Scaled to fit cluster capacity
🔧
BASH — Right-size the deployment
kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 "Allocated resources"
kubectl scale deploy/easypj-api -n s31-jobpost --replicas=4
kubectl get pods -n s31-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — All Pods Running Within Capacity

After scaling to fit available capacity, all pods run successfully. Always check node resources before scaling.

💡 Key takeaway: Always check kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 Allocated before scaling. If pods are Pending with "Insufficient" errors, either scale down, reduce requests, or add nodes.
