kubectl get ns s31-jobpost 2>&1
S32
🧪 SCENARIO S32 — Category 2: App Deployment Strategy

RollingUpdate Corrupts Data — Should Use Recreate for Schema Changes

The Problem: The easypj database migration adds a new NOT NULL column. The Deployment uses RollingUpdate — new pods (with the schema change) and old pods (without it) run simultaneously. Half the writes fail because old pods don't have the new column. For breaking schema changes, you must use Recreate strategy: stop ALL old pods first, then start new ones.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Strategy comparison
1

📋 Deploy with RollingUpdate During Breaking Change (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj DB team added a mandatory phone_number column to the users table. They deployed the schema change with RollingUpdate. New pods expect phone_number to exist, old pods don't have it. During the rollout, users on old pods get errors when the app tries to insert into the new column. Data inconsistency spreads as old and new pods write different schemas.
📁 MANIFESTS for S32:
s32-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── 01-deployment.yaml  ← BUG: RollingUpdate during breaking schema change!
BASH — Deploy with wrong strategy for schema change
kubectl create ns s32-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s32-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate    # ❌ BUG! Should be Recreate for breaking schema!
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
      maxSurge: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
EOF
kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s32-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A2 strategy
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Strategy is RollingUpdate — old and new pods run simultaneously during deploy
✗2. Breaking schema changes need ALL old pods stopped before new ones start
✗3. RollingUpdate with schema change = data inconsistency!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check strategy: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s32-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy.type}'
→ RollingUpdate — wrong for breaking changes!
2Root cause: RollingUpdate during breaking schema change causes old and new pods to run simultaneously — data inconsistency
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Data inconsistency → Schema change + RollingUpdate
②
Breaking change needs Recreate strategy
③
Recreate: stop ALL old → start ALL new
④
Downside: brief downtime (acceptable for schema)
⑤
Patch strategy → Recreate → Safe deployment!

Tenet: Use RollingUpdate for zero-downtime deploys of backward-compatible changes. Use Recreate when old and new versions cannot coexist (breaking schema changes, incompatible APIs). On CKAD, knowing which strategy to apply is critical.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s32-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy.type}' RollingUpdate ← ❌ Wrong for schema changes
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s32-jobpost -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy.type}' Recreate ✅ Safe for breaking schema changes
🔧
BASH — Patch strategy
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s32-jobpost -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Recreate"}}}'
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s32-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Recreate Strategy Set

With Recreate strategy, Kubernetes stops ALL old pods before starting any new ones. Safe for breaking schema changes.

💡 Key takeaway: Use RollingUpdate for zero-downtime (backward-compatible changes). Use Recreate when old and new versions CANNOT coexist (breaking schema, incompatible APIs).

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s32-jobpost
kubectl get ns s32-jobpost 2>&1
S33
🧪 SCENARIO S33 — Category 2: App Deployment Namespaces

Dev Pod Consumes All Resources — No ResourceQuota on Namespace

The Problem: The easypj-dev namespace has no ResourceQuota. A developer deploys a memory-intensive test that consumes all available cluster resources, starving the production namespace. Your job: create a ResourceQuota that limits dev to 2Gi memory and 2 CPU, protecting production from dev workloads.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Namespace isolation
1

📋 Deploy to Dev Without ResourceQuota (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj-dev namespace was created without a ResourceQuota. A new developer ran a load test that spawned 50 pods with 500Mi each — consuming 25Gi of memory. Production pods in easypj-prod started getting OOMKilled because the dev namespace had no limits. The entire job board went down because of a dev environment.
📁 MANIFESTS for S33:
s33-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── 01-resourcequota.yaml  ← ResourceQuota to protect the namespace
BASH — Apply ResourceQuota to protect namespace
kubectl create ns s33-jobpost
# ❌ BUG! No ResourceQuota — namespace can consume unlimited resources!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: dev-quota
  namespace: s33-jobpost
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "2"
    requests.memory: "2Gi"
    limits.cpu: "4"
    limits.memory: "4Gi"
    pods: "10"
EOF
kubectl get resourcequota -n s33-jobpost
kubectl describe quota dev-quota -n s33-jobpost
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. No ResourceQuota → namespace has no resource limits
✗2. Dev workloads can consume ALL cluster resources, starving production
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check quotas: kubectl get resourcequota -n s33-jobpost
→ If empty or not restrictive enough, namespace can consume unlimited resources
2Root cause: Missing or insufficient ResourceQuota allows a namespace to consume all cluster resources, affecting other namespaces
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Production pods OOMKilled → Resource starvation
②
Check dev namespace → No ResourceQuota
③
Dev workload consuming all resources
④
Create ResourceQuota on dev namespace
⑤
Production protected from dev!

Tenet: ResourceQuota limits aggregate resource consumption per namespace. Always set quotas on dev/test namespaces to prevent them from affecting production. Combine with LimitRange to set default resource requests/limits on pods. On CKAD, ResourceQuota and LimitRange are essential namespace management tools.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get resourcequota -n s33-jobpost No resources found ← No limits! Dev can consume everything!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl describe quota dev-quota -n s33-jobpost Resource Used Hard requests.cpu 0 2 ✅ Limited! requests.memory 0 2Gi ✅ Limited! pods 0 10 ✅ Limited!
🔧
BASH — Create ResourceQuota
kubectl create quota dev-quota -n s33-jobpost --hard=requests.cpu=2,requests.memory=2Gi,limits.cpu=4,limits.memory=4Gi,pods=10
kubectl describe quota dev-quota -n s33-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — Namespace Protected by Quota

ResourceQuota now limits the namespace to 2 CPU, 2Gi memory, and 10 pods. Dev workloads can no longer starve production.

💡 Key takeaway: Always set ResourceQuota on dev/test namespaces. Without it, a single runaway workload can consume all cluster resources and take down production. Combine with LimitRange for default pod limits.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s33-jobpost
kubectl get ns s33-jobpost 2>&1
S34
🧪 SCENARIO S34 — Category 2: App Deployment Diff

kubectl diff Shows Unintended Changes — Someone Edited Live Object

The Problem: You prepare a Deployment update, run kubectl diff to preview changes, and see unexpected modifications — someone edited the live Deployment directly instead of updating the YAML. kubectl diff reveals the drift between your local YAML and the live state. Your job: use kubectl diff to detect and reconcile configuration drift.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Configuration management
1

📋 Deploy, Then Manually Edit Live Object (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: During an incident, an SRE manually patched the Deployment to increase replicas from 3 to 6. The original YAML file still says 3. Next sprint, a developer updates the YAML (changing image) and applies it — the replicas silently revert from 6 to 3, causing a capacity incident. kubectl diff would have caught this drift before applying.
📁 for S34:
s34-jobpost namespace/
├── 00-namespace.yaml
└── deploy.yaml (replicas: 3, but live has replicas: 6!)
BASH — Simulate live state drift and detect with diff
kubectl create ns s34-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' > /tmp/deploy.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s34-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
EOF
kubectl apply -f /tmp/deploy.yaml
# Simulate manual edit: someone scales to 6 without updating YAML
kubectl scale deploy easypj-api -n s34-jobpost --replicas=6
# ❌ BUG! YAML says 3, live is 6 — drift detected!
kubectl diff -f /tmp/deploy.yaml
# Shows: -replicas: 6  +replicas: 3  ← YAML would OVERWRITE the manual change!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. YAML says replicas: 3, but live has replicas: 6 — configuration DRIFT!
✗2. Applying YAML would silently revert replicas to 3 — causing capacity loss!
✗3. kubectl diff catches this BEFORE the destructive apply
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Always diff before apply: kubectl diff -f manifest.yaml
→ Shows exactly what changes will be made to the live state
2Root cause: Live state drifts from source YAML when manual edits bypass version control — kubectl diff detects this drift
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Need to update Deployment → kubectl diff first
②
Diff shows replicas: 6→3 → Someone changed live!
③
Reconcile: update YAML to 6 → No more drift
④
Apply YAML → No unintended changes
⑤
Always diff before apply in production!

Tenet: kubectl diff -f is the safety net before applying changes. It shows a colored diff of what would change. If you see unexpected changes (like replicas shrinking), someone edited the live object directly. Reconcile the YAML first, then apply. On CKAD, kubectl diff is a best practice for infrastructure-as-code.

🔧
BASH — Reconcile drift
kubectl diff -f /tmp/deploy.yaml
sed -i 's/replicas: 3/replicas: 6/' /tmp/deploy.yaml
kubectl diff -f /tmp/deploy.yaml  # Should show no changes!
kubectl apply -f /tmp/deploy.yaml
✓

✅ Verify — No Unintended Changes

After reconciling the YAML, kubectl diff shows no changes. The apply is now safe.

💡 Key takeaway: kubectl diff -f is your safety net. Always run it before kubectl apply in production. If diff shows unexpected changes (like shrinking replicas), someone edited the live object — reconcile YAML first.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s34-jobpost
rm -f /tmp/deploy.yaml
kubectl get ns s34-jobpost 2>&1
S35
🧪 SCENARIO S35 — Category 2: App Deployment DaemonSet

DaemonSet RollingUpdate Gaps — maxUnavailable: 2 on 3 Nodes

The Problem: The Fluentd DaemonSet is updated with RollingUpdate and maxUnavailable: 2. On a 3-node cluster, 2 nodes lose their Fluentd pod simultaneously — no log collection on those nodes during the update. Your job: set safe DaemonSet update parameters.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — DaemonSet updates
1

📋 Deploy DaemonSet with Aggressive Update Strategy (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The Fluentd DaemonSet needed an urgent security patch. The SRE set maxUnavailable: 2 to speed up the rollout. On a 3-node kind cluster, 2 nodes simultaneously had no Fluentd pod — 67% of logs were lost during the update window. The security team couldn't audit those 3 minutes.
📁 for S35:
s35-jobpost namespace/
BASH — Deploy DaemonSet with unsafe update params
kubectl create ns s35-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: fluentd
  namespace: s35-jobpost
spec:
  updateStrategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 2    # ❌ BUG! 2 of 3 nodes lose Fluentd at once!
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: fluentd
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: fluentd
    spec:
      tolerations:
      - key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
        operator: Exists
        effect: NoSchedule
      containers:
      - name: fluentd
        image: alpine:3.19
        command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF
kubectl get ds fluentd -n s35-jobpost -o yaml | grep -A3 updateStrategy
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. maxUnavailable: 2 on 3 nodes → 67% log coverage loss during updates!
✗2. Audit logs missing during the update window — compliance violation!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Safe default: maxUnavailable: 1 ensures only 1 node without Fluentd at a time
→ For 3 nodes, only 33% coverage loss instead of 67%
2Root cause: maxUnavailable: 2 is too aggressive for a 3-node cluster — causes log collection gaps during DaemonSet updates
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Log gaps during DaemonSet updates
②
Check updateStrategy → maxUnavailable:2
③
3 nodes, 2 unavailable → 67% gap
④
Set maxUnavailable:1 → Only 33% gap
⑤
Safe DaemonSet updates achieved!

Tenet: DaemonSet RollingUpdate maxUnavailable should be 1 (or 10% for large clusters). Unlike Deployments, DaemonSets run exactly one pod per node — losing 2+ nodes of coverage during updates can cause significant gaps. On CKAD, understanding DaemonSet update strategies is important.

🔧
BASH — Patch DaemonSet
kubectl patch ds fluentd -n s35-jobpost -p '{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"maxUnavailable":1}}}}'
kubectl get ds fluentd -n s35-jobpost -o yaml | grep maxUnavailable
✓

✅ Verify — Safe DaemonSet Update

With maxUnavailable: 1, only one node at a time loses Fluentd during updates. Log coverage stays at 67%+ during rollouts.

💡 Key takeaway: DaemonSet maxUnavailable should be 1 (or 10% for large clusters). Unlike Deployments, DaemonSets run one pod per node — losing 2+ nodes of coverage causes significant observability gaps.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s35-jobpost
kubectl get ns s35-jobpost 2>&1
S36
🧪 SCENARIO S36 — Category 2: App Deployment StatefulSet

StatefulSet Pods Have Random DNS — ClusterIP Instead of Headless Service

The Problem: The PostgreSQL StatefulSet uses a regular ClusterIP Service instead of a headless Service (clusterIP: None). Pods get random DNS names instead of stable identities like postgres-0.easypj-db.svc.cluster.local. The application can't resolve individual pod addresses. Your job: create a headless Service for stable network identity.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — StatefulSet networking
1

📋 Deploy StatefulSet with Regular ClusterIP Service (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The database team deployed PostgreSQL as a StatefulSet. Each pod should be reachable at easypj-db-0.easypj-db.s36-jobpost.svc.cluster.local. But the Service was created as a regular ClusterIP — DNS queries for individual pod names fail. The app can't connect to specific database instances for read/write splitting.
📁 for S36:
s36-jobpost namespace/
BASH — Deploy StatefulSet with wrong Service type
kubectl create ns s36-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: s36-jobpost
spec:
  clusterIP: 10.96.100.50   # ❌ BUG! Regular ClusterIP — not headless!
  selector:
    app: easypj-db
  ports:
  - port: 5432
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: s36-jobpost
spec:
  serviceName: easypj-db
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
EOF
kubectl get svc easypj-db -n s36-jobpost
# → CLUSTER-IP shows an IP — should be "None" for headless!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Service CLUSTER-IP is 10.96.100.50 — should be None for StatefulSet!
✗2. Individual pod DNS (easypj-db-0.easypj-db...) won't resolve
✗3. App can't connect to specific pods for read/write splitting!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check Service type: kubectl get svc easypj-db -n s36-jobpost
→ CLUSTER-IP not None — This is a regular Service, not headless!
2Root cause: StatefulSet requires a headless Service (clusterIP: None) for stable per-pod DNS — using a regular ClusterIP breaks pod identity resolution
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Can't reach individual pods → DNS issue
②
Check Service → ClusterIP not None
③
Headless Service = clusterIP: None
④
Delete and recreate with clusterIP: None
⑤
Per-pod DNS resolves correctly!

Tenet: StatefulSets need a headless Service (clusterIP: None) for stable network identity. The headless Service creates DNS A records for each pod: <pod>.<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. A regular ClusterIP Service only resolves to a single virtual IP — individual pods aren't directly reachable. On CKAD, headless Services for StatefulSets is a key concept.

🔧
BASH — Delete and recreate with clusterIP: None
kubectl delete svc easypj-db -n s36-jobpost
kubectl expose sts easypj-db -n s36-jobpost --name=easypj-db --port=5432 --cluster-ip=None
kubectl get svc easypj-db -n s36-jobpost
# → CLUSTER-IP: None ✅ Headless!
✓

✅ Verify — Headless Service Created

With clusterIP: None, each pod gets its own DNS A record. The app can now connect to specific pods.

💡 Key takeaway: StatefulSets require a headless Service (clusterIP: None) for stable per-pod DNS: pod-name.service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local. Regular ClusterIP Services only give a single virtual IP — individual pods aren't directly reachable.

BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s36-jobpost
kubectl get ns s36-jobpost 2>&1

🧪 SCENARIO S37 — Category 2: App Deployment History

Can't Rollback to Old Version — revisionHistoryLimit Too Low

The Problem: The easypj API has been updated 15 times. A critical bug was found in production — you need to rollback to revision 3 (the last known good version). But kubectl rollout history only shows revisions 6-15. revisionHistoryLimit is set to 10 — revisions 1-5 were automatically cleaned up. You can't rollback that far. Your job: increase revisionHistoryLimit for better audit trail.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Revision management
1

📋 Deploy with Low revisionHistoryLimit (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The platform team set revisionHistoryLimit to 3 (the default is 10) to save etcd space. After 8 deployments, they discovered a data corruption bug introduced in revision 2 that only manifested weeks later. Revisions 1-5 were gone — no way to audit what changed or rollback to the safe version. The team had to redeploy from scratch.
📁 for S37:
s37-jobpost namespace/
BASH — Deploy with low history limit
kubectl create ns s37-jobpost
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s37-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 1
  revisionHistoryLimit: 3    # ❌ BUG! Only keeps last 3 revisions!
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
EOF
# Simulate 5 updates — only last 3 will be kept!
for v in 2 3 4 5 6; do
  kubectl set image deploy/easypj-api nginx=nginx:1.$v -n s37-jobpost --record
  kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s37-jobpost
done
kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-api -n s37-jobpost
# → Only revisions 4, 5, 6 shown — 1-3 are GONE!
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check history: kubectl rollout history deploy/easypj-api -n s37-jobpost → Only 3 revisions!
✗2. Can't rollback to early versions — revisions cleaned up!
✗3. Audit trail incomplete — which change introduced the bug?
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check history limit: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s37-jobpost -o yaml | grep revisionHistoryLimit
→ revisionHistoryLimit: 3 — only 3 old ReplicaSets are retained!
2Root cause: revisionHistoryLimit set too low — old ReplicaSets (revisions) are cleaned up, making rollback to early versions impossible
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Need to rollback far → Check history
②
Only 3 revisions available → Limit too low
③
Default is 10 → Someone reduced it
④
Increase to 20 → More history retained
⑤
Can now audit and rollback to any recent version!

Tenet: revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) controls how many old ReplicaSets are kept for rollback. Setting it too low (0-3) saves etcd space but removes your ability to audit changes or rollback to older versions. Set it to at least 10 for production deployments. On CKAD, understanding revision history is important for troubleshooting.

🔧
BASH — Patch deployment
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s37-jobpost -p '{"spec":{"revisionHistoryLimit":20}}'
kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s37-jobpost -o yaml | grep revisionHistoryLimit
✓

✅ Verify — Revision History Retained

With revisionHistoryLimit: 20, up to 20 old ReplicaSets are retained. Future deployments will preserve history for rollback and auditing.

💡 Key takeaway: revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) controls rollback depth. Setting it below 10 saves etcd space but removes audit trail and rollback capability. Set to 10-20 for production.

S38
🧪 SCENARIO S38 — Category 2: App Deployment Config

ConfigMap Updated But Some Pods Still Use Old Config

The Problem: The easypj-web ConfigMap was updated with new ALLOWED_HOSTS. Some pods restarted and picked up the new config, but others didn't — inconsistent configuration across replicas. Pods that haven't restarted are still using the old ConfigMap mounted at startup. Your job: perform a rolling restart of ALL pods to pick up the new ConfigMap.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — ConfigMap updates
1

📋 Update ConfigMap Without Restarting All Pods (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The security team added a new domain to ALLOWED_HOSTS. They updated the ConfigMap and expected pods to pick it up. But ConfigMap changes mounted as volumes take time to propagate (kubelet sync period ~60s). Some pods got the update, some didn't. New users on updated pods could access the new domain; users on old pods got 400 Bad Request.
📁 for S38:
s38-jobpost namespace/
BASH — Update ConfigMap, observe inconsistent pods
kubectl create ns s38-jobpost
kubectl create cm web-config -n s38-jobpost --from-literal=ALLOWED_HOSTS=easypj.com
kubectl create deploy easypj-web -n s38-jobpost --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=3
# Update ConfigMap — pods WON'T automatically pick it up!
kubectl create cm web-config -n s38-jobpost --from-literal=ALLOWED_HOSTS=easypj.com,new.easypj.com --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
# ❌ BUG! Some pods still use old ConfigMap — inconsistent config!
kubectl exec -it $(kubectl get pods -n s38-jobpost -o name | head -1) -n s38-jobpost -- cat /etc/config/ALLOWED_HOSTS || echo "File not mounted yet"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. ConfigMap updated, but some pods still show OLD values
✗2. Inconsistent behavior across replicas — some accept new domain, some don't!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1ConfigMap updates are not instantaneous: The kubelet syncs ConfigMap volumes periodically
→ Pods must be restarted (or use a sidecar to watch for changes) to get updated ConfigMaps
2Root cause: Updated ConfigMap not propagated to all running pods — must perform rolling restart to ensure consistent configuration
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
ConfigMap changed → Check if pods see it
②
Some pods have old config → Not propagated
③
kubectl rollout restart → All pods recreate
④
New pods mount updated ConfigMap
⑤
Consistent configuration across all replicas!

Tenet: ConfigMaps mounted as volumes are updated by the kubelet periodically (default ~60s). For immediate propagation, use kubectl rollout restart deploy/NAME to perform a rolling restart. This creates new pods that mount the updated ConfigMap. On CKAD, knowing how to propagate ConfigMap changes is essential.

🔧
BASH — Restart to pick up new ConfigMap
kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-web -n s38-jobpost
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-web -n s38-jobpost
kubectl get pods -n s38-jobpost
✓

✅ Verify — All Pods Using New Config

After rolling restart, all pods mount the updated ConfigMap. Configuration is consistent across all replicas.

💡 Key takeaway: ConfigMap updates don't automatically propagate to running pods. Use kubectl rollout restart deploy/NAME for a graceful rolling restart that picks up new ConfigMap values on all replicas.

S40
🧪 SCENARIO S40 — Category 2: App Deployment Decision

Choose the Right Deployment Strategy — Decision Matrix Scenario

The Problem: The easypj platform team is designing their deployment pipeline. They need to choose between Recreate, RollingUpdate, Canary, and Blue/Green for three different components: (1) a banking payments API (zero-downtime required), (2) a nightly batch job processor (downtime acceptable), (3) a user-facing web app (gradual rollout preferred). Wrong strategy choices cause outages, data loss, or failed rollbacks. Your job: create a decision matrix matching each strategy to the right scenario.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Strategy analysis
1

📋 Apply Wrong Strategy to Each Component (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj team applied RollingUpdate to ALL components. The payments API had a brief window of mixed versions during rollout (old and new pods serving transactions simultaneously) — causing double-charges. The batch processor used Blue/Green (unnecessarily complex — wastes resources). The web app used Recreate (causing 30s downtime on every deploy). Each component needs a different strategy.
📁 for S40:
s40-jobpost namespace/ (analysis and decision scenario)
BASH — Observe the consequences of wrong strategies
kubectl create ns s40-jobpost
# Scenario 1: Payments API — ❌ Using RollingUpdate (should be Blue/Green)
# Old and new versions run simultaneously → transaction conflicts!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payments-api
  namespace: s40-jobpost
spec:
  replicas: 2
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate   # ❌ Wrong for payments — need Blue/Green!
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: payments
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: payments
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
EOF
# Scenario 2: Batch processor — ❌ Using Blue/Green (overkill)
# Wastes resources running two full stacks for a batch job
# Scenario 3: Web app — ❌ Using Recreate (downtime on every deploy)
echo "Decision matrix: Match strategy to component requirements!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Payments API with RollingUpdate → mixed versions = transaction conflicts
✗2. Batch processor with Blue/Green → double resources, unnecessary complexity
✗3. Web app with Recreate → downtime on every deploy
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Decision matrix:
→ Payments API: Blue/Green (zero-downtime, instant rollback, no mixed versions)
→ Batch processor: Recreate (downtime acceptable, simple, no resource waste)
→ Web app: Canary or RollingUpdate (gradual rollout, validate with real traffic)
2Root cause: One-size-fits-all deployment strategy — each component has different availability and consistency requirements
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Payments = zero-downtime + no mixed versions → Blue/Green
②
Batch = downtime OK + simple → Recreate
③
Web = gradual rollout + real-traffic validation → Canary
④
General stateless = zero-downtime + simple → RollingUpdate
⑤
Match strategy to requirements — one size does NOT fit all!

Tenet: Deployment strategies are not interchangeable. Blue/Green is best for critical systems needing instant rollback. Canary is best for validating changes with real users. RollingUpdate is the default for stateless apps. Recreate is best when simplicity matters more than uptime or when versions can't coexist. On CKAD, matching the right strategy to the right scenario demonstrates architectural understanding.

📟 Decision Matrix
Strategy Best For Downtime Rollback Complexity Recreate Batch jobs, migrations Yes Manual Low RollingUpdate Stateless APIs None Automatic Low Canary User-facing apps None Manual Medium Blue/Green Payments, critical sys None Instant High
🔧
Correct strategy assignment
# Payments API → Blue/Green (zero-downtime, no mixed versions)
kubectl patch deploy payments-api -n s40-jobpost -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Recreate"}}}' # Simulating Blue/Green via Service switch
# Batch processor → Recreate (downtime acceptable, simple)
# Web app → RollingUpdate (default, good for stateless apps)
echo "✅ Strategies aligned with component requirements!"
✓

✅ Verify — Correct Strategies Applied

Each component now uses the deployment strategy that matches its availability, consistency, and complexity requirements.

💡 Key takeaway: Payments → Blue/Green. Batch → Recreate. Web → Canary or RollingUpdate. Match strategy to requirements, not habit.

S41
🧪 SCENARIO S41 — Category 3: Observability Liveness Probe

Pod Restarts Every 90 Seconds — Liveness Probe Kills Healthy Django App

The Problem: The easypj API pods keep restarting every 90 seconds even though the application code is fine and users aren't complaining about errors. The SRE team configured a liveness probe that checks /health/ every 3 seconds and restarts the pod after only 2 failures. During normal operation, Django's garbage collector occasionally pauses for 2-3 seconds — enough to cause two consecutive probe timeouts within 6 seconds. Kubernetes kills perfectly healthy pods because the probe is too aggressive. Users experience random HTTP 502 errors during GC cycles. Your job: tune the liveness probe to tolerate transient slowness while still catching truly dead pods.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production-like single-node cluster on "easy"
1

📋 Deploy API with Overly Aggressive Liveness Probe (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: It's 3 AM. The on-call engineer's pager won't stop buzzing — "easypj-api pods restarting." The pods restart every ~90 seconds across all 3 replicas. The app itself is fine — Django responds to requests, database queries complete, Redis cache is warm. The culprit: a liveness probe template copied from a "Kubernetes best practices" blog that used periodSeconds: 3 and failureThreshold: 2. The blog author was testing a fast Go microservice, not a Python Django app with periodic garbage collection. Two consecutive slow GC cycles = 2 probe failures = Kubernetes sends SIGKILL. The engineer needs to tune the probe for Python's runtime characteristics.
📁 S41 STANDALONE PROJECT — copy everything below to your Ubuntu terminal: 
~/s41-observability/
├── 00-namespace.yaml          ← kubectl create ns s41-observability
├── 01-deployment.yaml         ← Deployment with aggressive liveness probe (BUG HERE)
├── 02-service.yaml            ← ClusterIP Service on port 8000
└── 03-test-pod.yaml           ← BusyBox pod for testing from inside cluster
BASH — Copy this entire block to your Ubuntu terminal. Creates namespace + deploys buggy app. 
# ============================================
# SCENARIO S41: Liveness Probe Kills Healthy Django
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

# STEP 1: Create isolated namespace
kubectl create ns s41-observability

# STEP 2: Deploy the easypj API with an AGGRESSIVE liveness probe
# This app simulates a Django+Gunicorn server that occasionally
# has slow GC pauses (3-5s) — enough to trigger the buggy probe
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s41-observability
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
    scenario: s41
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-alpine
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
        args:
        - |
          # Simulates a Django+Gunicorn app with occasional GC pauses
          cat > /app.py << 'PYEOF'
          import http.server, random, time, sys, json
          class HealthHandler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
              def do_GET(self):
                  if self.path == "/health/":
                      # Simulate occasional GC pause (1 in 5 chance of 4s delay)
                      if random.random() < 0.20:
                          time.sleep(4)  # Simulates Python GC collection
                  self.send_response(200)
                  self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                  self.end_headers()
                  self.wfile.write(json.dumps({"status":"ok"}).encode())
              def log_message(self, format, *args):
                  sys.stderr.write(f"{time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')} {self.client_address[0]} {format%args}\n")
          http.server.HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8000), HealthHandler).serve_forever()
          PYEOF
          python3 /app.py
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
          name: http
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          periodSeconds: 3        # ❌ BUG! Checks every 3 seconds — too frequent!
          failureThreshold: 2     # ❌ BUG! Only 2 failures = pod is killed!
          timeoutSeconds: 2       # ❌ BUG! 2s timeout + 3s period = GC pause triggers failure
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          periodSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 2
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "64Mi"
            cpu: "100m"
          limits:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s41-observability
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api
  ports:
  - port: 8000
    targetPort: 8000
    name: http
  type: ClusterIP
EOF

# STEP 3: Create a test pod to observe restarts from inside the cluster
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-client
  namespace: s41-observability
spec:
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
EOF

echo "=== Waiting for pods to be ready ==="
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=easypj-api -n s41-observability --timeout=60s 2>/dev/null || true
echo ""
echo "=== Initial pod status ==="
kubectl get pods -n s41-observability -o wide
echo ""
echo "=== Watch pod restarts for 60 seconds (press Ctrl+C to stop) ==="
echo "Look for RESTARTS column increasing!"
kubectl get pods -n s41-observability -w &
WATCH_PID=$!
sleep 60
kill $WATCH_PID 2>/dev/null
echo ""
echo "=== Final pod status — check RESTARTS count ==="
kubectl get pods -n s41-observability
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pod restarts: kubectl get pods -n s41-observability → RESTARTS column increasing every ~90 seconds
✗2. Check probe config: kubectl describe deploy easypj-api -n s41-observability | grep -A6 Liveness → periodSeconds: 3, failureThreshold: 2, timeoutSeconds: 2
✗3. The math: 3s period × 2 failures = pod killed after only 6 seconds of slowness!
✗4. Check container logs for restart reasons: kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api -n s41-observability --previous --tail=5 → Shows normal traffic before kill
✗5. The app IS healthy — GC pauses are normal. The probe is the problem, not the app!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Read the liveness probe spec: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s41-observability -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].livenessProbe}' | python3 -m json.tool
→ periodSeconds: 3, failureThreshold: 2, timeoutSeconds: 2 — EXTREMELY aggressive!
2Calculate tolerance window: periodSeconds × failureThreshold = 3s × 2 = 6 seconds total
→ Any endpoint taking >2s for TWO consecutive checks = pod killed. Python GC can easily cause this.
3Check last restart reason: kubectl describe pod -n s41-observability -l app=easypj-api | grep -A2 "Last State"
→ "Reason: Error, Exit Code: 137" — SIGKILL from kubelet after liveness failure
4Compare with production recommendations: Liveness should tolerate 30-60 seconds of transient issues.
periodSeconds ≥ 10, failureThreshold ≥ 3-5, timeoutSeconds ≥ 5 for Python/Django apps
5Root cause: Liveness probe periodSeconds:3 + failureThreshold:2 = pod killed after 6 seconds of probe failure — GC pauses trigger unnecessary restarts of healthy pods
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pods restarting → Check liveness probe config
②
periodSeconds:3 + failureThreshold:2 = 6s window
③
Python GC pauses > timeoutSeconds → Probe fails
④
Tune: periodSeconds:15, failureThreshold:5 → 75s tolerance
⑤
Restarts stop! 75s window absorbs GC pauses

Tenet: The liveness probe should answer "is this pod BRAIN-DEAD?" — not "is this pod occasionally slow?" A properly tuned liveness probe for interpreted languages (Python, Ruby, Node.js) needs a tolerance window of at least 30-60 seconds. The formula: periodSeconds × failureThreshold = tolerance window. For Go/Rust apps: 3×3=9s may be fine. For Python/Django: 10-15×5=50-75s is appropriate. The liveness probe's ONLY job is to restart truly deadlocked pods — not to detect performance issues.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n s41-observability NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-6d4f8b9c-x2k9m 1/1 Running 4 (90s ago) 7m ← 4 restarts in 7 min! easypj-api-6d4f8b9c-m7p3q 1/1 Running 3 (85s ago) 7m
$ kubectl describe deploy easypj-api -n s41-observability | grep -A6 Liveness Liveness: http-get http://:8000/health/ delay=5s timeout=2s period=3s #success=1 #failure=2 ← period=3s × failure=2 = pod killed after 6 seconds of slowness!
$ kubectl describe pod -n s41-observability -l app=easypj-api | grep -A3 "Last State" Last State: Terminated Reason: Error Exit Code: 137 ← SIGKILL from kubelet (liveness probe failure) Started: Mon, 11 Jun 2026 03:14:22 +0000
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n s41-observability NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-7e9d2f4a-y5n8r 1/1 Running 0 5m ✅ No restarts! easypj-api-7e9d2f4a-k3w1m 1/1 Running 0 5m ✅ Stable!
$ kubectl describe deploy easypj-api -n s41-observability | grep -A6 Liveness Liveness: http-get http://:8000/health/ delay=10s timeout=5s period=15s #success=1 #failure=5 ✅ period=15s × failure=5 = 75 seconds tolerance — GC pauses absorbed!
🔧
BASH — Patch deployment with production-safe liveness probe values 
# Fix the liveness probe using kubectl patch
# Production values for Python/Django:
#   periodSeconds: 15  (check every 15 seconds — not every 3!)
#   failureThreshold: 5  (need 5 consecutive failures to restart)
#   timeoutSeconds: 5   (give the endpoint 5 seconds to respond)
#   initialDelaySeconds: 10 (wait 10 seconds before first check)
#   Tolerance window: 15s × 5 = 75 seconds!

kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s41-observability --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/periodSeconds","value":15},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/failureThreshold","value":5},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/timeoutSeconds","value":5},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/initialDelaySeconds","value":10}
]'

# Wait for rolling update to complete
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s41-observability --timeout=120s

# Verify the fix — watch for 120 seconds, restarts should NOT increase
echo "=== Monitoring pod restarts for 2 minutes ==="
echo "RESTARTS count should stay at 0 after the update"
for i in $(seq 1 12); do
  kubectl get pods -n s41-observability -l app=easypj-api --no-headers
  sleep 10
done
✓

✅ Verify — Stable Pods, No Unnecessary Restarts

After tuning the liveness probe to periodSeconds: 15 and failureThreshold: 5, pods now have a 75-second tolerance window. Python GC pauses (3-5s) no longer trigger restarts. The pods remain stable — RESTARTS column stays at 0. The app still responds to health checks, but transient slowness no longer triggers SIGKILL.

💡 Key takeaway: The liveness probe's tolerance window = periodSeconds × failureThreshold. For interpreted languages (Python/Ruby/Node.js), use a window of 45-90 seconds. For compiled languages (Go/Rust), 15-30 seconds may suffice. Never set periodSeconds below 10 for production — it wastes CPU on health checks and kills pods during normal variance. On the CKAD exam, probe tuning is a core skill — you WILL be asked to fix aggressive probes.

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get ns s41-observability 2>&1

S42
🧪 SCENARIO S42 — Category 3: Observability Readiness Probe

Pod Running But Gets No Traffic — Readiness Probe Path Typo Returns 404

The Problem: The easypj API pod shows Running but READY: 0/1. The Service has no endpoints — all traffic gets "connection refused." The readiness probe was configured to check /healthz (copied from a Kubernetes blog example) but the actual Django health endpoint is /health/. Every probe request returns HTTP 404, so the pod stays "not ready" forever. Users can't access the API even though the application is fully functional. Your job: find the path mismatch and correct it so traffic flows.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-node lab with cp, wk1, wk2
1

📋 Deploy API with Wrong Readiness Probe Path (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The DevOps engineer deployed a new version of easypj-api. The deployment YAML was assembled from multiple sources: the base template from the platform team, the readiness probe config from a "Kubernetes Health Checks" tutorial, and the image tag from the CI pipeline. The tutorial used /healthz as the health endpoint (common in Go/Kubernetes ecosystem), but Django's health check is at /health/. The pod starts, Gunicorn binds to port 8000, everything looks fine — except the readiness probe returns 404 every time. The Service won't add the pod to its endpoints because it's "not ready." The app is running but utterly unreachable.
📁 S42 STANDALONE PROJECT: 
~/s42-observability/   (all commands self-contained below)
├── 00-namespace.yaml
├── 01-deployment.yaml  ← BUG: readinessProbe httpGet path: /healthz (WRONG!)
├── 02-service.yaml
└── 03-test-pod.yaml
BASH — Copy entire block. Creates namespace + deploys app with wrong probe path.

# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)

kubectl create ns s42-observability

# Deploy easypj API with a readiness probe that checks the WRONG path
# The app serves /health/ but the probe checks /healthz → always 404

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s42-observability
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
    scenario: s42
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-alpine
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
        args:
        - |
          cat > /app.py << 'PYEOF'
          import http.server, json, sys, time
          class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
              def do_GET(self):
                  if self.path == "/health/":
                      self.send_response(200)
                      self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json")
                      self.end_headers()
                      self.wfile.write(json.dumps({"status":"healthy","uptime":"3h"}).encode())
                  elif self.path == "/api/":
                      self.send_response(200)
                      self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json")
                      self.end_headers()
                      self.wfile.write(json.dumps({"jobs":[],"total":0}).encode())
                  else:
                      self.send_response(404)
                      self.end_headers()
              def log_message(self, f, *a):
                  sys.stderr.write(f"{time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')} {f%a}\n")
          http.server.HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0",8000), Handler).serve_forever()
          PYEOF
          python3 /app.py
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
          name: http
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz     # ❌ BUG! Django endpoint is /health/ NOT /healthz!
            port: 8000
          periodSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 3
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 2

          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          periodSeconds: 15

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check probe configuration: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s42-observability -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].readinessProbe}' | python3 -m json.tool
→ "path": "/healthz" — This is the Kubernetes convention, NOT the Django convention!
2Verify what the app actually serves: Get a pod IP: POD_IP=$(kubectl get pod -n s42-observability -l app=easypj-api -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.podIP}') then kubectl exec test-client -n s42-observability -- wget -q -O- http://$POD_IP:8000/health/
→ Returns 200 OK! The app IS healthy at /health/!
3Test the probe path: kubectl exec test-client -n s42-observability -- wget -q -O- http://$POD_IP:8000/healthz
→ Returns 404! The probe path doesn't exist!
4Root cause: Readiness probe path is /healthz but the application health endpoint is at /health/ — probe always returns 404, pod stays "not ready," Service has no endpoints
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod Running but 0/1 Ready → Readiness failing
②
Endpoints empty → Probe failed, pod excluded
③
kubectl describe → "statuscode: 404" → Wrong path!
④
Verify actual endpoint → /health/ returns 200
⑤
Fix probe path → Pod Ready → Endpoints populated!

Tenet: A pod showing "Running" but "0/1 Ready" means the readiness probe is failing. Always check kubectl describe pod for the probe failure reason — it shows the exact HTTP status code. Common causes: wrong path (this scenario), wrong port, TLS required but probe uses HTTP, or the app really is broken. On CKAD, diagnosing a pod that's Running but receiving no traffic is a classic exam task.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n s42-observability NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-5c8f7d9b-m3k9p 0/1 Running 0 3m ← 0/1 Ready! easypj-api-5c8f7d9b-x7w2q 0/1 Running 0 3m
$ kubectl get endpoints easypj-api -n s42-observability NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-api <none> 3m ← NO endpoints! Service can't route traffic!
$ kubectl describe pod -n s42-observability -l app=easypj-api | grep -A3 Readiness Readiness: http-get http://:8000/healthz delay=5s timeout=2s period=5s Warning Unhealthy Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 404 Warning Unhealthy Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 404
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n s42-observability NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-7d9e2a4b-y5n8r 1/1 Running 0 45s ✅ Ready! easypj-api-7d9e2a4b-k3w1m 1/1 Running 0 45s ✅ Ready!
$ kubectl get endpoints easypj-api -n s42-observability NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-api 10.244.1.5:8000,10.244.2.3:8000 45s ✅ Endpoints populated!

  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/readinessProbe/httpGet/path","value":"/health/"}
]'

# Wait for rolling update
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s42-observability --timeout=60s

# Verify pods are now Ready

kubectl get pods -n s42-observability -o wide

# Verify Service has endpoints now

echo "=== Service endpoints after fix ==="

# Test connectivity from test-client

echo "=== Testing API from inside cluster ==="

echo ""
✓

✅ Verify — Pods Ready, Endpoints Populated, Traffic Flows

After correcting the readiness probe path from /healthz to /health/, the probe returns 200 OK. The pods become Ready (1/1), the Service discovers them and populates its endpoints, and traffic flows normally. The key lesson: always verify probe paths match the actual application endpoints — don't copy-paste probe configs from tutorials without checking.

💡 Key takeaway: Readiness probe has one job: determine if the pod should receive traffic. If it fails, the pod is removed from ALL Service endpoints. A path typo = pod permanently excluded = users get "connection refused." Always kubectl describe pod to see the probe failure reason — the HTTP status code tells you exactly what's wrong. On the CKAD exam, a 0/1 Ready pod with a 404 probe error is a classic "fix the path" task.

S43
🧪 SCENARIO S43 — Category 3: Observability Startup Probe

Django Killed Before Boot Completes — Missing Startup Probe

The Problem: Django with DEBUG=False, database migrations, static file collection, and cache warming needs 55+ seconds to fully boot. The liveness probe starts after initialDelaySeconds: 20 and kills the pod at 30 seconds (20s delay + 2 failures × 5s period). The pod enters a CrashLoopBackOff cycle — it boots for 30 seconds, gets killed, restarts, boots 30 seconds, gets killed... It can never complete startup. There is no startup probe to tell Kubernetes "I'm still booting, don't kill me." Your job: add a startup probe that protects the long boot sequence, then let liveness take over after startup succeeds.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production node "easy" with slow-boot simulation
1

📋 Deploy Slow-Booting Django WITHOUT Startup Probe (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Friday deployment. The easypj team pushed v3.2 with DEBUG=False (production mode). Django now needs to: run 3 pending database migrations (8s), collect static files (12s), warm the template cache (10s), and load the Gunicorn master process with 4 workers (15s). Total: ~45-55 seconds. The deployment YAML has no startupProbe — only a liveness probe that starts at 20 seconds with 2 failures before kill (20 + 2×5 = 30s total). Django hasn't even started Gunicorn at 30 seconds. The pod is murdered before its first HTTP response. It restarts... and dies again. Forever. The CI pipeline reports "deployment successful" (the pod was created), but the app is in an infinite boot-kill loop.

kubectl create ns s43-observability

# Deploy a simulated slow-booting Django app (55s startup)

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s43-observability
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
    scenario: s43
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: easypj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: easypj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-alpine
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
        args:
        - |
          # Simulates a slow-booting Django application (55 seconds total)

          echo "=== Django v3.2 Booting (DEBUG=False) ==="
          echo "[1/4] Running database migrations..."
          sleep 15
          echo "      Migrations complete."
          echo "[2/4] Collecting static files..."
          sleep 12
          echo "      Static files collected (142 files)."
          echo "[3/4] Warming template cache..."
          sleep 10
          echo "      Cache warm (87 templates loaded)."
          echo "[4/4] Starting Gunicorn with 4 workers..."
          sleep 18
          echo "      Gunicorn listening on 0.0.0.0:8000"
          echo "=== BOOT COMPLETE (55 seconds) ==="
          # Now start the actual HTTP server

          cat > /app.py << 'PYEOF'
import http.server, json, sys, time
class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        if self.path == "/health/":
            self.send_response(200)
            self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json")
            self.end_headers()
            self.wfile.write(json.dumps({"status":"ok","boot_time":"55s"}).encode())
        else:

    def log_message(self,f,*a):sys.stderr.write(f"{time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')} {f%a}\n")

          python3 /app.py
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8000
          name: http
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
          initialDelaySeconds: 20  # ❌ BUG! App needs 55s but probe starts at 20s!
          periodSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 2       # ❌ BUG! 2 failures × 5s = killed at ~30s!
          timeoutSeconds: 2
        # ❌ BUG! No startupProbe configured at all!
        # Without startupProbe, liveness kills the pod before boot completes

        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000

          failureThreshold: 2
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
---

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Pod RESTARTS: kubectl get pods -n s43-observability → RESTARTS column increments every ~60 seconds — CrashLoopBackOff!
✗2. Liveness timeline: initialDelaySeconds:20 + (failureThreshold:2 × periodSeconds:5) = killed at ~30 seconds!
✗3. App boot timeline: migrations(15s) + static(12s) + cache(10s) + gunicorn(18s) = 55 seconds — but killed at 30s!
✗4. Container logs show: "Starting Gunicorn..." but never "listening on 0.0.0.0:8000" — killed mid-boot!
✗5. No startupProbe in the Deployment spec — Kubernetes doesn't know the app needs time to boot.
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check last termination reason: kubectl describe pod -n s43-observability -l app=easypj-api | grep -A5 "Last State"
→ "Reason: Error, Exit Code: 137" — SIGKILL from liveness probe failure!
2Check container logs for boot progress: kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api -n s43-observability --previous
→ Stopped at "[3/4] Warming template cache..." — never reached Gunicorn!
3Calculate required boot time vs probe window: App needs 55s. Probe window: 20 + (2×5) = 30s.
→ 55s > 30s — the app CANNOT boot within the liveness window!
4Solution: Add startupProbe with failureThreshold:30, periodSeconds:3 → 90s boot grace. While startup probe runs, liveness is DISABLED.
Without startupProbe, Kubernetes uses liveness probe during boot — the app gets killed before it can start serving
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod restarts during boot → Check boot time vs liveness
②
App needs 55s, liveness window = 30s → Killed mid-boot
③
No startupProbe configured → Add it
④
startupProbe: 30 failures × 3s = 90s grace
⑤
Liveness DISABLED until startup succeeds → Pod boots!

Tenet: The startup probe was introduced in Kubernetes 1.16 specifically for slow-starting applications. While the startup probe is active, the liveness probe is DISABLED. Once startup succeeds, liveness takes over. The startup probe doesn't restart the container on failure — it just waits. Configure: failureThreshold × periodSeconds = max boot time. If your app takes > initialDelaySeconds + (failureThreshold × periodSeconds) for liveness, you NEED a startup probe. On CKAD, recognizing when a startup probe is needed is a key skill.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n s43-observability NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-9d4f8b2c-m7k3p 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 4 (30s ago) 4m
$ kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api -n s43-observability --previous | tail -5 [1/4] Running database migrations... Migrations complete. [2/4] Collecting static files... Static files collected (142 files). [3/4] Warming template cache... ← KILLED HERE! Never reached Gunicorn
$ kubectl describe pod -n s43-observability -l app=easypj-api | grep -A3 "Last State" Last State: Terminated Reason: Error Exit Code: 137 ← SIGKILL (liveness probe failure during boot)
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n s43-observability NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-2e7f5a9d-x4k8m 1/1 Running 0 65s ✅ Booted completely!
🔧
BASH — Add startupProbe to protect slow boot
# Add a startupProbe that allows up to 90 seconds for boot

# 30 failures × 3 second period = 90 seconds maximum boot time

kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s43-observability --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/startupProbe","value":{
    "httpGet":{"path":"/health/","port":8000},
    "failureThreshold":30,
    "periodSeconds":3,
    "timeoutSeconds":2
  }}
]'

# Wait for the rollout — pod will now boot fully

echo "=== Waiting for pod to boot (up to 90s) ==="
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s43-observability --timeout=120s

echo ""
echo "=== Pod status — should show 1/1 Ready ==="
kubectl get pods -n s43-observability

echo ""
echo "=== Boot logs — should show all 4 stages complete ==="
kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api -n s43-observability
✓

✅ Verify — Pod Boots Completely, All Stages Pass

With the startup probe configured (30 failures × 3s = 90 seconds grace), Django completes all 4 boot stages. The liveness probe is disabled during startup, so the pod isn't killed prematurely. Once the startup probe succeeds, liveness takes over to monitor ongoing health. The app is fully operational.

💡 Key takeaway: startupProbe is your "boot guardian." Use it for ANY app that takes >30 seconds to start (Django with migrations, Java Spring Boot, Node.js with npm install). The formula: failureThreshold × periodSeconds ≥ max_expected_boot_time × 1.5. Without it, you either make the liveness probe dangerously tolerant or your app never boots. On CKAD, a pod in CrashLoopBackOff that shows boot progress in logs = add a startupProbe.

🧪 SCENARIO S44 — Category 3: Observability All Probes

Three Probes, Three Bugs — startup, Liveness & Readiness All Misconfigured

The Problem: The easypj team added all three probes (startup, liveness, readiness) from a template, but each has a bug: (1) startup probe has failureThreshold:5 with periodSeconds:3 = only 15s grace (app needs 40s), (2) liveness probe has timeoutSeconds:1 but the app sometimes takes 2s during GC, (3) readiness probe has initialDelaySeconds:0 so it runs DURING startup and fails, keeping pod out of Service even after boot. The result: pods constantly restart, never reach Ready, and the Service stays empty. Your job: fix all three probes so they work as a chain.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Quick dev cluster for probe experimentation
1

📋 Deploy App with THREE Probe Bugs (CONTAINS ALL BUGS)

📖 APP STORY: The platform team provided a "standard probe template" for all microservices. The easypj team applied it without modification. The template was designed for a fast-booting Go microservice (15s boot, 50ms response times). Applied to a Python Django app, it fails three ways: the startup window is too short, the liveness timeout doesn't account for GC pauses, and the readiness probe fires during boot. The app is in a death spiral — it restarts endlessly and never serves traffic.

├── deploy.yaml    ← ALL THREE PROBES have bugs
├── service.yaml
└── test-pod.yaml

# ============================================


kubectl create ns s44-observability

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s44-observability
  labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s44}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: easypj-api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-alpine
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          echo "Booting Django (40s total)..."; sleep 40
          cat > /app.py << 'PYEOF'
import http.server,json,time,random,sys
class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        if self.path=="/health/":
            if random.random()<0.15: time.sleep(2.5)
            self.send_response(200)
            self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json")
            self.end_headers()
            self.wfile.write(json.dumps({"status":"ok"}).encode())
        else: self.send_response(404); self.end_headers()
    def log_message(self,f,*a):sys.stderr.write(f"{time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')} {f%a}\n")
http.server.HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0",8000),H).serve_forever()
PYEOF
          python3 /app.py
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000, name: http}]
        startupProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /health/, port: 8000}
          failureThreshold: 5     # ❌ BUG 1! 5×3s=15s grace but app needs 40s!
          periodSeconds: 3
          timeoutSeconds: 2
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /health/, port: 8000}
          periodSeconds: 10
          failureThreshold: 3
          timeoutSeconds: 1       # ❌ BUG 2! 1s timeout but GC pauses take 2-3s!
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /health/, port: 8000}
          periodSeconds: 5
          failureThreshold: 2

⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Three Bugs Manifest

✗1. BUG 1 (startup): failureThreshold:5 × periodSeconds:3 = 15s grace. App needs 40s → startup probe fails, pod restarts!
✗2. BUG 2 (liveness): timeoutSeconds:1 — GC pauses take 2.5s → liveness probe times out, pod killed!
✗3. BUG 3 (readiness): initialDelaySeconds:0 — probe fires during boot, gets 404, pod stays NotReady!
✗4. Combined effect: pod restarts → never boots → never Ready → Service empty → app DOWN!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find All Three Root Causes

1Bug 1 fix: startup failureThreshold should be ≥ ceil(40s ÷ 3s) = 14. Use 15 for safety margin.
Startup probe: failureThreshold:5=15s < 40s needed → pod never passes startup → infinite restart loop
2Bug 2 fix: liveness timeoutSeconds should be > max GC pause (2.5s). Use 5s.
Liveness timeout:1s < 2.5s GC pause → probe times out on healthy pod → unnecessary kill
3Bug 3 fix: When startupProbe exists, readiness initialDelaySeconds can be 0 (kubelet waits for startup to succeed first).
Readiness initialDelaySeconds:0 is actually fine WITH startupProbe — kubelet waits for startup to pass. The real issue is bugs 1+2 preventing startup from ever passing.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Probe chain: startup → readiness+liveness
②
All probes broken → death spiral
③
Fix startup: 15×3s=45s > 40s needed
④
Fix liveness: timeout 5s > 2.5s GC pause
⑤
Readiness auto-waits for startup → All fixed!

Tenet: The three probes form a chain: startup guards boot → liveness monitors health → readiness controls traffic. All three must be tuned to the app's actual behavior. A template designed for Go won't work for Python. Always measure: boot time, p99 response time for health endpoint, and GC pause duration before setting probe values. On CKAD, you may see a pod that never stabilizes — check ALL probes, not just one.

📟 AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n s44-observability NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-api-7f3d2b5a-x9k2m 1/1 Running 0 55s ✅
🔧

kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s44-observability --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/startupProbe/failureThreshold","value":15},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/startupProbe/periodSeconds","value":3},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/timeoutSeconds","value":5},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/periodSeconds","value":15},
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/failureThreshold","value":5}
]'
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s44-observability --timeout=120s
kubectl get pods,ep -n s44-observability
✓

✅ Verify — All Three Probes Working in Harmony

Startup: 15 failures × 3s = 45s grace (app boots in 40s). Liveness: 5s timeout absorbs GC pauses. Readiness: waits for startup to pass, then controls Service membership. Pod reaches Running 1/1, Service has endpoints, traffic flows.

💡 Key takeaway: The probe chain is: startup → (liveness + readiness). Startup MUST succeed before the others matter. Fix startup first, then liveness timeout, then readiness timing. Each probe has a specific job — don't confuse them.

🧪 SCENARIO S45 — Category 3: Observability Logs

CrashLoopBackOff — kubectl logs Shows Nothing (Need --previous)

The Problem: The easypj API pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. You run kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api -n s45-observability and see... nothing. Empty. The container just started fresh and hasn't logged anything yet. The crash happened in the PREVIOUS container instance — you need --previous to see those logs. The pod crashes because the Django settings module path has a typo: easypj.setting (missing 's'). The error message is in the PREVIOUS container's logs, not the current one. Your job: use the right log flags to find why the pod is crashing.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-node with crash debugging

📋 Deploy App That Crashes Immediately (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A junior developer pushed a Django settings change at 4:55 PM on Friday. The Deployment rolled out. Pods started crashing. The developer ran kubectl logs and saw "nothing" — so they assumed the image was corrupted and spent 2 hours debugging the Docker build. The real error was in the PREVIOUS container logs: "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'easypj.setting'" — a one-character typo. The current container was empty because the app crashed in 0.2 seconds. kubectl logs shows the CURRENT container, not the one that crashed.

echo ""
echo "=== Pod status ==="
kubectl get pods -n s45-observability
echo ""
echo "=== TRY: kubectl logs (CURRENT container — probably empty!) ==="
kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api -n s45-observability
echo ""
echo "^^^ See? Empty or minimal! The crash happened in the PREVIOUS container."
echo ""
echo "=== NOW TRY: kubectl logs --previous (the CRASHED container) ==="
kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api -n s45-observability --previous
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✗1. Pod STATUS: kubectl get pods -n s45-observability → CrashLoopBackOff
✗2. kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api -n s45-observability → EMPTY or shows only "Starting..." (current container)
✗3. kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api -n s45-observability --previous → Shows the REAL error: ModuleNotFoundError!
✗4. Without --previous, the root cause is invisible!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Always Check --previous for CrashLoopBackOff

1kubectl logs shows CURRENT container — after a crash, a new container starts fresh. Its logs are empty.
→ For CrashLoopBackOff, ALWAYS use --previous first!
2kubectl logs --previous shows the PREVIOUS (crashed) container's stdout/stderr
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'easypj.setting' — typo in settings module path!
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pod CrashLoopBackOff → kubectl logs = empty
②
Container restarted → Current logs are fresh
③
kubectl logs --previous → Shows crash error!
④
Fix the settings typo → Redeploy
⑤
Pod runs! Always --previous first for crashes.

Tenet: kubectl logs --previous is the #1 command for CrashLoopBackOff debugging. It retrieves logs from the PREVIOUS (crashed) container instance. Combine with --tail=50 to see the last 50 lines leading to the crash. Other useful flags: --timestamps (show when each line was logged), --since=5m (last 5 minutes), -f (follow/stream). On CKAD, you WILL encounter CrashLoopBackOff — and --previous is how you diagnose it.

📟 BEFORE/AFTER
$ kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api -n s45-observability (empty — current container just started, no output yet)
$ kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api -n s45-observability --previous Starting easypj API v3.2... Loading Django settings from easypj.setting... ERROR: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'easypj.setting' Did you mean 'easypj.settings'? ← Found it!
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s45-observability --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args","value":[
    "import sys,time; print('Starting easypj API v3.2...'); print('Loading Django settings from easypj.settings...'); time.sleep(0.5); print('Settings loaded successfully!'); import http.server,json; class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):\n    def do_GET(self):\n        self.send_response(200)\n        self.send_header('Content-Type','application/json')\n        self.end_headers()\n        self.wfile.write(json.dumps({'status':'ok'}).encode())\nhttp.server.HTTPServer(('0.0.0.0',8000),H).serve_forever()"
  ]}
]'
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s45-observability --timeout=60s
kubectl get pods -n s45-observability
✓

✅ Verify — Pod Running, Logs Show Normal Output

The settings module path is corrected, the pod starts successfully, and kubectl logs (without --previous) now shows healthy output. The key lesson: for CrashLoopBackOff, always run kubectl logs --previous FIRST — it will save you hours of debugging.

kubectl get ns s45-observability 2>&1

Can't Exec Into Container — Distroless Image Has No Shell

The Problem: The easypj API is running in production, but you can't kubectl exec into it. The production image uses a distroless base (no shell, no package manager, no debugging tools). Running kubectl exec -it easypj-api-xxx -- /bin/bash returns "exec: /bin/bash: no such file or directory". You need to inspect environment variables, check network connectivity, and view files — but there's no shell! Your job: use kubectl debug with an ephemeral container that shares the target pod's process namespace, or use alternative debugging approaches.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production distroless image debugging
1

📋 Deploy Distroless App & Try to Exec Into It (THE BUG IS THE IMAGE)

📖 APP STORY: The security team mandated distroless images for all production workloads. The easypj team migrated from python:3.12-slim to gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12. Three days later, on-call gets paged — API latency is spiking. The engineer runs kubectl exec -it pod -- bash and gets "no such file or directory." There is no bash, sh, ash, or any shell in the distroless image. No curl, wget, ping, nslookup, or apt. The container is a black box. The engineer needs to debug without a shell.
📁 S46 STANDALONE PROJECT:
~/s46-observability/
├── deploy.yaml    ← Uses gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12 (no shell!)
└── service.yaml
BASH — Deploy distroless app, then try and fail to exec.
# ============================================

# SCENARIO S46: Distroless — No Shell for kubectl exec

# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)

# ============================================


kubectl create ns s46-observability

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s46-observability
  labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s46}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: easypj-api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        # ❌ This distroless image has NO shell, NO curl, NO package manager!

        image: gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
        command: ["/hello"]
        args: ["--port=8080"]
        ports: [{containerPort: 8080}]
        env:
        - name: DATABASE_URL
          value: "postgresql://user:pass@easypj-db:5432/jobpost"
        - name: REDIS_URL
          value: "redis://easypj-redis:6379/0"
        - name: SECRET_KEY
          value: "django-insecure-s46-test-key-change-me"
        - name: DEBUG
          value: "false"
        resources: {requests: {memory: "32Mi", cpu: "50m"}, limits: {memory: "64Mi", cpu: "200m"}}
---

kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s46-observability}
spec:
  selector: {app: easypj-api}

EOF

echo "=== Waiting for pods ==="
sleep 10
kubectl get pods -n s46-observability
echo ""
echo "=== TRY: kubectl exec with bash (WILL FAIL!) ==="
kubectl exec -n s46-observability deploy/easypj-api -- /bin/bash 2>&1 || true
echo ""
echo "=== TRY: kubectl exec with sh (WILL FAIL!) ==="
kubectl exec -n s46-observability deploy/easypj-api -- /bin/sh 2>&1 || true
echo ""
echo "^^^ See? No shell! Distroless images don't include bash or sh."
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Shell Access Denied

✗1. kubectl exec ... -- /bin/bash → "exec: /bin/bash: no such file or directory"
✗2. kubectl exec ... -- /bin/sh → "exec: /bin/sh: no such file or directory"
✗3. No curl, wget, ping, nslookup, apt, apk — the image has NOTHING but the Go binary.
✗4. You need to see env vars, check files, test network — but can't get a shell!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Work Around the Missing Shell

1Option A — kubectl debug with ephemeral container: kubectl debug -it deploy/easypj-api -n s46-observability --image=busybox --target=api
→ Creates a temporary container in the same pod with a shell! Shares process namespace!
2Option B — kubectl exec with specific command: kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n s46-observability -- /hello --help
→ You can still run the app binary itself — just not a shell!
3Option C — kubectl describe + logs: kubectl describe pod shows env vars in the spec section!
Distroless is secure by design — no shell = smaller attack surface. Use kubectl debug for interactive troubleshooting.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
exec fails → Image has no shell (distroless)
②
Use kubectl debug with busybox image
③
Ephemeral container shares pod namespace
④
Now you have a shell! Debug away.
⑤
Distroless = secure, kubectl debug = rescue hatch

Tenet: Distroless images are the "secure by default" choice for production — no shell, no package manager, minimal attack surface. But they require different debugging approaches. kubectl debug creates an ephemeral container in the target pod with a full debugging image (busybox, ubuntu, netshoot). Use --target to share the target container's process namespace. On CKAD, knowing how to debug distroless containers is an advanced skill.

📟 Key Commands
$ kubectl debug -it deploy/easypj-api -n s46-observability --image=busybox --target=api Targeting container "api". If you don't see processes, the container may not share ProcessNamespace. / # cat /proc/1/environ ← See env vars of target container! / # nslookup easypj-db ← Test DNS resolution / # wget -qO- localhost:8080 ← Test the app endpoint / # exit
🔧
BASH — Three techniques for distroless debugging
# Technique 1: kubectl debug (BEST — gives you a full shell)

kubectl debug -it deploy/easypj-api -n s46-observability --image=busybox --target=api
# Inside the ephemeral container:

#   cat /proc/1/cmdline    → See target container command

#   cat /proc/1/environ    → See target container env vars

#   nslookup SERVICE_NAME  → Test DNS

#   wget -qO- localhost:PORT → Test app


# Technique 2: kubectl exec to run the app binary directly

kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n s46-observability -- /hello --help

# Technique 3: kubectl describe (shows env vars in Container spec)

kubectl describe pod -n s46-observability -l app=easypj-api | grep -A10 "Environment:"
✓

✅ Lesson Learned — Distroless Debugging Workflow

Distroless images are production best practice but require different debugging: kubectl debug for interactive sessions, kubectl describe for env vars, kubectl logs for output. Never add a shell to production images — use kubectl debug instead.

kubectl delete ns s46-observability
kubectl get ns s46-observability 2>&1

🧪 SCENARIO S47 — Category 3: Observability kubectl describe

Pod Stuck Pending — Read Events to Find Resource Shortage

The Problem: A new easypj API pod is stuck in Pending for 10+ minutes. kubectl get pods just shows "Pending" — no explanation. You need to use kubectl describe pod to read the Events section, which reveals: "0/2 nodes are available: 2 Insufficient memory." The pod requests 8Gi of memory but the nodes only have 4Gi each. Your job: use kubectl describe to find WHY the pod can't schedule, then fix the resource requests.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — 3-node cluster (cp, wk1, wk2)
1

📋 Deploy Pod with Impossible Resource Request (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A new data processing feature requires "8Gi of memory" according to the architecture doc. The developer copied this number directly into the Deployment YAML without checking the actual cluster capacity. The 3 kind nodes have 4Gi, 4Gi, and 4Gi of allocatable memory. A pod requesting 8Gi can never schedule — no single node has that much free memory. kubectl get pods just shows "Pending" forever. Only kubectl describe reveals the scheduling failure reason in Events.
📁 S47 STANDALONE:
~/s47-observability/  (all commands below)
BASH — Deploy pod requesting more memory than any node has.
# ============================================

# SCENARIO S47: Pod Stuck Pending — Resource Shortage

# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)

# ============================================


kubectl create ns s47-observability

# First, check actual node capacity

echo "=== Current node memory capacity ==="
kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 "Capacity:" | grep -E "cpu|memory|Name:"

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-data-processor
  namespace: s47-observability
  labels: {app: easypj-data, scenario: s47}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: processor
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep", "3600"]
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "8Gi"    # ❌ BUG! No single node has 8Gi of allocatable memory!
        cpu: "500m"
      limits:
        memory: "8Gi"
        cpu: "1000m"
EOF

echo ""
echo "=== Pod status — will show Pending ==="
kubectl get pods -n s47-observability -o wide
echo ""
echo "=== CRITICAL: kubectl describe pod — read the Events! ==="
kubectl describe pod easypj-data-processor -n s47-observability | tail -15
⚠

⚠️ Observe — kubectl get shows Pending, kubectl describe reveals why

✗1. kubectl get pods -n s47-observability → STATUS: Pending — no explanation!
✗2. kubectl describe pod easypj-data-processor -n s47-observability → Events: "0/N nodes are available: N Insufficient memory"
✗3. Pod requests 8Gi but nodes have only ~3-4Gi allocatable each → IMPOSSIBLE to schedule!
🔍

🔍 Debug — kubectl describe Events is your diagnostic window

1kubectl describe has the BEST debugging info: Events section shows exactly why the scheduler can't place the pod.
→ "Insufficient memory" = request > available on all nodes
2Check node capacity: kubectl describe nodes | grep -A5 "Allocated resources"
Pod requests 8Gi but max allocatable per node is ~4Gi — request exceeds ANY single node
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
Pod Pending → kubectl describe pod
②
Read Events section → "Insufficient memory"
③
Check node capacity vs pod request
④
Reduce request to fit available capacity
⑤
Pod schedules! Events section = diagnostic gold.

Tenet: kubectl describe is the #1 diagnostic command for Kubernetes. Its Events section tells you exactly what the scheduler, kubelet, and controllers are doing. For Pending pods: look for scheduling failures. For CrashLoopBackOff: look for probe failures and exit codes. For PVC issues: look for provisioning failures. Always read Events before anything else.

📟 Key Output
$ kubectl describe pod easypj-data-processor -n s47-observability | tail -10 Events: Type Reason Age From Message ---- ------ ---- ---- ------- Warning FailedScheduling 2m default-scheduler 0/3 nodes available: 1 Insufficient memory (node cp) 1 Insufficient memory (node wk1) 1 Insufficient memory (node wk2) ← ALL nodes lack memory for 8Gi request!
🔧
BASH
# Delete pod with impossible request, recreate with realistic request

kubectl delete pod easypj-data-processor -n s47-observability
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-data-processor, namespace: s47-observability, labels: {app: easypj-data, scenario: s47}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: processor
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    resources:
      requests: {memory: "128Mi", cpu: "100m"}   # ✅ Fits any node!
      limits: {memory: "256Mi", cpu: "500m"}
EOF
kubectl get pods -n s47-observability -o wide
✓

✅ Verify — Pod Running After Reducing Request

After reducing the memory request from 8Gi to 128Mi, the pod schedules immediately. The Events section in kubectl describe was the key — it precisely identified "Insufficient memory" on all nodes.

kubectl delete ns s47-observability
kubectl get ns s47-observability 2>&1
