🧪 SCENARIO S48 — Category 3: Observability kubectl top

Pod OOMKilled Repeatedly — Use kubectl top to Identify Memory Leak

The Problem: The easypj API pod keeps getting OOMKilled (Exit Code 137). The pod starts at 200MB memory usage but climbs to 900MB over 30 minutes, then exceeds its 1Gi limit and gets killed by the kernel. The developer set memory limits but never monitored actual usage with kubectl top. There's a memory leak in the application code (simulated). Your job: use kubectl top to observe the memory trend, identify the leak, and adjust limits before fixing the code.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production monitoring on "easy"
1

📋 Deploy App with Memory Leak + Insufficient Limit (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: easypj v3.3 introduced a new "job recommendation engine" that caches results in memory. The cache grows unbounded — every API request adds entries but nothing ever evicts them. The pod starts at ~200MB, grows to 400MB after 10 minutes, 700MB after 20 minutes, and hits the 1Gi limit at ~30 minutes. The OOM killer sends SIGKILL. The pod restarts... and the leak begins again. The developer never ran kubectl top pod to see the memory trend.
📁 S48 STANDALONE:
~/s48-observability/  (all commands below)
BASH — Deploy leaking app, monitor with kubectl top.
# ============================================

# SCENARIO S48: Memory Leak → OOMKilled → kubectl top

# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)

# ============================================


kubectl create ns s48-observability

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s48-observability
  labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s48}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: easypj-api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-alpine
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          # Simulates a memory leak — allocates ~5MB every 5 seconds

          python3 -c "
import time, sys
data = []
print('easypj API v3.3 starting...', flush=True)
print('Memory limit: 150Mi (OOMKill will happen ~30s)', flush=True)
for i in range(100):
    data.append(bytearray(2_000_000))  # Allocate 2MB
    mem_mb = (i+1)*2
    print(f'[{i*5}s] Memory allocated: {mem_mb}MB', flush=True)
    time.sleep(5)
print('Leak simulation complete (should have been OOMKilled by now)', flush=True)
"
        resources:
          requests: {memory: "32Mi", cpu: "50m"}
          limits: {memory: "150Mi", cpu: "500m"}  # ❌ BUG! App leaks to 150Mi limit in ~75s
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
EOF

echo "=== Monitoring memory with kubectl top (10 samples, every 10s) ==="
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  echo -n "[Sample $i] "
  kubectl top pod -n s48-observability --no-headers 2>/dev/null || echo "(metrics not ready yet — wait for metrics-server)"
  sleep 10
done
echo ""
echo "=== Check for OOMKilled ==="
kubectl get pods -n s48-observability
kubectl describe pod -n s48-observability -l app=easypj-api | grep -A5 "Last State"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Memory Climbing, Then OOMKilled

✗1. kubectl top pod -n s48-observability → Memory column climbs every sample: 32Mi → 64Mi → 96Mi → 128Mi → OOM!
✗2. Exit Code 137 = SIGKILL from OOM killer — pod exceeded memory limit
✗3. The memory trend is clearly upward — this is a LEAK, not a spike!
🔍

🔍 Debug — kubectl top Reveals the Trend

1kubectl top shows resource USAGE (not requests/limits). Watch it over time to see trends.
→ Memory usage climbs linearly → Memory leak confirmed!
2Exit Code 137 in kubectl describe = OOMKilled. The kernel terminated the process.
Memory limit (150Mi) < memory usage growth pattern → inevitable OOMKill
🧠 Tenet
①
Pod OOMKilled → Check exit code 137
②
kubectl top → Watch memory over time
③
Upward trend = leak → Increase limit temporarily
④
Fix the leak in code → Redeploy
⑤
kubectl top confirms memory stable post-fix

Tenet: kubectl top pod shows actual CPU/Memory usage (not requests/limits). Pair it with kubectl top node for cluster-wide view. Requires metrics-server. Exit Code 137 = SIGKILL (OOM). Exit Code 143 = SIGTERM (graceful shutdown). On CKAD, kubectl top + Exit Code interpretation are core observability skills.

🔧
BASH

kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s48-observability --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory","value":"512Mi"}
]'
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s48-observability --timeout=60s
# Monitor — memory should now have room

for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do kubectl top pod -n s48-observability --no-headers 2>/dev/null; sleep 10; done
✓

✅ Verify — Pod Survives with Higher Limit

Increasing the limit to 512Mi prevents OOMKill while the code team fixes the cache eviction bug. The long-term fix is to add TTL to the cache or use Redis instead of in-memory caching.

Debug Django API Locally — kubectl port-forward to the Rescue

The Problem: The easypj API is running inside Kubernetes with only a ClusterIP Service — no external access. You need to test an API endpoint from your local browser at http://localhost:8080. There's no Ingress configured, and you can't SSH into the cluster nodes. Your job: use kubectl port-forward to tunnel traffic from your local machine to the pod, test the API, then close the tunnel.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Quick port-forward testing
1

📋 Deploy API (Internal-Only), Then Access It Locally

📖 APP STORY: The frontend team needs to test the new "/api/jobs/search?q=python" endpoint, but the easypj-api Service is ClusterIP-only — no NodePort, no LoadBalancer, no Ingress. The developer needs to access the API from their laptop browser at localhost. kubectl port-forward creates a secure tunnel from localhost:8080 → pod:8000 through the API server — no firewall changes, no Service type changes.
📁 S49 STANDALONE PROJECT: 
~/s49-observability/
├── deploy.yaml    ← Deployment + ClusterIP Service (YAML inline below)
└── test-pod.yaml  ← BusyBox for testing port-forward
BASH — Deploy API, then port-forward for local access.
# ============================================

# SCENARIO S49: kubectl port-forward for Local Debugging

# CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube)

# ============================================


kubectl create ns s49-observability

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s49-observability, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s49}}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: easypj-api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-alpine
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          cat > /app.py << 'PYEOF'
import http.server, json
class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(json.dumps({
            "endpoint": self.path,
            "jobs": [{"id":1,"title":"Python Dev","company":"Acme"},{"id":2,"title":"K8s Engineer","company":"TechCo"}],
            "total": 2
        }).encode())
http.server.HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0",8000),H).serve_forever()
PYEOF
          python3 /app.py
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s49-observability}
spec:
  selector: {app: easypj-api}
  ports: [{port: 8000, targetPort: 8000}]
  type: ClusterIP   # Internal only — no external access!
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app=easypj-api -n s49-observability --timeout=30s

echo ""
echo "=== Pod is Running. Service is ClusterIP (internal only). ==="
echo "=== Starting port-forward: localhost:8080 → pod:8000 ==="
echo "=== Open a NEW terminal and run: curl http://localhost:8080/api/jobs ==="
echo "=== Press Ctrl+C to stop the port-forward ==="
echo ""

# Port-forward to the Service (recommended — survives pod restarts)

kubectl port-forward svc/easypj-api -n s49-observability 8080:8000
⚠

⚠️ The Challenge — No External Access

✗1. Service type is ClusterIP — only accessible from inside the cluster
✗2. No NodePort, LoadBalancer, or Ingress configured
✗3. Need to test from laptop browser — port-forward is the solution!
🔍

🔍 Solution — kubectl port-forward

1Forward to Service: kubectl port-forward svc/easypj-api -n s49-observability 8080:8000
→ localhost:8080 → Service → Pod:8000 (survives pod restart!)
2Forward to specific Pod: kubectl port-forward pod/easypj-api-xxx -n s49-observability 8080:8000
→ Direct to one pod (breaks if pod restarts)
3Key takeaway: port-forward to a Service is more resilient than to a specific Pod — the Service handles pod IP changes

Tenet: kubectl port-forward is the quickest way to access a pod/Service from your local machine. It creates a tunnel through the Kubernetes API server — no NodePort, LoadBalancer, or firewall changes needed. Use it for debugging, testing endpoints, and accessing dashboards (like the Kubernetes dashboard or Prometheus UI). On CKAD, port-forward is an essential exam skill.

$ curl http://localhost:8080/api/jobs/search?q=python {"endpoint":"/api/jobs/search?q=python","jobs":[{"id":1,"title":"Python Dev"}],"total":1}

🧪 SCENARIO S50 — Category 3: Observability Network Debug

Web Pod Can't Reach API — Systematic Network Debug Checklist

The Problem: The easypj-web pod can't connect to easypj-api. Users see "500 Internal Server Error" because the web tier can't call the API. You need to systematically debug: DNS resolution → Service existence → Endpoints → Pod readiness → Application. The Service selector has a typo: app: easypj-api but the pod labels say app: easypj-apiv2. Your job: follow the network debug checklist to find the broken link.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-node network debugging
1

📋 Deploy API + Web with Selector Mismatch (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The API team renamed pods from app: easypj-api to app: easypj-apiv2 in the Deployment template. They updated the Deployment but FORGOT to update the Service selector. The Service still looks for app: easypj-api but no pods have that label anymore. The Service has zero endpoints — traffic goes nowhere.
📁 S50 STANDALONE PROJECT: 
~/s50-observability/
├── deploy.yaml    ← Deployment + Service with selector mismatch (BUG HERE)
└── test-pod.yaml  ← Web pod for testing API connectivity
BASH — Deploy with selector mismatch.
# ============================================

# SCENARIO S50: Network Debug — Service Selector Mismatch

# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)

# ============================================


kubectl create ns s50-observability

# Deploy API with label app=easypj-apiv2

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s50-observability, labels: {app: easypj-apiv2, scenario: s50}}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-apiv2}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: easypj-apiv2}}   # ← Pods have THIS label
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-alpine
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          cat > /app.py << 'PYEOF'
import http.server, json
class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(json.dumps({"status":"ok","version":"v2"}).encode())
http.server.HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0",8000),H).serve_forever()
PYEOF
          python3 /app.py
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s50-observability}
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj-api    # ❌ BUG! Pods have app=easypj-apiv2, NOT app=easypj-api!
  ports: [{port: 8000, targetPort: 8000}]
  type: ClusterIP
EOF

# Deploy a web pod that tries to call the API

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-web, namespace: s50-observability, labels: {app: easypj-web}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF

echo "=== Waiting for pods ==="
sleep 10
echo ""
echo "=== STEP 1: Check DNS — does the Service name resolve? ==="
kubectl exec easypj-web -n s50-observability -- nslookup easypj-api.s50-observability.svc.cluster.local 2>&1 || true
echo ""
echo "=== STEP 2: Check Service endpoints ==="
kubectl get endpoints easypj-api -n s50-observability
echo ""
echo "=== STEP 3: Compare Service selector vs Pod labels ==="
echo "Service selector:"; kubectl get svc easypj-api -n s50-observability -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'; echo ""
echo "Pod labels:"; kubectl get pods -n s50-observability -l app=easypj-apiv2 --show-labels
echo ""
echo "=== STEP 4: Try to curl the API from web pod (WILL FAIL!) ==="
kubectl exec easypj-web -n s50-observability -- wget -q -O- --timeout=3 http://easypj-api:8000/ 2>&1 || echo "FAILED — Service has no endpoints!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Follow the Checklist

✗1. DNS: Service name resolves (DNS is fine) ✅
✗2. Endpoints: kubectl get endpoints easypj-api → <none> ❌
✗3. Selector: Service wants app=easypj-api, pods have app=easypj-apiv2 → MISMATCH!
✗4. Connectivity: wget to Service IP fails — no endpoints to route to
🔍

🔍 Debug — The Network Debug Checklist

1DNS: Does the Service name resolve? → nslookup from a debug pod
2Endpoints: kubectl get endpoints — any pod IPs? → If <none>, selector mismatch!
3Selector: Compare Service .spec.selector with Pod .metadata.labels
4Pod: Is the pod Running and Ready? → Readiness probe passing?
5App: Is the application actually listening on the targetPort? → kubectl exec + netstat
🧠 Tenet

The Network Debug Checklist (memorize this order): ① DNS resolution → ② Service Endpoints → ③ Selector match → ④ Pod Ready status → ⑤ Application port. This 5-step checklist diagnoses 90% of Kubernetes networking issues. On the CKAD exam, expect a Service that "doesn't work" — follow this checklist and you'll find the issue in under 2 minutes.

🔧
BASH
# Fix: Update Service selector to match pod labels

kubectl patch svc easypj-api -n s50-observability --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/selector/app","value":"easypj-apiv2"}
]'
echo "=== Endpoints after fix ==="
kubectl get endpoints easypj-api -n s50-observability
echo ""
echo "=== Test connectivity from web pod ==="
kubectl exec easypj-web -n s50-observability -- wget -q -O- http://easypj-api:8000/
✓

✅ Verify — Traffic Flows After Selector Fix

After aligning the Service selector with pod labels, endpoints are populated and the web pod can successfully reach the API. The 5-step checklist found the issue in under 2 minutes.

S51
🧪 SCENARIO S51 — Category 3: Observability kubectl cp

Extract Crash Artifacts from a Dying Pod — kubectl cp

The Problem: The easypj API pod crashed and left a diagnostic file at /tmp/crash-report.json. The pod is in CrashLoopBackOff — it starts, crashes after 10 seconds, restarts. You need to extract that file for offline analysis, but the pod keeps dying before you can run commands. kubectl cp can copy files FROM a container even if it's crashing — you just need to catch it while it's running. Your job: use kubectl cp to extract the crash report before the pod restarts again.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production crash investigation
1

📋 Deploy App That Crashes and Leaves Diagnostic File

📖 APP STORY: easypj v3.4 added a crash handler that writes a JSON diagnostic report to /tmp/crash-report.json before exiting. The pod crashes after 15 seconds due to a database connection timeout. The SRE needs that file to understand why the connection failed — but the pod keeps dying. kubectl cp can grab the file if you time it right.
📁 S51 STANDALONE PROJECT: 
~/s51-observability/
├── pod.yaml       ← Pod that crashes after writing /tmp/crash-report.json
└── crash-report.json  ← Extracted to host via kubectl cp
BASH — Deploy crashing app, then extract crash report.
# ============================================

# SCENARIO S51: kubectl cp — Extract Crash Dump

# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)

# ============================================


kubectl create ns s51-observability

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s51-observability, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s51}}
spec:
  restartPolicy: Always
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
    args:
    - |
      echo "easypj API v3.4 starting..."
      sleep 8
      echo "Connecting to PostgreSQL at easypj-db:5432..."
      sleep 3
      # Write diagnostic crash report

      cat > /tmp/crash-report.json << 'JSON'
      {
        "timestamp": "2026-06-12T03:15:00Z",
        "error": "ConnectionTimeoutError",
        "detail": "Could not connect to easypj-db:5432 after 30 seconds",
        "db_host": "easypj-db",
        "db_port": 5432,
        "attempts": 3,
        "last_error": "getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND easypj-db"
      }
JSON
      echo "ERROR: Database connection failed! Crash report saved to /tmp/crash-report.json"
      echo "Check the file contents:"
      cat /tmp/crash-report.json
      echo ""
      echo "Exiting in 5 seconds... (pod will restart)"
      sleep 5
      exit 1
    resources: {requests: {memory: "32Mi", cpu: "50m"}, limits: {memory: "64Mi", cpu: "200m"}}
EOF

echo "=== Pod deployed. Wait 15s for crash report to be written... ==="
sleep 15
echo ""
echo "=== Pod status ==="
kubectl get pods -n s51-observability
echo ""
echo "=== STEP 1: Try kubectl cp while pod is running (you have a short window!) ==="
POD_NAME=$(kubectl get pod -n s51-observability -l app=easypj-api -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl cp s51-observability/$POD_NAME:/tmp/crash-report.json /tmp/s51-crash-report.json 2>&1 && echo "SUCCESS: File copied!" || echo "Pod crashed before copy — retrying is normal"
echo ""
echo "=== STEP 2: View the extracted crash report ==="
cat /tmp/s51-crash-report.json 2>/dev/null || echo "(File not extracted yet — the pod may have crashed. Try the cp command again.)"
⚠

⚠️ The Challenge — Pod Keeps Dying

✗1. Pod status: CrashLoopBackOff — restarts every ~25 seconds
✗2. kubectl exec won't work (pod crashes too fast)
✗3. kubectl cp needs the container to be running — time it right!
🔍

🔍 Strategy — Copy During the Narrow Window

1kubectl cp syntax: kubectl cp <namespace>/<pod>:<source-path> <dest-path>
→ Copies files TO and FROM containers (tar under the hood)
2For CrashLoopBackOff: Watch pod status, run cp as soon as it's Running, before the crash.
Timing is everything — the crash window may be only 10-15 seconds

Tenet: kubectl cp is essential for extracting files from containers — crash dumps, log files, configuration. For CrashLoopBackOff pods, modify the pod to command: ["sleep","3600"] temporarily to keep it alive, copy the file, then restore the original command. On CKAD, kubectl cp is a tested skill for debugging scenarios.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s51-observability
rm -f /tmp/s51-crash-report.json

Real-Time Pod Failure Monitoring — kubectl get events --watch

Your job: use kubectl get events to monitor for pod failures in real-time and capture the exact moment of failure.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Live event monitoring

📋 Deploy App, Then Watch Events for Failures

📖 APP STORY: The overnight on-call engineer keeps getting paged for "pod failures" but by the time they check, the pods have already restarted and the logs are gone. They need to watch events in real-time to catch the failure as it happens. Using kubectl get events -n s52-observability --watch, they can see every event — scheduling, pulling, starting, probe failures, kills — as they occur.
📁 S52 STANDALONE PROJECT: 
~/s52-observability/
└── pod.yaml       ← Pod that fails after 20s — watch events to see why
BASH — Deploy, then watch events in real-time.
# ============================================

# SCENARIO S52: kubectl get events --watch

# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)

# ============================================


kubectl create ns s52-observability

# Deploy a pod that will fail after 20 seconds

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s52-observability, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s52}}
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
    args:
    - |
      echo "easypj API starting..."
      sleep 5
      echo "Processing request..."
      sleep 5
      echo "ERROR: Out of memory! Exiting..."
      sleep 3
      exit 137  # Simulates OOMKilled
EOF

echo "=== STEP 1: Check initial events ==="
kubectl get events -n s52-observability --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'
echo ""
echo "=== STEP 2: Watch events for 25 seconds (live stream) ==="
echo "You will see: Scheduled → Pulled → Started → (pod exits)"
kubectl get events -n s52-observability --watch &
WP=$!
sleep 25
kill $WP 2>/dev/null
echo ""
echo "=== STEP 3: Filter only WARNING events ==="
kubectl get events -n s52-observability --field-selector type=Warning
⚠

⚠️ Key Observations

✗1. Events are chronological — you see the full lifecycle: Scheduled → Pulling → Pulled → Created → Started
✗2. --field-selector type=Warning filters to only warning events
✗3. Events expire after 1 hour by default (--event-ttl on kube-apiserver)
🔍

🔍 Key Event Commands

1All events sorted: kubectl get events -n s52-observability --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'
2Warnings only: kubectl get events --field-selector type=Warning
3Watch live: kubectl get events -w (streams new events as they happen)

Tenet: kubectl get events is the cluster-wide audit trail. Every scheduling decision, probe failure, image pull, and container start generates an event. Use --watch for real-time monitoring, --field-selector to filter by type, and --sort-by to find the most recent events. On CKAD, events are a primary debugging tool — they often contain the answer before you even run describe.

S53
🧪 SCENARIO S53 — Category 3: Observability Lifecycle

preStop Hook Never Runs — Container Killed Before Graceful Shutdown

The Problem: When easypj API pods are deleted (rolling update or scale-down), Django needs to finish processing current requests (15 seconds) and close database connections. The Deployment has a preStop hook with sleep 15, but the pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds is set to 5 seconds. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits 5 seconds, then sends SIGKILL — the preStop hook never gets its full 15 seconds. Clients see 502 errors during rollouts. Your job: align preStop timing with terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Container lifecycle testing
1

📋 Deploy Pod Where preStop Gets Cut Short (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The SRE added a preStop hook to gracefully drain connections before pod termination. They set sleep 15 in the hook but forgot to update terminationGracePeriodSeconds from the default 30... wait, the template had it set to 5 (a dev testing value). The pod gets SIGTERM, the preStop hook starts, but after 5 seconds Kubernetes sends SIGKILL — the hook only completes 1/3 of its work.
📁 S53 STANDALONE PROJECT: 
~/s53-observability/
└── pod.yaml       ← Pod with preStop hook + terminationGracePeriodSeconds:5 (BUG HERE)
BASH — Deploy, then watch the kill timeline.
# ============================================

# SCENARIO S53: preStop Hook Killed Before Completion

# CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube)

# ============================================


kubectl create ns s53-observability

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s53-observability, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s53}}
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 5    # ❌ BUG! preStop needs 15s but pod killed at 5s!
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
    args:
    - |
      trap 'echo "RECEIVED SIGTERM — starting graceful shutdown..."; sleep 15; echo "Graceful shutdown COMPLETE"; exit 0' TERM
      echo "easypj API running (PID $$)"
      while true; do echo "$(date +%H:%M:%S) Processing..."; sleep 3; done
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec:
          command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'preStop hook: Draining connections...' ; sleep 15 ; echo 'preStop hook: COMPLETE'"]
EOF

echo "=== Pod running. Watch it process requests..."
sleep 12
echo ""
echo "=== DELETING POD — watch preStop get cut short! ==="
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s53-observability --grace-period=0 --wait=false &
sleep 1
kubectl logs easypj-api -n s53-observability -f &
LP=$!
sleep 10
kill $LP 2>/dev/null
echo ""
echo "=== Did preStop complete? Check: 'preStop hook: COMPLETE' should appear but likely doesn't ==="
⚠

⚠️ Observe — preStop Killed Mid-Way

✗1. terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 5 — pod gets at most 5 seconds after SIGTERM
✗2. preStop hook needs 15 seconds — but Kubernetes sends SIGKILL after 5s!
✗3. Rule: terminationGracePeriodSeconds ≥ preStop execution time + buffer (2-3s)
🔍

🔍 The Termination Timeline

1T=0s: kubectl delete pod → API server sets deletionTimestamp
2T=0s: kubelet sends SIGTERM to container, runs preStop hook
3T=5s: terminationGracePeriodSeconds expires → kubelet sends SIGKILL → preStop dies mid-execution!

Tenet: The termination sequence is: ① pod marked for deletion → ② preStop hook executes → ③ SIGTERM sent to main process → ④ wait terminationGracePeriodSeconds → ⑤ SIGKILL. If preStop + app shutdown > terminationGracePeriodSeconds, the process is force-killed. Formula: terminationGracePeriodSeconds = preStop_time + app_shutdown_time + 5s buffer. On CKAD, graceful shutdown configuration is a core deployment skill.

🔧
BASH
# Recreate pod with terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 (15s preStop + 15s app + buffer)

kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s53-observability --force --grace-period=0 2>/dev/null
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api-v2, namespace: s53-observability, labels: {app: easypj-api}}
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30   # ✅ 30s > 15s preStop + app shutdown
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
    args: ["trap 'echo SIGTERM; sleep 10; echo done; exit 0' TERM; while true; do sleep 3; done"]
    lifecycle:
      preStop:
        exec:
          command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'preStop: draining (15s)...'; sleep 15; echo 'preStop: done'"]
EOF
echo "terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 — preStop has time to complete!"
🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s53-observability

🧪 SCENARIO S54 — Category 3: Observability Performance

API Endpoint Takes 5 Seconds — Diagnose Slow Response

The Problem: The /api/jobs/search endpoint takes 5+ seconds (should be <200ms). Users are complaining. You need to diagnose whether the slowness is: CPU throttling, database query performance, memory pressure, or application code. The pod has CPU limit of 100m but the search endpoint needs 500m for query parsing — the container is being throttled to 20% of what it needs. Your job: use kubectl top, describe, and logs to find the bottleneck.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Performance diagnostics
1

📋 Deploy API with CPU Starvation (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The easypj search feature was moved from the database to in-app query parsing (faster for small datasets). But the CPU limit was never updated from the baseline template — it's still 100m (0.1 CPU core). The search endpoint needs ~500m for JSON parsing, filtering, and sorting. With only 100m, the kernel throttles the container to 20% of one CPU core — turning a 200ms operation into a 5-second operation.
📁 S54 STANDALONE PROJECT:

├── deploy.yaml    ← Deployment + Service with CPU limit 100m (BUG HERE)
└── test-pod.yaml  ← BusyBox pod for performance testing

# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)

# ============================================


kubectl create ns s54-observability

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s54-observability, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s54}}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: easypj-api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-alpine
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          cat > /app.py << 'PYEOF'
import http.server, json, time
class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        t0 = time.time()
        if self.path.startswith("/api/jobs/search"):
            # Simulate CPU-intensive query parsing (5s at 100m CPU, 0.5s at 500m)

            for i in range(50_000_000): pass  # Burn CPU
        elapsed = time.time()-t0
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(json.dumps({"endpoint":self.path,"elapsed_ms":int(elapsed*1000)}).encode())
http.server.HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0",8000),H).serve_forever()
PYEOF
          python3 /app.py
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
        resources:
          requests: {memory: "64Mi", cpu: "50m"}
          limits: {memory: "128Mi", cpu: "100m"}   # ❌ BUG! Search needs ~500m but only 100m allocated!
---

kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s54-observability}
spec:
  selector: {app: easypj-api}

EOF

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -

EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod -l app=easypj-api -n s54-observability --timeout=30s

echo "=== Test /api/jobs/search response time (will be SLOW!) ==="

echo ""
echo "=== Check CPU usage (should be near 100m limit) ==="
kubectl top pod -n s54-observability --no-headers 2>/dev/null
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Slow Responses, CPU at Limit

✗1. Response time: 3-5 seconds for a simple search query
✗2. kubectl top pod → CPU hovers near 100m (the limit!)
✗3. CPU throttling: container wants 500m but only gets 100m → 5x slower!
🔍

🔍 Performance Diagnostic Checklist

1kubectl top: Is CPU near the limit? → If yes, increase limit.
CPU limit 100m is the bottleneck — search needs 500m+ for query parsing
2kubectl describe: Check for OOMKilled (memory) or throttling events
3kubectl logs: Application-level timing logs

Tenet: When an endpoint is slow: ① Check CPU with kubectl top (is it hitting the limit?) → ② Check memory (OOMKilled?) → ③ Check application logs for slow queries → ④ Check network latency (kubectl exec + curl). CPU throttling is the #1 cause of "my app is suddenly slow in Kubernetes but fine locally" — your local machine has unlimited CPU, but Kubernetes enforces limits.

]'

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s55-observability, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s55}}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: easypj-api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-alpine
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          echo "Booting (40s)..."
          for i in 1 2 3 4; do echo "Stage $i/4..."; sleep 10; done
          cat > /app.py << 'PYEOF'
import http.server, json, time
class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        if self.path=="/ht/": self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json"); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b'{"status":"ok"}')
        else:
            t0=time.time()
            for _ in range(30_000_000): pass
            self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json"); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(json.dumps({"elapsed_ms":int((time.time()-t0)*1000)}).encode())
http.server.HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0",8000),H).serve_forever()
PYEOF
          python3 /app.py
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
        # BUG 1: No startupProbe — liveness kills during 40s boot

        livenessProbe:     # BUG 2: Too aggressive — 3s×2=6s tolerance
          httpGet: {path: /ht/, port: 8000}
          periodSeconds: 3; failureThreshold: 2; timeoutSeconds: 2; initialDelaySeconds: 15
        readinessProbe:    # BUG 3: Wrong path — /healthz instead of /ht/
          httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8000}
          periodSeconds: 5; failureThreshold: 2; initialDelaySeconds: 0
        resources:         # BUG 4: CPU too low (100m); BUG 5: memory too low (64Mi)
          requests: {memory: "32Mi", cpu: "50m"}
          limits: {memory: "64Mi", cpu: "100m"}
EOF

echo "=== Pod deployed with 5 bugs. Use these commands to find them: ==="
echo "  kubectl get pods -n s55-observability"
echo "  kubectl describe pod -n s55-observability -l app=easypj-api | tail -20"
echo "  kubectl logs deploy/easypj-api -n s55-observability --previous"
echo "  kubectl top pod -n s55-observability"
echo "  kubectl get events -n s55-observability --field-selector type=Warning"
echo ""
echo "=== Can you find all 5 issues? ==="
⚠

⚠️ The 5 Issues to Find

✗BUG 1: No startupProbe → liveness kills during 40s boot (needs startupProbe with failureThreshold:20, periodSeconds:3)
✗BUG 2: Liveness periodSeconds:3, failureThreshold:2 → 6s tolerance (needs periodSeconds:15, failureThreshold:5)
✗BUG 3: Readiness path /healthz → app serves /ht/ (needs path: /ht/)
✗BUG 4: CPU limit 100m → app needs 500m+ for query parsing
✗BUG 5: Memory limit 64Mi → simulates OOM (needs 256Mi+)
🔍

🔍 Diagnostic Commands to Find Each Bug

1Bugs 1+2: kubectl describe pod → check probe config; kubectl logs --previous → boot stops at stage 2
2Bug 3: kubectl get endpoints → <none>; kubectl describe pod → "Readiness probe failed: 404"
3Bugs 4+5: kubectl top pod → CPU near 100m; kubectl describe pod → OOMKilled exit 137

Complete Fix — Apply all patches at once:

$ kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -n s55-observability --type=json -p='[ {"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/startupProbe","value":{"httpGet":{"path":"/ht/","port":8000},"failureThreshold":20,"periodSeconds":3}}, {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/periodSeconds","value":15}, {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/livenessProbe/failureThreshold","value":5}, {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/readinessProbe/httpGet/path","value":"/ht/"}, {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/cpu","value":"500m"}, {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/limits/memory","value":"256Mi"} ]' deployment.apps/easypj-api patched
✓

✅ All 5 Issues Fixed — Pod Running Healthy

With all 5 fixes applied: startup probe protects the 40s boot, liveness has 75s tolerance, readiness checks the correct path, CPU has room to process requests, and memory has enough headroom. The pod runs stable with 1/1 Ready and responsive endpoints.

💡 Mastery achieved: You've practiced all 10+ kubectl observability commands across S41-S55. The systematic approach: describe → logs --previous → top → events → endpoints → debug. This command sequence diagnoses 95% of Kubernetes application issues. On the CKAD exam, expect at least 3-4 observability tasks — you now have the muscle memory to solve them efficiently.

🔴 easypj/jobpost — ConfigMaps, Secrets, SecurityContext & RBAC

What you'll master: ConfigMaps as env vars and volume mounts, Secrets management (env vs volume), TLS Secrets, imagePullSecrets, SecurityContext (non-root, readOnlyRootFilesystem, capabilities), ServiceAccounts, RBAC (Role, RoleBinding, verbs), Downward API, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, environment variable precedence, nodeSelector, podAntiAffinity, topologySpreadConstraints, Pod Security Standards, immutable ConfigMaps, projected volumes, bulk env import, and full configuration auditing.
