S56
🧪 SCENARIO S56 — Category 4: Config & Security ConfigMap

Nginx Config Overwritten — ConfigMap Mount Erases Entire Directory

The Problem: The easypj-web pod uses an Nginx sidecar for static files. The team created a ConfigMap with a custom default.conf and mounted it at /etc/nginx/conf.d/. But instead of adding just the one file, the mount replaced the entire directory — wiping out all other Nginx config files that were part of the container image. Nginx fails to start because nginx.conf (in the parent directory) references files that no longer exist. The fix: use subPath: default.conf to mount only that specific file without overwriting the directory. Your job: fix the volume mount to preserve existing directory contents.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production-like cluster on node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy Pod with ConfigMap Volume That Wipes Directory (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The platform team wants every microservice to use a standardized Nginx configuration. They created a ConfigMap with the custom default.conf and mounted it into the Nginx sidecar at /etc/nginx/conf.d/. What they didn't realize: mounting a volume at a directory path REPLACES the entire directory. The original /etc/nginx/conf.d/ from the container image (which contained other essential config snippets) is gone. Nginx starts, can't find referenced files, and crashes. The web frontend is down.
📁 S56 STANDALONE PROJECT: 
~/s56-config/
├── deploy.yaml    ← Pod with ConfigMap volume mount (BUG: no subPath!)
└── nginx-cm.yaml  ← ConfigMap with default.conf
BASH — Copy entire block. Deploys ConfigMap + Pod with directory-wiping mount. 

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S56: ConfigMap Mount Wipes Directory
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s56-config

# Create ConfigMap with custom nginx default.conf
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nginx-config
  namespace: s56-config
data:
  default.conf: |
    server {
        listen 80;
        server_name localhost;
        location / {
            root /usr/share/nginx/html;
            index index.html;
        }
        location /health {
            return 200 "OK";
        }
    }
EOF

# Deploy pod with ConfigMap mounted at /etc/nginx/conf.d/
# ❌ BUG! This REPLACES the entire directory — wiping other nginx config files!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: s56-config
  labels:
    app: easypj-web
    scenario: s56
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
    volumeMounts:
    - name: nginx-conf
      mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d    # ❌ BUG! Replaces entire directory!
  volumes:
  - name: nginx-conf
    configMap:
      name: nginx-config
EOF

# Wait and check — Nginx will fail because other config files are gone
sleep 10
echo "=== Pod status ==="
kubectl get pods -n s56-config
echo ""
echo "=== Check Nginx logs ==="
kubectl logs easypj-web -n s56-config 2>&1 || true
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Pod status: kubectl get pods -n s56-config → Pod may show errors or CrashLoopBackOff
✗2. Check mounted files: kubectl exec easypj-web -n s56-config -- ls /etc/nginx/conf.d/ → Only default.conf — other files GONE!
✗3. Nginx needs other files from the image (like mime.types includes) — those are wiped!
✗4. Mounting a volume at a directory path REPLACES everything that was there from the image
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check what files exist in the mounted directory: kubectl exec easypj-web -n s56-config -- ls -la /etc/nginx/conf.d/
→ Only default.conf exists — all original container image files are wiped!
2The problem: Kubernetes volume mounts replace the ENTIRE directory at mountPath — not merge with it.
→ Use subPath to mount only a specific file without affecting other files in the directory
3Root cause: ConfigMap volume mounted at directory path /etc/nginx/conf.d replaces the entire directory — wiping essential Nginx config files from the container image
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Nginx fails after ConfigMap mount → Check directory
②
ls /etc/nginx/conf.d/ → Only default.conf
③
Volume mount REPLACES directory, doesn't merge
④
Fix: use subPath to mount single file
⑤
Nginx starts — all files preserved!

Tenet: Kubernetes volume mounts at a directory path completely replace whatever was in that directory from the container image. This is by design — volumes are mounted ON TOP of existing paths. To add just one file without wiping the directory, use subPath to mount a single key from a ConfigMap/Secret as a file. On CKAD, this is one of the most commonly tested ConfigMap/Secret concepts.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec easypj-web -n s56-config -- ls /etc/nginx/conf.d/ default.conf ← ONLY this file! All original Nginx configs GONE!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec easypj-web -n s56-config -- ls /etc/nginx/conf.d/ default.conf fastcgi.conf mime.types uwsgi_params ✅ All original files preserved!
🔧
BASH — Recreate pod with subPath 

# Delete old pod
kubectl delete pod easypj-web -n s56-config

# Recreate with subPath — mounts only default.conf, preserves other files
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-web
  namespace: s56-config
  labels:
    app: easypj-web
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
    volumeMounts:
    - name: nginx-conf
      mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
      subPath: default.conf    # ✅ Only mounts THIS file!
  volumes:
  - name: nginx-conf
    configMap:
      name: nginx-config
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/easypj-web -n s56-config --timeout=30s
kubectl exec easypj-web -n s56-config -- ls /etc/nginx/conf.d/
✓

✅ Verify — Single File Mounted, Directory Preserved

With subPath: default.conf, only that one file is mounted at /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf. All other files from the container image remain intact. Nginx starts successfully with both the custom config and the built-in configuration files.

💡 Key takeaway: Volume mounts REPLACE directories at mountPath. Use subPath to mount individual files without wiping the directory. subPath works with ConfigMaps, Secrets, and PersistentVolumes. On the CKAD exam, "ConfigMap mounted but app can't find other config files" = check for missing subPath.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
kubectl delete ns s56-config
kubectl get ns s56-config 2>&1
S57
🧪 SCENARIO S57 — Category 4: Config & Security ConfigMap

ConfigMap Updated but Pods Still Use Old Values — No Auto-Reload

The Problem: The easypj team updated the ALLOWED_HOSTS in the ConfigMap to add a new domain. They ran kubectl apply — the ConfigMap was updated. But pods are STILL using the OLD value! ConfigMaps mounted as environment variables are only read at pod startup. Updating the ConfigMap does NOT restart pods or update their env vars. Users trying to access the new domain get rejected. Your job: trigger a rolling restart so pods pick up the new ConfigMap values.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-node for rollout testing
1

📋 Deploy App with ConfigMap, Then Update ConfigMap — Pods Ignore Change (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The marketing team registered a new domain "easypj-jobs.com". The DevOps engineer updated the ConfigMap: ALLOWED_HOSTS: "easypj.com,easypj-jobs.com". They verified the ConfigMap was updated. But traffic to the new domain still gets rejected. The pods were started BEFORE the ConfigMap update — they still have the old environment variable values. ConfigMaps mounted as env vars are NOT dynamically updated. The engineer needs to restart the pods.
📁 S57 STANDALONE PROJECT:
~/s57-config/
├── deploy.yaml    ← Deployment using ConfigMap as envFrom (BUG: no auto-reload)
└── configmap.yaml ← ConfigMap that gets updated
BASH — Deploy, update ConfigMap, observe pods ignore change.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S57: ConfigMap Update — Pods Ignore New Values
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s57-config

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: easypj-settings
  namespace: s57-config
data:
  ALLOWED_HOSTS: "easypj.com"
  DEBUG: "false"
  LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s57-config
  labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s57}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: easypj-api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          echo "ALLOWED_HOSTS=$ALLOWED_HOSTS"
          echo "Server started. Send request to verify host."
          while true; do sleep 30; done
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: easypj-settings
EOF

echo "=== Initial ALLOWED_HOSTS value ==="
kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api -n s57-config --tail=2
echo ""
echo "=== UPDATING ConfigMap — adding new domain ==="
kubectl patch cm easypj-settings -n s57-config -p '{"data":{"ALLOWED_HOSTS":"easypj.com,easypj-jobs.com"}}'
echo "ConfigMap UPDATED!"
echo ""
sleep 5
echo "=== Pod STILL shows OLD value (no auto-restart!) ==="
kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api -n s57-config --tail=2
echo ""
echo "^^^ See? Pods still have OLD ALLOWED_HOSTS! Need rollout restart!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error

✗1. ConfigMap updated: kubectl get cm easypj-settings -n s57-config -o yaml | grep ALLOWED_HOSTS → Shows new value ✅
✗2. Pod env: kubectl exec deploy/easypj-api -n s57-config -- env | grep ALLOWED_HOSTS → Shows OLD value! ❌
✗3. ConfigMaps as env vars are read at pod STARTUP only — updates don't propagate!
✗4. New domain traffic rejected — users locked out of new domain!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Why Pods Ignore ConfigMap Changes

1envFrom reads at startup: When a pod starts, kubelet reads the ConfigMap and sets env vars. After that, there's no mechanism to update running pods.
→ This is by design — env vars are static after process start
2Solution: Trigger a rolling restart so new pods pick up the updated ConfigMap
ConfigMap updates do NOT trigger pod restarts — pods must be manually restarted or use a tool like stakater/Reloader
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet
①
ConfigMap updated → Check if pods see change
②
Pods still have old value → env vars are static
③
kubectl rollout restart → New pods get new ConfigMap
④
For auto-reload: mount ConfigMap as volume file
⑤
Volume mounts update within ~60s (kubelet sync)

Tenet: ConfigMaps as env vars are STATIC after pod startup. ConfigMaps as volume mounts update automatically (kubelet syncs every ~60s). For values that change frequently, use volume mounts instead of env vars, or use stakater/Reloader for automatic rolling restarts. On CKAD, this is a core ConfigMap concept.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get cm easypj-settings -n s57-config -o jsonpath='{.data.ALLOWED_HOSTS}' easypj.com,easypj-jobs.com ← ConfigMap IS updated
$ kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api -n s57-config --tail=1 ALLOWED_HOSTS=easypj.com ← OLD value (pods NOT restarted yet!)
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api -n s57-config deployment.apps/easypj-api restarted
$ kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api -n s57-config --tail=1 ALLOWED_HOSTS=easypj.com,easypj-jobs.com ✅ New pods pick up updated ConfigMap!
🔧
BASH — Restart to pick up new ConfigMap

# Method 1: kubectl rollout restart (K8s 1.15+)
kubectl rollout restart deploy/easypj-api -n s57-config
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api -n s57-config --timeout=60s
kubectl logs -l app=easypj-api -n s57-config --tail=1
✓

✅ Verify — Pods Now Use Updated ConfigMap

After the rolling restart, new pods read the updated ConfigMap at startup and have the correct ALLOWED_HOSTS value including the new domain.

💡 Key takeaway: ConfigMap changes do NOT auto-propagate to running pods. Use kubectl rollout restart deploy/<name> for env vars, or mount as volume files for automatic updates. stakater/Reloader can automate this.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s57-config
kubectl get ns s57-config 2>&1
S58
🧪 SCENARIO S58 — Category 4: Config & Security Secret

Database Password Exposed — Secret as Env Var Visible in kubectl describe

The Problem: The easypj team stored the PostgreSQL password in a Secret and mounted it as an environment variable via envFrom.secretRef. An auditor ran kubectl describe pod and saw the database password in plain text in the Environment section. Secrets mounted as env vars are visible to anyone with pod read access. Your job: switch to mounting the Secret as a volume (tmpfs) where values are files — not visible in kubectl describe.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production secret hardening on node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy App with Secret as Env Var — Password Visible (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The security audit flagged the easypj deployment: "Database password visible in kubectl describe pod." The team stored credentials in a Kubernetes Secret (good) but exposed them via envFrom (bad). When Secrets are used as environment variables, they appear in plain text in kubectl describe pod — accessible to anyone with pod read permissions. Mounting as a volume (tmpfs) keeps values as files that don't appear in describe output.
📁 S58 STANDALONE:
~/s58-config/
├── secret.yaml    ← Secret with DB credentials
└── deploy.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: envFrom exposes password in describe!
BASH — Deploy with Secret as env var, then view in describe.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S58: Secret as Env Var — Password Exposed
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s58-config

# Create Secret with DB credentials
kubectl create secret generic easypj-db-creds -n s58-config \
  --from-literal=POSTGRES_USER=easypj \
  --from-literal=POSTGRES_PASSWORD=SuperSecret123! \
  --from-literal=POSTGRES_DB=jobpost

# Deploy pod using Secret as ENV VAR (password will be visible!)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s58-config
  labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s58}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    envFrom:
    - secretRef:
        name: easypj-db-creds    # ❌ BUG! Values visible in kubectl describe!
EOF

echo "=== CRITICAL: View the pod — password is in PLAIN TEXT! ==="
kubectl describe pod easypj-api -n s58-config | grep -A5 "Environment:"
echo ""
echo "^^^ Anyone with pod read access can see the database password!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Password Exposed

✗1. kubectl describe pod easypj-api -n s58-config → Environment section shows POSTGRES_PASSWORD: SuperSecret123!
✗2. Anyone with pod read RBAC can see all env vars — including Secrets!
✗3. env vars are also visible in /proc/<pid>/environ inside the container
🔍

🔍 Debug — Secret as Env Var vs Volume Mount

1envFrom exposes values: kubectl describe shows ALL environment variables including Secret values
→ This is a known Kubernetes design — env vars are visible in pod spec
2Volume mount hides values: Secrets mounted as volumes are stored in tmpfs — NOT visible in kubectl describe
Secret as envFrom exposes credentials to anyone with pod read access — use volume mounts for sensitive data
🧠 Tenet
①
Auditor flags password in describe → envFrom leak
②
Switch to volume mount → values are files
③
kubectl describe no longer shows password
④
App reads from /etc/secrets/POSTGRES_PASSWORD
⑤
Secret values protected from casual snooping!

Tenet: Secrets as env vars = visible in kubectl describe. Secrets as volume mounts = files in tmpfs, not in describe. For highly sensitive data (passwords, API keys, TLS keys), always use volume mounts. The app reads from files instead of env vars. On CKAD, understanding Secret exposure via envFrom is a key security concept.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe pod easypj-api -n s58-config | grep -A5 Environment Environment: POSTGRES_USER: easypj POSTGRES_PASSWORD: SuperSecret123! ← EXPOSED in plain text! POSTGRES_DB: jobpost
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl describe pod easypj-api -n s58-config | grep -A5 Environment (No Environment section — Secret is volume-mounted, not in describe!)
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s58-config -- cat /etc/secrets/POSTGRES_PASSWORD SuperSecret123! ✅ App still reads password from file — but not exposed in describe!
🔧
BASH — Switch to volume mount
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s58-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s58-config, labels: {app: easypj-api}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","cat /etc/secrets/POSTGRES_PASSWORD; sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: db-creds
      mountPath: /etc/secrets
      readOnly: true
  volumes:
  - name: db-creds
    secret:
      secretName: easypj-db-creds    # ✅ Mounted as files — NOT visible in describe!
EOF
echo "=== Check describe — NO password in Environment section! ==="
kubectl describe pod easypj-api -n s58-config | grep -A5 "Environment:" || echo "(No Environment section — Secret is volume-mounted)"
✓

✅ Verify — Password No Longer Exposed

With the Secret mounted as a volume, kubectl describe no longer shows the password. The app can still read credentials from /etc/secrets/POSTGRES_PASSWORD.

💡 Key takeaway: Secret as envFrom = visible in kubectl describe AND /proc/pid/environ. Secret as volume = files in tmpfs, not in describe. For production, always use volume mounts for sensitive credentials.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s58-config
S59
🧪 SCENARIO S59 — Category 4: Config & Security TLS Secret

HTTPS Broken — TLS Secret Created with Wrong Type (Opaque)

The Problem: The easypj team created a Secret for TLS certificates to enable HTTPS on the Ingress. They used kubectl create secret generic (Opaque type) instead of kubectl create secret tls. The Ingress can't use the certificate because it expects the kubernetes.io/tls type with tls.crt and tls.key keys — not an Opaque Secret with custom-named keys. HTTPS returns the default fake certificate. Your job: recreate the Secret with the correct type and key names.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-node for Ingress/TLS testing
1

📋 Create TLS Secret with Wrong Type (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The security team mandated HTTPS for all services. The DevOps engineer generated a self-signed certificate and created a Secret. But they used kubectl create secret generic easypj-tls --from-file=cert.pem --from-file=key.pem. This creates an Opaque Secret with keys named "cert.pem" and "key.pem". The Ingress controller expects a kubernetes.io/tls Secret with keys named "tls.crt" and "tls.key". The Ingress can't find the certificate — it serves the default "Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate."
📁 S59 STANDALONE:
~/s59-config/
├── cert.pem    ← Self-signed TLS certificate
└── key.pem     ← Private key
BASH — Create wrong-type Secret

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S59: TLS Secret — Wrong Type (Opaque instead of kubernetes.io/tls)
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s59-config

# Generate self-signed cert
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout /tmp/s59-key.pem -out /tmp/s59-cert.pem \
  -subj "/CN=easypj.example.com/O=easypj"

# ❌ BUG! Creates Opaque Secret with wrong key names!
kubectl create secret generic easypj-tls -n s59-config \
  --from-file=cert.pem=/tmp/s59-cert.pem \
  --from-file=key.pem=/tmp/s59-key.pem

echo "=== Check Secret type — should be kubernetes.io/tls but is Opaque ==="
kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n s59-config -o jsonpath='{.type}'
echo ""
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Wrong Type, Wrong Keys

✗1. Secret type: kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n s59-config → TYPE: Opaque (should be kubernetes.io/tls)
✗2. Secret keys: cert.pem, key.pem — Ingress expects tls.crt and tls.key
✗3. Ingress will either error or serve default fake certificate
🔍

🔍 Debug — TLS Secret Requirements

1Correct type: kubernetes.io/tls
→ Ingress controllers look for this specific type
2Correct keys: tls.crt (certificate) and tls.key (private key)
Opaque Secret with custom key names is invisible to Ingress TLS termination
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Ingress serves fake cert → Check Secret
②
Secret type is Opaque, keys: cert.pem/key.pem
③
Ingress expects kubernetes.io/tls + tls.crt/tls.key
④
Recreate with kubectl create secret tls
⑤
HTTPS works — correct certificate served!

Tenet: TLS Secrets MUST have type kubernetes.io/tls with keys tls.crt and tls.key. Use kubectl create secret tls <name> --cert=<cert-file> --key=<key-file> — it automatically sets the correct type and key names. NEVER use kubectl create secret generic for TLS. On CKAD, creating TLS Secrets with the correct type is a tested skill.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n s59-config NAME TYPE DATA AGE easypj-tls Opaque 2 5m ← ❌ WRONG TYPE! Should be kubernetes.io/tls!
$ kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n s59-config -o jsonpath='{.data}' | jq 'keys' ["cert.pem", "key.pem"] ← ❌ WRONG KEYS! Should be tls.crt and tls.key!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl delete secret easypj-tls -n s59-config && kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls -n s59-config --cert=/tmp/s59-cert.pem --key=/tmp/s59-key.pem secret "easypj-tls" deleted secret/easypj-tls created
$ kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n s59-config NAME TYPE DATA AGE easypj-tls kubernetes.io/tls 2 5s ✅ Correct type!
🔧
BASH
kubectl delete secret easypj-tls -n s59-config
kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls -n s59-config \
  --cert=/tmp/s59-cert.pem --key=/tmp/s59-key.pem
kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n s59-config
✓

✅ Verify — Secret Has Correct Type and Keys

The Secret now has type kubernetes.io/tls with data keys tls.crt and tls.key. The Ingress can now use it for TLS termination.

💡 Key takeaway: kubectl create secret tls automatically sets the correct type and key names. Never use generic/Opaque for TLS certificates — the Ingress controller won't recognize them.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s59-config
rm -f /tmp/s59-key.pem /tmp/s59-cert.pem
S60
🧪 SCENARIO S60 — Category 4: Config & Security imagePullSecrets

ImagePullBackOff — docker-registry Secret Created in Wrong Namespace

The Problem: The easypj team moved their Docker images to a private registry. They created a docker-registry Secret with credentials — but created it in the default namespace while the Deployment is in the easypj namespace. imagePullSecrets are namespace-scoped — a Secret in namespace A cannot be used by a pod in namespace B. The pods get ImagePullBackOff because Kubernetes can't find the credentials. Your job: create the Secret in the correct namespace.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production namespace isolation on node "easy"
1

📋 Create Secret in Wrong Namespace (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The DevOps engineer created the docker-registry Secret while their kubectl context was pointing to the default namespace. They didn't specify -n easypj. The Secret was created in default. The Deployment in s60-config references the Secret via imagePullSecrets — but Kubernetes can't find it. Secrets are namespace-scoped. The Deployment is in one namespace, the Secret in another — they can't see each other.
📁 S60 STANDALONE:
~/s60-config/
├── secret.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: Secret in default namespace
└── deploy.yaml    ← Deployment in s60-config namespace
BASH — Create Secret in wrong namespace, deploy in another.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S60: imagePullSecrets — Wrong Namespace
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s60-config

# ❌ BUG! Secret created in DEFAULT namespace, not s60-config!
kubectl create secret docker-registry easypj-regcred \
  --docker-server=myregistry.azurecr.io \
  --docker-username=easypj \
  --docker-password=TestPass123! \
  --docker-email=dev@easypj.com
# NOTE: No -n flag — goes to default namespace!

# Deploy in s60-config — references a Secret that doesn't exist there!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s60-config
  labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s60}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: nginx:alpine
  imagePullSecrets:
  - name: easypj-regcred    # ❌ BUG! Secret exists in default, NOT s60-config!
EOF

echo "=== Pod status — will show ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff ==="
kubectl get pods -n s60-config
echo ""
echo "=== Check events ==="
kubectl describe pod easypj-api -n s60-config | tail -5
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Secret Not Found in Namespace

✗1. Pod events: kubectl describe pod easypj-api -n s60-config | tail -5 → "secret easypj-regcred not found"
✗2. Secret exists in default: kubectl get secret easypj-regcred → Found!
✗3. Secret NOT in s60-config: kubectl get secret easypj-regcred -n s60-config → NotFound
✗4. Secrets are NAMESPACE-SCOPED — pods can only reference Secrets in their own namespace!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Cross-Namespace Secret Access Not Possible

1Secrets (like all namespaced resources) are scoped to a namespace
→ A pod in ns-A can only reference Secrets in ns-A
2imagePullSecrets must exist in the SAME namespace as the pod
Secret created in default namespace, Deployment in s60-config — cross-namespace Secret references are not supported
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod shows ImagePullBackOff → Check events
②
Event: "secret easypj-regcred not found"
③
Secret exists in default, NOT in pod''s namespace
④
Secrets are namespace-scoped — cross-ns not possible
⑤
Create Secret in SAME namespace → pod pulls image!

Tenet: Secrets, ConfigMaps, and all namespaced resources are scoped to their namespace. A pod can only reference Secrets in its own namespace. For imagePullSecrets, create the docker-registry Secret in EVERY namespace that needs to pull from the private registry. Alternatively, add the Secret to the default ServiceAccount of the namespace so all pods automatically get it. On CKAD, namespace-scoping of Secrets is a key concept.

🔧
BASH
kubectl create secret docker-registry easypj-regcred -n s60-config \
  --docker-server=myregistry.azurecr.io \
  --docker-username=easypj \
  --docker-password=TestPass123! \
  --docker-email=dev@easypj.com
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s60-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s60-config, labels: {app: easypj-api}}
spec:
  containers: [{name: api, image: nginx:alpine}]
  imagePullSecrets: [{name: easypj-regcred}]
EOF
kubectl get pods -n s60-config
✓

✅ Verify — Secret Found, Pod Running

With the docker-registry Secret in the same namespace as the pod, Kubernetes can authenticate to the private registry and pull the image.

💡 Key takeaway: imagePullSecrets must be in the SAME namespace as the pod. Always verify namespace with -n flag when creating Secrets. Use kubectl get secret -A | grep regcred to find which namespace has the Secret.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s60-config
kubectl delete secret easypj-regcred 2>/dev/null
S61
🧪 SCENARIO S61 — Category 4: Config & Security SecurityContext

Pod Crashes on Startup — runAsUser Set but Files Owned by Root

The Problem: The security team mandated non-root containers. The easypj team added runAsUser: 1000 to the pod securityContext. But the container image was built with all files owned by root. When the container starts as UID 1000, it can't write to any directory or execute files owned by root. The app crashes with "Permission denied" on startup. Your job: fix the file permissions so the non-root user can run the application.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-node for security testing
1

📋 Deploy with runAsUser but Root-Owned Container Files (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Security audit: "All containers must run as non-root." The team added runAsUser: 1000 and runAsNonRoot: true to the Deployment. The pod starts, tries to write to /app/logs/ (owned by root, mode 755), and crashes with "PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/app/logs/app.log'". The container user (UID 1000) doesn't own any files in the image.
📁 S61 STANDALONE:
~/s61-config/
└── deploy.yaml    ← runAsUser:1000 but root-owned files
BASH — Deploy non-root pod with root-owned files.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S61: runAsUser with Root-Owned Files
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s61-config

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s61-config, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s61}}
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsUser: 1000
    runAsNonRoot: true
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
    args:
    - |
      mkdir -p /app/logs
      # ❌ BUG! /app/logs owned by root, UID 1000 can't write!
      echo "Trying to write to /app/logs/app.log..."
      echo "App started" > /app/logs/app.log 2>&1
      echo "Write result: $?"
      cat /app/logs/app.log 2>&1 || echo "FAILED: Permission denied"
      sleep 3600
EOF

sleep 5
echo "=== Pod logs ==="
kubectl logs easypj-api -n s61-config
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Permission Denied

✗1. Pod logs show: Permission denied when writing to /app/logs/
✗2. Container runs as UID 1000 but all image files owned by root (UID 0)
✗3. Non-root user cannot write to root-owned directories (mode 755)
🔍

🔍 Debug — Fix File Ownership

1Solution A: Add USER 1000 in Dockerfile before creating files (files get correct ownership)
→ Long-term fix: rebuild the image with non-root user
2Solution B: Use fsGroup: 1000 in pod securityContext (changes volume group ownership)
runAsUser:1000 + root-owned files = Permission denied — fix with fsGroup or rebuild image
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod crashes with "Permission denied" → Check logs
②
Writing to /app/logs/ fails for UID 1000
③
runAsUser:1000 set but files owned by root (UID 0)
④
Fix: initContainer chowns + fsGroup:1000
⑤
Non-root container writes successfully!

Tenet: Setting runAsUser doesn't change file ownership in the container image. The files inside the image keep their original ownership. To run as non-root, either: (1) use USER in the Dockerfile so all subsequent files are owned by that user, (2) use fsGroup to change group ownership on mounted volumes, or (3) use an initContainer to chown directories at startup. On CKAD, understanding the gap between runAsUser and file ownership is critical.

🔧
BASH
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s61-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s61-config, labels: {app: easypj-api}}
spec:
  securityContext: {runAsUser: 1000, runAsNonRoot: true, fsGroup: 1000}
  initContainers:
  - name: fix-perms
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","mkdir -p /app/logs && chown -R 1000:1000 /app/logs"]
    volumeMounts: [{name: app-logs, mountPath: /app/logs}]
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'App started' > /app/logs/app.log && cat /app/logs/app.log && sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts: [{name: app-logs, mountPath: /app/logs}]
  volumes: [{name: app-logs, emptyDir: {}}]
EOF
kubectl logs easypj-api -n s61-config
✓

✅ Verify — Non-Root Container Writes Successfully

With fsGroup:1000 and an initContainer that sets correct ownership, the non-root container can now write to its directories.

💡 Key takeaway: runAsUser changes the UID but not file ownership. Use fsGroup for shared volumes, initContainers for chown, or rebuild the image with USER directive.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s61-config
S62
🧪 SCENARIO S62 — Category 4: Config & Security SecurityContext

Django Crashes — readOnlyRootFilesystem Blocks Writes to /tmp

The Problem: The security team enabled readOnlyRootFilesystem: true on all pods. Django needs to write temporary files to /tmp for file uploads and /var/run for PID files. With the root filesystem read-only, Django crashes because it can't create these files. The fix: mount emptyDir volumes at writable paths. Your job: add emptyDir volumes for all directories that need write access.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production hardening on node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy with readOnlyRootFilesystem but No Writable Volumes (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Security mandated read-only root filesystems. The team added readOnlyRootFilesystem: true to the securityContext and redeployed. Django crashed immediately — it needs /tmp for uploaded resume files, /var/run for Gunicorn PID, and /var/cache for template cache. All these paths are on the root filesystem which is now read-only.
📁 S62 STANDALONE:
~/s62-config/
└── deploy.yaml    ← readOnlyRootFilesystem:true but no emptyDirs
BASH — Deploy read-only pod without writable volumes.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S62: readOnlyRootFilesystem Without emptyDir
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s62-config

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s62-config, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s62}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
    args:
    - |
      echo "Trying to create /tmp/upload.txt..."
      echo "test" > /tmp/upload.txt 2>&1
      echo "Result: $?"
      sleep 3600
    securityContext:
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true    # ❌ BUG! /tmp is now read-only!
EOF

sleep 5
echo "=== Pod logs ==="
kubectl logs easypj-api -n s62-config
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Read-Only Filesystem Error

✗1. Pod logs: cannot create /tmp/upload.txt: Read-only file system
✗2. Every path on the root filesystem is now read-only — including /tmp, /var/run, /var/cache
🔍

🔍 Debug — Mount emptyDir at Writable Paths

1Mount emptyDir volumes at /tmp, /var/run, /var/cache — these override the read-only filesystem at those paths
readOnlyRootFilesystem:true without emptyDir volumes at writable paths = application crashes
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
App crashes — can''t write to /tmp → Check securityContext
②
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true — entire FS is RO
③
App needs /tmp, /var/run, /var/cache writable
④
Mount emptyDir volumes at writable paths
⑤
App runs with readOnlyRootFilesystem + writable volumes!

Tenet: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true is a critical security hardening measure, but it requires planning. Any path the application writes to must be backed by a writable volume (emptyDir, persistentVolume, hostPath). Common writable paths: /tmp, /var/run, /var/cache, /var/log. Mount emptyDir volumes at these paths to preserve security while allowing writes.

🔧
BASH
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s62-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s62-config, labels: {app: easypj-api}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo test > /tmp/upload.txt && cat /tmp/upload.txt && sleep 3600"]
    securityContext:
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
    volumeMounts:
    - {name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}
    - {name: var-run, mountPath: /var/run}
  volumes:
  - {name: tmp, emptyDir: {}}
  - {name: var-run, emptyDir: {}}
EOF
kubectl logs easypj-api -n s62-config
✓

✅ Verify — Writes Succeed with emptyDir Volumes

With emptyDir volumes mounted at /tmp and /var/run, the application can write to these paths while the root filesystem remains read-only for security.

💡 Key takeaway: readOnlyRootFilesystem + emptyDir at writable paths = security + functionality. Always audit write paths before enabling readOnlyRootFilesystem.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s62-config
S63
🧪 SCENARIO S63 — Category 4: Config & Security Capabilities

Nginx Can't Bind to Port 80 — Dropped ALL Capabilities Including NET_BIND_SERVICE

The Problem: The security team hardened containers by dropping ALL Linux capabilities. But Nginx runs as a non-root user and needs NET_BIND_SERVICE to bind to port 80. With capabilities dropped to an empty list, Nginx can't bind and crashes. Your job: drop ALL capabilities, then explicitly add back only NET_BIND_SERVICE.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — Quick security testing
1

📋 Deploy Nginx with ALL Capabilities Dropped (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Security audit recommendation: "Drop all Linux capabilities." The team applied: capabilities: drop: ["ALL"]. But Nginx runs as UID 101 (nginx user) and needs NET_BIND_SERVICE to bind to privileged port 80. Dropping ALL capabilities without adding back NET_BIND_SERVICE means Nginx can't bind to port 80. The web server fails to start.
📁 S63 STANDALONE:
~/s63-config/
└── deploy.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: drop ALL caps but no NET_BIND_SERVICE
BASH — Deploy with ALL capabilities dropped.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S63: Dropped ALL Caps — Can't Bind Port 80
# CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s63-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-web, namespace: s63-config, labels: {app: easypj-web, scenario: s63}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    securityContext:
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]    # ❌ BUG! Also drops NET_BIND_SERVICE needed for port 80!
      runAsUser: 101
    ports: [{containerPort: 80}]
EOF
sleep 8
kubectl logs easypj-web -n s63-config 2>&1 | tail -5
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Port Binding Failed

✗1. Nginx logs: "bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (13: Permission denied)"
✗2. Non-root user needs NET_BIND_SERVICE to bind to ports below 1024
🔍

🔍 Debug — Add Back NET_BIND_SERVICE

1Fix: drop ALL, then add only NET_BIND_SERVICE
Drop ALL removes all capabilities including NET_BIND_SERVICE needed for non-root port binding below 1024

Tenet: drop: ["ALL"] is recommended, but you must add back the specific capabilities your application needs. Common additions: NET_BIND_SERVICE (bind to low ports as non-root), SYS_TIME (set system time), CHOWN (change file ownership). Always test after hardening.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs easypj-web -n s63-config nginx: [emerg] bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (13: Permission denied) nginx: [emerg] bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (13: Permission denied) nginx: [emerg] still could not bind()
$ kubectl get pods -n s63-config NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-web 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 3 2m
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n s63-config NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-web 1/1 Running 0 30s
$ kubectl logs easypj-web -n s63-config nginx: [notice] using the "epoll" event method nginx: [notice] nginx/1.27.0 nginx: [notice] start worker process 30 ✅ Nginx bound to port 80 successfully (NET_BIND_SERVICE granted)
🔧
BASH
kubectl delete pod easypj-web -n s63-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-web, namespace: s63-config, labels: {app: easypj-web}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    securityContext:
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
        add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]    # ✅ Only capability needed!
      runAsUser: 101
    ports: [{containerPort: 80}]
EOF
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/easypj-web -n s63-config --timeout=30s
kubectl get pods -n s63-config
✓

✅ Verify — Nginx Binds Successfully

With NET_BIND_SERVICE added back, Nginx can bind to port 80 as non-root while all other unnecessary capabilities remain dropped.

💡 Key takeaway: drop ALL + add only what's needed = principle of least privilege for Linux capabilities. Audit your app''s capability needs before hardening.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s63-config
S64
🧪 SCENARIO S64 — Category 4: Config & Security RBAC

Pod Gets 403 Forbidden — RoleBinding Bound to Wrong ServiceAccount

The Problem: The easypj API pod needs to list pods in its namespace for a monitoring dashboard. The team created a Role, RoleBinding, and ServiceAccount — but the RoleBinding references default ServiceAccount instead of the custom easypj-api-sa. The pod gets 403 Forbidden because it''s using the custom SA but the RoleBinding grants permissions to the default SA. Your job: fix the RoleBinding to reference the correct ServiceAccount.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-node RBAC testing
1

📋 Deploy with RBAC Bound to Wrong ServiceAccount (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The monitoring dashboard needs to list pods. The team created: ServiceAccount (easypj-api-sa), Role (pod-reader with get/list on pods), and RoleBinding. But the RoleBinding''s subjects array points to kind: ServiceAccount, name: default — the default SA, not easypj-api-sa. The pod uses easypj-api-sa but gets 403 because the permissions are on the default SA.
📁 S64 STANDALONE:
~/s64-config/
├── sa.yaml           ← ServiceAccount: easypj-api-sa
├── role.yaml          ← Role: pod-reader (get/list pods)
└── rolebinding.yaml   ← ❌ BUG: subjects point to "default" SA!
BASH — Deploy with RBAC bound to wrong SA.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S64: RoleBinding — Wrong ServiceAccount
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s64-config
kubectl create sa easypj-api-sa -n s64-config
kubectl create role pod-reader -n s64-config --verb=get,list --resource=pods

# ❌ BUG! RoleBinding references "default" SA, not "easypj-api-sa"!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: {name: pod-reader-binding, namespace: s64-config}
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: default            # ❌ BUG! Should be "easypj-api-sa"!
  namespace: s64-config
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
EOF

# Test as the custom SA — should FAIL (403 Forbidden)
echo "=== Testing as easypj-api-sa (should FAIL) ==="
kubectl auth can-i list pods -n s64-config --as=system:serviceaccount:s64-config:easypj-api-sa
echo ""
echo "=== Testing as default SA (should PASS — wrong SA has the permission!) ==="
kubectl auth can-i list pods -n s64-config --as=system:serviceaccount:s64-config:default
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Wrong SA Has Permissions

✗1. easypj-api-sa → kubectl auth can-i list pods → no (pod gets 403!)
✗2. default SA → kubectl auth can-i list pods → yes (wrong SA has permission!)
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the RoleBinding Mistake

1Check RoleBinding subjects: kubectl get rolebinding pod-reader-binding -n s64-config -o yaml | grep -A3 subjects
RoleBinding subjects point to name: default instead of name: easypj-api-sa

Tenet: RoleBinding connects a Role to subjects (users, groups, ServiceAccounts). If the subject name is wrong, the permissions go to the wrong entity. Always verify with kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa> before deploying. On CKAD, RBAC debugging with auth can-i is a tested skill.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods -n s64-config --as=system:serviceaccount:s64-config:easypj-api-sa no ← 403 Forbidden! The custom SA has NO permissions!
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods -n s64-config --as=system:serviceaccount:s64-config:default yes ← Wrong SA got the permission instead!
$ kubectl get rolebinding pod-reader-binding -n s64-config -o yaml | grep -A3 subjects subjects: - kind: ServiceAccount name: default ← BUG! Should be "easypj-api-sa" namespace: s64-config
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods -n s64-config --as=system:serviceaccount:s64-config:easypj-api-sa yes ✅ Custom SA now has the correct RBAC permissions!
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch rolebinding pod-reader-binding -n s64-config --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/subjects/0/name","value":"easypj-api-sa"}
]'
echo "=== Verify: easypj-api-sa should now have list access ==="
kubectl auth can-i list pods -n s64-config --as=system:serviceaccount:s64-config:easypj-api-sa
✓

✅ Verify — Correct SA Has Permissions

The custom ServiceAccount now has list pods permission. Use kubectl auth can-i to verify any SA''s permissions before deploying workloads.

💡 Key takeaway: RoleBinding subjects must match the ServiceAccount name EXACTLY. Use kubectl auth can-i --as to test permissions before deploying. RBAC mistakes are one of the hardest bugs to diagnose because pods just get 403 with no clear error.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s64-config
S65
🧪 SCENARIO S65 — Category 4: Config & Security RBAC

Pod Can Get One Pod But Can''t List All — Missing "list" Verb

The Problem: The monitoring pod needs to list all pods in the namespace. The Role has get verb on pods, so kubectl get pod easypj-api-xxx works — but kubectl get pods returns 403 Forbidden. "get" retrieves a SINGLE named resource. "list" retrieves ALL resources of that type. They are different verbs. Your job: add the "list" verb to the Role.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — RBAC debugging on node "easy"
1

📋 Create Role with Only "get" Verb (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The monitoring dashboard calls the Kubernetes API to show all running pods. The developer created a Role with "get" on pods — they thought "get" meant "retrieve information." "get" allows retrieving ONE specific pod by name. "list" allows listing ALL pods. The dashboard calls LIST, not GET — and gets 403 Forbidden.
📁 S65 STANDALONE:
~/s65-config/
├── sa.yaml              ← ServiceAccount: monitor-sa
├── role.yaml             ← ❌ BUG: only "get" verb — missing "list"!
└── rolebinding.yaml      ← Binds role to monitor-sa
BASH — Create Role with only "get" (missing "list").

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S65: RBAC — Missing "list" Verb
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s65-config
kubectl create sa monitor-sa -n s65-config

# ❌ BUG! Only "get" — missing "list" verb!
kubectl create role pod-reader -n s65-config --verb=get --resource=pods
kubectl create rolebinding pod-reader-binding -n s65-config \
  --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=s65-config:monitor-sa

echo "=== Can get a specific pod? ==="
kubectl auth can-i get pod/test -n s65-config --as=system:serviceaccount:s65-config:monitor-sa
echo "=== Can LIST all pods? (should FAIL!) ==="
kubectl auth can-i list pods -n s65-config --as=system:serviceaccount:s65-config:monitor-sa
echo ""
echo "^^^ "get" works but "list" fails — they are DIFFERENT verbs!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — get Works, list Fails

✗1. kubectl auth can-i get pod/test → yes ✅
✗2. kubectl auth can-i list pods → no ❌
✗3. "get" = single named resource. "list" = all resources of type. DIFFERENT VERBS!
🔍

🔍 Debug — RBAC Verbs Matter

1Common RBAC verbs: get (single), list (all), watch (stream), create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection
"get" retrieves one resource by name — "list" retrieves all resources — they are separate verbs that must be explicitly granted

Tenet: Kubernetes RBAC verbs are specific: get (single named resource), list (all resources of type), watch (streaming updates), create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection. If your app lists pods but the Role only has "get", it will fail. Always use kubectl auth can-i to test exact permissions.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl auth can-i get pod/test -n s65-config --as=system:serviceaccount:s65-config:monitor-sa yes ← "get" works for single pods
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods -n s65-config --as=system:serviceaccount:s65-config:monitor-sa no ← "list" FAILS! The dashboard can't list all pods!
$ kubectl get role pod-reader -n s65-config -o yaml | grep verbs verbs: - get ← BUG! Only "get" — missing "list"!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl auth can-i list pods -n s65-config --as=system:serviceaccount:s65-config:monitor-sa yes ✅ "list" verb added — dashboard can now list all pods!
$ kubectl get role pod-reader -n s65-config -o yaml | grep verbs verbs: - get - list ✅ Both verbs now granted
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch role pod-reader -n s65-config --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/rules/0/verbs/-","value":"list"}
]'
echo "=== Verify: list pods should now work ==="
kubectl auth can-i list pods -n s65-config --as=system:serviceaccount:s65-config:monitor-sa
✓

✅ Verify — Both get and list Work

With "list" verb added, the SA can now list all pods. Remember: get ≠ list in Kubernetes RBAC.

💡 Key takeaway: get, list, and watch are three separate RBAC verbs. Always grant all three if your app needs to query resources. Use kubectl auth can-i to verify.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s65-config
S66
🧪 SCENARIO S66 — Category 4: Config & Security Downward API

POD_IP Shows Pod Name — Wrong fieldPath in Downward API

The Problem: The monitoring system needs POD_IP for metrics. The team configured the Downward API but used fieldPath: metadata.name for POD_IP. The env var POD_IP contains the pod NAME (e.g., "easypj-api-7d9f8b-x2k9m") instead of the pod IP (e.g., "10.244.1.5"). The correct fieldPath for IP is status.podIP. Your job: fix the fieldPath references.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Downward API testing
1

📋 Deploy with Wrong Downward API fieldPath (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The logging system needs POD_NAME, POD_NAMESPACE, POD_IP, and NODE_NAME. The developer looked up "Kubernetes Downward API" and copied fieldPaths from a blog — but the blog had an error. POD_IP uses fieldPath: metadata.name (which gives the pod name, not IP). The correct fieldPath for pod IP is status.podIP.
📁 S66 STANDALONE:
~/s66-config/
└── deploy.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: POD_IP fieldRef uses metadata.name instead of status.podIP
BASH — Deploy with wrong fieldPaths.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S66: Downward API — Wrong fieldPath
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s66-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s66-config, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s66}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo NAME=$POD_NAME IP=$POD_IP NODE=$NODE_NAME; sleep 3600"]
    env:
    - {name: POD_NAME, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}}
    - {name: POD_IP, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}}   # ❌ BUG! metadata.name = pod NAME, not IP!
    - {name: NODE_NAME, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: spec.nodeName}}}
EOF
sleep 3
echo "=== Pod env — POD_IP shows WRONG value! ==="
kubectl logs easypj-api -n s66-config
⚠

⚠️ Observe — POD_IP Shows Pod Name

✗1. Pod logs: IP=easypj-api — that''s the pod NAME, not the IP!
✗2. Correct fieldPath for IP: status.podIP
🔍

🔍 Debug — Downward API fieldPaths

1Common fieldPaths: metadata.name, metadata.namespace, metadata.uid, metadata.labels, metadata.annotations, spec.nodeName, spec.serviceAccountName, status.podIP, status.hostIP
metadata.name = pod name (string), status.podIP = pod IP address — used wrong fieldPath for POD_IP

Tenet: Downward API fieldPaths reference specific fields in the pod manifest. Common mistakes: using metadata.name for IP, using metadata.name for namespace (correct is metadata.namespace), using status.podIP for node name. On CKAD, knowing the correct fieldPaths is essential.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs easypj-api -n s66-config NAME=easypj-api IP=easypj-api NODE=kind-control-plane ^^^^^^^^^^^^ ❌ BUG! IP shows pod NAME, not IP address!
$ kubectl get pod easypj-api -n s66-config -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}' 10.244.1.7 ← Actual pod IP should be this, not "easypj-api"
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl logs easypj-api -n s66-config NAME=easypj-api IP=10.244.1.7 NODE=kind-control-plane ^^^^^^^^^^ ✅ Correct! status.podIP gives the real IP
🔧
BASH
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s66-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s66-config, labels: {app: easypj-api}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo NAME=$POD_NAME IP=$POD_IP NODE=$NODE_NAME; sleep 3600"]
    env:
    - {name: POD_NAME, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}}
    - {name: POD_IP, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: status.podIP}}}    # ✅ Fixed!
    - {name: NODE_NAME, valueFrom: {fieldRef: {fieldPath: spec.nodeName}}}
EOF
kubectl logs easypj-api -n s66-config
✓

✅ Verify — POD_IP Shows Correct IP Address

With the correct fieldPath, POD_IP now contains the actual pod IP address. Use kubectl explain pod.spec to find available Downward API fields.

💡 Key takeaway: Downward API fieldPaths: metadata.name (pod name), metadata.namespace, spec.nodeName, status.podIP, status.hostIP. Use kubectl explain to find available fields.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s66-config
S67
🧪 SCENARIO S67 — Category 4: Config & Security Env Vars

ConfigMap Value Ignored — Hardcoded env Overrides envFrom

The Problem: The easypj team set DATABASE_URL in a ConfigMap (correct value: postgresql://easypj-db:5432/jobpost). But the Deployment also has a hardcoded env: - name: DATABASE_URL value: "sqlite:///db.sqlite3". In Kubernetes, env takes PRECEDENCE over envFrom. The hardcoded value wins — Django connects to the wrong database. Your job: remove the hardcoded env so the ConfigMap value is used.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Env precedence debugging on node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy with Both env and envFrom — Hardcoded Wins (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The staging database was migrated to PostgreSQL. The team updated the ConfigMap with the new DATABASE_URL. But Django still connects to SQLite! The Deployment template has a hardcoded env entry for DATABASE_URL from the initial dev setup. In Kubernetes env var resolution, env (hardcoded) takes precedence over envFrom (ConfigMap/Secret). The ConfigMap update is completely ignored.
📁 S67 STANDALONE:
~/s67-config/
├── configmap.yaml    ← DATABASE_URL: postgresql://... (correct value)
└── deploy.yaml       ← ❌ BUG: hardcoded env DATABASE_URL overrides ConfigMap!
BASH — Deploy with env overriding envFrom.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S67: Env Var Precedence — hardcoded wins
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s67-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: {name: easypj-config, namespace: s67-config}
data:
  DATABASE_URL: "postgresql://easypj-db:5432/jobpost"
  DEBUG: "false"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s67-config, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s67}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo DATABASE_URL=$DATABASE_URL; sleep 3600"]
    env:
    - name: DATABASE_URL
      value: "sqlite:///db.sqlite3"    # ❌ BUG! This OVERRIDES ConfigMap value!
    envFrom:
    - configMapRef:
        name: easypj-config
EOF
sleep 3
echo "=== DATABASE_URL from pod — shows HARDCODED value, not ConfigMap! ==="
kubectl logs easypj-api -n s67-config
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Hardcoded Value Used, ConfigMap Ignored

✗1. Pod logs: DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///db.sqlite3 — the hardcoded value!
✗2. ConfigMap has: DATABASE_URL: postgresql://... — but it''s IGNORED!
✗3. env takes PRECEDENCE over envFrom — hardcoded values always win
🔍

🔍 Debug — Env Var Resolution Order

1Kubernetes env var precedence (highest to lowest):
① env (hardcoded) → ② envFrom (ConfigMap/Secret) → ③ Image defaults
Hardcoded env entry for DATABASE_URL overrides the ConfigMap value — env wins over envFrom

Tenet: Kubernetes env var precedence: env > envFrom > image defaults. If a variable is defined in both env and envFrom, the env value wins. To use ConfigMap values exclusively, remove the hardcoded env entry entirely. On CKAD, understanding env var precedence is tested.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs easypj-api -n s67-config DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///db.sqlite3 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ❌ Hardcoded env wins — ConfigMap IGNORED!
$ kubectl get cm easypj-config -n s67-config -o jsonpath='{.data.DATABASE_URL}' postgresql://easypj-db:5432/jobpost ← ConfigMap has the correct value, but it's overridden!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl logs easypj-api -n s67-config DATABASE_URL=postgresql://easypj-db:5432/jobpost ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ ✅ ConfigMap value used correctly!
🔧
BASH
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s67-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s67-config, labels: {app: easypj-api}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo DATABASE_URL=$DATABASE_URL; sleep 3600"]
    envFrom:
    - configMapRef:
        name: easypj-config          # ✅ Only ConfigMap — no hardcoded override!
EOF
kubectl logs easypj-api -n s67-config
✓

✅ Verify — ConfigMap Value Used

With the hardcoded env removed, the ConfigMap value for DATABASE_URL is now used correctly.

💡 Key takeaway: env (hardcoded) > envFrom (ConfigMap/Secret). Never mix both for the same variable name. Use envFrom for externalized config, env only for pod-specific overrides.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s67-config
S68
🧪 SCENARIO S68 — Category 4: Config & Security ResourceQuota

Deployment Rejected — ResourceQuota Exceeded in Namespace

The Problem: The easypj-dev namespace has a ResourceQuota limiting total memory to 2Gi. A developer deploys a new service requesting 3Gi — kubectl apply fails with "exceeded quota." The developer didn''t check namespace quotas before deploying. Your job: understand how ResourceQuota blocks deployments and adjust requests to fit.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — ResourceQuota enforcement
1

📋 Set ResourceQuota, Then Try to Exceed It (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The platform team set a 2Gi memory ResourceQuota on the dev namespace to prevent runaway workloads. A developer deploying a new ML service requests 3Gi. kubectl apply is REJECTED — the quota calculator sees the request would push total requested memory over 2Gi.
📁 S68 STANDALONE:
~/s68-config/
├── quota.yaml    ← ResourceQuota: requests.memory=2Gi
└── pod.yaml      ← ❌ BUG: requests 3Gi memory — exceeds quota!
BASH — Set quota, then deploy pod that exceeds it.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S68: ResourceQuota Exceeded
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s68-config
kubectl create quota dev-quota -n s68-config --hard=requests.memory=2Gi,requests.cpu=2
echo "=== Quota set: 2Gi memory, 2 CPU ==="
kubectl describe quota dev-quota -n s68-config
echo ""
echo "=== Try to deploy pod requesting 3Gi (WILL FAIL!) ==="
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-ml, namespace: s68-config}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: ml-worker
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "3Gi"    # ❌ BUG! Exceeds 2Gi namespace quota!
        cpu: "500m"
EOF
echo ""
echo "=== Check quota usage ==="
kubectl describe quota dev-quota -n s68-config
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Pod Rejected by Quota

✗1. kubectl apply output: "Error from server (Forbidden): exceeded quota"
✗2. Pod requests 3Gi but namespace quota is 2Gi
🔍

🔍 Debug — Check Quota Before Deploying

1Always check: kubectl describe quota -n <ns> before deploying
Pod memory request (3Gi) exceeds namespace ResourceQuota (2Gi) — deployment blocked

Tenet: ResourceQuota enforces aggregate resource limits at the namespace level. Pods that would exceed the quota are rejected at admission time — they don''t even get scheduled. Always check kubectl describe quota before deploying to understand namespace limits.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl apply -f pod.yaml Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "pod.yaml": pods "easypj-ml" is forbidden: exceeded quota: dev-quota, requested: requests.memory=3Gi, used: requests.memory=0, limited: requests.memory=2Gi ← 3Gi > 2Gi quota — REJECTED!
$ kubectl describe quota dev-quota -n s68-config Name: dev-quota Namespace: s68-config Resource Used Hard -------- ---- ---- requests.cpu 0 2 requests.memory 0 2Gi ← Quota: 2Gi max
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl apply -f pod-fixed.yaml pod/easypj-ml created ✅ Pod fits within quota now!
$ kubectl describe quota dev-quota -n s68-config Resource Used Hard requests.cpu 500m 2 requests.memory 256Mi 2Gi ← 256Mi < 2Gi — safely within quota
🔧
BASH
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-ml, namespace: s68-config}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: ml-worker
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "512Mi"    # ✅ Fits within 2Gi quota
        cpu: "500m"
EOF
kubectl get pods -n s68-config
✓

✅ Verify — Pod Deploys Within Quota

With memory request reduced to 512Mi, the pod fits within the namespace quota and deploys successfully.

💡 Key takeaway: ResourceQuota blocks pods at admission time. Check kubectl describe quota before deploying. Requests are counted against quota, limits are enforced at runtime.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s68-config

The Problem: The easypj-db pod needs SSD storage. The Deployment has nodeSelector: disktype: ssd. But NO node in the cluster has the label disktype=ssd. The pod stays Pending forever because no node matches the selector. Your job: either add the label to a node or fix the selector.

1

📋 Deploy with nodeSelector for Non-Existent Label (CONTAINS THE BUG)

But the cluster was set up without labeling any nodes as SSD. The scheduler looks for a node with disktype=ssd, finds none, and leaves the pod in Pending forever.
📁 S69 STANDALONE:
~/s69-config/
└── pod.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: nodeSelector: disktype=ssd but no node has this label!
BASH — Deploy pod that requires non-existent label.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S69: nodeSelector — Missing Node Label
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s69-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-db, namespace: s69-config, labels: {app: easypj-db, scenario: s69}}
spec:
  nodeSelector:

echo "=== Check events ==="

⚠

⚠️ Observe — Pod Can''t Schedule

✗1. Pod STATUS: Pending — will never schedule
✗2. Events: "0/N nodes are available: node(s) didn''t match Pod''s node affinity/selector"
🔍

🔍 Debug — Check Node Labels

1Check existing node labels: kubectl get nodes --show-labels | grep disktype → No matches!
nodeSelector: disktype=ssd but no node has this label — pod can never schedule

Tenet: nodeSelector requires the label to EXIST on at least one node. If no node has the label, the pod stays Pending forever. Always verify node labels with kubectl get nodes --show-labels before using nodeSelector. Alternative: use kubectl label node <name> disktype=ssd to add labels.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n s69-config NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-db 0/1 Pending 0 2m
$ kubectl describe pod easypj-db -n s69-config | tail -5 Events: Type Reason Message Warning FailedScheduling 0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector. ← No node has label disktype=ssd!
$ kubectl get nodes --show-labels | grep disktype (no output) ← Confirmed: no node has disktype label
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl label node kind-control-plane disktype=ssd && kubectl get pods -n s69-config node/kind-control-plane labeled NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE easypj-db 1/1 Running 0 30s ✅ Scheduled after adding label!
🔧
BASH
NODE=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl label node $NODE disktype=ssd
echo "=== Node labeled. Pod should now schedule ==="
kubectl get pods -n s69-config -w &
WP=$!; sleep 10; kill $WP 2>/dev/null
kubectl get pods -n s69-config
✓

✅ Verify — Pod Scheduled After Adding Label

After adding the disktype=ssd label to a node, the pod immediately schedules and starts running. Always ensure node labels exist before using nodeSelector.

💡 Key takeaway: nodeSelector + no matching label = pod Pending forever. Use kubectl get nodes --show-labels to verify before deploying. For more flexible scheduling, use nodeAffinity with preferredDuringScheduling.

S70
🧪 SCENARIO S70 — Category 4: Config & Security Scheduling

3 Replicas on 2-Node Cluster — podAntiAffinity Blocks Third Pod

The Problem: The easypj API uses requiredDuringScheduling podAntiAffinity to spread pods across nodes. With 3 replicas on a 2-node cluster, the third pod can''t schedule — each node already has one API pod, and the anti-affinity rule says pods can''t share nodes. Your job: change to preferredDuringScheduling (soft preference) so the third pod can schedule on any node.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Scheduling on single-node "easy"
1

📋 Deploy with Hard Anti-Affinity on Small Cluster (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: For high availability, the team added podAntiAffinity to spread API pods across nodes. They used requiredDuringScheduling (hard rule). The cluster has only 2 worker nodes. With 3 replicas, 2 pods schedule on separate nodes — but the third pod has nowhere to go (both nodes already have an API pod, and the hard anti-affinity rule prevents co-location).
📁 S70 STANDALONE:
~/s70-config/
└── deploy.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: requiredDuringScheduling with 3 replicas on small cluster!
BASH — Deploy with too-strict anti-affinity.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S70: podAntiAffinity Too Strict
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s70-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s70-config, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s70}}
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: easypj-api}}
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:    # ❌ BUG! Hard rule — 3 replicas on 1-node = 2 stuck!
          - labelSelector:
              matchLabels:
                app: easypj-api
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname

EOF

echo "=== Pod status — 2 will be Pending on single-node cluster ==="

⚠

⚠️ Observe — Pods Stuck Pending

✗1. 3 replicas but only 1 Running — 2 Pending due to hard anti-affinity on single-node cluster
✗2. requiredDuringScheduling = hard rule — pods CANNOT violate it
🔍

🔍 Debug — Switch to Soft Anti-Affinity

1Solution: Use preferredDuringScheduling (soft preference) — scheduler tries to spread pods but will co-locate if necessary
Hard anti-affinity (requiredDuringScheduling) with more replicas than nodes = pods stuck Pending forever

Tenet: requiredDuringScheduling = hard rule (pod won''t schedule if violated). preferredDuringScheduling = soft preference (scheduler tries but will co-locate if needed). For HA on small clusters, use preferred. For strict isolation (e.g., security), use required.

$ kubectl get pods -n s70-config -o wide NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE NODE easypj-api-8e0g9c-a1b2c 1/1 Running 0 30s node-1 easypj-api-8e0g9c-b3d4e 1/1 Running 0 30s node-1 easypj-api-8e0g9c-c5f6g 1/1 Running 0 30s node-1 ← All 3 Running! Soft anti-affinity allows co-location ✅

kubectl delete deploy easypj-api -n s70-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -

With soft anti-affinity, all 3 pods schedule successfully — the scheduler tries to spread them but co-locates when necessary.

💡 Key takeaway: requiredDuringScheduling = hard (pod won''t schedule if violated). preferredDuringScheduling = soft (best effort). Use hard for strict rules, soft for HA on limited nodes.

S71
🧪 SCENARIO S71 — Category 4: Config & Security Immutable

CI Pipeline Overwrites Production ConfigMap — Make It Immutable

The Problem: A CI pipeline accidentally ran kubectl apply against production and overwrote the easypj-prod ConfigMap with staging values. Production went down for 45 minutes. ConfigMaps and Secrets are mutable by default — anyone with write access can change them. The fix: set immutable: true to prevent accidental modifications. Your job: make the ConfigMap immutable and understand the delete+recreate workflow for intentional updates.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Production protection on node "easy"
1

📋 Create Immutable ConfigMap, Then Try to Update — It Gets Rejected! (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Post-incident review: "How did staging values end up in production?" Answer: The CI pipeline used the same kubectl context and overwrote the production ConfigMap. Kubernetes Secrets and ConfigMaps are mutable by default. Setting immutable: true prevents ANY modifications — even well-intentioned ones. For intentional updates, you must delete and recreate with a new name.
📁 S71 STANDALONE:
~/s71-config/
└── configmap.yaml    ← immutable: true — protected from accidental changes
BASH — Create ConfigMap, make immutable, then try to update.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S71: Immutable ConfigMap
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s71-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: easypj-prod-config
  namespace: s71-config
immutable: true      # ✅ Protected from accidental changes!
data:
  DATABASE_URL: "postgresql://easypj-db:5432/jobpost"
  DEBUG: "false"
EOF

echo "=== Try to update — will be REJECTED! ==="
kubectl patch cm easypj-prod-config -n s71-config -p '{"data":{"DEBUG":"true"}}' 2>&1
echo ""
echo "^^^ Immutable ConfigMaps cannot be updated — must delete and recreate!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Update Rejected

✗1. kubectl patch fails: "ConfigMap is immutable and cannot be modified"
✗2. Immutable protects from accidental CI overwrites — but requires delete+recreate for changes
🔍

🔍 Debug — Immutable Resource Workflow

1To update: Delete old ConfigMap → Create new ConfigMap with different name (e.g., easypj-prod-config-v2) → Update Deployment to reference new name → Rolling restart
Immutable resources cannot be patched or updated at all — intentional changes require delete+recreate with versioned names

Tenet: immutable: true on ConfigMaps and Secrets prevents ALL modifications (even well-intentioned ones). For updates: delete old, create new with versioned name, update Deployment reference, rollout restart. This forces intentional, traceable configuration changes.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl patch cm easypj-prod-config -n s71-config -p '{"data":{"DEBUG":"true"}}' Error from server (Invalid): ConfigMap "easypj-prod-config" is invalid: metadata.resourceVersion: Invalid value: 0x0: must be specified for an update ← Immutable ConfigMaps CANNOT be modified — even by kubectl patch!
$ kubectl get cm easypj-prod-config -n s71-config -o jsonpath='{.immutable}' true ← Confirmed: ConfigMap is immutable
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix (Intentional Update Workflow)
$ kubectl delete cm easypj-prod-config -n s71-config && kubectl create cm easypj-prod-config-v2 -n s71-config --from-literal=DEBUG=true --from-literal=DATABASE_URL=postgresql://easypj-db:5432/jobpost && kubectl get cm -n s71-config configmap "easypj-prod-config" deleted configmap/easypj-prod-config-v2 created NAME DATA AGE easypj-prod-config-v2 2 5s ✅ New version created, old deleted
🔧
BASH — Versioned update workflow
kubectl delete cm easypj-prod-config -n s71-config
kubectl create cm easypj-prod-config-v2 -n s71-config --from-literal=DEBUG=true --from-literal=DATABASE_URL=postgresql://easypj-db:5432/jobpost
kubectl get cm -n s71-config
✓

✅ Verify — Immutable ConfigMaps Prevent CI Accidents

With immutable: true, any attempt to modify the ConfigMap is rejected. Intentional changes follow the delete+recreate+versioned-name workflow, making all configuration changes intentional and traceable.

💡 Key takeaway: Set immutable: true on production ConfigMaps and Secrets to prevent accidental overwrites by CI pipelines. For updates: delete old, create new with versioned name (e.g., easypj-prod-config-v2).

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s71-config
S72
🧪 SCENARIO S72 — Category 4: Config & Security Projected Volume

Config Missing — Projected Volume Key Overwritten by Another Source

The Problem: Django needs config from a ConfigMap, credentials from a Secret, and pod info from the Downward API — all in ONE directory. The team used a projected volume. But both the ConfigMap and Secret have a key named DATABASE_URL. The Secret''s DATABASE_URL overwrites the ConfigMap''s DATABASE_URL because projected volumes process sources in order — later sources overwrite earlier ones with the same key. Your job: fix the conflicting key names.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Volume projection testing
1

📋 Deploy with Conflicting Keys in Projected Volume (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The platform team consolidated config into a projected volume at /etc/app-config/. They combined ConfigMap, Secret, and DownwardAPI. Both ConfigMap and Secret have a key called "DATABASE_URL" — the Secret''s value (credentials URL) overwrites the ConfigMap''s value (connection string). Django gets a connection string with embedded credentials instead of the expected format.
📁 S72 STANDALONE:
~/s72-config/
├── configmap.yaml    ← DATABASE_URL key (connection string)
├── secret.yaml       ← ❌ BUG: also has DATABASE_URL — will overwrite ConfigMap!
└── pod.yaml          ← Projected volume combining all 3 sources
BASH — Deploy projected volume with conflicting keys.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S72: Projected Volume — Key Conflict
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s72-config
kubectl create cm app-config -n s72-config --from-literal=DATABASE_URL=postgresql://db:5432/jobpost --from-literal=DEBUG=false
kubectl create secret generic app-secret -n s72-config --from-literal=DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@db:5432/jobpost --from-literal=API_KEY=sk-abc123

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s72-config, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s72}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","cat /etc/app-config/DATABASE_URL; echo '---'; ls /etc/app-config/; sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - {name: app-config, mountPath: /etc/app-config}
  volumes:
  - name: app-config
    projected:
      sources:
      - configMap: {name: app-config}    # DATABASE_URL from ConfigMap
      - secret: {name: app-secret}        # ❌ BUG! Also has DATABASE_URL — overwrites ConfigMap!
      - downwardAPI:
          items:
          - {path: "pod-name", fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}
EOF
sleep 3
echo "=== Check which DATABASE_URL won ==="
kubectl exec easypj-api -n s72-config -- cat /etc/app-config/DATABASE_URL
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Secret Value Overwrites ConfigMap

✗1. DATABASE_URL file contains the Secret''s value — ConfigMap''s value is lost!
✗2. Later sources in projected volumes overwrite earlier sources with same key name
🔍

🔍 Debug — Rename Conflicting Keys

1Fix: Use unique key names across all sources in a projected volume
Projected volume sources with same key name cause silent data loss — later sources overwrite earlier ones

Tenet: Projected volumes combine multiple sources (ConfigMaps, Secrets, DownwardAPI, ServiceAccountToken) into one directory. If two sources have the same key, the LAST source listed wins — silently overwriting earlier values. Always use unique key names or separate mount paths for conflicting keys.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s72-config -- cat /etc/app-config/DATABASE_URL postgresql://user:pass@db:5432/jobpost ← Secret's value with EMBEDDED CREDENTIALS overwrote ConfigMap!
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s72-config -- ls /etc/app-config/ DATABASE_URL ← Only ONE file! ConfigMap's DATABASE_URL was silently overwritten API_KEY DEBUG pod-name
$ kubectl get cm app-config -n s72-config -o jsonpath='{.data.DATABASE_URL}' postgresql://db:5432/jobpost ← ConfigMap's correct value — LOST in projection!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s72-config -- ls /etc/app-config/ DB_URL ← ConfigMap key renamed to DB_URL ✅ DB_CREDS ← Secret key renamed to DB_CREDS ✅ DEBUG API_KEY pod-name ← No more conflicts — all sources have unique keys!
🔧
BASH — Use unique key names
kubectl delete cm app-config -n s72-config; kubectl delete secret app-secret -n s72-config
kubectl create cm app-config -n s72-config --from-literal=DB_URL=postgresql://db:5432/jobpost --from-literal=DEBUG=false
kubectl create secret generic app-secret -n s72-config --from-literal=DB_CREDS=postgresql://user:pass@db:5432/jobpost --from-literal=API_KEY=sk-abc123
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s72-config 2>/dev/null
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s72-config, labels: {app: easypj-api}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","cat /etc/app-config/DB_URL; echo '---'; ls /etc/app-config/; sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts: [{name: app-config, mountPath: /etc/app-config}]
  volumes:
  - name: app-config
    projected:
      sources:
      - configMap: {name: app-config}
      - secret: {name: app-secret}
EOF
kubectl exec easypj-api -n s72-config -- ls /etc/app-config/
✓

✅ Verify — No Key Conflicts, All Sources Intact

With unique key names (DB_URL from ConfigMap, DB_CREDS from Secret), all values are correctly available in the projected volume without any overwrites.

💡 Key takeaway: Projected volumes combine sources in order — later sources with same key names silently overwrite earlier ones. ALWAYS use unique key names across all projected volume sources.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s72-config
