🧪 SCENARIO S73 — Category 4: Config & Security envFrom

Empty Environment Variables — Creating ConfigMap from .env File with Comments

The Problem: The team created a ConfigMap from a .env file using --from-env-file. The .env file has comments (# Database settings) and blank lines. kubectl creates ConfigMap keys for the comments and blank lines — resulting in empty or garbage environment variables. Django gets an empty DATABASE_URL because the real value is on the line after a comment. Your job: clean the .env file before creating the ConfigMap.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Config generation on node "easy"
1

📋 Create ConfigMap from Dirty .env File (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The developer copied the .env file from the Git repo directly into a ConfigMap. The .env file has explanatory comments and blank lines for readability. kubectl create configmap --from-env-file treats EVERY non-empty line as a KEY=VALUE pair. Comment lines become keys with empty values, blank lines are ignored but can shift key-value associations.
📁 S73 STANDALONE:
~/s73-config/
├── .env               ← ❌ BUG: has comments (# lines) and blank lines!
├── configmap.yaml     ← Created from dirty .env — garbage keys
└── pod.yaml           ← envFrom uses dirty ConfigMap
BASH — Create ConfigMap from dirty .env.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S73: .env File with Comments → Empty ConfigMap Keys
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s73-config

cat > /tmp/s73-dirty.env << 'ENVEOF'
# Database Configuration
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://easypj-db:5432/jobpost
# Redis Configuration
REDIS_URL=redis://easypj-redis:6379/0
# Feature Flags
DEBUG=false
ENVEOF

# ❌ BUG! Creates keys from comment lines!
kubectl create cm easypj-env -n s73-config --from-env-file=/tmp/s73-dirty.env
echo "=== ConfigMap data — check for garbage keys! ==="
kubectl get cm easypj-env -n s73-config -o yaml | grep -A20 "^data:"
echo ""
echo "=== Create a pod using this ConfigMap ==="
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s73-config, labels: {app: easypj-api}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","env | sort; sleep 3600"]

    - configMapRef: {name: easypj-env}
EOF
sleep 3
echo "=== Environment variables from pod ==="
kubectl logs easypj-api -n s73-config

⚠️ Observe — Garbage Env Vars

✗1. kubectl get cm shows extra keys from comment lines
✗2. Pod env shows empty or malformed variables
🔍

🔍 Debug — Clean .env File First

1Clean the .env file: Remove comments (lines starting with #) and blank lines before creating ConfigMap
--from-env-file treats comment lines and empty lines as key-value pairs — creating garbage ConfigMap entries

Tenet: kubectl create configmap --from-env-file processes every line. Use grep to filter: grep -v '^#' .env | grep -v '^$' > clean.env before importing. Alternatively, use --from-literal for individual keys to avoid this issue entirely.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get cm easypj-env -n s73-config -o yaml | grep -A15 "^data:" data: "# Database Configuration": "" ← Garbage key! "# Feature Flags": "" ← Garbage key! "# Redis Configuration": "" ← Garbage key! DATABASE_URL: postgresql://easypj-db:5432/jobpost DEBUG: "false" REDIS_URL: redis://easypj-redis:6379/0
$ kubectl logs easypj-api -n s73-config | head -5 # Database Configuration= ← Empty/garbage env var! # Redis Configuration= ← Empty/garbage env var! # Feature Flags= ← Empty/garbage env var! DATABASE_URL=postgresql://easypj-db:5432/jobpost DEBUG=false
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix

🔧
BASH

kubectl delete cm easypj-env -n s73-config

kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s73-config 2>/dev/null

S74
🧪 SCENARIO S74 — Category 4: Config & Security TLS Secret

TLS Certificate Corrupted — Multiline PEM Pasted into YAML Wrong

The Problem: A developer created a TLS Secret by manually pasting a multi-line PEM certificate into a YAML file and applying it. The indentation was wrong — the PEM data wasn''t properly formatted. The Secret was created but the certificate data is garbled. Browsers show "Certificate Invalid" errors. Your job: use kubectl create secret tls instead of manually writing TLS YAML.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube) — TLS Secret creation
1

📋 Create TLS Cert, Then Make Secret the Wrong Way — Opaque Type + Wrong Keys (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The developer generated a TLS certificate for the job board domain. Instead of using kubectl create secret tls, they copy-pasted the PEM data into a YAML file. The multi-line certificate lost its line breaks during the paste, or the YAML indentation corrupted the base64 encoding. The Secret exists but the certificate data is invalid.
📁 S74 STANDALONE:
~/s74-config/
├── cert.pem    ← TLS certificate (generated by openssl)
└── key.pem     ← Private key (generated by openssl)
⚠️ NEVER write TLS Secret in YAML — use kubectl create secret tls!
BASH — Generate cert, create Secret the WRONG way.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S74: TLS Secret — Never Write in YAML
# CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s74-config
openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 \
  -keyout /tmp/s74-key.pem -out /tmp/s74-cert.pem \
  -subj "/CN=easypj.example.com"

echo "=== THE RIGHT WAY: kubectl create secret tls ==="
kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls -n s74-config \
  --cert=/tmp/s74-cert.pem --key=/tmp/s74-key.pem
echo "=== Secret type and keys ==="
kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n s74-config -o jsonpath='{.type}{"\n"}{.data}' | head -c 100
echo ""
echo "✅ kubectl create secret tls handles multiline PEM automatically!"
echo "❌ NEVER manually paste PEM data into YAML — use kubectl create secret tls"
⚠

⚠️ Key Lesson

✗1. Manually pasting multiline PEM into YAML breaks indentation and encoding
✗2. kubectl create secret tls handles encoding, line breaks, and type automatically
🔍

🔍 Debug — Always Use kubectl create secret tls

1Golden rule: kubectl create secret tls <name> --cert=<file> --key=<file>
Manually writing TLS Secrets in YAML leads to encoding errors, wrong types, and corrupted certificates

Tenet: NEVER write TLS Secrets in YAML manually. Always use kubectl create secret tls which handles: base64 encoding, correct type (kubernetes.io/tls), correct key names (tls.crt, tls.key), and multiline PEM formatting. On CKAD, this is a frequently tested command.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix — Manual YAML approach)
$ cat tls-secret.yaml # ❌ Manually pasted PEM in YAML apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: {name: easypj-tls} type: Opaque ← BUG 1: Wrong type! Should be kubernetes.io/tls data: cert: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi... ← BUG 2: Wrong key name! Should be tls.crt key: LS0tLS1CRUdJTi... ← BUG 3: Wrong key name! Should be tls.key # BUG 4: Base64 may be corrupted from copy-paste
$ curl -k https://easypj.example.com curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate ← Certificate invalid — garbled PEM from manual YAML!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls -n s74-config --cert=/tmp/s74-cert.pem --key=/tmp/s74-key.pem && kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n s74-config -o jsonpath='{.type}{"\n"}{.data}' | head -c 100 secret/easypj-tls created kubernetes.io/tls ← ✅ Correct type! {"tls.crt":"LS0tLS1...","tls.key":"LS0tLS1..."} ← ✅ Correct key names!
$ curl -k https://easypj.example.com HTTP/1.1 200 OK ✅ TLS working — valid certificate!
🔧
BASH — The correct way every time
kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls -n s74-config --cert=/tmp/s74-cert.pem --key=/tmp/s74-key.pem
kubectl get secret easypj-tls -n s74-config -o jsonpath='{.type}'
✓

✅ Verify — TLS Secret Has Correct Type and Keys

kubectl create secret tls automatically sets type kubernetes.io/tls and key names tls.crt and tls.key — the Ingress controller recognizes and uses it for TLS termination.

💡 Key takeaway: NEVER write TLS Secrets in YAML manually. ALWAYS use kubectl create secret tls --cert= --key=. It handles base64 encoding, correct type, correct key names, and multiline PEM automatically. This is a CKAD exam essential.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s74-config; rm -f /tmp/s74-*.pem

├── secret.yaml          ← BUG 2: Secret envFrom exposes password

🧪 SCENARIO S76 — Category 4: Config & Security LimitRange

Dev Pods Consume All Resources — LimitRange Defaults Set Too High

The Problem: A LimitRange was created in the dev namespace to set default resource limits. But the defaults were set to cpu: 2, memory: 4Gi — production-level defaults in a dev namespace. Developers deploy pods without specifying resources, and each pod gets 2 CPU / 4Gi by default, quickly exhausting the cluster. Your job: set appropriate LimitRange defaults for a development namespace.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Create LimitRange with Excessive Defaults — 2CPU/4Gi for Dev! (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The platform team copy-pasted the production LimitRange to the dev namespace. Every pod without explicit resources gets 2 CPU and 4Gi memory by default. With 10+ developers deploying pods, the cluster is perpetually starved.
📁 S76 STANDALONE:
~/s76-config/
├── limitrange.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: default 2 CPU / 4Gi for DEV namespace!
└── pod.yaml           ← Pod gets excessive defaults
BASH — Create LimitRange with way-too-high defaults.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S76: LimitRange Defaults Too High
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s76-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata: {name: dev-limits, namespace: s76-config}
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:
      cpu: "2000m"       # ❌ BUG! 2 CPU default for DEV!
      memory: "4Gi"      # ❌ BUG! 4Gi default for DEV!
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: "1000m"
      memory: "2Gi"
EOF
echo "=== LimitRange created with production-like defaults ==="
kubectl describe limitrange dev-limits -n s76-config
echo ""
echo "=== Deploy pod without resources — gets 2CPU/4Gi by default! ==="
kubectl run test-pod -n s76-config --image=busybox:1.36 -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pod test-pod -n s76-config -o yaml | grep -A4 resources
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Excessive Defaults

✗1. Pod gets 2 CPU / 4Gi by default — way too much for dev!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Set Dev-Appropriate Defaults

1Dev defaults: defaultRequest: 100m/128Mi, default: 500m/256Mi
Production LimitRange defaults copied to dev — pods consume excessive resources without explicit limits

Tenet: LimitRange sets default requests/limits for pods that don''t specify them. Use appropriate defaults per environment: dev (100m/128Mi), staging (250m/512Mi), prod (500m/1Gi+). Always check LimitRange with kubectl describe before debugging resource issues.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe limitrange dev-limits -n s76-config Type Resource Min Max Default Request Default Limit Container cpu - - 1000m 2000m ← 2 CPU default for DEV! Container memory - - 2Gi 4Gi ← 4Gi default for DEV!
$ kubectl get pod test-pod -n s76-config -o yaml | grep -A4 resources resources: limits: cpu: "2" ← Pod got 2 CPU by default! memory: 4Gi ← Pod got 4Gi by default! requests: cpu: "1" memory: 2Gi ← Way too much for a dev namespace!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl describe limitrange dev-limits -n s76-config Type Resource Min Max Default Request Default Limit Container cpu - - 100m 500m ← Dev-appropriate! Container memory - - 128Mi 256Mi ← Dev-appropriate!
🔧
BASH
kubectl delete limitrange dev-limits -n s76-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata: {name: dev-limits, namespace: s76-config}
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default: {cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi"}
    defaultRequest: {cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi"}
EOF
echo "✅ Dev-appropriate defaults set"
✓

✅ Verify — Dev-Appropriate Defaults Applied

With defaultRequest: 100m/128Mi and default: 500m/256Mi, developer pods get reasonable resource allocations without overwhelming the cluster.

💡 Key takeaway: LimitRange sets defaults for pods without explicit resources. Use environment-appropriate defaults: dev=100m/128Mi, staging=250m/512Mi, production=500m/1Gi+. Always check with kubectl describe limitrange.

🧪 SCENARIO S77 — Category 4: Config & Security PSS

Pod Creation Rejected — Pod Security Standard Baseline Blocks hostNetwork

The Problem: The security team applied the baseline Pod Security Standard to the namespace. A monitoring pod that uses hostNetwork: true for network metrics is now rejected at admission time. The baseline policy prohibits hostNetwork. Your job: understand PSS enforcement and either remove hostNetwork or apply the correct policy level.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Apply Baseline PSS, Then Try Deploying hostNetwork Pod — Admission Rejects It! (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The security team enforced baseline PSS: "enforce=baseline". A monitoring pod that needs hostNetwork for accurate node-level metrics is now blocked. Baseline PSS prohibits: hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC, hostPorts, AppArmor, SELinux, /proc mount, and privileged containers.
📁 S77 STANDALONE:
~/s77-config/
└── pod.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: hostNetwork: true — blocked by baseline PSS!
BASH — Apply baseline PSS, try deploying hostNetwork pod.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S77: PSS Baseline Blocks hostNetwork
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s77-config
kubectl label ns s77-config pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline --overwrite
echo "=== Baseline PSS enforced on namespace ==="
echo ""
echo "=== Try to deploy pod with hostNetwork (WILL BE REJECTED!) ==="
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: monitor-agent, namespace: s77-config}
spec:
  hostNetwork: true    # ❌ BUG! Baseline PSS prohibits hostNetwork!
  containers:
  - name: agent
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF
echo ""
echo "=== Check if pod was created ==="
kubectl get pods -n s77-config 2>&1
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Pod Rejected by PSS

✗1. kubectl apply output: "violates PodSecurity 'baseline:latest': hostNetwork"
✗2. Baseline PSS is a built-in admission controller — no external tools needed
🔍

🔍 Debug — PSS Levels

1PSS levels: privileged (unrestricted), baseline (minimally restrictive, blocks known escalations), restricted (heavily restricted, follows hardening best practices)
Baseline PSS blocks hostNetwork — either remove hostNetwork from pod or use privileged PSS level with explicit exception

Tenet: Pod Security Standards (PSS) enforces pod security at the namespace level via built-in admission. Three levels: privileged, baseline, restricted. Use kubectl label ns <name> pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=<level> to apply. On CKAD, understanding PSS levels and what each blocks is important.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl apply -f monitor-pod.yaml Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "monitor-pod.yaml": pods "monitor-agent" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "baseline:latest": hostNetwork (container "agent" must not set securityContext.hostNetwork=true) ← Baseline PSS REJECTS hostNetwork!
$ kubectl get pods -n s77-config No resources found in s77-config namespace. ← Pod was blocked at admission — never created!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl label ns s77-config pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged --overwrite && kubectl apply -f monitor-pod.yaml namespace/s77-config labeled pod/monitor-agent created ✅ Created with privileged PSS!
$ kubectl get pods -n s77-config NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE monitor-agent 1/1 Running 0 10s ✅ Monitoring pod running!
🔧
BASH — Switch to privileged PSS level
kubectl label ns s77-config pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged --overwrite
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: monitor-agent, namespace: s77-config}
spec:
  hostNetwork: true
  containers:
  - {name: agent, image: busybox:1.36, command: ["sleep","3600"]}
EOF
kubectl get pods -n s77-config
✓

✅ Verify — Pod Created Under Privileged PSS

With privileged PSS level, the hostNetwork pod is now allowed. For production monitoring, consider using a dedicated namespace with privileged PSS and strict RBAC.

💡 Key takeaway: Pod Security Standards (PSS) has 3 levels: privileged, baseline, restricted. Baseline blocks: hostNetwork, hostPID, hostIPC, hostPorts. Use kubectl label ns with pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce to set the level. Always check PSS before deploying privileged workloads.

S78
🧪 SCENARIO S78 — Category 4: Config & Security Downward API

Label Files Are Empty — fieldPath Uses annotations Instead of labels

The Problem: The monitoring system reads pod labels (version, environment) from files in /etc/pod-info/. The Downward API volume was configured but the version and environment files are empty. The developer used fieldPath: metadata.annotations[''version''] instead of metadata.labels[''version'']. Labels and annotations are different — the Downward API reads from the specified source, and the pod has labels (not annotations) for version/environment. Your job: fix the fieldPath to reference labels instead of annotations.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
1

📋 Deploy with Wrong fieldPath — Reads Annotations Not Labels (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The SRE team set up a monitoring agent that reads pod metadata from /etc/pod-info/. They configured a Downward API volume to expose version and environment. But the developer confused labels with annotations — they used fieldPath: metadata.annotations[''version'']. The pod has these as LABELS, not annotations. The files are created but they're EMPTY because annotations have no matching keys. The monitoring dashboard shows "unknown" for version and environment.
📁 S78 STANDALONE:
~/s78-config/
└── pod.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: fieldPath uses annotations instead of labels!
BASH — Deploy pod with wrong fieldPath for labels.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S78: Downward API Volume — Wrong fieldPath
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s78-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s78-config
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
    version: v2.1
    environment: production
    team: platform
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'version='$(cat /etc/pod-info/version); echo 'env='$(cat /etc/pod-info/environment); echo 'name='$(cat /etc/pod-info/pod-name); sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts:
    - {name: pod-info, mountPath: /etc/pod-info}
  volumes:
  - name: pod-info
    downwardAPI:
      items:
      - {path: "version", fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.annotations[''version'']}}       # ❌ BUG! Uses annotations — pod has LABELS not annotations!
      - {path: "environment", fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.annotations[''environment'']}} # ❌ BUG! Both files will be EMPTY!
      - {path: "pod-name", fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}                            # ✅ This one is correct
EOF
sleep 3
echo "=== Version file (should show v2.1 — but is EMPTY!) ==="
kubectl exec easypj-api -n s78-config -- cat /etc/pod-info/version
echo "(empty output above — version file exists but has no content!)"
echo ""
echo "=== All files in /etc/pod-info/ ==="
kubectl exec easypj-api -n s78-config -- ls -la /etc/pod-info/
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Version and Environment Files Are Empty

✗1. kubectl exec ... -- cat /etc/pod-info/version → EMPTY OUTPUT! File exists but has no content
✗2. kubectl exec ... -- cat /etc/pod-info/environment → EMPTY!
✗3. pod-name file IS populated — that fieldPath is correct
✗4. The pod has labels version=v2.1 and environment=production — but the Downward API is reading from annotations (which are empty)!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Labels vs Annotations in Downward API

1Check pod labels: kubectl get pod easypj-api -n s78-config --show-labels → version=v2.1, environment=production
→ Labels ARE set correctly on the pod
2Check Downward API fieldPath: kubectl get pod easypj-api -n s78-config -o yaml | grep -A2 fieldRef
fieldPath: metadata.annotations[''version''] — reads ANNOTATIONS but pod has LABELS! Labels and annotations are different maps — the Downward API reads from the one you specify.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Version file empty → Check fieldPath
②
fieldPath: metadata.annotations['version']
③
Pod has LABELS not annotations → fieldPath reads wrong source
④
Change to metadata.labels['version']
⑤
Files now populated — monitoring dashboard works!

Tenet: Kubernetes has TWO metadata maps: metadata.labels (for identifying/selecting resources) and metadata.annotations (for non-identifying metadata). The Downward API reads from whichever you specify in fieldPath. metadata.labels[''key''] reads from labels; metadata.annotations[''key''] reads from annotations. They are NOT interchangeable — confusing them is a common CKAD mistake.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s78-config -- cat /etc/pod-info/version (empty — no output!) ← Version file exists but has NO content!
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s78-config -- cat /etc/pod-info/environment (empty — no output!) ← Environment file also empty!
$ kubectl get pod easypj-api -n s78-config --show-labels NAME READY STATUS LABELS easypj-api 1/1 Running app=easypj-api,version=v2.1,environment=production,team=platform ← Labels ARE set! But fieldPath reads annotations (none exist)
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s78-config -- cat /etc/pod-info/version v2.1 ✅ Version label now correctly exposed as file!
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s78-config -- cat /etc/pod-info/environment production ✅ Environment label correctly exposed!
🔧
BASH — Patch the pod volume to use labels
kubectl delete pod easypj-api -n s78-config
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: s78-config
  labels: {app: easypj-api, version: v2.1, environment: production, team: platform}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","cat /etc/pod-info/version; cat /etc/pod-info/environment; sleep 3600"]
    volumeMounts: [{name: pod-info, mountPath: /etc/pod-info}]
  volumes:
  - name: pod-info
    downwardAPI:
      items:
      - {path: "version", fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.labels[''version'']}}        # ✅ Fixed: labels not annotations!
      - {path: "environment", fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.labels[''environment'']}}  # ✅ Fixed!
      - {path: "pod-name", fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.name}}
EOF
kubectl exec easypj-api -n s78-config -- cat /etc/pod-info/version
kubectl exec easypj-api -n s78-config -- cat /etc/pod-info/environment
✓

✅ Verify — Labels Correctly Exposed as Files

After changing metadata.annotations to metadata.labels, the version and environment files now contain the correct values. The monitoring dashboard can read pod metadata reliably.

💡 Key takeaway: Downward API fieldPaths are specific: metadata.labels[''key''] reads LABELS, metadata.annotations[''key''] reads ANNOTATIONS. They are different maps — always verify which one your pod uses. Labels are for selectors; annotations are for non-identifying metadata.

kubectl delete ns s78-config
S79
🧪 SCENARIO S79 — Category 4: Config & Security Secret

Secret Value Is Base64 Garbage — Double-Encoded by Mistake

The Problem: A developer created a Secret from a file that was ALREADY base64-encoded. kubectl create secret generic base64-encodes all values automatically. The password was base64-encoded twice — when the app decodes it, it gets base64 text instead of the original password. Your job: understand that kubectl auto-encodes values and ensure the source data is plain text.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube)
1

📋 Create Secret with Pre-Encoded Value — Double-Encoding Bug! (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The security guidelines say "passwords must be base64-encoded." The developer base64-encoded the password before storing it. Then kubectl base64-encodes it AGAIN when creating the Secret. The app gets double-base64-decoded garbage instead of the actual password.
📁 S79 STANDALONE:
~/s79-config/
⚠️ BUG: Pre-base64-encoded value → kubectl encodes AGAIN → double-encoding!
✅ FIX: Pass PLAIN TEXT — kubectl handles base64 encoding automatically
BASH — Demonstrate double-encoding problem.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S79: Double Base64 Encoding
# CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s79-config

# ❌ BUG! Value is PRE-ENCODED — kubectl will encode it AGAIN!
ALREADY_ENCODED=$(echo -n "MyPassword123" | base64)
kubectl create secret generic easypj-creds -n s79-config \
  --from-literal=password="$ALREADY_ENCODED"

echo "=== Secret value (base64-decoded once) ==="
kubectl get secret easypj-creds -n s79-config -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
echo ""
echo "^^^ Still base64! App would need to decode TWICE to get the real password."

echo ""
echo "=== THE RIGHT WAY: kubectl auto-encodes plain text ==="
kubectl create secret generic easypj-creds-correct -n s79-config \
  --from-literal=password="MyPassword123"
kubectl get secret easypj-creds-correct -n s79-config -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
echo ""
echo "✅ Plain text password — kubectl handled the encoding correctly!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Double Encoded

✗1. Decoding once still gives base64 text — not the original password
✗2. kubectl create secret ALWAYS base64-encodes — never pre-encode values!
🔍

🔍 Debug — kubectl ALWAYS Base64-Encodes, Never Pre-Encode

1Check the raw Secret data: kubectl get secret easypj-creds -n s79-config -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d → Still base64 text!
kubectl encode ONCE. If input is already base64, the result is double-encoded. ALWAYS pass PLAIN TEXT to kubectl create secret.

Tenet: kubectl create secret --from-literal and --from-file ALWAYS base64-encode the values automatically. Never pre-encode values before passing them to kubectl. The Secret''s .data field contains base64-encoded values — when mounted as a volume or env var, Kubernetes automatically decodes them.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix — Double-Encoded)
$ kubectl get secret easypj-creds -n s79-config -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d TXlQYXNzd29yZDEyMw== ← STILL base64! App decodes once and gets GARBAGE!
$ kubectl get secret easypj-creds -n s79-config -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d | base64 -d MyPassword123 ← Need to decode TWICE to get the real password!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get secret easypj-creds-correct -n s79-config -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d MyPassword123 ✅ Single decode gives the correct plaintext password!
$ echo "Golden rule: kubectl ALWAYS base64-encodes. Pass PLAIN TEXT values." Golden rule: kubectl ALWAYS base64-encodes. Pass PLAIN TEXT values.
🔧
BASH — The golden rule
kubectl create secret generic easypj-creds-correct -n s79-config --from-literal=password="MyPassword123"
kubectl get secret easypj-creds-correct -n s79-config -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
echo ""
echo "Single decode = plain text password. kubectl encoded it ONCE, as expected."
✓

✅ Verify — Correct Single-Encoded Secret

When you pass plain text to kubectl create secret, it encodes ONCE. When the application reads the value via volume mount, Kubernetes auto-decodes it — giving the original plain text.

💡 Key takeaway: kubectl create secret ALWAYS base64-encodes input values. NEVER pre-encode data before passing to kubectl — this causes double-encoding. Pass plain text values and let kubectl handle encoding.

⚠️ Audit Findings — 5 Security Issues

✗1. Runs as root (UID 0) — missing runAsNonRoot
✗2. Secrets exposed via envFrom — visible in kubectl describe
✗3. No resource requests/limits — can consume all node resources
✗4. All Linux capabilities present — no capability dropping
✗5. Default ServiceAccount — no RBAC isolation

🔍 Debug — Audit Checklist for Security Hardening

1Check running user: kubectl exec easypj-api -n s80-config -- id → uid=0(root) — should be non-root!
→ Add runAsNonRoot: true + runAsUser: 101
2Check Secrets exposure: kubectl describe pod easypj-api -n s80-config | grep -A5 Environment → DB_PASSWORD in plain text!
Secrets as envFrom are visible in kubectl describe — mount as volumes instead
3Check resources + capabilities + ServiceAccount: kubectl get pod easypj-api -n s80-config -o yaml → no resources, no capabilities drop, default SA

Complete security hardening checklist: ① runAsNonRoot + runAsUser, ② readOnlyRootFilesystem + emptyDirs, ③ drop ALL capabilities + add NET_BIND_SERVICE, ④ Secrets as volume mounts, ⑤ resource requests==limits (Guaranteed QoS), ⑥ dedicated ServiceAccount + minimal RBAC, ⑦ immutable ConfigMaps/Secrets. This is the CKAD security blueprint.

S81
🧪 SCENARIO S81 — Category 5: Services & Networking ClusterIP

Pods Can't Reach API Internally — Service targetPort Doesn't Match containerPort

The Problem: The easypj-api Deployment runs 3 pods on port 8000. A ClusterIP Service named "easypj-api" was created, but other pods get connection refused when curling easypj-api:8000. The Service has targetPort: 8080 but the container listens on port 8000 — the port numbers don't match. Your job: fix the targetPort so the Service routes traffic to the correct container port.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Single-node on "easy"
1

📋 Deploy API Pod + Service with Wrong targetPort (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The platform team created a ClusterIP Service so internal services can reach the easypj API. But the monitoring pod keeps getting "connection refused." The developer copied a Service YAML from another project and changed the name but forgot to update targetPort — it's still 8080 from the old project, while the Django app listens on 8000.
📁 S81 STANDALONE:
~/s81-networking/
├── deploy.yaml    ← Deployment: containerPort 8000
└── svc.yaml       ← ❌ BUG: targetPort: 8080 — doesn't match containerPort!
BASH — Deploy API + broken Service.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S81: ClusterIP — targetPort Mismatch
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s81-networking

# Deploy API pods (listening on port 8000)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s81-networking, labels: {app: easypj-api, scenario: s81}}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: easypj-api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: python:3.12-alpine
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c"]
        args:
        - |
          cat > /app.py << 'PYEOF'
import http.server, json
class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(json.dumps({"service":"easypj-api","pod":"PLACEHOLDER"}).encode())
import os, socket
http.server.HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0",8000),H).serve_forever()
PYEOF
          sed -i "s/PLACEHOLDER/$HOSTNAME/" /app.py
          python3 /app.py
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /, port: 8000}
          periodSeconds: 3; failureThreshold: 2
EOF

kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods -l app=easypj-api -n s81-networking --timeout=60s

# ❌ BUG! targetPort: 8080 — but container listens on 8000!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s81-networking}
spec:
  selector: {app: easypj-api}
  ports:
  - port: 8000
    targetPort: 8080    # ❌ BUG! Should be 8000!
    protocol: TCP
EOF

# Test with a debug pod — connection will FAIL!
kubectl run test-pod -n s81-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -- wget -qO- http://easypj-api:8000/ 2>&1 || echo "Connection REFUSED — targetPort mismatch!"
echo ""
echo "=== Check Endpoints ==="
kubectl get endpoints easypj-api -n s81-networking
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Connection Refused from Test Pod

✗1. wget http://easypj-api:8000/ → Connection refused or timeout
✗2. Endpoints exist: kubectl get endpoints easypj-api -n s81-networking → Shows pod IPs but on port 8080!
✗3. Pod is Running and Ready — but the Service routes to wrong port!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Service targetPort vs containerPort

1Check Service port mapping: kubectl describe svc easypj-api -n s81-networking | grep -A3 Port
→ targetPort: 8080, but containerPort is 8000!
2Check container port: kubectl get deploy easypj-api -n s81-networking -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].ports}'
Service targetPort (8080) doesn't match containerPort (8000) — traffic goes to wrong port on pod!
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
curl easypj-api:8000 fails → Check Service endpoints
②
Endpoints show pod IPs but wrong port → Check targetPort
③
targetPort: 8080 but containerPort: 8000 → MISMATCH!
④
Patch targetPort to 8000 → Endpoints update
⑤
curl works — Service routes correctly!

Tenet: Service port is the port the Service listens on. targetPort is the port on the pod that traffic is forwarded to. They don't have to be the same number, but targetPort MUST match the containerPort in the pod spec. If they don't match, the Service creates Endpoints pointing to a port where nothing is listening.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl run test -n s81-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -- wget -qO- http://easypj-api:8000/ wget: can't connect to remote host: Connection refused ← Service resolves but routes to wrong container port!
$ kubectl describe svc easypj-api -n s81-networking | grep -A3 Port Port: http 8000/TCP TargetPort: 8080/TCP ← ❌ BUG! Should be 8000! Endpoints: 10.244.1.5:8080,10.244.1.6:8080
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch svc easypj-api -n s81-networking -p '{"spec":{"ports":[{"port":8000,"targetPort":8000,"protocol":"TCP"}]}}' service/easypj-api patched
$ kubectl run test -n s81-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -- wget -qO- http://easypj-api:8000/ {"service":"easypj-api","pod":"easypj-api-7d9f8b-x2k9m"} ✅ API responding!
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch svc easypj-api -n s81-networking --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/ports/0/targetPort","value":8000}
]'
kubectl get endpoints easypj-api -n s81-networking
kubectl run test -n s81-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -- wget -qO- http://easypj-api:8000/
✓

✅ Verify — Service Routes to Correct Port

After fixing targetPort to 8000, the Service endpoints now point to the correct container port. Internal clients can reach the API via DNS name easypj-api:8000.

💡 Key takeaway: Service port = Service's listening port. targetPort = pod's port. targetPort MUST match the actual port your application listens on. Use kubectl describe svc to verify endpoint mappings.

Endpoints Empty — Service Selector Doesn't Match Pod Labels

The Problem: A Service "easypj-db" was created to expose the PostgreSQL pod. But kubectl get endpoints easypj-db shows <none> — the Service isn't routing to any pods. The Service selector says app: easypj but the pod labels are app: easypj-db, tier: backend. The selector must match pod labels EXACTLY. Your job: fix the Service selector to match the pod labels.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-node for Service testing
1

📋 Deploy PostgreSQL Pod + Service with Wrong Selector (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The DBA deployed a PostgreSQL pod with labels app: easypj-db, tier: backend. The platform team created a Service with selector app: easypj — thinking "easypj" would match all easypj apps. Kubernetes selectors are exact match, not prefix match. "app: easypj" doesn't match "app: easypj-db" — the Service has zero endpoints and all database connections fail.
📁 S82 STANDALONE:
~/s82-networking/
├── pod.yaml    ← PostgreSQL pod: labels {app: easypj-db, tier: backend}
└── svc.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: selector {app: easypj} — doesn't match pod labels!
BASH — Deploy pod + Service with wrong selector.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S82: Service Selector Mismatch
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s82-networking

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: s82-networking
  labels:
    app: easypj-db        # Pod label is "easypj-db"
    tier: backend
    scenario: s82
spec:
  containers:
  - name: postgres
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'PostgreSQL ready on 5432'; nc -lk -p 5432 -e echo 'DB_OK'"]
    ports: [{containerPort: 5432}]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-db, namespace: s82-networking}
spec:
  selector:
    app: easypj          # ❌ BUG! "easypj" ≠ "easypj-db" — NO match!
  ports:
  - port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
EOF

echo "=== Service Endpoints — will be EMPTY! ==="
kubectl get endpoints easypj-db -n s82-networking
echo ""
echo "=== Check pod labels ==="
kubectl get pods -n s82-networking --show-labels
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Endpoints Empty

✗1. kubectl get endpoints easypj-db -n s82-networking → <none> — NO endpoints!
✗2. Pod IS running: kubectl get pods -n s82-networking → easypj-db is Ready
✗3. Service selector: app=easypj, Pod labels: app=easypj-db — EXACT match required!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Service Selector Must Match Pod Labels Exactly

1Check pod labels: kubectl get pods -n s82-networking --show-labels
→ Pod has app=easypj-db, Service selector wants app=easypj — mismatch!
2Fix: Service selectors are AND-based exact match. All labels in the selector must exist on the pod with exactly the same values.
Service selector {app: easypj} doesn't match any pod — pods have {app: easypj-db}. Selectors are exact string match, not pattern/prefix match.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
DB connections fail → Check Service endpoints
②
kubectl get endpoints → <none> — no pods matched
③
Compare selector vs pod labels → app values differ
④
Patch selector to app: easypj-db
⑤
Endpoints populated → DB reachable!

Tenet: Service selectors use EXACT string matching. {app: easypj} matches ONLY pods with app=easypj — NOT app=easypj-db or app=easypj-api. Each key-value pair in the selector must match a pod label exactly. Selectors are AND-based: ALL specified labels must match.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get endpoints easypj-db -n s82-networking NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-db <none> 5m ← NO endpoints! Service can't route to any pod!
$ kubectl get pods -n s82-networking --show-labels NAME READY LABELS easypj-db 1/1 app=easypj-db,tier=backend,scenario=s82 ← Pod has app=easypj-db, but Service selector wants app=easypj!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch svc easypj-db -n s82-networking --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/selector/app","value":"easypj-db"}]' service/easypj-db patched
$ kubectl get endpoints easypj-db -n s82-networking NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-db 10.244.2.5:5432 6m ✅ Endpoint populated!
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch svc easypj-db -n s82-networking --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/selector/app","value":"easypj-db"}
]'
kubectl get endpoints easypj-db -n s82-networking
✓

✅ Verify — Service Now Routes to PostgreSQL Pod

After fixing the selector to app: easypj-db, the Service now matches the pod and creates the correct endpoint. All database connections succeed.

💡 Key takeaway: Service selectors are EXACT match, not pattern/prefix. {app: easypj} ≠ {app: easypj-db}. Always verify with kubectl get endpoints <svc> — empty endpoints = selector mismatch.

🔍 Debug — Find the Correct NodePort

1Check Service details: kubectl get svc easypj-web -n s83-networking -o wide

①

EOF

# Test DNS resolution from a debug pod
kubectl run test-pod -n s84-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -- nslookup easypj-db 2>&1 || true
echo ""
echo "=== Service resolves to wrong external name ==="
kubectl get svc easypj-db -n s84-networking -o jsonpath='{.spec.externalName}'
echo ""
⚠

⚠️ Observe — DNS Resolves to Old Endpoint

✗1. nslookup easypj-db → Returns CNAME to old RDS endpoint
✗2. Django connection fails: could not translate host name "easypj-db-old..."
✗3. The new RDS endpoint is: easypj-prod.xyz.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com
🔍

🔍 Debug — ExternalName Points to Decommissioned Host

1Check the ExternalName value: kubectl get svc easypj-db -n s84-networking -o jsonpath='{.spec.externalName}'
ExternalName references "easypj-db-old" — the old RDS instance was decommissioned. Must update to the new endpoint: "easypj-prod.xyz.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com"
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Django DB connection fails → Check Service
②
Service type is ExternalName → Check externalName
③
ExternalName points to OLD RDS endpoint
④
Update to new RDS endpoint
⑤
Django connects to new RDS successfully!

Tenet: ExternalName Services provide a DNS CNAME alias — they don't proxy traffic. When a pod resolves easypj-db, CoreDNS returns a CNAME pointing to the external host. The pod then connects directly to that external host. Always verify externalName is current — DNS resolution will happily point to a decommissioned host.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get svc easypj-db -n s84-networking -o jsonpath='{.spec.externalName}' easypj-db-old.xyz.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com ← OLD RDS, DECOMMISSIONED!
$ kubectl run test -n s84-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -- nslookup easypj-db Name: easypj-db.s84-networking.svc.cluster.local easypj-db.s84-networking.svc.cluster.local canonical name = easypj-db-old.xyz.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com ← CNAME points to OLD, non-existent host!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch svc easypj-db -n s84-networking -p '{"spec":{"externalName":"easypj-prod.xyz.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com"}}' service/easypj-db patched

🔧
BASH

kubectl get svc easypj-db -n s84-networking -o jsonpath='{.spec.externalName}'
✓

✅ Verify — ExternalName Points to New RDS

After updating the ExternalName to the new RDS endpoint, Django can resolve and connect to the production database. All jobs and user data are accessible.

💡 Key takeaway: ExternalName Services create DNS CNAME records — they don't proxy traffic. To update, patch the externalName field. ExternalName is great for external DBs, SaaS endpoints, and cross-cluster services.

StatefulSet Pods Have Same DNS Name — clusterIP Not Set to None

The Problem: easypj-db is now a StatefulSet with 3 replicas (postgres-0, postgres-1, postgres-2). Each pod needs its own stable DNS A record. A Service was created but clusterIP is set (not None) — all pods share a single DNS name instead of getting individual records. Direct pod-to-pod communication fails because DNS returns the Service IP, not individual pod IPs. Your job: make the Service headless by setting clusterIP: None.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — Multi-node StatefulSet
1

📋 Deploy StatefulSet + Regular Service (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The DBA set up a PostgreSQL StatefulSet for high availability. Each replica needs a stable network identity: postgres-0, postgres-1, postgres-2. But the developer created a regular ClusterIP Service — DNS returns a single virtual IP shared by all pods. The application can't address individual pods for read replicas, and replication setup fails.
📁 S85 STANDALONE:
~/s85-networking/
├── sts.yaml    ← StatefulSet: 3 replicas
└── svc.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: clusterIP set — should be None for headless!
BASH — Deploy StatefulSet with regular (non-headless) Service.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S85: Headless Service — clusterIP Not None
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s85-networking

# ❌ BUG! Regular Service — clusterIP is auto-assigned!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-db, namespace: s85-networking}
spec:
  selector: {app: easypj-db}
  ports:
  - port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
    name: postgres
# Missing clusterIP: None — this is a regular ClusterIP Service!
EOF

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata: {name: easypj-db, namespace: s85-networking}
spec:
  serviceName: easypj-db
  replicas: 3
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-db}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: easypj-db}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo Pod=$HOSTNAME; nc -lk -p 5432 -e echo $HOSTNAME"]
        ports: [{containerPort: 5432}]
EOF

sleep 10
echo "=== DNS resolution — returns single ClusterIP, not individual pod IPs ==="
kubectl run test -n s85-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -- nslookup easypj-db 2>&1 || true
echo ""
echo "=== Try to resolve individual pod DNS (will FAIL) ==="
kubectl run test2 -n s85-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -- nslookup easypj-db-0.easypj-db 2>&1 || echo "Individual pod DNS NOT available!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Individual Pod DNS Not Available

✗1. nslookup easypj-db → Returns single ClusterIP — all traffic goes through Service IP
✗2. nslookup easypj-db-0.easypj-db → NXDOMAIN — no individual pod DNS!
✗3. clusterIP is set — headless requires clusterIP: None!

🔍 Debug — Headless Service Requirements

1Check Service type: kubectl get svc easypj-db -n s85-networking → CLUSTER-IP shows an IP (not None)
Headless Services require clusterIP: None — this creates individual DNS A records for each pod instead of a single virtual IP
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod-to-pod communication fails → Check DNS
②
nslookup returns single IP → Not headless
③
kubectl get svc → CLUSTER-IP is set, not None
④
Set clusterIP: None → Recreate Service
⑤
Individual pod DNS works: pod-0.svc.ns!

Tenet: Headless Services (clusterIP: None) don't get a virtual IP. Instead, DNS returns A records for each ready pod. Pod DNS: <pod-name>.<service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Essential for StatefulSets, databases, and any app that needs to address individual pods.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get svc easypj-db -n s85-networking NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP PORT(S) AGE easypj-db ClusterIP 10.96.100.50 5432/TCP 5m ← clusterIP is 10.96.100.50 — NOT headless!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl delete svc easypj-db -n s85-networking && kubectl create service clusterip easypj-db -n s85-networking --tcp=5432:5432 --clusterip=None service/easypj-db created
$ kubectl get svc easypj-db -n s85-networking NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP PORT(S) AGE easypj-db ClusterIP None 5432/TCP 5s ✅ Headless!
🔧
BASH
kubectl delete svc easypj-db -n s85-networking
kubectl create service clusterip easypj-db -n s85-networking --tcp=5432:5432 --clusterip=None
kubectl get svc easypj-db -n s85-networking
✓

✅ Verify — Headless Service Created

With clusterIP: None, DNS returns individual pod A records. Each StatefulSet pod now has a stable DNS identity for direct communication.

💡 Key takeaway: Headless = clusterIP: None. DNS returns pod IPs instead of Service IP. Required for StatefulSets. Pod DNS: <pod>.<svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local.

Ingress Returns 404 — Missing ingressClassName

The Problem: An Ingress was created to route easypj.example.com to the easypj-web Service. But curl returns 404 Not Found from the default backend. 🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab) — NGINX Ingress controller pre-installed
1

📋 Deploy Web Service + Ingress Without ingressClassName (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The platform team deployed the NGINX Ingress controller and created an Ingress resource for the job board. But traffic keeps hitting the default backend 404 page. The Ingress YAML was copied from an old tutorial that used the deprecated kubernetes.io/ingress.class annotation — but this cluster uses the modern ingressClassName field. Without it, no controller claims the Ingress.
📁 S86 STANDALONE:
~/s86-networking/
├── deploy.yaml    ← Web Deployment
├── svc.yaml       ← ClusterIP Service
└── ingress.yaml   ← ❌ BUG: missing ingressClassName!
BASH — Deploy web + Ingress without ingressClassName.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S86: Ingress — Missing ingressClassName
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s86-networking
kubectl run easypj-web -n s86-networking --image=nginx:alpine --port=80 --labels=app=easypj-web
kubectl expose pod easypj-web -n s86-networking --port=80 --target-port=80

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: easypj-ingress, namespace: s86-networking}
spec:
# ❌ BUG! No ingressClassName — no controller picks this up!
  rules:
  - host: easypj.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service: {name: easypj-web, port: {number: 80}}
EOF

INGRESS_IP=$(kubectl get ingress easypj-ingress -n s86-networking -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}' 2>/dev/null || echo "PENDING")
echo "=== Ingress IP: $INGRESS_IP (may be pending — no ingressClassName!) ==="

curl -s -H "Host: easypj.example.com" http://$INGRESS_IP/ 2>&1 || echo "No IP assigned yet — check kubectl describe ingress"

⚠️ Observe — 404 or No IP Assigned

✗1. kubectl get ingress -n s86-networking → ADDRESS may show nothing or pending
✗2. curl returns 404 — default backend, not the web Service
✗3. No ingressClassName specified — no controller claims this Ingress!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Ingress Controller Class

1Check Ingress status: kubectl describe ingress easypj-ingress -n s86-networking — no events, no address
Without ingressClassName: nginx, the NGINX Ingress controller ignores this Ingress resource. Every Ingress must declare which controller should handle it.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
curl returns 404 → Check Ingress status
②
kubectl get ingress → No ADDRESS assigned
③
Missing ingressClassName → Add nginx
④
Controller picks up Ingress → IP assigned
⑤
curl returns 200 — web page served!

Tenet: Every Ingress needs ingressClassName to tell the cluster which Ingress controller should handle it. Without it, no controller claims the resource. Common values: nginx, traefik, haproxy. The deprecated kubernetes.io/ingress.class annotation still works but ingressClassName is the modern standard.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get ingress -n s86-networking NAME CLASS HOSTS ADDRESS AGE easypj-ingress <none> easypj.example.com 5m ← No address!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch ingress easypj-ingress -n s86-networking -p '{"spec":{"ingressClassName":"nginx"}}' ingress.networking.k8s.io/easypj-ingress patched ✅ Controller now handles it!
🔧
BASH

kubectl get ingress -n s86-networking
✓

✅ Verify — Ingress Routes Correctly

With ingressClassName: nginx, the controller picks up the Ingress and routes traffic to the web Service. curl -H "Host: easypj.example.com" http://INGRESS_IP/ returns the web page.

💡 Key takeaway: Always specify ingressClassName in Ingress specs. Check available controllers: kubectl get ingressclasses. The deprecated annotation still works but is not recommended for CKAD.

🧪 SCENARIO S87 — Category 5: Services & Networking Ingress TLS

HTTPS Serves Fake Cert — Ingress TLS References Wrong Secret Name

The Problem: A TLS Secret was created for easypj.example.com, but browsers still show "Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate". The Ingress tls section references secretName: easypj-cert but the actual Secret is named easypj-tls — a typo in the Ingress spec. Your job: fix the secretName in the Ingress TLS configuration.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
1

📋 Create TLS Secret + Ingress with Wrong secretName (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The security team mandated HTTPS. The DevOps engineer generated a cert, created a TLS Secret named "easypj-tls", and added TLS to the Ingress. But in the Ingress YAML, they typed secretName: "easypj-cert" — a name they used in staging. The production Secret is "easypj-tls". The Ingress can't find the Secret and falls back to the default fake certificate.
📁 S87 STANDALONE:
~/s87-networking/
├── cert.pem + key.pem    ← TLS certificate files
├── secret.yaml           ← TLS Secret: name=easypj-tls
└── ingress.yaml          ← ❌ BUG: tls secretName: easypj-cert!
BASH — Deploy TLS Secret + Ingress with wrong secretName.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S87: Ingress TLS — Wrong Secret Name
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s87-networking
kubectl run easypj-web -n s87-networking --image=nginx:alpine --port=80 --labels=app=easypj-web
kubectl expose pod easypj-web -n s87-networking --port=80

openssl req -x509 -nodes -days 365 -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout /tmp/s87-key.pem -out /tmp/s87-cert.pem -subj "/CN=easypj.example.com"
kubectl create secret tls easypj-tls -n s87-networking --cert=/tmp/s87-cert.pem --key=/tmp/s87-key.pem

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: easypj-ingress, namespace: s87-networking}
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts: [easypj.example.com]
    secretName: easypj-cert    # ❌ BUG! Secret is named "easypj-tls", not "easypj-cert"!
  rules:
  - host: easypj.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend: {service: {name: easypj-web, port: {number: 80}}}
EOF

echo "=== Check TLS Secret name vs Ingress reference ==="
echo "Secret names:"
kubectl get secrets -n s87-networking | grep tls
echo ""
echo "Ingress TLS secretName:"
kubectl get ingress easypj-ingress -n s87-networking -o jsonpath='{.spec.tls[0].secretName}'
echo ""
⚠

⚠️ Observe — TLS Secret Name Mismatch

✗1. kubectl get secrets -n s87-networking → Secret is "easypj-tls"
✗2. Ingress tls.secretName: "easypj-cert" — different name! ❌
✗3. curl -k https://easypj.example.com → "Kubernetes Ingress Controller Fake Certificate"
🔍

🔍 Debug — Secret Name Typo

1Compare Secret name vs Ingress reference: kubectl describe ingress easypj-ingress -n s87-networking | grep -A3 TLS
Ingress references secretName: easypj-cert, but actual Secret is easypj-tls — simple typo. Fix: correct secretName or recreate Secret with matching name.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Browser shows fake cert → Check Ingress TLS
②
kubectl describe ingress → Secret not found
③
secretName: easypj-cert ≠ actual: easypj-tls
④
Patch secretName → Controller finds cert
⑤
HTTPS serves correct certificate!

Tenet: Ingress TLS requires the Secret to exist in the SAME namespace and have the EXACT name specified in secretName. A mismatch causes the Ingress controller to fall back to its default fake certificate. Always verify with kubectl describe ingress and check for TLS errors in the Ingress controller logs.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl describe ingress easypj-ingress -n s87-networking | grep -A2 TLS TLS: easypj-cert terminates easypj.example.com ← References "easypj-cert" Events: Warning Secret "easypj-cert" not found ← SECRET NOT FOUND!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch ingress easypj-ingress -n s87-networking --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/tls/0/secretName","value":"easypj-tls"}]' ingress.networking.k8s.io/easypj-ingress patched ✅ TLS now uses correct Secret!
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch ingress easypj-ingress -n s87-networking --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/tls/0/secretName","value":"easypj-tls"}
]'
kubectl describe ingress easypj-ingress -n s87-networking | grep -A2 TLS
✓

✅ Verify — TLS Certificate Served Correctly

With the correct secretName, the Ingress controller finds the TLS Secret and serves the proper certificate. curl -k https://easypj.example.com now returns the web page with the correct cert.

💡 Key takeaway: TLS secretName must match EXACTLY. Check kubectl describe ingress for Secret not found warnings. The Secret must be kubernetes.io/tls type, in the same namespace, with tls.crt and tls.key keys.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s87-networking; rm -f /tmp/s87-*.pem
S88
🧪 SCENARIO S88 — Category 5: Services & Networking Ingress Path

/api Returns Web Pages Not API — Ingress Path Order Sends All Traffic to Web

The Problem: Two Ingress paths were configured: / → easypj-web and /api → easypj-api. But curl easypj.example.com/api/health returns HTML from the web service, not JSON from the API. The / path is listed first with pathType: Prefix — it matches EVERYTHING including /api/*, so all traffic goes to the web backend. Your job: reorder the paths so the more specific /api path takes priority.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube)
1

📋 Deploy Web + API with Wrong Ingress Path Order (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The frontend team needs /api/* requests routed to the Django REST API and everything else to the web frontend. The DevOps engineer created two paths in the Ingress but put / BEFORE /api. With pathType: Prefix, / is a prefix of /api/health — it matches first and routes API calls to the web server. The web server returns 404 HTML pages instead of API JSON responses.
📁 S88 STANDALONE:
~/s88-networking/
├── web-pod.yaml + web-svc.yaml
├── api-pod.yaml + api-svc.yaml
└── ingress.yaml   ← ❌ BUG: / path comes before /api — catches all traffic!
BASH — Deploy Web + API + Ingress with wrong path order.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S88: Ingress Path Order — / catches /api
# CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s88-networking

# Web pod
kubectl run easypj-web -n s88-networking --image=nginx:alpine --port=80 --labels=app=easypj-web
kubectl expose pod easypj-web -n s88-networking --port=80

# API pod
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s88-networking, labels: {app: easypj-api}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","cat>/app.py<<'X'\nimport http.server,json\nclass H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):\n def do_GET(self):\n  self.send_response(200);self.send_header('Content-Type','application/json');self.end_headers()\n  self.wfile.write(json.dumps({'api':'v1','path':self.path}).encode())\nhttp.server.HTTPServer(('0.0.0.0',8000),H).serve_forever()\nX\npython3 /app.py"]
    ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
EOF
kubectl expose pod easypj-api -n s88-networking --port=8000 --target-port=8000

# ❌ BUG! / path listed before /api — Prefix matches /api too!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: easypj-ingress, namespace: s88-networking}
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: easypj.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /                   # ❌ BUG! This Prefix matches /api too!
        pathType: Prefix
        backend: {service: {name: easypj-web, port: {number: 80}}}
      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix
        backend: {service: {name: easypj-api, port: {number: 8000}}}
EOF

echo "=== curl /api/health — gets WEB HTML, not API JSON! ==="
sleep 5
⚠

⚠️ Observe — /api Returns Web Content

✗1. curl /api/health returns HTML (from web), not JSON (from API)
✗2. pathType: Prefix on / matches /api/* — path order matters!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Path Precedence in Ingress

1The rule: NGINX Ingress processes paths in order. With Prefix matching, / is a prefix of /api/health — it matches first!
Put more specific paths (/api) BEFORE general paths (/) in the Ingress spec. NGINX Ingress uses first-match for Prefix paths.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
curl /api returns HTML → Wrong backend
②
Check Ingress paths → / before /api
③
Prefix / matches /api/* → First match wins
④
Reorder: /api first, then / → Fix!
⑤
/api → API JSON, / → Web HTML ✅

Tenet: Ingress paths with pathType: Prefix are matched in order — first match wins. Always list more specific paths (like /api/) BEFORE general paths (like /). For exact matching, use pathType: Exact. Some Ingress controllers use longest-prefix matching; NGINX uses first-match.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -s -H "Host: easypj.example.com" http://INGRESS_IP/api/health | head -1 <!DOCTYPE html> ← HTML from web, not JSON from API!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -s -H "Host: easypj.example.com" http://INGRESS_IP/api/health {"api":"v1","path":"/api/health"} ✅ JSON from API — path order fixed!
🔧
BASH
kubectl get ingress easypj-ingress -n s88-networking -o yaml > /tmp/s88-ingress.yaml
# Edit: swap path order — put /api BEFORE /
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: easypj-ingress, namespace: s88-networking}
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: easypj.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /api              # ✅ Specific path FIRST!
        pathType: Prefix
        backend: {service: {name: easypj-api, port: {number: 8000}}}
      - path: /                 # ✅ General path LAST!
        pathType: Prefix
        backend: {service: {name: easypj-web, port: {number: 80}}}
EOF
✓

✅ Verify — /api Routes to API, / Routes to Web

After reordering paths, /api/* requests go to the Django API and everything else goes to the web frontend.

💡 Key takeaway: Ingress path order matters with Prefix matching. More specific paths MUST come before general paths. Use pathType: Exact when you need precise matching.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s88-networking
S89
🧪 SCENARIO S89 — Category 5: Services & Networking NetworkPolicy

Web Can't Reach API After Applying NetworkPolicy — namespaceSelector Missing

The Problem: A NetworkPolicy was applied to allow easypj-web pods to connect to easypj-api on port 8000. But after applying, web pods can no longer reach the API. The policy has a podSelector matching the API pods and an ingress rule from web pods — but it's missing namespaceSelector: {} in the from clause. Without it, the policy only allows traffic from pods in the SAME namespace that ALSO match the podSelector — which don't exist. Your job: add namespaceSelector to allow traffic from web pods.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
1

📋 Deploy Web + API + NetworkPolicy Without namespaceSelector (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The security team applied a zero-trust policy: default-deny all traffic, then explicitly allow web-to-API. The engineer created a NetworkPolicy with an ingress rule matching web pods but forgot namespaceSelector: {}. The policy now says "allow from pods with app=easypj-web AND in namespace matching {}" — but the empty matchLabels means "match nothing." Web pods are blocked.
📁 S89 STANDALONE:
~/s89-networking/
├── web-pod.yaml + api-pod.yaml
└── netpol.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: missing namespaceSelector in ingress from!
BASH — Deploy pods + broken NetworkPolicy.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S89: NetworkPolicy — namespaceSelector Missing
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s89-networking

# API pod (target)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s89-networking, labels: {app: easypj-api}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'import http.server,json\nclass H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):\n def do_GET(self):self.send_response(200);self.send_header(\"Content-Type\",\"application/json\");self.end_headers();self.wfile.write(json.dumps({\"api\":\"ok\"}).encode())\nhttp.server.HTTPServer((\"0.0.0.0\",8000),H).serve_forever()' > /app.py; python3 /app.py"]
    ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
EOF
kubectl expose pod easypj-api -n s89-networking --port=8000

# Web pod (client)
kubectl run easypj-web -n s89-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --labels=app=easypj-web -- sleep 3600

# Test BEFORE policy: should work
kubectl exec easypj-web -n s89-networking -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://easypj-api:8000/ 2>&1 || echo "(may fail while API starts)"

# ❌ BUG! Missing namespaceSelector: {} in from clause!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-web-to-api, namespace: s89-networking}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-web}}   # ❌ BUG! No namespaceSelector — blocks traffic!
    ports: [{port: 8000, protocol: TCP}]
EOF

sleep 3
echo "=== Test AFTER policy (should FAIL) ==="
kubectl exec easypj-web -n s89-networking -- wget -qO- --timeout=5 http://easypj-api:8000/ 2>&1 || echo "BLOCKED — namespaceSelector missing!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Web Blocked from API

✗1. Before policy: wget to API works ✅
✗2. After policy: wget times out — BLOCKED ❌
✗3. podSelector matches web pods but without namespaceSelector, the rule doesn't apply correctly
🔍

🔍 Debug — namespaceSelector Required for Cross-Pod Rules

1Check the NetworkPolicy: kubectl describe netpol allow-web-to-api -n s89-networking
from clause has podSelector but no namespaceSelector. With only podSelector, it matches pods in the namespace selected by namespaceSelector. Default behavior differs between CNI plugins — always add namespaceSelector: {} to match pods in same namespace.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Web can't reach API → Check NetworkPolicy
②
Policy exists, podSelector matches → Still blocked
③
Missing namespaceSelector → Add {}
④
Policy now matches same-ns pods → Traffic flows
⑤
web → API connection restored!

Tenet: NetworkPolicy from rules combine podSelector AND namespaceSelector. Without namespaceSelector, behavior is CNI-dependent. To allow traffic from pods in the SAME namespace, add namespaceSelector: {} (selects all namespaces) or namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: <ns>}}. Always specify both selectors for predictable behavior.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec easypj-web -n s89-networking -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://easypj-api:8000/ wget: download timed out ← BLOCKED!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch netpol allow-web-to-api -n s89-networking --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/ingress/0/from/0/namespaceSelector","value":{}}]' networkpolicy.networking.k8s.io/allow-web-to-api patched ✅ Fixed!
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch netpol allow-web-to-api -n s89-networking --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/ingress/0/from/0/namespaceSelector","value":{}}
]'
kubectl exec easypj-web -n s89-networking -- wget -qO- http://easypj-api:8000/
✓

✅ Verify — Web Reaches API After Fix

With namespaceSelector: {} added, the NetworkPolicy correctly allows traffic from web pods in the same namespace to API pods on port 8000.

💡 Key takeaway: NetworkPolicy from rules require BOTH podSelector AND namespaceSelector for predictable behavior. Use namespaceSelector: {} for same-namespace traffic.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s89-networking
S90
🧪 SCENARIO S90 — Category 5: Services & Networking NetworkPolicy

API Can't Resolve DNS — NetworkPolicy Blocks Egress to CoreDNS

The Problem: A strict egress NetworkPolicy was applied to easypj-api pods: only allow TCP 5432 to PostgreSQL. The API pod can't resolve any DNS names — including the DB hostname. The policy blocks UDP/TCP port 53 to CoreDNS (10.96.0.10), so DNS queries fail, and PostgreSQL connections fail because the hostname can't be resolved. Your job: add an egress rule allowing DNS queries to CoreDNS.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy API + NetworkPolicy Blocking DNS (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The security team locked down API egress to ONLY PostgreSQL on port 5432. But they forgot DNS! The API pod tries to resolve the DB hostname, sends a DNS query to CoreDNS on UDP 53, and the NetworkPolicy drops the packet. DNS times out, PostgreSQL connection fails — the entire API is down despite the DB being reachable.
📁 S90 STANDALONE:
~/s90-networking/
├── api-pod.yaml
└── netpol.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: allows TCP 5432 but blocks UDP 53 (DNS)!
BASH — Deploy API + NetworkPolicy that blocks DNS.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S90: NetworkPolicy Blocks DNS
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s90-networking
kubectl run easypj-api -n s90-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --labels=app=easypj-api -- sleep 3600

# ❌ BUG! Allows TCP 5432 but NO DNS (UDP 53)!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: restrict-api-egress, namespace: s90-networking}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-db}}
    ports: [{port: 5432, protocol: TCP}]
# ❌ BUG! No DNS egress rule — pod can't resolve any hostnames!
EOF

sleep 3
echo "=== Try DNS resolution (will FAIL) ==="
kubectl exec easypj-api -n s90-networking -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local 2>&1 || echo "DNS BLOCKED!"
echo ""
echo "=== Try to reach DB hostname (will FAIL — DNS blocked) ==="
kubectl exec easypj-api -n s90-networking -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 http://easypj-db:5432 2>&1 || echo "Can't resolve easypj-db — DNS blocked!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — DNS Resolution Blocked

✗1. nslookup times out — DNS queries blocked by NetworkPolicy
✗2. DB hostname can't be resolved — connections fail before reaching TCP
🔍

🔍 Debug — DNS Needs Separate Egress Rule

1Check CoreDNS IP: kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns
Egress policy only allows TCP 5432 to DB pods. DNS queries (UDP 53 to CoreDNS) are dropped. ALWAYS add DNS egress rules when restricting pod egress: allow UDP+TCP port 53 to kube-dns service.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
API can't resolve DB hostname → DNS issue
②
nslookup times out → Check NetworkPolicy
③
Egress only allows TCP 5432 → DNS blocked!
④
Add UDP+TCP 53 to CoreDNS → Fix!
⑤
DNS resolves → DB connections work!

Tenet: When applying egress NetworkPolicies, ALWAYS include a rule for DNS (UDP 53 + TCP 53 to CoreDNS). Without DNS, pods can't resolve Service names, external hosts, or any domain — breaking all network communication. CoreDNS runs in kube-system; use namespaceSelector with matchLabels to target it.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s90-networking -- nslookup kubernetes.default ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached ← DNS blocked!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s90-networking -- nslookup kubernetes.default (after DNS egress rule added) Server: 10.96.0.10 Name: kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local ✅ DNS works!
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch netpol restrict-api-egress -n s90-networking --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/egress/-","value":{
    "to":[{"namespaceSelector":{"matchLabels":{"kubernetes.io/metadata.name":"kube-system"}},"podSelector":{"matchLabels":{"k8s-app":"kube-dns"}}}],
    "ports":[{"port":53,"protocol":"UDP"},{"port":53,"protocol":"TCP"}]
  }}
]'
kubectl exec easypj-api -n s90-networking -- nslookup kubernetes.default
✓

✅ Verify — DNS Resolution Works

With the DNS egress rule added, the API pod can resolve hostnames and connect to the database successfully.

💡 Key takeaway: Egress NetworkPolicies MUST include DNS (UDP+TCP 53 to kube-dns). Without DNS, pods are completely isolated from the network. Always test DNS resolution after applying egress policies.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s90-networking

🧪 SCENARIO S91 — Category 5: Services & Networking Multi-Port

Service Creation Fails — Both Ports Named "http"

The Problem: easypj-api exposes HTTP on port 8000 and Prometheus metrics on port 9090. A single Service was created with both ports, but kubectl apply fails with "port names must be unique". Both ports are named "http" — Kubernetes requires unique port names within a Service. Your job: rename the ports to unique names.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
1

📋 Create Multi-Port Service with Duplicate Names (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The observability team wants Prometheus to scrape metrics from the API pods. The platform engineer added port 9090 to the existing Service. They copy-pasted the port definition and forgot to change the name — both ports are "http". Kubernetes rejects the Service because port names must be unique (they're used for protocol identification and monitoring).
📁 S91 STANDALONE:
~/s91-networking/
└── svc.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: port 8000 and 9090 both named "http"!
BASH — Attempt to create Service with duplicate port name.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S91: Multi-Port Service — Duplicate Names
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s91-networking
kubectl run easypj-api -n s91-networking --image=python:3.12-alpine --labels=app=easypj-api --port=8000 -- sleep 3600

# ❌ BUG! Both ports named "http" — will be REJECTED!
echo "=== Attempting to create Service (will FAIL) ==="
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f - 2>&1
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s91-networking}
spec:
  selector: {app: easypj-api}
  ports:
  - name: http          # ❌ BUG!
    port: 8000
    targetPort: 8000
    protocol: TCP
  - name: http          # ❌ BUG! Duplicate name — must be unique!
    port: 9090
    targetPort: 8000
    protocol: TCP
EOF
echo ""
echo "^^^ Service creation FAILS — port names must be unique!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Service Rejected

✗1. kubectl apply fails: "port names must be unique within a Service"
✗2. Both ports named "http" — must be unique per Service
🔍

🔍 Debug — Port Names Must Be Unique

1Kubernetes requirement: Each port in a Service must have a unique name. Names are used for protocol selection (e.g., AppProtocol), monitoring, and EndpointSlice identification.
Duplicate port name "http" on ports 8000 and 9090 — rename second port to "metrics"
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
kubectl apply fails → Read error message
②
"Duplicate value: http" → Both ports named same
③
Port names must be unique per Service
④
Rename second port to "metrics"
⑤
Service created — http (8000) + metrics (9090)!

Tenet: Service port names MUST be unique. Common naming: http, https, metrics, grpc, postgres. Port names enable protocol-aware routing and are referenced by NetworkPolicy, monitoring, and service meshes. On CKAD, creating a multi-port Service with unique names is a tested skill.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl apply -f svc.yaml The Service "easypj-api" is invalid: spec.ports[1].name: Duplicate value: "http"
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl apply -f svc-fixed.yaml service/easypj-api created ✅ Ports "http" (8000) + "metrics" (9090)
🔧
BASH
kubectl expose pod easypj-api -n s91-networking --port=8000 --target-port=8000 --name=easypj-api --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl patch svc easypj-api -n s91-networking --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"add","path":"/spec/ports/-","value":{"name":"metrics","port":9090,"targetPort":8000,"protocol":"TCP"}}
]'
✓

✅ Verify — Multi-Port Service Created

With unique port names (http + metrics), the Service is created successfully. Prometheus can now scrape metrics on port 9090 while clients use port 8000 for API calls.

💡 Key takeaway: Service port names must be unique. Use descriptive names: http, https, metrics, grpc, debug. Port names are referenced by NetworkPolicies and service meshes.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s91-networking
