🧪 SCENARIO S92 — Category 5: Services & Networking Selectorless

External DB Unreachable — Service Endpoint Points to Old IP

The Problem: PostgreSQL was moved to an external VM (10.0.1.50). A selector-less Service + manual Endpoints was created, but Django still gets "connection refused". The Endpoint still points to the old VM IP (10.0.1.25) that was decommissioned. Endpoints don't auto-update for external services. Your job: update the Endpoint to the new IP.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Create Selector-less Service + Endpoint with Old IP (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The DBA moved PostgreSQL to a bigger VM at 10.0.1.50 and decommissioned the old VM at 10.0.1.25. The platform team updated DNS but forgot to update the Kubernetes Endpoint. Selector-less Services rely on manually managed Endpoints — Kubernetes doesn't auto-discover external IPs. Django connects to 10.0.1.25 which no longer exists.
📁 S92 STANDALONE:
~/s92-networking/
├── svc.yaml       ← Service without selector
└── endpoint.yaml  ← ❌ BUG: IP 10.0.1.25 (old VM) — should be 10.0.1.50!
BASH — Create selector-less Service with old endpoint IP.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S92: Selector-less Service — Wrong Endpoint IP
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s92-networking

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-db, namespace: s92-networking}
spec:
  ports: [{port: 5432, targetPort: 5432, protocol: TCP}]
# No selector — manual Endpoints required!
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Endpoints
metadata: {name: easypj-db, namespace: s92-networking}
subsets:
- addresses:
  - ip: 10.0.1.25    # ❌ BUG! Old decommissioned VM IP!
  ports:
  - port: 5432
EOF

echo "=== Endpoint IP (wrong!) ==="
kubectl get endpoints easypj-db -n s92-networking -o jsonpath='{.subsets[0].addresses[0].ip}'
echo ""
echo "=== Try connecting (will fail — old IP) ==="
kubectl run test -n s92-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 10.0.1.25:5432 2>&1 || echo "Connection REFUSED — old IP!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Old IP in Endpoint

✗1. kubectl get endpoints easypj-db -n s92-networking → Shows 10.0.1.25:5432
✗2. The new DB IP is 10.0.1.50 — endpoint must be manually updated!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Manual Endpoints Don't Auto-Update

1Check Endpoint: kubectl get endpoints easypj-db -n s92-networking -o yaml | grep "ip:"
Selector-less Services require manual Endpoint management. When external IPs change, you must update the Endpoint resource. Kubernetes won't auto-discover or update external endpoints.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
DB connections fail → Check Endpoints
②
Endpoint IP: 10.0.1.25 → Old decommissioned VM
③
Manual Endpoints don't auto-update
④
Patch to new IP: 10.0.1.50
⑤
Service routes to new DB — connections work!

Tenet: Selector-less Services + manual Endpoints let you expose external resources inside the cluster. But Endpoints must be MANUALLY maintained — no auto-discovery. Use ExternalName for DNS-based external services; use selector-less for IP-based. Always verify endpoint IPs after external migrations.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get endpoints easypj-db -n s92-networking NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-db 10.0.1.25:5432 5m ← OLD IP!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch endpoints easypj-db -n s92-networking --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/subsets/0/addresses/0/ip","value":"10.0.1.50"}]' endpoints/easypj-db patched ✅ Updated to new IP 10.0.1.50!
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch endpoints easypj-db -n s92-networking --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/subsets/0/addresses/0/ip","value":"10.0.1.50"}
]'
kubectl get endpoints easypj-db -n s92-networking
✓

✅ Verify — Endpoint Points to New IP

The Service now routes to the new PostgreSQL VM. Django connections succeed.

💡 Key takeaway: Manual Endpoints require manual updates. After external migrations, always verify with kubectl get endpoints. Consider ExternalName Services for DNS-based external services.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s92-networking

api.easypj.com Returns Web — Second Host Rule Missing from Ingress

The Problem: Two Ingress resources were created: one for www.easypj.com → web and one for api.easypj.com → API. But api.easypj.com returns the web frontend HTML. 1

📋 Create Two Ingresses — API Has Typo in Host (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: Marketing wants www.easypj.com for the job board and api.easypj.com for developers. Two separate Ingress resources were created. But the API Ingress has "api.easypj.com" — missing the 'j' in "easypj". The Host header doesn't match, so NGINX falls through to the default backend or the web Ingress.
📁 S93 STANDALONE:
~/s93-networking/
├── web-svc.yaml + api-svc.yaml
└── ingress-api.yaml   ← ❌ BUG: host "api.easypj.com" — typo!
BASH — Deploy two Ingresses, API has typo.

# SCENARIO S93: Multi-Host Ingress — Typo in Host
# CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube)
# ============================================

kubectl run web -n s93-networking --image=nginx:alpine --port=80 --labels=app=web
kubectl expose pod web -n s93-networking --port=80
kubectl run api -n s93-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --labels=app=api -- sleep 3600
kubectl expose pod api -n s93-networking --port=8000 --target-port=8000

kubectl create ingress web-ingress -n s93-networking --class=nginx --rule="www.easypj.com/*=web:80"

# ❌ BUG! Host has TYPO: "easypj" instead of "easypj"!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: api-ingress, namespace: s93-networking}
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: api.easypj.com    # ❌ BUG! Missing 'j' — should be "easypj"!
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend: {service: {name: api, port: {number: 8000}}}
EOF

echo "=== curl api.easypj.com (correct host) — gets WEB, not API! ==="
echo "=== curl api.easypj.com (typo host) — might hit API ==="
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Wrong Host Returns Wrong Content

✗1. api.easypj.com returns web HTML — host doesn't match API Ingress!
✗2. Ingress host has typo: "easypj" should be "easypj"
🔍

🔍 Debug — Check Ingress Host Field

1Check hosts: kubectl get ingress -n s93-networking
api-ingress host is "api.easypj.com" — typo in domain name. Host matching is exact string comparison. Fix: correct the host spelling.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
api.easypj.com returns web → Wrong backend
②
Check Ingress hosts → "api.easypj.com"
③
Typo: missing 'j' in "easypj" → No match
④
Patch host to "api.easypj.com"
⑤
Correct host routes to API!

Tenet: Ingress host matching is EXACT string comparison. A single character typo means the rule never matches. Always verify Ingress hosts with kubectl get ingress and test with curl -H "Host: correct-host". Use kubectl describe ingress to see all configured rules.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -s -H "Host: api.easypj.com" http://INGRESS_IP/ <!DOCTYPE html>... ← WEB page, not API! Host mismatch!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch ingress api-ingress -n s93-networking --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/rules/0/host","value":"api.easypj.com"}]' && curl -s -H "Host: api.easypj.com" http://INGRESS_IP/ API v1 response ✅ Correct host routes to API!
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch ingress api-ingress -n s93-networking --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/rules/0/host","value":"api.easypj.com"}
]'
kubectl get ingress -n s93-networking
✓

✅ Verify — Both Hosts Route Correctly

After fixing the typo, www.easypj.com → web and api.easypj.com → API.

💡 Key takeaway: Ingress hosts are exact match. Typos cause silent failures — traffic falls through to default backend. Always verify with curl -H "Host:".

Job Board Not Loading — Trace Network Path Browser → Ingress → Service → Pod → DB

The Problem: Users report "job board not loading." You need to trace the entire network path: Browser → DNS → Ingress → Service → Pod → Django → Service → PostgreSQL. 1

📋 Deploy Full Stack with ConfigMap Typo (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The full stack is deployed: web pod, API pod, DB pod, ClusterIP Services, and Ingress. Everything looks fine at first glance — pods are Running, Services have endpoints. But the ConfigMap has DATABASE_URL pointing to "easypj-db-old" instead of "easypj-db" — a Service name that doesn't exist. Django can't connect to the database, returns 500, and the job board shows a blank page.
📁 S94 STANDALONE — Find the Break:
~/s94-networking/
├── web-pod.yaml + api-pod.yaml + db-pod.yaml
├── web-svc.yaml + api-svc.yaml + db-svc.yaml
├── ingress.yaml
└── configmap.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: DATABASE_URL=easypj-db-old (wrong Service name!)
BASH — Deploy full stack with wrong DB Service name.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S94: Full Network Debug — Hop-by-Hop
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s94-networking

# DB pod
kubectl run easypj-db -n s94-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --labels=app=easypj-db --port=5432 -- sleep 3600
kubectl expose pod easypj-db -n s94-networking --port=5432

# API pod
kubectl run easypj-api -n s94-networking --image=python:3.12-alpine --labels=app=easypj-api --port=8000 -- sleep 3600
kubectl expose pod easypj-api -n s94-networking --port=8000

# Web pod
kubectl run easypj-web -n s94-networking --image=nginx:alpine --labels=app=easypj-web --port=80
kubectl expose pod easypj-web -n s94-networking --port=80

# ❌ BUG! ConfigMap has WRONG DB Service name!
kubectl create cm easypj-config -n s94-networking --from-literal=DATABASE_URL=easypj-db-old:5432

echo "=== START DEBUGGING ==="
echo "1. Test Ingress → Web: curl IngressIP -H 'Host: easypj.example.com'"
echo "2. Test Web → API: kubectl exec easypj-web -- wget easypj-api:8000"
echo "3. Test API → DB: kubectl exec easypj-api -- nslookup easypj-db-old"
echo "   ^^^ DNS resolution FAILS — easypj-db-old doesn't exist!"
echo "4. Fix: kubectl patch cm easypj-config -n s94-networking -p '{\"data\":{\"DATABASE_URL\":\"easypj-db:5432\"}}'"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — DNS Resolution Fails at DB Hop

✗HOP 3 (API→DB): nslookup easypj-db-old → NXDOMAIN — Service doesn't exist!
✗HOP 1+2: Ingress→Web and Web→API work fine ✅
✗Root cause: ConfigMap DATABASE_URL references "easypj-db-old" but real Service is "easypj-db"
🔍

🔍 Debug — Systematic Hop-by-Hop Network Tracing

1Method: Test each hop: Ingress→Service→Pod→DNS→DB. Isolate the failing hop.
API can't resolve easypj-db-old — it's a non-existent Service name in the ConfigMap. Fix the Service name to easypj-db.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Job board blank → Trace Browser→Ingress→Web
②
Web→API works, API→DB fails → Isolate DB hop
③
nslookup easypj-db-old → NXDOMAIN
④
ConfigMap has wrong Service name → Fix it
⑤
Full path works — job board loads!

Tenet: Network debugging is hop-by-hop: Browser→DNS→Ingress→Service→Pod→Service→Pod. Test each hop with curl, wget, nslookup from within the cluster. The error at one hop doesn't mean the problem is there — it could be a dependency. Always trace the FULL path.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec easypj-api -n s94-networking -- nslookup easypj-db-old Server: 10.96.0.10 ** server can't find easypj-db-old: NXDOMAIN ← Service doesn't exist!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl patch cm easypj-config -n s94-networking -p '{"data":{"DATABASE_URL":"easypj-db:5432"}}' configmap/easypj-config patched ✅ Correct Service name!
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch cm easypj-config -n s94-networking -p '{"data":{"DATABASE_URL":"easypj-db:5432"}}'
kubectl exec easypj-api -n s94-networking -- nslookup easypj-db
✓

✅ Verify — Full Path Working

After fixing the DB Service name, the full path works: Browser → Ingress → Web Service → Web Pod → API Service → API Pod → DB Service → DB Pod. Job board loads successfully.

💡 Key takeaway: Hop-by-hop debugging: test each link independently. curl Ingress → wget Service → nslookup downstream Service. The break point tells you exactly where to fix.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s94-networking
S95
🧪 SCENARIO S95 — Category 5: Services & Networking DNS Policy

Pod Can't Resolve Cluster Services — dnsPolicy Set to "None" Without Cluster DNS

The Problem: A legacy application needs a custom DNS server (8.8.8.8). The pod was configured with dnsPolicy: None and custom nameservers. The pod can resolve external names but NOT cluster-internal Services. The custom DNS config only lists 8.8.8.8 — CoreDNS (10.96.0.10) was forgotten. Your job: add the cluster DNS server to the custom DNS config.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
1

📋 Deploy Pod with dnsPolicy: None — Missing Cluster DNS (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: A legacy payroll system hardcodes Google DNS (8.8.8.8). The DevOps engineer set dnsPolicy: None with custom nameservers. The pod can ping google.com but can't resolve easypj-api or kubernetes.default — the custom DNS config doesn't include CoreDNS. All internal Service communication is broken.
📁 S95 STANDALONE:
~/s95-networking/
└── pod.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: dnsPolicy: None + customDNS missing CoreDNS IP!
BASH — Deploy pod with incomplete custom DNS.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S95: dnsPolicy None — Missing Cluster DNS
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s95-networking

# ❌ BUG! Only external DNS — no CoreDNS (10.96.0.10)!
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: legacy-app, namespace: s95-networking, labels: {app: legacy}}
spec:
  dnsPolicy: None
  dnsConfig:
    nameservers: [8.8.8.8, 8.8.4.4]    # ❌ BUG! Only external DNS — missing CoreDNS!
    searches: [s95-networking.svc.cluster.local]
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF

sleep 5
echo "=== External DNS works ==="
kubectl exec legacy-app -n s95-networking -- nslookup google.com 2>&1 | head -3
echo ""
echo "=== Cluster DNS FAILS ==="
kubectl exec legacy-app -n s95-networking -- nslookup kubernetes.default 2>&1 || echo "Cluster DNS RESOLUTION FAILED!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — External Works, Internal Fails

✗1. External: nslookup google.com → works ✅
✗2. Internal: nslookup kubernetes.default → FAILS ❌
✗3. Custom DNS missing CoreDNS IP (10.96.0.10)!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Always Include CoreDNS in Custom DNS

1Check CoreDNS IP: kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns → Usually 10.96.0.10
dnsPolicy: None requires MANUAL specification of ALL nameservers. Forgetting CoreDNS means no cluster-internal name resolution. Always include the cluster DNS IP in custom DNS configs.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
External DNS works, cluster DNS fails → Check config
②
dnsPolicy: None → Manual nameserver list
③
Only 8.8.8.8 listed → No CoreDNS!
④
Add kube-dns IP as primary nameserver
⑤
Both internal and external DNS work!

Tenet: dnsPolicy: None gives you full control but requires listing ALL nameservers. ALWAYS include CoreDNS (kube-dns Service IP) for cluster-internal resolution. Common pattern: CoreDNS first (for cluster names), then external DNS (for internet). Without CoreDNS, pods are isolated from cluster Services.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec legacy-app -n s95-networking -- nslookup kubernetes.default ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached ← No CoreDNS!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec legacy-app -n s95-networking -- nslookup kubernetes.default (after adding 10.96.0.10) Name: kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local ✅ Cluster DNS works!
🔧
BASH
DNS_IP=$(kubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}')
kubectl patch pod legacy-app -n s95-networking --type=json -p='[
  {"op":"replace","path":"/spec/dnsConfig/nameservers","value":["'$DNS_IP'","8.8.8.8","8.8.4.4"]}
]'
✓

✅ Verify — Both Internal and External DNS Work

With CoreDNS as the primary nameserver, the pod resolves cluster Services AND external domains.

💡 Key takeaway: dnsPolicy: None requires ALL nameservers to be listed. Always put CoreDNS FIRST for cluster resolution, then external DNS. dnsPolicy options: Default, ClusterFirst, ClusterFirstWithHostNet, None.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s95-networking
S96
🧪 SCENARIO S96 — Category 5: Services & Networking TrafficPolicy

Rate Limiter Blocks Everyone — externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster Hides Real Client IP

The Problem: The API rate limiter sees ALL requests coming from the SAME node IP (10.0.0.5) instead of individual client IPs. With the default externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster, the source IP is SNATed to the node's IP — every client appears to be the same. The rate limiter blocks ALL traffic after the first user hits the limit. Your job: set externalTrafficPolicy: Local to preserve client source IPs.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Deploy NodePort Service with Default Cluster Traffic Policy (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The API has IP-based rate limiting. After deploying, ALL users get rate-limited after the first request. The default externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster SNATs all traffic to the node IP. The rate limiter sees 10.0.0.5 for every request — it thinks one user made 1000 requests and blocks everyone.
📁 S96 STANDALONE:
~/s96-networking/
└── svc.yaml    ← ❌ BUG: externalTrafficPolicy defaults to Cluster (IP hidden)
BASH — Deploy Service, test client IP visibility.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S96: externalTrafficPolicy — Client IP Hidden
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s96-networking
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s96-networking, labels: {app: easypj-api}}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: python:3.12-alpine
    command: ["/bin/sh","-c","echo 'import http.server as s,json\nclass H(s.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):\n def do_GET(self):self.send_response(200);self.send_header(\"Content-Type\",\"application/json\");self.end_headers();self.wfile.write(json.dumps({\"client_ip\":self.client_address[0]}).encode())\ns.HTTPServer((\"0.0.0.0\",8000),H).serve_forever()'>/a.py;python3 /a.py"]
    ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
EOF

cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-api, namespace: s96-networking}
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector: {app: easypj-api}
  ports: [{port: 8000, targetPort: 8000, nodePort: 31080}]
# ❌ BUG! externalTrafficPolicy defaults to Cluster — hides real client IP!
EOF

NODE_IP=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')
sleep 5
echo "=== Client IP from API (will be NODE IP, not real client!) ==="
curl -s http://$NODE_IP:31080/
echo ""
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Client IP Is Node's IP

✗1. API returns {"client_ip":"10.0.0.5"} — the NODE's IP, not yours!
✗2. Rate limiter thinks all requests come from one IP → blocks everyone
🔍

🔍 Debug — externalTrafficPolicy Options

1Cluster (default): Traffic can go to any node's pod — source IP is SNATed to node IP
externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster hides real client IPs — use Local to preserve source IP for rate limiting, geo-blocking, and audit logging
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Rate limiter blocks everyone → Check client IP
②
API returns node IP, not real client IP
③
externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster → SNAT hides IP
④
Change to Local → Preserves source IP
⑤
Rate limiter sees real IPs — works correctly!

Tenet: externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster (default) = balanced, but hides client IP. externalTrafficPolicy: Local = preserves client IP, but only routes to pods on the same node. For rate limiting/geo-blocking/audit logging, use Local. Trade-off: Local may cause uneven load distribution across nodes.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ curl -s http://NODE_IP:31080/ {"client_ip":"10.0.0.5"} ← NODE IP, not client!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ curl -s http://NODE_IP:31080/ {"client_ip":"192.168.1.100"} ← REAL client IP! ✅
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch svc easypj-api -n s96-networking -p '{"spec":{"externalTrafficPolicy":"Local"}}'
curl -s http://$NODE_IP:31080/
✓

✅ Verify — Real Client IP Preserved

With externalTrafficPolicy: Local, the API sees the actual client IP. Rate limiting, geo-blocking, and audit logging now work correctly.

💡 Key takeaway: externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster (default, hides IP) vs Local (preserves IP, node-local routing). Use Local when client IP matters. Trade-off: Local may cause uneven pod distribution.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s96-networking
S97
🧪 SCENARIO S97 — Category 5: Services & Networking Debug

Service-to-Service Calls Take 2 Seconds — Too Many iptables Rules

The Problem: With 50+ Services, inter-service calls are taking 2+ seconds (should be <50ms). kube-proxy is running in iptables mode — each Service adds sequential iptables rules. With many Services, packet matching is O(n), causing latency. Your job: identify kube-proxy as the bottleneck and understand IPVS mode as the fix.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
1

📋 Create Many Services to Demonstrate Latency (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The platform has 50+ microservices. API responses that call other services take 2+ seconds. The SRE team checks: pods are fine, network isn't saturated, no packet loss. The issue is kube-proxy in iptables mode — every packet traverses ALL Service rules sequentially. With 50+ Services, that's hundreds of iptables rules evaluated per packet.
📁 S97 STANDALONE (Diagnostic):
~/s97-networking/
⚠️ No YAML files — this is a diagnostic scenario
✅ Check kube-proxy mode: kubectl logs kube-proxy-xxx | grep Proxier
✅ iptables = O(n) latency; IPVS = O(1) constant time
BASH — Check kube-proxy mode (diagnostic, not fixable in CKAD scope).

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S97: Network Latency — kube-proxy iptables
# CLUSTER: ksw → 2 (kind-cka-lab)
# ============================================

echo "=== Check kube-proxy mode ==="
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[0].command}' | grep -o 'proxy-mode=[a-z]*'
echo ""

echo "=== Count iptables rules (indicative) ==="
NODES=$(kubectl get nodes -o name | head -1)
kubectl debug $NODES -it --image=busybox:1.36 -- iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES 2>/dev/null | wc -l || echo "Cannot access node iptables (expected in CKAD)"

echo ""
echo "=== Measure Service latency ==="
kubectl create ns s97-networking 2>/dev/null
kubectl run test -n s97-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --rm -it --restart=Never -- time wget -qO- http://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local:443/version 2>&1 || echo "(expected timeout on 443)"

echo ""
echo "=== CKAD NOTE ==="
echo "kube-proxy iptables mode: O(n) rules, latency grows with Service count"
echo "kube-proxy IPVS mode: O(1) hash lookup, constant latency"
echo "Fix: change kube-proxy config to --proxy-mode=ipvs (cluster-admin task)"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — High Service Latency

✗1. Service-to-service calls take 2+ seconds instead of <50ms
✗2. kube-proxy mode: iptables — O(n) rule evaluation per packet
✗3. With 50+ Services, iptables NAT table has hundreds of sequential rules
🔍

🔍 Debug — kube-proxy Modes

1iptables: Sequential rule evaluation, O(n) with Service count. Good for small clusters. Default in most distributions.
iptables mode with many Services causes linear latency increase. IPVS mode uses kernel hash tables for O(1) Service lookup — recommended for clusters with 1000+ Services.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Service calls take 2+ seconds → Check network
②
Pods fine, no packet loss → Check kube-proxy
③
iptables mode: O(n) sequential rules
④
50+ Services = hundreds of rules per packet
⑤
Switch to IPVS: O(1) hash lookup → <50ms!

Tenet: kube-proxy modes: userspace (legacy, slow), iptables (default, O(n)), IPVS (recommended, O(1) hash table). For CKAD, know that iptables latency increases with Service count and IPVS is the production recommendation. Switching kube-proxy mode is a cluster-admin task, not typically on CKAD.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-proxy-xxxxx | grep "Using iptables" Using iptables Proxier ← iptables mode — O(n) latency!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-proxy-xxxxx | grep "Using ipvs" Using ipvs Proxier ← IPVS mode — O(1) latency! ✅
🔧
BASH
kubectl get cm kube-proxy -n kube-system -o yaml | grep mode
# Change mode: "iptables" → "ipvs" in kube-proxy ConfigMap
# Then restart kube-proxy daemonset
kubectl rollout restart ds kube-proxy -n kube-system
✓

✅ Understanding — IPVS vs iptables

IPVS mode provides O(1) Service lookup via kernel hash tables. Essential knowledge for CKAD networking troubleshooting. The actual mode switch requires cluster-admin privileges.

💡 Key takeaway: kube-proxy iptables: O(n) rules, latency ∝ Service count. IPVS: O(1) hash table, constant latency. Check mode: kubectl logs kube-proxy-xxx | grep "Proxier".

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up
kubectl delete ns s97-networking 2>/dev/null; echo "S97 is diagnostic-only — no persistent resources"

The Problem: The easypj production deployment has 5 networking issues: (1) Service selector mismatch causing empty endpoints, (2) Ingress missing ingressClassName, (3) NetworkPolicy blocking DNS egress, (4) ExternalName pointing to old RDS, (5) NodePort using wrong port number. Your job: systematic network audit using kubectl get, describe, endpoints, and exec.

1

📋 Deploy the Broken Stack — Find All 5 Networking Issues (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The final networking challenge. A new production deployment has 5 networking bugs from the scenarios you've practiced. Your mission: apply ALL diagnostic skills from S81-S97 to find and fix every issue. Use kubectl get svc/ingress/netpol/endpoints, describe, exec with wget/nslookup, and auth can-i to systematically audit.

~/s98-networking/

kubectl run api -n s98-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --labels=app=api -- sleep 3600

kubectl expose pod api -n s98-networking --port=8000 --target-port=8000

# BUG 1: Service with wrong selector

metadata: {name: easypj-db, namespace: s98-networking}

# BUG 2: Ingress without ingressClassName

# BUG 3: NetworkPolicy blocking DNS

⚠️ The 5 Issues to Find

✗BUG 1: Service selector {app: easypj-db} but no pod has that label → empty endpoints
✗BUG 2: Ingress missing ingressClassName → no controller picks it up
✗BUG 3: NetworkPolicy blocks ALL egress except TCP 5432 → DNS blocked
✗BUG 4: ExternalName → old-db.rds.amazonaws.com (decommissioned)
✗BUG 5: NodePort 32080 — check actual assigned port with kubectl get svc

🔍 Debug — Apply All Networking Diagnostic Skills

1Endpoints: kubectl get endpoints -n s98-networking → find empty ones

2Ingress: kubectl describe ingress main -n s98-networking → no address, no events
3NetworkPolicy: kubectl exec api -- nslookup kubernetes.default → times out
4ExternalName: kubectl get svc legacy-db -o jsonpath='{.spec.externalName}' → old endpoint
5NodePort: kubectl get svc api-ext → check PORT(S) for actual nodePort
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Audit all endpoints → Find empty ones
②
Check Ingress className + hosts
③
Test DNS from pods → NetworkPolicy blocks?
④
Verify ExternalName + NodePort assignments
⑤
Fix all 5 — complete networking mastery!

Complete networking audit methodology: ① Check all Service endpoints (kubectl get endpoints -A). ② Verify Ingress status and className. ③ Test pod-to-pod and pod-to-DNS connectivity. ④ Validate ExternalName/Endpoints for external services. ⑤ Verify NodePort/LoadBalancer port assignments. Systematic audit catches all 5 issues.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get endpoints -n s98-networking NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-db <none> 5m ← BUG 1: Empty!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get endpoints -n s98-networking NAME ENDPOINTS AGE easypj-db 10.244.2.5:5432 6m ✅ Fixed!
🔧

kubectl run easypj-db -n s98-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --labels=app=easypj-db -- sleep 3600

🧪 SCENARIO S99 — Category 5: Services & Networking LoadBalancer

LoadBalancer EXTERNAL-IP Stuck Pending — No Cloud Controller or MetalLB

The Problem: A Service of type LoadBalancer was created to expose easypj-web publicly. But EXTERNAL-IP stays <pending> forever. On-premises/bare-metal clusters don't have a cloud controller to provision external load balancers. Without MetalLB or a cloud provider, type: LoadBalancer will never get an external IP. Your job: diagnose why LoadBalancer is stuck and understand the alternatives (NodePort + external LB, or install MetalLB).

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm) — Bare-metal, no cloud LB controller
1

📋 Create LoadBalancer Service on Bare-Metal Cluster (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The marketing team wants a public IP for the job board. The platform engineer created a LoadBalancer Service. But this is a bare-metal kubeadm cluster — there's no AWS/GCP/Azure cloud controller to provision an external load balancer. The EXTERNAL-IP stays "pending" indefinitely. On bare metal, you need MetalLB or an external load balancer solution.
📁 S99 STANDALONE:
~/s99-networking/
└── svc.yaml    ← type: LoadBalancer on bare-metal — EXTERNAL-IP stuck pending!
BASH — Create LoadBalancer Service on bare-metal.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S99: LoadBalancer — EXTERNAL-IP Stuck Pending
# CLUSTER: ksw → 1 (kubeadm)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s99-networking
kubectl run easypj-web -n s99-networking --image=nginx:alpine --port=80 --labels=app=easypj-web

echo "=== Creating LoadBalancer Service (will stay pending on bare-metal!) ==="
kubectl expose pod easypj-web -n s99-networking --type=LoadBalancer --port=80 --name=easypj-web-lb

sleep 5
echo "=== Check EXTERNAL-IP — STUCK at ! ==="

echo "=== Check events ==="

echo "=== Solution: Install MetalLB, or use NodePort + external LB ==="
⚠

⚠️ Observe — EXTERNAL-IP Never Assigned

✗1. kubectl get svc easypj-web-lb -n s99-networking → EXTERNAL-IP: <pending>
✗2. Describe shows no events or "no cloud provider" warnings
✗3. Bare-metal = no AWS/GCP/Azure LB controller. Need MetalLB or NodePort.
🔍

🔍 Debug — LoadBalancer on Bare-Metal

1Check cloud controller: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep cloud-controller → No results
No cloud controller manager = LoadBalancer Services stay pending forever. Fix: install MetalLB for bare-metal LB IPs, or use NodePort + external LB (HAProxy/Nginx). For CKAD, type: NodePort is sufficient for testing.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
EXTERNAL-IP pending → Check cloud controller
②
No cloud-controller pod → Bare-metal cluster
③
LoadBalancer needs cloud LB OR MetalLB
④
Switch to NodePort for testing
⑤
NodePort works — immediate external access!

Tenet: LoadBalancer Services require a cloud controller (AWS/GCP/Azure) or MetalLB (bare-metal). On CKAD, you'll primarily use ClusterIP and NodePort. If EXTERNAL-IP stays pending, check for cloud controller or install MetalLB. In CKAD exam environments, LoadBalancer may work if the exam cluster has a controller configured.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get svc easypj-web-lb -n s99-networking NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) easypj-web-lb LoadBalancer 10.96.50.100 <pending> 80/TCP ← STUCK!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get svc easypj-web-lb -n s99-networking NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) easypj-web-lb LoadBalancer 10.96.50.100 192.168.1.200 80/TCP ✅
🔧
BASH
kubectl patch svc easypj-web-lb -n s99-networking -p '{"spec":{"type":"NodePort"}}'
kubectl get svc easypj-web-lb -n s99-networking
NODE_PORT=$(kubectl get svc easypj-web-lb -n s99-networking -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}')
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.addresses[?(@.type=="InternalIP")].address}')
echo "Now accessible at: http://$NODE_IP:$NODE_PORT"
✓

✅ Verify — NodePort Works on Bare-Metal

Switching to NodePort immediately assigns a port and makes the Service accessible. For production bare-metal, install MetalLB for real LoadBalancer IPs.

💡 Key takeaway: LoadBalancer type requires cloud controller OR MetalLB. On bare-metal/on-prem, EXTERNAL-IP stays pending forever. CKAD workaround: use NodePort. Production fix: MetalLB.

🧪 SCENARIO S100 — Category 5: Services & Networking Capstone

NetworkPolicy Not Taking Effect — CNI Plugin Doesn't Support It

The Problem: You applied a NetworkPolicy to deny all ingress to easypj-db pods. But web pods can STILL connect to the database. The NetworkPolicy was created successfully, but the CNI plugin (Flannel by default) doesn't enforce NetworkPolicies — only Calico, Cilium, Weave, and similar CNIs support them. Your job: diagnose why NetworkPolicies aren't enforced and understand the CNI requirement.

🖥️ CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube)
1

📋 Deploy Pods + NetworkPolicy That Won't Work (CONTAINS THE BUG)

📖 APP STORY: The security team created a strict NetworkPolicy to isolate the database. They applied it, verified it exists, but traffic still flows freely. The cluster uses Flannel as its CNI — Flannel provides pod networking but does NOT enforce NetworkPolicy. NetworkPolicies are Kubernetes resources, but they require a CNI that supports them (Calico, Cilium, Weave Net).
📁 S100 STANDALONE:
~/s100-networking/
├── web-pod.yaml + db-pod.yaml
└── netpol.yaml    ← Created but NOT enforced — CNI doesn't support it!
BASH — Deploy pods + NetworkPolicy that won't be enforced.

# ============================================
# SCENARIO S100: NetworkPolicy — CNI Doesn't Support
# CLUSTER: ksw → 6 (minikube)
# ============================================

kubectl create ns s100-networking
kubectl run easypj-db -n s100-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --labels=app=easypj-db --port=5432 -- nc -lk -p 5432 -e echo 'DB_OK' &
kubectl run easypj-web -n s100-networking --image=busybox:1.36 --labels=app=easypj-web -- sleep 3600

# Create NetworkPolicy to DENY all ingress to DB
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: deny-db-ingress, namespace: s100-networking}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-db}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
# No ingress rules = deny all!
EOF

sleep 5
echo "=== NetworkPolicy created ==="
kubectl get netpol -n s100-networking

echo "=== Test: web pod tries to connect to DB (should be BLOCKED, but...) ==="
kubectl exec easypj-web -n s100-networking -- wget -qO- --timeout=3 10.244.1.X:5432 2>&1 || echo "(test depends on actual pod IP)"

echo ""
echo "=== Check CNI — does it support NetworkPolicy? ==="
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|cilium|weave|flannel|kindnet"
echo "Flannel/kindnet = NO NetworkPolicy support!"
echo "Calico/Cilium/Weave = NetworkPolicy IS enforced!"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — NetworkPolicy Exists But Traffic Still Flows

✗1. kubectl get netpol -n s100-networking → Policy exists ✅
✗2. Web pod can STILL reach DB pod — NetworkPolicy NOT enforced! ❌
✗3. CNI is Flannel/kindnet — does NOT support NetworkPolicy!
🔍

🔍 Debug — NetworkPolicy Requires Compatible CNI

1Check CNI: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|cilium|weave|flannel"
NetworkPolicies are Kubernetes API resources but enforcement depends on the CNI plugin. Flannel/kindnet don't enforce them. Must use Calico, Cilium, or Weave Net for NetworkPolicy enforcement.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
NetworkPolicy created → Check if enforced
②
Traffic still flows despite deny-all policy
③
Check CNI → Flannel/kindnet = no NetPol support
④
NetworkPolicy needs Calico/Cilium/Weave
⑤
CKAD exam clusters HAVE NetPol support!

Tenet: NetworkPolicy resources are created in Kubernetes API, but enforcement requires a CNI plugin that implements them. Compatible CNIs: Calico, Cilium, Weave Net, Kube-router, Antrea. Incompatible: Flannel, kindnet. On CKAD, the exam cluster WILL support NetworkPolicy — but you should know that the CNI must support it.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep flannel kube-flannel-ds-xxxxx 1/1 Running ← Flannel = NO NetworkPolicy support!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep calico calico-node-xxxxx 1/1 Running ← Calico = NetworkPolicy ENFORCED! ✅
🔧
BASH
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E "calico|cilium|weave|flannel|kindnet"
echo "If you see flannel/kindnet: NetworkPolicies WON'T be enforced"
echo "If you see calico/cilium/weave: NetworkPolicies WILL be enforced"
echo "CKAD exam clusters HAVE NetworkPolicy support enabled"

🌳 Decision Trees — Overview & Implementation GuideDT0

🧭 15 Diagnostic Flowcharts for CKAD Troubleshooting — How to Use & Apply Every Tree

Decision Trees are your systematic diagnostic framework for the CKAD exam. Instead of guessing, you follow a proven yes/no path from symptom → root cause → fix. This overview explains how to implement each tree during the exam and during real-world debugging.

🧠 The Decision Tree Methodology — 4-Step Diagnostic Loop

🔍
1. OBSERVE
Identify the symptom
k get pods, k describe
What STATUS do you see?
→
🌳
2. NAVIGATE
Pick the matching tree
Start at the top node
Answer YES/NO → follow arrows
→
🔧
3. FIX
Execute the fix shown
at the leaf node
Use the key commands box
→
✅
4. VERIFY
Confirm the fix worked
k get pods -w
Check STATUS changes to Running

🔬 Anatomy of a Decision Tree — How to Read Each Tree

🔍 START = The symptom you see
↓
❓ DECISION = Yes/No question
↙️ YES       ↘️ NO
✅ YES → FIX
Problem identified!
Execute the solution here.
Then go to Step 4: VERIFY
❌ NO → NEXT DECISION
Keep going down the tree.
Each NO answer eliminates
one possible root cause.
↓
📋 KEY COMMANDS BOX (bottom of every tree)
Copy-paste ready kubectl commands for this tree's diagnostic workflow
🔵 Blue = Start / Entry Point
🟡 Yellow = Decision / Question
🟢 Green = Fix / Solution
🔴 Red = Continue / Key Commands

🗺️ Decision Tree Index — Find Your Tree by Symptom

Tree Trigger Symptom CKAD Domain Difficulty Exam Freq Root Cause Categories
DT1 Pod STATUS = Pending 1. App Design 🟢 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Scheduling, Resources, Taints, PVC, Quota
DT2 STATUS = CrashLoopBackOff 3. Observability 🟡 ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Exit codes, App errors, Env vars, Probes

🎯 Exam Day Implementation Strategy

Step 1: Read the question — identify the symptom (Pending? CrashLoop? Not reachable?)
Step 2: Jump to the matching Decision Tree (use the table above)
Step 3: Run the START command (k describe pod, k get events, etc.)
Step 4: Follow YES/NO branches — each is ONE kubectl command
Step 5: At the leaf FIX node, execute the fix shown
Step 6: VERIFY: k get pods -w, k rollout status, k describe
⚡ EXAM HACK: If you hit a dead end after 3-4 nodes, flag the question and move on. Return with fresh eyes. The tree guarantees you've checked all common causes.

🏢 Real-World DevOps Integration

📋 Runbooks: Convert each tree into a team runbook page — "If Pending, follow DT1"
🤖 Automation: Script the START commands into a diagnostic script: ./diag-pod.sh PODNAME
📊 Alert Routing: Map alert types to Decision Trees — OOMKilled alert → auto-suggest DT7
🔗 CI/CD Hooks: Post-deployment health check runs START commands, suggests tree on failure
📈 Metrics: Track which trees are used most → identify systemic issues
🧠 On-Call Training: New engineers learn trees first — systematic before intuitive

🎬 Real Example — Walk Through DT4: "Service Not Reachable" with easypj/jobpost

📋 Scenario: Your easypj/jobpost Django app is deployed. Frontend pods can't reach the easypj-api Service. You run kubectl get svc easypj-api — it EXISTS. But kubectl exec frontend-pod -- curl easypj-api:8000 times out.
🔍 OBSERVE: Service unreachable → Jump to DT4
❓ k get endpoints easypj-api → <none> → YES! No endpoints → selector mismatch
❓ k get svc easypj-api -o yaml → selector: app: easypj → But pods have label: app: django-easypj
🔧 FIX: k edit svc easypj-api → change selector to app: django-easypj
✅ VERIFY: k get endpoints easypj-api → 10.244.1.5:8000 ✅ → curl works! 🎉
⏱️ Total time: 45 seconds. Without the tree? You might spend 5+ minutes guessing. This is the power of systematic diagnosis.

🔗 Tree Relationship Map — How Trees Cross-Reference Each Other

🔗 Pod Startup Chain
DT3: ImagePull? → DT1: Pending? → DT2: CrashLoop? → RUNNING ✅
🔗 Probe Troubleshooting Chain
DT9: Liveness? → DT8: Readiness? → DT4: Service? → TRAFFIC FLOWS ✅
🔗 Network Debug Chain
DT4: Internal Svc? → DT13: Ingress? → DT14: External? → DT10: NetPol?
🔗 Config & Security Chain
DT11: Missing Key? → DT6: Not Updating? → DT12: RBAC? → DT7: OOM?

# 2. What are the events?

🚀 Diagnostic Speed Aliases — Paste at Exam Start

alias kd='kubectl describe'
alias kevents='kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp'
alias klogp='kubectl logs --previous'
alias kend='kubectl get endpoints'
alias krs='kubectl rollout status'
alias krh='kubectl rollout history'

Combine with Appendix I aliases for maximum exam speed.

⚠️ When to Use Trees vs When NOT to

✅ DO USE when: You see a clear symptom (Pending, CrashLoop, Forbidden, 404). The tree guarantees you check ALL common causes in order.
✅ DO USE when: You're stuck and guessing. The tree gives you a systematic path instead of random debugging.
❌ SKIP when: The symptom is obvious from k describe output (e.g., "ImagePullBackOff: authentication required" → clearly DT3, just fix the secret).
❌ SKIP when: You already know the fix from experience. Trees are your safety net, not a mandatory checklist for every issue.

🌳 DT1: Pod Stuck in PendingDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: kubectl get pods shows STATUS = Pending — pod never starts

🧭 Decision Flow — Start at the top, follow Yes/No branches

🔍 START: Pod STATUS = Pending
⬇️ kubectl describe pod POD
❓ Events show "FailedScheduling"?
✅ YES ↓ ❌ NO → Check ImagePullBackOff (DT3)
❓ "Insufficient cpu/memory"?
✅ YES → FIX: Reduce requests or add nodes ❌ NO ↓
❓ "node(s) didn't match nodeSelector"?
✅ YES → FIX: k get nodes --show-labels, fix selector ❌ NO ↓
❓ "taints and tolerations"?
✅ YES → FIX: Add toleration or remove taint ❌ NO ↓
❓ PVC not binding?
✅ YES → FIX: Check StorageClass, PV availability ❌ NO ↓
❓ ResourceQuota exceeded?
✅ YES → FIX: k describe resourcequota, increase or delete ❌ NO → Re-check describe output for custom scheduler/priority
🔑 Key Commands: k describe pod POD | grep -A10 Events · k get nodes -o wide · k describe node NODE | grep -A5 Taints · k get pvc · k describe resourcequota

🌳 DT2: CrashLoopBackOffDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: Pod STATUS = CrashLoopBackOff — container starts then crashes repeatedly

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: Pod STATUS = CrashLoopBackOff
⬇️ kubectl logs POD --previous
❓ Exit code 137 (SIGKILL) = OOMKilled?
✅ YES → Go to DT7 (OOMKilled) ❌ NO ↓
❓ Exit code 1/2 = application error?
✅ YES → FIX: Read logs, fix app config/DB connection ❌ NO ↓
❓ "command not found" or "no such file"?
✅ YES → FIX: Wrong command/args or missing binary ❌ NO ↓
❓ Missing environment variable / ConfigMap key?
✅ YES → FIX: k describe pod → check env section ❌ NO ↓
❓ Liveness probe killing it? (check Events)
✅ YES → Go to DT9 (Liveness Probe) ❌ NO → k exec POD -- cat /var/log/app.log
🔑 Key Commands: k logs POD --previous · k describe pod POD | grep -A5 "State:" · k get events | grep POD · k exec POD -- printenv

🌳 DT3: ImagePullBackOffDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: Pod STATUS = ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull — image cannot be pulled

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff
⬇️ kubectl describe pod POD | grep -A5 Events
❓ Image name/typo? (e.g., nginx vs nginyx)
✅ YES → FIX: k edit pod or redeploy with correct image ❌ NO ↓
❓ Tag doesn't exist? (e.g., :latst vs :latest)
✅ YES → FIX: Check docker pull IMAGE:TAG locally first ❌ NO ↓
❓ Private registry — missing imagePullSecrets?
✅ YES → FIX: k create secret docker-registry REGSEC --docker-server=X --docker-username=U --docker-password=P ❌ NO ↓
❓ Registry credentials expired?
✅ YES → FIX: Recreate docker-registry secret ❌ NO ↓
❓ Network to registry blocked? (proxy/firewall)
✅ YES → FIX: Check egress/NetworkPolicy, proxy settings ❌ NO → Verify image exists: docker manifest inspect IMAGE:TAG
🔑 Key Commands: k describe pod POD | grep -i image · k get secrets · k describe sa SA · k run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- wget -O- https://registry.example.com

🌳 DT4: Service Not ReachableDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: Other pods or external clients cannot reach the Service

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: Service not reachable
⬇️ kubectl get endpoints SVC
❓ ENDPOINTS column is EMPTY (<none>)?
✅ YES → Selector mismatch! ↓ ❌ NO → Endpoints exist — issue is network path ↓
❓ Service labels match Pod labels?
✅ NO → FIX: Align spec.selector with pod labels ❌ YES but still empty? → Check targetPort vs containerPort
❓ Pods Ready? k get pods -l APP=LABEL
✅ NOT READY → Check Readiness Probe (DT8) ❌ READY but unreachable ↓
❓ NetworkPolicy blocking? k get netpol
✅ YES → Go to DT10 (NetworkPolicy) ❌ NO → Test DNS: nslookup SVC.NS.svc.cluster.local
🔑 Key Commands: k get endpoints SVC · k describe svc SVC · k get pods -o wide --show-labels · k run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- nslookup SERVICE.NAMESPACE.svc.cluster.local

🌳 DT5: Deployment Rollout StuckDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: kubectl rollout status hangs — new ReplicaSet pods not becoming ready

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: Deployment rollout stuck
⬇️ kubectl rollout status deploy/NAME + k describe deploy
❓ "replicaset exceeded its progress deadline"?
✅ YES → New pods are failing ↓ ❌ NO → Check conditions in describe output
❓ New pods crashing? k get pods -l APP=X
✅ YES → Go to DT2 (CrashLoopBackOff) or DT3 (ImagePull) ❌ NO ↓
❓ Insufficient cluster resources? (describe)
✅ YES → FIX: k top nodes, reduce requests or add nodes ❌ NO ↓
❓ Probe failure? Readiness not passing?
✅ YES → Go to DT8 (Readiness Probe Failing) ❌ NO → k rollout undo deploy/NAME to recover
🔑 Key Commands: k rollout status deploy/NAME --watch · k describe deploy NAME | grep -A10 Conditions · k rollout history deploy/NAME · k rollout undo deploy/NAME

🌳 DT6: ConfigMap Update Not ReflectedDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: Updated ConfigMap — but running pods still see old values

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: ConfigMap updated — pods don't see it
⬇️ kubectl describe pod POD | grep -A5 "Environment\|Mounts"
❓ ConfigMap consumed via env var (envFrom)?
✅ YES → Env vars DON'T auto-update! RESTART the pod. ❌ NO → Volume mount ↓
❓ ConfigMap mounted as volume — using subPath?
✅ YES → subPath does NOT auto-update! Remove subPath or restart. ❌ NO → Volume should auto-update in ~60s (kubelet sync period)
❓ ConfigMap marked as immutable?
✅ YES → Delete + recreate ConfigMap (can't edit immutable) ❌ NO → App may cache values — check app-level reload
🔑 Key Commands: k get cm NAME -o yaml · k describe pod POD · k exec POD -- cat /etc/config/KEY · k rollout restart deploy/NAME

🌳 DT7: OOMKilled (Exit Code 137)Decision Tree

🔍 Symptom: Pod restarted with Exit Code 137 — container killed by kernel OOM killer

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: Pod OOMKilled (Exit 137)
⬇️ kubectl describe pod POD | grep "OOMKilled"
❓ Memory limit set?
✅ NO → FIX: Set memory limit (container can consume all node memory) ❌ YES ↓
❓ Limit too low for normal operation?
✅ YES → FIX: Increase memory limit (monitor with k top pod) ❌ NO ↓
❓ Memory usage grows over time (leak)?
✅ YES → FIX: Fix memory leak or add HPA + increase limit ❌ NO ↓
❓ Node under memory pressure?
✅ YES → FIX: k describe node → check Conditions; evict pods or add nodes ❌ NO → Check QoS: Guaranteed (req==limit) is safest
🔑 Key Commands: k describe pod POD | grep -A5 "Last State" · k top pod · k top node · k describe node | grep -A3 "MemoryPressure"

🌳 DT8: Readiness Probe FailingDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: Pod Running but NOT Ready — not receiving traffic from Service

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: Pod Running 1/2 or 0/1 (READY)
⬇️ kubectl describe pod POD | grep -A10 "Readiness"
❓ Probe path/port wrong? (404, connection refused)
✅ YES → FIX: Correct httpGet.path or httpGet.port ❌ NO ↓
❓ initialDelaySeconds too short? (app not started yet)
✅ YES → FIX: Increase initialDelaySeconds (or use startupProbe) ❌ NO ↓
❓ Dependency not available? (DB, cache, API)
✅ YES → FIX: Ensure backend services are running first ❌ NO ↓
❓ failureThreshold reached? (probe failed N times)
✅ YES → FIX: Increase failureThreshold or fix underlying issue ❌ NO → Check app logs: k logs POD
🔑 Key Commands: k describe pod POD | grep -A15 Readiness · k logs POD · k exec POD -- curl localhost:PORT/healthz · k get events | grep POD

🌳 DT9: Liveness Probe Killing Healthy PodDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: Pod restarts even though the app is healthy — probe is too aggressive

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: Liveness probe kills healthy pod
⬇️ kubectl describe pod POD | grep -A10 Liveness
❓ periodSeconds too short? (e.g., 1s)
✅ YES → FIX: Increase periodSeconds (5-10s minimum recommended) ❌ NO ↓
❓ failureThreshold too low? (e.g., 1)
✅ YES → FIX: Set failureThreshold=3+ to tolerate transient failures ❌ NO ↓
❓ App needs long startup — missing startupProbe?
✅ YES → FIX: Add startupProbe — liveness waits for startup to pass ❌ NO ↓
❓ timeoutSeconds too short for slow endpoint?
✅ YES → FIX: Increase timeoutSeconds (default=1, try 5-10) ❌ NO → Liveness endpoint doing too much work — simplify it
🔑 Golden Rule: Liveness probe should ONLY check if app is alive (not stuck). It should NOT check dependencies. Use readiness probe for dependency checks.

🌳 DT10: NetworkPolicy Blocking TrafficDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: Previously working connections suddenly blocked — NetworkPolicy may be the culprit

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: Traffic blocked — suspect NetworkPolicy
⬇️ kubectl get networkpolicy -A
❓ Default deny-all policy exists?
✅ YES → Everything blocked by default — need explicit allow rules ❌ NO ↓
❓ podSelector matches YOUR pod? k describe netpol
✅ NOT MATCHING → Policy doesn't apply — look elsewhere ❌ MATCHING ↓
❓ Port correct in ingress/egress rule?
✅ NO → FIX: Add correct port to policy or create new allow rule ❌ YES ↓
❓ namespaceSelector missing? (cross-ns traffic)
✅ YES → FIX: Add namespaceSelector: matchLabels: {} ❌ NO → Check CNI supports NetworkPolicy: k get pods -n kube-system | grep calico\|cilium\|weave
🔑 Key Commands: k get netpol -A · k describe netpol NAME -n NS · k run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- wget -O- --timeout=2 TARGET:PORT

🌳 DT11: ConfigMap/Secret Missing KeyDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: Pod fails to start — "configmap references a key that does not exist"

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: "key not found" or pod won't start
⬇️ kubectl describe pod POD | grep -A10 Events
❓ ConfigMap/Secret exists? k get cm,secret -n NS
✅ NO → FIX: Create the ConfigMap/Secret first ❌ YES ↓
❓ Key name exact match? (case sensitive!)
✅ MISMATCH → FIX: Keys are CASE SENSITIVE! "DB_HOST" ≠ "db_host" ❌ YES ↓
❓ Created from correct source? k describe cm NAME
✅ WRONG DATA → FIX: Recreate with correct --from-literal=KEY=VALUE ❌ NO ↓
❓ optional: false (default) — pod won't start without key
✅ YES → FIX: Set optional: true in volume/env reference, or provide the key ❌ NO → Verify with: k get cm NAME -o jsonpath='{.data}'
🔑 Key Commands: k get cm NAME -o jsonpath='{.data}' | jq · k get secret NAME -o jsonpath='{.data.KEY}' | base64 -d · k create cm NAME --from-literal=KEY=VALUE --dry-run=client -o yaml

🌳 DT12: RBAC Permission DeniedDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: "Error from server (Forbidden)" — user or ServiceAccount lacks permissions

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: "Error from server (Forbidden)"
⬇️ kubectl auth can-i VERB RESOURCE -n NS --as=system:serviceaccount:NS:SA
❓ ServiceAccount exists in namespace?
✅ NO → FIX: k create sa NAME -n NS ❌ YES ↓
❓ Role/ClusterRole exists?
✅ NO → FIX: k create role NAME --verb=get,list --resource=pods -n NS ❌ YES ↓
❓ RoleBinding links SA to Role? k get rolebinding
✅ NO → FIX: k create rolebinding NAME --role=R --serviceaccount=NS:SA -n NS ❌ YES ↓
❓ Verb correct? (get≠list, create≠patch, watch for watch)
✅ MISSING VERB → FIX: Add the specific verb to the Role ❌ NO → Check API group: deployments is in apps group!
🔑 Key Commands: k auth can-i --list -n NS --as=system:serviceaccount:NS:SA · k describe role NAME -n NS · k describe rolebinding NAME -n NS

🌳 DT13: Ingress Not RoutingDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: Ingress resource created but traffic not reaching the backend — 404 or timeout

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: Ingress not routing — 404/timeout
⬇️ kubectl get ingress -A — check ADDRESS column
❓ ADDRESS column empty? Ingress controller running?
✅ YES → FIX: Install ingress controller (nginx, traefik, etc.) ❌ NO ↓
❓ Host header matches? k describe ingress
✅ MISMATCH → FIX: Correct host field or use curl -H "Host: correct.host" to test ❌ YES ↓
❓ Backend Service + port correct?
✅ NO → FIX: Ensure service name and port match Ingress backend spec ❌ YES ↓
❓ TLS misconfigured? (cert error)
✅ YES → FIX: Verify TLS secret exists with k get secret TLSNAME ❌ NO → Test: curl -v -H "Host: HOST" http://INGRESS_IP/PATH
🔑 Key Commands: k describe ingress NAME -n NS · k get svc -n NS · k get pods -n ingress-nginx · k logs deploy/ingress-nginx-controller -n ingress-nginx

🌳 DT14: Pod Can't Access External ServiceDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: Pod cannot reach external APIs, databases, or URLs outside the cluster

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: Pod can't reach external service
⬇️ kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- nslookup google.com
❓ DNS resolves? nslookup returns IP?
✅ NO → FIX: Check CoreDNS (k logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns) ❌ YES (resolves) ↓
❓ Egress NetworkPolicy blocking? k get netpol
✅ YES → Go to DT10 — add egress allow rule to NetworkPolicy ❌ NO ↓
❓ Proxy required? (HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY)
✅ YES → FIX: Set env: HTTP_PROXY / NO_PROXY in pod spec ❌ NO ↓
❓ NAT gateway / firewall issue? k get nodes -o wide
✅ YES → FIX: Check cloud NAT, security groups, or corporate proxy ❌ NO → Test raw connectivity: nc -vz HOST PORT or wget -O- URL
🔑 Key Commands: k run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- sh · nslookup HOST · wget -O- URL · nc -vz HOST PORT · k run test --image=nicolaka/netshoot --rm -it -- sh

🌳 DT15: Multi-Container Communication FailureDecision Tree

🔍 Symptom: Containers in the same pod can't communicate via localhost or shared volumes

🧭 Decision Flow

🔍 START: Containers in same pod can't communicate
⬇️ kubectl exec POD -c CONTAINER -- netstat -tlnp
❓ Wrong port? Containers share network namespace (localhost works)
✅ YES → FIX: Verify target container is listening on correct port ❌ NO ↓
❓ initContainer failed? (app container may not start)
✅ YES → FIX: k logs POD -c INITNAME — fix initContainer issue ❌ NO ↓
❓ Shared volume permission issue? k exec POD -- ls -la /shared
✅ YES → FIX: Set securityContext.fsGroup or chmod in initContainer ❌ NO ↓
❓ Container startup order? (postStart hook?)
✅ YES → FIX: Use initContainer for ordering; all regular containers start together ❌ NO → Test localhost: k exec POD -c C1 -- wget -O- localhost:PORT
🔑 Key Commands: k exec POD -c CONTAINER -- COMMAND · k logs POD -c CONTAINER · k explain pod.spec.containers · k get pod POD -o yaml | grep -A20 containers

📋 ANSWER KEY — Q1–Q200 with Domain, Difficulty & Answer Hint
# Domain Ans Topic / Hint Level
📦 DOMAIN 1: Application Design & Build (Q1–Q40)
Q1App DesignDDockerfile: multi-stage builds preserve build deps in builder stage only🟢
Q2App DesignB.dockerignore: *.txt wildcard blocks requirements.txt from build context🟢
Q3App DesignADocker layer caching: COPY requirements.txt BEFORE COPY . maximizes cache🟡
Q4App DesignCCMD vs ENTRYPOINT: CMD is default args, ENTRYPOINT is the executable🟡
Q5App DesignBUSER directive: changes container user, must exist or be created first🟢
Q6App DesignAEXPOSE is documentation-only; actual port binding happens in CMD/ENTRYPOINT🟢
Q7App DesignDWORKDIR creates AND cds into directory; prefer over RUN cd /app🟢
Q8App DesignCARG vs ENV: ARG is build-time only, ENV persists in container runtime🟡
Q9App DesignACOPY --from=builder copies from previous stage; key to multi-stage builds🟡
Q10App DesignBImage tags: latest is mutable; always use specific tags in production🟢
Q11–Q20App Design—Dockerfile best practices, image registries, distroless, layer optimization🟡
Q21–Q40App Design—Pod design, initContainers, sidecars, volumes, multi-container patterns🔴
🚀 DOMAIN 2: Deployments & Rollouts (Q41–Q70)
Q41DeploymentsCDeployment strategy: RollingUpdate vs Recreate — Recreate for schema changes🟡
Q42DeploymentsAkubectl rollout undo: goes back ONE revision; use --to-revision for specific🟡
Q43DeploymentsBmaxUnavailable + maxSurge: control rollout parallelism and capacity🔴
Q44DeploymentsDkubectl set image: updates container image; triggers rolling update🟢
Q45–Q55Deployments—Jobs, CronJobs, DaemonSets, StatefulSets, canary, blue-green strategies🟡
Q56–Q70Deployments—Helm, Kustomize, Helm rollback, immutable fields, upgrade strategies🔴
🔍 DOMAIN 3: Observability & Debugging (Q71–Q100)
Q71ObservabilityBkubectl logs --previous: retrieves logs from PREVIOUS crashed container🟢
Q72ObservabilityAlivenessProbe vs readinessProbe: liveness restarts, readiness removes from Service🟡
Q73ObservabilityCstartupProbe: protects slow-starting containers from liveness kills🟡
Q74ObservabilityDProbe timing: periodSeconds × failureThreshold = total tolerance window🔴
Q75–Q100Observability—kubectl describe, events, top, port-forward, debug containers, OOMKilled🟡
🔐 DOMAIN 4: Configuration & Security (Q101–Q150)
Q101Config/SecurityBConfigMap as envFrom: values static after pod start; volume mounts auto-update🟡
Q102Config/SecurityASecret as env var: visible in kubectl describe; volume mount hides from describe🟡
Q103Config/SecurityDsecurityContext: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, capabilities drop🔴
Q104Config/SecurityCRBAC: Role + RoleBinding — verbs must match exactly (get ≠ list)🔴
Q105–Q150Config/Security—Downward API, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, nodeSelector, affinity, PSS🟡
🌐 DOMAIN 5: Services & Networking (Q151–Q200)
Q151NetworkingBClusterIP: targetPort must match containerPort, port is Service's listening port🟢
Q152NetworkingAService selector: EXACT match required; empty endpoints = selector mismatch🟡
Q153NetworkingDIngress: ingressClassName required; missing = no controller picks up resource🟡
Q154NetworkingCNetworkPolicy: namespaceSelector + podSelector combined; DNS must be allowed🔴
Q155–Q200Networking—NodePort, Headless, ExternalName, Ingress TLS/paths/hosts, DNS, CNI🟡

📄 Dockerfile — Annotated Line by Line

DOCKERFILE — Copy to ~/jobpost/Dockerfile 
# ============================================================
# easypj/jobpost — Production Multi-Stage Dockerfile
# CKAD Reference Implementation
# ============================================================

# ═══════════ STAGE 1: BUILDER ═══════════
# Purpose: Compile dependencies, build wheels
# This stage has gcc, python3-dev, libpq-dev — NEVER ships to production
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Install BUILD-TIME dependencies only
# gcc + python3-dev: needed to compile psycopg2 C extension
# libpq-dev: PostgreSQL client libraries for psycopg2
# --no-install-recommends: skip optional packages (smaller layer)
# rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*: clean apt cache (saves ~50MB)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc python3-dev libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# COPY requirements FIRST — maximizes Docker layer cache
# If requirements.txt hasn't changed, all subsequent layers are cached
# This is the #1 Docker build optimization technique!
COPY requirements.txt .

# Install Python packages as the BUILD user
# --user: installs to /root/.local (not system-wide)
# --no-cache-dir: don't cache pip downloads (saves ~200MB)
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt


# ═══════════ STAGE 2: RUNTIME ═══════════
# Purpose: Minimal production image — no compilers, no dev headers
# Fresh FROM = all build tools from Stage 1 are GONE
FROM python:3.12-slim

WORKDIR /app

# Create non-root user FIRST (before COPY — layer caching)
# UID 1000: standard non-root user for Kubernetes securityContext
# -m: create home directory /home/django
RUN useradd -m -u 1000 django && \
    apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    # libpq-dev: RUNTIME libs only (psycopg2 needs libpq.so at runtime)
    libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# COPY from builder stage — only the COMPILED packages, not the tools!
# --from=builder: references Stage 1
# /root/.local: where pip --user installed packages in Stage 1
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /usr/local

# COPY application code LAST — maximizes cache for previous layers
# .dockerignore should exclude: .git, __pycache__, *.pyc, .env, venv/
COPY . .

# Switch to non-root user — container CANNOT run as root now
# Kubernetes securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true will match this
USER django

# EXPOSE is DOCUMENTATION only — actual port binding is in CMD
# Kubernetes uses containerPort, not EXPOSE
EXPOSE 8000

# HEALTHCHECK — Docker-level health (separate from K8s probes)
# Checks Django health endpoint every 30s
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=5s --retries=3 \
    CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/ht/')" || exit 1

# CMD: the process that runs when container starts
# EXEC form (JSON array) — PID 1 receives signals directly
# gunicorn: production WSGI server (NEVER use manage.py runserver in prod)
# --bind=0.0.0.0:8000: listen on all interfaces (required for K8s)
# easypj.wsgi: Django's WSGI application entry point
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind=0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers=4", "--timeout=120", "easypj.wsgi"]

📊 Layer Visualization — Build Order & Cache Strategy

LAYER 1 — FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder ← Cached (base image rarely changes)
LAYER 2 — WORKDIR /app ← Cached (always same)
LAYER 3 — RUN apt-get install gcc... ← Occasional rebuild (security patches)
LAYER 4 — COPY requirements.txt . ← 🔑 CACHE KEY! Changes when deps change
LAYER 5 — RUN pip install -r requirements.txt ← Rebuilds only when LAYER 4 changes
LAYER 6 — FROM python:3.12-slim (Runtime) ← STAGE 2: fresh base, no build tools!
LAYER 7 — RUN useradd django ← Cached
LAYER 8 — COPY --from=builder /root/.local ← Copies only compiled packages
LAYER 9 — COPY . . ← 🔑 Changes on every code edit (FAST — only this layer)
LAYER 10 — USER django, EXPOSE, HEALTHCHECK, CMD ← Cached

🔑 = Cache boundary. Everything ABOVE a changed layer is rebuilt. Put frequently-changing layers (COPY .) LAST.

⚡ Build & Run Commands

BASH — Build the production image
# Build with specific tag (NEVER use :latest in production)
docker build -t easypj/jobpost:v3.2 .

# Verify the image
docker images easypj/jobpost:v3.2

# Check image layers
docker history easypj/jobpost:v3.2

# Run locally for testing
docker run -d -p 8000:8000 --name jobpost easypj/jobpost:v3.2

# Test health endpoint
curl http://localhost:8000/ht/

# Push to registry
docker tag easypj/jobpost:v3.2 myregistry.azurecr.io/easypj/jobpost:v3.2
docker push myregistry.azurecr.io/easypj/jobpost:v3.2

✅ Production Dockerfile Checklist

✅ Multi-stage build (builder ≠ runtime)
✅ Non-root user (USER django, UID 1000)
✅ COPY requirements.txt BEFORE COPY . (cache)
✅ --no-install-recommends (smaller layers)
✅ rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* (clean cache)
✅ pip --no-cache-dir (no pip cache)
✅ EXEC form CMD (JSON array, not shell string)
✅ HEALTHCHECK (Docker-level health)
✅ Specific image tag (:v3.2, not :latest)
✅ .dockerignore excludes .git, __pycache__, .env
✅ slim base image (not alpine — avoids musl issues)
✅ gunicorn (production WSGI, not runserver)

⚠️ Common Dockerfile Mistakes

❌ COPY . . before COPY requirements.txt . — breaks caching

❌ Shell form CMD python app.py — no signals to PID 1

❌ :latest tag in production — mutable, untraceable

❌ Single-stage with gcc — bloated image (800MB+)

❌ pip install without --no-cache-dir — wastes 200MB

🥚 Pod Imperative: k run NAME --image=IMG $do > pod.yaml
YAML — pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: easypj-api
    tier: backend
spec:
  containers:
  - name: api
    image: easypj/jobpost:v3.2
    ports:
    - containerPort: 8000
    env:
    - name: DEBUG
      value: "false"
    resources:
      requests: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}
      limits:   {cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi}
🚀 Deployment Imp: k create deploy NAME --image=IMG $do
YAML — deploy.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: easypj-api
  namespace: default
  labels: {app: easypj-api}
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1
      maxSurge: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: easypj-api}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: easypj/jobpost:v3.2
        ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /ht/, port: 8000}
          periodSeconds: 5
🗄️ StatefulSet Imp: k create sts NAME --image=IMG $do
YAML — sts.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: easypj-db
  namespace: default
spec:
  serviceName: easypj-db         # Must match headless Service name!
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: easypj-db}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: easypj-db}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15
        ports: [{containerPort: 5432}]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: pgdata
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:          # Each pod gets its OWN PVC!
  - metadata: {name: pgdata}
    spec:
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
      resources: {requests: {storage: 10Gi}}
⚡ Job & CronJob Imp: k create job/cronjob
YAML — job.yaml + cronjob.yaml
# === JOB ===
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata: {name: db-migrate}
spec:
  completions: 1
  parallelism: 1
  backoffLimit: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: easypj/jobpost:v3.2
        command: ["python","manage.py","migrate"]
      restartPolicy: Never      # Job MUST use Never or OnFailure

# === CRONJOB ===
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata: {name: db-backup}
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"         # 5 fields: min hour day month weekday
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid     # Allow | Forbid | Replace
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: backup
            image: postgres:15
            command: ["pg_dump","-h","easypj-db","-U","easypj","jobpost"]
          restartPolicy: OnFailure

🌐 Services & Ingress

🔌 ClusterIP / NodePort / LoadBalancer Imp: k expose deploy NAME --port=P --type=TYPE
YAML — svc.yaml (3 types)
# === CLUSTERIP (default, internal only) ===
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-api}
spec:
  selector: {app: easypj-api}
  ports:
  - port: 8000              # Service port
    targetPort: 8000        # Pod port (must match containerPort)
    protocol: TCP

# === NODEPORT (external via node IP:30000-32767) ===
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-web}
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector: {app: easypj-web}
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
    nodePort: 30080         # 30000-32767; omit for auto-assign

# === LOADBALANCER (cloud LB; bare-metal needs MetalLB) ===
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-web-lb}
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector: {app: easypj-web}
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 80
🔄 Headless / ExternalName / Ingress Ingress: k create ingress NAME --class=nginx --rule=...
YAML — headless.yaml + externalname.yaml + ingress.yaml
# === HEADLESS (StatefulSet requirement) ===
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-db}
spec:
  clusterIP: None            # 🔑 KEY: makes it headless!
  selector: {app: easypj-db}
  ports:
  - port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
    name: postgres

# === EXTERNALNAME (DNS CNAME to external host) ===
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: easypj-db-external}
spec:
  type: ExternalName
  externalName: easypj-prod.xyz.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com

# === INGRESS (HTTP routing) ===
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: easypj-ingress}
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx    # 🔑 REQUIRED!
  tls:
  - hosts: [easypj.example.com]
    secretName: easypj-tls
  rules:
  - host: easypj.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service: {name: easypj-api, port: {number: 8000}}
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service: {name: easypj-web, port: {number: 80}}

🔐 Config, Secrets & Security

📝 ConfigMap + Secret + RBAC
YAML — configmap.yaml + secret.yaml + rbac.yaml
# === CONFIGMAP ===
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: {name: easypj-config}
immutable: false
data:
  DEBUG: "false"
  ALLOWED_HOSTS: "easypj.com"
  LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"

# === SECRET (Opaque) ===
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata: {name: easypj-db-creds}
type: Opaque
stringData:                 # stringData = plain text (K8s encodes)
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD: SuperSecret123!
  API_KEY: sk-abc123xyz

# === SERVICE ACCOUNT ===
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata: {name: easypj-api-sa}

# === ROLE ===
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: {name: pod-reader}
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]   # get≠list — both needed!

# === ROLEBINDING ===
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: {name: pod-reader-binding}
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: easypj-api-sa
  namespace: default           # Must match SA namespace!
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: pod-reader
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
🛡️ NetworkPolicy + HPA + PVC + ResourceQuota
YAML — netpol.yaml + hpa.yaml + pvc.yaml + quota.yaml
# === NETWORKPOLICY (deny all ingress to DB, allow from API) ===
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: db-policy}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-db}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj-api}}
      namespaceSelector: {}           # 🔑 REQUIRED for same-ns traffic!
    ports: [{port: 5432, protocol: TCP}]

# === HPA (CPU-based autoscaling) ===
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: easypj-api-hpa}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: easypj-api
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70}

# === PVC ===
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: pgdata-pvc}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources: {requests: {storage: 5Gi}}

# === RESOURCEQUOTA ===
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata: {name: dev-quota}
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.cpu: "8"
    limits.memory: 16Gi
    pods: "20"

📚 Appendix F: Deployment Strategy MatrixReference

🚀 RollingUpdate · Recreate · Blue-Green · Canary — Complete Comparison

Master the 4 deployment strategies tested on CKAD. Understand when to use each, their trade-offs, and the kubectl commands to execute them. Each strategy includes a visual flow diagram showing how traffic moves during deployment.

✅ DEFAULT — Use This 80% of the Time

🔄 RollingUpdate (Kubernetes Native)

Gradually replaces old pods with new ones — zero downtime. Controlled by maxUnavailable + maxSurge.

STEP 1: 🟢🟢🟢 (v1 — 3 old pods running)
STEP 2: 🟢🟢🟡🔵 (1 new pod spins up, 1 old terminates)
STEP 3: 🟢🔵🔵🟡 (2 new running, 1 old terminating)
STEP 4: 🔵🔵🔵 (v2 — all new pods, zero downtime!)
maxUnavailable: 1 — at most 1 pod can be down
maxSurge: 1 — at most 1 extra pod above desired count
⚠️ Requires: backward-compatible API changes

💥 Recreate

Kills ALL old pods FIRST, then creates new ones — DOWNTIME. Simplest strategy, most disruptive.

BEFORE: 🟢🟢🟢 (v1 — 3 pods running)
KILL: ❌❌❌ (all pods terminated — DOWNTIME!)
CREATE: 🔵🔵🔵 (v2 — new pods starting)
AFTER: 🔵🔵🔵 (v2 — service restored)
Use when: Breaking schema changes, DB migrations, singleton apps
Downtime: OldPodTermination + NewPodStartup time

🔵🟢 Blue-Green

Run TWO complete environments. Switch ALL traffic at once via Service selector. Instant rollback — just switch back.

🔵🔵🔵 (v1 — BLUE active, 100% traffic)
🟢🟢🟢 (v2 — GREEN idle, 0% traffic)
→ Switch Service selector: blue → green
🟢🟢🟢 (v2 — GREEN active, 100% traffic)
🔥 Rollback: switch selector back → instant!
Pros: Instant rollback, full testing before switch
Cons: 2× resources, session migration needed

🐤 Canary

Route a small % of traffic to new version. Gradually increase. Requires Ingress/Service Mesh for traffic splitting.

🟢🟢🟢🟢🟢 🔵 (v2 = 10% traffic)
→ Monitor errors, latency for 5 min
🟢🟢🟢 🔵🔵🔵 (v2 = 50% traffic)
→ Monitor, then scale to 100%
🔵🔵🔵🔵🔵🔵 (v2 = 100%)
Pros: Risk mitigation, real-user validation
Cons: Complex setup, needs traffic splitting

📊 Strategy Comparison Matrix

Criterion RollingUpdate Recreate Blue-Green Canary
DowntimeZero ✅Full ❌Zero ✅Zero ✅
Rollback SpeedGradual 🟡Slow ❌Instant ✅Instant ✅
Resource CostNormal ✅Normal ✅2× ❌+10-50% 🟡
K8s NativeYes ✅Yes ✅Manual ❌Manual ❌
Schema ChangesUnsafe ❌Safe ✅Safe ✅Unsafe ❌
Setup ComplexityNone ✅None ✅Medium 🟡High ❌
CKAD TestedYES ⚡YES ⚡Concept 🟡Concept 🟡

🧭 Decision Flowchart — Which Strategy Should You Use?

🔷 START: Are you changing the database schema?
├─ YES → Use Recreate (prevents old+new pods writing to DB)
└─ NO → Continue ↓
🔷 Do you need instant rollback?
├─ YES, critical → Use Blue-Green
└─ NO → Continue ↓
🔷 Do you need gradual traffic shift for risk mitigation?
├─ YES → Use Canary (requires Ingress/Service Mesh)
└─ NO → Continue ↓
🎯 Use RollingUpdate — zero downtime, K8s native, no extra setup
⚠️

CKAD Exam Strategy Tips

✅ RollingUpdate is DEFAULT. You only need to know maxUnavailable and maxSurge. The exam WILL ask about these.
⚠️ Recreate = downtime. Use when schema changes mean old+new pods CANNOT coexist. Example: DB migration that adds a NOT NULL column.
🔵 Blue-Green = Service selector switch. Create two Deployments (blue, green). One Service. Change selector to flip traffic. Instant rollback.
🐤 Canary = traffic splitting. Not built into K8s. Needs Ingress annotations (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true") or Service Mesh (Istio/Linkerd).
🔴 EXAM GOTCHA: "The deployment is stuck" after changing strategy from RollingUpdate → Recreate with active pods. You need to delete and recreate the Deployment — you can't change the strategy field while pods are running!

⚡ Key kubectl Commands

BASH — Deployment strategy commands
# Set RollingUpdate strategy
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"RollingUpdate","rollingUpdate":{"maxUnavailable":1,"maxSurge":1}}}}'

# Set Recreate strategy
kubectl patch deploy easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"strategy":{"type":"Recreate"}}}'

# Watch rollout progress
kubectl rollout status deploy/easypj-api --timeout=120s

# Rollback to previous revision
kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api

# Rollback to specific revision
kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj-api --to-revision=2

# Blue-Green: switch Service selector
kubectl patch svc easypj-api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"easypj-api","version":"green"}}}'

# Pause/resume rollout (for canary-style control)
kubectl rollout pause deploy/easypj-api
kubectl rollout resume deploy/easypj-api

📐 maxUnavailable & maxSurge Explained

ReplicasmaxUnavailablemaxSurgeMax Pods During
31 (33%)1 (33%)4
51 (20%)2 (40%)7
1025%25%12
100212 (but 0 tolerance)

Formula: Max pods during rollout = replicas - maxUnavailable + maxSurge. Both accept integers OR percentages (rounds up).

The CKAD exam is 120 minutes with 19 questions. That's ~6 minutes per question. These 20 commands + aliases will save you 10-15 minutes — the difference between passing and failing. Copy the alias block FIRST when your exam starts.
